optionA: modelBuilder.Entity<Course>().Property(c => c.Fee).HasMaxLength(10, 2);
optionB: modelBuilder.Entity<Course>().Property(c => c.Fee).IsRequired(10, 2);
optionC: modelBuilder.Entity<Course>().Property(c => c.Fee).HasPrecision(10, 2);
optionD: modelBuilder.Entity<Course>().HasKey(c => c.Fee).HasColumnType("10,2");
correctAnswerText: modelBuilder.Entity<Course>().Property(c => c.Fee).HasPrecision(10, 2);
explanation: HasPrecision(10, 2) (EF Core 5+) sets precision and scale; HasColumnType("decimal(10,2)") also works. Without it EF Core uses decimal(18,2) and logs a warning.

prompt: A list shows size items per page, ordered by name, for a 1-based page number. Which query is right?
optionA: db.Courses.OrderBy(c => c.Title).ThenBy(c => c.Id).Skip(page * size).Take(size)
optionB: db.Courses.OrderBy(c => c.Title).ThenBy(c => c.Id).Take(size).Skip((page - 1) * size)
optionC: db.Courses.Skip((page - 1) * size).Take(size).OrderBy(c => c.Title).ThenBy(c => c.Id)
optionD: db.Courses.OrderBy(c => c.Title).ThenBy(c => c.Id).Skip((page - 1) * size).Take(size)
correctAnswerText: db.Courses.OrderBy(c => c.Title).ThenBy(c => c.Id).Skip((page - 1) * size).Take(size)
explanation: Order first (with a unique tiebreaker), then skip the previous pages, then take one page; EF Core emits OFFSET ... FETCH. Ordering after paging sorts an arbitrary page, and Take before Skip empties later pages.

prompt: A search has an optional city and an optional minimum CGPA. How do you build one SQL query that applies only the filters supplied?
optionA: Write four separate queries, one for every combination of the two filters
optionB: Load db.Students.ToList() and then apply each supplied filter with Where
optionC: Add both Where calls always, passing null to switch an unused filter off
optionD: Start from IQueryable<Student> q = db.Students and add q = q.Where(...) per filter
correctAnswerText: Start from IQueryable<Student> q = db.Students and add q = q.Where(...) per filter
explanation: Each Where on an IQueryable composes into the same expression, so one SELECT carries exactly the supplied conditions. ToList first loads every student into memory.

prompt: You must load invoices with their Lines and each line's Course entity, to modify them. Which query does it?
optionA: db.Invoices.Include(i => i.Lines.Course)
optionB: db.Invoices.Include(i => i.Lines).ThenInclude(l => l.Course)
optionC: db.Invoices.Include(i => i.Lines).Include(l => l.Course)
optionD: db.Invoices.ThenInclude(i => i.Lines).Include(l => l.Course)
correctAnswerText: db.Invoices.Include(i => i.Lines).ThenInclude(l => l.Course)
explanation: ThenInclude continues from the previous Include, here from each line to its Course. A second Include starts again from Invoice, and Lines.Course does not compile on a collection.

prompt: Raise the fee of every course in category 3 by 10% in a single statement (EF Core 8). Which code does it?
optionA: await db.Courses.Where(c => c.CategoryId == 3).ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(c => c.Fee, c => c.Fee * 1.10m));
optionB: foreach (var c in db.Courses.Where(c => c.CategoryId == 3)) c.Fee *= 1.10m; await db.SaveChangesAsync();
optionC: await db.Courses.Where(c => c.CategoryId == 3).UpdateAsync(c => c.Fee = c.Fee * 1.10m); await db.SaveChangesAsync();
optionD: db.Courses.UpdateRange(db.Courses.Where(c => c.CategoryId == 3)); await db.SaveChangesAsync(); // Fee * 1.10m
correctAnswerText: await db.Courses.Where(c => c.CategoryId == 3).ExecuteUpdateAsync(s => s.SetProperty(c => c.Fee, c => c.Fee * 1.10m));
explanation: ExecuteUpdateAsync with SetProperty becomes one UPDATE ... SET Fee = Fee * 1.10 WHERE CategoryId = 3. The loop sends an UPDATE per row; UpdateAsync does not exist, and UpdateRange changes nothing.

prompt: You must call a hand-written query filtering by a user-typed roll number. Which EF Core 8 call is safe?
optionA: db.Students.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Students WHERE RollNo = {rollNo}")
optionB: db.Students.FromSqlRaw("SELECT * FROM Students WHERE RollNo = '" + rollNo + "'")
optionC: db.Database.ExecuteSqlRaw("SELECT * FROM Students WHERE RollNo = " + rollNo)
optionD: db.Students.FromSqlRaw($"SELECT * FROM Students WHERE RollNo = '{rollNo}'")
correctAnswerText: db.Students.FromSql($"SELECT * FROM Students WHERE RollNo = {rollNo}")
explanation: FromSql (EF Core 7+) takes a FormattableString and turns each {hole} into a parameter. FromSqlRaw with an interpolated or concatenated string pastes input into SQL, and ExecuteSqlRaw returns no rows.

prompt: A PUT endpoint receives { id, phone } to change only a student's phone and must return 404 for an unknown id. Which approach fits?
optionA: FindAsync(id); if null return NotFound; set Phone; SaveChangesAsync
optionB: db.Add(new Student { Id = id, Phone = phone }); SaveChangesAsync
optionC: db.Attach(new Student { Id = id }); SaveChangesAsync; then set Phone
optionD: db.Update(new Student { Id = id, Phone = phone }); SaveChangesAsync
correctAnswerText: FindAsync(id); if null return NotFound; set Phone; SaveChangesAsync
explanation: Loading then copying sends only the changed column and lets you detect a missing row. Update on a new object overwrites every other column with defaults, and Add tries an INSERT.

prompt: Students take many courses and courses have many students, and each pairing has an EnrolledOn date and a Grade. How should it be modelled?
optionA: An Enrolment entity with StudentId, CourseId, EnrolledOn and Grade, keyed by both ids
optionB: A Grades string column on Student holding a comma-separated list per course
optionC: A CourseId column on Student and a StudentId column on Course, both required
optionD: List<Course> on Student and List<Student> on Course, with no join class at all
correctAnswerText: An Enrolment entity with StudentId, CourseId, EnrolledOn and Grade, keyed by both ids
explanation: When the link carries data, it is an entity: two one-to-many relationships through Enrolment with a composite key. The skip-navigation form (EF Core 5+) has nowhere to put EnrolledOn or Grade.

prompt: Deleting a Batch must be refused while students still belong to it. Which configuration does that?
optionA: HasOne(s => s.Batch).WithMany(b => b.Students).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.SetNull)
optionB: HasOne(s => s.Batch).WithMany(b => b.Students).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict)
optionC: HasOne(s => s.Batch).WithMany(b => b.Students).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Cascade)
optionD: HasOne(s => s.Batch).WithMany(b => b.Students).IsRequired(false) with no OnDelete
correctAnswerText: HasOne(s => s.Batch).WithMany(b => b.Students).OnDelete(DeleteBehavior.Restrict)
explanation: Restrict (or NoAction) makes the delete fail with a foreign-key error while dependants exist. Cascade deletes the students, and SetNull or an optional FK orphans them.

prompt: A dashboard tile shows how many students have unpaid fees. Which line is right?
optionA: await db.Students.CountAsync(s => s.FeeDue > 0)
optionB: (await db.Students.ToListAsync()).Count(s => s.FeeDue > 0)
optionC: (await db.Students.Where(s => s.FeeDue > 0).ToListAsync()).Count
optionD: db.Students.AsEnumerable().Where(s => s.FeeDue > 0).Count()
correctAnswerText: await db.Students.CountAsync(s => s.FeeDue > 0)
explanation: CountAsync with a predicate becomes SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE, returning one number. The others load rows, or every row, into memory just to count them.

prompt:
var top = db.Students.ToList().Where(s => s.Cgpa > 9).Take(10);
The table has 400,000 rows and the endpoint is slow. Why?
optionA: ToList runs first and loads every student; the filter then runs in memory
optionB: The query runs twice, once for Where and once more for Take, on the server
optionC: Where on a decimal column cannot be translated, so EF Core retries in memory
optionD: Take(10) is ignored by EF Core, so all students matching Where come back
correctAnswerText: ToList runs first and loads every student; the filter then runs in memory
explanation: ToList enumerates the DbSet immediately — SELECT of all 400,000 rows — and Where and Take run as LINQ to Objects. Put ToList last so the filter and TOP go to SQL.

prompt: With UseLazyLoadingProxies on, a report loops over 300 enrolments printing e.Student.Name. The log shows 301 SELECTs. What is happening?
optionA: Each first read of Student fires its own query: the N+1 problem
optionB: Proxies always run each query twice, to check for concurrency
optionC: The log counts each column read, so 301 lines is only one query
optionD: EF Core re-runs the enrolment query once for every row it prints
correctAnswerText: Each first read of Student fires its own query: the N+1 problem
explanation: One query loads the enrolments; each proxy navigation then loads its student on first access — 300 more. Project the name, or Include Student, to make it one query.

optionA: The context was disposed between the two calls by Task.WhenAll
optionB: One context runs one operation at a time; these two overlap on it
optionC: Task.WhenAll is not supported by EF Core, only await on each task
optionD: CountAsync cannot be used on two different DbSets of a context
correctAnswerText: One context runs one operation at a time; these two overlap on it
explanation: A DbContext is not thread-safe and does not allow parallel queries. Await each call in turn, or use separate context instances (for example from IDbContextFactory) for real parallelism.

prompt: A service loads student 7 with tracking to validate it, then calls db.Update(dtoMappedStudent) where dtoMappedStudent also has Id 7. It throws "cannot be tracked because another instance with the same key value...". Why?
optionA: Update cannot be used after any query has been run on the same context
optionB: The context already tracks a Student 7, and two instances cannot share a key
optionC: The DTO-mapped object lacks a RowVersion, which Update always requires
optionD: Ids above zero must be attached first, and only then can they be updated
correctAnswerText: The context already tracks a Student 7, and two instances cannot share a key
explanation: Identity resolution allows one instance per key per context. Copy the DTO values onto the tracked entity (or load with AsNoTracking if you really mean to attach another instance).

optionA: The entity was never tracked, so SaveChanges has no change to write
optionB: Phone is a string, and strings are compared by reference so it looks same
optionC: FirstAsync returns a copy that is discarded before SaveChanges runs
optionD: SaveChanges needs Update called first for every change in EF Core 8
correctAnswerText: The entity was never tracked, so SaveChanges has no change to write
explanation: AsNoTracking entities are invisible to the change tracker, so nothing is Modified. Query with tracking when you intend to change the entity.

prompt: An endpoint runs db.Courses.Update(new Course { Id = dto.Id, Title = dto.Title }); await db.SaveChangesAsync();. Afterwards the course's Fee is 0. Why?
optionA: SaveChanges resets numeric columns that are not part of the posted DTO
optionB: Fee is set to 0 by a database DEFAULT whenever an UPDATE skips the column
optionC: Update deletes the row and inserts a new one carrying only the given values
optionD: Update marks every property Modified, so the default Fee of 0 is written too
correctAnswerText: Update marks every property Modified, so the default Fee of 0 is written too
explanation: Update on a detached object marks all properties as modified, so the UPDATE writes every column — including Fee = 0 from the new object. Load and copy, or mark only Title as modified.

prompt: A Student loaded by another context is set as enrolment.Student, then db.Enrolments.Add(enrolment); SaveChanges fails with an IDENTITY_INSERT error on Students. Why?
optionA: Add marks the whole reachable graph Added, so it tries to insert the student
optionB: The student's Id is regenerated by SQL Server whenever it is referenced
optionC: SaveChanges inserts the enrolment twice, once per navigation direction
optionD: Enrolments cannot reference students that were loaded asynchronously
correctAnswerText: Add marks the whole reachable graph Added, so it tries to insert the student
explanation: Add marks every untracked entity reachable from the enrolment as Added, even with a key set, so EF Core tries INSERT INTO Students with an explicit Id. Set enrolment.StudentId instead, or attach the student first.

prompt: A prototype called db.Database.EnsureCreated(). The team then adds migrations, and dotnet ef database update fails: "There is already an object named 'Students'". Why?
optionA: Migrations work only on databases that have no tables in the dbo schema
optionB: The Students table must be renamed before each new migration is applied
optionC: EnsureCreated locks the tables, so migrations cannot alter them afterwards
optionD: EnsureCreated made the tables without history rows, so migrations rerun them
correctAnswerText: EnsureCreated made the tables without history rows, so migrations rerun them
explanation: EnsureCreated builds the schema from the model with no __EFMigrationsHistory, so the initial migration thinks nothing exists and tries to create the tables again. Use one approach from the start.

prompt: db.Students.Include(s => s.Attempts).Include(s => s.Payments) is slow; a student with 40 attempts and 12 payments yields 480 rows. What fixes the multiplication?
optionA: Add AsSplitQuery() so each collection is loaded by its own SELECT
optionB: Swap the order of the two Include calls so the smaller one is first
optionC: Add AsNoTracking(), which removes the duplicate rows from the join
optionD: Replace Include with ThenInclude so the joins nest instead of multiply
correctAnswerText: Add AsSplitQuery() so each collection is loaded by its own SELECT
explanation: Two collection joins in one query return every attempt–payment combination. AsSplitQuery (EF Core 5+) sends one SELECT per collection; order and tracking do not change the row count.

prompt:
IEnumerable<Student> All() => db.Students;
A caller writes All().Where(s => s.City == "Pune").Take(5). What SQL runs?
optionA: Nothing: IEnumerable cannot be enumerated over a DbSet
optionB: One SELECT per student, checking each city one at a time
optionC: SELECT TOP(5) ... WHERE City = N'Pune', fully on the server
optionD: A SELECT of every student; the filter and Take run in memory
correctAnswerText: A SELECT of every student; the filter and Take run in memory
explanation: Typed as IEnumerable, the later Where and Take bind to LINQ to Objects, so EF Core sees only db.Students and loads the whole table. Return IQueryable, or better, take the filter as a parameter.

prompt: An API runs on four instances behind a load balancer, and each calls db.Database.Migrate() at startup. Your judgement?
optionA: Apply migrations as a deploy step: a reviewed idempotent script or a bundle
optionB: Let each developer run database update against production from a laptop
optionC: Good: Migrate is safe however many instances call it at the same moment
optionD: Switch to EnsureCreated at startup, as it is the production-grade version
correctAnswerText: Apply migrations as a deploy step: a reviewed idempotent script or a bundle
explanation: Several instances migrating at once can race, and no one reviews the SQL. migrations script --idempotent (reviewable) or migrations bundle (EF Core 6+) runs once, as part of the deployment.

prompt: To avoid "creating a context per request", a developer registers the DbContext as a singleton. Your judgement?
optionA: Good, provided every query in the app uses AsNoTracking from then on
optionB: Make it transient instead, so each repository method gets three copies
optionC: Keep it scoped: a shared context breaks under concurrency and goes stale
optionD: Good: one context is faster because its tracker caches every entity
correctAnswerText: Keep it scoped: a shared context breaks under concurrency and goes stale
explanation: Concurrent requests would hit one non-thread-safe context, and its tracker would hold stale entities for ever. Contexts are cheap; if creation cost matters, AddDbContextPool reuses them safely.

prompt: Two counsellors edit the same lead; the second save throws DbUpdateConcurrencyException. Which response is best?
optionA: Wrap the save in Serializable so the conflict is silently resolved
optionB: Reload current values, show them, and let the user reapply or cancel
optionC: Remove the RowVersion column so the exception can never happen
optionD: Catch it and call SaveChanges again until it finally succeeds
correctAnswerText: Reload current values, show them, and let the user reapply or cancel
explanation: The exception exists to stop a lost update. Blind retry or removing the token overwrites the other user's work; GetDatabaseValuesAsync lets you show the current row and decide deliberately.

prompt: GET /api/courses returns 2,000 courses as JSON and never modifies them. Which query style is best?
optionA: A projection to a DTO, or AsNoTracking, since nothing will be saved
optionB: A tracking query with every navigation Included, to be complete
optionC: A tracking query, so the entities are ready if an edit comes later
optionD: Load the courses once at startup into a static list for all users
correctAnswerText: A projection to a DTO, or AsNoTracking, since nothing will be saved
explanation: Tracking builds snapshots and an identity map for nothing on a read-only path. A DTO projection fetches only the needed columns; AsNoTracking at least skips the tracker.

prompt: A null navigation crashes a page, and a teammate proposes enabling lazy-loading proxies app-wide to fix it. Your judgement?
optionA: Load it on purpose with Include or a projection; proxies invite N+1
optionB: Agree, but only in production, where the extra queries are cached
optionC: Make every navigation required, so EF Core always loads it for you
optionD: Agree: lazy loading is the EF Core default and should be restored
correctAnswerText: Load it on purpose with Include or a projection; proxies invite N+1
explanation: Proxies make the crash disappear by issuing a query per navigation read, which turns loops into N+1. The null is telling you the query did not ask for the data; ask for it explicitly.

prompt: An API returns Student entities directly, with Batch and Batch.Students navigations, as its JSON response. Your judgement?
optionA: Return DTOs: entities leak columns and their navigations form a cycle
optionB: Good: returning entities avoids writing any mapping code at all
optionC: Good, provided the API only ever returns one student per request
optionD: Good, as long as lazy loading is on so every navigation is filled
correctAnswerText: Return DTOs: entities leak columns and their navigations form a cycle
explanation: Student → Batch → Students is a reference cycle for the serializer, and entities expose every column (fees, internal flags) and couple the API contract to the schema. A DTO says exactly what is returned.

prompt: A nightly job must purge about 200,000 audit rows older than a year (EF Core 8). Which approach is best?
optionA: Load every row with AsNoTracking, then Remove and SaveChanges them
optionB: Loop over the rows, calling Remove and SaveChanges once for each one
optionC: Where(a => a.At < cutoff).ExecuteDeleteAsync(): one set-based DELETE
optionD: Load the rows with ToListAsync, RemoveRange them, then SaveChanges
correctAnswerText: Where(a => a.At < cutoff).ExecuteDeleteAsync(): one set-based DELETE
explanation: ExecuteDelete (EF Core 7+) sends one DELETE ... WHERE without loading anything. RemoveRange still loads 200,000 entities and sends a DELETE per row, and AsNoTracking changes neither cost.

prompt: Payment has a required int StudentId, so EF Core defaults to Cascade. Should the team keep that default?
optionA: No: set Restrict so deleting a student cannot silently delete payments
optionB: Yes: the default is always right, since EF Core chose it from the model
optionC: No: make StudentId optional so the payments are deleted more safely
optionD: Yes, because SQL Server stops a cascade from reaching financial tables
correctAnswerText: No: set Restrict so deleting a student cannot silently delete payments
explanation: A required relationship cascades by default, which would erase payment records with the student. Choose Restrict (or soft-delete students) for valuable data; making the FK optional just orphans the rows.

prompt: A migration already applied to the shared test database turns out to have a wrong column length. What is the right fix?
optionA: Add a new migration that alters the column; never edit an applied one
optionB: Drop the shared database and rebuild it with EnsureCreated
optionC: Edit the applied migration file and run database update again
optionD: Delete its row from __EFMigrationsHistory and edit the migration
correctAnswerText: Add a new migration that alters the column; never edit an applied one
explanation: Databases that already ran the migration will never run an edited version, so environments drift apart. A new migration moves every database forward the same way.

prompt: Someone proposes making split queries the global default with UseQuerySplittingBehavior(SplitQuery). What trade-off should the team weigh?
optionA: None: split queries are strictly better and always send one SELECT
optionB: Split queries cannot be combined with Where, OrderBy or projections
optionC: More round trips, and the SELECTs are not one consistent snapshot
optionD: Split queries turn off change tracking for every entity they load
correctAnswerText: More round trips, and the SELECTs are not one consistent snapshot
explanation: Splitting avoids cartesian explosion but sends one SELECT per collection; without a transaction, data can change between them. It suits multi-collection Includes, not necessarily every query.

prompt: Which type holds the list of service registrations you build in Program.cs before the container exists?
optionA: IConfiguration
optionB: IServiceCollection
optionC: IServiceScope
optionD: IServiceProvider
correctAnswerText: IServiceCollection
explanation: You add registrations to IServiceCollection (builder.Services). builder.Build() turns that list into an IServiceProvider, which then creates instances.

prompt: Which registration method gives one shared instance per HTTP request in ASP.NET Core?
optionA: AddSingleton
optionB: AddHostedService
optionC: AddTransient
optionD: AddScoped
correctAnswerText: AddScoped
explanation: ASP.NET Core opens a scope per request, and a scoped service is created once per scope. Singleton is once per app; transient is new on every injection.

prompt: Which IServiceProvider method throws InvalidOperationException when the requested service was never registered?
optionA: GetService<T>()
optionB: GetRequiredService<T>()
optionC: CreateScope()
optionD: GetServices<T>()
correctAnswerText: GetRequiredService<T>()
explanation: GetRequiredService<T> throws when no registration exists. GetService<T> returns null instead, and GetServices<T> returns an empty sequence.

prompt: With what lifetime does AddDbContext<T>() register the context by default?
optionA: Thread-local
optionB: Transient
optionC: Singleton
optionD: Scoped
correctAnswerText: Scoped
explanation: AddDbContext registers the context as scoped, so the services in one request share one change tracker and two requests never share a context.

prompt: Which environment variable sets the environment name (Development, Production) of an ASP.NET Core app?
optionA: ASPNETCORE_HOSTING_MODE
optionB: DOTNET_BUILD_PROFILE
optionC: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
optionD: APP_ENVIRONMENT_NAME
correctAnswerText: ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT
explanation: ASP.NET Core reads ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT (the generic host also reads DOTNET_ENVIRONMENT). With neither set, the environment is Production.

prompt: Which options interface exposes CurrentValue and an OnChange callback for settings that change while the app runs?
optionA: IOptionsSnapshot<T>
optionB: IOptionsFactory<T>
optionC: IOptions<T>
optionD: IOptionsMonitor<T>
correctAnswerText: IOptionsMonitor<T>
explanation: IOptionsMonitor<T> is a singleton that tracks reloads: CurrentValue is always the latest value and OnChange notifies you. IOptions<T> is computed once.

prompt: Which type do you inject to log from OrderService with the category set to that class's full name?
optionA: ILogger<OrderService>
optionB: TextWriter
optionC: ILogEntry<OrderService>
optionD: ILoggerProvider
correctAnswerText: ILogger<OrderService>
explanation: ILogger<T> uses the full name of T as its category, which is what appsettings filtering matches on. The host registers it for any T with no extra code.

prompt: Which log level sits between Information and Error?
optionA: Trace
optionB: Debug
optionC: Critical
optionD: Warning
correctAnswerText: Warning
explanation: From lowest to highest: Trace, Debug, Information, Warning, Error, Critical (and None for switching a category off).

prompt: In IConfiguration, which character joins a section name to a child key, as in reading the Port value under Smtp?
optionA: A colon, as in Smtp:Port
optionB: A dot, as in Smtp.Port
optionC: A slash, as in Smtp/Port
optionD: A hash, as in Smtp#Port
correctAnswerText: A colon, as in Smtp:Port
explanation: Configuration flattens nested sections into keys joined by a colon. Environment variables spell the same key with a double underscore, which the provider maps back to a colon.

prompt: In .NET 8, which method registers a singleton INotifier under the key "sms"?
optionA: AddSingletonFor<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms")
optionB: AddNamedSingleton<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms")
optionC: AddTaggedSingleton<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms")
optionD: AddKeyedSingleton<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms")
correctAnswerText: AddKeyedSingleton<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms")
explanation: Keyed services arrived in .NET 8: AddKeyedSingleton, AddKeyedScoped and AddKeyedTransient, consumed with [FromKeyedServices(key)] or GetRequiredKeyedService.

prompt: Why does constructor injection make a class easier to unit test?
optionA: Constructors run faster than property setters do
optionB: The test can pass a fake for each dependency itself
optionC: The container runs inside every test automatically
optionD: Interfaces compile into smaller test assemblies
correctAnswerText: The test can pass a fake for each dependency itself
explanation: A class that receives its dependencies can be built in a test with new and fakes, without any container. A class that news up SmtpClient itself cannot be isolated.

prompt: Why must a BackgroundService create a scope itself before it resolves a DbContext?
optionA: No request exists, so nothing opens a scope for it
optionB: A BackgroundService is registered as transient
optionC: A scope is what opens the database connection
optionD: DbContext refuses to run outside a controller
correctAnswerText: No request exists, so nothing opens a scope for it
explanation: ASP.NET Core opens a scope per HTTP request. A hosted service is a singleton outside any request, so it uses IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() and disposes the scope when done.

prompt: What is a "captive dependency"?
optionA: A service whose constructor throws at startup
optionB: A shorter-lived service held by a longer-lived one
optionC: A service registered twice with two lifetimes
optionD: A dependency the container can resolve only once
correctAnswerText: A shorter-lived service held by a longer-lived one
explanation: When a singleton receives a scoped or transient service, it keeps that instance for the life of the app, so the short-lived object outlives its intended lifetime.

prompt: Why does the container dispose a singleton it created but not one registered as AddSingleton<IClock>(new FixedClock())?
optionA: Instances passed in are disposed on every request
optionB: Singletons are never disposed by the container
optionC: It disposes only the instances it constructed itself
optionD: FixedClock cannot implement IDisposable as a value
correctAnswerText: It disposes only the instances it constructed itself
explanation: The container owns what it builds: scoped instances at the end of the scope, singletons at shutdown. An instance you created and handed over stays your responsibility.

prompt: Why do libraries usually register their defaults with TryAddSingleton rather than AddSingleton?
optionA: So a registration the app already made is kept
optionB: So the service is created lazily on first use
optionC: So the type is registered under every interface
optionD: So the library's registration always wins at runtime
correctAnswerText: So a registration the app already made is kept
explanation: TryAdd* adds the descriptor only when the service type has no registration yet, so an application that registered its own implementation first keeps it.

prompt: Why does an environment variable on the server override the same key in appsettings.json?
optionA: appsettings.json is ignored once any variable is set
optionB: Later sources win, and env vars load after the JSON files
optionC: The host sorts every source alphabetically by its name
optionD: Environment variables are read-only to the JSON provider
correctAnswerText: Later sources win, and env vars load after the JSON files
explanation: The default builders add appsettings.json, appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets (Development), environment variables and command-line arguments, each overriding the earlier ones.

prompt: What does adding ValidateOnStart() to an AddOptions<SmtpOptions>() chain change?
optionA: Validation errors are logged and the defaults are used
optionB: A bad setting stops the app at startup, not on first use
optionC: The options class no longer needs data annotations
optionD: Settings are re-validated on every request that reads them
correctAnswerText: A bad setting stops the app at startup, not on first use
explanation: Without ValidateOnStart, validation runs the first time the options are resolved, which may be the first email hours later. With it, a broken deploy fails immediately.

prompt: In _logger.LogInformation("Order {OrderId} by {UserId}", userId, orderId), how are the arguments matched to the placeholders?
optionA: Not at all; mismatched names make the call throw
optionB: By type, so the int goes to the numeric placeholder
optionC: By name, so each value finds its matching placeholder
optionD: By position, so OrderId receives the value of userId
correctAnswerText: By position, so OrderId receives the value of userId
explanation: Placeholders are filled in order. The names only label the stored values, so swapping the arguments silently records the user id as OrderId.

prompt: Why is a mutable List<string> field on a singleton service risky in a web API?
optionA: The container clears the field after each request
optionB: Every concurrent request shares that one instance
optionC: Singletons are recreated whenever memory is low
optionD: Lists cannot be stored in container-built objects
correctAnswerText: Every concurrent request shares that one instance
explanation: One singleton serves all requests at once. List<T> is not thread-safe, and data written for one user is visible to the next; keep singletons stateless or use concurrent types.

prompt: Why does the app run as Development on a laptop but as Production on a server where nothing was configured?
optionA: Development is only used when a debugger is attached to it
optionB: The SDK detects a server OS and switches the app to Production
optionC: dotnet run reads launchSettings.json; with no variable it is Production
optionD: The server's appsettings.Production.json selects the environment
correctAnswerText: dotnet run reads launchSettings.json; with no variable it is Production
explanation: launchSettings.json (used by dotnet run and Visual Studio) sets ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development. A deployed app does not read it, and with no variable the host defaults to Production.

prompt: A CurrentUser service holds the id and roles of whoever made the request, read once from the token. Which lifetime fits?
optionA: Singleton with a [ThreadStatic] field for the id
optionB: Scoped, so each request has its own instance
optionC: Transient, so it is rebuilt on every injection
optionD: Singleton, so the roles are read only once
correctAnswerText: Scoped, so each request has its own instance
explanation: Per-request data belongs in a scoped service: shared by everything in that request, never by two requests. A singleton would mix users; transient would rebuild it repeatedly.

prompt: An in-memory cache of currency exchange rates is refreshed hourly and should be shared by every request. Which lifetime fits?
optionA: Scoped, so each request loads its own copy
optionB: Singleton, using thread-safe collections inside
optionC: Scoped, with the rates copied into a static
optionD: Transient, so readers never see stale rates
correctAnswerText: Singleton, using thread-safe collections inside
explanation: A cache that all requests share is app-wide state, so it is a singleton. Because requests use it concurrently, it needs thread-safe storage such as ConcurrentDictionary.

prompt: ReportService(IClock clock, string outputFolder) cannot be resolved because nothing supplies the string. Which change fixes it the usual way?
optionA: Register ReportService as a singleton instead of scoped
optionB: Mark the parameter with the [FromServices] attribute
optionC: Rename outputFolder to match the key in appsettings.json
optionD: Bind a ReportOptions section and inject IOptions<ReportOptions>
correctAnswerText: Bind a ReportOptions section and inject IOptions<ReportOptions>
explanation: The container supplies registered services, not settings. Binding a section to an options class and injecting IOptions<T> is the standard way to give a service its configuration.

prompt: appsettings.json sets Smtp:Port to 25, the environment has Smtp__Port=465, and the app starts with --Smtp:Port=2600. Which port does it use?
optionA: 465, since environment variables always win in the end
optionB: 25, since appsettings.json is the configured base file
optionC: The app fails to start because the key is set twice
optionD: 2600, since command-line arguments are added last
correctAnswerText: 2600, since command-line arguments are added last
explanation: Command-line arguments are the last default source, so they override environment variables, which override the JSON files. Setting a key in several sources is normal.

prompt: Logging:LogLevel has "Default": "Information" and "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning". Which entry is written?
optionA: A Trace from the category Shop.Api.Program class
optionB: A Debug from category Shop.Services.OrderService
optionC: An Information from Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing
optionD: A Warning from category Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing
correctAnswerText: A Warning from category Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing
explanation: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing matches the "Microsoft.AspNetCore" prefix, minimum Warning, so its Warning passes and its Information does not. Shop.* uses Default, Information, so Debug and Trace are dropped.

prompt: A catch block must log a failed save with its stack trace. Which call is correct?
optionA: _logger.LogError($"Saving order {id} failed: {ex.Message}")
optionB: _logger.LogError(ex, "Saving order {OrderId} failed", id)
optionC: _logger.LogInformation("Saving order {OrderId} failed", id)
optionD: _logger.LogError("Saving order failed: " + ex.Message)
correctAnswerText: _logger.LogError(ex, "Saving order {OrderId} failed", id)
explanation: The exception is its own first parameter, so providers record its type, message and stack trace, and the template keeps OrderId searchable. ex.Message alone loses the stack trace.

prompt: A BackgroundService must delete stale carts every hour through ShopDbContext. Which approach is correct?
optionA: Call app.Services.GetRequiredService<ShopDbContext>() each run
optionB: Inject ShopDbContext into the worker constructor and keep it
optionC: Register ShopDbContext as a singleton just for the worker class
optionD: Inject IServiceScopeFactory, and per run create a scope to resolve it
correctAnswerText: Inject IServiceScopeFactory, and per run create a scope to resolve it
explanation: The worker is a singleton, so a context injected into it would be captive. Creating a scope per run gives a fresh context that is disposed with the scope.

prompt: A singleton RateLimiter must pick up a changed RateLimit:PerMinute without a restart. What should it inject?
optionA: IOptions<RateLimitOptions>, reading Value on every call
optionB: IOptionsSnapshot<RateLimitOptions> in its constructor
optionC: IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitOptions>, reading CurrentValue
optionD: A RateLimitOptions object registered with AddSingleton
correctAnswerText: IOptionsMonitor<RateLimitOptions>, reading CurrentValue
explanation: IOptions<T>.Value is created once. IOptionsSnapshot<T> is scoped and cannot go into a singleton. IOptionsMonitor<T>.CurrentValue reflects reloads in a singleton.

prompt: Program.cs has grown sixty registrations for the data layer. What is the usual way to organise them?
optionA: A second IServiceProvider built just for the data classes
optionB: An AddDataLayer(this IServiceCollection services) extension method
optionC: Moving the registrations into each class's static constructor
optionD: A static ServiceLocator class that every service calls into
correctAnswerText: An AddDataLayer(this IServiceCollection services) extension method
explanation: Grouping registrations in IServiceCollection extension methods keeps Program.cs readable and still gives one composition root, with no service locator.

prompt: The app registers AddScoped<IPaymentGateway, RazorpayGateway>(), then a test factory adds AddScoped<IPaymentGateway, FakeGateway>(). What does a controller receive?
optionA: FakeGateway, as the last registration for a type wins
optionB: Nothing; the provider rejects a duplicate type
optionC: Both, combined into one composite gateway object
optionD: RazorpayGateway, as the first registration is kept
correctAnswerText: FakeGateway, as the last registration for a type wins
explanation: Resolving a single IPaymentGateway uses the last registration. That is why test factories can swap a real service for a fake by adding theirs afterwards.

prompt: In Development the API fails at startup with "Cannot consume scoped service 'AppDbContext' from singleton 'ReportCache'". What is wrong?
optionA: AppDbContext was registered twice with two lifetimes
optionB: The connection string for AppDbContext is not configured
optionC: ReportCache is missing a public parameterless constructor
optionD: A singleton takes the scoped context in its constructor
correctAnswerText: A singleton takes the scoped context in its constructor
explanation: ReportCache would keep one AppDbContext for the life of the app. Make it scoped, or keep it singleton and create a scope with IServiceScopeFactory when it needs the database.

prompt: The same build starts fine in Production but fails in Development with a scoped-from-singleton error. Why the difference?
optionA: Scope validation is on by default only in Development
optionB: Production registers DbContext as a singleton instead
optionC: Production skips building services until first request
optionD: Development uses a different service container library
correctAnswerText: Scope validation is on by default only in Development
explanation: The default builders enable ValidateScopes and ValidateOnBuild in Development. In Production the captive dependency is not reported, but the bug is still there.

prompt: Resolving OrderService fails with "A circular dependency was detected". OrderService(InvoiceService) and InvoiceService(OrderService). What is the cause?
optionA: InvoiceService lacks an interface of its own
optionB: Each class needs the other in its constructor
optionC: Both services were registered with AddScoped
optionD: OrderService was registered after InvoiceService
correctAnswerText: Each class needs the other in its constructor
explanation: The container cannot build A without B or B without A. Move the shared logic into a third service both depend on, or rethink which class owns the work.

prompt: SmtpOptions.Host is an empty string in Production. appsettings.json has a "Mail" section; Program.cs binds GetSection("Smtp"). Why?
optionA: IOptions<T> cannot be injected into an email service
optionB: Keys differ in letter case between JSON and the class
optionC: The bound section name does not match the JSON one
optionD: Production ignores appsettings.json for all sections
correctAnswerText: The bound section name does not match the JSON one
explanation: Binding a section that does not exist leaves every property at its default, without an error. Keys are case-insensitive, so case is not the problem; validation would have caught it.

prompt: LogDebug calls in Shop.Services.OrderService never appear. Logging:LogLevel has only "Default": "Information". Why?
optionA: The logger category needs its own provider registration
optionB: Debug is below the Information minimum for that category
optionC: ILogger<T> discards messages from service classes
optionD: Debug messages are written only when a debugger attaches
correctAnswerText: Debug is below the Information minimum for that category
explanation: A message is written when its level is at or above the minimum for its category. With only Default set to Information, Debug (1) is below Information (2) and is dropped.

prompt: A loop calls app.Services.GetRequiredService<ReportWriter>() thousands of times; ReportWriter is a transient IDisposable. Memory keeps growing. Why?
optionA: The root provider holds each disposable until shutdown
optionB: GetRequiredService clones the object every time it runs
optionC: Transient services are cached for the life of the scope
optionD: IDisposable objects can never be garbage collected
correctAnswerText: The root provider holds each disposable until shutdown
explanation: The provider tracks disposable instances it creates so it can dispose them later. From the root, "later" is shutdown, so each one is kept alive. Resolve them inside a short-lived scope.

prompt: Program.cs calls app.Services.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>().Database.Migrate() and Development reports "Cannot resolve scoped service from root provider". Fix?
optionA: Create a scope and resolve the context from that scope
optionB: Call GetService instead of GetRequiredService there
optionC: Register AppDbContext as a singleton for migrations
optionD: Move the call to before builder.Build() is called
correctAnswerText: Create a scope and resolve the context from that scope
explanation: A scoped service must come from a scope. using var scope = app.Services.CreateScope(); then scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>() gives a context that is disposed afterwards.

prompt: Program.cs calls AddSingleton<IClock, FakeClock>() and then services.AddAuditing(), which calls AddSingleton<IClock, SystemClock>(). SystemClock is injected. Why?
optionA: AddSingleton ignores every registration after the first
optionB: The library's Add came later, so its registration wins
optionC: Library registrations always outrank the application
optionD: FakeClock is dropped because it is not a sealed class
correctAnswerText: The library's Add came later, so its registration wins
explanation: For a single IClock the last registration wins. Register yours after AddAuditing, or the library should have used TryAddSingleton so the existing registration survives.

prompt: A hot loop calls _logger.LogDebug($"Row {i} = {value}") with Debug switched off, yet profiling shows heavy string allocation there. Why?
optionA: Disabled log calls are still sent to the console provider
optionB: The logger buffers disabled messages to replay them later
optionC: LogDebug always formats its message twice per call
optionD: The interpolated string is built before the level is checked
correctAnswerText: The interpolated string is built before the level is checked
explanation: An interpolated string is evaluated as an argument before LogDebug runs. A message template passes the values unformatted, so nothing is built when the level is disabled.

prompt: A singleton TokenService injects IOptionsSnapshot<JwtOptions>, and Development fails at startup. Why?
optionA: IOptionsSnapshot works only inside minimal API handlers
optionB: Snapshots are loaded only after the first HTTP request
optionC: IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, so a singleton cannot hold it
optionD: JwtOptions must be a record to be bound from settings
correctAnswerText: IOptionsSnapshot is scoped, so a singleton cannot hold it
explanation: IOptionsSnapshot<T> is registered as scoped so it can recompute per request. Injecting it into a singleton is a captive dependency; use IOptions<T> or IOptionsMonitor<T>.

prompt: A teammate proposes passing IServiceProvider into every class and resolving what each needs inside its methods. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Reject it: IServiceProvider cannot be injected into classes
optionB: Reject it: needs become hidden and tests must build a container
optionC: Accept it: fewer constructor parameters make classes simpler
optionD: Accept it: resolving on demand is faster than injecting at start
correctAnswerText: Reject it: needs become hidden and tests must build a container
explanation: A service locator hides a class's real dependencies, moves missing registrations from startup to runtime, and forces tests to configure a provider. Keep GetRequiredService at the edges.

prompt: Someone suggests registering DbContext as a singleton "to save database connections". How should this be judged?
optionA: Accept: a singleton context makes saving changes atomic
optionB: Reject: EF Core refuses to compile a singleton context
optionC: Reject: it is not thread-safe and its tracker only grows
optionD: Accept: one context means only one connection is opened
correctAnswerText: Reject: it is not thread-safe and its tracker only grows
explanation: One context shared by concurrent requests fails, and its change tracker keeps every entity forever. Connection pooling already reuses connections; AddDbContextPool reuses contexts safely.

prompt: Where should the production SQL Server password for the API live?
optionA: appsettings.Production.json, since only ops deploy it
optionB: A constant in code, so the build cannot lose the value
optionC: An environment variable or vault, never a committed file
optionD: User secrets on the server, as they are kept encrypted
correctAnswerText: An environment variable or vault, never a committed file
explanation: A committed password stays in git history forever. User secrets are a Development-only convenience and are not encrypted. Production reads secrets from the environment or a vault.

prompt: A reviewer insists every class must get an interface before it can be injected. What is the sound position?
optionA: Agree: interfaces are what make constructor injection thread-safe
optionB: Agree: the container cannot inject a concrete class directly
optionC: Interfaces belong at seams; plain classes can register as themselves
optionD: Disagree: interfaces stop the container from choosing lifetimes
correctAnswerText: Interfaces belong at seams; plain classes can register as themselves
explanation: AddScoped<OrderService>() works fine. Interfaces earn their place where you need a fake or a second implementation: databases, email, payment, the clock.

prompt: An API must pick a payment gateway per request from the customer's country. Which design fits?
optionA: Inject one IPaymentGateway and let the container choose
optionB: new up the right gateway class inside each controller
optionC: A resolver that picks among injected gateways by country
optionD: [FromKeyedServices] on the parameter with a country key
correctAnswerText: A resolver that picks among injected gateways by country
explanation: A keyed-service attribute fixes the key at compile time, and a single injection always gets the last registration. A choice made from request data needs code: a resolver over IEnumerable<IPaymentGateway> or keyed lookups.

prompt: A required Smtp:Host may be missing in a new environment. Should the app fail at startup or start and fail when the first email is sent?
optionA: Start anyway, since email is a minor part of the app
optionB: Fail at startup, so a broken deploy never takes traffic
optionC: Fail on first send, as that error message is clearer
optionD: Start anyway and use localhost as a silent fallback
correctAnswerText: Fail at startup, so a broken deploy never takes traffic
explanation: ValidateOnStart turns a missing required setting into an immediate, visible failure during deploy instead of a surprise hours later. Silent fallbacks hide misconfiguration.

prompt: A developer wants _logger.LogInformation("Login {@Request}", request) on the login endpoint to debug failures. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Accept: structured logs mask fields named Password
optionB: Reject: the @ operator is not supported by ILogger
optionC: Reject: the destructured request stores the password too
optionD: Accept: log files are only readable by the developers
correctAnswerText: Reject: the destructured request stores the password too
explanation: Destructuring records every property, including the password. Logs are copied and kept for months; log the email or user id, never credentials or tokens.

prompt: A singleton cache uses a plain Dictionary and occasionally throws under load. Which fix keeps its purpose?
optionA: Make it scoped so two requests never share the cache
optionB: Keep the Dictionary; its reads and writes are atomic
optionC: Make it transient so each caller gets its own Dictionary
optionD: Keep it singleton and use ConcurrentDictionary or a lock
correctAnswerText: Keep it singleton and use ConcurrentDictionary or a lock
explanation: The cache exists to be shared, so changing the lifetime defeats it. Dictionary is not safe for concurrent writes; a concurrent collection, a lock or IMemoryCache is the fix.

prompt: When is the [LoggerMessage] source generator worth adopting over ordinary message templates?
optionA: Everywhere, since plain templates lose structured data
optionB: Never in .NET 8, as it was replaced by interpolation
optionC: On hot paths that log very often, where cost matters
optionD: Only for Error logs, which must include the exception
correctAnswerText: On hot paths that log very often, where cost matters
explanation: Templates already give structured fields. The generator removes per-call parsing and boxing, which matters on code paths that log thousands of times a second.

prompt: A 200-line console tool has three classes with constructor injection. Must it use the generic host and a container?
optionA: No: but then the classes must create their own dependencies
optionB: Yes: constructor injection only works with a container
optionC: No: wiring them with new in Main is a fine composition root
optionD: Yes: the classes cannot be unit tested without a host
correctAnswerText: No: wiring them with new in Main is a fine composition root
explanation: Dependency injection is the design; the container is a convenience. Building the graph by hand in Main keeps every benefit, including fakes in tests.

prompt: What is the name of the cross-platform web server built into ASP.NET Core?
optionA: Tomcat
optionB: Jetty
optionC: Nginx
optionD: Kestrel
correctAnswerText: Kestrel
explanation: Kestrel is the in-process HTTP server every ASP.NET Core app runs on. IIS or Nginx may sit in front as a reverse proxy, but Kestrel serves the app.

prompt: Which pipeline method adds terminal middleware that never calls the next component?
optionA: app.Map(...)
optionB: app.UseWhen(...)
optionC: app.Use(...)
optionD: app.Run(...)
correctAnswerText: app.Run(...)
explanation: app.Run registers a terminal delegate: it handles the request and nothing after it executes. app.Use receives next and may call it; Map and UseWhen branch the pipeline.

prompt: Which attribute on a controller turns on the automatic 400 response for an invalid model?
optionA: [Route]
optionB: [FromBody]
optionC: [ApiController]
optionD: [Produces]
correctAnswerText: [ApiController]
explanation: [ApiController] adds automatic ValidationProblemDetails responses, binding-source inference, required attribute routing and ProblemDetails bodies for error results.

prompt: Which status code reports that a POST created a resource, with a Location header pointing at it?
optionA: 201 Created
optionB: 204 No Content
optionC: 202 Accepted
optionD: 200 OK
correctAnswerText: 201 Created
explanation: 201 Created tells the client a new resource exists and the Location header says where. 202 means accepted for later processing; 204 means success with no body.

prompt: What media type does a ProblemDetails error response carry?
optionA: text/problem-details
optionB: application/problem+json
optionC: application/error+xml
optionD: application/json+error
correctAnswerText: application/problem+json
explanation: RFC 9457 (which replaced RFC 7807) defines application/problem+json with the standard fields type, title, status, detail and instance.

prompt: In minimal APIs (.NET 7+), which method collects endpoints under one shared prefix such as /api/products?
optionA: UseGroup
optionB: MapGroup
optionC: MapPrefix
optionD: MapArea
correctAnswerText: MapGroup
explanation: app.MapGroup("/api/products") returns a RouteGroupBuilder; endpoints mapped on it share the prefix and any conventions such as RequireAuthorization or WithTags.

prompt: Which controller helper returns 201 and builds the Location header from another action's name and route values?
optionA: LocalRedirect
optionB: CreatedAtAction
optionC: RedirectToAction
optionD: AcceptedAtRoute
correctAnswerText: CreatedAtAction
explanation: CreatedAtAction(nameof(GetById), new { id }, dto) generates the URL of GetById for that id and returns 201 with the DTO as the body.

prompt: Which package does the .NET 8 webapi template use to generate the OpenAPI document and Swagger UI?
optionA: AutoMapper
optionB: Serilog.AspNetCore
optionC: Newtonsoft.Json
optionD: Swashbuckle.AspNetCore
correctAnswerText: Swashbuckle.AspNetCore
explanation: The .NET 8 template adds Swashbuckle.AspNetCore with AddSwaggerGen, UseSwagger and UseSwaggerUI. (Later versions moved to Microsoft.AspNetCore.OpenApi.)

prompt: Which interface, new in .NET 8, lets a class turn an exception into a response for UseExceptionHandler?
optionA: IProblemWriter
optionB: IFaultMapper
optionC: IErrorResponder
optionD: IExceptionHandler
correctAnswerText: IExceptionHandler
explanation: A class implementing IExceptionHandler.TryHandleAsync is registered with AddExceptionHandler<T>() and is called by the UseExceptionHandler middleware.

prompt: Which JSON serializer does ASP.NET Core 8 use by default for request and response bodies?
optionA: Newtonsoft.Json
optionB: DataContractJsonSerializer
optionC: System.Text.Json
optionD: JavaScriptSerializer
correctAnswerText: System.Text.Json
explanation: System.Text.Json is the built-in default. Newtonsoft.Json can be plugged in with AddNewtonsoftJson but is no longer needed for most APIs.

prompt: In app.Use(async (ctx, next) => { A; await next(ctx); B; }), when does B run?
optionA: After the rest of the pipeline has finished
optionB: Before any later middleware begins to run
optionC: In parallel with the endpoint on another thread
optionD: Only when a later middleware throws an error
correctAnswerText: After the rest of the pipeline has finished
explanation: Code before await next runs on the way in; code after it runs on the way out, once everything later — including the endpoint — has produced the response.

prompt: Why is UseExceptionHandler placed first in the pipeline?
optionA: It must run before Kestrel accepts the connection
optionB: Later placement disables the logging of exceptions
optionC: It can only catch exceptions from middleware after it
optionD: It sets up the DI scope the other middleware use
correctAnswerText: It can only catch exceptions from middleware after it
explanation: Middleware wraps what comes after it. An exception thrown by a component placed before the handler never passes through the handler, so it cannot be turned into ProblemDetails.

prompt: Why does GET /api/products/abc return 404 for a route template "{id:int}"?
optionA: The int conversion throws, which maps to a 404
optionB: Route values that are not numbers are discarded
optionC: The constraint stops the route from matching at all
optionD: Model binding fails and [ApiController] answers 404
correctAnswerText: The constraint stops the route from matching at all
explanation: A route constraint decides whether a route matches. With no match there is no endpoint, hence 404. Without the constraint the route matches, binding "abc" to int fails, and the answer is 400.

prompt: Why does an API return a ProductDto rather than the EF Core Product entity?
optionA: Returning entities disables model validation on input
optionB: DTOs make the database queries run asynchronously
optionC: The contract stays stable and internal fields stay hidden
optionD: Entities cannot be serialised by System.Text.Json at all
correctAnswerText: The contract stays stable and internal fields stay hidden
explanation: A DTO is shaped for clients: renaming a column does not break them, server-only fields never leak, and navigation cycles cannot reach the serializer.

prompt: What is the difference in meaning between a 4xx and a 5xx status?
optionA: 4xx: the client must change the request; 5xx: the server failed
optionB: 4xx: an authentication issue; 5xx: a validation issue
optionC: 4xx: a temporary failure; 5xx: a permanent one to give up on
optionD: 4xx: the request was logged; 5xx: it was not logged at all
correctAnswerText: 4xx: the client must change the request; 5xx: the server failed
explanation: A 4xx tells the caller that retrying the same request will not help. A 5xx says the server broke, which is why a duplicate SKU is 409 and never 500.

prompt: What does declaring an action as ActionResult<ProductDto> give over IActionResult?
optionA: It validates the returned DTO before it is serialised
optionB: It returns a DTO or a result, and OpenAPI learns the type
optionC: It makes the action run asynchronously on its own
optionD: It forces every response to be 200 with a JSON body
correctAnswerText: It returns a DTO or a result, and OpenAPI learns the type
explanation: ActionResult<T> lets the method return a T (200) or any result such as NotFound(), and tells the OpenAPI generator what the success body looks like. IActionResult hides that type.

prompt: In minimal APIs, why return TypedResults.Ok(dto) with a Results<Ok<ProductDto>, NotFound> type rather than Results.Ok(dto)?
optionA: Results.Ok(dto) cannot write a JSON body for complex types
optionB: Each outcome is a concrete type that OpenAPI and tests can see
optionC: TypedResults are required for the endpoint to be routed
optionD: TypedResults serialise to JSON faster than the IResult helpers
correctAnswerText: Each outcome is a concrete type that OpenAPI and tests can see
explanation: TypedResults return concrete types and the Results<...> union lists every outcome, so the OpenAPI document and unit tests know them. Results.Ok returns a plain IResult.

prompt: Why is a scoped DbContext the right lifetime in a web API?
optionA: It lets every request see the others' unsaved changes
optionB: Only scoped contexts are allowed to call SaveChangesAsync
optionC: A scoped context keeps its connection open between requests
optionD: One request shares one tracker, and no two requests share it
correctAnswerText: One request shares one tracker, and no two requests share it
explanation: Services in one request work on the same change tracker and save together, while concurrent requests each get their own context, which matters because DbContext is not thread-safe.

prompt: Why pass the action's CancellationToken into ToListAsync(ct)?
optionA: An abandoned request also stops its database query
optionB: Queries without a token are not sent to SQL Server
optionC: It caches the result until the token is cancelled
optionD: The token makes the query run inside a transaction
correctAnswerText: An abandoned request also stops its database query
explanation: ASP.NET Core signals the token when the client disconnects. Passing it on lets EF Core cancel the command instead of finishing work nobody will read.

prompt: Why is "this SKU must not already exist" checked in the service rather than with a data annotation on the DTO?
optionA: Validation attributes are ignored on POST request bodies
optionB: Services run before model binding, so they see it first
optionC: Data annotations cannot check any string property at all
optionD: It needs the database, and a duplicate is a 409, not a 400
correctAnswerText: It needs the database, and a duplicate is a 409, not a 400
explanation: Annotations check the shape of the input in isolation. Uniqueness depends on current data, belongs to the business rules, and is a conflict with existing state.

optionA: A in, B in, B out, A out
optionB: A in, A out, B in, B out
optionC: B in, A in, A out, B out
optionD: A in, B in, A out, B out
correctAnswerText: A in, B in, B out, A out
explanation: Middleware nests: A calls B, B calls the endpoint, then B finishes before control returns to A. The way out is the reverse of the way in.

prompt: PUT /api/products/5 tries to set SKU "NB-02", which product 8 already uses. Which response fits?
optionA: 400 Bad Request
optionB: 404 Not Found
optionC: 500 Internal Server Error
optionD: 409 Conflict
correctAnswerText: 409 Conflict
explanation: The request is well formed and product 5 exists; it conflicts with the current state of another record. That is 409. A unique-index exception surfacing as 500 is the bug to avoid.

prompt: For app.MapPost("/api/products", (CreateProductRequest req, IProductStore store) => ...), where do req and store come from?
optionA: req from the query string; store from the JSON body
optionB: req from the route; store from a static instance
optionC: req from the JSON body; store from the DI container
optionD: Both from the JSON body, matched by parameter name
correctAnswerText: req from the JSON body; store from the DI container
explanation: Minimal APIs infer sources: a complex type binds from the JSON body, a type registered in DI is injected, route names bind from the route and simple types from the query.

prompt: Page 3 of products, 20 per page, ordered by Id. Which query is correct?
optionA: db.Products.Skip(40).Take(20).OrderBy(p => p.Id)
optionB: db.Products.OrderBy(p => p.Id).Take(20).Skip(40)
optionC: db.Products.OrderBy(p => p.Id).Skip(40).Take(20)
optionD: db.Products.OrderBy(p => p.Id).Skip(60).Take(20)
correctAnswerText: db.Products.OrderBy(p => p.Id).Skip(40).Take(20)
explanation: Pages 1 and 2 cover 40 rows, so skip 40 and take 20, after ordering. Ordering after paging sorts an arbitrary slice; taking before skipping returns nothing.

prompt: GetById is [HttpGet("{id:int}")]. After creating dto, which line returns a correct 201?
optionA: return CreatedAtAction(nameof(GetById), dto);
optionB: return CreatedAtAction("GetById", new { productId = dto.Id }, dto);
optionC: return CreatedAtAction(nameof(GetById), new { id = dto.Id }, dto);
optionD: return Ok(CreatedAtAction(nameof(GetById), dto.Id));
correctAnswerText: return CreatedAtAction(nameof(GetById), new { id = dto.Id }, dto);
explanation: The route values must supply every parameter of the target route, by its name: id. A wrong name fails link generation with a 500, and Ok(...) wraps the result as a 200 body.

prompt: A booking DTO must have EndDate after StartDate. Which approach validates this in a controller API?
optionA: Put [Compare("StartDate")] on the EndDate property
optionB: Add a {endDate:datetime} route constraint on the action
optionC: Implement IValidatableObject on the DTO and compare them
optionD: Put [Range] on EndDate with StartDate as its minimum
correctAnswerText: Implement IValidatableObject on the DTO and compare them
explanation: Attribute arguments must be constants, and [Compare] checks equality. IValidatableObject.Validate (or a FluentValidation rule) can compare two properties, and [ApiController] returns the 400.

prompt: A GET list endpoint only reads products to return as DTOs. Which query shape is best?
optionA: Attach each entity to the context, then copy it out
optionB: Load the entities with ToList, then map in a foreach
optionC: Load every row with Include, then filter in memory
optionD: Project with Select into ProductDto before ToListAsync
correctAnswerText: Project with Select into ProductDto before ToListAsync
explanation: A Select projection fetches only the needed columns and is never tracked. Loading full tracked entities first, or filtering after materialising, wastes memory and time.

prompt: Every ProblemDetails response must carry the request's traceId. Where is this done once for the whole API?
optionA: A route constraint that copies the id into the URL
optionB: A [ProducesResponseType] attribute on every action
optionC: AddProblemDetails(o => o.CustomizeProblemDetails = ...)
optionD: A try/catch in each controller action that adds it
correctAnswerText: AddProblemDetails(o => o.CustomizeProblemDetails = ...)
explanation: CustomizeProblemDetails runs for every ProblemDetails the app writes — validation, status code pages and exception handling — so one callback adds the extension everywhere.

prompt: The /// summaries on your actions should appear as descriptions in Swagger UI. What must you do?
optionA: Nothing; Swashbuckle reads the C# source files directly
optionB: Add [Description] attributes to the controller classes only
optionC: Install the XML formatter with AddXmlSerializerFormatters
optionD: Enable GenerateDocumentationFile and call IncludeXmlComments
correctAnswerText: Enable GenerateDocumentationFile and call IncludeXmlComments
explanation: The compiler writes the comments to an XML file only when GenerateDocumentationFile is set in the project, and AddSwaggerGen must be told to read it with IncludeXmlComments.

prompt: Swagger UI should be served while developing but not in production. Which Program.cs code does that?
optionA: if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseSwagger(); app.UseSwaggerUI(); }
optionB: app.UseSwaggerUI(); placed after app.Run() so production never reaches it
optionC: if (builder.Services.Count > 0) { app.UseSwagger(); app.UseSwaggerUI(); }
optionD: app.UseSwagger(); app.UseSwaggerUI(); with [Conditional("DEBUG")] above them
correctAnswerText: if (app.Environment.IsDevelopment()) { app.UseSwagger(); app.UseSwaggerUI(); }
explanation: The template wraps the Swagger middleware in an environment check. Anything placed after app.Run() never executes, and [Conditional] applies to method declarations, not calls.

prompt: Program.cs calls AddControllers(), the controllers have [Route] attributes, yet every URL returns 404. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: AddProblemDetails() is never called
optionB: The controllers lack a constructor
optionC: UseHttpsRedirection() is missing
optionD: app.MapControllers() is never called
correctAnswerText: app.MapControllers() is never called
explanation: AddControllers registers the services; MapControllers adds the controller endpoints to routing. Without it, no route exists and every request is a 404.

prompt: A POST from a test client returns 415 Unsupported Media Type, though the body is valid JSON. What is wrong?
optionA: The action is missing an [HttpPost] attribute
optionB: The request has no Content-Type: application/json
optionC: The DTO has a required property left as null
optionD: The JSON property names are in the wrong case
correctAnswerText: The request has no Content-Type: application/json
explanation: [FromBody] input formatters choose by Content-Type. With none, or text/plain, no formatter accepts the body and ASP.NET Core returns 415 before the action runs.

prompt: DELETE /api/products/7 returns 405 Method Not Allowed. What does that tell you?
optionA: The route template has an {id:int} constraint
optionB: The product 7 does not exist in the database at all
optionC: The user is not allowed to delete this product
optionD: The path matched, but no endpoint there handles DELETE
correctAnswerText: The path matched, but no endpoint there handles DELETE
explanation: 405 means routing found endpoints for that path but none for the method. Add an [HttpDelete("{id:int}")] action; a missing record would be 404 and a refused user 403.

prompt: Custom middleware that throws is registered before app.UseExceptionHandler(). Clients get no ProblemDetails for its errors. Why?
optionA: AddProblemDetails ignores exceptions from middleware
optionB: The handler only wraps the middleware placed after it
optionC: UseExceptionHandler catches only controller exceptions
optionD: Exceptions thrown in middleware are always swallowed
correctAnswerText: The handler only wraps the middleware placed after it
explanation: The exception handler catches what happens inside the next(...) call it makes. Code that runs before it is outside that call, so its exceptions bypass the handler.

prompt: A middleware writes "checked" to the response body and then calls next. Later the controller returns 404 and the log shows "StatusCode cannot be set because the response has already started". Why?
optionA: Kestrel only allows one status change per connection
optionB: Middleware may not write to a response body at all
optionC: Writing the body sent the headers, so the status is fixed
optionD: The controller returned 404 instead of throwing an error
correctAnswerText: Writing the body sent the headers, so the status is fixed
explanation: The first write sends the status line and headers. After that the status cannot change. Middleware that calls next must not write the body; one that answers should short-circuit.

prompt: GET /api/orders/5 returns the Order entity with Customer loaded, and Customer has an Orders list. The response is a 500. What is the cause?
optionA: Order lacks a [Key] attribute on its Id property
optionB: The serializer finds an Order-Customer-Orders cycle
optionC: System.Text.Json cannot write a decimal property
optionD: The Customer navigation was loaded lazily too late
correctAnswerText: The serializer finds an Order-Customer-Orders cycle
explanation: System.Text.Json throws a JsonException on an object cycle. Returning a DTO that includes only what the client needs removes the cycle and the leaked fields.

prompt: An action declared ActionResult<ProductDto> does return _service.Find(id); and the client gets 204 for a missing id instead of 404. Why?
optionA: Find throws, and the exception becomes a 204
optionB: A null value in ActionResult<T> is written as 204
optionC: The [ApiController] attribute maps 404 to 204
optionD: The client sent a HEAD request instead of GET
correctAnswerText: A null value in ActionResult<T> is written as 204
explanation: Returning null as the value gives 204 No Content. A missing resource must be reported explicitly: if (dto is null) return NotFound();

prompt: Swagger UI shows "Failed to load API definition" after a teammate added a public helper method to a controller. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The public method has no HTTP verb, so it looks like an action
optionB: The project lacks an XML documentation file for the method
optionC: Helper methods must be static to appear in the document
optionD: Swagger UI cannot show controllers with more than ten actions
correctAnswerText: The public method has no HTTP verb, so it looks like an action
explanation: Swashbuckle treats public controller methods as actions and fails on one without an HTTP method. Make the helper private or mark it [NonAction].

prompt: A list ordered by OrderBy(e => e.StartsAt) and paged with Skip/Take shows the same event on pages 1 and 2. Why?
optionA: Many rows share StartsAt, so their order is not stable
optionB: EF Core caches page 1 and returns it for page 2
optionC: StartsAt must be indexed before paging can work
optionD: Skip and Take are applied in memory after loading
correctAnswerText: Many rows share StartsAt, so their order is not stable
explanation: Rows with equal sort keys come back in no guaranteed order, so each page query can cut them differently. Add a unique tie-breaker: ThenBy(e => e.Id).

prompt: An endpoint runs (await db.Products.ToListAsync()).Where(p => p.Price < 100). It is slow on a large table. Why?
optionA: The Price comparison is translated into a full-text search
optionB: Where clauses on decimal columns cannot be indexed at all
optionC: Every row is loaded before the filter is applied in memory
optionD: ToListAsync runs on a single thread and blocks the server
correctAnswerText: Every row is loaded before the filter is applied in memory
explanation: ToListAsync materialises the whole table; the Where then runs in C#. Filtering on the IQueryable before ToListAsync sends WHERE Price < @p to SQL Server.

prompt: A new microservice has five endpoints and no MVC filters. A teammate says controllers are mandatory for a "real" API. What is the sound judgement?
optionA: Minimal APIs are only for prototypes and must be replaced
optionB: Controllers are required: minimal APIs cannot return JSON
optionC: Minimal APIs suit it well; both styles are fully supported
optionD: Controllers are required: only they can use dependency injection
correctAnswerText: Minimal APIs suit it well; both styles are fully supported
explanation: Minimal APIs are a supported production style, lean and well suited to a small service. Controllers bring [ApiController] conventions and filters that larger APIs may want.

prompt: A team plans a generic IRepository<T> over EF Core "because every app needs one". What is the best judgement?
optionA: Required: services cannot use a DbContext without a repository layer
optionB: DbContext is already a unit of work; add repositories only when they earn it
optionC: Good idea if GetAll returns IEnumerable<T> for the services to filter
optionD: Required: EF Core queries are unsafe unless a repository wraps them
correctAnswerText: DbContext is already a unit of work; add repositories only when they earn it
explanation: DbSet is already a repository and DbContext a unit of work. A generic GetAll returning IEnumerable pulls whole tables into memory; specific repositories are fine when queries are complex or reused.

prompt: An API returns 200 with { "success": false, "error": "Not found" } for every failure. How should this be judged?
optionA: Wrong: JSON bodies may not be sent with a 200 response
optionB: Fine: the JSON body describes the error well enough
optionC: Fine: using one status keeps the client code simpler
optionD: Wrong: clients, caches and monitors trust the status line
correctAnswerText: Wrong: clients, caches and monitors trust the status line
explanation: Retry logic, caches, logs and dashboards read the status code. A failure reported as 200 is counted as a success everywhere; use 404, 409, 400 with ProblemDetails.

prompt: Should a 500 response include the exception's Message so clients can see what went wrong?
optionA: Yes: but only when the exception came from EF Core
optionB: No: unexpected messages may leak SQL, paths or data
optionC: Yes: clients need the exact message to retry correctly
optionD: No: ProblemDetails has no field for any text at all
correctAnswerText: No: unexpected messages may leak SQL, paths or data
explanation: An unexpected exception message can contain SQL, file paths or personal data. Your own expected exceptions carry client-safe messages; unknown ones get a generic 500 and a full log entry.

prompt: An export endpoint pages through 2 million rows with Skip/Take, and later pages get slower and slower. What is the better design?
optionA: Cache every page in memory after the first request
optionB: Raise the page size until only one page is needed
optionC: Remove the ORDER BY so SQL Server can return faster
optionD: Keyset paging: ask for rows after the last key seen
correctAnswerText: Keyset paging: ask for rows after the last key seen
explanation: OFFSET still walks past every skipped row. Seeking with WHERE (StartsAt, Id) > (last values) on an index costs the same for every page; the trade-off is no jumping to page 57.

prompt: A teammate wants to drop DTOs and return entities because "mapping is boilerplate". Which consequence matters most?
optionA: Responses become larger but otherwise behave the same
optionB: The OpenAPI document can no longer be generated at all
optionC: Entities make every endpoint slower than DTOs would
optionD: A column rename becomes a breaking change for clients
correctAnswerText: A column rename becomes a breaking change for clients
explanation: With entities as the contract, every schema change reaches clients, server-owned fields leak and can be over-posted, and navigation cycles break serialisation.

prompt: The React form already validates every field. Does the API still need validation?
optionA: Yes: the API is callable directly, so it must check input
optionB: No: [ApiController] trusts input from a same-origin client
optionC: No: duplicate validation wastes server CPU on each request
optionD: Only for PUT requests, as POST input is checked by React
correctAnswerText: Yes: the API is callable directly, so it must check input
explanation: Client validation is a convenience for the user. Anyone can call the API with curl or Postman, so the server must enforce every rule itself.

prompt: To debug a production issue, someone proposes enabling the developer exception page in Production. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Accept: it is the only way to see production errors
optionB: Reject: it shows stack traces and code to any caller
optionC: Reject: it only works when a debugger is attached
optionD: Accept: it is harmless as long as HTTPS is enforced
correctAnswerText: Reject: it shows stack traces and code to any caller
explanation: The developer page exposes stack traces, source lines and request data. Production errors belong in logs with a trace id that the ProblemDetails body returns to the client.

prompt: Partners need your API's OpenAPI spec in production. What is the sound approach?
optionA: Skip the spec and let partners read your controller code
optionB: Publish the JSON spec or serve it behind authentication
optionC: Email them screenshots of the Development Swagger UI
optionD: Serve an open Swagger UI on the public production URL
correctAnswerText: Publish the JSON spec or serve it behind authentication
explanation: An open try-it UI advertises your attack surface. The spec itself is a contract clients can generate code from, so share the JSON file or protect the endpoint.

prompt: An action calls _service.GetAsync(id).Result to avoid making the action async. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Accept: blocking is fine because ASP.NET Core has no limit
optionB: Reject: blocking holds a thread per request and risks starvation
optionC: Reject: .Result always deadlocks in ASP.NET Core 8 apps
optionD: Accept: .Result is the same as await but with less code
correctAnswerText: Reject: blocking holds a thread per request and risks starvation
explanation: Blocking on a task ties up a thread-pool thread while the database works; under load the pool starves. ASP.NET Core has no synchronization context, so it does not always deadlock, but it scales badly.

prompt: Which middleware reads the bearer token and sets HttpContext.User?
optionA: UseAuthentication
optionB: UseCors
optionC: UseRouting
