optionD: UseAuthorization
correctAnswerText: UseAuthentication
explanation: UseAuthentication runs the scheme's handler, which validates the credential and builds the ClaimsPrincipal. UseAuthorization then decides using that principal.

prompt: Which attribute lets one action be called without logging in, inside a controller marked [Authorize]?
optionA: [SkipAuthentication]
optionB: [AllowAnonymous]
optionC: [PublicEndpoint]
optionD: [IgnoreAuthorize]
correctAnswerText: [AllowAnonymous]
explanation: [AllowAnonymous] overrides [Authorize] and the fallback policy for that endpoint. Minimal APIs use .AllowAnonymous() for the same effect.

prompt: What is the type of HttpContext.User (User in a controller)?
optionA: AuthenticationTicket
optionB: IdentityUser
optionC: JwtSecurityToken
optionD: ClaimsPrincipal
correctAnswerText: ClaimsPrincipal
explanation: User is a ClaimsPrincipal: one or more identities, each a set of claims such as nameidentifier, email and role. IdentityUser is the database entity, not the request's principal.

prompt: How does ASP.NET Core Identity's default PasswordHasher store a password?
optionA: A PBKDF2 hash with a random per-password salt
optionB: A single unsalted SHA-256 hash of the text
optionC: An MD5 hash with one salt shared by all users
optionD: An AES encryption under an application key
correctAnswerText: A PBKDF2 hash with a random per-password salt
explanation: PasswordHasher<TUser> uses PBKDF2 with a random 128-bit salt and many iterations (HMAC-SHA512, 100,000 since .NET 7). It is one-way: nothing can decrypt it.

prompt: Which NuGet package provides AddJwtBearer for validating JWTs in ASP.NET Core?
optionA: Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Stores
optionB: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Cors
optionC: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer
optionD: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies
correctAnswerText: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer
explanation: Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer adds the bearer handler, configured with TokenValidationParameters for issuer, audience, lifetime and signing key.

prompt: Which status does ASP.NET Core return when an authenticated user fails an authorization policy?
optionA: 400 Bad Request
optionB: 403 Forbidden
optionC: 404 Not Found
optionD: 401 Unauthorized
correctAnswerText: 403 Forbidden
explanation: A known user who fails a requirement is forbidden (403). An anonymous caller at a protected endpoint is challenged (401).

prompt: Which AuthorizationOptions property applies to every endpoint that has no authorization metadata at all?
optionA: FallbackPolicy
optionB: BasePolicy
optionC: GlobalPolicy
optionD: DefaultPolicy
correctAnswerText: FallbackPolicy
explanation: FallbackPolicy covers endpoints with no [Authorize] or [AllowAnonymous]. DefaultPolicy is what a bare [Authorize] uses; it does not touch unmarked endpoints.

prompt: Which interface marks a class as a requirement that an AuthorizationHandler<T> evaluates?
optionA: IAuthenticationHandler
optionB: IClaimsTransformation
optionC: IAuthorizationFilter
optionD: IAuthorizationRequirement
correctAnswerText: IAuthorizationRequirement
explanation: A requirement implements the marker interface IAuthorizationRequirement; a handler deriving from AuthorizationHandler<TRequirement> calls context.Succeed(requirement) when it is met.

prompt: Which registered JWT claim holds the time after which the token must be rejected?
optionA: aud
optionB: exp
optionC: iat
optionD: sub
correctAnswerText: exp
explanation: exp is the expiry, as seconds since the Unix epoch. iat is when the token was issued, sub the subject (user id), and aud the intended audience.

prompt: Which service do you inject to run a resource-based authorization check against a loaded record?
optionA: IAuthorizationService
optionB: SignInManager<AppUser>
optionC: IAuthenticationService
optionD: UserManager<AppUser>
correctAnswerText: IAuthorizationService
explanation: IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, resource, requirement) runs the handlers registered for that requirement and resource type and returns a result to act on.

prompt: A request with an expired token reaches an [AllowAnonymous] endpoint. What does the JWT bearer handler do?
optionA: Rejects the request with 401 before routing happens
optionB: Rejects the request with 403 for an invalid token
optionC: Refreshes the token and returns it in a header
optionD: Leaves the user anonymous, and the request continues
correctAnswerText: Leaves the user anonymous, and the request continues
explanation: Authentication only establishes identity. A failed token leaves User anonymous; refusing happens in authorization, and an [AllowAnonymous] endpoint does not refuse.

prompt: Why must a JWT's payload never hold secrets such as a password or an Aadhaar number?
optionA: The payload is logged by every HTTP proxy it passes
optionB: Its signature is removed when it reaches the browser
optionC: It is only Base64url-encoded, so anyone can read it
optionD: Claims longer than 32 characters break its signature
correctAnswerText: It is only Base64url-encoded, so anyone can read it
explanation: The signature stops tampering, not reading. Anyone holding the token can decode the payload, so claims carry only what is safe to show.

prompt: Why does Identity use a different random salt for every password?
optionA: A salt lets the server decrypt the password when it is needed
optionB: Equal passwords get different hashes, defeating precomputed tables
optionC: Salted hashes take up less space in the AspNetUsers table
optionD: A salt makes the hash safe to send to the browser later
correctAnswerText: Equal passwords get different hashes, defeating precomputed tables
explanation: With a per-password salt, two users with the same password have different hashes, and lookup tables built in advance are useless. The hash stays one-way.

prompt: Why should login return the same 401 for an unknown email and for a wrong password?
optionA: Different answers reveal which emails have accounts
optionB: Identity cannot tell the two cases apart internally
optionC: A 404 for unknown emails breaks the React login form
optionD: Using one status code lowers the server's logging cost
correctAnswerText: Different answers reveal which emails have accounts
explanation: If "no such user" differs from "wrong password", an attacker can enumerate registered emails and then focus guessing on real accounts.

prompt: Why are JWT access tokens kept short-lived, around 5 to 15 minutes?
optionA: Longer tokens no longer fit in an HTTP header
optionB: Browsers delete Authorization headers after 15 minutes
optionC: Signatures weaken the longer a token is in use
optionD: A JWT cannot be revoked; it works until it expires
correctAnswerText: A JWT cannot be revoked; it works until it expires
explanation: The server does not track issued JWTs, so logout or a password change cannot cancel one. A short life limits a stolen token; a revocable refresh token keeps users signed in.

prompt: A policy is built with RequireRole("Student").RequireClaim("email_verified", "true"). How do these requirements combine?
optionA: The claim is checked only if the role fails
optionB: The role is checked only on POST requests
optionC: Either one passing is enough to succeed
optionD: Both must pass for the policy to succeed
correctAnswerText: Both must pass for the policy to succeed
explanation: Within one policy every requirement must be satisfied. Alternatives inside a single requirement — such as several role names in one RequireRole — are OR.

prompt: What does ClockSkew in TokenValidationParameters do, and what is its default?
optionA: Delays a new token's validity; thirty seconds by default
optionB: Limits how often tokens may be issued; one per minute
optionC: Sets the access token lifetime; fifteen minutes by default
optionD: Allows tokens past exp by a margin; five minutes by default
correctAnswerText: Allows tokens past exp by a margin; five minutes by default
explanation: ClockSkew tolerates clocks that disagree between servers by accepting tokens slightly after exp. The default five minutes makes a 15-minute token last up to 20, so APIs often shorten it.

prompt: Why does a login endpoint call SignInManager.CheckPasswordSignInAsync(user, pw, lockoutOnFailure: true) rather than UserManager.CheckPasswordAsync?
optionA: It also counts failures and locks out repeated guessing
optionB: It issues the JWT access token as part of the same call
optionC: It checks the password faster than the UserManager does
optionD: It is the only one that compares against the stored hash
correctAnswerText: It also counts failures and locks out repeated guessing
explanation: Both verify the hash. CheckPasswordSignInAsync also records failed attempts and applies lockout (5 failures, 5 minutes by default) without issuing a cookie; CheckPasswordAsync counts nothing.

prompt: Why might GET /api/bookings/1043 return 404, not 403, when the booking belongs to someone else?
optionA: A 403 would log the caller out of the application
optionB: A 404 is the only status the ownership filter can send
optionC: A 403 would confirm the record exists to the caller
optionD: Browsers retry 403 responses again and again
correctAnswerText: A 403 would confirm the record exists to the caller
explanation: Filtering by owner in the query makes another user's record simply not found, which also avoids telling an attacker which ids are real.

prompt: An admin is demoted, but their existing token still passes [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]. Why?
optionA: Demotion requires the app to be restarted to apply
optionB: The Identity tables update only once a day by default
optionC: Role checks are cached by the authorization service
optionD: Roles in the token are a snapshot taken at login
correctAnswerText: Roles in the token are a snapshot taken at login
explanation: The token carries the role claims written when it was issued, and the API trusts them until exp. Short lifetimes bound how long a stale role lasts.

prompt: Which Program.cs order is correct for a JWT API that a React app on another origin calls?
optionA: UseAuthentication, MapControllers, UseAuthorization, UseCors
optionB: UseAuthorization, UseAuthentication, UseCors, MapControllers
optionC: MapControllers, UseCors, UseAuthentication, UseAuthorization
optionD: UseCors, UseAuthentication, UseAuthorization, MapControllers
correctAnswerText: UseCors, UseAuthentication, UseAuthorization, MapControllers
explanation: CORS answers preflights before auth refuses them; authentication sets User before authorization reads it; endpoints are mapped after both.

prompt: Only Students with the claim email_verified = "true" may book. Which registration expresses that rule once?
optionA: AddPolicy("VerifiedStudent", p => p.RequireRole("Student", "email_verified", "true"))
optionB: AddPolicy("VerifiedStudent", p => p.RequireAuthenticatedUser().AllowAnonymous())
optionC: AddPolicy("VerifiedStudent", p => p.RequireRole("Student").RequireClaim("email_verified", "true"))
optionD: AddPolicy("VerifiedStudent", p => p.RequireClaim("Student").RequireRole("email_verified"))
correctAnswerText: AddPolicy("VerifiedStudent", p => p.RequireRole("Student").RequireClaim("email_verified", "true"))
explanation: RequireRole checks role claims and RequireClaim checks a claim type with allowed values; both must pass. RequireRole with three strings means any of three roles.

prompt: Inside a controller action, where should the current user's id come from?
optionA: User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)
optionB: A UserId property in the JSON request body
optionC: Request.Headers["X-User-Id"] set by the client
optionD: Request.Query["userId"] sent by the React app
correctAnswerText: User.FindFirstValue(ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier)
explanation: Only the validated token is trustworthy. The query string, body and headers are chosen by the caller, so an id read from them lets anyone act as anyone.

prompt: A student may view only their own booking. Which query does that in one step?
optionA: db.Bookings.Where(b => b.UserId == id).FirstOrDefaultAsync()
optionB: db.Bookings.FindAsync(id), then return it if User is authenticated
optionC: db.Bookings.FirstOrDefaultAsync(b => b.Id == id && b.UserId == userId)
optionD: db.Bookings.FirstOrDefaultAsync(b => b.Id == id), checked by [Authorize]
correctAnswerText: db.Bookings.FirstOrDefaultAsync(b => b.Id == id && b.UserId == userId)
explanation: Putting ownership in the query means another user's booking is never loaded; a null result becomes 404. [Authorize] only proves someone is logged in.

prompt: The API sets a FallbackPolicy requiring an authenticated user. A new HealthController must stay public. What do you do?
optionA: Leave it without attributes; it stays public
optionB: Register it before calling AddAuthorization
optionC: Put [Authorize(Roles = "")] on the controller
optionD: Put [AllowAnonymous] on HealthController
correctAnswerText: Put [AllowAnonymous] on HealthController
explanation: The fallback policy applies to every endpoint without metadata, so an unmarked controller now requires login. Public endpoints opt out explicitly with [AllowAnonymous].

prompt: How should the API store the refresh tokens it issues?
optionA: A JWT with a one-year exp that is never stored at all
optionB: The raw token in a column, so it can be compared directly
optionC: A hash of a random value, with user, expiry and revoked flag
optionD: In the access token's payload, renewed on each request
correctAnswerText: A hash of a random value, with user, expiry and revoked flag
explanation: A refresh token is a long-lived credential. Store only its hash, like a password, with enough data to expire it, revoke it and rotate it on use.

prompt: Which Jwt:Key setting is acceptable for signing HS256 tokens in production?
optionA: The app name and the year, set in Program.cs code
optionB: Guid.NewGuid().ToString(), generated on each startup
optionC: "secret123", kept in the committed appsettings.json
optionD: 32 random bytes, Base64, from an environment variable
correctAnswerText: 32 random bytes, Base64, from an environment variable
explanation: HS256 needs at least 256 bits of real randomness, kept secret and shared by every instance. A short key is refused; a generated one logs everyone out on restart.

prompt: A JWT-only API needs UserManager and password hashing from Identity but no cookies. Which registration fits?
optionA: AddCookie() with the JWT handler as a fallback
optionB: AddDefaultIdentity<AppUser>() with the Identity UI
optionC: AddIdentity<AppUser, IdentityRole>() with defaults
optionD: AddIdentityCore<AppUser>() with the EF Core stores
correctAnswerText: AddIdentityCore<AppUser>() with the EF Core stores
explanation: AddIdentity registers Identity's cookie scheme as the default, so challenges redirect to a login page. AddIdentityCore gives the user store, hashing and UserManager without cookies.

prompt: Every minimal API endpoint under /api/admin must require the "AdminOnly" policy. Which code applies it to all of them?
optionA: app.MapGroup("/api/admin").WithTags("AdminOnly")
optionB: app.MapGroup("/api/admin").AllowAnonymous("AdminOnly")
optionC: app.MapGroup("/api/admin").RequireAuthorization("AdminOnly")
optionD: app.UseAuthorization("/api/admin", "AdminOnly")
correctAnswerText: app.MapGroup("/api/admin").RequireAuthorization("AdminOnly")
explanation: RequireAuthorization on a route group adds the policy to every endpoint mapped on it. WithTags only labels endpoints for OpenAPI.

prompt: In a WebApplicationFactory test, how do you call an [Authorize(Roles = "Librarian")] endpoint as a librarian without a real login?
optionA: Remove UseAuthorization from Program.cs in the test project
optionB: Send the header X-Role: Librarian; the API reads it in tests
optionC: Register a test authentication scheme that issues a Librarian role
optionD: Put [AllowAnonymous] on the action while the tests run
correctAnswerText: Register a test authentication scheme that issues a Librarian role
explanation: ConfigureTestServices can add a test AuthenticationHandler that returns a principal with the chosen role claims, so the real authorization rules are exercised.

prompt: Every protected endpoint returns 401 even with a freshly issued, valid token. Program.cs has app.UseAuthorization(); app.UseAuthentication();. What is wrong?
optionA: The bearer handler rejects tokens under a minute old
optionB: The token was issued for a different audience
optionC: Authorization runs while User is still anonymous
optionD: UseAuthentication must come after MapControllers
correctAnswerText: Authorization runs while User is still anonymous
explanation: Middleware runs in order. Authorization sees an anonymous principal and challenges, so every protected call is 401. Authentication must come first.

prompt: A Postman call to an [Authorize] API endpoint without a token returns 302 to /Account/Login instead of 401. What is the cause?
optionA: AddIdentity made Identity's cookie scheme the default
optionB: UseHttpsRedirection rewrites each 401 into a 302
optionC: The JWT bearer handler redirects anonymous callers
optionD: [ApiController] turns challenges into redirects
correctAnswerText: AddIdentity made Identity's cookie scheme the default
explanation: The cookie scheme challenges by redirecting to a login page. Use AddIdentityCore with JWT bearer as the default scheme, or set the default challenge scheme explicitly.

prompt: Tokens are refused with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="The audience 'campus-web' is invalid". Likeliest cause?
optionA: Issuing and validating read different Jwt:Audience values
optionB: The token has expired and ClockSkew is set to zero
optionC: The signing key is shorter than 32 bytes in this setup
optionD: The user has no role claims written in the token
correctAnswerText: Issuing and validating read different Jwt:Audience values
explanation: The aud claim written at login does not match ValidAudience. Commonly one config file has a typo or the token came from another environment; issue and validate from the same options.

prompt: After each deploy or restart, every user's token fails signature validation. What is the likely cause?
optionA: ClockSkew is reset to zero on every app restart
optionB: The tokens were signed with a key that is too long
optionC: The signing key is generated fresh when the app starts
optionD: The issuer claim includes the server's start time
correctAnswerText: The signing key is generated fresh when the app starts
explanation: A fallback such as Guid.NewGuid() as the key means each process signs and validates with a new key. Use one key from a secret store, shared by all instances.

prompt: A user who is in the Admin role in AspNetUserRoles gets 403 on [Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]. Decoding the token shows no role claim. What is wrong?
optionA: The [Authorize] attribute reads roles only from the cookie
optionB: Role names in Identity must be written in all capital letters
optionC: The Admin role must also be added to the fallback policy
optionD: The login endpoint never added the user's roles to the token
correctAnswerText: The login endpoint never added the user's roles to the token
explanation: The API knows only what the token says. Call GetRolesAsync at login and add a ClaimTypes.Role claim per role; the user must sign in again after a role change.

prompt: After logout, a copied access token keeps working, even a few minutes past its exp. Which explanation covers both facts?
optionA: The bearer handler ignores exp when a refresh token exists
optionB: JWTs cannot be revoked, and default ClockSkew adds 5 minutes
optionC: The browser cached the response for the protected endpoint
optionD: Logout failed to delete the token row from the database
correctAnswerText: JWTs cannot be revoked, and default ClockSkew adds 5 minutes
explanation: Logout can only drop the token client-side; the server still accepts it until exp plus ClockSkew. Short tokens, a small ClockSkew and revocable refresh tokens fix it.

prompt: Calls to one action fail with a 500, and the log says "The AuthorizationPolicy named: 'ManageEvent' was not found." What is the cause?
optionA: The policy was registered after AddAuthentication
optionB: The user lacks the claims the policy requires
optionC: The attribute names a policy that was never registered
optionD: The policy handler threw an exception internally
correctAnswerText: The attribute names a policy that was never registered
explanation: An unknown policy name is a configuration error, not a refusal, so it surfaces as a 500. Declare policy names as constants and test each one.

prompt: A custom requirement's policy returns 403 for every user, including those who meet the rule, and a breakpoint in its handler is never hit. Why?
optionA: Requirements only work when the user has the Admin role
optionB: The policy must be applied to the whole controller class
optionC: The handler should return Task.FromResult(true) to succeed
optionD: The handler was never registered as an IAuthorizationHandler
correctAnswerText: The handler was never registered as an IAuthorizationHandler
explanation: Handlers are found through DI. If none is registered for the requirement, nothing calls Succeed, so the policy fails for every authenticated user.

prompt: GET /api/orders/{id} is [Authorize] and runs db.Orders.FindAsync(id). Any logged-in customer can read any order by changing the id. What is missing?
optionA: A route constraint of {id:int} on the action
optionB: A longer signing key for the access tokens
optionC: A check that the order belongs to the caller
optionD: An [Authorize(Roles = "Customer")] attribute
correctAnswerText: A check that the order belongs to the caller
explanation: This is broken object-level authorization, the top OWASP API risk. Authentication proves who the caller is; the query must also restrict the order to the caller's user id.

prompt: Two handlers serve one requirement: OwnerHandler calls Succeed for the owner, and SuspendedHandler calls context.Fail() for suspended users. A suspended owner calls the endpoint. Result?
optionA: Denied, because Fail wins even when another handler succeeds
optionB: Allowed, because one handler called Succeed for the owner
optionC: Allowed or denied, depending on which handler ran first
optionD: A 500, because two handlers gave conflicting results
correctAnswerText: Denied, because Fail wins even when another handler succeeds
explanation: Authorization succeeds only if every requirement is met and no handler called Fail. An explicit Fail overrides any Succeed, whatever the order.

prompt: The React app must hold the access token. Which assessment of the options is fair?
optionA: localStorage is safe because only your own scripts can read it
optionB: A cookie is always worse, as cookies are readable by any site
optionC: An httpOnly cookie hides it from scripts but brings CSRF to handle
optionD: Where it lives does not matter once the token has been signed
correctAnswerText: An httpOnly cookie hides it from scripts but brings CSRF to handle
explanation: Any script on the page can read localStorage, so one XSS bug leaks the token. An httpOnly cookie resists that, but the browser sends it automatically, so CSRF defences are needed.

prompt: Role names such as "Organiser,Admin" are repeated on thirty endpoints. What is the better design?
optionA: Check roles with if statements inside every action
optionB: More roles, one per endpoint, checked by role name
optionC: Named policies, so each rule is defined once and reused
optionD: Drop roles and give every user the same permissions
correctAnswerText: Named policies, so each rule is defined once and reused
explanation: A policy names a rule once; endpoints refer to it, and changing who may manage events is a one-line change rather than a hunt through attributes.

prompt: A teammate says hiding the Delete button for non-owners in React is enough protection. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Accept: CORS stops other tools from calling the API
optionB: Reject: the API can be called directly, so it must check
optionC: Reject: React cannot hide buttons based on the user
optionD: Accept: users cannot call endpoints that have no button
correctAnswerText: Reject: the API can be called directly, so it must check
explanation: The UI is a convenience. curl, Postman or a script call the API without your React app, so ownership must be enforced on the server.

prompt: To avoid building refresh tokens, someone proposes 7-day access tokens. How should this be judged?
optionA: Accept: a longer token means fewer logins for users
optionB: Accept: signed tokens cannot be stolen or replayed
optionC: Reject: a stolen or stale token stays valid for a week
optionD: Reject: the JWT format cannot hold an exp of 7 days
correctAnswerText: Reject: a stolen or stale token stays valid for a week
explanation: An access token cannot be revoked, so its lifetime is how long a theft or a removed role lasts. Short access tokens with revocable, rotated refresh tokens limit that window.

prompt: In .NET 8, MapIdentityApi issues bearer tokens. Another service must validate them too. What is the sound judgement?
optionA: They are opaque to other services; issue JWTs for that case
optionB: They are standard JWTs, so any service can validate them
optionC: They must be decrypted with the user's password hash
optionD: They work anywhere once both services share a database
correctAnswerText: They are opaque to other services; issue JWTs for that case
explanation: MapIdentityApi's tokens are protected by ASP.NET Core Data Protection, not JWTs, and are meant for the same app. Cross-service validation needs a JWT with a shared or public key.

prompt: Several services must validate tokens that one auth service issues. Why is RS256 often preferred over HS256 here?
optionA: HS256 tokens cannot be validated by ASP.NET Core 8
optionB: RS256 tokens are encrypted, so their claims stay hidden
optionC: RS256 tokens never expire, so refresh is not needed
optionD: Validators need only the public key, so they cannot sign
correctAnswerText: Validators need only the public key, so they cannot sign
explanation: With HS256 every validator holds the signing secret and could mint tokens. With RS256 only the issuer has the private key; others validate with the public key.

prompt: To save database lookups, a developer wants the student's phone number and Aadhaar number in the JWT. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Accept: HTTPS removes the payload before the browser sees it
optionB: Reject: the payload is readable by anyone holding the token
optionC: Reject: JWT payloads can hold only numeric claim values
optionD: Accept: the signature keeps the claims private from others
correctAnswerText: Reject: the payload is readable by anyone holding the token
explanation: Signing protects integrity, not confidentiality. Keep claims to ids and roles, and fetch personal data from the database when it is needed.

prompt: A developer stores refresh tokens in plain text because "the database is private". What is the sound judgement?
optionA: Fine: the tokens expire, so plain text adds no risk
optionB: Fine: refresh tokens are useless without the password
optionC: Encrypt them with the JWT signing key instead
optionD: Hash them: a leaked table would hand over live sessions
correctAnswerText: Hash them: a leaked table would hand over live sessions
explanation: Backups, logs and SQL injection leak tables. A refresh token works like a password for weeks, so store only its hash and compare hashes.

prompt: Should a team rely on remembering [Authorize] on each new controller, or set a fallback policy requiring authentication?
optionA: Attributes: fallback policies cannot coexist with roles
optionB: Attributes: a fallback policy slows every request down
optionC: Fallback: a forgotten attribute fails closed, not open
optionD: Neither: protect the API with CORS rules instead
correctAnswerText: Fallback: a forgotten attribute fails closed, not open
explanation: With a fallback policy, forgetting an attribute makes the endpoint require login instead of exposing it. Public endpoints become an explicit [AllowAnonymous] list you can review.

prompt: Lockout after failed logins lets an attacker lock a victim out on purpose. What is the balanced judgement?
optionA: Keep lockout short and add rate limiting; guessing is the bigger risk
optionB: Replace lockout by telling users which emails exist
optionC: Turn lockout off, since denial of service is worse than guessing
optionD: Lock accounts permanently so attackers give up guessing them
correctAnswerText: Keep lockout short and add rate limiting; guessing is the bigger risk
explanation: Unlimited guessing breaks weak passwords. A short lockout with rate limiting by IP slows guessing while limiting the damage of deliberate lockouts.

prompt: On which TCP port does a default SQL Server instance listen unless it is reconfigured?
explanation: A default SQL Server instance listens on TCP 1433. 3306 is MySQL, 5432 is PostgreSQL and 1521 is the Oracle listener.

prompt: Which SQL Server column type stores variable-length Unicode text such as names in Telugu or Hindi?
optionA: NVARCHAR(n)
optionB: VARCHAR(n)
optionC: VARBINARY(n)
optionD: CHAR(n)
correctAnswerText: NVARCHAR(n)
explanation: NVARCHAR stores Unicode (UTF-16), so any script survives. VARCHAR and CHAR use a code page under the usual collations, and VARBINARY holds raw bytes, not text.

prompt: Which function returns the last IDENTITY value generated by an insert in the current scope and session?
optionA: NEWID()
optionB: ROWCOUNT_BIG()
optionC: SCOPE_IDENTITY()
optionD: IDENT_CURRENT()
correctAnswerText: SCOPE_IDENTITY()
explanation: SCOPE_IDENTITY() is limited to the current session and scope, so a trigger's insert cannot change it. IDENT_CURRENT reads a table's last value from any session; NEWID makes a GUID.

prompt: Which T-SQL keyword returns only the first five rows of an ordered SELECT?
optionA: TOP (5)
optionB: ROWNUM <= 5
optionC: LIMIT 5
optionD: FIRST 5 ONLY
correctAnswerText: TOP (5)
explanation: T-SQL has no LIMIT: SELECT TOP (5) ... ORDER BY ... takes the first five. LIMIT is MySQL and PostgreSQL, ROWNUM is Oracle.

prompt: Which SQL Server edition is free, has every Enterprise feature, and is licensed only for development and testing?
optionA: Developer
optionB: Web
optionC: Standard
optionD: Express
correctAnswerText: Developer
explanation: Developer edition is the full feature set for non-production use. Express is free for production but capped (10 GB per database); Standard and Web are paid.

prompt: Which type is the recommended choice for a new column that stores a date and a time of day?
optionA: TIMESTAMP
optionB: DATETIME2
optionC: SMALLDATETIME
optionD: DATE
correctAnswerText: DATETIME2
explanation: DATETIME2 has a wider range and finer precision than DATETIME and SMALLDATETIME. TIMESTAMP in SQL Server is a synonym for rowversion, not a date, and DATE has no time part.

prompt: Which SQL Server type holds a GUID, the value a C# Guid maps to?
optionA: UNIQUEIDENTIFIER
optionB: SQL_VARIANT
optionC: ROWVERSION
optionD: BIGINT
correctAnswerText: UNIQUEIDENTIFIER
explanation: UNIQUEIDENTIFIER is the 16-byte GUID type, read with GetGuid in ADO.NET. ROWVERSION is an auto-changing binary stamp, and BIGINT is a 64-bit integer.

prompt: In SQL Server, which principal is created at the server level and is what a client authenticates as?
optionA: A schema
optionB: A database role
optionC: A login
optionD: A database user
correctAnswerText: A login
explanation: A login lets you connect to the server. A database user, mapped to that login, is what gets permissions inside one database; schemas and roles are database-level too.

prompt: What is the name of the default schema that tables land in when no schema is given?
optionA: master
optionB: public
optionC: sys
optionD: dbo
correctAnswerText: dbo
explanation: dbo is the default schema for most users, which is why tables are written dbo.Orders. public is PostgreSQL's default; master is a system database and sys holds catalog views.

prompt: Which T-SQL construct catches a runtime error so the code can roll back and re-raise it?
optionA: BEGIN TRY ... END TRY BEGIN CATCH ... END CATCH
optionB: TRY { ... } CATCH (SqlException ex) { ... }
optionC: ON ERROR GOTO handler ... RESUME NEXT
optionD: BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN ... END
correctAnswerText: BEGIN TRY ... END TRY BEGIN CATCH ... END CATCH
explanation: T-SQL uses BEGIN TRY / BEGIN CATCH blocks, with THROW; inside CATCH to re-raise. The braces form is C#, ON ERROR is VB, and EXCEPTION WHEN is PL/SQL.

prompt: Why is a Unicode literal written N'సాయి' rather than 'సాయి' when inserting into an NVARCHAR column?
optionA: The N prefix makes the insert faster but changes nothing that is stored
optionB: The N prefix is needed only when the column also has a UNIQUE constraint
optionC: Without N the literal is VARCHAR and is converted through a code page first
optionD: Without N the value is stored in upper case by the default collation
correctAnswerText: Without N the literal is VARCHAR and is converted through a code page first
explanation: A plain '...' literal is VARCHAR, so characters outside the database code page become ? before they ever reach the NVARCHAR column. N'...' keeps the literal Unicode.

prompt: How do ISNULL and COALESCE differ in T-SQL?
optionA: ISNULL is standard SQL and COALESCE is a T-SQL extension with two arguments
optionB: COALESCE returns the last non-NULL argument, ISNULL returns the first one
optionC: ISNULL takes two arguments and keeps the first one's type; COALESCE takes many
optionD: They are identical; COALESCE is simply an older spelling of the same function
correctAnswerText: ISNULL takes two arguments and keeps the first one's type; COALESCE takes many
explanation: ISNULL(a, b) has exactly two arguments and the result has a's type, so a VARCHAR(3) first argument truncates the fallback. COALESCE is standard SQL, takes any number, and returns the first non-NULL.

prompt: Why can a SQL Server table have only one clustered index?
optionA: A second clustered index would need a second copy of the whole server
optionB: The clustered index is the table itself, its rows stored in key order
optionC: SQL Server limits every table to one index of any kind for licensing
optionD: The clustered index is only a hint, and two hints would contradict
correctAnswerText: The clustered index is the table itself, its rows stored in key order
explanation: The leaf level of a clustered index holds the data rows, sorted by the key, and rows can be physically ordered only one way. Nonclustered indexes are separate structures, and a table may have many.

prompt: Why should an invoice amount be stored as DECIMAL(12,2) rather than FLOAT?
optionA: FLOAT columns cannot be added together with SUM in a GROUP BY query
optionB: DECIMAL takes fewer bytes than FLOAT for every possible amount stored
optionC: DECIMAL is exact, while FLOAT cannot hold values like 0.10 exactly
optionD: FLOAT always rounds amounts to whole rupees when the row is inserted
correctAnswerText: DECIMAL is exact, while FLOAT cannot hold values like 0.10 exactly
explanation: FLOAT is binary floating point, so decimal fractions are approximated and totals drift by tiny amounts. DECIMAL(p,s) stores the exact digits, which is what money needs.

prompt: Why does OFFSET ... FETCH need an ORDER BY, ideally ending in a unique column?
optionA: ORDER BY makes SQL Server cache the result so later pages are free
optionB: The unique column is needed only so the query can use a clustered index
optionC: OFFSET counts from the end of the table unless ORDER BY is present
optionD: Without a fixed, total order the rows on each page are not guaranteed
correctAnswerText: Without a fixed, total order the rows on each page are not guaranteed
explanation: OFFSET-FETCH is part of the ORDER BY clause, and a set has no order of its own. If the order has ties, rows can move between pages; adding Id makes the order total.

prompt: What is a common table expression (WITH name AS (...)) in SQL Server?
optionA: A named subquery that exists only for the one statement that follows it
optionB: A temporary table written to tempdb that lasts until the session ends
optionC: A stored view saved in the database and shared by every later query
optionD: A cached result that SQL Server reuses across batches for a few minutes
correctAnswerText: A named subquery that exists only for the one statement that follows it
explanation: A CTE names a query for the single statement after it; nothing is stored. A temp table (#t) persists for the session, and a view is a saved object.

prompt: An Orders table uses INT IDENTITY(1,1) and the ids run 1, 2, 3, 5. What is the usual explanation?
optionA: Row 4 was moved to another page and now shows a different id in SELECT
optionB: The column was declared wrong; IDENTITY guarantees gapless numbering
optionC: An insert that took 4 failed or rolled back, and IDENTITY never reuses values
optionD: IDENTITY skips any number already used as a value in another table
correctAnswerText: An insert that took 4 failed or rolled back, and IDENTITY never reuses values
explanation: IDENTITY values are handed out outside the transaction, so a rolled-back or failed insert burns its number; a service restart can also skip a cached block. Never rely on gapless ids.

prompt: Scores are 90, 90 and 80. What numbers do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK give, ordered by score descending?
optionA: All three give 1,1,2, since equal scores tie
optionB: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3; RANK 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK 1,1,2
optionC: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3; RANK 1,1,2; DENSE_RANK 1,1,3
optionD: ROW_NUMBER 1,1,3; RANK 1,1,2; DENSE_RANK 1,2,3
correctAnswerText: ROW_NUMBER 1,2,3; RANK 1,1,3; DENSE_RANK 1,1,2
explanation: ROW_NUMBER always counts 1,2,3 (ties broken arbitrarily). RANK gives ties the same number and then leaves a gap; DENSE_RANK gives ties the same number with no gap.

prompt: A plain (non-indexed) view dbo.ActiveCustomers is queried after new customers are inserted. Why does it show them?
optionA: The view holds a snapshot, but SELECT falls back to the table on a miss
optionB: Views copy their rows nightly, and inserts trigger an extra early refresh
optionC: SQL Server rebuilds every view automatically after each INSERT statement
optionD: The view stores only its query, which runs against the tables each time
correctAnswerText: The view stores only its query, which runs against the tables each time
explanation: A normal view is a saved SELECT; querying it runs that SELECT against the base tables, so it is always current. Only an indexed view materialises its rows.

prompt: What does SET NOCOUNT ON at the top of a stored procedure change?
optionA: It stops @@ROWCOUNT from being set, so row checks no longer work at all
optionB: It turns off the transaction log for the statements in the procedure
optionC: It stops the "rows affected" messages being sent back for each statement
optionD: It makes COUNT(*) inside the procedure return zero for faster queries
correctAnswerText: It stops the "rows affected" messages being sent back for each statement
explanation: NOCOUNT suppresses the DONE_IN_PROC "(n rows affected)" messages, saving round-trip chatter. @@ROWCOUNT is still set, so IF @@ROWCOUNT = 0 keeps working.

prompt: A course catalogue shows 25 courses per page, newest first. Which clause returns page 4?
optionA: ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC OFFSET 4 ROWS FETCH NEXT 25 ROWS ONLY
optionB: ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC OFFSET 75 ROWS FETCH NEXT 25 ROWS ONLY
optionC: ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC LIMIT 25 OFFSET 75
optionD: ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC OFFSET 100 ROWS FETCH NEXT 25 ROWS ONLY
correctAnswerText: ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC, Id DESC OFFSET 75 ROWS FETCH NEXT 25 ROWS ONLY
explanation: Page 4 skips three full pages: (4 − 1) × 25 = 75 rows. OFFSET counts rows, not pages, and LIMIT is not T-SQL.

prompt: For each student you need only their most recent exam attempt from dbo.Attempts (StudentId, TakenAt, Score). Which query does it?
optionA: SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY StudentId ORDER BY TakenAt DESC) AS rn FROM dbo.Attempts AS a WHERE a.rn = 1 ORDER BY StudentId
optionB: WITH a AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY StudentId ORDER BY TakenAt DESC) AS rn FROM dbo.Attempts) SELECT * FROM a WHERE rn = 1
optionC: SELECT TOP (1) WITH TIES * FROM dbo.Attempts ORDER BY ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY StudentId, TakenAt DESC) DESC
optionD: SELECT StudentId, MAX(TakenAt) AS TakenAt, MAX(Score) AS Score FROM dbo.Attempts GROUP BY StudentId ORDER BY StudentId
correctAnswerText: WITH a AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY StudentId ORDER BY TakenAt DESC) AS rn FROM dbo.Attempts) SELECT * FROM a WHERE rn = 1
explanation: Number each student's attempts newest first in a CTE, then keep rn = 1. A window function cannot be filtered in the same SELECT's WHERE, and the GROUP BY version pairs the latest date with the best score, which may come from a different attempt.

prompt: Fees in dbo.Courses must never be negative, and the rule needs a name you can drop later. Which statement adds it?
optionA: ALTER TABLE dbo.Courses ADD CONSTRAINT CK_Courses_Fee CHECK (Fee >= 0);
optionB: CREATE RULE CK_Courses_Fee ON dbo.Courses FOR Fee VALUES (>= 0);
optionC: ALTER TABLE dbo.Courses ADD CHECK CK_Courses_Fee WHERE Fee >= 0;
optionD: ALTER TABLE dbo.Courses ALTER COLUMN Fee DECIMAL(10,2) UNSIGNED;
correctAnswerText: ALTER TABLE dbo.Courses ADD CONSTRAINT CK_Courses_Fee CHECK (Fee >= 0);
explanation: ADD CONSTRAINT name CHECK (condition) creates a named check that every insert and update must pass. SQL Server has no UNSIGNED, and the other two are not valid syntax.

prompt: The hot query is WHERE BranchId = @b AND PaidOn >= @from AND PaidOn < @to on dbo.Payments. Which index serves it best?
optionA: CREATE INDEX IX_Payments_Branch ON dbo.Payments (BranchId) INCLUDE (Amount);
optionB: Two separate indexes, one on BranchId and one on PaidOn, of the same table
optionC: CREATE INDEX IX_Payments_PaidOn_Branch ON dbo.Payments (PaidOn, BranchId);
optionD: CREATE INDEX IX_Payments_Branch_PaidOn ON dbo.Payments (BranchId, PaidOn);
correctAnswerText: CREATE INDEX IX_Payments_Branch_PaidOn ON dbo.Payments (BranchId, PaidOn);
explanation: Equality column first, range column last: the seek goes straight to BranchId = @b and reads one contiguous PaidOn range. With PaidOn first, the branch filter applies across the whole date range.

prompt: Which INSERT returns the new IDENTITY Id of dbo.Batches as a result set in the same statement?
optionA: INSERT INTO dbo.Batches (Name) OUTPUT INSERTED.Id VALUES (N'Batch 9');
optionB: INSERT INTO dbo.Batches (Name) VALUES (N'Batch 9') RETURNING Id;
optionC: INSERT INTO dbo.Batches (Name) VALUES (N'Batch 9'); SELECT MAX(Id);
optionD: INSERT INTO dbo.Batches (Name) SELECT IDENTITY() VALUES (N'Batch 9');
correctAnswerText: INSERT INTO dbo.Batches (Name) OUTPUT INSERTED.Id VALUES (N'Batch 9');
explanation: OUTPUT INSERTED.Id sits between the column list and VALUES and returns the generated value. RETURNING is PostgreSQL, and MAX(Id) races with other sessions.

prompt: You need each day's sales with a running total since the start of the month, from dbo.DailySales (SaleDate, Amount). Which expression gives the running total?
optionA: SUM(Amount) OVER (PARTITION BY SaleDate ORDER BY SaleDate)
optionB: LAG(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY SaleDate) + Amount
optionC: SUM(Amount) GROUP BY SaleDate ORDER BY SaleDate ASC
optionD: SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY SaleDate ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
correctAnswerText: SUM(Amount) OVER (ORDER BY SaleDate ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING)
explanation: An ordered window from the first row to the current one accumulates. PARTITION BY SaleDate sums each day alone, and LAG adds only the previous day.

prompt: PlacedAt is a DATETIME2 holding UTC. Which predicate finds orders from the last 7 days and can still seek an index on PlacedAt?
optionA: WHERE PlacedAt >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, SYSUTCDATETIME())
optionB: WHERE CONVERT(DATE, PlacedAt) >= GETDATE() - 7
optionC: WHERE DATEADD(DAY, 7, PlacedAt) >= SYSUTCDATETIME()
optionD: WHERE DATEDIFF(DAY, PlacedAt, SYSUTCDATETIME()) <= 7
correctAnswerText: WHERE PlacedAt >= DATEADD(DAY, -7, SYSUTCDATETIME())
explanation: Leaving the column bare and doing the arithmetic on the constant side keeps the predicate SARGable. Wrapping PlacedAt in DATEDIFF, DATEADD or CONVERT forces each row to be computed.

prompt: A new column must record when each row was created, in UTC, without the application sending it. Which definition fits?
optionA: CreatedAt DATETIME2 NOT NULL CONSTRAINT DF_T_CreatedAt DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME()
optionB: CreatedAt DATETIME2 NOT NULL CONSTRAINT DF_T_CreatedAt CHECK (SYSUTCDATETIME())
optionC: CreatedAt TIMESTAMP NOT NULL, which SQL Server fills with the current UTC time
optionD: CreatedAt DATETIME2 NULL IDENTITY(SYSUTCDATETIME(), 1) for automatic stamping
correctAnswerText: CreatedAt DATETIME2 NOT NULL CONSTRAINT DF_T_CreatedAt DEFAULT SYSUTCDATETIME()
explanation: A named DEFAULT constraint fills the column when an insert omits it. TIMESTAMP is rowversion (binary, not a date), CHECK validates rather than fills, and IDENTITY is numeric only.

prompt: SELECT Status, Amount FROM dbo.Invoices WHERE StudentId = @s runs constantly. An index on StudentId exists, and the plan shows a Key Lookup per row. What change removes the lookups?
optionA: Make StudentId the clustered key and drop the primary key on Id
optionB: Recreate the index on (StudentId) with INCLUDE (Status, Amount)
optionC: Rebuild the existing index on StudentId with a higher fill factor
optionD: Add a separate nonclustered index on (Status, Amount) to the table
correctAnswerText: Recreate the index on (StudentId) with INCLUDE (Status, Amount)
explanation: Included columns are stored at the index's leaf, so the query is answered from the index alone. An index on Status, Amount cannot seek on StudentId, and a rebuild changes nothing about the columns.

prompt: dbo.EnrolStudent has parameters @StudentId INT, @CourseId INT and @EnrolmentId INT OUTPUT. Which call puts the new id into @Id?
optionA: DECLARE @Id INT; EXEC @Id OUTPUT = dbo.EnrolStudent @StudentId = 4, @CourseId = 9;
optionB: DECLARE @Id INT; SET @Id = EXEC dbo.EnrolStudent @StudentId = 4, @CourseId = 9;
optionC: DECLARE @Id INT; EXEC dbo.EnrolStudent @StudentId = 4, @CourseId = 9, @EnrolmentId = @Id;
optionD: DECLARE @Id INT; EXEC dbo.EnrolStudent @StudentId = 4, @CourseId = 9, @EnrolmentId = @Id OUTPUT;
correctAnswerText: DECLARE @Id INT; EXEC dbo.EnrolStudent @StudentId = 4, @CourseId = 9, @EnrolmentId = @Id OUTPUT;
explanation: An OUTPUT parameter is copied back only when the caller also writes OUTPUT after the argument. EXEC cannot be assigned with SET, and EXEC @x = proc captures only the RETURN status.

prompt: dbo.Admissions has an index on AdmittedOn, yet WHERE YEAR(AdmittedOn) = 2025 AND MONTH(AdmittedOn) = 6 shows an Index Scan of every row. Why?
optionA: Functions wrap the column, so SQL Server cannot seek to a key range
optionB: YEAR and MONTH are slow functions that always disable every index
optionC: Two conditions on one column always force SQL Server into a scan
optionD: The index is stale and needs a rebuild before it can be sought
correctAnswerText: Functions wrap the column, so SQL Server cannot seek to a key range
explanation: The index is sorted by AdmittedOn, not by YEAR(AdmittedOn), so a computed predicate must check each row. AdmittedOn >= '2025-06-01' AND AdmittedOn < '2025-07-01' can seek.

prompt: A database uses the default SQL_Latin1_General_CP1_CI_AS collation and a column is NVARCHAR(100). A script runs INSERT INTO dbo.Patients (Name) VALUES ('लक्ष्मी'); and SELECT shows ?????. What went wrong?
optionA: NVARCHAR cannot hold Devanagari, so the column must be changed to VARCHAR
optionB: The collation is case-insensitive, which replaces non-Latin letters with ?
optionC: SSMS cannot display Hindi, though the stored value is correct in the table
optionD: The literal lacks the N prefix, so it became VARCHAR and lost the characters
correctAnswerText: The literal lacks the N prefix, so it became VARCHAR and lost the characters
explanation: Without N the literal is VARCHAR in the database code page, which has no Devanagari, so each character became ? before the insert. The column is fine; write N'लक्ष्मी'.

prompt: INSERT INTO dbo.Enrolments (StudentId, CourseId) VALUES (42, 7); fails with Msg 547 naming FK_Enrolments_Students. What is the cause?
optionA: Course 7 has reached a maximum size enforced by the foreign key
optionB: There is no row in dbo.Students with Id 42 for the key to reference
optionC: The Students table is locked by a report running at the same time
optionD: StudentId 42 already has an enrolment, and keys must be unique
correctAnswerText: There is no row in dbo.Students with Id 42 for the key to reference
explanation: Msg 547 on an insert means the referenced parent row does not exist — here student 42. A duplicate would break a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY constraint instead, with a different message.

prompt: SELECT Batch, Passed * 100.0 / Appeared FROM dbo.Results; fails with "Divide by zero error encountered." for one batch. Which rewrite fixes it?
optionA: CAST(Passed AS FLOAT) * 100 / Appeared, as floats divide by zero safely
optionB: Passed * 100.0 / Appeared WITH (NOLOCK) to skip rows that cannot divide
optionC: Passed * 100.0 / ISNULL(Appeared, 0), so that zero becomes a safe value
optionD: Passed * 100.0 / NULLIF(Appeared, 0), giving NULL where nobody appeared
correctAnswerText: Passed * 100.0 / NULLIF(Appeared, 0), giving NULL where nobody appeared
explanation: NULLIF(Appeared, 0) turns a zero divisor into NULL, and anything divided by NULL is NULL. ISNULL only replaces NULL, and FLOAT division by zero still raises the error in T-SQL.

prompt: After INSERT INTO dbo.Orders ..., code reads SELECT @@IDENTITY and gets an id that belongs to dbo.OrderAudit. An AFTER INSERT trigger on Orders writes to OrderAudit. Why?
optionA: The trigger runs first, so the Orders insert never received an identity
optionB: @@IDENTITY always returns the identity of the table with the highest id
optionC: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity in the session, including the trigger's
optionD: OrderAudit and Orders share one IDENTITY sequence across the database
correctAnswerText: @@IDENTITY returns the last identity in the session, including the trigger's
explanation: @@IDENTITY is session-wide across scopes, so the trigger's insert overwrites it. SCOPE_IDENTITY() or OUTPUT INSERTED.Id returns the Orders value.

prompt: RollNo is VARCHAR(10); most values are digits, a few are 'TBD'. SELECT * FROM dbo.Students WHERE RollNo = 1024; fails converting 'TBD' to int. Why?
optionA: The error comes from an index on RollNo that stores only integers
optionB: VARCHAR columns cannot be compared with anything but N'' literals
optionC: The literal 1024 is too long to fit in a VARCHAR(10) comparison
optionD: INT outranks VARCHAR, so SQL Server converts every RollNo value to int
correctAnswerText: INT outranks VARCHAR, so SQL Server converts every RollNo value to int
explanation: With mixed types, the lower-precedence side is converted: the column becomes INT, and 'TBD' cannot. Compare with a string, RollNo = '1024', which also keeps the index usable.

optionA: The payment is committed while the balance is left unchanged
optionB: The transaction stays open forever because COMMIT is skipped
optionC: Both are committed, because a CHECK error is only a warning
optionD: Nothing is committed, as the CHECK failure rolls everything back
correctAnswerText: The payment is committed while the balance is left unchanged
explanation: With XACT_ABORT OFF a constraint violation ends only that statement; the batch reaches COMMIT and keeps the insert. SET XACT_ABORT ON plus TRY...CATCH makes the pair all-or-nothing.

prompt: Email is VARCHAR(200) with an index. The query is fast in SSMS but slow from the C# app, whose plan shows CONVERT_IMPLICIT on Email and an Index Scan. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The app sends the parameter as NVARCHAR, so the VARCHAR column is converted
optionB: SSMS caches the rows in memory, while the application reads from the disk
optionC: The app connects as a different login, and logins each have their own index
optionD: The app uses async calls, and async queries cannot use indexes in SQL Server
correctAnswerText: The app sends the parameter as NVARCHAR, so the VARCHAR column is converted
explanation: A C# string parameter defaults to NVARCHAR. Comparing it with a VARCHAR column converts the column side, which under a SQL collation prevents a seek. Send it as VarChar with the right size.

prompt: An AFTER DELETE trigger on dbo.Students does DECLARE @Id INT; SELECT @Id = Id FROM deleted; INSERT dbo.Archive (StudentId) VALUES (@Id);. A cleanup deletes 30 students in one statement. What ends up in Archive?
optionA: Thirty rows, but only if the delete statement ran inside a transaction
optionB: Thirty rows, because a DELETE trigger fires once for every row it removes
optionC: One row, because the trigger fires once per statement with all 30 in deleted
optionD: No rows, because AFTER triggers cannot read the deleted pseudo-table at all
correctAnswerText: One row, because the trigger fires once per statement with all 30 in deleted
explanation: SQL Server triggers are statement-level. Assigning a variable from deleted keeps one arbitrary row. INSERT dbo.Archive (StudentId) SELECT Id FROM deleted archives all thirty.

prompt: A list pages with ORDER BY City OFFSET @skip ROWS FETCH NEXT 20 ROWS ONLY. Users report one student appearing on page 1 and page 2, and another on neither. Why?
optionA: Many rows share a City, so their order is not fixed between the two queries
optionB: City must be indexed for OFFSET to work, otherwise the rows are random
optionC: OFFSET skips rows by physical page, which changes when data is compressed
optionD: FETCH NEXT reads 20 rows plus one extra row to check for a following page
correctAnswerText: Many rows share a City, so their order is not fixed between the two queries
explanation: Rows that tie on City may come back in a different order each time, so a row can cross a page boundary. ORDER BY City, Id makes the order total and the pages stable.

prompt: A team wants Orders keyed by Id UNIQUEIDENTIFIER DEFAULT NEWID() as the clustered primary key, so ids are hard to guess in URLs. Your judgement?
optionA: Good, but use NVARCHAR(36) for the GUID, so it can be read in query results
optionB: Good choice: random GUIDs spread the inserts and make the table faster to fill
optionC: Drop the primary key entirely and leave the table as a heap with the GUID column
optionD: Cluster on an INT or BIGINT IDENTITY; keep the GUID as a unique nonclustered key
correctAnswerText: Cluster on an INT or BIGINT IDENTITY; keep the GUID as a unique nonclustered key
explanation: A random clustered key inserts all over the B-tree, splitting pages and fragmenting the table, and widens every nonclustered index. A narrow, increasing clustered key plus a unique GUID column gives both.

prompt: An attendance table takes thousands of inserts a minute. A developer proposes an index on every one of its twelve columns "so any query is fast". Your judgement?
optionA: Index only for the queries that run; each index slows every insert
optionB: Refuse all indexes: an insert-heavy table should always be a heap
optionC: Agree, as long as every index is clustered so the lookups are free
optionD: Agree: indexes cost nothing on writes, only some space on the disk
correctAnswerText: Index only for the queries that run; each index slows every insert
explanation: Each index is maintained on every insert, update and delete of its columns, and costs disk and memory. Build indexes for the real query workload, checked against the plans.

prompt: Which split of responsibilities between a .NET API and SQL Server is the soundest default?
optionA: Every rule in C#, with no constraints so the API can manage the data
optionB: Every rule in stored procedures, the API only passing parameters on
optionC: Rules in triggers, since triggers run on every write from any client
optionD: Business rules in tested C#; integrity in keys, constraints and FKs
correctAnswerText: Business rules in tested C#; integrity in keys, constraints and FKs
explanation: C# rules are unit-tested, reviewed and released with the app, and app servers are cheap to scale. Constraints still guard the data against every client, including a bug or a manual script.

prompt: Should FK_Invoices_Students be ON DELETE CASCADE, so deleting a student also deletes their invoices?
optionA: No: use ON DELETE SET DEFAULT so the invoices move to student number 1
optionB: Yes, but only if the invoices table also has a clustered index on StudentId
optionC: No: keep financial records; refuse the delete or deactivate the student
optionD: Yes: cascading keeps the database small, and invoices are easy to rebuild
correctAnswerText: No: keep financial records; refuse the delete or deactivate the student
explanation: Invoices are records the business must keep; a cascade silently destroys them along with the student. NO ACTION makes the delete fail visibly, and a status flag retires the student.

prompt: A developer wants an AFTER INSERT trigger on dbo.Admissions to call an external SMS service for each new admission. Your judgement?
optionA: Send it from the application after commit; triggers run inside the transaction
optionB: Good: the trigger guarantees an SMS for every admission, whatever the client
optionC: Good, as long as the trigger uses a cursor to send one message per row
optionD: Use an INSTEAD OF trigger, so the SMS goes out before the row is written
correctAnswerText: Send it from the application after commit; triggers run inside the transaction
explanation: A trigger runs inside the inserting transaction: a slow call holds locks, a failure rolls the admission back, and a rollback cannot recall a sent SMS. Do side effects in the app after the commit.

prompt: A team's production API connects to SQL Server as sa "to avoid permission errors". What should they do instead?
optionA: A dedicated login mapped to a user with only the rights the app needs
optionB: Keep sa but put its password in appsettings.json rather than the code
optionC: Use sa only for writes and a second sysadmin login for all the reads
optionD: Grant the db_owner role to the public role so every login has access
correctAnswerText: A dedicated login mapped to a user with only the rights the app needs
explanation: sa is sysadmin: an injection bug in the app could then drop databases or read every one on the server. A least-privilege login limits the damage to what the app may legitimately do.

prompt: An app serving users in India and the Gulf stores PaidAt with GETDATE() on a server in IST. What is the better design?
optionA: Keep GETDATE(), since IST is the zone most of the users happen to live in
optionB: Store UTC with SYSUTCDATETIME() in DATETIME2 and convert when displaying
optionC: Store the time as NVARCHAR text, with the time zone name written after it
optionD: Store each time in the user's local zone, so every report reads naturally
correctAnswerText: Store UTC with SYSUTCDATETIME() in DATETIME2 and convert when displaying
explanation: UTC is unambiguous and survives a server move. Local server time ties the data to one machine's settings, and text dates cannot be compared or indexed as dates.

prompt: A schema declares every text column, including Email and PinCode, as NVARCHAR(MAX) "to never truncate". Your judgement?
optionA: Size columns to the data; a MAX column cannot be an index key column
optionB: Good: MAX columns are stored and indexed exactly like NVARCHAR(50)
optionC: Use CHAR(4000) instead, so every value has a predictable fixed width
optionD: Good, but change them to TEXT, which is the modern long-text type
correctAnswerText: Size columns to the data; a MAX column cannot be an index key column
explanation: NVARCHAR(MAX) cannot be an index key, so Email cannot get the unique index it needs, and a size limit is itself validation. TEXT is deprecated, and CHAR(4000) pads every value.

prompt: A report query went from 80 ms to 9 seconds after a data load. Which first step is best?
optionA: Move the database to a bigger server before looking at the query at all
optionB: Capture the actual plan; compare estimated with actual rows and read IO
optionC: Add every index the missing-index hint lists, then run the report again
optionD: Restart the SQL Server service, since slow queries mean a memory leak
correctAnswerText: Capture the actual plan; compare estimated with actual rows and read IO
explanation: Measure before changing anything: the plan shows scans, lookups and wrong estimates (stale statistics after a load are common), and SET STATISTICS IO gives a number to compare. Hints are suggestions, not orders.

prompt: A coaching institute expects its database to reach about 40 GB in two years and plans to run production on Developer edition. Your judgement?
optionA: Use Express instead, which has no size limit once it runs on a Linux server
optionB: Fine, as long as the server never has more than a hundred users connected
optionC: Fine: Developer edition is free and has every feature, so it suits production
optionD: Not allowed: Developer is non-production; Express caps at 10 GB, so buy Standard
correctAnswerText: Not allowed: Developer is non-production; Express caps at 10 GB, so buy Standard
explanation: Developer edition is licensed for development and test only. Express is free for production but limits each database to 10 GB, so a 40 GB database needs a paid edition such as Standard.

prompt: Which reference stays pointing at cell B2 whichever direction the formula is copied?
optionD: B2
explanation: The $ before the column and before the row lock both, so the reference never moves. $B2 locks only the column and B$2 only the row; B2 moves with every copy.

prompt: Which Excel 2021/365 lookup function matches exactly by default, can return a column to the left of the key, and takes an if_not_found argument?
optionA: LOOKUP
optionB: XLOOKUP
optionC: VLOOKUP
optionD: HLOOKUP
correctAnswerText: XLOOKUP
explanation: XLOOKUP(lookup, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found]) is exact by default and takes separate arrays, so direction does not matter. VLOOKUP looks only rightwards and defaults to approximate match.

prompt: What does FALSE as the fourth argument of VLOOKUP ask for?
optionA: An exact match of the lookup value
optionB: A case-sensitive match of the value
optionC: A match searched from the bottom up
optionD: The approximate, nearest-below match
correctAnswerText: An exact match of the lookup value
explanation: range_lookup FALSE (or 0) means exact match, returning #N/A if the key is absent. Omitting it means TRUE, an approximate match that needs a sorted first column.

prompt: Which shortcut turns a range of records into an Excel Table that grows with new rows?
optionA: Ctrl+T
optionB: Ctrl+G
optionC: Ctrl+Shift+L
optionD: Alt+=
correctAnswerText: Ctrl+T
explanation: Ctrl+T creates a Table with structured references that expand as rows are added. Ctrl+Shift+L only toggles filter arrows; Alt+= inserts AutoSum; Ctrl+G opens Go To.

prompt: Which error does an exact-match lookup return when the key is not in the lookup range?
optionA: #REF!
optionB: #VALUE!
optionC: #N/A
optionD: #NAME?
correctAnswerText: #N/A
explanation: #N/A means "value not available". #REF! is an invalid reference, #VALUE! a wrong type in a calculation, and #NAME? an unknown function or name.

prompt: In SUMIFS, which argument comes first?
optionA: The number of criteria pairs
optionB: The first criterion value
optionC: The range to be summed
optionD: The first criteria range
correctAnswerText: The range to be summed
explanation: SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range1, criteria1, ...) puts the sum range first. The older SUMIF puts it last, which is a common source of mixed-up formulas.

prompt: Which error does a dynamic-array formula such as =UNIQUE(A2:A100) show when cells it needs to fill are occupied?
optionA: #N/A
optionB: #NUM!
optionC: #SPILL!
optionD: #CALC!
correctAnswerText: #SPILL!
explanation: Dynamic arrays (Excel 2021/365) spill into neighbouring cells; anything in the way gives #SPILL!. #CALC! comes from, for example, FILTER finding nothing with no if_empty argument.

prompt: How does Excel store a date such as 03-Jan-2025?
optionA: As three numbers: day, month, year
optionB: As seconds since 1 January 1970
optionC: As a serial number counting days
optionD: As text in the chosen format
correctAnswerText: As a serial number counting days
explanation: On the default 1900 system, 1-Jan-1900 is 1 and 03-Jan-2025 is 45660; the date format only controls display. That is why dates can be subtracted and why a text date cannot.

prompt: Which function removes leading and trailing spaces and reduces repeated inner spaces to one?
optionA: SUBSTITUTE
optionB: PROPER
optionC: CLEAN
optionD: TRIM
correctAnswerText: TRIM
explanation: TRIM fixes the spaces that make "Pune " differ from "Pune". CLEAN strips non-printing characters, PROPER changes case, and SUBSTITUTE replaces given text.

prompt: Which Excel 2021/365 function returns the distinct values of a range as a spilled list?
optionA: UNIQUE
optionB: DISTINCT
optionC: FILTER
optionD: SORT
correctAnswerText: UNIQUE
explanation: UNIQUE(range) spills one copy of each value. Excel has no DISTINCT function; FILTER keeps rows meeting a condition and SORT orders them.

prompt: One amount in a column sits on the left of its cell though nobody set the alignment. Why does that matter?
optionA: It is a formula result, which pivots cannot aggregate
optionB: It has a currency format, which SUM rounds to rupees
optionC: It is text that looks like a number, and SUM will skip it
optionD: It is a negative number, which Excel aligns to the left
correctAnswerText: It is text that looks like a number, and SUM will skip it
explanation: By default numbers align right and text left. A left-aligned "amount" is text, which SUM ignores without any error, so the total comes out too low.

prompt: A cell formatted to two decimals shows 2.50 but holds 2.4987. What do formulas that use it see?
optionA: 2.5, because Excel rounds stored values on formatting
optionB: 2, because a formatted number is truncated in formulas
optionC: 2.50, because formulas read what the cell displays
optionD: 2.4987, because a format changes only how a value looks
correctAnswerText: 2.4987, because a format changes only how a value looks
explanation: Number formats change display, not the stored value, so totals of displayed figures can disagree by a rupee. Use ROUND in the formula when the rounded value is what should be used.

prompt: In a multiplication grid, the formula uses $A2 for the row header and B$1 for the column header. Why the mixed references?
optionA: Mixed references are needed whenever a formula multiplies
optionB: The $ signs stop the formula being copied out of the grid
optionC: Mixed references calculate faster than fully absolute ones
optionD: Each keeps the header fixed in one direction while the other moves
correctAnswerText: Each keeps the header fixed in one direction while the other moves
explanation: $A2 keeps column A when copied right but lets the row change going down; B$1 keeps row 1 when copied down but lets the column change. One formula then fills the whole grid.

prompt: Why is wrapping every lookup in IFERROR(..., 0) risky in a revenue sheet?
optionA: IFERROR makes the lookup switch to an approximate match
optionB: IFERROR recalculates the whole workbook on every edit
optionC: It returns text "0", which SUM then refuses to add up
optionD: It turns any error, including a mistyped key, into a believable 0
correctAnswerText: It turns any error, including a mistyped key, into a believable 0
explanation: IFERROR catches every error type, so a broken reference or a key with a trailing space becomes a silent zero. Use IFNA or XLOOKUP's if_not_found for the expected "not found" case and let other errors show.

prompt: Why do merged city headings, blank rows between months and typed "Total" rows break a pivot table?
optionA: A pivot ignores rows whose city is written only once
optionB: A pivot cannot read cells that carry any formatting at all
optionC: A pivot treats each row as one record with its own values
optionD: Merged cells make a pivot sort the cities alphabetically
correctAnswerText: A pivot treats each row as one record with its own values
explanation: Pivots, filters and SUMIFS need one record per row with every field filled. Merged headings leave rows with no city, blank rows split the range, and total rows are counted as extra orders.

prompt: A Revenue field dropped into a pivot's Values shows "Count of Revenue". What does that tell you?
optionA: The pivot was built from an Excel Table
optionB: At least one Revenue cell is text or blank
optionC: Revenue is stored with too many decimals
optionD: Revenue holds a few negative amounts
correctAnswerText: At least one Revenue cell is text or blank
explanation: Excel picks Sum only when every cell in the field is a number. Count is the first sign of text-numbers or blanks; find them, fix them and set Value Field Settings to Sum.

prompt: Why does INDEX-MATCH survive a column inserted inside the lookup table when VLOOKUP(key, A:F, 4, FALSE) breaks?
optionA: INDEX-MATCH always searches the whole sheet for the value
optionB: INDEX-MATCH recalculates whenever a column is added to the table
optionC: VLOOKUP cannot read beyond the fourth column of any range
optionD: MATCH finds a position and INDEX reads a named column, not a count
correctAnswerText: MATCH finds a position and INDEX reads a named column, not a count
explanation: VLOOKUP's 4 is a hard-coded column count, so an inserted column shifts the result to the wrong field. INDEX(F:F, MATCH(key, A:A, 0)) refers to the return column itself, and can also look left.

prompt: What does an approximate-match VLOOKUP (TRUE) return, and what does it require?
optionA: The smallest key above the value; keys sorted ascending
optionB: The first key that contains the value; keys sorted descending
optionC: The nearest key above or below; keys in any order
optionD: The largest key not above the value; keys sorted ascending
correctAnswerText: The largest key not above the value; keys sorted ascending
explanation: Approximate match walks a sorted first column and returns the row of the largest key less than or equal to the lookup value — right for slabs and bands, wrong for IDs.

prompt: Which situation most clearly says the analysis should move from a worksheet to a database query?
optionA: A one-off what-if on next quarter's price with Goal Seek
optionB: A 400-row product list that needs one lookup column added
optionC: Several million transaction rows joined monthly to two other tables
optionD: A chart of twelve monthly totals for a team presentation
correctAnswerText: Several million transaction rows joined monthly to two other tables
explanation: A worksheet holds 1,048,576 rows, and repeated joins of large tables are what SQL is built for. The other tasks are small, one-off or presentational — exactly what a spreadsheet does well.

prompt: Why build a pivot on an Excel Table (tblSales) rather than on the range A1:E500?
optionA: After a refresh the pivot includes rows added to the Table
optionB: A range source makes the pivot read only the first 500 rows ever
optionC: A Table source lets a pivot count distinct values by default
optionD: A pivot on a Table refreshes every time a cell is edited
correctAnswerText: After a refresh the pivot includes rows added to the Table
explanation: A Table grows as rows are added, so the pivot's source grows with it; a fixed range leaves new rows out. Either way the pivot still needs Refresh — it does not update by itself.

prompt:
A1:C6
City   | Category | Amount
Pune   | Grocery  | 1200
Mumbai | Grocery  | 800
Pune   | Fashion  | 2500
Pune   | Grocery  | 600
Mumbai | Fashion  | 1500

What does =COUNTIFS(A2:A6,"Pune",C2:C6,">=1000") return?
explanation: Pune rows have 1200, 2500 and 600; two of them are at least 1000. COUNTIFS counts rows meeting every condition.

prompt:
A1:C6
City   | Category | Amount
Pune   | Grocery  | 1200
Mumbai | Grocery  | 800
Pune   | Fashion  | 2500
Pune   | Grocery  | 600
Mumbai | Fashion  | 1500

What does =SUMIFS(C2:C6,A2:A6,"Pune",B2:B6,"Grocery") return?
explanation: Rows that are both Pune and Grocery are 1200 and 600, summing to 1800. 4300 is all Pune, and 2000 all Grocery.

prompt:
A1:C6
City   | Category | Amount
Pune   | Grocery  | 1200
Mumbai | Grocery  | 800
Pune   | Fashion  | 2500
Pune   | Grocery  | 600
Mumbai | Fashion  | 1500

What does =AVERAGEIFS(C2:C6,B2:B6,"Fashion") return?
explanation: Fashion rows are 2500 and 1500; their average is 4000 / 2 = 2000. 1320 is the average of all five amounts.

prompt: D2 holds =$B2*C$1. It is copied to E3 (one column right, one row down). What formula does E3 hold?
explanation: $B keeps column B and the row moves 2 to 3; C$1 keeps row 1 and the column moves C to D. So E3 has =$B3*D$1.

prompt:
A discount slab table (F2:G5) is sorted ascending:
From | Rate
0    | 0%
500  | 5%
2000 | 10%
5000 | 15%

What does =VLOOKUP(1999,F2:G5,2,TRUE) return?
optionB: #N/A
explanation: Approximate match returns the largest key not above 1999, which is 500, so the rate is 5%. 2000 would be the first value to get 10%.

prompt: A2 holds the date 28-Feb-2024 and B2 holds 01-Mar-2024. What does =B2-A2 return, formatted as a number?
optionC: #VALUE!
explanation: Dates are day serial numbers, so subtraction counts days. 2024 is a leap year, so 29 February lies between them: 2 days.

prompt: A2 holds the order code PUN-1042. What does =LEFT(A2,FIND("-",A2)-1) return?
optionA: PU
optionB: PUN
optionC: PUN-
correctAnswerText: PUN
explanation: FIND returns 4, the position of the hyphen, so LEFT takes 3 characters: PUN. In Excel 365, =TEXTBEFORE(A2,"-") gives the same.

prompt: Profit is =Units*(Price-Cost)-Fixed with Units 400, Cost 150 and Fixed 20000. Goal Seek sets Profit to 40000 by changing Price. What price does it find?
In one month a pivot shows North 1,20,000, South 80,000 and West 50,000. With Show Values As > % of Column Total, what does South show?
explanation: The column total is 2,50,000, and 80,000 / 2,50,000 = 0.32, so 32.00%. North shows 48.00% and West 20.00%; the column adds to 100%.

prompt: B2 holds 74. What does =IFS(B2>=80,"A",B2>=60,"B",TRUE,"C") return?
optionA: #N/A
optionB: B
optionC: C
optionD: A
correctAnswerText: B
explanation: IFS returns the result for the first true condition: 74 fails >=80 and passes >=60, so "B". TRUE as the last condition acts as the "otherwise" case. IFS needs Excel 2019 or later.

prompt: =XLOOKUP(B2,tblProducts[ProductID],tblProducts[Price]) gives #N/A for P103, though P103 is plainly in the product list. =B2=F4 (the list cell) returns FALSE. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The keys differ invisibly, such as a trailing space
optionB: The price column is formatted as currency text
optionC: Structured references cannot be used in XLOOKUP
optionD: XLOOKUP needs the product list sorted ascending
correctAnswerText: The keys differ invisibly, such as a trailing space
explanation: Two keys that look equal but compare FALSE differ invisibly: a trailing space from an export, or a number stored as text on one side. LEN reveals it; TRIM or VALUE fixes it.

prompt: =SUM(D2:D400) is below the billing system. =COUNT(D2:D400) is 381 and =COUNTA(D2:D400) is 399. What should you check first?
optionA: Whether 18 cells have the wrong decimal format
optionB: Whether 18 amounts are stored as text
optionC: Whether 18 amounts are negative refunds
optionD: Whether 18 rows are hidden by a filter
correctAnswerText: Whether 18 amounts are stored as text
explanation: COUNT counts numbers and COUNTA counts non-empty cells, so 18 cells hold something that is not a number — text-numbers, which SUM skips silently. SUM includes hidden rows anyway.

prompt: The January total from =SUM(D2:D300) is exactly twice what finance reports. What is the likely cause?
optionA: Excel counts merged cells twice when it sums
optionB: Typed subtotal rows sit inside the summed range
optionC: Each amount is formatted with two decimal places
optionD: The range includes the column header by mistake
correctAnswerText: Typed subtotal rows sit inside the summed range
explanation: Subtotal rows after each city or month add every order a second time. Take totals out of the data (or use SUBTOTAL(9, ...) both for the subtotals and the total, which skips other SUBTOTAL cells).

prompt: E2 holds =D2*F1 to apply the GST rate in F1. E2 is right, but E3 down to E200 all show 0. What is the fix?
optionA: Make it =D2*$F$1 so the rate cell stays fixed
optionB: Fill column F with the rate down to row 200
optionC: Format column E as a number with two decimals
optionD: Make it =$D$2*F1 so the amount cell stays fixed
correctAnswerText: Make it =D2*$F$1 so the rate cell stays fixed
explanation: F1 is relative, so copying down turns it into F2, F3 and so on — empty cells, hence 0. Locking it with $F$1 (F4) or naming it GST_Rate fixes every row. Filling F would hide the bug.

prompt: An order for P109, which is not in the catalogue, shows a price of ₹899 — another product's price. The formula is =VLOOKUP(B2,F2:I5,4). What is wrong?
optionA: The catalogue range should begin at row 1, not at row 2
optionB: Column 4 is outside F2:I5, so Excel wraps round to column 1
optionC: VLOOKUP returns the last row of the range when keys are text
optionD: Without FALSE it does an approximate match and returns a near key
correctAnswerText: Without FALSE it does an approximate match and returns a near key
explanation: The missing fourth argument defaults to TRUE, approximate match, which returns the nearest key below instead of #N/A. Add FALSE or use XLOOKUP, which is exact by default.

prompt: Fifty rows were added below a sales range yesterday; after Refresh All the pivot totals are unchanged. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The new rows were sorted, which pivots ignore until regrouped
optionB: The pivot's source is a fixed range that ends above the new rows
optionC: Pivots read new rows only after the workbook is reopened
optionD: Refresh All updates only the pivot charts, not the pivot tables
correctAnswerText: The pivot's source is a fixed range that ends above the new rows
explanation: A fixed source such as A1:E500 does not grow. Change Data Source to an Excel Table so future rows are included, then refresh.

prompt: A pivot shows months in the order Apr, Aug, Dec, Feb, Jan... The month field was built with =TEXT(OrderDate,"mmm"). Why, and what is the fix?
optionA: The pivot sorts by revenue; switch the sort to manual order
optionB: TEXT returns numbers; wrap it in VALUE to sort them properly
optionC: The dates are wrong; re-enter them in the day-month-year form
optionD: The months are text sorting A–Z; group the real date by month
correctAnswerText: The months are text sorting A–Z; group the real date by month
explanation: TEXT returns text, and text sorts alphabetically. Grouping the real date field by months (and years) keeps calendar order, as does a month-start date formatted as mmm.

prompt: =UNIQUE(tblSales[Region]) shows #SPILL! even though the cells below look empty. The formula sits in a column of tblSales itself. What is the cause?
