prompt: Which PyTorch loss is the usual choice for predicting delivery time in minutes?
optionA: nn.CrossEntropyLoss
optionB: nn.BCEWithLogitsLoss
optionC: nn.NLLLoss
optionD: nn.MSELoss
correctAnswerText: nn.MSELoss
explanation: Delivery time is a continuous number, a regression target: mean squared error (or L1 / Huber) fits. The other three are classification losses.

prompt: What does a dropout layer do during training?
optionA: Randomly zeroes a fraction of activations on each forward pass
optionB: Stops training when the validation loss starts to go back up
optionC: Removes the training rows that the model finds hardest to fit
optionD: Deletes the weights that are closest to zero after each epoch
correctAnswerText: Randomly zeroes a fraction of activations on each forward pass
explanation: Dropout zeroes each activation with probability p during training, so no unit can rely on any other. Stopping on validation loss is early stopping.

prompt: What does early stopping do?
optionA: Stops when the training loss reaches zero and saves the final weights
optionB: Stops when validation loss stops improving and keeps the best weights
optionC: Stops each epoch early, after half of the batches, to save on compute
optionD: Stops after a fixed number of epochs chosen before the training began
correctAnswerText: Stops when validation loss stops improving and keeps the best weights
explanation: It tracks validation loss each epoch, waits a patience number of epochs without improvement, then stops and restores the best state seen.

prompt: What does calling model.eval() change?
optionA: Dropout turns off and batch norm uses its running statistics
optionB: Gradients stop being computed for any tensor inside the model
optionC: The model moves from the GPU to the CPU for faster predictions
optionD: All weights are frozen so that no later training can change them
correctAnswerText: Dropout turns off and batch norm uses its running statistics
explanation: eval() switches layer behaviour for inference. It does not freeze weights or stop gradient tracking — that is torch.no_grad() — and it does not move the model.

prompt: What does weight decay do to a network's weights during training?
optionA: Rounds them to fewer decimal places to save memory
optionB: Shrinks them a little towards zero at every step
optionC: Lowers the learning rate a little after every step
optionD: Removes the smallest of them at the end of each epoch
correctAnswerText: Shrinks them a little towards zero at every step
explanation: Weight decay is an L2-style penalty: each step pulls every weight slightly towards zero, which discourages large weights and overfitting. Lowering the learning rate over time is a schedule.

prompt: What does a PyTorch model's state_dict() contain?
optionA: The Python source code of the model class and its methods
optionB: Its learned tensors (weights, biases, buffers) keyed by name
optionC: The full training history of losses for every past epoch
optionD: A copy of the training data that the model was fitted on
correctAnswerText: Its learned tensors (weights, biases, buffers) keyed by name
explanation: The state_dict maps parameter and buffer names to tensors. To load it you rebuild the model class in code and call load_state_dict.

prompt: What is data augmentation when training an image model?
optionA: Generating labels for unlabelled images with the current model
optionB: Random label-preserving changes to training images each epoch
optionC: Adding test images to the training set to get more examples
optionD: Raising the image resolution so that the model sees more detail
correctAnswerText: Random label-preserving changes to training images each epoch
explanation: Flips, crops, small rotations and colour jitter show the network a slightly different version of each training image, which reduces overfitting. It is applied to training data only.

prompt: Why does a standard PyTorch loop call optimizer.zero_grad() every step?
optionA: It frees the training batch from memory before the next one
optionB: backward() adds to .grad, so old gradients would pile up
optionC: It resets the learning rate to its starting value each step
optionD: step() refuses to run unless the gradients were just cleared
correctAnswerText: backward() adds to .grad, so old gradients would pile up
explanation: Gradients accumulate by design, which allows deliberate accumulation over several small batches. A normal loop must clear them, or each step pushes with the sum of all previous gradients.

prompt: Why can a learning rate that is too large make the loss bounce around or blow up?
optionA: Each step overshoots the minimum and lands somewhere worse
optionB: A large rate makes the model memorise the training data
optionC: A large rate makes the batches smaller, so gradients are noisy
optionD: A large rate stops backward() from reaching the first layers
correctAnswerText: Each step overshoots the minimum and lands somewhere worse
explanation: With too big a step the weights jump past the low point, sometimes further up the other side, so the loss oscillates or diverges to nan. Too small a rate converges, just slowly.

prompt: What is true of the gradient computed from a mini-batch of 16 rows?
optionA: It is exact, since every batch is drawn from the same dataset
optionB: It is an unbiased but noisy estimate of the full-data gradient
optionC: It is biased towards zero, so small batches always learn slowly
optionD: It points in a random direction unrelated to the full gradient
correctAnswerText: It is an unbiased but noisy estimate of the full-data gradient
explanation: Averaged over many batches, mini-batch gradients match the full gradient; their spread falls roughly with the square root of the batch size. Some noise even helps escape flat regions.

prompt: Why is early stopping driven by a validation split rather than by the test set?
optionA: Any choice made on the test set makes its score optimistic
optionB: The test set cannot be passed through a model in eval mode
optionC: Validation loss falls faster, so training finishes sooner
optionD: The test set is too small for the loss to be computed on it
correctAnswerText: Any choice made on the test set makes its score optimistic
explanation: Picking the epoch, learning rate or architecture by test score tunes the model to those rows. The validation split absorbs those choices, and the test set is scored once at the end.

prompt: What does the Adam optimiser add on top of plain SGD?
optionA: Automatic early stopping when the training loss stops falling
optionB: A second backward pass that checks every gradient is correct
optionC: Momentum and a per-parameter step size from past gradients
optionD: A fixed learning rate that is the same for every single weight
correctAnswerText: Momentum and a per-parameter step size from past gradients
explanation: Adam keeps running averages of gradients (momentum) and of squared gradients, and scales each parameter's step by them. That makes it far less sensitive to the learning rate than SGD.

prompt: Why should numeric inputs be standardised before training a network?
optionA: A huge input makes a huge gradient for its weights, so one rate cannot suit all
optionB: It turns the features into integers, which train faster on most kinds of GPUs
optionC: Standardising removes outliers, which networks are unable to learn from at all
optionD: Networks can only read values between 0 and 1, and anything else is clipped
correctAnswerText: A huge input makes a huge gradient for its weights, so one rate cannot suit all
explanation: The gradient for a first-layer weight is proportional to its input. Income in rupees (~40,000) next to a count (~3) gives steps thousands of times too big for one and tiny for the other. Fit the scaler on training rows only.

prompt: Why is a pretrained model fine-tuned with a learning rate 10 to 100 times smaller than one trained from scratch?
optionA: Pretrained weights have no gradients except in the head
optionB: Small learning rates are needed to fit larger batch sizes
optionC: Large steps would overwrite the useful pretrained weights
optionD: A small rate lets the tokenizer or image pipeline adapt
correctAnswerText: Large steps would overwrite the useful pretrained weights
explanation: The pretrained weights already encode useful features; fine-tuning should nudge them toward the task. A big step moves them far from that start and throws away the benefit of pretraining.

prompt: Why is a pretrained backbone often frozen while a new classification head is trained first?
optionA: The random head's large early gradients would damage pretrained features
optionB: Frozen layers train faster, so they converge before the head is added
optionC: Freezing removes the need to use the preprocessing the model expects
optionD: PyTorch cannot compute gradients for pretrained layers until later
correctAnswerText: The random head's large early gradients would damage pretrained features
explanation: A fresh head starts random with large errors. Training it first, then unfreezing the top of the backbone at a much smaller learning rate, protects what pretraining learned.

prompt: Why wrap evaluation in torch.no_grad() as well as calling model.eval()?
optionA: no_grad skips building the backward graph, saving memory and time
optionB: no_grad converts the outputs to NumPy arrays for the metric code
optionC: no_grad switches dropout off, which eval() on its own does not do
optionD: no_grad stops the weights from being changed by the optimiser later
correctAnswerText: no_grad skips building the backward graph, saving memory and time
explanation: eval() changes layer behaviour (dropout, batch norm); no_grad stops autograd recording the computation. They do different jobs, and evaluation wants both.

prompt: Why fix the random seeds before comparing two training settings?
optionA: Otherwise a difference may come from initialisation and shuffling
optionB: PyTorch refuses to train twice in one session without a set seed
optionC: Fixed seeds make every network reach the same final loss as others
optionD: Seeds control the learning rate, which must match for a fair test
correctAnswerText: Otherwise a difference may come from initialisation and shuffling
explanation: Weight initialisation, data shuffling and dropout are random, and they move results by small amounts. Fixing seeds (and ideally running several) separates a real effect from luck.

prompt: A training set has 25,000 rows, the DataLoader uses batch_size=64 (drop_last=False), and training runs 12 epochs. How many weight updates happen?
explanation: 25,000 / 64 = 390.6, and the partial last batch counts: 391 steps per epoch; 391 × 12 = 4,692. 4,680 drops the partial batch; 391 is one epoch.

prompt: A single weight w = 1.0 has loss (2w − 3)². After one plain SGD step with learning rate 0.1, what is w?
explanation: dL/dw = 2(2w − 3) × 2 = 4(2w − 3) = −4 at w = 1. w ← 1 − 0.1 × (−4) = 1.4, moving towards the minimum at 1.5. 0.6 steps up the gradient instead of down.

prompt: A 3-class model outputs logits [2.0, 0.0, −1.0] and the true class is index 1. What is nn.CrossEntropyLoss for this example, to two decimals?
explanation: Softmax gives [0.844, 0.114, 0.042]; the loss is −ln(0.114) = 2.17. 0.17 would be the loss if the true class were index 0; 0.11 is the probability itself, not its negative log.

prompt: Roughly what cross-entropy loss should an untrained, freshly initialised 10-class classifier show on its first batch?
optionA: About 10, one per class
optionB: About 2.30, which is ln 10
optionC: About 0.10, which is 1 / 10
optionD: About 0.69, which is ln 2
correctAnswerText: About 2.30, which is ln 10
explanation: Small random weights give near-uniform probabilities of 1/10, so the loss is −ln(0.1) = 2.303. A first loss far above that points to a bug: unscaled inputs, wrong labels or a broken head.

prompt: Validation loss by epoch: 1: 0.62, 2: 0.55, 3: 0.51, 4: 0.50, 5: 0.52, 6: 0.53, 7: 0.49, 8: 0.50, 9: 0.51, 10: 0.52. With patience 3, when does training stop and which weights are restored?
optionA: Stops after epoch 6; restores epoch 4
optionB: Stops after epoch 10; restores epoch 10
optionC: Stops after epoch 7; restores epoch 4
optionD: Stops after epoch 10; restores epoch 7
correctAnswerText: Stops after epoch 10; restores epoch 7
explanation: Epochs 5 and 6 are worse than 0.50 but only two in a row, so training continues; epoch 7 sets a new best (0.49) and resets the count. Epochs 8–10 make three without improvement: stop, reload epoch 7.

prompt: PyTorch uses inverted dropout. With nn.Dropout(p=0.25) in training mode, what happens to the activations that are kept?
optionA: They are left exactly as they were
optionB: They are multiplied by 0.25 instead
optionC: They are multiplied by 1/0.75 ≈ 1.33
optionD: They are multiplied by 0.75 to match
correctAnswerText: They are multiplied by 1/0.75 ≈ 1.33
explanation: Kept units are scaled by 1/(1 − p) during training so the expected value is unchanged; at eval time nothing is dropped or scaled. Multiplying by 0.75 would shrink the layer's output.

prompt: A model outputs logits of shape (32, 3) for a 3-class problem. Which target tensor should go into nn.CrossEntropyLoss?
optionA: Shape (32,), float32 class numbers 1 to 3
optionB: Shape (32, 1), float32 class numbers 1 to 3
optionC: Shape (32,), int64 class indices from 0 to 2
optionD: Shape (3,), int64 counts of each class in it
correctAnswerText: Shape (32,), int64 class indices from 0 to 2
explanation: CrossEntropyLoss takes one integer class index per row, numbered 0…k−1 (or a (32, 3) float tensor of class probabilities). Float indices raise a dtype error and labels 1–3 put 3 out of bounds.

prompt: Only 32 images fit in GPU memory, but the recipe calls for an effective batch of 128. How should gradient accumulation be set up?
optionA: Call zero_grad() before each micro-batch, then step() once after all 4
optionB: Backward on 4 micro-batches, each loss divided by 4, then one step
optionC: Multiply the learning rate by 4 and keep stepping after every 32 images
optionD: Run 4 optimizer.step() calls per micro-batch, each with lr divided by 4
correctAnswerText: Backward on 4 micro-batches, each loss divided by 4, then one step
explanation: Gradients add up across backward() calls, so 4 backward passes on 32 images, each loss scaled by 1/4, give the mean gradient of 128 images; then one step() and one zero_grad(). Zeroing between them throws the accumulation away.

prompt: A new head on a pretrained ResNet trains with AdamW at 1e-3. You now unfreeze the last backbone block in its own parameter group. Which learning rate fits that group?
optionA: About 1e-5 to 1e-4
optionB: About 1e-2, ten times higher
optionC: About 1.0, to move it quickly
optionD: Exactly 1e-3, the same as the head
correctAnswerText: About 1e-5 to 1e-4
explanation: Pretrained weights get a rate 10–100 times smaller than the fresh head, so 1e-5 to 1e-4 here. A higher rate would wipe out the features you are fine-tuning.

prompt: torch.optim.AdamW with lr=1e-3 and weight_decay=0.01 applies its decay as w ← w × (1 − lr × weight_decay). By how much does that decay alone shrink a weight of 2.0 in one step?
optionA: By 0.2
explanation: 2.0 × 1e-3 × 0.01 = 0.00002 per step. The decay is scaled by the learning rate, which is why 0.01 at lr 1e-3 is gentle and only adds up over thousands of steps.

prompt:
The loss falls for a few steps, then wanders upwards and bounces, even at a small learning rate:
for xb, yb in train_dl:
    loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
    loss.backward()
    opt.step()
What is the bug?
optionA: model.train() is missing, so the weights are frozen for every step
optionB: opt.step() must come before loss.backward(), or the update is stale
optionC: The loss is computed on the batch, but it must be on the whole data
optionD: No opt.zero_grad(), so each step uses the sum of all past gradients
correctAnswerText: No opt.zero_grad(), so each step uses the sum of all past gradients
explanation: backward() adds into .grad, so without zero_grad the gradient grows every step and the updates get ever larger. Call opt.zero_grad() at the start of each step.

prompt: A 3-class model ends in nn.Softmax(dim=1) and is trained with nn.CrossEntropyLoss. Accuracy looks fine, but the training loss never goes below about 0.55. Why?
optionA: Three classes set a floor of ln 3 on any cross-entropy loss value
optionB: CrossEntropyLoss needs class weights whenever there are 3 classes
optionC: Softmax is applied twice, so the loss cannot fall below −ln(e/(e+2))
optionD: The learning rate is too low for the loss to pass the class balance
correctAnswerText: Softmax is applied twice, so the loss cannot fall below −ln(e/(e+2))
explanation: CrossEntropyLoss applies log-softmax to its input. Feeding it probabilities in [0, 1] means even a perfect [1, 0, 0] becomes e/(e + 2) = 0.576, a loss of 0.551. Return logits from the model.

prompt: A 5-class rating model (ratings 1–5) raises "IndexError: Target 5 is out of bounds." on the first batch. Its last layer is nn.Linear(64, 5). What is wrong?
optionA: The last layer needs 6 outputs, one for each label value
optionB: The labels run 1–5, but class indices must run 0–4
optionC: The batch has more rows than the number of the classes
optionD: The labels are float, but CrossEntropyLoss needs int64
correctAnswerText: The labels run 1–5, but class indices must run 0–4
explanation: Five logits are indexed 0–4, so label 5 has no logit. Subtract 1 (or encode with LabelEncoder) and keep the mapping. Adding a sixth output would create a class that never appears.

prompt: A demand-forecast network's training MSE stalls at 41.0; the target's variance is 40.6. The log shows "Using a target size (torch.Size([32])) that is different to the input size (torch.Size([32, 1]))". Diagnosis?
optionA: The targets need scaling, since MSE cannot fall below the variance
optionB: The warning is harmless here; the loss is high because daily demand is noisy
optionC: The model is underfitting and needs more hidden units to beat the mean
optionD: Broadcasting compares all 32 predictions with all 32 targets; squeeze the output
correctAnswerText: Broadcasting compares all 32 predictions with all 32 targets; squeeze the output
explanation: (32, 1) minus (32,) broadcasts to (32, 32), so each prediction is scored against every target and the best the model can do is predict the mean — an MSE equal to the variance. Squeeze the output to (32,).

prompt: With dropout p = 0.5, the running training loss is 0.41 while validation loss (in eval mode) is 0.36 every epoch. The split is random from one source. What is the most likely explanation?
optionA: The model is underfitting and needs a larger network to close the gap
optionB: The validation set has leaked into training, so it is scored too kindly
optionC: model.eval() was forgotten, so validation used the training weights
optionD: Dropout is active only while training, so the training loss is inflated
correctAnswerText: Dropout is active only while training, so the training loss is inflated
explanation: In training mode half the units are dropped, which handicaps the model; in eval mode the full network runs. A validation loss a little below training loss is normal with dropout.

prompt:
Four runs of one binary classifier, training loss per epoch:
A: 0.693 0.693 0.693 0.693
B: 0.61 0.58 nan nan
C: 0.52 0.31 0.12 0.03 (validation 0.50 0.53 0.71 1.05)
D: 0.66 0.61 0.57 0.53 (validation 0.66 0.62 0.58 0.54)
Which reading is correct?
optionA: A not learning, B overfitting, C diverged, D underfitting for good
optionB: A not learning, B diverged, C overfitting, D healthy but unfinished
optionC: A converged, B diverged, C healthy and finished, D overfitting badly
optionD: A diverged, B overfitting, C not learning yet, D finished and healthy
correctAnswerText: A not learning, B diverged, C overfitting, D healthy but unfinished
explanation: A is stuck at ln 2 (50/50 on everything); B went to nan (lower the rate, check inputs, clip); C's validation rises as training falls; D's curves fall together, so train longer.

prompt: The notebook's best validation loss was at epoch 6; the job ran 80 epochs and saved model.state_dict() at the end. In production the model is clearly worse than the notebook suggested. Why?
optionA: The model was saved in eval mode, which switches off its dropout
optionB: The saved weights are from epoch 80, long after overfitting began
optionC: Production data always scores lower than validation data does
optionD: state_dict() loses the batch-norm statistics, so the model degrades
correctAnswerText: The saved weights are from epoch 80, long after overfitting began
explanation: The notebook's number came from epoch 6, but the file holds epoch 80. Keep a copy of the best state during training (early stopping) and save that one.

prompt: On 60,000 rows, raising the batch size from 32 to 2,048 at the same learning rate and 5 epochs made validation loss clearly worse. What is the main reason?
optionA: Each epoch fell from 1,875 steps to 30, so far fewer updates were made
optionB: Large batches always overfit, because each step sees more of the data
optionC: The DataLoader cannot shuffle batches that large, so order effects arise
optionD: Large batches give biased gradients, so the model learns the wrong thing
correctAnswerText: Each epoch fell from 1,875 steps to 30, so far fewer updates were made
explanation: 60,000 / 32 = 1,875 steps per epoch, against ⌈60,000 / 2,048⌉ = 30. Large batches need a higher learning rate or more epochs to make the same progress.

prompt: A network takes loan amount in rupees (up to 50 lakh) and applicant age in years. With plain SGD at 1e-3, the loss jumps to 10³⁰ in two steps. What should be fixed first?
optionA: Add dropout, since a loss of that size is a sign of overfitting
optionB: Standardise the inputs, with a scaler fitted on training rows only
optionC: Switch to sigmoid hidden units, which keep every activation small
optionD: Train for more epochs, since the loss settles after a warm-up phase
correctAnswerText: Standardise the inputs, with a scaler fitted on training rows only
explanation: Gradients for the loan-amount weights are proportional to values in the lakhs, so one step at 1e-3 is enormous. Standardising puts features on similar scales; also check for inf or NaN in the data.

prompt: A frozen ResNet with a logistic probe scores 0.95 on validation. The team then unfreezes the whole backbone with a new random head and trains everything at lr 1e-2 from the start; validation drops to 0.71. Why?
optionA: The random head's gradients and a high rate wrecked the pretrained features
optionB: Training more parameters needs more epochs before accuracy recovers
optionC: The probe overfit, and 0.71 is the honest figure for this image dataset
optionD: Unfreezing always lowers accuracy, so pretrained layers must stay frozen
correctAnswerText: The random head's gradients and a high rate wrecked the pretrained features
explanation: Train the head first with the backbone frozen, then unfreeze the top block(s) at 1e-5 to 1e-4. Fine-tuning done that way usually matches or beats the probe; done at 1e-2 it erases what pretraining learned.

prompt: A 76,000-parameter network memorises 450 tabular training rows: training loss reaches 0, validation loss climbs from epoch 4. Which plan is the soundest response?
optionA: More epochs at a lower learning rate until validation turns down
optionB: Early stopping and a smaller net, judged against a logistic baseline
optionC: Drop the validation split and train on all 450 rows instead
optionD: Double the width, since a bigger network generalises better
correctAnswerText: Early stopping and a smaller net, judged against a logistic baseline
explanation: Early stopping does most of the work, dropout and weight decay help at the margin, and a smaller network has less to memorise. With so little tabular data, a simple regularised model may well win outright.

prompt: For a new small network on a fresh problem, which optimiser setting is the most sensible starting point?
optionA: Plain SGD at 5.0, since bigger steps reach the minimum first
optionB: AdamW at 1.0, since adaptive optimisers ignore the rate
optionC: Plain SGD at 1e-6, since small steps can never diverge
optionD: AdamW at about 1e-3, then adjust by reading the curves
correctAnswerText: AdamW at about 1e-3, then adjust by reading the curves
explanation: AdamW at 1e-3 trains most small networks with no tuning and applies weight decay correctly. Tuned SGD with a schedule can match it, but it needs more search; extreme rates either diverge or barely move.

prompt: Training on a GPU, how should the batch size be chosen?
optionA: Always 1, because single examples give the most exact gradient possible
optionB: Any size; batch size has no effect on the result, only on the speed
optionC: Always the whole dataset, because full batches give the best final model
optionD: A size in the usual 32–256 range that fits, retuning lr and epochs with it
correctAnswerText: A size in the usual 32–256 range that fits, retuning lr and epochs with it
explanation: Batch size trades speed per epoch against the number and noise of steps. Pick one that fits memory, usually 32–256, and adjust the learning rate or epochs when you change it.

prompt: A team tried 40 combinations of learning rate, dropout and width, scored each on the test set, and reports the best test accuracy, 0.912. How should that number be judged?
optionA: Optimistic: the test set chose the model, so a fresh holdout is needed
optionB: Fair, provided all 40 runs used the same random seed throughout
optionC: Pessimistic, since 40 runs means the best model was undertrained
optionD: Fair, since each of the 40 runs was scored on the same untouched test
correctAnswerText: Optimistic: the test set chose the model, so a fresh holdout is needed
explanation: Picking the maximum of 40 noisy test scores builds in luck. Select on a validation split (or cross-validation), then score the chosen model once on a test set that played no part.

prompt: A marketplace has 60 labelled photos per category for 4 new categories. Which training plan is best?
optionA: Probe a frozen pretrained model first, then fine-tune it in two stages
optionB: Fine-tune every layer of a pretrained model at once at a high rate
optionC: Wait until 5,000 photos per category exist before training anything
optionD: Train a small CNN from scratch for many epochs with heavy augmentation
correctAnswerText: Probe a frozen pretrained model first, then fine-tune it in two stages
explanation: A frozen backbone with a linear probe is cheap and often strong on a small set. Fine-tuning then trains the head first and unfreezes the top block at a small rate. From scratch, 60 photos cannot teach a network to see.

prompt: A model reads handwritten digits from scanned bank forms. Which augmentation plan is the most defensible?
optionA: No augmentation at all, since scans of the forms never vary at all
optionB: Every augmentation available, applied to validation images as well
optionC: Small rotations, shifts and contrast changes, on training images only
optionD: Horizontal and vertical flips, since they double the data for free
correctAnswerText: Small rotations, shifts and contrast changes, on training images only
explanation: Augmentations must keep the label true: a flipped 6 can read as a 9, and mirrored digits do not occur on forms. Validation and test images are never augmented, so they reflect real inputs.

prompt: One run with dropout 0.3 gives validation AUC 0.781 and one run with dropout 0.5 gives 0.778. Is that enough to pick 0.3?
optionA: Yes, as long as both runs used the same learning rate and batch size
optionB: No; repeat each over several seeds and compare the gap with the spread
optionC: Yes; any higher validation AUC is a reason to choose that setting
optionD: No; dropout settings can only be compared on the test set itself
correctAnswerText: No; repeat each over several seeds and compare the gap with the spread
explanation: A 0.003 difference is easily within run-to-run variation from initialisation and shuffling. Several seeds per setting show whether the gap is larger than that noise.

prompt: For a long fine-tuning run of a pretrained model, which learning-rate plan is most commonly the better choice?
optionA: A random rate redrawn at each step to escape local minima
optionB: A constant rate of 1e-2 for every step from start to finish
optionC: A rate that rises steadily throughout so the model speeds up
optionD: A short warm-up, then a gradual decay of the learning rate
correctAnswerText: A short warm-up, then a gradual decay of the learning rate
explanation: Warm-up avoids large early updates while the optimiser's statistics settle and the new head is random; decay lets the weights settle later. Schedules from torch.optim.lr_scheduler implement both.

prompt: A 10-hour training job may be killed and must resume exactly where it stopped. What should each checkpoint save?
optionA: Model and optimiser state_dicts, the epoch, and any scheduler state
optionB: Only the latest loss value, so training can restart from that point
optionC: The whole notebook session pickled, including the data loaders too
optionD: Only the model's state_dict, which holds everything needed to resume
correctAnswerText: Model and optimiser state_dicts, the epoch, and any scheduler state
explanation: Adam's moment estimates and the scheduler's position live outside the model; without them the resumed run behaves differently. For inference alone, the model's state_dict is enough.

prompt: Before launching a 6-hour training run of a new model, which cheap check best catches a broken loop or loss?
optionA: Score the untrained model on the test set and record its accuracy
optionB: Train on about 50 rows and confirm the loss can be driven near zero
optionC: Check that the model's parameter count is above one million exactly
optionD: Run the full job at a tiny learning rate to see whether it can finish
correctAnswerText: Train on about 50 rows and confirm the loss can be driven near zero
explanation: A working model and loop can memorise a tiny subset. If the loss will not fall there, the data, labels, loss wiring or optimiser step is broken — found in a minute rather than six hours.

prompt: In self-attention, how is each token's new vector formed?
optionA: By copying the vector of the token just before it
optionB: By averaging the vectors of the whole vocabulary
optionC: As a weighted average of all tokens' value vectors
optionD: From its own vector only, passed through a ReLU
correctAnswerText: As a weighted average of all tokens' value vectors
explanation: Each token's query is compared with every token's key; a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the output is the weighted sum of the values. Every token can draw on every other in one step.

prompt: Where do a token's query, key and value vectors come from?
optionA: Three different tokenizers applied to the same text
optionB: The previous, current and next tokens in the input
optionC: Three learned projections of that token's vector
optionD: Three fixed random vectors that never get trained
correctAnswerText: Three learned projections of that token's vector
explanation: Each token vector x is multiplied by learned matrices W_q, W_k and W_v. Training adjusts these so that query–key matches pick out useful context.

prompt: How does a transformer get information about word order?
optionA: A recurrent layer runs over the sequence beforehand
optionB: The tokenizer sorts tokens so that order is implied
optionC: Position information is added to the token embeddings
optionD: Attention reads tokens strictly from left to right
correctAnswerText: Position information is added to the token embeddings
explanation: Self-attention by itself treats the input as a set. Learned or fixed position vectors, or rotary encodings, give the model order.

prompt: BERT, DistilBERT and MiniLM belong to which transformer family?
optionA: Recurrent models, which read one token at a time in order
optionB: Decoders, which predict each next token from earlier ones
optionC: Encoders, which read the whole input in both directions
optionD: Encoder–decoders, which rewrite an input as a new output
correctAnswerText: Encoders, which read the whole input in both directions
explanation: Encoders are pretrained by filling in masked words with context from both sides, which suits classification, extraction and embeddings. GPT-style models are decoders.

prompt: What is a GPT-style decoder pretrained to do?
optionA: Fill in randomly masked words using both sides
optionB: Translate between two languages given in pairs
optionC: Classify whole documents into a set of topics
optionD: Predict the next token from the tokens before it
correctAnswerText: Predict the next token from the tokens before it
explanation: Decoders see only earlier tokens and learn next-token prediction, which is why they generate text. Filling masked words with context on both sides is the encoder objective.

prompt: What does a subword tokenizer such as BERT's WordPiece do with a word that is not in its vocabulary?
optionA: Splits it into smaller pieces that are in the vocabulary
optionB: Replaces it with a single unknown-word token every time
optionC: Adds it to the vocabulary and gives it a fresh embedding
optionD: Drops it from the input before the model can see it
correctAnswerText: Splits it into smaller pieces that are in the vocabulary
explanation: "refund" becomes "ref" + "##und", romanised Hindi breaks into fragments, and so on. The vocabulary is fixed after pretraining, so rare words cost more tokens rather than being lost.

prompt: What does the attention_mask returned by a Hugging Face tokenizer mark?
optionA: Which positions are real tokens (1) and which are padding (0)
optionB: Which tokens the model should predict during its pretraining
optionC: Which words carry the most meaning in the input sentence
optionD: Which heads of the model are switched on for this batch
correctAnswerText: Which positions are real tokens (1) and which are padding (0)
explanation: Texts in a batch are padded to the same length; the mask tells the model to ignore the padded positions so they do not affect the real tokens.

prompt: What is multi-head attention?
optionA: Attention computed once per layer and shared by every later layer
optionB: Attention applied separately to each of the tokens on its own
optionC: One attention run several times in a row on its own previous output
optionD: Several attentions run in parallel on different learned projections
correctAnswerText: Several attentions run in parallel on different learned projections
explanation: Each head has its own query, key and value projections, so different heads can track different relations; their outputs are concatenated and projected back to the model width.

prompt: In a BERT-style classifier, what is the [CLS] token used for?
optionA: It pads short texts to the length of the longest
optionB: Its final vector is read by the classification head
optionC: It replaces any word missing from the vocabulary
optionD: It marks where each sentence ends inside the input
correctAnswerText: Its final vector is read by the classification head
explanation: The tokenizer adds [CLS] at the start and [SEP] at the end. BERT's sequence-classification head reads the [CLS] position's final hidden state; padding uses [PAD].

prompt: Which transformer family, such as T5 or BART, is built for translation and summarisation?
optionA: Recurrent-only
optionB: Encoder–decoder
optionC: Encoder-only
optionD: Decoder-only
correctAnswerText: Encoder–decoder
explanation: An encoder reads the whole input and a decoder writes the output while attending to it, which fits turning one text into another.

prompt: Why did attention-based transformers replace RNNs and LSTMs for most language work?
optionA: They need far less memory than an RNN on long input sequences
optionB: All positions run in parallel and any two are one step apart
optionC: They can be trained without any labelled or unlabelled data
optionD: They read one token at a time, which preserves word order
correctAnswerText: All positions run in parallel and any two are one step apart
explanation: An RNN must process step by step and squeeze early words through its hidden state. Attention processes the whole sequence at once and connects distant tokens directly — at a quadratic memory cost.

prompt: Why are query–key dot products divided by √d before the softmax?
optionA: Their spread grows with d; scaling stops the softmax saturating
optionB: It halves the memory that the attention matrix takes up on a GPU
optionC: It turns the dot products into cosine similarities between tokens
optionD: It makes each row of attention weights add up to exactly one
correctAnswerText: Their spread grows with d; scaling stops the softmax saturating
explanation: Dot products of d-dimensional vectors have a spread that grows like √d. Unscaled, large d pushes the softmax to nearly one-hot and its gradients vanish. The softmax itself makes rows sum to one.

prompt: Why do transformers have a maximum context length?
optionA: Each token is processed after the one before it, which is slow
optionB: Position vectors cannot represent numbers above a few hundred
optionC: Attention compares every pair of tokens, so cost grows with length²
optionD: The vocabulary has a fixed size, which caps the number of tokens
correctAnswerText: Attention compares every pair of tokens, so cost grows with length²
explanation: n tokens give an n × n score matrix per head per layer, so doubling the length roughly quadruples that compute and memory. The limit is set where that becomes too expensive.

prompt: Why does a decoder mask each token from attending to the tokens after it during training?
optionA: Later tokens are less important, so their weights are dropped
optionB: It is learning to predict the next token, so it must not see it
optionC: Later tokens are padding, and padding must always be ignored
optionD: Attending forwards would double the memory the model needs
correctAnswerText: It is learning to predict the next token, so it must not see it
explanation: With next-token prediction, seeing future tokens would let the model copy the answer. The causal mask makes training match generation, where the future does not exist yet.

prompt: Why must a model and its tokenizer be loaded from the same checkpoint?
optionA: A mismatched tokenizer is much slower, which causes request timeouts
optionB: The tokenizer chooses the device the model will run on at inference
optionC: Each token id points to a row of that model's own embedding table
optionD: Tokenizers hold part of the model weights, which must be complete
correctAnswerText: Each token id points to a row of that model's own embedding table
explanation: Token id 2025 means "not" only in one vocabulary. Another tokenizer sends different ids, so the model reads the wrong embeddings and its output is nonsense even though it runs.

prompt: Why does romanised Hinglish text usually need more tokens per word than English for an English-trained tokenizer?
optionA: Hindi words are always longer than English words, letter for letter
optionB: The tokenizer inserts a language tag before every Hindi word
optionC: The tokenizer translates each Hindi word into several English ones
optionD: Its words are rare in the vocabulary, so they split into pieces
correctAnswerText: Its words are rare in the vocabulary, so they split into pieces
explanation: The subword vocabulary was built mostly from English, so "nahi" becomes "nah" + "##i". More tokens per message means less room in the context and higher cost on per-token APIs.

prompt: You load a pretrained encoder with AutoModelForSequenceClassification and num_labels=5, and the library reports the classifier weights as newly initialised. What does that mean?
optionA: The model is already fine-tuned, and the report is only informational
optionB: The download failed, so the whole model is starting from random weights
optionC: The tokenizer is missing, so the model will not accept any input text
optionD: The pretrained body loaded; a new 5-label head must now be trained
correctAnswerText: The pretrained body loaded; a new 5-label head must now be trained
explanation: The checkpoint has no head for your five labels, so one is created at random. That is expected before fine-tuning; until it is trained, its predictions are random.

prompt: Why is each attention and feed-forward sub-layer in a transformer wrapped in a residual connection and layer normalisation?
optionA: They add word order, which attention alone cannot represent
optionB: They keep gradients and activations stable through deep stacks
optionC: They cut the number of heads needed in each attention layer
optionD: They replace the softmax, which is too slow for long sequences
correctAnswerText: They keep gradients and activations stable through deep stacks
explanation: Residuals give the gradient a direct path through dozens of blocks and layer norm keeps activations in range, which is what lets transformers be stacked 12 to 100+ layers deep.

prompt: Why can a pretrained transformer reach good accuracy from a few thousand labelled tickets when a model trained from scratch cannot?
optionA: Pretraining on vast text already taught it language and paraphrase
optionB: Labels matter less to transformers than to other types of model
optionC: Pretrained models have fewer parameters, so they need less data
optionD: Pretrained models were trained on these same tickets beforehand
correctAnswerText: Pretraining on vast text already taught it language and paraphrase
explanation: Pretraining on huge unlabelled text learns general language; fine-tuning only has to adapt it to the task. From scratch, a few thousand tickets cannot teach a model what words mean.

prompt: A Hugging Face sentiment pipeline returns {"label": "NEGATIVE", "score": 0.98}. What does 0.98 mean?
optionA: The model's own confidence, which says nothing about its accuracy
optionB: That 98% of similar reviews in its training data were negative
optionC: That the review contains 98% negative words by the token count
optionD: A 98% chance that the review really is negative, as measured
correctAnswerText: The model's own confidence, which says nothing about its accuracy
explanation: The score is a softmax output. On text unlike its training data a model can be confidently wrong; only evaluation on labelled samples of your own text tells you how often it is right.

prompt: A query has dot products 3 and 1 with two keys, d = 4, and the two values are 10 and 30. What does scaled dot-product attention output, to one decimal?
explanation: Scale by √4 = 2: scores 1.5 and 0.5. Softmax: 0.731 and 0.269. Output 0.731 × 10 + 0.269 × 30 = 15.4. Without scaling the weights would be 0.881 / 0.119, giving 12.4; 20.0 is a plain average.

prompt: A token's raw query–key scores are 12, 6 and 0, with head dimension d = 36. What scores go into the softmax?
optionB: 4, 2 and 0
optionC: 2, 1 and 0
correctAnswerText: 2, 1 and 0
explanation: Divide by √36 = 6: 2, 1 and 0. Dividing by d itself (36) gives 0.33 and 0.17; leaving them unscaled makes the softmax sharper than intended.

prompt: A model's input grows from 1,024 to 4,096 tokens. How many attention scores does one head in one layer now compute, and how many times more is that?
optionA: 4,096 scores, 4 times more
optionB: 1,048,576 scores, 16 times more
optionC: 16,777,216 scores, 16 times more
optionD: 16,777,216 scores, 4 times more
correctAnswerText: 16,777,216 scores, 16 times more
explanation: Every token scores every token: 4,096² = 16,777,216, against 1,024² = 1,048,576 — a factor of (4,096 / 1,024)² = 16 for a 4× longer input.

prompt: nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=128, num_heads=8) has projections for Q, K, V and the output, each 128 × 128 with a bias. How many parameters is that?
explanation: Four projections × (128 × 128 + 128) = 4 × 16,512 = 66,048. The number of heads does not change it: the 128 dimensions are split into 8 heads of 16. 65,536 forgets the biases.

prompt: A BERT-base layer has model width 768 and 12 attention heads. What is each head's dimension, and what are its scores divided by?
optionA: 64, divided by 64
optionB: 768, divided by 27.7
optionC: 12, divided by 3.5
optionD: 64, divided by 8
correctAnswerText: 64, divided by 8
explanation: The width is split across heads: 768 / 12 = 64 per head, and scores are divided by √64 = 8. Each head works in its own 64-dimensional space.

prompt: Two tickets tokenise to 5 and 8 ids (including [CLS] and [SEP]) and are batched with padding=True. What is the attention_mask row for the first ticket?
explanation: The batch is padded to the longest text, 8. BERT-style tokenizers pad on the right by default, so the first ticket has five real tokens (1) followed by three padding positions (0).

prompt: A decoder reads 4 tokens with a causal mask. How many (query, key) pairs are allowed, counting each token attending to itself?
explanation: Token 1 sees 1 position, token 2 sees 2, token 3 sees 3, token 4 sees 4: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, the lower triangle with the diagonal. 16 is full attention; 6 leaves out the diagonal.

prompt: A logistics firm must tag merchant names, amounts and dates in 10 lakh invoices a month and has 5,000 tagged invoices. Which approach fits best?
optionA: A decoder LLM prompted on every invoice with no labels used
optionB: An encoder–decoder trained to translate invoices into tags
optionC: A small encoder fine-tuned for token classification (NER)
optionD: A word2vec model, which tags entities by word similarity
correctAnswerText: A small encoder fine-tuned for token classification (NER)
explanation: Extraction with plenty of labels at high volume is an encoder task: a token-classification head on a small fine-tuned encoder is accurate and cheap per invoice. Regexes can still handle fixed formats.

prompt: LoRA adds a rank-16 update B·A to a frozen 1,024 × 1,024 weight matrix. How many trainable parameters is that, as a share of the matrix?
explanation: B is 1,024 × 16 and A is 16 × 1,024: 2 × 1,024 × 16 = 32,768 parameters, against 1,024² = 1,048,576 in the full matrix — 3.1%.

prompt: Five token vectors, with no position information added, go through an nn.TransformerEncoderLayer. You then shuffle the five inputs and run it again. What comes out?
optionA: An error, because the layer needs its tokens to be sorted
optionB: The same five output vectors, shuffled in the same way
optionC: Five new vectors, since attention depends on token order
optionD: The same five vectors in their original, unshuffled order
correctAnswerText: The same five output vectors, shuffled in the same way
explanation: Self-attention and the per-token feed-forward layer treat the input as a set, so permuting inputs permutes outputs identically (checked in PyTorch). That is why position information must be added.

prompt: A fine-tuned ticket classifier scored 0.88. After a teammate "only updated the tokenizer" to a newer model's, it scores 0.30, with no errors raised. What happened?
optionA: The new token ids index the wrong rows of the model's embedding table
optionB: Tokenizers must be retrained monthly, and the new one is out of date
optionC: The new tokenizer is slower, so the requests timed out and scored as wrong
optionD: The new tokenizer removes stop words, which the classifier relied on
correctAnswerText: The new token ids index the wrong rows of the model's embedding table
explanation: The model learned one vector per id of its own vocabulary. Save model and tokenizer together (save_pretrained to one directory) and score ten known tickets after every load.

prompt: A service loads what it believes is the team's fine-tuned classifier. The load report lists classifier.weight and classifier.bias as newly initialised, and predictions look random. Diagnosis?
optionA: The load report is normal, and the predictions are just noisy
optionB: It loaded the base model, not the fine-tuned checkpoint
optionC: The GPU ran out of memory, so the head was silently dropped
optionD: The tokenizer was not loaded, so the inputs were all padding
correctAnswerText: It loaded the base model, not the fine-tuned checkpoint
explanation: A fine-tuned checkpoint contains its trained head; a newly initialised head means the weights came from somewhere without one. Point the loader at the saved fine-tuned directory.

prompt: A call-reason classifier tokenises with truncation=True, max_length=128. Accuracy is 0.91 on short calls and 0.68 on long ones, where the customer states the reason near the end. What is the cause?
optionA: Long calls have more stop words, which should have been removed
optionB: Long calls are cut at 128 tokens, so their reason is never seen
optionC: Attention cannot connect tokens more than 64 positions apart
optionD: The learning rate was too high for the longest training examples
correctAnswerText: Long calls are cut at 128 tokens, so their reason is never seen
explanation: Truncation is silent. Check the token-length distribution; raise max_length towards the model's limit, keep head and tail, or split into windows and combine predictions. Report accuracy by length band.

prompt: A student trains a small text-generating decoder. Training loss drops almost to zero within an epoch, but generated text is gibberish. The attention has no causal mask. Why?
optionA: The loss is too low, which always makes a generator repeat itself
optionB: The model is too small, so it memorised the corpus but cannot generalise
optionC: Without a mask the padding is attended, which corrupts the outputs
optionD: Each position could see the next token, so it learned to copy it
correctAnswerText: Each position could see the next token, so it learned to copy it
explanation: Without the mask, predicting token t+1 is trivial because it is in the input. At generation time the future is not there, so the shortcut fails. Add the causal (upper-triangle) mask.

prompt: A ticket scored on its own and the same ticket scored inside a padded batch get different predictions. The code calls model(input_ids=batch["input_ids"]). What is wrong?
optionA: The tokenizer padded on the left, which a BERT model cannot read
optionB: The model is in eval mode, which makes batches nondeterministic
optionC: attention_mask is not passed, so the padding is attended to
optionD: Batching always changes results, so tickets must be scored singly
correctAnswerText: attention_mask is not passed, so the padding is attended to
explanation: Without the mask, real tokens attend to [PAD] positions, and how many there are depends on the batch. Pass attention_mask (or **batch); then the same ticket gives the same output in any batch.

prompt: A pretrained NER pipeline tags "Zepto" and "PhonePe" as PER (person) with scores of 0.8–0.9 in Indian support tickets. What explains this, and what follows?
optionA: The aggregation strategy is wrong; switching it will fix the entity types
optionB: NER models cannot read brand names, so regexes must replace the model
optionC: The scores are high, so the tags are right and the brands are names of people
optionD: It was trained on text without these brands; evaluate and fine-tune on tickets
correctAnswerText: It was trained on text without these brands; evaluate and fine-tune on tickets
explanation: A model trained on news text has not met these names, and its confidence does not reflect that. Measure it on labelled tickets; fine-tune on a few hundred, and use regexes for fixed patterns such as UPI ids.

prompt: On reviews written in wording unseen during training, a fully fine-tuned encoder scores 0.83 while frozen embeddings from the same encoder plus logistic regression score 0.87. Training data had only a few phrasings per class. Most likely reason?
optionA: The fine-tuned model used a smaller vocabulary than before
optionB: Fine-tuning always loses to frozen embeddings on text tasks
optionC: Updating every weight on narrow data fitted those phrasings
optionD: Logistic regression is a stronger head than any transformer
correctAnswerText: Updating every weight on narrow data fitted those phrasings
explanation: With little variety, fine-tuning partly specialises the model to the training wording; the frozen encoder keeps its general sense of paraphrase. With varied data the order often flips — test on held-out wording.

prompt: Fine-tuning DistilBERT with AdamW at lr 1e-2, the loss jumps around and the model ends up predicting the majority class for every review. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: AdamW is unsuitable for transformers, which need plain SGD instead
optionB: The classes are imbalanced, which no learning rate can ever overcome
optionC: A rate far too high for pretrained weights; use about 2e-5 to 5e-5
optionD: Too few epochs; transformers need dozens of epochs to leave the majority
correctAnswerText: A rate far too high for pretrained weights; use about 2e-5 to 5e-5
explanation: Pretrained transformers are fine-tuned at roughly 1e-5 to 1e-4. At 1e-2 the updates destroy the pretrained representation, and the model collapses to the easiest constant answer.

prompt: Training ran fine with max_length=512 and batch 16. After raising max_length to 2,048 at the same batch size, the GPU runs out of memory. Why such a jump?
optionA: Padding tokens use more memory than real tokens, and there are more
optionB: Attention score matrices grow 16-fold when the length grows 4-fold
optionC: A longer max_length adds more layers to the model automatically
optionD: The vocabulary grows with max_length, so the embedding table expands
correctAnswerText: Attention score matrices grow 16-fold when the length grows 4-fold
explanation: Each head stores an n × n score matrix: (2,048 / 512)² = 16 times larger, on top of the activations that grow linearly. Cut the batch size, use gradient accumulation, or a memory-efficient attention kernel.

prompt: A zero-shot NLI classification pipeline with 8 candidate labels takes about 8 times as long per ticket as a fine-tuned encoder of the same size. Why?
optionA: It uses a decoder, which generates each label word by word
optionB: It downloads its model again for each label it has to score
optionC: It runs the model once per (ticket, label) pair, so 8 passes
optionD: It tokenises each ticket 8 times, which dominates the run time
correctAnswerText: It runs the model once per (ticket, label) pair, so 8 passes
explanation: Zero-shot NLI scores "This text is about {label}" as a separate premise–hypothesis pair for each label. It needs no training data, but its cost grows with the number of labels.

prompt: An insurer must sort 3 lakh claim notes a month into 12 reasons. It has 8,000 labelled notes, and the notes may not leave its servers. Which approach is best?
optionA: Send every note to an external LLM API with a carefully written prompt
optionB: Train a large transformer from scratch on the insurer's own claim notes
optionC: Use an encoder–decoder to rewrite each claim note as its reason label
optionD: Fine-tune a small encoder in-house, compared against a TF-IDF baseline
correctAnswerText: Fine-tune a small encoder in-house, compared against a TF-IDF baseline
explanation: Labels and volume favour a fine-tuned small encoder, and the data rule rules out an external API without masking and a contract. A baseline shows whether the encoder earns its cost.

prompt: A team has no labelled tickets and must start routing next week. Later, volume will reach lakhs a day. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Train a transformer from scratch now on the raw, unlabelled tickets alone
optionB: Prompt an LLM now and keep calling it for every ticket at any volume
optionC: Fine-tune a small encoder now, using the ticket text with no labels at all
optionD: Prompt an LLM now, measured on a hand-labelled set; later distil to an encoder
correctAnswerText: Prompt an LLM now, measured on a hand-labelled set; later distil to an encoder
explanation: Prompting needs no training labels but still needs a labelled sample to be evaluated. Its audited labels then train a small encoder that is cheaper and faster at high volume.

prompt: A company needs one large model adapted separately for 15 clients, on a single modest GPU. Why is LoRA a strong choice over full fine-tuning?
optionA: LoRA always gives higher accuracy than full fine-tuning on every task
optionB: Small per-client adapters train in less memory and share one base model
optionC: LoRA retrains the tokenizer for each client, which full tuning cannot
optionD: LoRA needs no labelled examples, so the clients need not provide data
correctAnswerText: Small per-client adapters train in less memory and share one base model
explanation: LoRA freezes the base weights and learns a low-rank update per matrix, a few percent of the parameters. Fifteen small adapters on one shared base are cheap to train and store; accuracy is usually close to, not always above, full tuning.

prompt: A manager proposes pretraining a BERT-sized model from scratch on the company's 2 lakh support tickets "so it truly knows our language". How do you judge it?
optionA: Sound, provided the model is trained for at least 100 epochs
optionB: Unnecessary, because tickets need no language understanding
optionC: Almost never worth it; adapt a pretrained model and measure
optionD: Sound, since in-house text beats any general pretraining data
correctAnswerText: Almost never worth it; adapt a pretrained model and measure
explanation: Pretraining needs far more text and compute than one company's tickets provide. Fine-tuning a pretrained encoder (or continued pretraining on the tickets, if tests show a gap) gets the domain words without starting from zero.

prompt: 95% of tickets are under 180 tokens, and the longest are 1,200. The encoder accepts 512. Which max_length policy is most defensible?
optionA: 1,200, by editing the config so the model accepts longer inputs
optionB: About 256, then check accuracy on the long tickets separately
optionC: Always 512, since a longer limit can never cost anything at all
optionD: 64, since most of the meaning sits in the first few words anyway
correctAnswerText: About 256, then check accuracy on the long tickets separately
explanation: Attention cost grows with length², so a limit that covers nearly all tickets keeps training and serving cheap. Long tickets are then measured on their own and handled with windows if they suffer. Positions beyond the pretrained limit have no trained embeddings.

prompt: A team plans to label 50,000 reviews with a prompted LLM and fine-tune a small encoder on those labels. What is the key condition for this to be sound?
optionA: The encoder must be larger than the LLM, or it cannot learn the labels
optionB: Audit the LLM labels on a human gold set; the encoder inherits their errors
optionC: The LLM labels must be used unseen, since auditing biases the dataset
optionD: None; labels produced by an LLM are always as good as careful human labels
correctAnswerText: Audit the LLM labels on a human gold set; the encoder inherits their errors
explanation: The student model learns the teacher's mistakes too. Measure the LLM labeller against a human-labelled sample (accuracy, kappa, per-class recall) first, then check the encoder against the same gold set.

prompt: Tickets arrive in English and romanised Hinglish. Should the team pick a multilingual encoder over an English one as its base model?
optionA: No; English models always win, because Hinglish is written in Latin letters
optionB: Test both on labelled tickets; "multilingual" may not cover romanised Hindi
optionC: Yes; a multilingual model always handles any mix of languages best
optionD: Yes, provided the multilingual model is the larger of the two on offer
correctAnswerText: Test both on labelled tickets; "multilingual" may not cover romanised Hindi
explanation: Many multilingual models learned Hindi in Devanagari, not Hindi typed in Latin letters, and can do worse on Hinglish. Only scores on your own language mix decide it.

prompt: For a loan-complaint classifier, a colleague shows one head's attention weights peaking on "not" and calls this the explanation of the decision. How should that be judged?
optionA: Conclusive, provided the weight on "not" is above one half in value
optionB: Meaningless, since attention weights are random after fine-tuning
optionC: Suggestive only; one head's weights are not a faithful explanation
optionD: Conclusive, since attention weights are the model's actual reasons
correctAnswerText: Suggestive only; one head's weights are not a faithful explanation
explanation: There are many heads and layers, and values and later layers transform what attention selects. Test explanations directly — remove or change words and watch the prediction — and measure behaviour on labelled cases.

prompt: A device must classify 30-step sensor sequences locally, with 3,000 labelled examples and tight memory. A colleague insists a transformer is required. How do you judge it?
optionA: Correct; transformers beat recurrent models on every kind of sequence
optionB: Neither is suitable; sequence data always needs a pretrained LLM
optionC: Not required; a small GRU or LSTM may suit, so compare on validation
optionD: Correct, because short sequences cannot be handled by recurrent cells
correctAnswerText: Not required; a small GRU or LSTM may suit, so compare on validation
explanation: Transformers win on long text at scale; on short sequences with little data and tight memory, small recurrent or convolutional models are often as good and lighter. Measure rather than assume.

prompt: A production script calls pipeline("sentiment-analysis") with no model argument. Why is that a poor practice?
optionA: Without a model name the pipeline returns labels but never any scores
optionB: Pipelines without a model argument run only on a GPU, never on a CPU
optionC: The default model can change between versions; name and pin the model
optionD: The default model is always multilingual, which slows English text
correctAnswerText: The default model can change between versions; name and pin the model
explanation: The task default is chosen for demos and may change with the library version, silently changing predictions. Name the model (and ideally its revision) and record it with every evaluation.

prompt: How does a sentence embedding differ from a TF-IDF vector of the same text?
optionA: It is a few hundred dense learned numbers, not one weight per word
optionB: It is longer, with one column for every word in the whole vocabulary
optionC: It is the same vector, only normalised to a length of exactly one
optionD: It is a list of the keywords, sorted from most to least important
correctAnswerText: It is a few hundred dense learned numbers, not one weight per word
explanation: TF-IDF is sparse: one column per vocabulary term, mostly zeros. An embedding model maps any text to a fixed, dense vector (384 numbers for MiniLM) learned so that similar meanings land close together.

prompt: What range of values can the cosine similarity of two vectors take?
optionA: From −100 to 100
optionB: From 0 to 1 only
optionC: From 0 to infinity
optionD: From −1 to 1
correctAnswerText: From −1 to 1
explanation: Cosine is a·b / (‖a‖‖b‖), the cosine of the angle between the vectors: 1 for the same direction, 0 for perpendicular, −1 for opposite. Many text models rarely produce negative values in practice.

prompt: What does a word-embedding model such as word2vec or GloVe give each word?
optionA: A new vector for each sentence it appears in
optionB: One fixed vector, the same in every sentence
optionC: A count of how often it appears in a corpus
optionD: A single id number from the model's vocabulary
correctAnswerText: One fixed vector, the same in every sentence
explanation: Static word embeddings store one vector per word, so "bank" has the same vector in "river bank" and "bank account". Transformer (contextual) embeddings change with the sentence.

prompt: What is a sentence-embedding model such as all-MiniLM-L6-v2?
optionA: A tokenizer that splits sentences into words and counts each of them
optionB: A transformer tuned so one pooled vector per text suits similarity
optionC: A classifier that labels each sentence with one of a fixed set of topics
optionD: A dictionary that maps each sentence to its translation in English
correctAnswerText: A transformer tuned so one pooled vector per text suits similarity
explanation: It is a transformer fine-tuned, usually on sentence pairs, so that the pooled vector for a whole text places paraphrases close together. It outputs vectors, not labels.

prompt: Once two embeddings are normalised to length 1, what is their dot product equal to?
optionA: Their Euclidean distance
optionB: Always exactly one
optionC: Their cosine similarity
optionD: The sum of their lengths
correctAnswerText: Their cosine similarity
explanation: Cosine is a·b divided by both lengths; with unit-length vectors the division is by 1. That is why systems normalise once and use the fast dot product.

prompt: What is a PyTorch nn.Embedding(num_embeddings, embedding_dim) layer?
optionA: A pretrained sentence model loaded from a model hub
optionB: A learned lookup table with one vector per integer id
optionC: A layer that computes cosine similarity between rows
optionD: A one-hot encoder that turns ids into sparse vectors
correctAnswerText: A learned lookup table with one vector per integer id
explanation: It holds a num_embeddings × embedding_dim weight matrix; id i returns row i. The rows are trained with the rest of the network.

prompt: An embedding model is described as "384-dimensional". What does that mean?
optionA: It was trained on 384 million sentences of mixed languages
optionB: It can read texts of at most 384 words before cutting them
optionC: It has 384 layers, each adding one dimension of meaning
optionD: Every text, short or long, becomes a vector of 384 numbers
correctAnswerText: Every text, short or long, becomes a vector of 384 numbers
explanation: The dimension is the length of the output vector and is fixed for a model. How much text it can read is its maximum sequence length, a separate number.

prompt: What does an approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) index do?
optionA: Finds close vectors fast without checking all, at a small risk of misses
optionB: Finds the exact nearest vector by comparing the query against all of them
optionC: Translates each query into keywords and runs a full-text search on them
optionD: Compresses each vector into one number so that it can be sorted quickly
correctAnswerText: Finds close vectors fast without checking all, at a small risk of misses
explanation: Indexes such as HNSW or IVF (in FAISS, vector databases or pgvector) trade a little recall for search over millions of vectors in milliseconds. Brute force is exact but scales with the collection.

prompt: In a sentence-embedding model, what is mean pooling?
optionA: Averaging the token vectors of real tokens into one vector
optionB: Taking the largest value in each column of the vectors
optionC: Keeping only the vector of the first token in the text
optionD: Adding the vectors of the text's nouns and verbs only
correctAnswerText: Averaging the token vectors of real tokens into one vector
explanation: The transformer gives one vector per token; mean pooling averages them, using the attention mask so padding is left out. Using only the first ([CLS]) token is a different pooling.

prompt: In a tabular network, what is an entity embedding for a column such as merchant or city?
optionA: A text description of each category, embedded by a language model
optionB: A learned vector for each category value, trained with the model
optionC: The average target value of each category, used as a feature
optionD: A one-hot column for each value, added to the input table
correctAnswerText: A learned vector for each category value, trained with the model
explanation: Each category value gets a row in an embedding table, learned during training so that values that behave alike end up close. The vectors can also be extracted and fed to a tree model.

prompt: Why does a transformer give "bank" different vectors in "river bank" and "bank account", when word2vec does not?
optionA: The transformer reads only the word before, which differs here
optionB: word2vec ignores rare words, and "bank" is rare in its training
optionC: The transformer stores a separate vocabulary entry for each meaning
optionD: Each token's vector is built from the other words via attention
correctAnswerText: Each token's vector is built from the other words via attention
explanation: Contextual models compute each token's vector from the whole sentence, so the surrounding words change it. Static models look up one stored vector per word.

prompt: Why can "refund not received" and "refund received, thank you" have a high cosine similarity?
optionA: Cosine ignores word order, so the two texts are treated the same
optionB: Embeddings capture shared topic strongly and negation weakly
optionC: Short texts always score high, whatever they actually contain
optionD: The model has stored these two sentences as a known duplicate
correctAnswerText: Embeddings capture shared topic strongly and negation weakly
explanation: Both are about a refund, so they sit close; the opposite outcome is a small shift in the vector (0.77 in the lesson). Close is not the same as equivalent, which matters for duplicates and answers.

prompt: Why is there no universal cosine value, such as 0.7, that means "similar"?
optionA: Cosine values change every time the same two texts are embedded once again
optionB: Each model spreads its scores differently, so thresholds must be set per model
optionC: Cosine only ranks results, so its values cannot be compared with a number
optionD: A threshold of 0.5 is universal; it is only 0.7 that varies across models
correctAnswerText: Each model spreads its scores differently, so thresholds must be set per model
explanation: One model may score unrelated tickets at 0.2, another at 0.6. Choose thresholds on labelled pairs from your own data for the model you use, and redo it if the model changes.

prompt: Why should every cached embedding be stored with the name and version of the model that made it?
optionA: Providers charge per version, so the name is needed to reconcile the invoices
optionB: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared
optionC: The version sets the vector's length, which is needed to read it back from disk
optionD: Models expire after a year, so the version tells you when to delete the vector
correctAnswerText: Vectors from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared
explanation: Even with the same dimension, two models' axes mean different things. Knowing which model produced each vector prevents silent mixing and tells you what must be re-embedded after an upgrade.

prompt: An English sentence-embedding model scores "paisa kat gaya" (money deducted) as barely similar to "amount debited". Why?
optionA: Cosine similarity cannot be used for texts of different lengths
optionB: It saw little romanised Hindi in training, so it cannot place it
optionC: The two phrases mean different things, so the score is correct
optionD: The vectors were not normalised, which pushes cosine towards 0
correctAnswerText: It saw little romanised Hindi in training, so it cannot place it
explanation: A model places only what it has learned. Even multilingual models often learned Hindi in Devanagari, not typed in Latin letters, so any model must be tested on your own language mix.

prompt: A small sentence model reads at most 256 tokens. What happens when a 900-token product review is embedded with it?
optionA: Everything after the limit is cut off silently, so it is not represented
optionB: The model raises an error and refuses to embed the review at all
optionC: The model reads the whole review but at lower precision per token
optionD: The model summarises the review first, then embeds the summary
correctAnswerText: Everything after the limit is cut off silently, so it is not represented
explanation: Tokenizers truncate at max_length without warning, so the vector reflects only the start. Check token lengths, and split long texts and combine their vectors if the end matters.

prompt: With only 2,000 labelled tickets, why does logistic regression on frozen sentence embeddings often beat it on TF-IDF for new wording?
optionA: The embedding model learned paraphrase from far more text than 2,000 tickets
optionB: Logistic regression only works properly on dense inputs, never sparse ones
optionC: The embedding model was trained on these very tickets before it was released
optionD: Embeddings have more columns, and more columns always raise the accuracy
correctAnswerText: The embedding model learned paraphrase from far more text than 2,000 tickets
explanation: This is transfer learning with no fine-tuning: the encoder brings knowledge that similar meanings sit close, so the classifier generalises to wording absent from its labels.

prompt: For unit-length embeddings, why do ranking by smallest Euclidean distance and by largest cosine give the same order?
optionA: Euclidean distance and cosine are always numerically equal on any vectors
optionB: They do not; Euclidean ranking reverses cosine ranking on unit vectors
optionC: Both ignore the vectors' directions, so both depend only on the lengths
optionD: Squared distance equals 2 − 2·cosine, so one falls as the other rises
correctAnswerText: Squared distance equals 2 − 2·cosine, so one falls as the other rises
explanation: ‖a − b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² − 2a·b = 2 − 2cos when both lengths are 1. The two orderings agree, so an index can use either.

prompt: Why are k-means clusters of ticket embeddings used to discover themes rather than adopted as labels?
optionA: Clusters follow wording and language as well as the intent
optionB: Embeddings contain no information about what tickets mean
optionC: k-means cannot be run on vectors with more than 100 columns
optionD: Clusters change every time the data is loaded from the disk
correctAnswerText: Clusters follow wording and language as well as the intent
explanation: Clusters group by whatever dominates the vectors — Hinglish tickets often cluster together whatever they are about. People read samples per cluster and define the label set themselves.

prompt: Why should you use the pooling method stated on a sentence model's card rather than any pooling that seems reasonable?
optionA: Other pooling methods raise an error when the model is loaded for use
optionB: The model was trained so that only that pooled vector suits similarity
optionC: The pooling decides the vector's length, which must match the index
optionD: Pooling affects only speed, and the card lists the fastest method
correctAnswerText: The model was trained so that only that pooled vector suits similarity
explanation: A model trained with mean pooling did not learn to make its [CLS] vector useful for similarity, and vice versa. The wrong pooling still returns vectors, just worse ones.

prompt: Two embeddings, shortened to four dimensions, are a = (2, 0, 1, 2) and b = (1, 2, 2, 0). What is their cosine similarity?
explanation: a·b = 2 + 0 + 2 + 0 = 4; ‖a‖ = √9 = 3 and ‖b‖ = √9 = 3; cosine = 4 / 9 = 0.444. 4.000 is the raw dot product before dividing by the lengths.

prompt: Two unit-length embeddings have cosine similarity 0.8. What is the Euclidean distance between them?
optionA: About 0.20
optionB: About 0.40
optionC: About 0.63
optionD: About 1.26
correctAnswerText: About 0.63
explanation: ‖a − b‖² = 2 − 2 × 0.8 = 0.4, so the distance is √0.4 = 0.632. 0.40 is the squared distance; 0.20 is 1 − cosine.

prompt: How many learnable parameters does nn.Embedding(50000, 384) hold?
explanation: One 384-number row for each of 50,000 ids: 50,000 × 384 = 19,200,000. An embedding table has no bias, so 19,250,000 adds one that does not exist.

prompt: A unit-length query q = (0.6, 0.8) is compared with three unit-length documents: d1 = (1, 0), d2 = (0, 1), d3 = (0.8, 0.6). In what order does cosine similarity rank them?
explanation: With unit vectors cosine is the dot product: d1 0.6, d2 0.8, d3 0.48 + 0.48 = 0.96. So d3 (0.96), then d2 (0.80), then d1 (0.60).

prompt: A short text in a padded batch has token vectors (2, 4), (4, 0) and a padding vector (0, 0), with attention mask [1, 1, 0]. What does masked mean pooling give?
explanation: Sum the real tokens and divide by the mask total: ((2 + 4) / 2, (4 + 0) / 2) = (3, 2). Averaging all three positions, padding included, gives (2, 1.33) — a vector that depends on the batch.

prompt:
For duplicate tickets, agents labelled 300 pairs. Cosine thresholds give:
0.70 → precision 0.85, recall 0.92
0.80 → precision 0.94, recall 0.81
0.90 → precision 0.99, recall 0.42
The rule is "precision at least 0.90, then the highest recall". Which threshold?
optionB: None of the three
explanation: 0.70 fails the precision rule (0.85). Both 0.80 and 0.90 pass it, and 0.80 keeps far more recall (0.81 against 0.42).

prompt: A help centre stores 1 lakh (100,000) document embeddings of 384 dimensions as float32. How much memory do the raw vectors take?
optionA: About 154 MB
optionB: About 1.5 GB
optionC: About 38 MB
optionD: About 15 MB
correctAnswerText: About 154 MB
explanation: 100,000 × 384 numbers × 4 bytes = 153,600,000 bytes ≈ 154 MB. 38 MB forgets the 4 bytes per float32 number; an index adds some overhead on top.

prompt: Sentence vectors are made by averaging static word vectors. What is the cosine similarity between "dog bites man" and "man bites dog"?
optionA: About −1, since the meanings are each other's reverse
optionB: About 0.5, since half of the word positions differ
optionC: Exactly 0, since the subject and object are swapped
optionD: Exactly 1, since the same words give the same average
correctAnswerText: Exactly 1, since the same words give the same average
explanation: An average of the same three vectors is the same vector whatever the order, so cosine is 1. Averaged static vectors cannot see order; contextual models can.

prompt: Of 300 labelled ticket pairs, 60 are true duplicates. A cosine threshold flags 55 pairs, of which 50 are true duplicates. What are its precision and recall?
optionA: Precision 0.92, recall 0.18
optionB: Precision 0.91, recall 0.83
optionC: Precision 0.83, recall 0.91
optionD: Precision 0.17, recall 0.83
correctAnswerText: Precision 0.91, recall 0.83
explanation: Precision = 50 flagged correctly / 55 flagged = 0.909. Recall = 50 found / 60 true duplicates = 0.833. Swapping them is the common slip.

prompt: Query q = (1, 0). Unnormalised documents d1 = (3, 3) and d2 = (1, 0.2). Which document is top by raw dot product, and which by cosine?
optionA: Dot: d1 (3.0); cosine: d2 (0.98)
optionB: Dot: d1 (3.0); cosine: d1 (0.71)
optionC: Dot: d2 (1.0); cosine: d1 (0.71)
optionD: Dot: d2 (1.0); cosine: d2 (0.98)
correctAnswerText: Dot: d1 (3.0); cosine: d2 (0.98)
explanation: Dot products are 3.0 and 1.0, so the longer d1 wins. Cosines are 3 / 4.24 = 0.71 and 1 / 1.02 = 0.98, so d2 points much more nearly the query's way. Unnormalised dot products reward length.

prompt: Unrelated tickets ("otp not coming", "kyc rejected") score cosine 0.55–0.75, so the duplicate rule merges almost everything. The code takes last_hidden_state[:, 0] from a model whose card says mean pooling. Diagnosis?
optionA: The [CLS] vector was never trained for similarity; use masked mean pooling
