optionD: RRF needs an odd number of ranked lists to settle any ties
correctAnswerText: A poor rewrite then cannot lose what the user really typed
explanation: Generated queries can drift or drop a code; keeping the original as one ranked list means its results still take part in fusion. RRF accepts any number of lists, and all queries use the same model.

prompt: Why do golden-set labels name a source file and a short exact quote rather than a chunk id?
optionA: Chunk ids would let the model see the answer during the test
optionB: Chunk ids change with chunking, the very thing being compared
optionC: Vector stores never return chunk ids along with their results
optionD: Quotes take less storage than chunk ids in the evaluation file
correctAnswerText: Chunk ids change with chunking, the very thing being compared
explanation: A new chunk size renumbers every chunk, so id labels only fit the chunking that made them. A quote is found in whichever chunk now holds it, letting two chunkings be scored on one set.

prompt: Why is recall@k best reported with k equal to the number of chunks the prompt actually receives?
optionA: A larger k would always give a lower and harsher score
optionB: Recall cannot be computed for any k other than 5 or 10
optionC: The vector store returns exactly k results for each query
optionD: Only those chunks can inform the answer the model writes
correctAnswerText: Only those chunks can inform the answer the model writes
explanation: If the model sees five chunks, a relevant chunk at rank 8 cannot help, so recall@5 is the number that limits answer quality. Recall rises, not falls, as k grows.

prompt: Why should a router whose scores all fall below threshold search every index rather than pick one?
optionA: Searching every index is always faster than searching one
optionB: Low confidence means it does not know; guessing may miss
optionC: Low scores prove the question is outside the domain served
optionD: Indexes refuse queries whose routing score is below threshold
correctAnswerText: Low confidence means it does not know; guessing may miss
explanation: Low router scores show the router is unsure, not that the question is out of scope. Widening the search is safe; retrieval's own threshold then handles genuinely off-topic questions.

prompt: Why does a golden set written by someone reading the policy PDFs make every retrieval design look good?
optionA: Questions written by staff are always too short to score
optionB: Reading the PDFs changes their embeddings in the index
optionC: Such sets contain no unanswerable questions by definition
optionD: Its questions copy the documents' wording, so all match
correctAnswerText: Its questions copy the documents' wording, so all match
explanation: Questions phrased from the text share its words, so even weak retrieval finds the passage. Real helpdesk questions bring the paraphrases, codes and Hinglish that separate good designs from bad ones.

prompt: Why does the answer prompt still receive the recent conversation when retrieval used a condensed question?
optionA: The reply must respond to what the user said, in context
optionB: Providers reject prompts that do not repeat earlier turns
optionC: History is needed to compute each chunk's embedding again
optionD: The condensed question is too long to include in a prompt
correctAnswerText: The reply must respond to what the user said, in context
explanation: The rewrite exists to search well. The answer should read naturally against the real conversation and can recover details the rewrite missed, so it gets the history plus the retrieved chunks.

prompt: BM25 ranks chunks [A, B, C]; vector search ranks [B, D, A]. With RRF and k = 60, what is the fused order?
optionA: A, then B, then D, then C
optionB: B and A tied, then C, then D
optionC: A, then B, then C, then D
optionD: B, then A, then D, then C
correctAnswerText: B, then A, then D, then C
explanation: B = 1/62 + 1/61 ≈ 0.03252; A = 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.03227; D = 1/62 ≈ 0.01613; C = 1/63 ≈ 0.01587. B edges A because its worse rank (2nd) beats A's worse rank (3rd).

prompt: Five questions each have one relevant chunk, found at ranks 1, 4, 2, not at all, and 1. What are recall@3 and MRR?
optionA: recall@3 = 0.60 and MRR = 0.55
optionB: recall@3 = 0.75 and MRR = 0.69
optionC: recall@3 = 0.60 and MRR = 0.69
optionD: recall@3 = 0.80 and MRR = 0.55
correctAnswerText: recall@3 = 0.60 and MRR = 0.55
explanation: Ranks 1, 2 and 1 are in the top 3, so recall@3 = 3/5 = 0.60. MRR = (1 + 0.25 + 0.5 + 0 + 1) / 5 = 0.55. Leaving the miss out of the average gives 0.69.

prompt: Which BM25 tokeniser, applied to lower-cased text, keeps expense codes such as "exp-71" as one token?
optionA: re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*", text)
optionB: re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text) on every input
optionC: re.split(r"[-\s]+", text) splitting on hyphens
optionD: re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text) with digits dropped
correctAnswerText: re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*", text)
explanation: The optional hyphen group joins "exp" and "71" into "exp-71". The plain [a-z0-9]+ pattern splits the code into "exp" and "71", which match every EXP code equally; dropping digits loses the code entirely.

prompt: An HR handbook arrives as a Word file using Heading 1 and Heading 2 styles. Which parsing and chunking fits?
optionA: Embed the whole handbook as one chunk to keep all context
optionB: Convert to PDF, then cut fixed 1,000-character chunks from it
optionC: Split on every full stop so each sentence is its own chunk
optionD: Split by heading styles, prefix the path, size-limit sections
correctAnswerText: Split by heading styles, prefix the path, size-limit sections
explanation: python-docx exposes style names, which is structure for free. Heading-based sections with the heading path prefixed keep each rule with its context; one huge chunk averages topics and single sentences lose context.

prompt: For one question, 2 of the top 5 retrieved chunks are relevant. What is precision@5 for that question?
explanation: Precision@k is the share of the top k that is relevant: 2 / 5 = 0.40. It matters when chunks cost tokens, because irrelevant ones are paid for and can distract the model.

prompt: A question needs three passages, c, d and e. The top 5 results contain c and e but not d. What is recall@5?
optionA: About 0.40
optionB: About 0.67
optionC: About 0.33
optionD: Exactly 1.0
correctAnswerText: About 0.67
explanation: Recall@k is relevant passages found in the top k divided by all relevant passages: 2 / 3 ≈ 0.67. Dividing by k (2/5 = 0.40) gives precision instead.

prompt: A condense step turned "Is 12BB due before March for L5?" into a rewrite that no longer contains "12BB". What should the pipeline do?
optionA: Search with both original and rewrite, then fuse the lists
optionB: Search with the rewrite only, since it reads more naturally
optionC: Refuse to answer until the user repeats the question again
optionD: Raise the temperature and request a different rewrite
correctAnswerText: Search with both original and rewrite, then fuse the lists
explanation: Codes and numbers in the original must survive the rewrite. When a check finds one missing, searching with both and fusing keeps the exact code in play; a fresh sampled rewrite may drop it again.

prompt: An employee asks, "Can I claim LTA for a Goa trip, and do I need to keep the tickets?" Which retrieval step fits?
optionA: Send it straight to the model without any retrieval
optionB: Embed only the first clause, since one topic is enough
optionC: Lower the top-k to 1 so only the best chunk is returned
optionD: Generate sub-queries on eligibility and proof, then fuse
correctAnswerText: Generate sub-queries on eligibility and proof, then fuse
explanation: The question needs two passages — eligibility and proof of travel. Multi-query retrieval searches each need (plus the original) and fuses them with RRF, so both passages reach the prompt.

prompt: A golden set includes 8 questions the policies cannot answer. How should those 8 be scored?
optionA: Drop them, since a question with no answer cannot be scored
optionB: Count them as hits whenever any chunk at all is returned
optionC: Check the top re-ranker score stays below the refusal line
optionD: Include them in recall@5 with an expected rank of one
correctAnswerText: Check the top re-ranker score stays below the refusal line
explanation: Their expected set is empty, so recall does not apply. What matters is that retrieval finds nothing convincing, so the best score stays under the threshold and the assistant declines.

prompt: Using the course's rule of thumb, what overlap suits fixed 400-token chunks of a policy manual?
optionA: Exactly 400 tokens
optionB: About 200 to 300 tokens
optionC: None; overlap always hurts
optionD: About 40 to 60 tokens
correctAnswerText: About 40 to 60 tokens
explanation: Overlap of 10–15% protects a sentence near a boundary: 40–60 tokens for 400-token chunks. Half or full overlap duplicates most of each chunk; structure-aware chunks need little overlap, but fixed ones benefit.

prompt: Chunks are BM25-tokenised with a lower-casing regex, but queries with question.split(). "When is Form 12BB due?" scores 0 on the Form 12BB chunk. Why?
optionA: The Form 12BB chunk is too long for BM25 to give it a score
optionB: The query keeps capitals and "due?", so no tokens match
optionC: BM25 needs vector scores as input before it can rank chunks
optionD: BM25 cannot score any token that contains digit characters
correctAnswerText: The query keeps capitals and "due?", so no tokens match
explanation: split() yields "Form", "12BB" and "due?" while the chunks hold "form", "12bb" and "due". Tokenised the same way, the chunk scored 3.93 and ranked first; one shared tokenize() fixes it.

prompt: For "what is exp-70 for", BM25 scores the EXP-71 chunk above EXP-70. The EXP-71 chunk contains "costs for transfers". Diagnosis?
optionA: BM25 needs a re-ranker before it can match codes at all
optionB: BM25 treats exp-70 and exp-71 as the same rare token
optionC: A stop word ("for") is adding score; drop it on both sides
optionD: The EXP-70 chunk is shorter, and BM25 always favours long text
correctAnswerText: A stop word ("for") is adding score; drop it on both sides
explanation: Words like "for" carry no meaning but still add score when they match. Removing a short stop-word list from both queries and chunks lets the exact code decide.

prompt: After chunk size changes from 500 to 300 characters, recall@5 drops from 0.86 to 0.11, yet manual spot checks look fine. Likeliest cause?
optionA: Labels are chunk ids, and re-chunking renumbered them
optionB: The vector index must be retrained after re-chunking
optionC: Shorter chunks lose nearly all meaning when embedded
optionD: Recall@5 is undefined when chunks are shorter than k
correctAnswerText: Labels are chunk ids, and re-chunking renumbered them
explanation: A collapse that manual testing does not confirm points at the measurement. Id labels now point at different text; relabelling as source plus quote gives a metric that survives the change.

prompt: Multi-query retrieval raised latency on every request, yet the golden set shows gains only on compound questions. What does this indicate?
optionA: It is wasted on simple asks; trigger it only when needed
optionB: The golden set is wrong, since multi-query always helps
optionC: Simple questions need more generated queries, not fewer
optionD: The fusion step is broken and should be rewritten fully
correctAnswerText: It is wasted on simple asks; trigger it only when needed
explanation: Decomposition helps questions that need several passages and adds a model call plus extra searches to all others. Running it only for long or multi-part questions keeps the gain and drops most of the cost.

prompt: Second and third chat turns get poor answers, while the same questions asked fresh are fine. Logs show the retriever embedding "What about Chennai?". Diagnosis?
optionA: The raw follow-up was embedded; it needs condensing first
optionB: The vector index was rebuilt between the first and second turn
optionC: The chat history is too short for the model to see the topic
optionD: Chennai is missing from the embedding model's vocabulary
correctAnswerText: The raw follow-up was embedded; it needs condensing first
explanation: A follow-up depends on the previous turn, so on its own it matches nothing useful. A condense step turns it into a standalone question for search; the answer step still sees the history.

prompt: Average recall@5 is flat after adding BM25, but the slice report shows code questions up sharply and paraphrases down. What does this reveal?
optionA: BM25 had no effect, since the overall average did not move
optionB: The code questions should be removed as unrepresentative
optionC: The average hid two opposing effects; fix the paraphrase loss
optionD: Slices are noise, and only the overall average should count
correctAnswerText: The average hid two opposing effects; fix the paraphrase loss
explanation: BM25 helps exact codes and its noise can hurt paraphrases. Slices expose what the average hides; stop words, fusion or a re-ranker may repair the loss, then both slices are re-measured.

prompt: A developer drops re-ranked chunks scoring under 0.5, "the probability midpoint", and relevant chunks start vanishing. What is wrong?
optionA: The scores are unbounded logits, so 0.5 means nothing
optionB: Re-rankers score relevant chunks low only for Hindi text
optionC: Re-rankers only work when the threshold is exactly zero
optionD: The threshold belongs before re-ranking, not after it
correctAnswerText: The scores are unbounded logits, so 0.5 means nothing
explanation: Cross-encoders of this kind return raw logits — runs in the course gave 5.18 and −0.69 — so a relevant chunk can fall below 0.5. Any refusal threshold is read off the golden set for that model.

prompt: A multilingual embedding model fixed Devanagari Hindi queries, but romanised Hinglish ones still score near zero against English policies. Where does the fix belong?
optionA: Before retrieval: rewrite the question into English for search
optionB: After retrieval: translate the chunks into Hinglish for display
optionC: At ingestion: store a Hinglish copy of every policy chunk
optionD: In the threshold: lower it until Hinglish queries return chunks
correctAnswerText: Before retrieval: rewrite the question into English for search
explanation: The failure is the search itself, so the query must be put in the documents' language before retrieval; the answer can still be written in the user's language. Lowering the threshold only admits noise.

prompt: Answers from a two-column policy PDF mix unrelated rules. Printing the parsed text shows lines from both columns interleaved. What should change?
optionA: Raise chunk overlap so the two columns are joined back up
optionB: Ask the model in the prompt to ignore unrelated sentences
optionC: Use a layout-aware parser and check its output before chunking
optionD: Switch to a larger embedding model that can follow columns
correctAnswerText: Use a layout-aware parser and check its output before chunking
explanation: The text was garbled before chunking, so nothing downstream can repair it. A parser that keeps reading order on multi-column pages (PyMuPDF, or a layout-aware tool) fixes the input, which is checked by eye.

prompt: "Can I carry casual leave forward?" gets the earned-leave rule. The retrieved fixed-size chunk holds the end of one section and the start of the next. Root fix?
optionA: Raise overlap so the next section appears in full as well
optionB: Add "do not confuse leave types" to the system prompt
optionC: Retrieve more chunks so the right section also appears
optionD: Chunk by headings and prefix each with its heading path
correctAnswerText: Chunk by headings and prefix each with its heading path
explanation: The chunk crosses a section boundary and loses which heading each sentence belongs to. Structure-aware chunks keep each rule under its own heading; more overlap or more chunks keep the confusion.

prompt: On a 50-question set, a re-ranker lifts recall@5 from 0.84 to 0.85 and adds 0.4 s per question. What is the soundest verdict?
optionA: A failure, since a re-ranker must add at least ten points
optionB: Proof the golden set is broken, since recall barely moved
optionC: A clear win, since any rise in recall is worth shipping
optionD: About one question, likely noise, for a certain latency cost
correctAnswerText: About one question, likely noise, for a certain latency cost
explanation: On 50 questions 0.01 is half a question, within noise, while the latency is real. Check the misses and MRR, grow the set, and decide with cost in view; there is no fixed gain a re-ranker must deliver.

prompt: Hybrid + re-rank lifts recall@5 from 0.78 to 0.86; codes go 0.50 → 0.90, paraphrases 0.85 → 0.83, at +0.35 s. Ship it?
optionA: No, since any slice getting worse must block a release
optionB: Yes, without checks, since the average went up by 0.08
optionC: Likely yes, after checking latency and the lost paraphrase
optionD: No, since 0.35 seconds is too slow for any assistant
correctAnswerText: Likely yes, after checking latency and the lost paraphrase
explanation: The gain is large and lands where hybrid search should help; the paraphrase drop is about one question. Confirm the latency fits the product's budget and look at the lost question before shipping.

prompt: Which plan for a 60-question golden set for an HR policy assistant is best?
optionA: Real tickets in slices, unanswerables, source-and-quote labels
optionB: Questions written from the PDFs, labelled with their chunk ids
optionC: Sixty plain questions from one team, labelled by the developer
optionD: Generated questions only, so the set can grow without limit
correctAnswerText: Real tickets in slices, unanswerables, source-and-quote labels
explanation: Real helpdesk questions sliced into plain, paraphrase, codes, follow-ups, Hinglish and unanswerable — labelled by source and quote, reviewed by HR — measure what users meet. PDF-copied or single-source sets flatter every design.

prompt: Every retrieval design now scores 1.00 on a 10-question set, and a manager proposes ending evaluation work. How do you judge that?
optionA: Wrong: the set has saturated and needs harder questions
optionB: Right: switching the metric to nDCG would add nothing
optionC: Wrong: the scores prove the evaluation code is broken
optionD: Right: perfect scores show that retrieval is finished
correctAnswerText: Wrong: the set has saturated and needs harder questions
explanation: A set nobody fails cannot show a gain or a regression. Adding codes, paraphrases, Hinglish and follow-ups until the best system misses some makes it useful again; perfect scores do not imply buggy code.

prompt: A team proposes that the routing model decide whether a contractor's question may reach the salary-bands index. How do you judge it?
optionA: Unsafe: wording can steer a router; enforce access in code
optionB: Safe, provided the router runs at temperature 0 every time
optionC: Safe: routers read the user's role from the conversation
optionD: Unsafe only because salary data cannot be stored as vectors
correctAnswerText: Unsafe: wording can steer a router; enforce access in code
explanation: Routing is a model's judgement and the question text can steer it. Who may see what must be enforced by filters or collections the role cannot reach, checked in server code; vectors can hold such data under proper access control.

prompt: A blog post reports HyDE raising recall. Your corpus is full of exact limits and dates. What is the sound adoption plan?
optionA: Adopt it only with a higher temperature for the draft
optionB: Measure it per slice; drafts may invent wrong figures
optionC: Adopt it everywhere, since it was shown to raise recall
optionD: Reject it outright, since generated text is never useful
correctAnswerText: Measure it per slice; drafts may invent wrong figures
explanation: A hypothetical answer helps when questions and documents are worded very differently, but it can carry wrong numbers that pull wrong chunks. Run the golden set by slice before deciding, rather than trusting another corpus.

prompt: Routing across HR, travel and IT indexes misroutes vague questions. Which router design is best justified?
optionA: Ask users to choose the right index before every question
optionB: A single merged index, with routing removed and no filters
optionC: Only one-line descriptions, matched to the top score always
optionD: Rules for codes, a fixed-label classifier, and a wide fallback
correctAnswerText: Rules for codes, a fixed-label classifier, and a wide fallback
explanation: Obvious cases such as "EXP-" codes go by rule; a classifier with structured output from a fixed set of routes handles vague wording; and an unsure result widens the search instead of guessing.

prompt: A condense call runs on every chat turn, including the first, and median latency has risen. Which change is soundest?
optionA: Run it on a larger model to make up for the added delay
optionB: Remove it entirely, since rewrites never help retrieval
optionC: Skip it on first turns, log rewrites, and measure follow-ups
optionD: Condense the retrieved chunks instead of the user question
correctAnswerText: Skip it on first turns, log rewrites, and measure follow-ups
explanation: A first message has nothing to resolve, so the call is pure cost there. Logging the rewrite and measuring a follow-up slice before and after shows whether the remaining calls earn their latency.

prompt: 500-character chunks beat 200-character ones on recall@5 (0.88 vs 0.81); misses at 200 are table rows cut from their headers. What should the team do?
optionA: Average the two sizes to 350 and ship that without measuring
optionB: Pick 200, since smaller chunks are always more precise to embed
optionC: Pick 500, and still fix table parsing since it fails at any size
optionD: Pick 500 and stop there, since the bigger chunks hid the issue
correctAnswerText: Pick 500, and still fix table parsing since it fails at any size
explanation: Recall@5 limits what the model sees, so 500 wins; but the miss list exposed a parsing fault the larger chunks merely masked. Record scores, set version and commit so the next change starts from a known baseline.

prompt: On a small plain-prose corpus with no codes, hybrid search scored below vector-only and only hybrid plus re-rank matched it. Which decision fits?
optionA: Keep vector-only until a harder set shows hybrid gains
optionB: Ship hybrid alone, since it is the industry standard
optionC: Ship hybrid plus re-rank, since more stages are better
optionD: Drop the golden set, since it disagrees with practice
correctAnswerText: Keep vector-only until a harder set shows hybrid gains
explanation: Hybrid search is not automatically an improvement — BM25 noise can leak into fusion. With no gain shown and real latency added, the simpler design stays until codes or acronyms in a harder set justify the extra stages.

prompt: In a vector store such as Qdrant, what is a point's payload?
optionA: The query that was used to retrieve the point most recently
optionB: JSON metadata stored with the vector, used to filter and cite
optionC: The list of neighbour links the index keeps for that point
optionD: The raw bytes of the vector, compressed for faster transfer
correctAnswerText: JSON metadata stored with the vector, used to filter and cite
explanation: A point is an id, a vector and a payload: fields such as source, page, section, company_id and effective date. Filters read the payload and citations come from it; Chroma calls the same thing metadata.

prompt: What kind of structure is an HNSW index?
optionA: A set of k-means clusters, searched one nearest list at a time
optionB: A hash table that maps each vector to an exact bucket id
optionC: A sorted B-tree of vectors ordered by their first dimension
optionD: A layered graph of neighbour links, walked from the top down
correctAnswerText: A layered graph of neighbour links, walked from the top down
explanation: HNSW links each vector to about m neighbours across layers; a search enters at the sparse top layer, walks greedily towards the query and drops down. Clustered lists describe IVF instead.

prompt: How does an IVF (inverted file) vector index answer a query?
optionA: It looks up the query's words in an inverted word list
optionB: It searches only the probes nearest k-means clusters
optionC: It compares the query with every stored vector in turn
optionD: It walks a layered neighbour graph from the top layer
correctAnswerText: It searches only the probes nearest k-means clusters
explanation: IVF clusters vectors into lists with k-means and, at query time, scans only the probes clusters nearest the query. Despite the name, it is not a keyword inverted index.

prompt: In pgvector, which operator gives cosine distance between two vectors?
explanation: <=> is cosine distance, <-> is Euclidean (L2) distance and <#> is negative inner product. The operator used in ORDER BY must match the index's operator class for the index to be used.

prompt: What does the HNSW parameter ef_search control?
optionA: How many dimensions are kept from each stored vector
optionB: How many results the database returns to the caller
optionC: How many neighbour links each vector stores in the graph
optionD: How many candidates a query keeps while it walks the graph
correctAnswerText: How many candidates a query keeps while it walks the graph
explanation: ef_search is query-time effort: higher keeps more candidates, finds more true neighbours and is slower. Links per vector is m; the number returned is the limit or top k.

prompt: For a collection in cosine space, what number does a Chroma query return for each result?
optionA: A rank, from 1 for the best result to k for the last
optionB: A probability between 0 and 1 that it is relevant
optionC: A distance, 1 − cosine, where lower means closer
optionD: A similarity, the cosine, where higher means closer
correctAnswerText: A distance, 1 − cosine, where lower means closer
explanation: Chroma reports distance, so 0.617 is a closer match than 0.79. Qdrant reports similarity, where higher is better — the opposite convention, and a common source of inverted thresholds.

prompt: Which values does Qdrant accept as point ids?
optionA: Any string, such as file#0
optionB: Unsigned integers or UUIDs
optionC: Only sequential integers
optionD: Only the vector's own hash
correctAnswerText: Unsigned integers or UUIDs
explanation: Qdrant ids are unsigned integers or UUIDs; "leave.md#0" raises a "not a valid UUID" error. A uuid5 of the readable chunk id gives a stable valid id, with the readable id kept in the payload.

prompt: What characterises exact (brute-force) vector search?
optionA: Approximate results, because it skips most stored vectors
optionB: Perfect results, with cost growing linearly with the data
optionC: Approximate results, with cost that stays fixed as data grows
optionD: Perfect results, but only when vectors are 128-dimensional
correctAnswerText: Perfect results, with cost growing linearly with the data
explanation: Brute force compares the query with every vector, so it never misses a true neighbour but its cost grows with the collection. Below roughly a hundred thousand vectors it is often fast enough.

prompt: In an HNSW index, what do the build parameters m and ef_construction set?
optionA: Query effort and the number of results returned per query
optionB: The vector dimension and the distance metric to be used
optionC: Links per vector and build effort, so quality and memory
optionD: The number of clusters and how many of them are probed
correctAnswerText: Links per vector and build effort, so quality and memory
explanation: m is roughly the number of neighbours each vector links to and ef_construction is the effort spent building the graph; together they set index quality, memory and build time. Clusters and probes belong to IVF.

prompt: Which collection setting is fixed at creation and cannot be changed later without rebuilding?
optionA: The distance metric, such as cosine, dot or L2
optionB: The number of results returned by each query
optionC: The filter conditions that queries may apply
optionD: The payload fields that each point may carry
correctAnswerText: The distance metric, such as cosine, dot or L2
explanation: A collection has one dimension and one distance metric, set when it is created; changing either means rebuilding. Result count and filters are per query, and payloads are flexible JSON.

prompt: Why should a team compare its ANN index's top 10 with exact search on sample queries?
optionA: Exact search is required by law for any production system
optionB: ANN indexes return results in random order on every query
optionC: The comparison rebuilds the graph, making it more accurate
optionD: ANN trades some recall for speed, and that loss must be known
correctAnswerText: ANN trades some recall for speed, and that loss must be known
explanation: An approximate index can miss true nearest neighbours. Measuring overlap with exact results on a sample shows how much, and ef_search or probes are raised until recall is around 0.95 or better.

prompt: Why should an IVF index be built after the vectors are loaded rather than on an empty table?
optionA: IVF needs to know the final row count to set its dimension
optionB: Its clusters are learnt from the data that is already there
optionC: An IVF index on an empty table raises an error at every query
optionD: Loading data into an IVF index is impossible once it exists
correctAnswerText: Its clusters are learnt from the data that is already there
explanation: IVF runs k-means over existing vectors to form its lists. Built on little or no data, the clusters do not reflect the real distribution and recall suffers; HNSW does not have this ordering constraint.

prompt: Why can applying a strict tenant filter after an ANN search return few or no results?
optionA: Filters change the distance metric for the filtered points
optionB: Filtering resets ef_search to zero for the filtered query
optionC: The nearest neighbours may all belong to other tenants
optionD: ANN indexes cannot store any metadata next to the vectors
correctAnswerText: The nearest neighbours may all belong to other tenants
explanation: If the top 10 is chosen first and filtered afterwards, a small tenant's chunks may never be among those 10. Filtering during the graph walk ranks only the tenant's own points.

prompt: Why create a payload index on every field a Qdrant collection is filtered by?
optionA: It converts the vectors so they match the filter field
optionB: Without it, filters are silently ignored by the database
optionC: It is needed to store the field in the payload at all
optionD: Without it, filtered searches slow down as the data grows
correctAnswerText: Without it, filtered searches slow down as the data grows
explanation: A payload index lets the engine apply the filter efficiently during the search. Without one the filter still works but must inspect payloads point by point, so filtered queries get slower with scale.

prompt: Why does a pgvector HNSW index built with vector_cosine_ops go unused for a query ordered by <->?
optionA: An index serves only its own operator, and <-> is L2
optionB: HNSW indexes are used only for tables under a million rows
optionC: The <-> operator always forces an exact parallel scan
optionD: pgvector disables indexes when a WHERE clause is present
correctAnswerText: An index serves only its own operator, and <-> is L2
explanation: vector_cosine_ops serves <=>. With <-> the planner cannot use the index and falls back to a sequential scan — correct results, slowly, with no error. Match the operator or create an L2 index.

prompt: Why derive point ids with uuid5 of the chunk id rather than with uuid4?
optionA: uuid5 is the same each run, so upserts replace old points
optionB: uuid5 also encrypts the chunk id stored in the payload
optionC: uuid5 values are shorter, so the index uses less memory
optionD: uuid4 values are rejected by Qdrant as invalid point ids
correctAnswerText: uuid5 is the same each run, so upserts replace old points
explanation: uuid5 is deterministic: the same chunk id always gives the same UUID, so re-ingesting overwrites. uuid4 is random and valid, but every run inserts new points and the collection keeps growing.

prompt: Why can upserting a revised document by chunk id still leave outdated text searchable?
optionA: If the new version has fewer chunks, old extras survive
optionB: Old chunks are cached by the store for thirty days by default
optionC: Upserts are applied only after the index is fully rebuilt
optionD: Upsert keeps the old vector and replaces only the payload
correctAnswerText: If the new version has fewer chunks, old extras survive
explanation: Upsert replaces points whose ids match and leaves the rest. When a policy shrinks from 14 chunks to 9, ids 9–13 stay behind quoting the old rules; delete by source first, then insert.

prompt: Why does marking a policy as superseded need no re-embedding of its chunks?
optionA: Only metadata changes; the text and its vector are the same
optionB: Vectors are recomputed by the store whenever payloads change
optionC: Embedding models ignore any text that is marked as superseded
optionD: Superseded chunks are deleted, so they need no vectors at all
correctAnswerText: Only metadata changes; the text and its vector are the same
explanation: The chunk text has not changed, so its vector is still right. A payload or metadata update — Qdrant set_payload, Chroma update with metadatas — is enough, and filters then exclude it.

prompt: Why pass your own embeddings to Chroma's upsert instead of only the documents?
optionA: Passing embeddings turns on cosine distance by default
optionB: Chroma refuses documents longer than 256 characters
optionC: Otherwise Chroma embeds with its own default model
optionD: Documents passed alone are stored but never indexed
correctAnswerText: Otherwise Chroma embeds with its own default model
explanation: Given only documents, Chroma applies its default embedding function — a different model from the one your queries use, so the spaces do not match. Passing vectors yourself keeps one model on both sides.

prompt: Why is pgvector attractive to a team that already runs PostgreSQL?
optionA: It is always faster than every dedicated vector database
optionB: Vectors sit beside its data with SQL, joins and backups
optionC: It needs no index at all to search millions of vectors
optionD: It embeds text automatically inside its SQL functions
correctAnswerText: Vectors sit beside its data with SQL, joins and backups
explanation: pgvector keeps vectors in the database the team already operates: SQL filters, joins to permission tables, transactions and existing backups. It still needs an index for speed and does not embed text itself.

prompt: Which Chroma where clause keeps chunks for company "acme" from year 2025 onwards?
optionA: {"company": "acme", "year": {"$gte": 2025}} with no $and
optionB: {"$and": [{"company": "acme"}, {"year": {"$lte": 2025}}]}
optionC: {"$and": [{"company": "acme"}, {"year": {"$gte": 2025}}]}
correctAnswerText: {"$and": [{"company": "acme"}, {"year": {"$gte": 2025}}]}
explanation: Chroma needs $and to combine more than one condition, and $gte means "2025 or later". $or would admit other companies' chunks, and $lte selects older ones.

prompt: Which Qdrant filter keeps company 17's chunks but excludes those whose status is "archived"?
optionA: must on company_id = 17, and must on status = archived
optionB: must on company_id = 17, and must_not on status = archived
optionC: must_not on company_id = 17, and must on status = archived
optionD: should on company_id = 17, and should on status = archived
correctAnswerText: must on company_id = 17, and must_not on status = archived
explanation: must conditions all have to hold and must_not conditions must all fail, which is exactly "company 17 and not archived". should means at least one holds; must on status keeps only archived chunks.

prompt: A pgvector table has an HNSW index with vector_cosine_ops. Which query returns one company's five closest chunks using that index?
optionA: WHERE company_id = $2 ORDER BY embedding <-> $1 LIMIT 5
optionB: WHERE company_id = $2 ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 DESC LIMIT 5
optionC: WHERE company_id = $2 ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5
optionD: WHERE embedding <=> $1 > 0.5 ORDER BY company_id LIMIT 5
correctAnswerText: WHERE company_id = $2 ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5
explanation: <=> is cosine distance and matches vector_cosine_ops; ascending order puts the closest first. <-> is L2 and skips the index; DESC returns the farthest chunks; ordering by company_id does no nearest-neighbour search.

prompt: A store will hold 2 million chunks as 768-dimension float32 vectors. Roughly how much do the raw vectors need, before the HNSW graph?
optionA: About 3.1 GB, at 1,536 bytes per vector
optionB: About 6.1 GB, at 3,072 bytes per vector
optionC: About 61 GB, at 30,720 bytes per vector
optionD: About 1.5 GB, at 768 bytes per vector
correctAnswerText: About 6.1 GB, at 3,072 bytes per vector
explanation: float32 is 4 bytes: 768 × 4 = 3,072 bytes per vector, × 2,000,000 ≈ 6.1 GB. The graph links and payloads come on top; 768 bytes per vector would be int8 quantisation.

prompt: The travel policy has been rewritten and re-chunked. What should ingestion do in the vector store?
optionA: Delete every point whose source is the file, then insert
optionB: Drop and rebuild the whole collection for every change
optionC: Upsert the new chunks only, trusting ids to cover the rest
optionD: Insert the new chunks and leave the old ones beside them
correctAnswerText: Delete every point whose source is the file, then insert
explanation: Deleting by source removes every old chunk, however many the new version has, and the insert adds the current ones. Upsert alone leaves orphans; rebuilding everything for one file causes needless downtime.

prompt: The 2024 leave policy must now be marked status "superseded" in Qdrant. Which operation fits?
optionA: Re-embed every chunk with the status inserted in the text
optionB: set_payload on its points, leaving the vectors as they are
optionC: Delete the points and upload them to a second collection
optionD: Recreate the collection with a new distance metric set
correctAnswerText: set_payload on its points, leaving the vectors as they are
explanation: Only metadata changes, so a payload update is enough; queries then exclude superseded points with a must_not filter. Re-embedding or moving collections does work the change does not need.

prompt: On 200 sample queries, the HNSW top 10 overlaps exact search by only 0.88. What should you do first?
optionA: Accept it, since approximate indexes cannot be tuned at all
optionB: Switch the metric from cosine to L2 and rebuild the index
optionC: Lower ef_search so each query finishes faster than before
optionD: Raise ef_search and re-measure until overlap passes ~0.95
correctAnswerText: Raise ef_search and re-measure until overlap passes ~0.95
explanation: ef_search is the query-time knob: more candidates find more true neighbours at some latency cost. Re-measure after each change; rebuilding with higher m or ef_construction is the next lever if needed.

prompt: A Chroma collection in cosine space returns a distance of 0.30 for a chunk. What cosine similarity is that?
explanation: Chroma's cosine distance is 1 − similarity, so similarity = 1 − 0.30 = 0.70. Converting at the store boundary lets the rest of the code use one "higher is better" convention.

prompt: A pgvector ivfflat index with lists = 100 misses many true neighbours. Which setting do you raise first?
optionA: ivfflat.probes, so more clusters are searched per query
optionB: lists, raised to 10,000 without rebuilding the index
optionC: hnsw.ef_search, so the graph keeps more candidates
optionD: The LIMIT, so that more rows come back from the query
correctAnswerText: ivfflat.probes, so more clusters are searched per query
explanation: IVF recall depends on how many of its lists a query scans; probes raises that at some cost in speed. hnsw.ef_search does nothing for an ivfflat index, and lists only changes on rebuild.

prompt: A client company asks for all its data to be deleted from a shared multi-tenant RAG store. What does the job include?
optionA: Delete the source files only, since vectors hold no text
optionB: Remove its company_id from the router so it is never searched
optionC: Mark its points superseded so filters hide them from users
optionD: Delete its points by company_id, its files and caches; verify zero
correctAnswerText: Delete its points by company_id, its files and caches; verify zero
explanation: Every point with that company_id, the source files, parsed text and caches keyed by the tenant must go, then a count query should return zero. Hiding is not deleting, and payloads usually hold the chunk text.

prompt: Search over 2 million pgvector rows takes 1.4 s and EXPLAIN shows a Seq Scan. The index uses vector_cosine_ops; the query orders by <#>. Diagnosis?
optionA: <#> is inner product, which a cosine index cannot serve
optionB: EXPLAIN always shows a Seq Scan for vector columns
optionC: pgvector cannot index tables larger than one million rows
optionD: The query needs DESC, as inner product sorts in reverse
correctAnswerText: <#> is inner product, which a cosine index cannot serve
explanation: <#> is negative inner product and needs vector_ip_ops; with vector_cosine_ops only <=> uses the index. The planner falls back to scanning every row, correct but slow, so check EXPLAIN after any query change.

prompt: After each nightly re-ingest, the same passage appears several times in results and the point count keeps rising. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The HNSW graph duplicates points when it is rebalanced
optionB: Nightly backups are being restored into the live store
optionC: Payload indexes copy each point once for every field
optionD: Point ids are random per run, so upserts never replace
correctAnswerText: Point ids are random per run, so upserts never replace
explanation: With ids from uuid4 (or any per-run value), every ingest inserts fresh points beside the old ones. uuid5 of the chunk id makes the id stable so upsert overwrites.

prompt: Moving from Chroma to Qdrant, a developer keeps "keep if score <= 0.4". The bot now cites irrelevant chunks and drops good ones. Why?
optionA: Qdrant has no metadata filters, so all chunks appear
optionB: Qdrant returns similarity, so the rule keeps the worst
optionC: Qdrant normalises scores so that all land near 0.4
optionD: Qdrant scores run from 0 to 100, so every chunk passes
correctAnswerText: Qdrant returns similarity, so the rule keeps the worst
explanation: Chroma reports distance (lower is closer) and Qdrant similarity (higher is closer), so a rule written for one selects the opposite chunks in the other. Convert at the store boundary and test with a known pair.

prompt: Every query now fails with "expected dim: 384, got 1536" after the query service was moved to a hosted embedding API. What happened?
optionA: The collection lost its index and must be rebuilt
optionB: Payload indexes limit queries to 384 dimensions only
optionC: Queries use a different model from the stored vectors
optionD: The hosted API returns vectors without normalising them
correctAnswerText: Queries use a different model from the stored vectors
explanation: The collection holds 384-dimension vectors from a local model; queries now come from a 1,536-dimension model. Padding or truncating would hide the error but not make the spaces comparable — re-embed into a new collection.

prompt: One HNSW collection serves 300 companies. Code takes the top 10 and then keeps the caller's company; small companies often get nothing. Diagnosis?
optionA: Top 10 is too few; raising it to 50 fully solves the issue
optionB: Small companies' vectors need a score boost before ranking
optionC: Post-filtering; filter inside the search on an indexed field
optionD: The index m is too small to reach small companies' vectors
correctAnswerText: Post-filtering; filter inside the search on an indexed field
explanation: Other tenants fill the top 10 before the filter runs. Filtering during the search, with a payload index or a SQL WHERE, ranks only the caller's chunks; a larger k only makes the failure rarer.

prompt: A Qdrant server's unfiltered searches stay fast, but searches filtered by company_id slow steadily as data grows. What is most likely missing?
optionA: A payload index on company_id
optionB: A second vector per point
optionC: A larger ef_construction value
optionD: A shorter vector dimension
correctAnswerText: A payload index on company_id
explanation: Only the filtered path degrades, which points at the filter itself. Creating a payload index on company_id lets Qdrant apply it efficiently during the search; graph and vector settings affect all queries alike.

prompt: A Chroma collection created with default settings ranks some chunks differently from the cosine scores the team computes offline with the same vectors. Why?
optionA: Chroma ranks by the order in which chunks were inserted
optionB: Chroma rounds vectors to integers before it compares them
optionC: Chroma defaults to L2; cosine must be set when it is created
optionD: Offline cosine is wrong, since cosine needs a GPU to compute
correctAnswerText: Chroma defaults to L2; cosine must be set when it is created
explanation: Chroma's default space is L2. For unnormalised vectors L2 also counts length, so rankings drift from cosine. The metric is fixed at creation, so the collection must be rebuilt with cosine space.

prompt: After moving from brute force to HNSW with a low ef_search, a few known-correct chunks no longer appear in the top 10. What is going on?
optionA: The approximate walk stops early and misses true neighbours
optionB: HNSW only returns chunks that were inserted most recently
optionC: HNSW deleted those chunks to keep the graph within memory
optionD: The vectors were re-normalised when the graph was built
correctAnswerText: The approximate walk stops early and misses true neighbours
explanation: HNSW trades recall for speed; a small candidate list ends the search before every true neighbour is found. Measure overlap with exact search and raise ef_search until it is acceptable.

prompt: An ivfflat index was created on an empty table during migration, then 500,000 rows were loaded. Recall is poor even with more probes. Diagnosis?
optionA: The rows were loaded in the wrong order for the clusters
optionB: Its clusters came from no data; rebuild it after loading
optionC: probes is ignored whenever the table was empty at creation
optionD: ivfflat cannot hold more than 100,000 rows in any table
correctAnswerText: Its clusters came from no data; rebuild it after loading
explanation: IVF learns its list centres from the data present at build time. Built on an empty table, the clusters do not describe the real vectors, so even generous probing scans the wrong lists; rebuild after loading.

prompt: An FAQ shrank from 20 chunks to 12 and was re-ingested by upsert. The bot still quotes a question that was removed. Diagnosis?
optionA: The embedding model remembers text from earlier ingestions
optionB: Upsert failed because the chunk count did not match before
optionC: Eight old chunks were never deleted and remain searchable
optionD: The new chunks were rejected because their ids already exist
correctAnswerText: Eight old chunks were never deleted and remain searchable
explanation: Upsert overwrote ids 0–11 and left 12–19, which still hold the removed content. Delete by source (or delete ids not in the new set) before inserting the new version.

prompt: A team runs PostgreSQL, has 300,000 chunks, and must join results to its permissions tables. Which store is best justified?
optionA: pgvector, keeping vectors next to the data they must join
optionB: A new dedicated vector database, since it benchmarks faster
optionC: A flat file of vectors, searched by a loop in the app code
optionD: An in-memory prototype store, since the corpus is small
correctAnswerText: pgvector, keeping vectors next to the data they must join
explanation: At this size pgvector performs well, and SQL joins, transactions and the existing backups favour it. A second database adds operations for no gain the workload needs; prototype and flat-file options lack durability.

prompt: Vectors are the main workload: 50 million points, heavy filtered search per tenant, no existing database to reuse. Which choice fits best?
optionA: An embedded prototype store, run inside the web process
optionB: A relational table with no vector index, filtered in SQL
optionC: Brute-force search in application memory on every query
optionD: A dedicated vector store with in-search filters and indexes
correctAnswerText: A dedicated vector store with in-search filters and indexes
explanation: When vectors dominate and filtered search must scale, a dedicated store such as Qdrant with payload indexes and filtering during the graph walk is the fit. Embedded or brute-force options do not scale to 50 million.

prompt: A two-day hackathon demo searches 2,000 FAQ chunks on one laptop. Which store choice is most sensible?
optionA: A replicated vector cluster with payload indexes on all fields
optionB: pgvector with an IVF index tuned for many millions of rows
optionC: An embedded store such as Chroma, kept as simple as possible
optionD: A custom HNSW library written from scratch for the demo
correctAnswerText: An embedded store such as Chroma, kept as simple as possible
explanation: Chroma suits prototypes and small embedded apps; at 2,000 chunks even brute force is instant. Cluster operations and index tuning are effort the demo does not need — choose on operations, not benchmarks.

prompt: How should a RAG service for many client companies isolate tenants in its vector store?
optionA: A router model that infers the company from the question's wording
optionB: A tenant id that the client app sends in the body of each request
optionC: One shared collection with no filter, trusting the model to stay quiet
optionD: Server-set tenant filter on an indexed field; own collections if strict
correctAnswerText: Server-set tenant filter on an indexed field; own collections if strict
explanation: The tenant comes from the authenticated session on the server and is applied as an indexed filter inside every search; where isolation or deletion must be absolute, a collection per tenant is the simplest guarantee. Request fields and model judgements can be forged or steered.

prompt: Index memory must shrink and slightly lower recall is acceptable. Which change is best justified?
optionA: Lower m or try IVF, then re-measure recall against exact
optionB: Raise ef_search, which reduces the memory each query uses
optionC: Raise m and ef_construction to build a denser graph
optionD: Switch the metric to L2, which halves index memory
correctAnswerText: Lower m or try IVF, then re-measure recall against exact
explanation: Fewer links per vector, or IVF's lighter structure, cut memory at some cost in recall — which must then be measured. A denser graph uses more memory; ef_search is a query-time setting and the metric does not change storage.

prompt: An engineer sets ef_search to 1,000 on every query "to get the best recall". How should this be judged?
optionA: Choose it from a measured recall-versus-latency curve
optionB: Correct, since a higher ef_search never costs anything
optionC: Wrong, since ef_search can never be set above 100
optionD: Correct, since it also cuts the memory the graph uses
correctAnswerText: Choose it from a measured recall-versus-latency curve
explanation: Each step up in ef_search buys less recall for more latency. Measure overlap with exact search at several values and pick the smallest that meets the target, usually around 0.95, within the latency budget.

prompt: When a policy is replaced, should its old chunks be deleted from the store or kept with version metadata?
optionA: Deleted, then re-added whenever someone asks
optionB: Kept with version and dates, filtered out by default
optionC: Kept with no metadata, letting the model choose
optionD: Deleted, since old rules are never needed again
correctAnswerText: Kept with version and dates, filtered out by default
explanation: Version and effective-date metadata with a default filter excludes superseded rules from normal answers while still allowing "what was the rule last year?". Leaving the choice to the model invites mixed answers.

prompt: A blog shows store X 20% faster than pgvector on a public benchmark. Your team runs only Postgres, with 200,000 vectors and fast queries today. Switch?
optionA: No: dedicated vector stores are never faster than pgvector
optionB: Yes: a 20% benchmark lead outweighs every operational cost
optionC: Yes: pgvector cannot be used once a team has over 100,000 rows
optionD: No: decide on operations and your own load, not that benchmark
correctAnswerText: No: decide on operations and your own load, not that benchmark
explanation: Queries are already fast and a second database adds operations, backups and failure modes. A benchmark on someone else's data is weak evidence; move when your own load shows a need.

prompt: A team weighs running BM25 as a separate service against storing dense and sparse vectors per point and fusing with RRF in one store query. What favours the single-store design?
optionA: Sparse vectors make the dense half of the search unnecessary
optionB: A separate BM25 service cannot ever handle codes or acronyms
optionC: In-store fusion guarantees higher recall on every question
optionD: One query applies the same filters to both lists, one system
correctAnswerText: One query applies the same filters to both lists, one system
explanation: Prefetching a dense and a sparse list in one query keeps tenant and version filters consistent and removes a second system to run. Fusion quality is unchanged in principle, so it must still be checked on the golden set.

prompt: A team must move its store to a new embedding model with no downtime. Which migration plan is best?
optionA: Average old and new vectors per chunk so both spaces still work
optionB: Overwrite vectors in place, one document at a time, while live
optionC: Re-embed new documents only and keep the old vectors as they are
optionD: New collection beside the old, compare on the golden set, switch
correctAnswerText: New collection beside the old, compare on the golden set, switch
explanation: Vectors from two models are not comparable, so a mixed store breaks search. Building the new collection alongside, recording the model name with it, and switching the alias only after it wins on the golden set avoids downtime and regressions.

prompt: Which source gives an eval set its most valuable cases, according to the course?
optionA: Examples copied from the model provider's documentation
optionB: The first two hundred rows of last week's request logs
optionC: Questions an LLM writes in bulk from a short list of topics
optionD: Complaints and thumbs-down answers with a known wrong output
correctAnswerText: Complaints and thumbs-down answers with a known wrong output
explanation: A complaint is a real input with a known failure, which is exactly what an eval set must catch. Generated questions are cleaner than real ones, and "the first 200 rows" is not a stratified sample.

prompt: In a well-written eval case, what does the expectation describe?
optionA: The token count the answer has to reach
optionB: What any good answer must do or contain
optionC: The exact reference wording to be matched
optionD: The temperature the model must run at
correctAnswerText: What any good answer must do or contain
explanation: Good answers can be worded many ways, so the expectation states required facts, citations, refusals or fields. An exact reference string fails correct paraphrases; token counts and temperature are not expectations.

prompt: What is a held-out eval set?
optionA: Cases generated afresh by a model on each run
optionB: Cases removed because their labels were wrong
optionC: Cases the prompt is tuned against every day
optionD: Cases kept back and run only before a release
correctAnswerText: Cases kept back and run only before a release
explanation: A held-out set is never looked at while tuning, so its score is an honest estimate. The cases you tune against are the dev set, and a prompt tuned on them overfits to them.

prompt: Which of these is a deterministic check on an LLM output?
optionA: Parsing the reply into a schema and checking a field
optionB: Sampling the answer five times and taking a vote
optionC: Asking three reviewers to rate the answer 1 to 5
optionD: Asking a second model whether the tone is polite
correctAnswerText: Parsing the reply into a schema and checking a field
explanation: Schema parsing and exact field comparison give the same verdict every time, cost nothing and are never wrong about what they check. A judge model, human ratings and voting are all opinions or samples.

prompt: What is LLM-as-judge in evaluation?
optionA: A person who checks every model answer before it ships
optionB: A metric that counts the words shared with a reference
optionC: A model that writes new cases to add to the eval set
optionD: A second model grading answers against a written rubric
correctAnswerText: A second model grading answers against a written rubric
explanation: A judge is another model prompted with a rubric to score open-ended qualities. Generating cases, human review and word-overlap metrics are separate tools; the judge is itself a prompt that can be wrong.

prompt: What does Cohen's kappa measure when a judge is checked against human graders?
optionA: Agreement beyond what chance alone would produce
optionB: How many tokens the judge spends per verdict
optionC: How long the judge takes to grade each answer
optionD: The share of answers that the judge marked PASS
correctAnswerText: Agreement beyond what chance alone would produce
explanation: Kappa = (observed − chance) / (1 − chance). It corrects raw agreement for the agreement two raters would reach by guessing at their own pass rates, which raw agreement does not.

prompt: In RAG evaluation, what is recall@k?
optionA: The share of gold chunks found in the top k results
optionB: The number of chunks stored in the vector index
optionC: The rank at which the first relevant chunk appears
optionD: The share of top-k chunks that the model then quoted
correctAnswerText: The share of gold chunks found in the top k results
explanation: Recall@k asks how many of the chunks that hold the answer were retrieved in the top k. The rank of the first hit is what reciprocal rank uses; what the model quoted is a generation question.

prompt: What does faithfulness (groundedness) measure for a RAG answer?
optionA: How many of the retrieved chunks it chose to cite
optionB: How closely its wording matches the reference answer
optionC: The share of its claims supported by the retrieved context
optionD: Whether the model produced it at temperature zero
correctAnswerText: The share of its claims supported by the retrieved context
explanation: Faithfulness splits the answer into claims and checks each against the retrieved context; one unsupported claim in a policy answer is a hallucination. It needs no reference answer, unlike correctness.

prompt: In an eval gate, what is a floor?
optionA: The largest drop allowed against the last baseline run
optionB: The smallest number of cases the CI job will accept
optionC: The lowest temperature the model is allowed to use
optionD: An absolute minimum a metric must meet, whatever the baseline
correctAnswerText: An absolute minimum a metric must meet, whatever the baseline
explanation: A floor such as "safety at 100%" applies whatever last month's score was. The allowed drop against the baseline is the separate no-regression rule; a gate needs both.

prompt: What is shadow testing of a new prompt or model?
optionA: A small share of users is served its answers for feedback
optionB: Its answers are shown to everyone, with a beta label on top
optionC: Live requests copied to it, with users shown only current answers
optionD: It runs only on the held-out eval set, on a nightly schedule
correctAnswerText: Live requests copied to it, with users shown only current answers
explanation: In shadow mode the candidate's answers are logged and scored offline; no user sees them. Serving a small share of users is a canary, which comes later and does expose users.

prompt: Why is a 50-case eval set poor at telling an 88% prompt from a 91% one?
optionA: The judge model tires and grows lenient after forty cases
optionB: Fifty cases always overstate the pass rate of a newer prompt
optionC: Pass rates can only be compared on sets of exactly 100 cases
optionD: Its 95% range is about ±8 points, so 3 points is within noise
correctAnswerText: Its 95% range is about ±8 points, so 3 points is within noise
explanation: With n = 50 and p ≈ 0.9 the standard error is about 0.042, so the 95% range is roughly ±8 points. A 3-point change is inside it. Small sets are noisy, not biased upward, and judges do not tire.

prompt: Why should an eval report give pass rates per slice and not only overall?
optionA: Per-slice rates use fewer tokens than one overall run
optionB: A large slice can hide a small one that fails badly
optionC: An overall rate cannot be calculated from JSONL results
optionD: Most CI systems refuse to store a single overall number
correctAnswerText: A large slice can hide a small one that fails badly
explanation: "92% overall" can be 98% on English and 68% on Hinglish. Slice rates, each with a floor, reveal the failure the average hides. Token use and file formats have nothing to do with it.

prompt: Why is an exact-match reference string a poor expectation for an open-ended answer?
optionA: Exact match needs a judge model to run, which costs more
optionB: Correct answers vary in wording and would wrongly fail
optionC: Reference strings cannot be kept in a versioned file
optionD: Exact match passes answers that contain wrong numbers
correctAnswerText: Correct answers vary in wording and would wrongly fail
explanation: A perfectly good answer worded differently fails an exact match, so the check is too strict, not too lenient. Required facts, citations and refusals are the robust expectations; exact match needs no judge.

prompt: Why can embedding similarity to a reference not certify a factual answer?
optionA: It only works on answers shorter than one sentence in length
optionB: It needs a human to label every answer before it can be used
optionC: It measures topic closeness, so a wrong number still scores high
optionD: It changes value every time the same answer is embedded
correctAnswerText: It measures topic closeness, so a wrong number still scores high
explanation: "Refunds take 2 days" and "Refunds take 10 days" are near-identical vectors. Similarity is useful to flag answers that drifted off topic, never to certify facts, which need must-contain checks or a judge with the source.

prompt: Why does the course advise one criterion and a PASS/FAIL verdict per judge call?
optionA: A 1–10 scale is not allowed in JSON output by most providers
optionB: Binary verdicts let the judge skip reading the source text
optionC: Judges can only return one token, so two values never fit
optionD: Vague scales drift and get lenient; a binary call is checkable
correctAnswerText: Vague scales drift and get lenient; a binary call is checkable
explanation: An undefined 1–10 scale clusters around 7–9 for good and bad answers alike. One precise criterion with a defined binary verdict, given the material a human grader would have, can be checked against people.

prompt: Why is raw agreement with human graders a misleading score for a judge?
optionA: Raw agreement counts only failed answers, never the passed ones
optionB: Humans disagree with each other too often for agreement to count
optionC: A judge that always says PASS agrees often when most answers pass
optionD: Raw agreement falls whenever the judge runs at temperature zero
correctAnswerText: A judge that always says PASS agrees often when most answers pass
explanation: If 70% of answers are good, a judge that passes everything agrees 70% of the time and has learnt nothing (kappa 0). Kappa and recall on human-failed answers expose this; raw agreement does not.

prompt: Why can a RAG answer be correct yet unfaithful?
optionA: Faithfulness counts only answers that copy the reference text
optionB: It may come from the model's memory when no context supported it
optionC: A correct answer is unfaithful whenever recall@k is above 0.9
optionD: Correct answers are always unfaithful when they cite a chunk
correctAnswerText: It may come from the model's memory when no context supported it
explanation: If nothing relevant was retrieved and the model answered from pre-training, the answer can be right today and wrong next time. For a policy assistant, faithful to your documents comes first.

prompt: Why does an eval gate need floors as well as a no-regression rule?
optionA: No-regression rules only apply to the first release of a feature
optionB: Baselines expire monthly, after which only floors are checked
optionC: Floors are cheaper to compute than a baseline comparison
optionD: A slice can stay below acceptable forever without ever dropping
correctAnswerText: A slice can stay below acceptable forever without ever dropping
explanation: No-regression only stops things getting worse; a safety slice stuck at 96% passes every week. A 100% floor forces it to be fixed. Cost and baseline age are not the reason.

prompt: When two prompts are compared on the same cases, why do only the disagreements matter?
optionA: Disagreeing cases are the only ones the judge is able to grade
optionB: Only disagreeing cases are cheap enough to run on the real model
optionC: Cases both pass or both fail say nothing about which is better
optionD: Agreeing cases are always wrongly labelled and should be dropped
correctAnswerText: Cases both pass or both fail say nothing about which is better
explanation: A case both prompts pass, or both fail, carries no information about the difference. A paired (McNemar / sign) test asks whether the split of the disagreements could be a coin flip.

prompt: Why are two scores comparable only when they come from the same eval set version?
optionA: Added or changed cases shift the score for any prompt
optionB: A new version re-orders cases, and order sets the score
optionC: Each version is graded by a different judge model by design
optionD: Versions use different pass marks that cannot be converted
correctAnswerText: Added or changed cases shift the score for any prompt
explanation: New cases are often harder ones from complaints, so any prompt scores lower on the new version. Re-run the baseline on the same version before comparing; case order does not affect the score.

prompt: A Kannada-and-English bank support bot scores 96% on an eval set generated entirely by a model, but complaints are rising. What should be added?
optionA: Real cases sampled from logs and complaint tickets, by slice
optionB: A stricter judge that fails any answer longer than 80 words
optionC: A higher temperature so the bot's answers vary more often
optionD: Another hundred generated cases in the same polished style
correctAnswerText: Real cases sampled from logs and complaint tickets, by slice
explanation: Generated questions are polite and well-formed; real users mix languages, make typos and ask two things at once. Logs and complaints bring that reality in. More of the same synthetic cases repeats the blind spot.

prompt: A team wants a pass-rate estimate within about ±3 points at 95% confidence for a bot near 90%. Roughly how many cases do they need?
optionA: Around 40,000 cases
optionB: Around 50 cases
optionC: Around 20 cases
optionD: Around 400 cases
correctAnswerText: Around 400 cases
explanation: At p = 0.9, 1.96 × √(0.09 / 400) ≈ 0.029, about ±3 points. Fifty cases give about ±8 points; 40,000 is far more than needed for this precision.

prompt: A ticket triage model returns JSON with a priority of P1–P4. Which check should run first in its eval?
optionA: Parse the JSON and compare the priority with the label
optionB: Compute embedding similarity to a reference ticket reply
optionC: Ask a judge to rate how sensible the priority looks, 1–10
optionD: Measure ROUGE between the output and a written rationale
correctAnswerText: Parse the JSON and compare the priority with the label
explanation: A priority is a structured field with one right value, so an exact comparison is free and unambiguous. A judge adds cost and noise to a question with a definite answer; ROUGE and similarity do not measure the label.

prompt: Retrieved, in rank order: h4, h9, h2, h7. The gold chunks are h2 and h5. What is recall@3?
explanation: The top 3 are h4, h9 and h2; one of the two gold chunks (h2) is among them, so recall@3 = 1/2. h5 was never retrieved. 0.33 is the reciprocal of h2's rank, not recall.

prompt: Retrieved, in rank order: p8, p1, p6. The only gold chunk is p6. What is the reciprocal rank?
optionA: One third, about 0.33
optionB: Zero, as it is not ranked first
optionC: One, since it was retrieved
optionD: Three, the rank itself
correctAnswerText: One third, about 0.33
explanation: Reciprocal rank is 1 / (rank of the first gold chunk) = 1/3. It is zero only when no gold chunk is retrieved, and 1 only when the gold chunk is first; 3 is the rank, not its reciprocal.

prompt: Safety was 100% at baseline. A PR scores 99% overall and 95% on safety; safety has a 100% floor and there is a 2-point no-regression allowance. What should the gate do?
optionA: Pass: a 5-point drop on one slice is ordinary judge noise
optionB: Pass: the overall score is high and within the allowance
optionC: Warn only, since floors apply to the overall pass rate
optionD: Block: safety is below its floor, whatever the overall score
correctAnswerText: Block: safety is below its floor, whatever the overall score
explanation: Safety at 95% breaks its absolute 100% floor and also falls more than 2 points below baseline. A high overall rate does not excuse a slice that must never fail.

prompt: A pairwise judge picks whichever answer is shown first, in both orders. How should that comparison be recorded?
optionA: As a win for the longer answer, which the judge preferred
optionB: As a tie, since the verdict followed position not content
optionC: As a win for whichever answer was shown first originally
optionD: As a judge crash, to be re-run until the verdicts differ
correctAnswerText: As a tie, since the verdict followed position not content
explanation: A verdict that flips with the order is position bias. Running both orders and keeping only consistent verdicts removes it; here neither answer has been shown to be better.

prompt: Which of these changes should trigger the real-model eval run in CI for an HR assistant?
optionA: Renaming a CSS class on the chat page's send button
optionB: Updating the README's setup steps for new developers
optionC: Changing the retriever's k from 4 to 8 in the config file
optionD: Adding a unit test for the date-formatting helper
correctAnswerText: Changing the retriever's k from 4 to 8 in the config file
explanation: Anything that changes outputs is a release: prompts, model settings, retrieval configuration, tools, guardrail rules. A retrieval k change alters every answer; styling, docs and helper tests do not.

prompt: A team wants a new model in front of real users, a few at first, watching thumbs-down and escalations. Which approach fits?
optionA: Swapping the model alias for everyone on one night
optionB: A canary at a small share of traffic, then widen
optionC: Shadow mode, logging its answers without showing them
optionD: Running the held-out set again on a different laptop
correctAnswerText: A canary at a small share of traffic, then widen
explanation: A canary serves the candidate to a small share of users and widens as signals stay healthy. Shadow mode shows nobody, so it cannot measure user reactions; a big-bang switch has no safety margin.

prompt: A production answer wrongly told an employee that casual leave carries forward. Beyond fixing the prompt, what completes the fix?
optionA: Add the input to the eval set with the behaviour wanted
optionB: Raise the judge's pass mark for every leave question
optionC: Ask the employee to rephrase and try the question again
optionD: Delete the conversation from the logs so it is not reused
correctAnswerText: Add the input to the eval set with the behaviour wanted
explanation: Every bug becomes a case: the failing input, redacted, with the expected behaviour (here must-contain "lapse"). Then a future change cannot quietly bring the bug back.

prompt: A RAG case scores recall@3 = 0 and the answer is wrong. What should the team investigate?
optionA: The judge rubric, since recall@3 = 0 is always a labelling error
optionB: Generation: the prompt, since the model ignored good context
optionC: The temperature, since randomness hid the right chunk from it
optionD: Retrieval: chunking, embeddings or k, since the text never arrived
correctAnswerText: Retrieval: chunking, embeddings or k, since the text never arrived
explanation: With recall@3 = 0 the answer was never in the context, so no prompt could have produced it. The fix is on the retrieval side, re-measured with recall on the affected cases.

prompt: Recall@5 is 0.96 but faithfulness is 0.58 on a policy assistant. Which explanation fits the numbers best?
optionA: The right text arrives, but the answers go beyond it
optionB: The chunks are far too large to be retrieved correctly
optionC: The embedding model maps different policies to one vector
optionD: The eval set holds too few cases to measure recall at all
correctAnswerText: The right text arrives, but the answers go beyond it
explanation: High recall means the context usually holds the answer; low faithfulness means the model adds claims. Work on the prompt (answer only from context, cite each claim) or the model, not on retrieval settings.

prompt: A faithfulness judge shows 0.85 raw agreement and kappa 0.58, and catches 3 of the 6 answers humans failed. What is the main problem?
optionA: Kappa is undefined because the classes are not balanced
optionB: It fails too many good answers, so releases would stall
optionC: It misses half the real failures, so bad releases would pass
optionD: Its agreement is too high to be believable for any judge
correctAnswerText: It misses half the real failures, so bad releases would pass
explanation: Recall on human failures of 50% means half the bad answers sail through. Kappa 0.58 is only moderate; the fix is a sharper rubric, re-measured on a fresh sample. The judge is lenient, not strict.

prompt: An eval passes the answer "GST is filed quarterly" because its embedding similarity to "GST is filed monthly" is 0.96. What is the design fault?
optionA: The pass threshold was too low and should be raised to 0.99
optionB: Embeddings must be normalised before cosine is computed
optionC: Similarity was used to certify a fact it cannot distinguish
optionD: The reference should have been written in shorter words
correctAnswerText: Similarity was used to certify a fact it cannot distinguish
explanation: Sentences about the same topic sit close whatever the key fact says. Raising the threshold does not fix it; the fact needs a must-contain check or a judge given the source text.

prompt: A judge keeps passing long, confident answers that add rules not in the policy. Which bias and gap explain this best?
optionA: Self-preference, since all long answers come from humans
optionB: Low temperature, which makes judges favour short answers
optionC: Position bias, since long answers are always shown first
optionD: Verbosity bias, with no source text to check claims against
correctAnswerText: Verbosity bias, with no source text to check claims against
explanation: Judges tend to reward length, and a judge without the policy text cannot tell a confident invention from a supported claim. Add "length is not a merit", give it the source, and test with a padded wrong answer.

prompt: After two weeks of tuning a prompt on every dev case, the dev set scores 99% but the held-out set scores 84%. What happened?
optionA: The prompt overfitted to the dev cases it was tuned on
optionB: The held-out set must contain wrongly labelled cases
optionC: The held-out set is too large to give a stable estimate
optionD: The model provider changed the model during the two weeks
correctAnswerText: The prompt overfitted to the dev cases it was tuned on
explanation: Tuning against the same cases again and again overfits the prompt to them, like training on the test set. The held-out set is the honest estimate; blaming its labels without evidence hides the problem.

prompt: On 200 shared cases, prompt B passes 12 that A fails and A passes 9 that B fails. What is the honest reading?
optionA: A is better, because the cases it won are harder by nature
optionB: The test is invalid, since both prompts used the same cases
optionC: A 12-to-9 split of disagreements is no evidence of a difference
optionD: B is better, because it passes three more of the same cases
correctAnswerText: A 12-to-9 split of disagreements is no evidence of a difference
explanation: Only the 21 disagreements carry information, and 12 against 9 is close to a coin flip. Using the same cases is what makes the comparison fair. The 9 cases A won are the regressions B would ship.

prompt: A "friendlier tone" PR is blocked: leave edge cases fell from 100% to 0%. The diff swapped "give no number the context lacks" for "always give a clear answer". What is the cause?
optionA: Leave cases cannot be scored once the tone is informal
optionB: The eval set changed version in the same pull request
optionC: Friendly greetings use up tokens needed for the citations
optionD: The new line pushes the model to invent definite rules
correctAnswerText: The new line pushes the model to invent definite rules
explanation: "Always give a clear answer" removed the guard against invented numbers, so the model now states a carry-forward limit the policy lacks. Read the failing cases and the diff, not just the totals; tone itself was not the problem.

prompt: A new prompt passed the offline gate, but in a 5% canary the escalation rate doubled. What does this most likely show?
optionA: The gate's floors were set much too strictly to be useful
optionB: The eval gate must have been run on the wrong branch
optionC: Real traffic holds cases the eval set does not yet cover
optionD: The canary share was too small to show any real signal
correctAnswerText: Real traffic holds cases the eval set does not yet cover
explanation: The eval set is what the team thought of; production is what users do. Roll back or hold the canary, find the escalated cases, and add them to the set as the next version.

prompt: An HR case expects must_contain "lapse". A correct answer says unused leave "expires on 31 December" and fails. What is the fault?
optionA: The answer should have been checked by exact match instead
optionB: The model is wrong, since "expires" differs from "lapse"
optionC: Must-contain checks cannot run on lowercase text at all
optionD: The expectation pins one word instead of the fact itself
