prompt: Why does deleting a user's row from the main table rarely complete erasure in an AI feature?
optionA: Deleted rows are always restored automatically from the nightly backup
optionB: Embeddings, caches, logs and datasets hold copies no foreign key links
optionC: Relational databases cannot delete rows that contain free-form text
optionD: The model provider's weights have absorbed the user's data at inference
correctAnswerText: Embeddings, caches, logs and datasets hold copies no foreign key links
explanation: AI features copy text into vector stores, caches, prompt logs, eval sets and fine-tuning files. Inference calls do not normally put data into a provider's weights.

prompt: Why does a screening pipeline remove protected details the task does not need before the model sees them?
optionA: It lets the model infer those details more accurately
optionB: It makes the prompt shorter, which is the main benefit of it
optionC: The model cannot be swayed by a detail it never receives
optionD: The law forbids storing any name in a résumé database
correctAnswerText: The model cannot be swayed by a detail it never receives
explanation: Minimising inputs removes the channel through which a learnt skew can act. The model should never be asked to infer gender, religion or caste either.

prompt: Why report a support bot's answer quality separately for English, Hinglish and Tamil?
optionA: An overall average can hide a slice that is much worse
optionB: Regulators only accept metrics reported in one language
optionC: Each language needs a completely different model to run
optionD: Separate reports make the overall score look higher
correctAnswerText: An overall average can hide a slice that is much worse
explanation: Uneven quality across languages or accents is a form of bias. Slice metrics with their own floors expose it; one blended number lets the majority slice mask it.

prompt: Why should an HR assistant say plainly what it cannot help with and offer a route to a person?
optionA: It stops the model from ever making a mistake in its answers
optionB: It lets the company avoid keeping any logs of the conversation
optionC: Users can then judge its answers and reach help it cannot give
optionD: It reduces the number of tokens the model has to generate
correctAnswerText: Users can then judge its answers and reach help it cannot give
explanation: Transparency — saying it is an AI, showing sources, stating limits and offering a human — lets people calibrate their trust. It does not make the model error-free.

prompt: Why do enterprise customers increasingly ask vendors about ISO/IEC 42001 rather than only the NIST AI RMF?
optionA: Organisations can be certified against 42001; the RMF has no certification
optionB: The NIST AI RMF applies only to US government departments and agencies
optionC: ISO/IEC 42001 is mandatory by law for every AI product sold in India
optionD: The NIST AI RMF was withdrawn and replaced entirely by ISO/IEC 42001
correctAnswerText: Organisations can be certified against 42001; the RMF has no certification
explanation: A certificate is third-party evidence a vendor review can rely on. The NIST framework is voluntary guidance widely used as vocabulary, but it does not certify anyone.

prompt: Why should governance evidence — gate results, prompt versions, approvals — be produced automatically as work happens?
optionA: It allows the team to skip evaluation runs before a prompt change
optionB: Audits sample evidence; if finding it takes a week, controls are not working
optionC: Auditors refuse any document that a human being has written by hand
optionD: Automatic evidence removes the need for anyone to own a risk at all
correctAnswerText: Audits sample evidence; if finding it takes a week, controls are not working
explanation: An auditor asks for the eval run before the last change and who approved it. Evidence stored per release answers that in minutes and shows the controls actually run.

prompt: Why should a system store each consent together with its purpose and timestamp?
optionA: So the consent can be treated as permanent and never withdrawn
optionB: So the user never has to be shown a notice about their data
optionC: So code can check consent covers this purpose before processing
optionD: So the consent record can be shared with advertisers later on
correctAnswerText: So code can check consent covers this purpose before processing
explanation: Consent is specific to a purpose and can be withdrawn. Recording purpose and time lets processing be checked against it and stopped when it is withdrawn.

prompt: A lender adds an LLM to its loan-application workflow. Which role should the model have?
optionA: Summarise the file; an officer decides, seeing the evidence too
optionB: Decide alone, but only for applicants below a set loan amount
optionC: Decide alone, with officers reviewing a sample once a quarter
optionD: Decide alone, and explain its decision in a polite email
correctAnswerText: Summarise the file; an officer decides, seeing the evidence too
explanation: For consequential decisions about people the model drafts and a person decides, with the evidence in front of them — not just the model's verdict.

prompt: A sales team quietly wired a model into its CRM without telling anyone. Which governance document should make such features visible?
optionA: The model card of the vendor
optionB: The acceptable-use slide deck
optionC: The quarterly sales forecast
optionD: The AI system inventory
correctAnswerText: The AI system inventory
explanation: The inventory lists every AI feature with its models, data sources, owner and risk tier. Shadow AI shows up there or nowhere.

prompt: A risk scores likelihood 4, impact 5. After controls it scores likelihood 2, impact 4. Risks with residual score above 6 must be treated. What is the decision?
optionA: Residual 8: accept it as it is
optionB: Residual 20: treat it further
optionC: Residual 8: treat it further
optionD: Residual 6: accept it as it is
correctAnswerText: Residual 8: treat it further
explanation: Residual risk is residual likelihood × residual impact = 2 × 4 = 8, above the threshold of 6, so it needs more treatment. 20 is the inherent score before controls.

prompt: A company writes down who may approve a model for production and who owns each AI risk. Which NIST AI RMF function is this?
optionA: Map
optionB: Govern
optionC: Measure
optionD: Manage
correctAnswerText: Govern
explanation: Govern covers culture, roles, policies and accountability. Map sets context, Measure evaluates risks and Manage treats them.

prompt: Before building a scholarship-eligibility assistant, a team lists its intended use, who is affected, what could go wrong and the legal duties. Which NIST AI RMF function is that?
optionA: Govern
optionB: Manage
optionC: Map
optionD: Measure
correctAnswerText: Map
explanation: Map establishes context: intended use, affected people, possible harms and obligations. Measuring those risks with tests comes next, under Measure.

prompt: A leave-request summariser sends each employee record to an external model. The record holds name, PAN, phone, leave dates and reason. What should be sent?
optionA: The whole record, since the provider is under a contract
optionB: Only the fields the summary needs, with identifiers redacted
optionC: Nothing at all; summaries must never use an external model
optionD: The whole record, encrypted, so the model can still read it
correctAnswerText: Only the fields the summary needs, with identifiers redacted
explanation: Data minimisation: send only what the task needs. A contract does not make extra fields necessary, and an outright ban ignores that minimised processing can be lawful.

prompt: A user of a RAG note-taking app withdraws consent. No law requires keeping their notes. What must the team do?
optionA: Keep the data but stop sending the user any marketing messages
optionB: Hide the account from search but keep all stored data for analytics
optionC: Delete only the notes created after the date consent was withdrawn
optionD: Stop processing and erase the notes from DB, vectors, caches and logs
correctAnswerText: Stop processing and erase the notes from DB, vectors, caches and logs
explanation: Withdrawal ends processing and the data is erased unless a law requires keeping it — every copy, including embeddings, caches and logs.

prompt: A college uses an LLM to shortlist students for placement interviews. Which test most directly checks whether a student's name changes the score?
optionA: Score identical profiles that differ only in the name
optionB: Ask a judge model whether the prompt sounds neutral
optionC: Compare this year's shortlist rate with last year's
optionD: Count how many names appear in the training corpus
correctAnswerText: Score identical profiles that differ only in the name
explanation: Only a counterfactual pair isolates the name. Year-on-year rates mix in many changes, and a judge reading the prompt says nothing about the model's behaviour.

prompt: A homework-help app for school students will process the children's questions. What does the DPDP Act add for this user group?
optionA: Stricter rules, including verifiable consent from a parent
optionB: An exemption, since school work is not personal data
optionC: Nothing; children's data is treated like any adult's data
optionD: A rule that data must be stored only on the child's phone
correctAnswerText: Stricter rules, including verifiable consent from a parent
explanation: The Act treats children's data more strictly, including verifiable parental consent. The detail is in the rules made under the Act, read with the legal team.

prompt: A security incident hits an Indian company's AI chatbot. Apart from DPDP duties on personal-data breaches, which body's directions on incident reporting apply?
optionA: SEBI
optionB: NASSCOM
optionC: CERT-In
optionD: TRAI
correctAnswerText: CERT-In
explanation: CERT-In directions require specified cybersecurity incidents to be reported within a short deadline. A security incident in an AI feature is still a security incident.

prompt: A résumé screener passes men and women at equal rates at threshold 6.0, yet counterfactual pairs score women 0.5 lower on identical résumés. What explains this?
optionA: There is no bias, because equal rates at one threshold settle the matter
optionB: The model is random, so any two runs will give different averages
optionC: The penalty is real; it moved nobody across 6.0 but would at another line
optionD: The pairs are invalid, since changing only the name is not a real test
correctAnswerText: The penalty is real; it moved nobody across 6.0 but would at another line
explanation: Changing only the name and getting a lower score is exactly what the pair is built to detect. Selection rates depend on where the threshold falls; at 6.75 the same model fails them.

prompt: A screener has no name effect, but takes 1.5 points off any résumé mentioning a career break for family care. How should the review treat this?
optionA: As an issue: it falls mostly on women, so it must be a deliberate policy
optionB: As fine: the rule never looks at names, so it cannot affect any group
optionC: As fine: career breaks are rare, so the effect is too small to matter
optionD: As a data bug: the model must have been given the wrong résumés
correctAnswerText: As an issue: it falls mostly on women, so it must be a deliberate policy
explanation: A neutral-looking rule can fall mostly on one group. It may or may not be acceptable, but it has to be a decision someone owns, not a habit the model picked up.

prompt: A cross-employee retrieval-leak risk goes from L2×I5 to L1×I5 after a metadata filter, and is accepted at residual 5. What does the unchanged impact tell you?
optionA: Controls cut likelihood, not harm, so the filter needs a test on every deploy
optionB: The impact score is wrong, since any control always lowers the impact too
optionC: The risk is now negligible, so it can be removed from the register entirely
optionD: The likelihood score is wrong, since filters cannot change how often leaks occur
correctAnswerText: Controls cut likelihood, not harm, so the filter needs a test on every deploy
explanation: If the control ever fails, the harm is as bad as before. That is the case for a CI test that proves the filter on every deploy, and a named owner of the acceptance.

prompt: An auditor asks for the eval run before the last prompt change and who approved it. It takes the team a week to dig it out. What is the underlying problem?
optionA: The prompt was changed too rarely for there to be any evidence to find
optionB: The model provider failed to send the team its monthly compliance report
optionC: Evidence is not generated as a by-product of releases, so controls are unproven
optionD: The auditor asked for too much, since prompt changes are not ever audited
correctAnswerText: Evidence is not generated as a by-product of releases, so controls are unproven
explanation: Gate results stored per release, prompts versioned in Git and approvals recorded make this a minutes-long lookup. If it takes a week, nobody can show the control ran.

prompt: An HR assistant scores 91% overall on its eval set. Split by language, Tamil questions score 6 points below English. What follows?
optionA: The Tamil eval rows must be mislabelled, since the average is high
optionB: The fix is to drop Tamil questions from the eval set in future runs
optionC: Nothing; the overall score is above target, so slices do not matter
optionD: A real gap the overall score hid; record it as a known limit and treat it
correctAnswerText: A real gap the overall score hid; record it as a known limit and treat it
explanation: Slice metrics exist to catch exactly this. The gap goes in the system card's known limits with a floor and a plan; deleting the slice only hides it.

prompt: Insurance claim reviewers accept the model's recommendation 99.6% of the time and open the claim documents in only a few cases. What is happening?
optionA: The documents are redundant, since the model has already read them
optionB: Reviewer fatigue, which a shorter daily quota of claims would solve
optionC: The model is near-perfect, and the acceptance rate is the proof of it
optionD: Automation bias: the human check is a rubber stamp, so the model decides
correctAnswerText: Automation bias: the human check is a rubber stamp, so the model decides
explanation: Acceptance without reading the evidence means no human judgement is applied. A high acceptance rate shows agreement, not accuracy; quotas alone do not make reviewers look.

prompt: After an employee's erasure request, the assistant still quotes text from their old grievance letter. Where is the copy most likely?
optionA: In the employee's own browser history only
optionB: In chunks and embeddings in the vector store
optionC: In the database row that was already deleted
optionD: In the model provider's pre-trained weights
correctAnswerText: In chunks and embeddings in the vector store
explanation: Retrieval can only quote what is still indexed. The letter's chunks were never linked to the deleted row; the erasure job has to reach the vector store too.

prompt: A team "proves" its screener is fair because a judge model rated the screening prompt as neutral and inclusive. What is wrong with that evidence?
optionA: Judge models are not allowed to read prompts written by other teams
optionB: It assesses the prompt's wording, not how the model scores real inputs
optionC: The judge should have rated the prompt as biased to be conservative
optionD: Nothing; a neutral prompt guarantees the model's outputs are neutral
correctAnswerText: It assesses the prompt's wording, not how the model scores real inputs
explanation: Bias is a property of behaviour. A neutrally worded prompt can still produce different scores for identical profiles; only tests on outputs, such as counterfactual pairs, show it.

prompt: A team fine-tunes a model on two years of customer support chats, unredacted, citing "we already had the data". Which two problems does the course flag?
optionA: Fine-tuning breaks copyright and the data is stored too cheaply
optionB: Support chats contain no personal data, so there is no issue
optionC: The chats are too old and too short to be used for training
optionD: No lawful purpose for training, and memorised personal data
correctAnswerText: No lawful purpose for training, and memorised personal data
explanation: Using chats to train needs its own lawful purpose under the DPDP Act, and a model can memorise and repeat training data, so redaction must happen before training.

prompt: A bank compares the share of women approved this year by its new LLM-assisted process with last year's manual share, and finds them equal. Why is this weak evidence of fairness?
optionA: Only the model's training loss can show whether a process is fair
optionB: Approval shares are private and cannot be legally compared across years
optionC: Applicants, rules and markets changed too, so the comparison is confounded
optionD: Equal shares prove fairness, so the evidence is strong, not weak at all
correctAnswerText: Applicants, rules and markets changed too, so the comparison is confounded
explanation: Many things differ between years. A counterfactual test holds everything fixed except the protected detail, which is what isolates the model's behaviour.

prompt: To cut hiring time, a manager proposes letting the LLM reject applicants automatically below a score. Which response is best?
optionA: Keep a person deciding; speed up review and track override and audit rates
optionB: Reject AI entirely, since no model may ever be used in hiring at all
optionC: Accept it, if candidates are told an AI was used after they are rejected
optionD: Accept it, since a consistent model is fairer than any human reviewer
correctAnswerText: Keep a person deciding; speed up review and track override and audit rates
explanation: Hiring is a consequential decision: the model drafts, a person decides, and the oversight is measured so it stays real. A total ban throws away legitimate help.

prompt: Counterfactual tests show a name effect in a screener. Which mitigation plan is strongest?
optionA: Strip unneeded details, keep the pairs in the eval set with a floor
optionB: Raise the threshold until the selection rates happen to be equal
optionC: Add "be fair to everyone" to the system prompt and close the issue
optionD: Ask the model to infer gender first so it can correct for it later
correctAnswerText: Strip unneeded details, keep the pairs in the eval set with a floor
explanation: Removing the detail cuts the channel and a gated test catches regressions. An instruction is untested hope, inferring gender is itself forbidden, and threshold-tuning hides the effect.

prompt: A Bengaluru AI vendor's biggest customer requires a certified AI management system by next year. Which plan fits?
optionA: Build toward ISO/IEC 42001, using NIST RMF terms to organise the risks
optionB: Ask the model provider to certify the vendor's own management system
optionC: Adopt the NIST AI RMF and request its certificate from NIST directly
optionD: Publish a model card for each model, which counts as certification
correctAnswerText: Build toward ISO/IEC 42001, using NIST RMF terms to organise the risks
explanation: Only 42001 offers certification of a management system. The NIST framework is a useful vocabulary but issues no certificate, and a model card is documentation.

prompt: A team proposes that any risk with residual score at or under the threshold is auto-accepted, with no owner recorded. What is the best judgement?
optionA: Approve it, but only if the threshold is lowered by one or two points
optionB: Approve it: below-threshold risks need no further thought or owner
optionC: Reject it: every accepted risk needs a named person who accepted it
optionD: Reject it: no risk may be accepted, every one must be fully removed
correctAnswerText: Reject it: every accepted risk needs a named person who accepted it
explanation: The register's value is the decisions it forces. An acceptance with no owner is no decision at all; demanding zero risk is impossible.

prompt: A Pune start-up's hiring assistant will also be sold to employers in the EU. How should the team plan its obligations?
optionA: Wait until a regulator writes to them before planning any obligations
optionB: Follow only the EU AI Act, since it overrides the DPDP Act in India
optionC: Follow only Indian law, since the company is registered in India
optionD: Meet DPDP duties and also the EU AI Act, which treats hiring as high risk
correctAnswerText: Meet DPDP duties and also the EU AI Act, which treats hiring as high risk
explanation: Products serving EU users also meet the EU AI Act, which puts its heaviest duties on high-risk uses such as hiring and credit. Indian duties still apply at home.

prompt: A developer thinks a new analytics feature falls under one of the DPDP Act's legitimate uses that need no consent. What is the right course?
optionA: Build it, since a blog post says analytics never needs consent
optionB: Ask the legal team to confirm it before building on that ground
optionC: Ask the model provider whether the exemption applies to them
optionD: Build it and add a consent screen only if users later complain
correctAnswerText: Ask the legal team to confirm it before building on that ground
explanation: The Act lists limited legitimate uses, and the operational detail is in rules made under it. Whether one applies is a legal question, not a guess in code or from a blog.

prompt: For debugging, engineers want every raw prompt to an HR assistant kept forever. Which logging policy best balances debugging and the DPDP Act?
optionA: Keep every raw prompt forever, since debugging is a legitimate business need
optionB: Keep every raw prompt, but move the logs to a cheaper storage tier after a year
optionC: Log nothing at all, since any prompt may contain personal data of an employee
optionD: Redact first, keep raw text for a sample with short retention and access logs
correctAnswerText: Redact first, keep raw text for a sample with short retention and access logs
explanation: Keeping personal data needs a purpose and should last no longer than needed. Redaction, sampling, short retention and restricted access keep debugging possible; logging nothing blinds the team.

prompt: Which design for a bank's support chatbot best meets the transparency practices the course teaches?
optionA: Uses a human name and photo so customers feel more at ease with it
optionB: Says it is an AI, cites sources, states its limits, offers an agent
optionC: Hides its sources so customers are not confused by policy documents
optionD: Answers every question, never saying "I cannot help with that"
correctAnswerText: Says it is an AI, cites sources, states its limits, offers an agent
explanation: People should know they are talking to an AI, see where answers come from, know what it cannot do and have a route to a human. A human persona misleads; hiding limits invites misplaced trust.

prompt: A company builds a RAG policy assistant on a hosted model it did not train. Which document should it write for the launch review?
optionA: A model card describing the hosted model's training data
optionB: Only the provider's marketing page, linked from the intranet
optionC: A system card for the whole pipeline, guardrails and oversight
optionD: No document, since the company did not train the model itself
correctAnswerText: A system card for the whole pipeline, guardrails and oversight
explanation: A model card is for a model you train or fine-tune. The product — retrieval, guardrails, human oversight, known failures — is described by a system card, which you own.

prompt: When should an AI feature's risk assessment and system card next be reviewed?
optionA: On a set schedule and on any model, prompt or data-source change
optionB: Only once a year, regardless of what changes in the meantime
optionC: Never; once approved, a system card stays valid indefinitely
optionD: Only after a customer complaint reaches senior management
correctAnswerText: On a set schedule and on any model, prompt or data-source change
explanation: A model, prompt or data-source change can alter every risk score, so it triggers a review alongside the regular cycle. A fixed annual review alone misses those changes.

prompt: Which GenAI application pattern runs a model offline over a large set of stored records, such as tagging two lakh old tickets?
optionA: Batch enrichment
optionB: Copilot in a product
optionC: Streaming gateway
optionD: Chat assistant
correctAnswerText: Batch enrichment
explanation: Batch enrichment processes many records with no user waiting, so throughput and cost count, not per-item latency. A chat assistant and a copilot both have a user waiting.

prompt: In distributed tracing, what is a span?
optionA: One timed step inside a request, with a parent and attributes
optionB: A rule that limits how many tokens one request may use
optionC: The total number of requests the service handled in a day
optionD: A copy of the full prompt kept for every user permanently
correctAnswerText: One timed step inside a request, with a parent and attributes
explanation: A trace is one request end to end; spans are its steps — retrieve, rerank, llm.call — each with a start, duration, status, parent and key-value attributes.

prompt: What belongs in the key of an exact answer cache for an LLM service?
optionA: The time of day and the server name that handled the first call
optionB: Only the raw user question, exactly as it was typed by the user
optionC: The user's browser type and the length of the generated answer
optionD: Model, prompt version, output-changing settings, normalised input
correctAnswerText: Model, prompt version, output-changing settings, normalised input
explanation: Everything that changes the output belongs in the key. Leave out the prompt version and users get last week's answers after a prompt release.

prompt: What does provider-side prompt caching do?
optionA: Saves every user prompt on the provider for training
optionB: Compresses the prompt so the model reads fewer words
optionC: Returns a stored answer whenever a question repeats
optionD: Bills a repeated identical prompt prefix at a discount
correctAnswerText: Bills a repeated identical prompt prefix at a discount
explanation: It makes re-reading the same long prefix cheaper and faster. It does not return a stored answer — that is your own answer cache.

prompt: What does time to first token (TTFT) measure?
optionA: How long until the first words of the answer arrive
optionB: How long the whole answer takes to finish generating
optionC: How long a cached answer stays valid before expiry
optionD: How long the vector store takes to build its index
correctAnswerText: How long until the first words of the answer arrive
explanation: TTFT is the wait before output starts. With streaming, users see words after about a second even when the full answer takes several more.

prompt: A POST starts several minutes of LLM work as a background job. What does it return straight away?
optionA: 202 Accepted with a job id
optionB: 504 Gateway Timeout, then retry
optionC: 200 OK with the full result
optionD: 201 Created with the summary
correctAnswerText: 202 Accepted with a job id
explanation: The handler validates, records and queues the job, then returns 202 with a job id the client follows by polling, server-sent events or a webhook.

prompt: What is an Idempotency-Key header for?
optionA: It tells the server which model version should be used
optionB: A repeated POST returns the same job instead of a new one
optionC: It encrypts the request body between client and server
optionD: It authenticates the client in place of an API key
correctAnswerText: A repeated POST returns the same job instead of a new one
explanation: The client sends one UUID per logical action; the server maps key to job id, so a retry or double-click does not start, and bill, a second job.

prompt: How does a token-bucket rate limiter treat a user?
optionA: An LLM token count per answer, cut off once it is reached
optionB: A capacity that refills steadily: bursts pass, abuse does not
optionC: A queue that serves every request in strict arrival order
optionD: A fixed number of requests per day, reset each midnight
correctAnswerText: A capacity that refills steadily: bursts pass, abuse does not
explanation: Each request takes a token; tokens refill at a set rate up to the capacity. A burst can use the stored tokens, but a sustained flood runs dry.

prompt: In an LLM gateway, what does a circuit breaker do?
optionA: Cuts power to the GPU when it gets too hot during inference
optionB: Stops calling a failing provider for a while after N failures
optionC: Blocks any prompt that is longer than the context window
optionD: Ends a chat after a fixed number of user and model turns
correctAnswerText: Stops calling a failing provider for a while after N failures
explanation: After repeated failures the breaker opens, so requests fail over immediately instead of each paying a timeout against a provider that is down.

prompt: How is word error rate (WER) for speech-to-text computed?
optionA: (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / reference words
optionB: (seconds of audio) / (seconds taken to transcribe it)
optionC: (characters wrong) / (characters in the transcript)
optionD: (correct words) / (words in the transcript produced)
correctAnswerText: (substitutions + deletions + insertions) / reference words
explanation: WER counts the edits that turn the transcript into the reference, divided by the number of reference words. Character error rate is a separate metric.

prompt: Why should a chat assistant stream its answers even though streaming does not make the full answer faster?
optionA: Streaming removes the need to set any timeout on model calls
optionB: Streaming cuts the number of output tokens the model generates
optionC: Streaming lets the provider charge less for each input token
optionD: Users judge speed by when words appear, not when the answer ends
correctAnswerText: Users judge speed by when words appear, not when the answer ends
explanation: Generation time grows with output length; streaming shows the first words in about a second, which is what the user feels. Token counts and prices are unchanged.

prompt: A RAG request uses 3,200 input and 250 output tokens. Why does trimming the prompt usually save more than capping the answer?
optionA: Short prompts stop the model from producing any output at all
optionB: Output tokens are always free, so capping answers saves nothing
optionC: Input tokens dominate the count, so they dominate the cost too
optionD: Providers bill only for the system prompt and never the rest
correctAnswerText: Input tokens dominate the count, so they dominate the cost too
explanation: In RAG, retrieved chunks and history make input the bulk of tokens. Halving 3,200 input tokens moves the bill far more than trimming 250 output tokens.

prompt: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff when retrying a rate-limited provider?
optionA: Without jitter the client library refuses to retry at all
optionB: Jitter guarantees that the second attempt always succeeds
optionC: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together
optionD: Random waits make each retry cheaper for the provider to bill
correctAnswerText: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together
explanation: Identical backoff makes every failed client hit the provider at the same instants, recreating the spike — a retry storm. Randomness spreads them out.

prompt: Why should neither a retry nor a fallback provider be used for a 400 Bad Request?
optionA: The request itself is malformed, so it will fail at every provider
optionB: A 400 is always caused by a network glitch that clears by itself
optionC: A 400 means the provider is down, so waiting is the only option
optionD: A 400 means the account has run out of credit with the provider
correctAnswerText: The request itself is malformed, so it will fail at every provider
explanation: Retry or fail over only on errors another attempt could fix: 429, 5xx and timeouts. A malformed request needs a code fix, not more attempts.

prompt: Why must each step of a queued LLM job check whether its output already exists?
optionA: Queues deliver at least once, so a job can run again after a crash
optionB: The model may refuse to answer the same document a second time
optionC: Workers run each job exactly once, so the check is only for speed
optionD: Brokers delete finished jobs, so the output must be looked up
correctAnswerText: Queues deliver at least once, so a job can run again after a crash
explanation: A worker can crash after the work but before acknowledging it; the broker redelivers. Idempotent steps make the re-run harmless, and side effects such as emails are recorded.

prompt: Why are personalised answers such as "what is my leave balance?" never put in a semantic cache?
optionA: A similar question from someone else would get this user's answer
optionB: Leave balances change every second, so no cache can be used at all
optionC: Semantic caches only store answers that contain citations to files
optionD: Personal questions are too short for an embedding model to encode
correctAnswerText: A similar question from someone else would get this user's answer
explanation: The question text is the same for every employee, so a similarity match would serve one person's data to another. Answers also depend on permissions, so caches are scoped.

prompt: Why put the system prompt and tool definitions first and the retrieved chunks and question last?
optionA: Provider prompt caching only helps when the prefix is identical
optionB: Retrieved chunks at the start are always billed at double rate
optionC: The question must be last or the provider rejects the request
optionD: Models ignore anything that appears after the first 500 tokens
correctAnswerText: Provider prompt caching only helps when the prefix is identical
explanation: Provider caching applies to a long identical prefix. Stable parts first and variable parts last maximise the shared prefix across calls.

prompt: Why budget and alert on p95 latency rather than average latency?
optionA: The average is always higher than p95, so it raises false alarms
optionB: The slowest requests are the ones users notice and complain about
optionC: p95 is the only latency figure that providers are able to report
optionD: p95 ignores the model call, so it isolates the retrieval step
correctAnswerText: The slowest requests are the ones users notice and complain about
explanation: An average hides a slow tail. p95 shows the experience of the slowest one in twenty requests, which is what drives complaints.

prompt: Why should an AI service's liveness check not call the model provider?
optionA: The provider rejects any request that arrives from a health probe
optionB: Liveness checks must finish within one millisecond to be accepted
optionC: Provider slowness would then restart healthy pods for no reason
optionD: Health checks are billed at a higher rate than normal requests
correctAnswerText: Provider slowness would then restart healthy pods for no reason
explanation: Liveness answers "is this process alive?". Tie it to an external provider and every provider hiccup kills pods. Readiness covers whether the index and model are loaded.

prompt: Why does cropping a shelf photo to the price label often beat sending a larger full photo to a vision model?
optionA: Cropping removes the need to validate the fields in code later
optionB: Larger photos are always read in black and white by the model
optionC: Fewer image tokens are billed, and the label text ends up larger
optionD: Vision models reject any photo wider than a single price label
correctAnswerText: Fewer image tokens are billed, and the label text ends up larger
explanation: An image is cut into patches that become tokens, and providers resize images. A crop costs less and keeps small text readable after resizing.

prompt: HR uploads offer letters and wants the CTC, joining date and location pulled into the HRMS. Which pattern is this, and what guards it?
optionA: Copilot: suggestions the HR user accepts or rejects in the screen
optionB: Batch enrichment: one prompt run once over all historical letters
optionC: Extraction: a validated schema, with failures sent to human review
optionD: Chat assistant: streamed answers with citations to the offer letter
correctAnswerText: Extraction: a validated schema, with failures sent to human review
explanation: A document in, a fixed structure out, no conversation: an extraction pipeline. Its failure mode is a wrong field silently stored, so validation and a review queue guard it.

prompt: A small model costs 0.0042 and a large one 0.042 price units per request. A router sends 85% to small and 15% to large. What is the blended cost per request?
optionA: About 0.0099
optionB: About 0.0420
optionC: About 0.0231
optionD: About 0.0042
correctAnswerText: About 0.0099
explanation: 0.85 × 0.0042 + 0.15 × 0.042 = 0.00357 + 0.0063 ≈ 0.00987, about 76% below always-large — and still more than double all-small, so the large-model share is worth watching.

prompt: A token bucket has capacity 5 and refills 0.5 tokens a second. A full bucket gets a burst of 7 requests at once. How many are allowed?
optionA: 5 allowed, 2 refused
optionB: 6 allowed, 1 refused
optionC: 7 allowed, 0 refused
optionD: 3 allowed, 4 refused
correctAnswerText: 5 allowed, 2 refused
explanation: The burst can spend the five stored tokens; refilling at 0.5 a second adds nothing within an instant, so the sixth and seventh are refused.

prompt: Input costs 1 and output costs 4 price units per million tokens. A request uses 2,400 input and 300 output tokens. What does it cost?
optionA: 0.0108 price units
optionB: 0.0012 price units
optionC: 0.0036 price units
optionD: 0.0027 price units
correctAnswerText: 0.0036 price units

prompt: A provider call can fail with 400, 401, 429, 503 or a timeout. Which should the client retry with backoff?
optionA: Only the 400 and the 503
optionB: 429, 503 and the timeout
optionC: 400, 401 and the timeout
optionD: All five of them equally
correctAnswerText: 429, 503 and the timeout
explanation: Rate limits, server errors and timeouts may clear. A 400 (malformed) or 401 (bad credentials) will fail again however often it is retried.

prompt: A "summarise 40 policy PDFs" button needs about two minutes of LLM work. How should the API be built?
optionA: Return 202 and a job id; a worker runs it; the client polls status
optionB: Keep the HTTP request open for two minutes until the work finishes
optionC: Run it in the browser by calling the model provider from JavaScript
optionD: Raise the gateway timeout to five minutes and run it in the handler
correctAnswerText: Return 202 and a job id; a worker runs it; the client polls status
explanation: Gateways cut idle connections, mobile networks drop and a blocked worker serves nobody. Slow work becomes a job with status, progress and a stored result.

prompt: HR uploads a new leave policy. Cached answers built on the old one must stop being served. What does the cache need?
optionA: Entries tagged with the documents they cite, deleted by tag on re-index
optionB: A cache kept in a Python dict so restarting the server clears it all
optionC: A longer time-to-live so answers stay in the cache for several months
optionD: Nothing; semantic similarity will notice that the policy has changed
correctAnswerText: Entries tagged with the documents they cite, deleted by tag on re-index
explanation: Tagging entries with cited document ids lets a re-index invalidate exactly the stale answers. A process-local dict is not shared by workers and is not a policy.

prompt: A CRM copilot can create tickets and update fields for the user. Whose permissions should its API calls carry?
optionA: No permissions, since it only suggests
optionB: The signed-in user's own permissions
optionC: The permissions of the CRM's admin
optionD: A service superuser key for reliability
correctAnswerText: The signed-in user's own permissions
explanation: A copilot must never be able to do what its user cannot. Writes also need confirmation and a log of who accepted what.

prompt: A team adds a semantic cache to a policy assistant with 40,000 questions a month. How should it choose the similarity threshold?
optionA: From labelled same-answer and different-answer pairs of its traffic
optionB: Use 0.80, the value most semantic-cache tutorials start with
optionC: Ask the embedding model to suggest a threshold for itself
optionD: Pick the threshold that gives the highest cache hit rate
correctAnswerText: From labelled same-answer and different-answer pairs of its traffic
explanation: "Sick leave" and "casual leave" questions scored 0.81 in the course — one word apart, different answers. Only labelled pairs from real traffic show where the line is safe.

prompt: Three calls have reference lengths 20, 50 and 30 words with 2, 4 and 4 errors. What is the corpus WER?
explanation: Corpus WER is total errors over total reference words: 10 / 100 = 0.10. The mean of per-call WERs (0.10, 0.08, 0.133) is about 0.104, which over-weights short calls.

prompt: An employee asks about paternity leave and gets the maternity-leave answer, marked as a semantic cache hit. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: A guessed threshold: the two questions embed above it but differ
optionB: The exact cache key was missing the prompt version of the answer
optionC: The provider returned a cached answer from its own prompt cache
optionD: The retry logic sent the question to a different model by mistake
correctAnswerText: A guessed threshold: the two questions embed above it but differ
explanation: Questions one word apart can embed very close together while needing different answers. The threshold must come from labelled pairs, and the cache be scoped.

prompt: After prompt answer-v4 goes live, half the answers keep the old format for exactly 24 hours. What is wrong?
optionA: The cache key lacks the prompt version, so v3 entries serve until expiry
optionB: Users' browsers cached the old page and did not request new answers
optionC: The new prompt is too long, so the provider silently used the old one
optionD: The model needs 24 hours to learn a new prompt before it can follow it
correctAnswerText: The cache key lacks the prompt version, so v3 entries serve until expiry
explanation: The 24 hours is the cache TTL. With the prompt version in the key, v4 lookups would miss the v3 entries immediately.

prompt: A 30-second provider blip becomes a 10-minute outage; request volume spikes in waves at fixed intervals. Which client behaviour explains it?
optionA: Retries without jitter, on all exceptions, with no cap on attempts
optionB: The token bucket refilled too slowly for normal daytime traffic
optionC: Streaming was switched on, which multiplies every request by ten
optionD: A semantic cache served answers that were too old for the users
correctAnswerText: Retries without jitter, on all exceptions, with no cap on attempts
explanation: Synchronised retries arrive in waves and keep the provider overloaded. Retry only 429, 5xx and timeouts, add full jitter, honour Retry-After and cap attempts.

prompt: After a deploy, 120 documents are summarised twice and managers get two emails. Workers use late acknowledgement. What went wrong?
optionA: Late acknowledgement is a bug and should always be switched off
optionB: Redelivery was correct; the task was not idempotent per document
optionC: The broker lost the jobs, and the client re-sent all of them again
optionD: The model produced two summaries because temperature was too high
correctAnswerText: Redelivery was correct; the task was not idempotent per document
explanation: Stopping workers mid-task means the broker redelivers, as it should. Skip documents already done, upsert keyed on job and document, and record emails so they are sent once.

prompt: A new release restarts every pod every 30 seconds. Liveness calls the provider and a 400 MB index loads at startup. What is the fix?
optionA: Raise the replica count so that some pods survive the restarts
optionB: Call the provider twice in liveness so one slow reply is tolerated
optionC: Remove all health checks so the orchestrator never restarts pods
optionD: Trivial liveness; readiness that turns green after the index loads
correctAnswerText: Trivial liveness; readiness that turns green after the index loads
explanation: Liveness should only prove the process is alive; readiness keeps traffic away until loading finishes. More replicas or no checks hide the problem or remove safety.

prompt: Traces show the request span but no llm.call child for summaries run in a thread pool. Why?
optionA: Work submitted to the pool does not carry the current trace context
optionB: Thread pools never call the model, so there is no span to record
optionC: LLM calls cannot be traced unless the provider supports tracing
optionD: The exporter drops any span that lasts longer than one second
correctAnswerText: Work submitted to the pool does not carry the current trace context
explanation: A plain executor.submit loses the context variable holding the current span, so the child starts a new trace or none. Instrument the executor or copy the context.

prompt: p95 latency doubled from 4 s to 8 s with no deploy. Per-span p95: retrieve 90→95 ms, rerank 180→175 ms, llm.call 3.1→7.2 s. Where should the team look?
optionA: The model call: tokens, attempts, routing share, or the provider
optionB: The network: every span grew by the same amount of time
optionC: Reranking: a slightly faster reranker means it has broken
optionD: Retrieval: the vector index must have been rebuilt overnight
correctAnswerText: The model call: tokens, attempts, routing share, or the provider
explanation: Per-span percentiles locate the time: only llm.call grew. Its attributes — input tokens, retries, model, cache hits — narrow it down further.

prompt: Receipt photos from one phone model come back with nonsense fields, though they look upright in the gallery. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The EXIF rotation flag was ignored, so the model saw them sideways
optionB: The model was rate-limited and returned random fields for them
optionC: That phone saves photos in a format the model cannot open at all
optionD: The receipts are in a regional language the model does not know
correctAnswerText: The EXIF rotation flag was ignored, so the model saw them sideways
explanation: Some phones store pixels sideways with a "rotate" flag that galleries honour. Apply the orientation (exif_transpose) before resizing, and add rotated photos to the eval set.

prompt: One collection holds text chunks and figures, both embedded with a CLIP-style model. Figures never rank in the top results. Why?
optionA: The modality gap: text scores higher against text than images do
optionB: Figures are stored at too high a resolution for the index to use
optionC: CLIP cannot embed images at all, only the captions beside them
optionD: The vector store sorts images after text by default, by design
correctAnswerText: The modality gap: text scores higher against text than images do
explanation: Text-to-text similarities sit systematically above text-to-image ones, so images lose every comparison. Use separate collections per modality merged by rank, or caption figures.

prompt: A transcript sounds perfect to the team, yet scores WER 0.158. The reference says "two thousand rupees"; the transcript says "2,000 rupees". What is wrong?
optionA: The reference transcript is wrong and should say "2,000 rupees"
optionB: The speech model is poor and should be replaced with a larger one
optionC: WER cannot be used on Indian English and should be dropped entirely
optionD: Numbers were not normalised the same way on both sides before scoring
correctAnswerText: Numbers were not normalised the same way on both sides before scoring
explanation: Unnormalised number formats count as errors. Normalise numbers, dates and currency identically on both sides, then the real errors remain.

prompt: A router cuts cost by 70% but eval-set quality drops slightly. Should it ship?
optionA: Ship at once, since a 70% saving outweighs any drop in quality
optionB: Never ship, since any quality drop at all is unacceptable here
optionC: Ship only if quality stays within the tolerance agreed in advance
optionD: Ship, but stop running the evaluation set so the drop is hidden
correctAnswerText: Ship only if quality stays within the tolerance agreed in advance
explanation: A router is good if quality stays within your threshold of "large model always" while the large share falls. The threshold, set beforehand, decides — not the size of the saving.

prompt: An HR assistant serves 30 client companies. Which caching design is soundest?
optionA: No scoping, but a high threshold so that wrong hits are very rare
optionB: A semantic cache only, since exact caching adds nothing in practice
optionC: Exact and semantic caches both scoped by tenant, prompt and permissions
optionD: One shared semantic cache across all tenants to maximise the hit rate
correctAnswerText: Exact and semantic caches both scoped by tenant, prompt and permissions
explanation: The worst failure is serving one company's policy to another. Scoping by tenant, prompt version and permissions prevents it; a high threshold only makes it rarer.

prompt: A paid feature re-summarises 400 PDFs per client on request, behind two API replicas. Which job runner fits?
optionA: A broker such as Redis with separate workers (Celery or RQ)
optionB: Run the work inside the POST handler and raise the timeout
optionC: FastAPI BackgroundTasks inside each API process, as it is simple
optionD: A thread queue inside one API replica, shared by both replicas
correctAnswerText: A broker such as Redis with separate workers (Celery or RQ)
explanation: BackgroundTasks and in-process queues die with the process and cannot be shared across replicas. Work users pay or wait for belongs on a broker with scalable workers.

prompt: A product manager wants the model to decide whether an employee is eligible for a loan against salary. Eligibility is a fixed rule. What is the best design?
optionA: Let the model decide, and have a human check one case in a hundred
optionB: Put the rule in the system prompt and let the model apply it
optionC: Fine-tune a model on past decisions so it learns the rule itself
optionD: Compute eligibility in code; let the model only explain the result
correctAnswerText: Compute eligibility in code; let the model only explain the result
explanation: Deterministic logic stays deterministic: a rule computed in code is exact and testable. The model is for language that varies, such as explaining the outcome.

prompt: Choosing a fallback model for when the main provider fails, which candidate is best?
optionA: A second model that has passed the same evaluation set
optionB: The newest model, untested, since newer is usually better
optionC: Any model, as long as it uses the same response format
optionD: The cheapest model on offer, since outages are rare anyway
correctAnswerText: A second model that has passed the same evaluation set
explanation: A fallback that answers badly is an outage with extra steps. It must meet the same quality bar as the main path, verified on the same evaluation set.

prompt: A team's dashboard tracks error rate, p95 latency and cost per request. What is the most important thing it is missing?
optionA: A chart of CPU temperature on the machines running the API
optionB: The total count of lines of code in the service repository
optionC: Quality signals such as thumbs-down and "I don't know" rates
optionD: The number of engineers who viewed the dashboard each day
correctAnswerText: Quality signals such as thumbs-down and "I don't know" rates
explanation: A wrong answer returns 200 OK. Thumbs-down rate, "I don't know" rate, sampled groundedness and retrieval scores catch failures that error rates never show.

prompt: Scanned supplier invoices come in hundreds of layouts, and reviewers must see where each value sits on the page. Which reading approach fits best?
optionA: Hybrid: OCR text and boxes plus the page image given to a vision model
optionB: A vision model alone, trusting the values it returns without boxes
optionC: Manual typing of every invoice, since no model can read a layout
optionD: OCR alone, with a single fixed template for every supplier's layout
correctAnswerText: Hybrid: OCR text and boxes plus the page image given to a vision model
explanation: A vision model copes with many layouts but gives no coordinates and can invent values; OCR keeps characters honest and gives boxes for the review screen. Together they cover both.

prompt: A company's deck search cannot answer questions about charts. What is the best default fix?
optionA: Raise the retrieval top-k until a chart happens to appear in results
optionB: Embed the chart images with CLIP in the same collection as the text
optionC: Ask users to retype the numbers from each chart into the search box
optionD: Caption each figure with a vision model and index captions as chunks
correctAnswerText: Caption each figure with a vision model and index captions as chunks
explanation: Captions and markdown tables turn figures into ordinary chunks, so existing embedding, hybrid search and re-ranking keep working. CLIP scores charts poorly and suffers the modality gap.

prompt: Two lakh product reviews must be summarised by next week. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Run all two lakh at once on the real-time API to finish quickest
optionB: Run all two lakh, then read a sample afterwards to check quality
optionC: Summarise them in a chat window one by one as time allows
optionD: Sample 200 and review them, then run a resumable job on a batch API
correctAnswerText: Sample 200 and review them, then run a resumable job on a batch API
explanation: The failure mode of batch work is a prompt bug found after 1.5 lakh rows. Review a sample first, then use a cheaper batch API with a resumable, idempotent job.

prompt: Which rule should send an extracted invoice to human review rather than straight to the ledger?
optionA: Every invoice, so the pipeline saves no effort at all for the team
optionB: Never; once the schema validates, the record is known to be correct
optionC: Only when the model says its own confidence is below 95 per cent
optionD: Any failed check, missing required field, large amount or new supplier
correctAnswerText: Any failed check, missing required field, large amount or new supplier
explanation: Route on evidence, not self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated. Validation failures, nulls, high amounts and unknown suppliers are evidence; a weekly sample of auto-approved ones keeps it honest.

prompt: In LoRA, W' = W + (alpha / r) · B·A. Which weights are trained?
optionA: W, A and B all together at once
optionB: Only the original weight matrix W
optionC: Only the scaling value alpha / r
optionD: Only the small matrices A and B
correctAnswerText: Only the small matrices A and B
explanation: LoRA freezes W and learns a low-rank correction B·A, which has r × (d_in + d_out) numbers per adapted matrix instead of d_in × d_out.

prompt: At step 0 of LoRA training, how are A and B initialised?
optionA: Both copied from the original weight matrix W
optionB: Both zero, so no gradient can flow through them
optionC: A random, B zero, so the model starts as the base
optionD: Both random, so the model starts slightly changed
correctAnswerText: A random, B zero, so the model starts as the base
explanation: With B at zero the product B·A is zero, so training starts from exactly the base model; A being random lets gradients flow into B.

prompt: What does QLoRA change compared with ordinary LoRA?
optionA: Every weight is trained, but gradients are stored in 4-bit
optionB: The adapters are trained in 4-bit while the base stays 32-bit
optionC: The frozen base is held in 4-bit NF4; adapters stay 16-bit
optionD: The base model is pruned to a quarter of its original layers
correctAnswerText: The frozen base is held in 4-bit NF4; adapters stay 16-bit
explanation: QLoRA loads the frozen base weights in 4-bit NF4 and de-quantises them on the fly; the LoRA adapters are still trained in 16-bit.

prompt: In the prompt-completion training format, which tokens count towards the loss by default?
optionA: Only the completion, the assistant's reply
optionB: Every token, prompt and completion alike
optionC: Only the special chat-template marker tokens
optionD: Only the prompt, the system and user turns
correctAnswerText: Only the completion, the assistant's reply
explanation: The prompt is masked, so the model learns to write the reply rather than to reproduce system prompts and customer messages.

prompt: Why must the end-of-turn token appear at the end of each assistant turn in the training data?
optionA: So the fine-tuned model learns when to stop
optionB: So the tokenizer can detect the language
optionC: So the trainer can count the training rows
optionD: So the loss is not computed on that turn
correctAnswerText: So the fine-tuned model learns when to stop
explanation: If the end-of-turn token is missing, the model never sees an example of stopping and keeps generating past its answer.

prompt: At inference, what does add_generation_prompt=True do in apply_chat_template?
optionA: Adds a default system prompt that the model was trained with
optionB: Inserts the end-of-turn token after the user's last message
optionC: Appends the expected answer so the model can check its work
optionD: Ends the string with the assistant marker so the model replies
correctAnswerText: Ends the string with the assistant marker so the model replies
explanation: The conversation is passed without the answer, and the template ends with the opening of an assistant turn, so the next tokens the model predicts are the reply.

prompt: What is catastrophic forgetting in fine-tuning?
optionA: The model forgets the system prompt within one reply
optionB: The trainer deletes the dataset after the first epoch
optionC: Narrow training damages abilities the base model had
optionD: The adapter file is lost when the notebook session ends
correctAnswerText: Narrow training damages abilities the base model had
explanation: Training hard on a narrow task can break general facts, instructions or safety refusals the base model handled well, which is why a general-ability set is re-run.

prompt: What does merge_and_unload() produce from a base model plus a LoRA adapter?
optionA: A plain model with the scaled B·A added into W
optionB: A second adapter that undoes the first adapter
optionC: An adapter file a tenth the size of the original
optionD: A quantised 4-bit copy of the base model only
correctAnswerText: A plain model with the scaled B·A added into W
explanation: Merging computes W + (alpha / r)·B·A once and returns an ordinary model that needs no PEFT library and has no adapter overhead — but is a full-size copy.

prompt: Roughly how many bytes per parameter does full fine-tuning with Adam in mixed precision need, before activations?
optionA: About 2 bytes
optionB: About 4 bytes
optionC: About 16 bytes
optionD: About 64 bytes
correctAnswerText: About 16 bytes
explanation: 2 (16-bit weight) + 2 (gradient) + 4 (fp32 master copy) + 8 (two Adam moments) ≈ 16 bytes per parameter.

prompt: What is the effective batch size in a training run on one GPU?
optionA: Per-device batch size + number of training epochs
optionB: Number of training rows ÷ number of training epochs
optionC: Per-device batch size × gradient accumulation steps
optionD: Maximum sequence length × per-device batch size
correctAnswerText: Per-device batch size × gradient accumulation steps
explanation: Gradient accumulation sums gradients over several micro-batches before one optimiser step, so the step sees batch × accumulation examples.

prompt: Why is fine-tuning a poor way to teach a model a telecom operator's monthly-changing tariffs?
optionA: Tariff data is too small to fit into a training dataset at all
optionB: Fine-tuned models are unable to output any numbers in replies
optionC: Facts would need retraining each change and cannot be cited
optionD: Fine-tuning can only change a model's tone, never its content
correctAnswerText: Facts would need retraining each change and cannot be cited
explanation: Changing facts belong in retrieval, which updates by re-indexing and can cite sources. A few hundred examples tend to teach answer style and invented content, not reliable facts.

prompt: Why should every training example carry, word for word, the system prompt that production will use?
optionA: The model learns behaviour in that context; another prompt is another input
optionB: The trainer refuses to start unless each row has the same exact length
optionC: The system prompt is where the loss is computed during the training run
optionD: It allows the production prompt to be dropped entirely after training
correctAnswerText: The model learns behaviour in that context; another prompt is another input
explanation: A fine-tune learns "given inputs like these, answer like this". A different or missing system prompt at serving time is a different input, and behaviour can drift.

prompt: Why remove duplicate examples before fine-tuning?
optionA: Duplicates make the adapter file larger than the base model
optionB: Duplicate rows are always mislabelled, so they teach wrong answers
optionC: Trainers crash with an error when two rows are exactly identical
optionD: They over-weight some examples and can leak into the test set
correctAnswerText: They over-weight some examples and can leak into the test set
explanation: Repeated rows pull the model towards them, and a duplicate that lands in both train and test makes the test flatter the model. Templated and synthetic data repeats a lot.

prompt: Why split support chats into train and test by time or by customer rather than at random?
optionA: Random splits always leave some intent class out of the training set
optionB: Random splits put near-siblings in both sets, so the test flatters
optionC: Trainers can only read data sorted in time order from oldest to newest
optionD: Splitting by time makes the training run finish noticeably faster
correctAnswerText: Random splits put near-siblings in both sets, so the test flatters
explanation: Zero exact overlaps is not enough: "bill 199 extra" in test with "bill 299 extra" in train is a near-copy. A split by source or time keeps the test genuinely unseen.

prompt: Why does LoRA cut GPU memory far more than its 1–4% trainable share alone suggests?
optionA: Gradients and optimiser states exist only for the adapter weights
optionB: LoRA trains in 1-bit precision, so every number is much smaller
optionC: LoRA runs only the first few layers of the model in each step
optionD: LoRA deletes the frozen weights from memory during each step
correctAnswerText: Gradients and optimiser states exist only for the adapter weights
explanation: In full fine-tuning, gradients, fp32 master copies and Adam moments dominate memory. With LoRA they exist only for a few million numbers; the frozen 16-bit weights dominate.

prompt: Why is LoRA's update scaled by alpha / r?
optionA: It keeps the size of the update comparable when r is changed
optionB: It decides how many epochs the trainer runs before stopping
optionC: It sets how many layers of the model receive an adapter
optionD: It converts the adapter from 16-bit to 4-bit before saving
correctAnswerText: It keeps the size of the update comparable when r is changed
explanation: Scaling by alpha / r means a higher rank does not automatically mean a bigger update. People set alpha to r or 2r and treat alpha and the learning rate as one knob.

prompt: Why compare a fine-tune against the base model with a few-shot prompt, not the base model zero-shot?
optionA: Few-shot prompts are what the trainer used to build the adapter
optionB: Zero-shot results cannot be scored automatically by any script
optionC: Comparisons with the zero-shot base are banned by model licences
optionD: Zero-shot is a straw man; few-shot is the cheap rival to beat
correctAnswerText: Zero-shot is a straw man; few-shot is the cheap rival to beat
explanation: In the course, five examples took the base model from 0/10 to 9/10 valid JSON. A fine-tune must earn its keep against the cheapest alternative that could do the job.

prompt: Why is a LoRA adapter useless without exactly the base model it was trained on?
optionA: Licences forbid loading an adapter on any other base model at all
optionB: The adapter stores the tokenizer, which no other model can read
optionC: Adapters are encrypted with a key that only one base model holds
optionD: It is a correction to specific weights; other weights it does not fit
correctAnswerText: It is a correction to specific weights; other weights it does not fit
explanation: B·A is learnt as a delta to one model's matrices. On another size, version or the base instead of the instruct model, it loads — or fails — and produces nonsense.

prompt: Why re-run the evaluation set after quantising a fine-tuned model for serving?
optionA: Quantising always improves accuracy, and the new numbers must be recorded
optionB: Quantised models use a different tokenizer that needs a fresh test set
optionC: Exact outputs such as JSON keys and labels show quantisation errors first
optionD: The evaluation set must be re-labelled whenever the model file changes
correctAnswerText: Exact outputs such as JSON keys and labels show quantisation errors first
explanation: Fine-tunes are often used for exact things, which is where quantisation hurts first. If escalation recall drops, step up to 8-bit or keep 16-bit.

prompt: Why can't fine-tuning make a model reveal salary bands "only to managers"?
optionA: Salary data is too sensitive to be tokenised by the trainer
optionB: Fine-tuning cannot change the model's behaviour towards anyone
optionC: Managers would need their own GPU to run the fine-tuned model
optionD: Whatever is in the weights is available to every user who asks
correctAnswerText: Whatever is in the weights is available to every user who asks
explanation: A fine-tuned model knows what it knows for everyone. Access control belongs outside the model, for example in retrieval filters built from the session.

prompt: A 30-layer model has q_proj 576×576 and v_proj 192×576 (out × in). With r = 8 on q_proj and v_proj only, how many LoRA parameters are trained?
explanation: Per matrix r × (d_in + d_out): 8 × (576 + 576) + 8 × (576 + 192) = 9,216 + 6,144 = 15,360 per layer; × 30 layers = 460,800. 15,360 forgets the layers.

prompt: Roughly how much GPU memory would full fine-tuning of an 8B-parameter model with Adam need, before activations?
optionA: About 32 GB
optionB: About 128 GB
optionC: About 16 GB
optionD: About 512 GB
correctAnswerText: About 128 GB
explanation: 8B × about 16 bytes per parameter ≈ 128 GB — several data-centre GPUs. 16 GB is roughly just the 16-bit weights.

prompt: 42 training rows, per-device batch 4, gradient accumulation 2, three epochs. About how many optimiser steps run?
explanation: 42 / 4 gives 11 micro-batches per epoch; two per optimiser step gives about 6 steps per epoch; three epochs give about 18. 33 counts micro-batches, not steps.

prompt: A bank wants its assistant to answer from loan policies that change every quarter, citing the clause. Which route fits first?
optionA: A longer system prompt with no retrieval
optionB: Fine-tune on the policies once per quarter
optionC: Full fine-tuning of a larger base model
optionD: Retrieval over the policies, with citations
correctAnswerText: Retrieval over the policies, with citations
explanation: Changing, citable knowledge is a retrieval problem. Re-indexing a document is cheap; retraining each quarter cannot cite and still invents content.

prompt: The allowed intents are recharge_failed, no_network, port_out, bill_dispute and sim_block. A row's reply is {"intent": "billing", "escalate": "yes"}. What should validation report?
optionA: Only that the reply is missing a "reply" key
optionB: Nothing; the reply is valid JSON, so it passes
optionC: Unknown intent, and escalate is not a boolean
optionD: Only that "billing" should be in upper case
correctAnswerText: Unknown intent, and escalate is not a boolean
explanation: "billing" is not one of the five intents and "yes" is a string, not true or false. Both make it a bad row; the model copies mistakes as faithfully as good answers.

prompt: Validation loss by epoch is 1.10, 0.92, 0.95, 1.04, 1.18 while training loss keeps falling. Which checkpoint should be kept?
optionA: The epoch-4 checkpoint
optionB: The epoch-2 checkpoint
optionC: The epoch-5 checkpoint
optionD: The epoch-1 checkpoint
correctAnswerText: The epoch-2 checkpoint
explanation: Validation loss is lowest after epoch 2; afterwards the model memorises. Keep the best checkpoint (load_best_model_at_end) and train less next time.

prompt: A SaaS firm has twelve customer-specific LoRA adapters on one base model and one GPU. How should it serve them?
optionA: Twelve GPUs, one for each merged customer model
optionB: Twelve merged models, each a full copy on the GPU
optionC: One base with all twelve adapters loaded at run time
optionD: One merged model that combines all twelve adapters
correctAnswerText: One base with all twelve adapters loaded at run time
explanation: Many adapters on one base is what multi-LoRA serving is for: one copy of the base in memory, the adapter chosen per request by name. Merging means full copies.

prompt: An adapter trained with r = 32 must be served by a multi-LoRA server started with a maximum LoRA rank of 16. What must change?
optionA: Raise the server's maximum rank to at least 32
optionB: Lower the adapter's alpha to 16 before loading
optionC: Merge the adapter, then set its rank to 16
optionD: Nothing; the server pads lower ranks automatically
correctAnswerText: Raise the server's maximum rank to at least 32
explanation: The server's maximum LoRA rank must be at least the adapter's r. Changing alpha does not change the rank of the matrices.

prompt: On an older 16 GB notebook GPU, the trainer stops with "your setup doesn't support bf16". What setting fixes it?
optionA: Load the base in 32-bit only
optionB: Raise gradient accumulation
optionC: bf16=True and fp16=True
optionD: bf16=False and fp16=True
correctAnswerText: bf16=False and fp16=True
explanation: The trainer defaults to bf16, which older GPUs and CPUs cannot do. Turn it off and use fp16 on the older GPU; newer GPUs keep bf16.

prompt: A fine-tune would cut each prompt by 1,800 tokens on 500,000 calls a month. How many input tokens a month does that save?
optionA: 90 million
optionB: 900 thousand
optionC: 9 billion
optionD: 900 million
correctAnswerText: 900 million
explanation: 1,800 × 500,000 = 900,000,000. That saving, priced from the current price page, is set against serving, training and labelling costs.

prompt: Loss falls nicely, but the fine-tune sometimes writes out the system prompt or a customer-style message. One batch shows 113 of 113 tokens counted in the loss. What is wrong?
optionA: The end-of-turn token was masked, so the model never stopped
optionB: Loss was computed on prompt tokens too; train on the reply only
optionC: The rank r was too small to store the system prompt properly
optionD: The learning rate was too low, so the model could not learn
correctAnswerText: Loss was computed on prompt tokens too; train on the reply only
explanation: With every token as a target, the model learns to produce prompts and user turns too. The prompt-completion format masks the prompt so only the reply is learnt.

prompt: LoRA setup fails with "target modules not found" on a Llama-style model. The config was copied from a BERT tutorial. What is the cause?
optionA: Llama-style models cannot be fine-tuned with LoRA adapters at all
optionB: Module names differ by architecture; list this model's own names
optionC: The tokenizer was not loaded before the LoRA configuration was set
optionD: The rank is too high for the number of layers in the base model
correctAnswerText: Module names differ by architecture; list this model's own names
explanation: BERT names its layers differently from Llama-style models (q_proj, v_proj and so on). Print the linear-layer names from the model, or use "all-linear".

prompt: A fine-tune scores well on the test set, but production drafts ignore the escalation rule. The serving code builds messages without a system turn. What explains it?
optionA: The adapter was overfitted, which only ever shows up in production
optionB: Production users write longer messages than the model can read
optionC: Serving used a different input; the template injected its own default
optionD: The test set was too large, so the scores cannot be trusted at all
correctAnswerText: Serving used a different input; the template injected its own default
explanation: Without an explicit system turn, the chat template may insert a default one, so production inputs differ from training. One build_messages function used by training, evaluation and serving prevents it.

prompt: An adapter loads without error, but every reply is gibberish. What should be checked first?
optionA: That the base model matches base_model_name_or_path in adapter_config
optionB: That the temperature is set high enough to allow creative answers
optionC: That the training loss reached exactly zero before the adapter saved
optionD: That the adapter file is under the GPU's maximum upload size limit
correctAnswerText: That the base model matches base_model_name_or_path in adapter_config
explanation: An adapter trained on a different base — another size, or the base rather than instruct model — can load and produce nonsense. Load exactly the recorded model and pin its revision.

prompt: From epoch 3, training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises. What is happening?
optionA: The validation set is a copy of the training set by mistake
optionB: The masking is wrong, so the prompt is being learnt as well
optionC: Underfitting: the model needs a much higher learning rate
optionD: Overfitting: the model is memorising the training rows
correctAnswerText: Overfitting: the model is memorising the training rows
explanation: Diverging curves mean memorisation. Keep the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss and train for fewer epochs. Copied validation rows would make the curves track each other instead.

prompt: Training and validation loss both stay flat and high for the whole run. Which causes should be checked?
optionA: Gradient checkpointing, which always stops the loss from falling
optionB: A learning rate too low, wrong masking, or a task beyond the model
optionC: Overfitting from too many epochs on a very small training set
optionD: A validation set that leaks near-copies of the training rows
correctAnswerText: A learning rate too low, wrong masking, or a task beyond the model
explanation: Flat and high means nothing is being learnt. Overfitting shows as diverging curves, and leaked validation rows make validation look too good, not flat.

prompt: After a short run, a support fine-tune returns valid-looking JSON with an invented intent and a rude reply. Both losses are still falling. What does this show?
optionA: The rude reply proves the base model is unsafe and cannot be fine-tuned
optionB: Format is learnt before content; it is undertrained, and outputs must be read
optionC: The model has overfitted, so the earliest checkpoint should be used
optionD: Valid JSON shows the run succeeded, so the content will fix itself in use
correctAnswerText: Format is learnt before content; it is undertrained, and outputs must be read
explanation: Falling losses mean training works but has not finished. The model picked up the shape first. Read real outputs before anyone sees the model, and validate the enum in code.

prompt: On 10 test rows the fine-tune gets 7 right and the prompted baseline 5. A manager calls the fine-tune better. What is the issue?
optionA: Nothing; two more correct answers is a clear 40% relative improvement
optionB: The fine-tune should be scored on its training rows to be fair to it
optionC: With 10 rows the intervals overlap; it needs hundreds, compared paired
optionD: The baseline was given examples, so the comparison is always invalid
correctAnswerText: With 10 rows the intervals overlap; it needs hundreds, compared paired
explanation: Around 70% on 10 rows the 95% interval is roughly ±28 points. Use a few hundred rows and count, on the same rows, where each wins and the other loses.

prompt: After ten epochs on a few dozen telecom rows, the fine-tune gets a simple capital-city question wrong that the base model answered. What does this point to?
optionA: The base model was wrong too, and only got lucky the first time
optionB: The adapter is too small to hold geography, so raise the rank
optionC: Catastrophic forgetting; run a general-ability set on base and tune
optionD: A tokenizer mismatch between the base model and the adapter files
correctAnswerText: Catastrophic forgetting; run a general-ability set on base and tune
explanation: Narrow, long training broke a fact the base knew. One question is an anecdote; a 50–200 item general set, plus the safety refusal set, turns it into a measurement.

prompt: Validation loss tracks training loss almost exactly. The dataset was generated from shared templates and split at random. What is the likely explanation?
optionA: Gradient accumulation copied the training loss into the validation log
optionB: The model generalises perfectly, so no test set is needed any more
optionC: Validation rows are siblings of training rows, so it flatters the model
optionD: The learning rate is too high, which always pulls the curves together
correctAnswerText: Validation rows are siblings of training rows, so it flatters the model
explanation: Template siblings in both splits make validation an easy copy of training. Split by template, source or time so the held-out rows are genuinely unseen.

prompt: "Our chatbot doesn't know our products. Should we fine-tune it?" Which answer is best?
optionA: Probably not: product facts change and need citing, so use retrieval
optionB: Yes, but fully fine-tune the whole model rather than using an adapter
optionC: Yes: fine-tuning is the standard way to add product knowledge to a model
optionD: No: a longer system prompt listing every product is always enough
correctAnswerText: Probably not: product facts change and need citing, so use retrieval
explanation: Knowledge that changes and must be cited is retrieval's job. If answers are still wrong with RAG, look at retrieval before the generator. A huge prompt of products scales poorly.

prompt: You must fine-tune an open 8B instruct model and the only GPU has 16 GB. Which method is the sound choice?
optionA: Prompt tuning only, since no adapter method fits on such a GPU
optionB: QLoRA: a 4-bit base with 16-bit LoRA adapters at a moderate rank
optionC: Full fine-tuning with a smaller batch size to make the memory fit
optionD: LoRA on a 16-bit base, since quantisation always ruins quality
correctAnswerText: QLoRA: a 4-bit base with 16-bit LoRA adapters at a moderate rank
