explanation: Full fine-tuning needs about 128 GB. A 16-bit base alone is about 16 GB before adapters and activations. QLoRA brings the weights to about 4–5 GB, so it fits.

prompt: A team has one fine-tune for one task and serves nothing else from that base. Which serving choice is best?
optionA: Keep a separate adapter so more could be added some day
optionB: Merge it into the base weights and serve one plain model
optionC: Serve the 4-bit QLoRA training base with the adapter on top
optionD: Retrain as a full fine-tune so there is no adapter to manage
correctAnswerText: Merge it into the base weights and serve one plain model
explanation: One task, one model: merge, removing adapter overhead and the PEFT dependency. Many adapters on one base: serve adapters. A QLoRA adapter merges into a 16-bit base, then re-evaluate.

prompt: A client's contract requires its customer data to stay on servers in India. Which fine-tuning route suits?
optionA: A provider's hosted fine-tuning, since the weights then stay with them
optionB: LoRA on an open-weight model, trained and served on your own hardware
optionC: No fine-tuning is possible at all when data must stay inside India
optionD: A provider's hosted fine-tuning, with the data uploaded once only
correctAnswerText: LoRA on an open-weight model, trained and served on your own hardware
explanation: Hosted fine-tuning keeps weights and serving with the provider. Open weights with LoRA let you keep data and model on your own servers — and you own every operational problem.

prompt: When should the rule for shipping a fine-tune — recall floor, accuracy gain, forgetting limit, no safety regressions — be written?
optionA: After the results, so the rule can fit what was found
optionB: Never; the training loss alone decides whether to ship
optionC: Only if the fine-tune turns out to lose to the baseline
optionD: Before the results are seen, so the numbers decide
correctAnswerText: Before the results are seen, so the numbers decide
explanation: A rule fixed first stops the effort already spent from bending the decision. Training loss is a training signal, not a ship decision.

prompt: A support fine-tune shows forgetting on the general-ability set. Which set of mitigations does the course recommend?
optionA: A larger rank, since forgetting means the adapter is too small
optionB: More epochs at a higher rate so the model relearns general facts
optionC: Fewer epochs or lower rate, mixed general data, task-only routing
optionD: Removing the general-ability set so the drop no longer appears
correctAnswerText: Fewer epochs or lower rate, mixed general data, task-only routing
explanation: Train less or more gently, lower the rank, mix 5–20% general data, and route only task traffic to the adapter so the forgetting never meets a general question.

prompt: Rare intents have few real examples, so a team plans to generate more with a strong model. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Generate thousands and train straight away, with no human review
optionB: Use only generated data, since it is cleaner than real customer chats
optionC: Copy each real rare example fifty times instead of generating more
optionD: Review a sample, dedupe, mix with real data, tag each row's source
correctAnswerText: Review a sample, dedupe, mix with real data, tag each row's source
explanation: Generated data is a draft: its errors become habits, it repeats and it smooths away real messy Hinglish. Check the provider's terms too. Copying rows only over-weights them.

prompt: A policy assistant uses RAG but keeps ignoring the required citation format. The team wants to fine-tune the generator. How should training examples be built?
optionA: With the policy text alone, so the model memorises all of the policies
optionB: With answers copied from a forum, since style matters more than source
optionC: With questions only and no context, so it learns to answer from memory
optionD: With retrieved passages in the prompt, so it learns behaviour, not facts
correctAnswerText: With retrieved passages in the prompt, so it learns behaviour, not facts
explanation: RAG plus a fine-tuned generator: retrieval supplies facts, the fine-tune teaches using context your way — cite the clause, answer in your JSON, say when the context is silent.

prompt: For a tone-and-format fine-tune, a teammate insists on r = 128 "because higher rank is always better". What is the best response?
optionA: Skip LoRA and fully fine-tune, since rank choice is too uncertain
optionB: Start near 16 on all-linear modules and raise r only if eval gains
optionC: Agree; the highest rank the GPU allows always gives the best model
optionD: Use r = 1, since tone needs no capacity in the adapter whatsoever
correctAnswerText: Start near 16 on all-linear modules and raise r only if eval gains
explanation: Format and tone rarely need high rank. Raising r is cheap to try, so measure on the evaluation set rather than assuming bigger is better.

prompt: A team has 60 labelled examples, no evaluation set and no one to own retraining, but wants to fine-tune next week. What should they do?
optionA: Go ahead, but train for 50 epochs to make the most of the 60 rows
optionB: Go ahead, and build the evaluation set later once it is in use
optionC: Hold off: build an eval set, prompt well, and gather more examples
optionD: Go ahead: 60 examples is plenty for any fine-tune if run long enough
correctAnswerText: Hold off: build an eval set, prompt well, and gather more examples
explanation: Fewer than about 100 good examples, no eval set and no owner are all signals against. Without an eval set nobody can tell whether the fine-tune beats a good prompt.

prompt: On the spectrum single call → workflow → agent, who decides the steps of a workflow?
optionA: The model, choosing each step at run time
optionB: Nobody, because there is only ever one step
optionC: A human operator approving each step live
optionD: Your code, along a path written in advance
correctAnswerText: Your code, along a path written in advance
explanation: A workflow's path is fixed in code and the model fills in each step. Choosing steps at run time is what makes something an agent; a single call has one step and no path at all.

prompt: In the prompt-chaining pattern, what is a gate?
optionA: A code check between steps that can stop the chain
optionB: A model call that picks which branch to take next
optionC: The final call that formats the answer for the user
optionD: A rate limiter placed in front of the provider API
correctAnswerText: A code check between steps that can stop the chain
explanation: A gate is a check, usually in code, on one step's output before the next step runs — "is the outline under ten points?". Picking a branch is routing, not gating.

prompt: In the parallelisation pattern, what is voting?
optionA: Letting the cheapest of several models decide alone
optionB: Asking users to rate each of several draft answers
optionC: Running one task several times and taking the majority
optionD: Splitting one task into independent parts run at once
correctAnswerText: Running one task several times and taking the majority
explanation: Voting repeats the same task and combines the results, which suits judgements like "is this message abusive?". Splitting a task into independent parts is the other form, sectioning.

prompt: In the orchestrator–workers pattern, who decides what the sub-tasks are?
optionA: The developer, who lists them in the code
optionB: A model call that plans them at run time
optionC: Each worker, which picks its own job from a queue
optionD: The user, who types one sub-task per message
correctAnswerText: A model call that plans them at run time
explanation: The orchestrator is a model call that decides the sub-tasks from the input, then hands them to workers. When the developer can list them in advance, the simpler sectioning pattern fits instead.

prompt: Which two roles make up the evaluator–optimizer pattern?
optionA: One call produces, another judges it against criteria
optionB: One call routes, another runs the chosen branch
optionC: One call plans, many worker calls execute the steps
optionD: One call retrieves, another writes the final answer
correctAnswerText: One call produces, another judges it against criteria
explanation: A producer drafts and an evaluator checks the draft against criteria and gives feedback, looping until it passes or a round limit is hit. Planning with workers is orchestrator–workers.

prompt: What cycle does a ReAct agent repeat until it answers?
optionA: Plan every step once, then execute without looking back
optionB: Reason, call a tool, observe the result, decide again
optionC: Classify the request once, then hand it to a branch
optionD: Draft, critique and revise until a critic passes it
correctAnswerText: Reason, call a tool, observe the result, decide again
explanation: ReAct decides each next step from everything seen so far, which is the agent → tools → agent loop. Planning once is plan-and-execute; draft-critique-revise is reflection; classify-and-hand-off is routing.

prompt: In plan-and-execute, what is the replanner's job?
optionA: Write the very first plan before any tool is called
optionB: Look at results so far and edit the remaining steps
optionC: Merge every step's output into the final answer
optionD: Run each step of the plan as a separate tool call
correctAnswerText: Look at results so far and edit the remaining steps
explanation: The replanner revisits the plan after results arrive, so a step that found "account closed" can change what follows. Writing the first plan is the planner's job, and running steps is the executor's.

prompt: Which list names the stopping conditions an agent loop should have?
optionA: A time cap only, set by the user for every request
optionB: A step cap only, since that also bounds the total cost
optionC: Success, step cap, budget cap, time cap, no-progress check
optionD: Success only, since the model decides when it is done
correctAnswerText: Success, step cap, budget cap, time cap, no-progress check
explanation: Each condition catches a different failure: a stuck model, a costly long history, a hung tool, a loop repeating itself. A step cap alone does not bound tokens, because calls grow longer as history grows.

prompt: Which pattern in an agent trace is the clearest sign of no progress?
optionA: The same tool called with the same arguments repeatedly
optionB: Two different tools requested in the same model reply
optionC: A tool call that returns a long result for the first time
optionD: A final answer that is shorter than the user's question
correctAnswerText: The same tool called with the same arguments repeatedly
explanation: Repeating an identical call that returns the same result means the model is going round in circles; no-progress detection stops it at once. Parallel tool calls and long results are normal.

prompt: Which of these is a cost of autonomy that a fixed workflow avoids?
optionA: The model cannot read tool results in its next call
optionB: Each model call can produce only plain text output
optionC: The same request can take a different path on each run
optionD: Tool schemas must be written as JSON instead of code
correctAnswerText: The same request can take a different path on each run
explanation: When the model chooses the path, two runs of one request can differ, which makes behaviour harder to predict and test. Agents do read tool results, and schemas and structured output exist either way.

prompt: Why does an agent's tenth model call usually cost more input tokens than its first?
optionA: Tool definitions are only sent from the tenth call on
optionB: Later calls switch automatically to a larger model
optionC: Each call resends the whole history, which has grown
optionD: The provider adds a surcharge after the ninth call
correctAnswerText: Each call resends the whole history, which has grown
explanation: Model calls are stateless, so every call carries the system prompt, the request and every earlier tool call and result. A twelve-round run pays for the first tool result twelve times.

prompt: Why does splitting a task into a prompt chain often improve quality?
optionA: The provider caches whole chains and replays them faster
optionB: Chains let the model skip steps that it finds unnecessary
optionC: Each step becomes a narrower prompt that is easier to get right
optionD: Chained calls share one context window and so save tokens
correctAnswerText: Each step becomes a narrower prompt that is easier to get right
explanation: An outline, then a draft from the outline, then a translation, are each easier than one prompt doing all three, and a gate can check each output. A chain is fixed; the model cannot skip steps.

prompt: Why can routing let a support desk use a cheaper model for some requests?
optionA: The classifier call answers most of the questions by itself
optionB: Cheaper models are required whenever tools are attached
optionC: Routing compresses the prompt so any model can handle it
optionD: Each class gets its own handler, and simple classes need less
correctAnswerText: Each class gets its own handler, and simple classes need less
explanation: Once a request is classified, code can send "where is my order" to a small model with one tool and keep the larger model for hard cases. Routing does not compress prompts or answer by itself.

prompt: Why do errors compound in an agent more than in a single model call?
optionA: Each tool result is less accurate than the one before it
optionB: Agents always run at a higher temperature than calls do
optionC: A wrong early step feeds every step that comes after it
optionD: The step limit forces the later steps to be rushed
correctAnswerText: A wrong early step feeds every step that comes after it
explanation: An agent's later decisions are built on its earlier results, so one bad lookup misleads everything after it. Temperature is a setting you choose, and tools do not degrade with each call.

prompt: Why can a plan-and-execute agent be checked before it does anything?
optionA: It runs every step in a dry-run mode on the very first pass
optionB: Its plan is written out first, so code or a person can review it
optionC: Its planner uses a model that is guaranteed to be correct
optionD: It never calls a tool until the user has typed the word approve
correctAnswerText: Its plan is written out first, so code or a person can review it
explanation: The plan is an explicit artefact made before execution, so it can be validated in code or shown to a human. Nothing makes a planner always right, which is why plans get reviewed and replanned.

prompt: Why should a reflection loop's critic be code wherever that is possible?
optionA: A model cannot read text that a different model has written
optionB: Code critics improve the tone of a draft more reliably
optionC: Code critics let the loop run safely without any round limit
optionD: Code checks exactly; a vague model critic passes nearly anything
correctAnswerText: Code checks exactly; a vague model critic passes nearly anything
explanation: Running the SQL, running the tests or checking each required clause gives a definite answer at no model cost. A model asked "is this good?" tends to approve. Tone is the one thing code cannot judge.

prompt: Why should a run stopped by a limit return an honest partial result rather than a made-up answer?
optionA: Errors are hidden from logs, so nobody would see them anyway
optionB: The user learns what was found and that the task is unfinished
optionC: A partial result is billed at a lower rate by the provider
optionD: An honest result lets the loop resume without a checkpoint
correctAnswerText: The user learns what was found and that the task is unfinished
explanation: A limit means the task did not finish; saying so ("I could not finish; here is what I found") lets the user or a human act. Claiming success on an unfinished task is the worst outcome of all.

prompt: Why is ReAct a good fit for investigation tasks such as a failed nightly import?
optionA: Its context stays the same size however long it runs
optionB: It uses fewer model calls than any other agent pattern
optionC: It never needs a step limit, since it observes each result
optionD: Each next step can depend on what the last step found
correctAnswerText: Each next step can depend on what the last step found
explanation: Investigation is exactly the case where the path cannot be fixed in advance. ReAct pays for that with more calls and a growing context, and it still needs stop conditions.

prompt: Why do teams start with the simplest design that works and add autonomy only on evidence?
optionA: Autonomous agents need a year of testing before release
optionB: Each step toward autonomy adds cost, latency and variance
optionC: Providers charge a higher token rate for agent requests
optionD: Simple designs are the only ones that can use tools at all
correctAnswerText: Each step toward autonomy adds cost, latency and variance
explanation: One call, then a chain or router, then loops and orchestrators, then a free agent: each move right costs more calls, slower answers and less predictable paths, so it has to fix a measured failure.

prompt: Why does "update every file that uses the old API" suit orchestrator–workers rather than sectioning?
optionA: Sectioning cannot run its model calls in parallel at all
optionB: Orchestrator–workers needs no model call to plan the work
optionC: Which files change is known only after searching at run time
optionD: Each file must be handled by one and the same worker call
correctAnswerText: Which files change is known only after searching at run time
explanation: Sectioning needs the parts known when you write the code; here the parts come from a search, so a planner call decides them. Sectioning does run in parallel, and the orchestrator is itself a model call.

prompt: A college app sends a student's statement of purpose to the model and saves the feedback it returns. A teammate calls it "our agent". What is it?
optionA: A workflow, because the feedback is saved afterwards
optionB: A multi-agent system, since a student and a model act
optionC: A single model call; code fixes the one and only step
optionD: An agent, because a model writes the saved output
correctAnswerText: A single model call; code fixes the one and only step
explanation: Nothing is chosen by the model: code calls it once and saves the result. That is a single call, however useful. Saving the output is ordinary code, not a workflow step the model takes.

prompt: A telecom chatbot gets SIM-swap, bill-dispute and plan-change requests, each needing its own tools and policy text. Which pattern should it start with?
optionA: Reflection, so every reply is critiqued before it is sent
optionB: One ReAct agent holding every tool for every request kind
optionC: Routing to a branch per request kind, plus an "other" branch
optionD: Parallel voting over three copies of the very same prompt
correctAnswerText: Routing to a branch per request kind, plus an "other" branch
explanation: Known request kinds with their own tools are the routing case: a cheap classification, then a focused branch, with "other" going to a person. One agent with everything carries every tool and policy on every call.

prompt: A vendor contract must be checked for payment, liability and termination issues, each by its own prompt. Which pattern fits, and why?
optionA: Chaining: each check needs the previous check's output first
optionB: Routing: only one of the three checks should ever be run
optionC: Voting: the three prompts decide each clause by a majority
optionD: Sectioning: the three checks are independent, so run them at once
correctAnswerText: Sectioning: the three checks are independent, so run them at once
explanation: Independent checks known in advance are sectioning: run all three at the same time and combine. Voting repeats one task; chaining is for steps that depend on each other.

prompt: A text-to-SQL feature must only return queries that actually run on the schema. Which loop design fits?
optionA: Generate ten queries in parallel and keep the longest of them
optionB: Generate, run on a test copy, feed errors back, cap the rounds
optionC: Ask a second model if the SQL looks correct, with no round cap
optionD: Generate once and show the SQL to the user without running it
correctAnswerText: Generate, run on a test copy, feed errors back, cap the rounds
explanation: Executing the query is an exact, code-based evaluator, and its error message is useful feedback. A round cap ends the loop when the question cannot be answered from the schema at all.

prompt: A ReAct agent averages 4 tool rounds per request, one tool per round. How many model calls should you estimate for a typical request?
optionA: 1: the tools do the rest after the first call
optionB: 5: one per round, plus one to write the answer
optionC: 8: two per round, one to call and one to read
optionD: 4: one per round, since the last one also answers
correctAnswerText: 5: one per round, plus one to write the answer
explanation: Each round is one model call that requests a tool; after the last result, one more call writes the answer. Tools are run by your code and need no model calls of their own.

prompt: A plan-and-execute agent makes a 3-step plan and has no replanner. How many model calls does one run make?
optionA: 4: one plan and then one call for each step
optionB: 3: one model call for each step of the plan
optionC: 6: two calls for every step, plan included
optionD: 5: one plan, one per step, and one final answer
correctAnswerText: 5: one plan, one per step, and one final answer
explanation: One call writes the plan, the executor makes one call per step, and a final call writes the answer: 1 + N + 1. Each executor call sees only its step, which is why it can be a smaller model.

prompt: A research agent for a Chennai law firm must never run past 2 minutes or 40,000 tokens. Where do these limits belong?
optionA: In each tool's description, so tools refuse late
optionB: In the user's request, so they choose each time
optionC: In the loop's code, checked after every step
optionD: In the system prompt, so the model keeps track
correctAnswerText: In the loop's code, checked after every step
explanation: Limits are only guarantees if code enforces them. A model told about a budget may still overrun it, and tools cannot see the run's total time or tokens.

prompt: An agent's log shows the same "case not found" error from search_cases three times in a row. The step limit is 20. What should the loop do now?
optionA: Carry on until step 20, since the limit is not reached
optionB: Stop on the repeated error and report what it tried
optionC: Hide the error and give the user a confident answer
optionD: Restart the run from scratch at a higher temperature
correctAnswerText: Stop on the repeated error and report what it tried
explanation: The same error three times is a no-progress signal; stopping now saves seventeen calls and gives an honest result. The step limit is a backstop, not a target to reach.

prompt: A bank's loan-rejection letters must name the grievance officer and state the reason code. How should the critic in a reflection loop be built?
optionA: Code checks the required clauses; a model judges only tone
optionB: One model asked "Is this letter good? Reply PASS or FAIL"
optionC: A second drafter whose letter replaces the first one
optionD: No critic; the drafting prompt lists the rules in capitals
correctAnswerText: Code checks the required clauses; a model judges only tone
explanation: Required clauses and codes are checkable exactly in code, so make that the critic and use a model only for what code cannot judge. A vague model critic passes nearly everything.

prompt: "Find the best 1-year FD across these 5 banks for a senior citizen" always means: look up 5 rates, add the senior bonus, rank. What should you build?
optionA: A supervisor with one specialist agent for each bank
optionB: A ReAct agent that decides which bank to look up next
optionC: A fixed workflow with the five look-ups run in parallel
optionD: A reflection loop that critiques the ranking until it passes
correctAnswerText: A fixed workflow with the five look-ups run in parallel
explanation: The shape never varies, so code owns it: five tool look-ups in parallel and one model call to write the answer from the table. A ReAct version would make about six calls over a growing history.

prompt: An agent "forgets" at step 4 a tool result it used at step 2. Each request is built from the system prompt, the user message and only the latest tool result. Diagnosis?
optionA: The step limit is set too low for a four-step task
optionB: Calls are stateless, and earlier results were never resent
optionC: The model's context window is too small for four steps
optionD: The provider deletes tool results after two model calls
correctAnswerText: Calls are stateless, and earlier results were never resent
explanation: The model knows only what is in the request. Dropping earlier tool calls and results erased them; the loop must append each result to the history (and trim deliberately if it grows).

prompt: An invoice bot built as an agent takes different paths on identical invoices and keeps failing audits. The steps are always extract, match the PO, save. Root cause?
optionA: The agent lacks a separate tool for each invoice field
optionB: Autonomy was spent on a task whose steps are fixed
optionC: The model's temperature is set too low for invoices
optionD: The audit log keeps too few of the agent's steps
correctAnswerText: Autonomy was spent on a task whose steps are fixed
explanation: Variance between runs is the price of letting the model choose the path; here there was nothing to choose. A workflow would run the same three steps every time and pass the audit.

prompt: A ReAct agent's cost per request roughly tripled when typical tasks grew from 4 to 10 rounds — more than the 2.5x growth in rounds. Why?
optionA: Each round resends a longer history, so tokens grow faster
optionB: The provider charges more per round after the fifth one
optionC: Tools return larger results the more often they are called
optionD: ReAct adds a hidden planning call every second round
correctAnswerText: Each round resends a longer history, so tokens grow faster
explanation: Input tokens per call grow with the history, so total tokens grow faster than the number of rounds. There is no hidden planning call or per-round surcharge.

prompt: A travel agent planned "book flight, book hotel, email itinerary". The flight step found no seats, yet a hotel was booked for those dates. What was missing?
optionA: A reflection critic that reviews the itinerary email
optionB: A replanner that edits the plan when results change it
optionC: A larger model for the planner, so plans come out better
optionD: A parallel fan-out so all three steps run at the same time
correctAnswerText: A replanner that edits the plan when results change it
explanation: A plan is fixed when it is made; without a replanner the executor carries on through a plan that no longer fits. A better planner cannot know the flight would be full.

prompt: A reflection loop for marketing copy always runs to its round limit; the critic keeps asking for "more energy". Diagnosis?
optionA: The round limit is too high for marketing copy tasks
optionB: The drafter and the critic must use different providers
optionC: The criteria are taste, not checkable, so nothing passes
optionD: The critic needs the full conversation history as well
correctAnswerText: The criteria are taste, not checkable, so nothing passes
explanation: Reflection pays off when quality is checkable. With taste-based criteria a critic can find fault forever (or approve everything). Define concrete criteria, or drop the loop.

prompt: A pipeline of four model steps, each right 95% of the time independently, gives correct end results only about 81% of the time. What explains it?
optionA: Each step's accuracy was measured on a different data set
optionB: The step limit cuts off one of the steps in one run in five
optionC: Errors multiply along the chain: 0.95 to the fourth is 0.81
optionD: The fourth step uses a weaker model than the other three
correctAnswerText: Errors multiply along the chain: 0.95 to the fourth is 0.81
explanation: For independent steps, end-to-end accuracy is the product of each step's accuracy. Nothing else needs to be wrong; this is why long chains need checks between steps.

prompt: A routed support bot gives billing answers to KYC questions about one time in eight. What should you check first?
optionA: The step limit set on the KYC branch's own agent loop
optionB: The classifier's accuracy, measured on its own labelled set
optionC: Whether the final answers are longer than the questions
optionD: Whether the billing branch has too many tools attached
correctAnswerText: The classifier's accuracy, measured on its own labelled set
explanation: Routing fails by misrouting, so evaluate the classifier alone on labelled requests and log every route. The branches' tools and limits only matter after the request reaches the right one.

prompt: An agent stopped by its step limit told the user "Your refund is done", though no refund tool ever ran. What is the design fault?
optionA: A limit stop must report honestly, never fake success
optionB: The step limit should be removed for refund requests
optionC: The refund tool should run automatically at the limit
optionD: The model should be told the limit in its system prompt
correctAnswerText: A limit stop must report honestly, never fake success
explanation: When a limit ends a run, code should return a fixed honest message ("I could not finish"), not let the model improvise. Removing the limit or acting automatically makes things worse.

prompt: An orchestrator–workers code migration gives every worker the whole repository and the full plan; workers are slow and costly. Diagnosis?
optionA: The plan should be hidden so the workers cannot read it
optionB: Workers need the user's original chat history as well
optionC: The orchestrator should handle every file by itself instead
optionD: Workers should get only their own sub-task and its files
correctAnswerText: Workers should get only their own sub-task and its files
explanation: The benefit of workers is a small, focused context each. Sending everything to every worker multiplies tokens and dilutes attention without helping any single file's change.

prompt: A design review estimated 3 model calls per request for a routed support bot; traces show an average of 7. Which finding best explains the gap?
optionA: The routing rule runs once for every word in the request
optionB: Tools are counted as model calls in the tracing dashboard
optionC: The classifier call is billed by the provider as several calls
optionD: Many requests fall to the "other" branch, a ReAct loop with tools
correctAnswerText: Many requests fall to the "other" branch, a ReAct loop with tools
explanation: An estimate holds only for the traffic mix it assumed. If a large share of requests misses the known kinds and falls to an open-ended branch, average calls rise; trace real runs to check.

prompt: A team proposes an autonomous agent for HR policy questions; nobody has tried a single retrieval-backed call yet. Best response?
optionA: Try one call with retrieval first, then measure it
optionB: Build the agent, since agents include single calls
optionC: Build a multi-agent team with an owner per policy
optionD: Skip retrieval and fine-tune a model on the policies
correctAnswerText: Try one call with retrieval first, then measure it
explanation: Policy Q&A is usually answered by retrieval plus one call. Measure that on real questions; only a measured failure justifies more calls and more variance.

prompt: Which justification for choosing an agent over a workflow would hold up in a design review?
optionA: Workflows cannot call more than one model per request
optionB: The next step depends on results we cannot know in advance
optionC: An agent removes the need to test each step separately
optionD: Agents are the newest approach and will impress stakeholders
correctAnswerText: The next step depends on results we cannot know in advance
explanation: Autonomy is worth its cost only when the path genuinely varies with what is found. Workflows can make many calls, and agents need more testing, not less.

prompt: A translation evaluator–optimizer loop passes 98% of first drafts on the eval set. What is the better design now?
optionA: Raise the round limit so the 2% get more chances to pass
optionB: Remove every check, since 98% is close enough to perfect
optionC: Drop the loop; keep a cheap check that flags the 2% for review
optionD: Add a second critic model to double-check every draft
correctAnswerText: Drop the loop; keep a cheap check that flags the 2% for review
explanation: If the first draft almost always passes, the loop mostly adds calls. Keeping the check catches the rare failure for a human; removing it ships those failures silently.

prompt: For an open-ended "why did UPI settlements fail last night?" investigation, which design is best?
optionA: Routing to one of three canned diagnosis prompts
optionB: Plan-and-execute with a fixed plan, no replanner
optionC: One call given every log line from the whole night
optionD: ReAct with step, budget and no-progress limits
correctAnswerText: ReAct with step, budget and no-progress limits
explanation: Each finding decides the next check, which is ReAct's case — bounded by stop rules. A fixed plan cannot adapt, canned prompts cannot investigate, and a night of logs will not fit or focus.

prompt: A team split one working agent into five specialists; quality is flat and cost has doubled. Which finding would justify keeping some split?
optionA: Five prompts are easier to keep in sync than just one
optionB: Each specialist can now use the same shared prompt
optionC: The architecture diagram now looks far more complete
optionD: One tool reads salary data that uploads must never reach
correctAnswerText: One tool reads salary data that uploads must never reach
explanation: Different permissions are a concrete reason: isolating the salary tool limits what injected text in an upload can reach. Appearance is not a reason, and shared prompts defeat specialisation.

prompt: Why might you prefer plan-and-execute over ReAct for a long report whose shape is predictable?
optionA: Plan-and-execute always makes fewer model calls than ReAct
optionB: ReAct cannot call more than one tool during a single run
optionC: Executor calls see one step, so a smaller model can do them
optionD: Plans cannot go wrong, so no step limits are needed at all
correctAnswerText: Executor calls see one step, so a smaller model can do them
explanation: Short, focused executor calls suit a cheaper model and the plan can be reviewed first. It can make more calls than ReAct, and plans can still go stale.

prompt: Which stopping design is strongest for a production research agent?
optionA: One high step cap, since that also bounds the token spend
optionB: A final answer only, trusting the model to judge when it is done
optionC: A final answer, plus step, token and time caps and repeat checks
optionD: A time cap only, because users care most about waiting
correctAnswerText: A final answer, plus step, token and time caps and repeat checks
explanation: Several independent ways out cover different failures. A step cap does not bound tokens as history grows, and a model alone may never decide it is done.

prompt: Two designs answer the same request: routing (2 calls, short context) and ReAct (6 calls, growing context). Quality is equal on the eval set. Which do you ship?
optionA: ReAct: more calls mean more careful reasoning
optionB: ReAct: a growing context improves later answers
optionC: Both, choosing one at random for each request
optionD: Routing: equal quality for fewer, shorter calls
correctAnswerText: Routing: equal quality for fewer, shorter calls
explanation: With quality equal on a representative eval set, the cheaper, faster and more predictable design wins. More calls are a cost, not a virtue.

prompt: For which output is a reflection loop most worth its extra model calls?
optionA: Code that must pass a known test suite before use
optionB: A one-line summary that users rarely read in full
optionC: A brainstorm list where any idea is acceptable
optionD: A casual greeting shown on the app's home screen
correctAnswerText: Code that must pass a known test suite before use
explanation: Reflection earns its calls where quality is checkable and matters; a test suite is an exact critic. Low-stakes or uncheckable output gains little from a critique loop.

prompt: Which task is the strongest candidate for an autonomous agent rather than a workflow?
optionA: Fixing a failed data import, where each check guides the next
optionB: Producing a weekly sales PDF with four fixed sections
optionC: Turning each support email into category, priority and reply
optionD: Translating every product description into Hindi and Tamil
correctAnswerText: Fixing a failed data import, where each check guides the next
explanation: An agent earns its cost when the number and order of steps depend on findings. The other three have steps known in advance and belong in workflows.

prompt: Which MCP primitive is meant to be invoked by the model itself?
optionA: Hosts, which the model starts as servers
optionB: Tools, which the model calls as actions
optionC: Resources, which the model loads by URI
optionD: Prompts, which the model picks as templates
correctAnswerText: Tools, which the model calls as actions
explanation: Tools are model-invoked. Resources are data the application chooses to attach, and prompts are templates the user picks, like a slash command. The host is the application, not something the model starts.

prompt: What does a Pydantic field typed Literal["casual", "sick", "earned"] become in the generated JSON Schema?
optionA: Three separate optional boolean properties
optionB: An integer code from 0 to 2, one per value
optionC: An enum listing exactly those three values
optionD: A free string with the values in its description
correctAnswerText: An enum listing exactly those three values
explanation: Literal becomes enum, so the model is offered only those values and cannot invent "annual". A free string with the values in prose is a hint the model may ignore.

prompt: Which fields make up the regular error shape a well-designed tool returns to the model?
optionA: ok, error, and either details, a hint or retryable
optionB: an empty string, so the model simply tries again
optionC: the exception class name and the server host name
optionD: a status code, the stack trace and the failing SQL
correctAnswerText: ok, error, and either details, a hint or retryable
explanation: A small, consistent shape tells the model what failed and what to do: which fields to fix, a hint such as "confirm the dates with the user", or that a retry may work. Traces and SQL leak internals and teach nothing.

prompt: What is served at 169.254.169.254 inside a typical cloud virtual machine?
optionA: The cloud provider's public DNS resolver for the VM
optionB: A reserved address that always refuses any HTTPS call
optionC: The metadata service, which can hand out credentials
optionD: The load balancer in front of the model provider API
correctAnswerText: The metadata service, which can hand out credentials
explanation: The link-local metadata endpoint issues instance credentials to whatever asks from inside the machine, so a fetch tool that reaches it is a server-side request forgery risk.

prompt: In a code-running tool, what does subprocess.run(..., timeout=5) actually limit?
optionA: The memory, CPU and network the code may use
optionB: Every child process the snippet goes on to start
optionC: Which files the code may read from the disk
optionD: Only how long the process it started may run
correctAnswerText: Only how long the process it started may run
explanation: A timeout limits time for the one process it started. It does not limit memory, files, network or processes that snippet spawns — which is why it is not a sandbox.

prompt: What are MCP tool annotations such as destructive_hint and read_only_hint?
optionA: Rate limits the client applies to each tool per minute
optionB: Hints so clients can ask for confirmation, not enforcement
optionC: Permissions the server enforces on every call it receives
optionD: Labels that hide the tool from the model's list of tools
correctAnswerText: Hints so clients can ask for confirmation, not enforcement
explanation: Annotations describe a tool so a well-behaved client can confirm before a destructive call. A client may ignore them, so any rule that matters is enforced by the server.

prompt: Which tool name follows the advice of a namespace plus a verb?
optionA: payroll_get_payslip
optionB: PayslipHelperV2
optionC: tool_3
optionD: getStuff
correctAnswerText: payroll_get_payslip
explanation: A namespace and a verb tell the model the family and the action, and keep names from colliding when MCP servers bring their own tools. The others say nothing about what the tool does.

prompt: When an MCP client launches a stdio server, which environment variables does the official Python SDK pass by default?
optionA: Every variable of the parent, secrets included
optionB: A short safe set such as PATH, plus any you add
optionC: None at all, so the server must hard-code paths
optionD: Only variables whose names begin with MCP_
correctAnswerText: A short safe set such as PATH, plus any you add
explanation: The SDK passes a small allow-list of system variables and merges what you give in env. Secrets in the parent are not handed to a server unless you pass them, which is worth keeping.

prompt: In a tool-calling loop, which message must appear in the history just before the tool-result messages?
optionA: The assistant message that contained the tool calls
optionB: Nothing; tool results can stand on their own
optionC: A system message listing which tools were used
optionD: A new user message repeating the original request
correctAnswerText: The assistant message that contained the tool calls
explanation: Each tool result answers a tool call by id, so the assistant message holding those calls must precede the results. Leaving it out is a common cause of a 400 on the second model call.

prompt: Which pair shows a read tool and a write tool correctly kept apart?
optionA: run_sql(query) for reads and writes
optionB: call_hr_api(method, path, body)
optionC: leave_tool(action="read" or "write")
optionD: get_leave_balance and apply_leave
correctAnswerText: get_leave_balance and apply_leave
explanation: Separate tools let reads run freely while the write is confirmed, logged and rate-limited. One tool with a mode, a generic API caller or raw SQL puts reads and writes behind one permission.

prompt: Why expose one apply_leave tool rather than tools mirroring the create, set-dates and submit endpoints?
optionA: Models are allowed to call only one tool per task
optionB: One call replaces planning three steps and passing an id
optionC: Endpoint tools cannot have JSON Schemas of their own
optionD: Three tools would expose the HR database password
correctAnswerText: One call replaces planning three steps and passing an id
explanation: Mirroring endpoints makes the model plan three calls, carry an id between them and get the order right — three chances to fail. A task-shaped tool removes that work.

prompt: Why must a tool's schema never include an employee_id argument for the person asking?
optionA: JSON Schema cannot express identifiers of that format
optionB: Identity fields make the schema too long for the model
optionC: The model fills arguments, so a user's text could change it
optionD: The provider strips identity fields before tools run
correctAnswerText: The model fills arguments, so a user's text could change it
explanation: Anything in the schema is chosen by the model, which follows what the user typed. The caller's identity must come from the authenticated request, where text cannot reach it.

prompt: Why should a tool's description say when NOT to use it?
optionA: Overlapping tools are told apart only by what they declare
optionB: It lowers the token count of the whole tool definition
optionC: It stops the tool's code from running on bad input
optionD: Providers reject descriptions without any negative rule
correctAnswerText: Overlapping tools are told apart only by what they declare
explanation: The model chooses from names, descriptions and schemas alone. When two tools could plausibly answer, an explicit boundary ("for balances use get_leave_balance") is what makes the choice reliable.

prompt: Why is the provider's tool_call_id a poor idempotency key for a write tool?
optionA: It is too short to be unique across all of your users
optionB: A retried call gets a new id, so the duplicate is missed
optionC: It is assigned only after the tool has finished running
optionD: The model can read and change the id in its next reply
correctAnswerText: A retried call gets a new id, so the duplicate is missed
explanation: An idempotency key must be the same for the same request. A model retrying after a timeout produces a new call id; a hash of what makes the request unique stays the same.

prompt: Why do forty tool definitions hurt an agent even on requests that use only two of them?
optionA: Unused tools run in the background and slow replies
optionB: All definitions ride on every call: more tokens, worse picks
optionC: Providers refuse any request carrying over ten tools
optionD: The model must call each defined tool once per task
correctAnswerText: All definitions ride on every call: more tokens, worse picks
explanation: Every definition is sent on every model call, so cost grows with the catalogue, and many similar tools make wrong choices more likely. Unused tools do not run.

prompt: Why does an MCP tool raise ToolError for an unknown leave_type rather than let the error crash?
optionA: ToolError closes the session so no bad call is ever retried
optionB: The client gets is_error with a message the model can act on
optionC: ToolError hides the failure from the server's own logs
optionD: Crashing tools are removed from the server automatically
correctAnswerText: The client gets is_error with a message the model can act on
explanation: ToolError is the anticipated-failure path: the call succeeds at the protocol level and returns is_error with your message, so the model can correct itself. Protocol errors are for malformed requests.

prompt: Why should an MCP tool get its own token for the payroll API rather than forward the caller's token?
optionA: A forwarded token acts beyond its audience and blurs the audit
optionB: Forwarded tokens are always too large for HTTP headers
optionC: Payroll services accept only tokens that never expire
optionD: The caller's token must be kept for the client's next call
correctAnswerText: A forwarded token acts beyond its audience and blurs the audit
explanation: A token is issued for one audience. Passing it on lets it act where it was never meant to, and the downstream log no longer shows which service acted. A token issued for payroll keeps both clear.

prompt: Why is a subprocess with a timeout and a cleared environment still not a sandbox for model-written code?
optionA: The timeout fires only after the output cap is reached
optionB: Python cannot start at all without the parent's environment
optionC: Subprocesses always run with administrator rights
optionD: It runs as your service user, with its files and network
correctAnswerText: It runs as your service user, with its files and network
explanation: Clearing env hides variables and the timeout bounds time, but the child can still read any file your service user can, open sockets and use all memory. Isolation must come from the OS or below.

prompt: Why do <untrusted_web_content> tags not, by themselves, make a web-reading agent safe?
optionA: Labels help the model treat text as data but guarantee nothing
optionB: The tags are stripped by the provider before the model call
optionC: Tags slow the model so much that the run times out
optionD: Models can read only the text that is outside any tags
correctAnswerText: Labels help the model treat text as data but guarantee nothing
explanation: Delimiters make it likelier the model treats fetched text as data, but it may still follow an instruction inside. What makes injection harmless is that the reading run cannot act without approval.

prompt: Why count consecutive failed tool calls separately from the agent's overall step limit?
optionA: A stuck model goes to a human before it wastes every step
optionB: The step limit counts only the successful tool calls
optionC: Most providers bill failed tool calls at double the rate
optionD: Errors in a row mean the tool must be redeployed
correctAnswerText: A stuck model goes to a human before it wastes every step
explanation: Errors let a model fix itself, but a confused one will try forever. A small budget of failures in a row hands over early, while the step limit still bounds the whole run.

prompt: A get_tickets tool takes a status that must be open, pending or closed. The model sometimes sends "resolved". Best schema change?
optionA: Make status optional so the model can leave it out
optionB: Add "use valid statuses" to the system prompt
optionC: Accept any string and map unknowns to open quietly
optionD: Make status an enum of the three allowed values
correctAnswerText: Make status an enum of the three allowed values
explanation: An enum moves the choice into the schema, so the model is offered only valid values and validation rejects anything else. Prompt pleading is unreliable, and silent mapping hides wrong results.

prompt: An apply_leave call arrives with the end date before the start date. What should the tool return?
optionA: The full Python traceback, so the model can see the cause
optionB: An error naming the rule, with a hint to recheck with the user
optionC: A success, after swapping the two dates so the request passes
optionD: An empty string, so the model decides what to try next
correctAnswerText: An error naming the rule, with a hint to recheck with the user
explanation: A business-rule error should say which rule broke and steer the model back to the human rather than guessing new dates. Silently swapping dates may file leave the employee never asked for.

prompt: A refund tool must be safe to call twice when the payment API times out. Which idempotency key fits?
optionA: The current timestamp to the millisecond
optionB: The tool_call_id the provider attached
optionC: A random UUID made at the start of each call
optionD: A hash of customer, order and refund amount
correctAnswerText: A hash of customer, order and refund amount
explanation: The key must be derived from what makes the refund unique, so a retry sends the same key and the payment API returns the original result. UUIDs, timestamps and call ids change on retry.

prompt: Your Streamable HTTP MCP server at a Bengaluru GCC receives a valid token that was issued for a different internal service. What should it do?
optionA: Forward it on to the service it was issued for
optionB: Accept it for read tools and refuse it for writes
optionC: Accept it, since its signature and expiry are valid
optionD: Reject it, because the audience is not this server
correctAnswerText: Reject it, because the audience is not this server
explanation: A token is valid only for its audience. Accepting tokens meant for other services lets any of them be replayed here; the verifier must check audience as well as signature and expiry.

prompt: A finance team's agent should only read leave balances from your HR MCP server. How do you enforce that?
optionA: Add "never apply leave" to the finance agent's prompt
optionB: Mark apply_leave with destructive_hint set to true
optionC: Grant only leave:read and check the scope in apply_leave
optionD: Leave apply_leave out of the server's instructions text
correctAnswerText: Grant only leave:read and check the scope in apply_leave
explanation: Scopes on the verified token, checked inside each tool, are enforcement the client cannot bypass. Prompts and annotations are requests to a client that may ignore them.

prompt: A fetch_page tool for an RBI-circular assistant must not reach internal addresses. What is the soundest check?
optionA: Check that the URL is shorter than two hundred characters
optionB: Allow every https URL, since TLS proves the site is safe
optionC: A host allow-list, with private IPs blocked after DNS lookup
optionD: Block any URL whose text contains the word "internal"
correctAnswerText: A host allow-list, with private IPs blocked after DNS lookup
explanation: An allow-list of hosts, plus blocking private and link-local addresses after resolution, stops requests to the metadata service and internal systems. TLS proves identity, not that a site is harmless.

prompt: An HR agent has 35 tools across leave, payroll, travel and IT, and often picks the wrong one. Which change fits first?
optionA: Route the request, then offer only that area's tools
optionB: Raise the temperature so the model explores more tools
optionC: Let the model call all 35 tools and merge the results
optionD: Add "IMPORTANT: choose carefully" to every description
correctAnswerText: Route the request, then offer only that area's tools
explanation: Routing first and offering a subset cuts the tokens and the confusable choices. Capital-letter pleading is unreliable, and a higher temperature makes choices less consistent.

prompt: Your MCP server should let users pick a "draft a leave email" template, like a slash command. Which primitive fits?
optionA: A sampling request sent from server to client
optionB: A prompt, which the user chooses in the client
optionC: A resource, which the app attaches by its URI
optionD: A tool, which the model calls when it decides to
correctAnswerText: A prompt, which the user chooses in the client
explanation: Prompts are user-chosen templates. Making it a tool hands the choice to the model, and a resource is data the application attaches, not a template the user runs.

prompt: fetch_page receives a 302 from an allow-listed domain to an unknown one. What should the tool do?
optionA: Retry the first URL until it stops redirecting
optionB: Follow it if the new page is under the size limit
optionC: Follow it, since the first host has passed the checks
optionD: Not follow it blindly: check the new host or refuse
correctAnswerText: Not follow it blindly: check the new host or refuse
explanation: A redirect is a new request to a new host. Following it blindly lets an allowed site send the agent anywhere, including internal addresses; size has nothing to do with permission.

prompt: Your loop gets a 400 on the second model call: a tool message does not answer any preceding tool call. What fix fits?
optionA: Retry the second call with a higher max token limit
optionB: Remove tool_call_id from each of the tool messages
optionC: Send the tool results as a user message instead
optionD: Append the assistant tool-call message before the results
correctAnswerText: Append the assistant tool-call message before the results
explanation: Results must answer calls the history contains. Append the assistant message with its tool_calls, then one tool message per call id; removing ids or relabelling results breaks the pairing.

prompt: search_policies is described "Searches policies." and get_policy "Gets a policy." A hotel-limit question sometimes pulls a 9,000-token document. Diagnosis?
optionA: The model's temperature is set too high for tool use
optionB: get_policy is missing a required argument in its schema
optionC: The 9,000-token policy is too long for the model to read
optionD: The descriptions overlap and neither says when to use it
correctAnswerText: The descriptions overlap and neither says when to use it
explanation: Both tools plausibly answer, so the model guesses. Say what each does and when not to use it, then add the question to the tool-selection eval set so the fix stays fixed.

prompt: An employee has two leave requests for one set of dates. The trace: HR API timeout, retryable true, then a second call carrying a fresh uuid4 key. Root cause?
optionA: The model should never retry calls marked retryable
optionB: Two requests mean the step limit was set too high
optionC: The HR API timed out because deduplication is slow
optionD: A new key per call made the retry look like a new request
correctAnswerText: A new key per call made the retry look like a new request
explanation: The first call had succeeded; the retry carried a different key, so the API created another request. Derive the key from employee, type and dates, and return the existing id on a repeat.

prompt: A banking agent's balance tool takes account_number as an argument. A user typed "check my brother's account 4471" and got its balance. What failed?
optionA: The account number was not validated against a regex
optionB: The tool should have masked all but the last four digits
optionC: The model should have refused, so its prompt is too weak
optionD: Identity came from a model-filled argument, not the session
correctAnswerText: Identity came from a model-filled argument, not the session
explanation: The schema gave the model a choice it must not have. Take the account from the authenticated user and check ownership in the tool; a stronger prompt still leaves the door open.

prompt: After a code run reports "timed out after 5s", a python process still pegs the server's CPU. Why?
optionA: Python ignores timeouts while it is printing to stdout
optionB: The timeout was given in minutes rather than in seconds
optionC: The snippet started a child that the timeout did not kill
optionD: Output capping keeps the process alive until it is read
correctAnswerText: The snippet started a child that the timeout did not kill
explanation: subprocess.run kills the process it started, not that process's children. A per-run container with a process limit, killed whole at the deadline, is the fix.

prompt: An MCP stdio server launched with command "npx" works on a laptop but fails at startup inside a slim Python container. Cause?
optionA: The container has no network, so stdio cannot connect
optionB: npx-based servers need an OAuth token to open a session
optionC: The stdio transport is disabled inside every container
optionD: A stdio server is a local child process, and Node is absent
correctAnswerText: A stdio server is a local child process, and Node is absent
explanation: Stdio means the client starts the server as a process on the same machine, so its runtime must be installed there. Either add Node to the image or run the server separately over HTTP.

prompt: After upgrading the MCP Python SDK to 2.x, a bridge fails with "'CallToolResult' object has no attribute 'isError'". Diagnosis?
optionA: The server stopped returning errors after the upgrade
optionB: The 2.x SDK uses snake_case; isError is only the wire name
optionC: isError was removed because tools can no longer fail
optionD: The bridge must now parse results as raw JSON-RPC text
correctAnswerText: The 2.x SDK uses snake_case; isError is only the wire name
explanation: In 2.x the result attributes are is_error and structured_content; the camelCase names exist only in the JSON. Pin the SDK, upgrade deliberately and run in-process client tests first.

prompt: A review of a web agent finds: allow-listed fetch, size caps, content tags, and send_email available in the same run with no approval. Which gap is the real risk?
optionA: The content tags should use a less common tag name
optionB: The size cap should be lower than two hundred kilobytes
optionC: The allow-list should include more news domains
optionD: A write tool is held in the run that reads untrusted text
correctAnswerText: A write tool is held in the run that reads untrusted text
explanation: Injected instructions in a page can steer the model; the damage they can do depends on what the run can act on. Remove the write tool from that run or put it behind human approval.

prompt: A product-search tool returns "" when nothing matches; the agent keeps rephrasing until the step limit. Best diagnosis?
optionA: The search tool should raise an exception on no results
optionB: An empty result gives no hint, so the model keeps guessing
optionC: The step limit is too low for agents that search a lot
optionD: The model needs a larger context to handle empty results
correctAnswerText: An empty result gives no hint, so the model keeps guessing
explanation: A result like "No products under 2000; the cheapest is 2199" tells the model what to do next. An empty string invites endless rephrasing; an exception gives it even less.

prompt: Input cost per task is high; the trace shows 8 model calls, each carrying about 11,000 tokens of tool definitions. What best explains the bill?
optionA: Some forty definitions are resent on each of the calls
optionB: The model calls every tool once to read its schema
optionC: Tool results are billed at a higher per-token rate
optionD: Definitions are cached, so cost is only output tokens
correctAnswerText: Some forty definitions are resent on each of the calls
explanation: Around forty definitions at roughly 280 tokens each, times eight calls, is about 90,000 input tokens before the user's words. Route to subsets or search over tools.

prompt: A team relied on destructive_hint so a client would confirm deletions, but a custom client deleted files without asking. What was wrong?
optionA: destructive_hint must be paired with read_only_hint
optionB: Annotations are hints; the server must enforce the rule
optionC: The client needed a newer protocol to read the hints
optionD: The tool name lacked a verb such as delete or remove
correctAnswerText: Annotations are hints; the server must enforce the rule
explanation: Clients may honour annotations or ignore them. A rule that matters — a scope, an approval, a check of who is calling — has to live on the server.

prompt: Which tool set is best for an agent that files employee expense claims?
optionA: create_claim, add_line, attach_receipt, then submit
optionB: submit_claim and get_claim_status, each task-shaped
optionC: call_expense_api(method, path, body) for everything
optionD: A single run_sql(query) over the claims database
correctAnswerText: submit_claim and get_claim_status, each task-shaped
explanation: Task-shaped tools leave the model nothing to sequence and split read from write. Endpoint mirrors add planning and ordering; generic API or SQL tools hand the model far too much power.

prompt: Which code-execution setup do you recommend for a multi-tenant data-analysis agent?
optionA: The API process itself, using exec() with limited globals
optionB: A subprocess with a timeout under the API's service user
optionC: One shared container for all users, kept warm for speed
optionD: A fresh sandbox per user, no network or secrets, capped output
correctAnswerText: A fresh sandbox per user, no network or secrets, capped output
explanation: Per-user isolation from the OS or a hosted sandbox, with no credentials and no network, means a hijacked snippet reaches nothing. Shared or in-process execution exposes every tenant.

prompt: Where should identity and permission decisions be made for an MCP server that other teams' agents call?
optionA: On the server, from the verified token's subject and scopes
optionB: In each client's system prompt, which lists allowed users
optionC: In the calling model, which reads the user's name from chat
optionD: In a header the client sets, trusted because it is internal
correctAnswerText: On the server, from the verified token's subject and scopes
explanation: Only the server can verify signature, expiry and audience, then read subject and scopes. Models, prompts and free-form headers can all be steered or forged.

prompt: An apply_leave agent keeps failing on "next Thursday" dates. Which change best removes the failure rather than just bounding it?
optionA: Give the model today's date, or resolve dates and confirm
optionB: Raise max_errors_in_a_row so the model has longer to fix it
optionC: Lower the step limit so the loop ends sooner each time
optionD: Tell the model in capitals to always use YYYY-MM-DD
correctAnswerText: Give the model today's date, or resolve dates and confirm
explanation: The error budget only bounds the damage. Giving the model today's date, or letting the tool resolve relative dates and return them for confirmation, lets it succeed.

prompt: Your internal catalogue grows to 300 tools exposed through MCP. Which approach scales best?
optionA: Merge everything into one generic do_anything tool
optionB: Search over tool descriptions and offer the top few
optionC: Offer 15 tools chosen at random for each request
optionD: Send all 300 definitions on every call to be safe
correctAnswerText: Search over tool descriptions and offer the top few
explanation: Embedding descriptions and offering the most relevant few keeps tokens and confusion low. All 300 every call is costly and inaccurate; one generic tool removes every schema safeguard.

prompt: Your team wants to connect a third-party MCP server found in a public registry. Which policy is soundest?
optionA: Run it with the service's full environment so it works
optionB: Trust it once it installs cleanly and lists its tools
optionC: Review it, limit its env, allow-list tools, approve writes
optionD: Let the model decide which of its tools are safe to use
correctAnswerText: Review it, limit its env, allow-list tools, approve writes
explanation: A third-party server is code you run and text your model reads; its descriptions and results can carry injection. Review it, give it only what it needs, and keep writes behind approval.

prompt: Which design best contains prompt injection for a support agent that reads NPCI pages and can raise payment disputes?
optionA: The reading run proposes; the app files on a user's click
optionB: Tell the model to ignore instructions in web pages
optionC: Strip all HTML so hidden text cannot reach the model
optionD: Fetch only pages whose titles mention UPI or NPCI
correctAnswerText: The reading run proposes; the app files on a user's click
explanation: When the run that reads untrusted text cannot act, the worst a hijacked run can do is give a wrong answer. Stripping HTML kept hidden paragraphs, and prompt rules are not guarantees.

prompt: Which tool error message is best both for the model and for security?
optionA: "Traceback (most recent call last): File ..."
optionB: "invalid arguments: start must be YYYY-MM-DD"
optionC: "psycopg2 error at db-prod-3: column start bad"
optionD: "Something went wrong, please try again later"
correctAnswerText: "invalid arguments: start must be YYYY-MM-DD"
explanation: It names the field and the format the model must use. Database errors and tracebacks leak internals and cost tokens; a generic message gives the model nothing to fix.

prompt: An HR MCP server exposes read and write leave tools to several teams. Which permission design is best?
optionA: Tool annotations alone, trusting clients to respect them
optionB: One shared admin key so every team's agent can do anything
optionC: Per-tool scopes from the token, read and write granted apart
optionD: A system-prompt rule telling each agent what it may call
correctAnswerText: Per-tool scopes from the token, read and write granted apart
explanation: Scopes checked in each tool against the verified token give each client exactly what it was granted. Shared admin keys ignore the caller, and prompts and annotations are not enforcement.

prompt: For a research agent's web-fetch tool, which combination of controls is strongest?
optionA: Block URLs containing "admin" and allow everything else
optionB: Any URL, but strip scripts and images from every page
optionC: Any https URL, since certificates prove a site is safe
optionD: https only, host allow-list, no blind redirects, size caps
correctAnswerText: https only, host allow-list, no blind redirects, size caps
explanation: Together these stop SSRF to internal addresses, redirects to unapproved hosts, data carried out in query strings, and huge or slow pages. Stripping scripts or keyword blocks stop none of that.

prompt: In a graph's state, what happens to a key with no reducer when a node returns a new value for it?
optionA: The new value replaces the old one
optionB: The two values are merged as a dict
optionC: The new value is appended to the old
optionD: The update is ignored after the first
correctAnswerText: The new value replaces the old one
explanation: Without a reducer a key is overwritten. A reducer such as operator.add is what makes a list append, and a custom function can merge dicts.

prompt: What does a LangGraph checkpointer save, and under what key?
optionA: The compiled graph's code, under a version tag
optionB: Every prompt sent to the model, under the user's email
optionC: A state snapshot after each step, under a thread_id
optionD: Only the final answer, under the name of the graph
correctAnswerText: A state snapshot after each step, under a thread_id
explanation: Each step's state is saved under the thread id, which is what makes history, pausing, resuming and surviving a crash possible. For a loan file the thread id is the application id.

prompt: What does a node achieve by returning Command(goto=..., update=...)?
optionA: It pauses the graph until a human resumes it
optionB: It updates state and picks the next node in one return
optionC: It saves a checkpoint to a separate database
optionD: It runs the next node in parallel with itself
correctAnswerText: It updates state and picks the next node in one return
explanation: Command combines a state update with routing, so a supervisor needs no separate router function. It does not create parallel branches or pauses.

prompt: What does a node started by Send(node, payload) receive as its input?
optionA: The list of every Send payload made
optionB: The previous node's return value only
optionC: The full graph state plus the payload
optionD: Only the payload it was sent
correctAnswerText: Only the payload it was sent
explanation: A Send branch sees only its payload. Anything else it needs, such as the user's question, must be put in the payload.

prompt: What does interrupt(value) do inside a node?
optionA: Skips the node and moves on to the next in line
optionB: Raises an error for the retry policy to handle
optionC: Cancels the run and discards its saved checkpoints
optionD: Pauses the run and surfaces value to a reviewer
correctAnswerText: Pauses the run and surfaces value to a reviewer
explanation: interrupt saves the run and returns the value to the caller (your UI shows it). On resume, the value passed in Command(resume=...) becomes what interrupt returns.

prompt: Which LangGraph durability mode writes checkpoints only when the graph exits?
optionA: exit
optionB: final
optionC: async
optionD: sync
correctAnswerText: exit
explanation: "sync" saves before the next step starts, "async" (the default) saves while the next step runs, and "exit" saves only at the end — so a hard crash leaves nothing to resume.

prompt: What does it mean for a side-effecting node to be idempotent?
optionA: It returns the same value however its inputs change
optionB: Running it twice has the same effect as running it once
optionC: It runs exactly once, because the framework guarantees it
optionD: It never writes anything into the graph's shared state
correctAnswerText: Running it twice has the same effect as running it once
explanation: Idempotency is about effects: a second run must not pay, email or book again. No framework guarantees exactly-once execution across crashes, so the node has to be safe to repeat.

prompt: What does g.add_edge(["search", "data"], "write") mean?
optionA: write runs as soon as either of the two finishes
optionB: write runs once, after both search and data finish
optionC: write runs twice, once after each of the two nodes
optionD: search and data run one after the other, then write
correctAnswerText: write runs once, after both search and data finish
explanation: A list of start nodes creates a join that waits for all of them. Two separate edges into write would trigger it from each.

prompt: What does max_concurrency in a run's config limit?
optionA: How many times a failing node is retried
optionB: How many interrupts may be pending at once
optionC: How many branches may run at the same time
optionD: How many steps the graph may take in total
correctAnswerText: How many branches may run at the same time
explanation: max_concurrency caps simultaneous branches, which keeps a fan-out inside the provider's rate limit. Total steps are bounded by the recursion limit; retries by the RetryPolicy.

prompt: Which checkpointer suits several workers that resume each other's runs?
optionA: A shared database such as Postgres
optionB: An InMemorySaver inside each worker
optionC: A SQLite file on each pod's own disk
optionD: None; the workers share their RAM
correctAnswerText: A shared database such as Postgres
explanation: Every worker must see the same checkpoints. In-memory state dies with the process and a per-pod SQLite file is invisible to the other pods.

prompt: Why must model output still be validated when the graph's state is declared as a TypedDict?
optionA: TypedDict state cannot be read by conditional edges
optionB: TypedDict converts every value to a string on save
optionC: TypedDict types are hints the framework does not check
optionD: TypedDict keys are dropped whenever a node returns them
correctAnswerText: TypedDict types are hints the framework does not check
explanation: A wrong type goes straight into a TypedDict state. Validate model output with Pydantic inside the node that calls the model, where the error can be handled, or use a Pydantic state.

prompt: Why make edge conditions short tests on state fields, such as confidence < 0.7?
optionA: LangGraph refuses any router that calls a model
optionB: Model routers cannot return more than two targets
optionC: State fields are cheaper to store than message text
optionD: Plain-code routers are deterministic, free and testable
correctAnswerText: Plain-code routers are deterministic, free and testable
explanation: A router that reads a field gives the same answer every time, costs nothing and has unit tests. "Route if the model seems unsure" is unfinished until unsure is a field.

prompt: Why keep a specialist's retrieved chunks inside its own sub-graph schema?
optionA: Private state makes the specialist run in parallel with others
optionB: Retrieved chunks cannot be stored in any shared state key
optionC: Others see a short summary: smaller context, smaller blast radius
optionD: Sub-graph schemas are encrypted at rest by the checkpointer
correctAnswerText: Others see a short summary: smaller context, smaller blast radius
explanation: Only the summary reaches the supervisor and writer, so their calls stay small and injected text in a document can steer only the specialist, whose output others treat as data.

prompt: Why add a turns counter to a supervisor when the framework already has a recursion limit?
optionA: It ends deliberately with an honest message, not a crash
optionB: The recursion limit only counts tool calls, not turns
optionC: A counter makes each supervisor call cheaper to run
optionD: The recursion limit resets itself after every hand-off
correctAnswerText: It ends deliberately with an honest message, not a crash
explanation: Past the cap the supervisor can say "I could not resolve this; passing it to HR". The recursion limit is a blunt last resort that ends in GraphRecursionError.

prompt: Why should a fan-out's join key results by id rather than trust their position in the list?
optionA: Positions are lost whenever a checkpoint is saved
optionB: Branches finish in any order, and resumes change the list
optionC: Send payloads are always processed alphabetically
optionD: Reducers always reverse the list at the end of a step
correctAnswerText: Branches finish in any order, and resumes change the list
explanation: Completion order depends on timing, and a recorded error or a resumed branch changes what is in the list. Each result should carry its id, and the join sorts by it.

prompt: Why must nothing with a side effect run before interrupt() in the same node?
optionA: interrupt() refuses to pause after any network call
optionB: The checkpoint is written before the node even starts
optionC: On resume the node runs again from its first line
optionD: Side effects before a pause are rolled back on resume
correctAnswerText: On resume the node runs again from its first line
explanation: The interrupted node re-executes from the top when resumed, so anything before interrupt runs twice. Keep the approval node free of side effects and act in the next node.

prompt: Why does invoking a paused thread with a new message not count as an approval?
optionA: New input starts a fresh run from START, not a resume
optionB: Paused threads silently ignore any new input given
optionC: New input deletes the thread's checkpoint history
optionD: New input is queued until the interrupt has expired
correctAnswerText: New input starts a fresh run from START, not a resume
explanation: Only Command(resume=...) supplies the value interrupt returns. New input runs the graph from START, reaches the approval again and pauses again.

prompt: Why must every side-effecting node be idempotent even when the graph has checkpoints?
optionA: Checkpoints store side effects and replay them on resume
optionB: The framework skips non-idempotent nodes on a resume
optionC: Idempotency makes checkpoint writes faster under load
optionD: Checkpoints sit between nodes, so an unfinished node reruns
correctAnswerText: Checkpoints sit between nodes, so an unfinished node reruns
explanation: A crash after the bank accepted a payout but before the node returned leaves no checkpoint for that node, so it runs again. Only an idempotency key stops the second payout.

prompt: Why does a RetryPolicy with the default retry_on not retry a TimeoutError?
optionA: TimeoutError is an OSError, which the default skips
optionB: The default policy retries only validation errors
optionC: Retries are disabled for nodes that call a model
optionD: Time-outs are retried only when max_attempts is over 5
correctAnswerText: TimeoutError is an OSError, which the default skips
explanation: The default retries ConnectionError and 5xx HTTP errors but treats OSError subclasses, which include TimeoutError, as not retryable. Name the exceptions you mean in retry_on.

prompt: Why do pending approvals in an agent need an expiry?
optionA: Reviewers cannot see requests older than one week
optionB: Checkpoints are deleted automatically after one day
optionC: A stale request may be approved on out-of-date facts
optionD: interrupt() raises an error after an hour by default
correctAnswerText: A stale request may be approved on out-of-date facts
explanation: A request left for weeks can be approved at an old price or salary. A job resumes expired ones with a reject decision, so they end cleanly and are logged.

prompt: Two nodes in one step each add a line to notes, declared as a plain list[str]. Which change lets both writes land?
optionA: Set a higher recursion_limit for that one run
optionB: Return notes as a single string, not a list
optionC: Declare notes as Annotated[list[str], operator.add]
