optionD: Run the two nodes in two separate graphs instead
correctAnswerText: Declare notes as Annotated[list[str], operator.add]
explanation: A key with no reducer accepts one value per step, and two writes raise InvalidUpdateError. An appending reducer merges them; giving each branch its own key also works.

prompt: Send("score_resume", {"resume_id": r}) branches need the job description to score each resume. How should they get it?
optionA: Put the job description into each Send payload
optionB: Have the join node pass it back to each branch
optionC: Read it from the graph state inside the branch
optionD: Store it in a global variable before fan-out
correctAnswerText: Put the job description into each Send payload
explanation: A Send branch receives only its payload, so reading graph state fails with a KeyError. Typing the payload with its own TypedDict makes such omissions visible in review.

prompt: A batch of three invoice approvals pauses in three parallel branches. How does the approval service resume all three?
optionA: update_state with all three answers, then invoke with new input
optionB: Restart the batch with the three answers already in the input
optionC: Three invoke calls with new input, one for each of the branches
optionD: One Command(resume=...) mapping each interrupt id to its answer
correctAnswerText: One Command(resume=...) mapping each interrupt id to its answer
explanation: Each pending Interrupt has an id, and resume accepts a mapping from id to value. update_state does not answer interrupts, and new input restarts the graph.

prompt: A paused refund run has the wrong order id, which the agent extracted. The reviewer wants to fix it and then approve. What do you do?
optionA: Send the right id as a new message on the same thread
optionB: Edit the checkpoint table's JSON by hand, then resume
optionC: Start a new run on a new thread with the corrected input
optionD: update_state with the right id, then resume with approve
correctAnswerText: update_state with the right id, then resume with approve
explanation: update_state writes into the paused thread as if a node had returned it, and the run continues from the pause. A new message restarts the graph; editing storage by hand bypasses reducers.

prompt: The resume endpoint receives {"action": "approve", "by": "ravi@ops"} in its request body. What should be recorded as the approver?
optionA: The signed-in user from the session, after a role check
optionB: Whatever name the model writes in its next reply
optionC: The "by" field, since the form shows the user's name
optionD: The thread id, since each thread has one approver
correctAnswerText: The signed-in user from the session, after a role check
explanation: A request body can be forged; the authenticated session cannot. Check the user has the approver role for this tenant, then record them from the session.

prompt: A fan-out over 60 contracts starts getting 429s; the provider plan allows 10 concurrent requests. Which setting fits?
optionA: recursion_limit of 10 in the run config
optionB: A RetryPolicy with max_attempts of 10
optionC: An operator.add reducer on the results
optionD: max_concurrency of 10 in the run config
correctAnswerText: max_concurrency of 10 in the run config
explanation: max_concurrency caps how many branches run at once, keeping requests within quota. The recursion limit counts steps, and retries alone keep hammering the limit.

prompt: In a contract fan-out, one PDF has no text layer and another branch hits a dropped connection. How should each be handled?
optionA: Retry the dropped connection; record the PDF as not reviewed
optionB: Retry both with back-off until each of them finally succeeds
optionC: Record both as not reviewed and never retry anything at all
optionD: Let both raise so the whole review stops for a fresh rerun
correctAnswerText: Retry the dropped connection; record the PDF as not reviewed
explanation: A dropped connection is transient, so a retry heals it. A missing text layer is permanent for that item, so retrying wastes time; record it so the report says what is missing.

prompt: A pay node in a month-end payout graph calls a bank API. Which idempotency key is right?
optionA: The current time to the millisecond, as a string
optionB: f"{thread_id}:{invoice_id}:pay", the same on every attempt
optionC: A counter that goes up each time the node starts
optionD: str(uuid.uuid4()), made at the top of the node each time
correctAnswerText: f"{thread_id}:{invoice_id}:pay", the same on every attempt
explanation: The key must be identical for every attempt of the same logical payment, so a crash, retry or resume produces the same key and the bank ignores the repeat.

prompt: On worker start-up, which threads should be resumed with invoke(None, cfg)?
optionA: Those whose next is empty, so they can run once more
optionB: Those with a non-empty next and no pending interrupt
optionC: Those with a pending interrupt, to skip the reviewer
optionD: Every thread, so nothing is ever left half finished
correctAnswerText: Those with a non-empty next and no pending interrupt
explanation: A non-empty next with no interrupt is a run a crash orphaned. Paused runs wait for a person, and an empty next means the run already finished.

prompt: A month-end payout graph makes slow bank calls. Which durability mode do you choose?
optionA: async: a lost checkpoint can never repeat any step
optionB: exit: the run is long, so checkpoints only slow it down
optionC: sync: a checkpoint write is cheap next to a bank call
optionD: none: idempotency keys make checkpoints redundant
correctAnswerText: sync: a checkpoint write is cheap next to a bank call
explanation: sync saves before each next step, so the least work repeats after a crash, and its cost is trivial beside a bank call. Under async a step may repeat; under exit a crash loses everything.

prompt: A research graph works with only web search enabled; enabling the database branch makes the first run fail with InvalidUpdateError at key 'notes'. Diagnosis?
optionA: Both branches write notes in one step, and it has no reducer
optionB: InvalidUpdateError means the database returned bad rows
optionC: Parallel branches are not allowed to share a START edge
optionD: The database branch returns notes before web search starts
correctAnswerText: Both branches write notes in one step, and it has no reducer
explanation: Two writes to a key with no reducer in one super-step are refused. Add an appending reducer, or give each branch its own key, which also makes the join clearer.

prompt: After a run on thread "KYC-77", app.get_state(cfg).next shows ('review',). What is the state of that run?
optionA: Never started; the thread has no history
optionB: Failed in review and will never run again
optionC: Paused before review, waiting to be resumed
optionD: Finished; review was the last node that ran
correctAnswerText: Paused before review, waiting to be resumed
explanation: next lists the nodes due to run from the latest checkpoint. A finished run shows an empty tuple, and an unknown thread has no values at all.

prompt: In a helpdesk graph, the billing specialist gets control from triage but answers about the wrong invoice. Triage's goto carried no update. Most likely cause?
optionA: No hand-off note: billing saw only what shared state held
optionB: Command.PARENT wipes the shared state during the jump
optionC: The supervisor reset the invoice id after the hand-off
optionD: Billing must reread the whole conversation every time
correctAnswerText: No hand-off note: billing saw only what shared state held
explanation: The receiving agent knows only what is in shared state. Write a note in the update — invoice id, what was asked — rather than hoping the next agent infers it.

prompt: Some requests end in GraphRecursionError; the trace alternates supervisor and policy_agent. policy_agent wrote its finding to a key the supervisor never reads. Root cause?
optionA: Command cannot route back to a node that has already run
optionB: The supervisor never saw the finding, and nothing capped turns
optionC: The recursion limit of 25 is too low for this supervisor
optionD: policy_agent should have called the supervisor's tools
correctAnswerText: The supervisor never saw the finding, and nothing capped turns
explanation: Two parts: findings must go to the shared key the supervisor's prompt is built from, and a turns counter must end the loop honestly. Raising the limit only spends more.

prompt: An offer-letter graph sends candidates two "your offer is being prepared" messages whenever a recruiter answers. A print at the top of recruiter_review appears twice. Diagnosis?
optionA: The send_offer node ran in two parallel branches at once
optionB: The message is sent before interrupt() in a node that reruns
optionC: The checkpointer saved recruiter_review's output twice
optionD: The recruiter clicked approve twice on the review screen
correctAnswerText: The message is sent before interrupt() in a node that reruns
explanation: On resume the interrupted node runs again from its first line. Move the message into the node that drafts the offer, which ran once and is checkpointed.

prompt: After Approve, the refund graph's propose node runs again and drafts a second refund. The front end posts {"messages": ["approved"]} to the run endpoint. Diagnosis?
optionA: The interrupt payload was too large to be resumed
optionB: The checkpointer lost the state when the user clicked
optionC: New input restarted the thread instead of resuming it
optionD: The propose node lacks an idempotency key for drafts
correctAnswerText: New input restarted the thread instead of resuming it
explanation: A message is new input, so the graph starts again from START, drafts again and pauses again. A resume endpoint calling Command(resume=decision) is the fix.

prompt: Approvals made an hour later fail with "nothing to resume" about a third of the time. The service runs on three pods, each with its own SQLite checkpoint file. Why?
optionA: Approvals made after an hour are refused by interrupt()
optionB: The resume often lands on a pod without that thread's state
optionC: SQLite deletes paused threads after about an hour
optionD: One pod in three runs an older version of the framework
correctAnswerText: The resume often lands on a pod without that thread's state
explanation: Each pod sees only its own file, so a resume routed to another pod finds no thread. Several workers need one shared checkpoint database such as Postgres.

prompt: One of four fan-out branches raised. With a checkpointer, invoke(None, cfg) re-ran only that branch; a colleague without one saw all four re-run. Why?
optionA: The colleague's join node ran before the failed branch
optionB: Pending writes exist only when max_concurrency is one
optionC: The checkpoint held pending writes of the three that finished
optionD: Without a checkpointer only failed branches are retried
correctAnswerText: The checkpoint held pending writes of the three that finished
explanation: Successful branches' writes are saved as pending writes, so a resume repeats only the failed task. With nothing saved, the whole fan-out starts over and every model call is paid again.

prompt: A payout graph logs a single attempt whenever the bank client raises a time-out, yet ConnectionError failures are retried. What explains this?
optionA: Time-outs are retried only when durability is set to sync
optionB: The default retry_on skips OSError subclasses like time-outs
optionC: max_attempts counts only exceptions raised by models
optionD: Bank clients switch off retries through their own headers
correctAnswerText: The default retry_on skips OSError subclasses like time-outs
explanation: TimeoutError is an OSError, which the default policy treats as not retryable, while ConnectionError is retried. Pass retry_on=(TimeoutError, ConnectionError) — after checking the node is idempotent.

prompt: A node pays a vendor, then emails them. An email time-out triggers a retry, and the bank log shows two payout requests, the second deduplicated. What is the design flaw?
optionA: The email should reuse the bank's idempotency key
optionB: Two side effects in one node, so a retry repeats both
optionC: The bank's deduplication should have refused the first
optionD: Retries should never be set on nodes with side effects
correctAnswerText: Two side effects in one node, so a retry repeats both
explanation: One side effect per node means a retry repeats only the step that failed. The key made the repeat harmless this time; splitting the node removes the repeat altogether.

prompt: For a helpdesk answering leave, payslip and policy questions, when would you choose a supervisor with specialists over one agent?
optionA: When salary tools need isolating and evals show no loss
optionB: Never, since a supervisor cannot route to sub-graphs
optionC: Always, because specialists are more accurate by design
optionD: When the diagram should show a more advanced system
correctAnswerText: When salary tools need isolating and evals show no loss
explanation: Separate permissions are a concrete reason to split, and running both versions on one eval set keeps the choice honest. Each specialist adds calls and hand-off losses.

prompt: Which durability choice suits a short, cheap, read-only summarisation graph?
optionA: sync, since every graph needs the safest setting
optionB: exit, accepting a full rerun after a rare crash
optionC: sync, plus an idempotency key on every read node
optionD: No checkpointer and a recursion limit of one
correctAnswerText: exit, accepting a full rerun after a rare crash
explanation: "exit" is for short runs that are cheap to repeat and have no side effects: a crash just means running again. Paying for per-step saves buys little here.

prompt: Which approval policy for a refund agent is most defensible?
optionA: Auto-approve every refund and audit a sample each month
optionB: Auto-approve a defined low-risk class; people review the rest
optionC: Let the model decide which refunds need a person to look
optionD: Send every refund to a person, whatever its amount or risk
correctAnswerText: Auto-approve a defined low-risk class; people review the rest
explanation: Sending everything to people produces rubber-stamping; sending nothing removes the check. A defined low-risk class, set in code, lets reviewers focus on cases worth a look.

prompt: Which approval-service design is most sound?
optionA: Approvals arrive as email replies parsed into resume calls
optionB: Any signed-in user may resume; the form records their name
optionC: Role-checked resume API, approver from session, expiry, audit
optionD: The model approves its own proposals below a limit it sets
correctAnswerText: Role-checked resume API, approver from session, expiry, audit
explanation: Who may approve, who did, how long a request stays open and what was decided are all checked or recorded server-side. Form fields, the model and parsed emails can all be forged or steered.

prompt: A team says checkpoints make idempotency keys unnecessary in their payout graph. Best judgement?
optionA: Right: checkpoints guarantee that each node runs exactly once
optionB: Right, provided the durability mode is set to async
optionC: Wrong: a crash mid-node reruns it, so keys are still needed
optionD: Wrong only for parallel branches; serial nodes are safe
correctAnswerText: Wrong: a crash mid-node reruns it, so keys are still needed
explanation: Checkpoints shrink repeated work; keys make what is repeated harmless. A crash test that kills a process mid-payout shows repeats happen, and the bank ignores them only because keys match.

prompt: For a monthly review of 40 vendor contracts, which overall failure design is best?
optionA: Catch every error and report all forty as reviewed anyway
optionB: Raise on any error so a person reruns the whole batch
optionC: Retry transient errors, record per-item failures, raise fatal ones
optionD: Retry every error five times, then drop that contract quietly
correctAnswerText: Retry transient errors, record per-item failures, raise fatal ones
explanation: Sorting by error kind lets transient faults heal, keeps one bad PDF from costing 39 results, and produces an honest "38 of 40 reviewed" report. Silent drops are incidents waiting to happen.

prompt: A research node sometimes hangs on a provider call for minutes. Which time-out approach is strongest?
optionA: A time.sleep watchdog in the node that checks a flag
optionB: Client time-outs on every call, plus node and run bounds
optionC: A run-level time-out only, since node bounds are noise
optionD: No time-outs; the recursion limit will end it in time
correctAnswerText: Client time-outs on every call, plus node and run bounds
explanation: An HTTP client time-out is the first and cheapest defence; node and run bounds catch the rest, and the checkpoint lets a later attempt resume. The recursion limit counts steps, not time.

prompt: An orchestrated agent gives a wrong answer now and then. Which debugging approach is best?
optionA: Swap in a stronger model and see whether the error goes away
optionB: Add more instructions to the supervisor's system prompt
optionC: Raise the recursion limit and rerun until the answer passes
optionD: Script a fake model, stream updates, check the bad node's input
correctAnswerText: Script a fake model, stream updates, check the bad node's input
explanation: A scripted model makes the run repeatable; streamed updates show the first node that wrote something wrong; checking its input (state or payload) finds the cause. Then keep the run as a test.

prompt: Model output that enters graph state must be well-formed. Which approach balances speed and safety?
optionA: No schema at all; later nodes cope with whatever arrives
optionB: TypedDict state, trusting the type hints to catch errors
optionC: Re-ask the model in every node until two outputs agree
optionD: TypedDict state, with Pydantic validation inside the node
correctAnswerText: TypedDict state, with Pydantic validation inside the node
explanation: Most teams keep a light TypedDict state and validate model output where it is produced, so the error is handled next to its cause. Type hints alone check nothing at run time.

prompt: Forty contracts, about 6 seconds each, and a quota of 10 concurrent requests. Which design is best?
optionA: One node that loops over all forty contracts in turn
optionB: Forty static edges from START with no concurrency limit
optionC: A Send per contract with no limit, retrying every 429
optionD: A Send per contract, max_concurrency 10, sort results by id
correctAnswerText: A Send per contract, max_concurrency 10, sort results by id
explanation: Ten-way parallelism cuts about four minutes to under half a minute without breaking the quota, and keying results by id keeps the report right. A loop is slow; no limit invites 429s.

prompt: In an agent built on a graph framework, what holds the short-term memory of one conversation?
optionA: A vector store shared by every user of the app
optionB: The thread's messages, saved by a checkpointer
optionC: A browser cookie that keeps the last answer only
optionD: The model's weights, updated after each reply
correctAnswerText: The thread's messages, saved by a checkpointer
explanation: Short-term memory is the conversation thread, persisted between requests by a checkpointer. A shared vector store is long-term memory, and model weights never change at run time.

prompt: What does long-term memory give an agent that short-term memory does not?
optionA: A longer context window for the current request
optionB: Protection against instructions in tool results
optionC: Facts that persist across separate conversations
optionD: Faster token generation on repeated questions
correctAnswerText: Facts that persist across separate conversations
explanation: Long-term memory carries facts and preferences from one thread to the next. It does not enlarge the window, speed up generation or defend against injection.

prompt: Which of these is an episodic memory about a user?
optionA: A team rule that claims need a manager in CC
optionB: The user's current leave balance in the HR system
optionC: A short summary of a past session and its outcome
optionD: The user's preferred reply language for all chats
correctAnswerText: A short summary of a past session and its outcome
explanation: Episodes summarise past sessions. Reply language is a preference, the CC rule is a procedure, and a live balance belongs in the system of record, not in memory.

prompt: In the memory store built in the course, what is a memory's id made of?
optionA: The embedding vector of the memory text itself
optionB: The time at which the conversation was started
optionC: A random UUID generated on every single write
optionD: The user id and a slot name, as in user:slot
correctAnswerText: The user id and a slot name, as in user:slot
explanation: A user:slot id means a new value for the same slot replaces the old one on upsert. A random id per write would pile contradictory memories side by side.

prompt: Which metadata on a memory lets a newer one win a conflict and shows why it is believed?
optionA: source and updated_at
optionB: thread_id and recursion_limit
optionC: collection name and index space
optionD: n_results and max_distance
correctAnswerText: source and updated_at
explanation: Recording where a memory came from and when it was updated lets the newer fact win and lets you show the user the reason. The other pairs are query or graph settings.

prompt: What does a max_distance threshold do when recalling memories?
optionA: Drops nearest memories that are not close enough
optionB: Sets how long a memory is kept before it expires
optionC: Limits how many users one collection can hold
optionD: Caps the number of tokens a memory may contain
correctAnswerText: Drops nearest memories that are not close enough
explanation: A nearest neighbour always exists; the threshold decides whether it is relevant enough to inject. It has nothing to do with capacity, expiry or memory length.

prompt: Which memories are better loaded as an always-present profile than retrieved by search?
optionA: Full tool results from the previous conversation
optionB: Long summaries of every past session with the user
optionC: Every memory whose distance is under the threshold
optionD: Small, always-relevant facts like name and language
correctAnswerText: Small, always-relevant facts like name and language
explanation: Name and preferred language matter on every turn and are tiny, so loading them always is cheaper and safer than hoping retrieval finds them. The long tail is retrieved.

prompt: What question does context engineering ask that prompt engineering does not?
optionA: Which words the system instruction should use
optionB: Which model provider has the cheapest tokens
optionC: How many examples a few-shot prompt should hold
optionD: What goes into the window on this particular step
correctAnswerText: What goes into the window on this particular step
explanation: Context engineering decides, step by step, which instructions, tools, memories, summaries and results enter the window. Wording the instruction is prompt engineering.

prompt: In context engineering, what does offloading a large tool result mean?
optionA: Storing it and giving the model a handle and summary
optionB: Moving it into the system prompt so it caches cheaply
optionC: Deleting it once the model has read it a single time
optionD: Sending it to a second model to answer on its behalf
correctAnswerText: Storing it and giving the model a handle and summary
explanation: Offloading keeps the bulky result outside the window: the model gets an id, a short summary and a tool to query it. Moving it into the system prompt still sends it every step.

prompt: What must stay identical across calls for a provider's prompt cache to be reused?
optionA: The final user message at the end of the prompt
optionB: The prompt's prefix, from its very first token
optionC: The temperature and the maximum output tokens
optionD: The number of tool results returned per step
correctAnswerText: The prompt's prefix, from its very first token
explanation: Prompt caching reuses an identical prefix. Anything that changes near the start — a timestamp, a user name — makes every prefix new and the cache misses.

prompt: Why are memories written with upsert under a stable slot id rather than appended as new rows?
optionA: So deleted memories can be recovered after a forget request
optionB: So each write costs less than an insert in the vector store
optionC: So the model can compare the old and new values by itself
optionD: So an updated fact replaces the old one, not sits beside it
correctAnswerText: So an updated fact replaces the old one, not sits beside it
explanation: With append, "Home city: Hyderabad" and "Home city: Bengaluru" both come back and the model guesses. Upsert under one slot keeps one current fact. Cost and recovery are not the reason.

prompt: Why does storing a memory as labelled text, such as "Home city: Bengaluru", improve recall?
optionA: Labels force the model to cite the memory in its final answer
optionB: Labels make the embedding model skip the distance computation
optionC: Short memories are ruled by phrasing; labels match questions
optionD: Labelled text is stored in a separate, faster index structure
correctAnswerText: Short memories are ruled by phrasing; labels match questions
explanation: Memories are short, so wording dominates similarity. "Home city: …" shares more with "which city am I in?" than a narrative sentence does. Labels change no index or computation.

prompt: Why must the user filter be applied inside the vector search rather than after it?
optionA: Other users' rows can take all k places and hide the user's own
optionB: Filtering inside the query skips embedding the question text
optionC: Filtering after the search is rejected by most vector stores
optionD: A post-filter changes the distances of the remaining results
correctAnswerText: Other users' rows can take all k places and hide the user's own
explanation: A post-filter lets other users' memories compete for the k results, so a user may get nothing relevant — and a forgotten post-filter leaks. Stores accept unfiltered queries, which is the danger.

prompt: Why must the user id for a memory lookup come from the verified request, not from the model?
optionA: Vector stores only accept ids that arrive in HTTP headers
optionB: Ids from the request are shorter and so cost fewer tokens
optionC: The model cannot produce strings in the right id format
optionD: Text the model reads could steer it into naming another user
correctAnswerText: Text the model reads could steer it into naming another user
explanation: Anything the model outputs can be influenced by what it reads, including injected text. The server's verified identity cannot. Format and token cost are not the concern.

prompt: Why does memory recall need a distance threshold even when the user filter is correct?
optionA: Vector stores refuse any query that has no threshold set
optionB: The threshold is what makes memory writes idempotent
optionC: Without it the store returns memories from other users too
optionD: A nearest memory always exists, even for unrelated questions
correctAnswerText: A nearest memory always exists, even for unrelated questions
explanation: Even "what is the capital of France?" has a nearest memory. Without a cut-off it is injected and the model mentions it. The user filter, not the threshold, stops cross-user leaks.

prompt: Why should an HR assistant call the leave tool rather than remember an employee's leave balance?
optionA: Tool calls are always cheaper than memory lookups
optionB: Memory stores cannot hold numbers, only plain text
optionC: Leave balances are too long to fit in one memory row
optionD: The balance changes, and a remembered copy goes stale
correctAnswerText: The balance changes, and a remembered copy goes stale
explanation: Memory is not the system of record. A balance changes with every request approved, so a stored copy is soon wrong. Memory stores can hold numbers; cost is not the issue.

prompt: Why should an assistant not store a user's Aadhaar number in memory "just in case"?
optionA: Numbers cannot be found again by similarity search
optionB: Aadhaar numbers are too long for most embedding models
optionC: Personal data needs a purpose; unneeded data is only risk
optionD: The model would refuse to answer once it saw the number
correctAnswerText: Personal data needs a purpose; unneeded data is only risk
explanation: Under the DPDP Act personal data needs a stated purpose and consent and must be erasable. Data held with no need is pure exposure. Length and searchability are beside the point.

prompt: Why does input token cost grow faster than linearly with the number of steps in an agent run?
optionA: Providers raise the per-token price after each step
optionB: The model's reasoning gets longer on each later step
optionC: Tool definitions are duplicated once for every step
optionD: Every step resends all the history gathered so far
correctAnswerText: Every step resends all the history gathered so far
explanation: Step k carries everything from steps 1 to k−1, so the total grows with the square of the run length. Prices and tool definitions do not change per step.

prompt: Why restate the current goal near the end of the context on a long agent run?
optionA: Restating it stops the model from calling any further tools
optionB: Models use the start and end of long contexts more reliably
optionC: The end of the context is never trimmed by the token budget
optionD: Providers only cache the final part of each request sent
correctAnswerText: Models use the start and end of long contexts more reliably
explanation: Facts in the middle of a long context are used less reliably than those at the edges, so a short task-state block at the end keeps the goal in view. Caching works on the prefix, not the end.

prompt: Why must a summary of dropped turns be told what to keep, such as ids, amounts and decisions?
optionA: Without ids the summary cannot be embedded for search
optionB: Summaries are lossy and can quietly change key facts
optionC: A summary is always longer than the turns it replaces
optionD: Providers reject summaries that contain no numbers
correctAnswerText: Summaries are lossy and can quietly change key facts
explanation: A summary that says "refund approved" when the tool said "requested" is a new bug. Telling it what must survive limits that loss. Providers impose no such rule.

prompt: A bank chatbot hears: "I prefer WhatsApp, my balance is ₹12,400, and here is my PAN." What goes into long-term memory?
optionA: Nothing, since memory stores only past episodes
optionB: All three, so the bot never has to ask again
optionC: The balance and the PAN, as they are exact facts
optionD: Only the WhatsApp contact preference
correctAnswerText: Only the WhatsApp contact preference
explanation: The preference is what memory is for. The balance lives in the core banking system and goes stale, and a PAN stored without a purpose breaks data minimisation.

prompt: Meena now prefers e-mail to WhatsApp. Her contact preference lives at meena:pref:contact. Which write is correct?
optionA: Lower the threshold so the newer memory ranks first
optionB: Ask the model to pick whichever preference is newer
optionC: Insert a new row and keep the WhatsApp one as history
optionD: Upsert the new preference under meena:pref:contact
correctAnswerText: Upsert the new preference under meena:pref:contact
explanation: Upserting under the same slot id replaces the outdated preference. Keeping both returns two contradictory memories and leaves the choice to the model.

prompt: You are writing recall() against one shared memory collection. Which query is correct?
optionA: query(..., where={"user_id": ctx.user_id})
optionB: query(...) with the user id added to the question
optionC: query(..., where={"user_id": tool_args["user"]})
optionD: query(..., n_results=50), then keep the user's rows
correctAnswerText: query(..., where={"user_id": ctx.user_id})
explanation: The filter goes inside the search and its value comes from the verified request context. Post-filtering can starve the user, a question prefix filters nothing, and a model-supplied id can be steered.

prompt: On a labelled set, relevant memories score 0.40–0.65 cosine distance and unrelated ones 0.78–0.95. Which max_distance fits?
optionA: About 0.72, between the two groups
optionB: 0.95, so that no memory is ever dropped
optionC: 0.30, so only near-exact matches pass
optionD: 0.85, inside the unrelated group's range
correctAnswerText: About 0.72, between the two groups
explanation: A threshold in the gap keeps every relevant memory and drops the unrelated ones. 0.95 injects noise, 0.30 drops real matches, and 0.85 lets some unrelated memories through.

prompt: A user says "forget everything about me". Where must the deletion reach?
optionA: Memory rows, thread checkpoints, summaries, logs, exports
optionB: Only the rows held in the long-term memory collection
optionC: Only the newest thread, as the older ones expire anyway
optionD: The memory rows, marked as hidden but kept for later use
correctAnswerText: Memory rows, thread checkpoints, summaries, logs, exports
explanation: The user's data lives in several places. Deleting only memory rows, waiting for expiry or hiding rows all keep personal data the user asked to erase.

prompt: A B2B HR assistant serves forty client companies. Which memory layout fits best?
optionA: One shared collection with no filters, for recall
optionB: A namespace per company at least, plus user filters
optionC: Every company's memories inside the system prompt
optionD: One collection per message, deleted after replying
correctAnswerText: A namespace per company at least, plus user filters
explanation: Separating per company makes a cross-client leak structurally impossible, and the user filter isolates people within a company. A shared unfiltered collection leaks by design.

prompt: A tool returns 36 months of payslips, but users ask about recent months. What tool and context design fits?
optionA: Return all 36 months so the model never lacks data
optionB: Put all the payslips in the system prompt each day
optionC: Add a months argument and clip results with a note
optionD: Return nothing and let the model recall the figures
correctAnswerText: Add a months argument and clip results with a note
explanation: Tool design and context design are one problem: ask for less, and clip with a note saying rows were cut and how to get more. Dropping data invites invented numbers.

prompt: A context builder must fit a 4,000-token budget. Which order of priority did the course use?
optionA: Recent turns first, then tools, then the system prompt
optionB: Oldest turns first, then the summary, then the tools
optionC: Memories first, then turns, then instructions if room
optionD: Instructions and tools, memories, summary, recent turns
correctAnswerText: Instructions and tools, memories, summary, recent turns
explanation: Instructions and tools are always needed; then the user's memories; then a summary of what was dropped; then as many recent turns as fit, with room reserved for the answer.

prompt: Where should "Today is 26 Oct 2026" go in an agent's prompt to keep the prompt cache useful?
optionA: Inside each tool definition's description field
optionB: Nowhere, since a date breaks caching anywhere
optionC: After the fixed system prompt and tool definitions
optionD: As the very first line, before the system prompt
correctAnswerText: After the fixed system prompt and tool definitions
explanation: The cache reuses an identical prefix, so stable content goes first and dynamic data after it. A date at the top or in tool descriptions changes the prefix every day.

prompt: A step needs a 60-page vendor contract read to extract the renewal date, notice period and penalty. What keeps the main context small?
optionA: Append a summary of each page to the main conversation
optionB: A sub-agent reads it in its own context, returns 3 facts
optionC: Load the whole contract into the main thread at start
optionD: Raise the context window so the contract fits easily
correctAnswerText: A sub-agent reads it in its own context, returns 3 facts
explanation: A sub-agent spends its own context on the pages and hands back only the result. Loading pages or sixty summaries still fills the main window with material it does not need.

prompt: After a refactor of the memory tool, Meena is told how Ravi pays his rent. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: The distance threshold was set slightly too high
optionB: The memory text was not written as labelled text
optionC: The memory query lost its user filter in the refactor
optionD: The two users' memories were embedded differently
correctAnswerText: The memory query lost its user filter in the refactor
explanation: A query with no where filter ranks every user's rows together, and Ravi's matched best. Thresholds and phrasing affect relevance, not whose memories are searched.

prompt: The assistant says Ravi lives in Hyderabad on some turns and Bengaluru on others. The store holds both. What went wrong?
optionA: Each write used a new id, so the move added a row
optionB: The profile was loaded only on the first turn
optionC: The embedding model cannot tell two cities apart
optionD: The threshold let another user's memory through
correctAnswerText: Each write used a new id, so the move added a row
explanation: With a fresh id per write the move appended instead of replacing, so both facts come back and the model picks one. A slot id with upsert keeps a single current value.

prompt: Users complain the assistant mentions their city in unrelated answers. recall() returns the top 3 with no cut-off. Diagnosis?
optionA: No user filter, so other users' cities are leaking
optionB: No threshold, so a nearest memory is always injected
optionC: The profile is reloaded on every turn of a thread
optionD: Memories are upserted rather than being appended
correctAnswerText: No threshold, so a nearest memory is always injected
explanation: The users see their own city, so the filter works; the problem is that some memory is always nearest. A tuned max_distance stops irrelevant memories being injected.

prompt: For "which city am I in?", the rent memory ranks above "Ravi moved to Bengaluru in October". What is the likely cause?
optionA: Narrative memory text shares little with the question
optionB: The collection uses cosine rather than dot product
optionC: The filter drops memories older than one month
optionD: n_results is too small to reach the city memory
correctAnswerText: Narrative memory text shares little with the question
explanation: Short memories are ranked by phrasing; a narrative sentence matches the question poorly. Rewriting as "Home city: Bengaluru" ranked it first. With normalised embeddings the metric does not reorder.

prompt: A provider rejects a trimmed request because its first kept message is a tool result. What is the fault?
optionA: Tool results must always be converted to user messages
optionB: The summary was placed after recent turns, not before
optionC: Trimming split a tool call from its result; drop the orphan
optionD: The budget was too large for the model's context window
correctAnswerText: Trimming split a tool call from its result; drop the orphan
explanation: A tool message must follow the assistant message that made the call. The builder should drop the orphan. Relabelling it as user text hides its origin and weakens injection defences.

prompt: Input cost doubled overnight with the same traffic, and the cached-token share fell near zero. What do you check first?
optionA: Whether the output token limit was raised in config
optionB: Whether the memory threshold was lowered in a release
optionC: Whether a change made the prompt prefix differ per call
optionD: Whether users began writing much longer messages
correctAnswerText: Whether a change made the prompt prefix differ per call
explanation: A collapse in cached tokens points at the prefix: a timestamp or user name added to the first line defeats the cache. Longer user messages would not zero the cached share.

prompt: Around step 18 an expense agent forgets the trip was to Pune, stated at step 2. The context is 30,000 tokens. Which explanation fits?
optionA: The fact is buried mid-context, where models attend least
optionB: Pune was filtered out by the memory distance threshold
optionC: The checkpointer drops messages older than 15 steps
optionD: The model cannot hold city names past 10,000 tokens
correctAnswerText: The fact is buried mid-context, where models attend least
explanation: The fact is still in the window but sits in the middle of a long context. A short task-state block at the end, and smaller tool results, fix it. No such hard limits exist.

prompt: Fixed prompt 2,000 tokens, tool output 1,500 per step, 20 steps: 325,000 input tokens. Clipping output to 300 gives 97,000. What does this show?
optionA: Clipping helps only for runs shorter than ten steps
optionB: Input grows linearly, so clipping saves exactly 80%
optionC: The fixed prompt dominates the cost of long agent runs
optionD: What each step leaves behind is the biggest cost lever
correctAnswerText: What each step leaves behind is the biggest cost lever
explanation: The fixed part contributes 40,000 either way; the per-step residue is resent on every later step and drives the total. Growth is quadratic, and the saving here is about 70%.

prompt: After summarisation, an agent tells a customer the refund was approved, though the tool had said "refund requested". Root cause?
optionA: The refund tool returned the wrong status to the agent
optionB: The lossy summary changed a key fact the agent trusted
optionC: The memory store held an older refund for the customer
optionD: The budget reserved too few tokens for the final answer
correctAnswerText: The lossy summary changed a key fact the agent trusted
explanation: The trace shows the right status from the tool; the summary rewrote it. Summaries must be told to keep statuses, ids and amounts verbatim.

prompt: A run went wrong and the trace holds only the user's message and the final answer. What is missing for diagnosis?
optionA: The model's weights at the moment the run took place
optionB: The assembled context the model saw, by part and tokens
optionC: The source code of the context assembly function
optionD: Every other user's memories, kept for comparison
correctAnswerText: The assembled context the model saw, by part and tokens
explanation: The first question is "what did the model actually see?" — instructions, tools, memories, summary, turns and tool results, with token counts per part. Other users' data must never be logged for this.

prompt: Weighing one shared memory collection with a user filter against a namespace per user, which statement is right?
optionA: One collection makes leaks impossible as ids are unique
optionB: Per-user namespaces return worse matches for queries
optionC: One collection is simpler, but one missing filter leaks all
optionD: Per-user namespaces cannot be deleted once they exist
correctAnswerText: One collection is simpler, but one missing filter leaks all
explanation: A filtered collection is simple and scales, but its safety rests on every query remembering the filter. Namespaces make a leak structurally impossible and deletion a single drop, at the cost of many small indexes.

prompt: A product manager wants the assistant to memorise each user's order statuses to save tool calls. Your judgement?
optionA: Reject: vector stores cannot hold order numbers
optionB: Accept, but keep only statuses older than a month
optionC: Reject: statuses change; the order tool is the source
optionD: Accept: memory is cheaper and equally accurate
correctAnswerText: Reject: statuses change; the order tool is the source
explanation: Order status changes several times a day, so remembered copies are wrong when it matters. The tool is the system of record. Storage capability is not the objection.

prompt: Designing memory for a lending app under the DPDP Act, which policy is strongest?
optionA: Store everything encrypted and delete it after ten years
optionB: Store whatever the model decides to remember by itself
optionC: Purpose-limited memories, consent and a tested erase path
optionD: Keep all memories but hide them from the support team
correctAnswerText: Purpose-limited memories, consent and a tested erase path
explanation: The Act asks for purpose, consent and erasure. Encryption alone does not justify keeping unneeded data, and letting the model decide or merely hiding data meets none of the three.

prompt: Should memories be extracted inside the live reply or by a job after the chat? Which default is better?
optionA: Never; reread the full history on every single turn
optionB: A background job after the chat, as structured output
optionC: Inside the reply, with the model writing raw queries
optionD: Inside the reply, so the user waits on every write
correctAnswerText: A background job after the chat, as structured output
explanation: A background job keeps the reply fast and produces structured slot/text/kind records that can be reviewed. Rereading all history does not scale, and raw model-written queries are unsafe.

prompt: A team fills the context exactly to the model's limit to keep the most history. Your verdict?
optionA: Sound: providers trim the output budget for you
optionB: Unsound: reserve room or the model cannot answer
optionC: Sound: more history always gives better answers
optionD: Unsound: contexts must stay under half the window
correctAnswerText: Unsound: reserve room or the model cannot answer
explanation: A context filled to the limit leaves no room for the reply, so a reserve is part of the budget. More history is not always better, and there is no half-window rule.

prompt: A tool can return a 2 MB transaction export that the agent must filter several times. Which design is best?
optionA: Clip to the first rows and never mention the cut
optionB: Offload it: a handle, a summary and a query tool
optionC: Ask the user to paste the relevant rows into chat
optionD: Paste the full export into the context only once
correctAnswerText: Offload it: a handle, a summary and a query tool
explanation: Offloading keeps the export out of every later step while letting the agent query it repeatedly. Pasting it once still resends it each step, and silent clipping invites wrong answers.

prompt: Preload all 30 HR policies into every request, or give the agent a search tool? Which is better?
optionA: Preload them: longer contexts improve accuracy
optionB: A search tool: fetch what this step needs, stay lean
optionC: A search tool, since preloading breaks tool calls
optionD: Preload them: the model can never miss a clause
correctAnswerText: A search tool: fetch what this step needs, stay lean
explanation: Retrieving just in time keeps the window small and the relevant clause prominent. Long preloaded contexts cost more and bury what matters; they do not break tool calling.

prompt: When is handing a sub-task to a sub-agent with its own context NOT worth it?
optionA: When the sub-task is small and its result is needed whole
optionB: When it reads many pages to extract a few short facts
optionC: When the main context is already close to its budget
optionD: When its output is a short and structured answer
correctAnswerText: When the sub-task is small and its result is needed whole
explanation: Sub-agents pay off when a lot of reading collapses into a small result. For a small task whose full output the main agent needs, the extra call adds cost and latency for nothing.

prompt: A team changes the context budget and ordering and ships without evals since "no prompt changed". Judge it.
optionA: Sound: budget changes affect cost, never correctness
optionB: Unsound: context changes alter behaviour; run the evals
optionC: Unsound only if the model provider changed as well
optionD: Sound: only system prompt edits can change behaviour
correctAnswerText: Unsound: context changes alter behaviour; run the evals
explanation: What the model sees is its prompt. Dropping or reordering content changes answers, so it goes through the same eval set as a prompt change, measuring cost and accuracy together.

prompt: Which audit approach to forget-me requests best balances proof of erasure with erasure itself?
optionA: Keep a full copy of what was deleted, for disputes
optionB: Keep the deleted memories hashed so they can be restored
optionC: Record that a deletion happened and when, not the data
optionD: Keep no record at all, since any record breaks erasure
correctAnswerText: Record that a deletion happened and when, not the data
explanation: An audit row proving that the request was honoured keeps no personal data. A copy or a restorable form defeats the erasure; no record leaves you unable to show compliance.

prompt: Which three layers is an agent evaluated on?
optionA: Outcome, trajectory and efficiency
optionB: Precision, recall and F1 of search
optionC: Fluency, tone and length of answer
optionD: Latency, uptime and error budget
correctAnswerText: Outcome, trajectory and efficiency
explanation: Did it succeed (the state of the world), how did it get there (tools, arguments, order, forbidden calls), and at what cost (steps, tokens, time).

prompt: What does tool-call recall measure against a reference trajectory?
optionA: The share of runs that succeeded once in k tries
optionB: The share of steps that met the latency budget
optionC: The share of reference calls the run actually made
optionD: The share of the run's calls that were in the reference
correctAnswerText: The share of reference calls the run actually made
explanation: Recall is about reference calls made; low recall usually means a skipped check. The share of the run's calls that were in the reference is precision.

prompt: What does pass^k report for a scenario run k times?
optionA: The share of the k runs that hit a token budget
optionB: The average number of steps across the k runs
optionC: Whether it succeeded on every one of the k runs
optionD: Whether it succeeded on at least one of k runs
correctAnswerText: Whether it succeeded on every one of the k runs
explanation: pass^k requires success every time; pass@k requires it once. Customer-facing agents need the former.

prompt: What three properties should a fake tool in a scenario suite have?
optionA: Live, cached and rate-limited
optionB: Random, silent and permissive
optionC: Recorded, recording and strict
optionD: Async, retried and idempotent
correctAnswerText: Recorded, recording and strict
explanation: Recorded: same input, same output. Recording: every call is kept for trajectory assertions. Strict: an unrecorded call fails the test instead of quietly returning {}.

prompt: What is a simulated user in an agent scenario suite?
optionA: A real customer's chat replayed word for word
optionB: A judge model that scores the agent's last answer
optionC: A load-testing tool sending parallel requests
optionD: A script or model playing the human side of a chat
correctAnswerText: A script or model playing the human side of a chat
explanation: The agent's behaviour depends on what the user says back, so a scripted responder or a persona-prompted model plays that side through the conversation.

prompt: In a reference written as constraints, what does a must-not-call rule do?
optionA: Skips that tool when the fake records responses
optionB: Fails the case outright if that call is ever made
optionC: Marks the call as optional for tool-call recall
optionD: Lowers the efficiency score by one step per call
correctAnswerText: Fails the case outright if that call is ever made
explanation: Forbidden calls are the most important line of a reference: one forbidden call fails the case whatever the outcome looked like.

prompt: What happens when a graph framework's recursion limit is reached during an agent run?
optionA: It switches the run to a cheaper fallback model
optionB: It returns a polite partial answer to the user
optionC: It pauses until a human approves more steps
optionD: It raises an error, ending the run with no answer
correctAnswerText: It raises an error, ending the run with no answer
explanation: The recursion limit is a crash-style backstop counted in graph steps. A graceful stop with a message needs your own budget checked by the router.

prompt: In an agent release process, what does one "agent version" bundle together?
optionA: The framework library's installed version
optionB: Every edit made to the prompt this month
optionC: The provider's name for its model snapshot
optionD: Prompt, model, tool descriptions and graph
correctAnswerText: Prompt, model, tool descriptions and graph
explanation: An agent's behaviour depends on all four, so they are released together under one version recorded on every trace and thread.

prompt: How is step efficiency computed for a scored agent run?
optionA: Successful runs over all runs of the scenario
optionB: Actual steps over the step budget for the run
optionC: Tokens used over the tokens in the reference
optionD: Reference steps over actual steps, capped at 1
correctAnswerText: Reference steps over actual steps, capped at 1
explanation: Efficiency is reference length divided by actual length, capped at 1. It must be read with recall, because a skipped step also looks efficient.

prompt: Which events does an agent API stream so a UI can show progress?
optionA: One final JSON body once the whole run completes
optionB: Change events from the checkpointer's database
optionC: Raw model tokens only, with no event types at all
optionD: Typed events such as step, approval_required, answer
correctAnswerText: Typed events such as step, approval_required, answer
explanation: Typed events let the UI show "looking up your order", "waiting for approval" and the answer. A single final body shows nothing for a run that takes a minute.

prompt: Why is checking the final message alone not enough to evaluate an agent?
optionA: Two runs can say the same while acting very differently
optionB: Final messages are too short to be scored by a judge
optionC: Judges cannot read messages written in Hinglish
optionD: The final message is never shown to users of agents
correctAnswerText: Two runs can say the same while acting very differently
explanation: An agent acts. One run may refund the right amount after checking the policy, another may skip the check and refund ten times too much, and both can end with the same polite sentence.

prompt: Why are tool calls compared as a multiset rather than a set?
optionA: A set collapses repeated calls, hiding wasted steps
optionB: A multiset sorts calls, so order is checked too
optionC: A multiset ignores arguments, so wording never matters
optionD: A set cannot hold tool names that contain dots
correctAnswerText: A set collapses repeated calls, hiding wasted steps
explanation: Repeated calls are exactly the waste you want precision to show. A set counts get_order twice as once, inflating precision. Multisets neither ignore arguments nor check order.

prompt: Why are free-text arguments, like search queries, left out of the exact-match call key?
optionA: Free text is too long to hash into a dictionary key
optionB: Search queries never affect what the tool returns
optionC: Two good phrasings never match, so valid runs score zero
optionD: The tool gateway strips free text before scoring
correctAnswerText: Two good phrasings never match, so valid runs score zero
explanation: "damaged item refund rules" and "refund policy damaged items" are equally good but never equal. Key on ids, amounts and dates; judge free text separately or by what it returned.

prompt: Why should a customer-facing agent be gated on pass^k rather than pass@k?
optionA: Customers need it to work every time, not once in k
optionB: pass^k is cheaper to compute on large scenario suites
optionC: pass@k cannot be computed for agents that use tools
optionD: pass^k ignores flaky cases, so the score is steadier
correctAnswerText: Customers need it to work every time, not once in k
explanation: A customer gets one run, so the agent must succeed consistently. pass@k rewards a case that works once in k tries, which suits a supervised assistant at best.

prompt: Why must a fake tool fail the test on a call that its recording does not cover?
optionA: Unrecorded calls make the scenario run much slower
optionB: Recording libraries crash on calls they do not know
optionC: A fake that returns {} lets a wrong lookup pass quietly
optionD: Strict fakes let tests run without any model calls
correctAnswerText: A fake that returns {} lets a wrong lookup pass quietly
explanation: A permissive fake hides an agent that looked up the wrong order and still happened to reach the expected outcome. Strictness turns that into a failure.

prompt: Why must an LLM-played simulated user not be told the scenario's expected outcome?
optionA: It cannot read structured outcomes like refund rows
optionB: It would refuse to play a user asking for refunds
optionC: It would steer the chat towards it, inflating scores
optionD: The outcome is too long for its persona prompt
correctAnswerText: It would steer the chat towards it, inflating scores
explanation: A user who knows the target outcome nudges the agent towards it, so the test measures the simulator's help, not the agent. It is told goals and facts only.

prompt: Why does a CI tier with scripted or replayed model responses not replace a nightly tier with the real model?
optionA: Replayed runs are not deterministic across machines
optionB: It catches broken code, not broken model judgement
optionC: Replayed runs cost more tokens than live model runs
optionD: CI cannot run tests written as parametrised suites
correctAnswerText: It catches broken code, not broken model judgement
explanation: Replays test the harness, wiring, tools and fakes deterministically and for free. Only the real model, run k times, measures the agent's behaviour.

prompt: Why keep your own step and token budget in state when the framework has a recursion limit?
optionA: The recursion limit is ignored when tools are called
optionB: A recursion limit can only be set once per server
optionC: State budgets make the model reason more carefully
optionD: It ends the run gracefully and counts money, not steps
correctAnswerText: It ends the run gracefully and counts money, not steps
explanation: The recursion limit crashes with no answer and counts graph steps. A budget in state, checked by the router, stops cleanly with a message and can cap tokens.

prompt: Why is a token budget needed in addition to a step budget for agent runs?
optionA: Providers bill per step, so tokens never affect cost
optionB: Tokens per step rise as history grows, so steps hide cost
optionC: Token budgets also block injected instructions
optionD: Step counts cannot be measured inside graph frameworks
correctAnswerText: Tokens per step rise as history grows, so steps hide cost
explanation: Each step resends the growing history, so later steps cost more than earlier ones. A drifting agent can stay under a step cap while spending far more tokens.

prompt: Why is each conversation thread pinned to the agent version it started on?
optionA: Threads cannot be read by any other server replica later
optionB: Each agent version can serve only one thread at a time
optionC: Pinning is what lets a dropped event stream be resumed
optionD: Its saved state fits that graph and behaviour stays steady
correctAnswerText: Its saved state fits that graph and behaviour stays steady
explanation: A checkpoint written by one graph may not fit a changed schema, and a conversation that changes behaviour mid-way confuses users. Replicas and streams are unrelated.

prompt: Reference: get_order → check_policy → issue_refund. A run makes those three plus two extra get_order calls. Precision and efficiency?
optionA: Precision 1.0 and efficiency 0.6
optionB: Precision 0.6 and efficiency 1.0
optionC: Precision 1.0 and efficiency 1.0
optionD: Precision 0.6 and efficiency 0.6
correctAnswerText: Precision 0.6 and efficiency 0.6
explanation: As a multiset, 3 of the 5 calls match the reference, so precision is 0.6; efficiency is 3 reference steps over 5 actual, 0.6. Recall is 1.0, which is why the run still succeeds.

prompt: Valid runs may find the order by id or by phone, and check policy before or after. How do you write the reference?
optionA: As one exact script, failing any run that differs from it
optionB: As every possible path, listed one by one in a long table
optionC: As constraints: must call, must precede, must not, max steps
optionD: As a set of acceptable final messages, judged on wording
correctAnswerText: As constraints: must call, must precede, must not, max steps
explanation: Constraints accept every valid path and still fail the wrong ones. One script fails good runs, final-message checks miss the trajectory, and enumerating paths does not scale.

prompt: You add a scenario for an undelivered order: "refund chahiye order 7781 ka, abhi tak nahi aaya". What must it specify?
optionA: The exact final reply text the agent has to produce
optionB: Recorded tool responses, expected outcome, forbidden calls
optionC: The temperature and the provider region for the run
optionD: Only the opening line; the model decides all the rest
correctAnswerText: Recorded tool responses, expected outcome, forbidden calls
explanation: A scenario fixes what the tools return, what the world should look like at the end (no refund), and what must never happen (issue_refund), plus a budget. Exact reply text is too brittle.

prompt: A case passes 90% of the time, independently. Roughly what is its pass^3?
optionA: About 0.90
optionB: About 0.73
optionC: About 0.97
optionD: About 0.27
correctAnswerText: About 0.73
explanation: Passing three independent runs is 0.9³ ≈ 0.73. 0.90 is the single-run rate, and 0.27 is the chance that at least one of the three runs fails. Flakiness compounds.

prompt: You must check the agent asked for the order number when it was missing. How should this be scored?
optionA: An exact match on the agent's final message text
optionB: Tool-call precision against the reference path
optionC: An LLM judge on the trace, with a yes/no rubric item
optionD: Step efficiency against the shortest known run
correctAnswerText: An LLM judge on the trace, with a yes/no rubric item
explanation: Asking a clarifying question leaves no state to check, so a calibrated judge reads the trace against a yes/no rubric item. Precision and efficiency cannot see it.

prompt: A team changes only the tool descriptions. What must run before release?
optionA: The nightly tier: real model, k runs, pass^k gate
optionB: Nothing, as descriptions do not affect behaviour
optionC: Only the CI tier, since no Python code changed
optionD: A manual check of the happy-path scenario only
correctAnswerText: The nightly tier: real model, k runs, pass^k gate
explanation: Tool descriptions are part of what the model reads, so they change behaviour. Only the real-model tier measures that; replayed CI runs would pass unchanged.

prompt: A run keeps calling search_policies with the same query. Which router guard stops it earliest?
optionA: A per-user daily cap on the number of runs started
optionB: A detector on the last three calls being identical
optionC: A token budget set far above the usual run size
optionD: A higher recursion limit so the search gets chances
correctAnswerText: A detector on the last three calls being identical
explanation: A repeated-call detector fires on the third identical call. A high token budget fires much later, a daily cap does not stop this run, and raising the recursion limit prolongs it.

prompt: A state field steps: int gets {"steps": 1} from each node, but the step budget never fires. Which change fixes it?
optionA: Raise the recursion limit so the budget has time
optionB: Reset the field to zero at the start of every node
optionC: Return the step count from the router function instead
optionD: Give the field an adding reducer so updates accumulate
correctAnswerText: Give the field an adding reducer so updates accumulate
explanation: Without a reducer each update replaces the value, so steps is always 1. Annotated[int, operator.add] sums them. Routers do not write state, and a higher limit only delays the crash.

prompt: A three-minute research run is in progress when the mobile app disconnects. What should the client do on reopening?
optionA: Restart the run from step one under a new thread id
optionB: Post the same message again so a fresh run starts
optionC: Wait, since a lost event stream can never be resumed
optionD: Reconnect to the run's event log from its last event id
correctAnswerText: Reconnect to the run's event log from its last event id
explanation: Runs on a worker write events to a log, so the client resumes with its Last-Event-ID. Posting again starts a second run that repeats the agent's work and its side effects.

prompt: A new agent version has passed the pass^k gate. How should it reach users?
optionA: A switch for every user at night when traffic is low
optionB: All threads at once, including ones mid-conversation
optionC: Only threads that hit an error on the old version
optionD: A canary slice of new threads, compared with the old
correctAnswerText: A canary slice of new threads, compared with the old
explanation: A canary on new threads compares success, steps, cost and budget stops against the old version while open threads stay pinned. A night-time switch is still unmeasured.

prompt: A run never checked the refund policy but refunded the right amount. It scores success, precision 1.0 and efficiency 1.0. What does the analysis reveal?
optionA: The ideal run, since outcome and precision are perfect
optionB: A scorer bug, since efficiency cannot be 1.0 for it
optionC: Success by luck; recall and order expose the skipped check
optionD: A failure, since every run must make exactly 5 calls
correctAnswerText: Success by luck; recall and order expose the skipped check
explanation: Recall is 0.67 and the order check fails: on a non-refundable item this run would refund anyway. Efficiency is capped at 1, so a skipped step looks efficient — never read one metric alone.

prompt: A scorer reports precision 0.75 for a run of five calls, three in the reference and one call repeated. By hand it is 0.6. Cause?
optionA: Calls compared as multisets, double-counting it
optionB: Arguments cast to strings before the comparison
optionC: Precision divided by reference length, not run's
optionD: Calls compared as sets, so the repeat counts once
correctAnswerText: Calls compared as sets, so the repeat counts once
explanation: As a set there are 4 distinct calls, 3/4 = 0.75; as a multiset there are 5, 3/5 = 0.6. Dividing by the reference length would give 1.0, not 0.75.

prompt: A run that searched "damaged item refund rules" scores recall 0 against "refund policy damaged items". Diagnosis?
optionA: The agent used the wrong tool for the policy lookup
optionB: Recall is computed over runs, not over tool calls
optionC: Free text is in the call key, so it can never match
optionD: The search tool returned nothing for either query
correctAnswerText: Free text is in the call key, so it can never match
explanation: Exact matching on free-text arguments scores good runs as failures. Key on normalised ids, amounts and dates; then rescore old runs and watch the false failures disappear.

prompt: After a refactor the agent looks up order 5531 instead of 5513, yet the scenario suite is green. Likely cause?
optionA: A permissive fake returned {} for the unrecorded call
optionB: The step budget was set far too high for the scenario
optionC: The scenario recorded too many tool responses for it
optionD: The simulated user gave the agent a wrong order number
correctAnswerText: A permissive fake returned {} for the unrecorded call
explanation: A permissive fake let the wrong lookup through and the outcome matched by chance. Assert tools.unrecorded == [] in every scenario, then break it once on purpose to prove the assertion works.

prompt: A prompt change makes the agent refund damaged items at once, skipping the photo. Which scenario fails, and what does it show?
optionA: The with-photo case; happy paths catch all regressions
optionB: The undelivered case; refusals fail on any prompt edit
optionC: The no-photo case; unhappy paths catch what happy ones miss
optionD: None; the change only affects the wording of replies
correctAnswerText: The no-photo case; unhappy paths catch what happy ones miss
explanation: The happy path still ends in a refund and passes. Only the scenario where a refund must not happen catches it — which is why half a good suite is refusals and missing information.

prompt: The audit log shows approval for a ₹1,240 refund, then an executed refund of ₹12,400. Root cause?
optionA: The approver mistyped the amount on the review screen
optionB: Approval was keyed by tool name, not the exact arguments
optionC: The idempotency key was reused for the second refund
optionD: The model was not told the refund limit in its prompt
correctAnswerText: Approval was keyed by tool name, not the exact arguments
explanation: An approval must belong to the exact call. Derive the id from tool and arguments and execute the stored call; a different amount is a new action needing its own approval.

prompt: A double-tapped Send produced two runs on one thread, both proposing a refund. What explains it?
optionA: The event stream replayed the first run's events
optionB: Two concurrent runs loaded one checkpoint and both acted
optionC: The simulated user sent its message twice by design
optionD: The recursion limit allowed the run to fork in two
correctAnswerText: Two concurrent runs loaded one checkpoint and both acted
explanation: Without one-active-run-per-thread, both requests read the same state and acted. Return 409 to the second, disable Send while streaming, and keep write tools idempotent.

prompt: After a release, median steps per run is flat but p95 doubled and the budget-stop rate rose. What does it suggest?
optionA: Some runs in the new version have started to loop
optionB: The tracing library is double-counting each span
optionC: Users are now asking simpler questions than before
optionD: The provider slowed down, so every run is slower
correctAnswerText: Some runs in the new version have started to loop
explanation: A tail that grows while the median holds is a subset of runs going round in circles, confirmed by more budget stops. A provider slowdown changes latency, not step counts.

prompt: An agent's SSE events arrive all at once in production but stream correctly on a laptop. Where do you look first?
optionA: The test suite replaying a recorded cassette
optionB: A proxy or CDN buffering the response in production
optionC: The checkpointer holding events until it saves
optionD: The recursion limit delaying output until reached
correctAnswerText: A proxy or CDN buffering the response in production
explanation: Working locally but batched behind infrastructure points at buffering — nginx proxy buffering, gzip or a CDN. The checkpointer and recursion limit do not hold events back.

prompt: A release lifts the overall pass rate from 88% to 91%, but Hinglish-tagged scenarios fall from 85% to 70%. Analysis?
optionA: Better, as Hinglish scenarios are a small share
optionB: Worse for Hinglish users; the total hides the regression
optionC: Noise, since per-tag rates are never meaningful
optionD: Better for everyone, since the overall rate went up
correctAnswerText: Worse for Hinglish users; the total hides the regression
explanation: Per-tag pass rates show who a release helps and hurts. A release that is better overall and worse on Hinglish is not better for the users who write Hinglish.

prompt: For a booking agent, should success be scored by a judge on the final message or by checking the booking store?
optionA: Check the store; a judge is a fallback where no state exists
optionB: Use both on every run, averaging their scores with equal weight
optionC: Use the judge, since it understands intent better than code
optionD: Neither; the trajectory metrics already imply the success
correctAnswerText: Check the store; a judge is a fallback where no state exists
explanation: Outcome means the world: is there exactly one booking, in the right slot and time zone? Code can check that exactly. A judge on wording is only for tasks with no state to inspect.

prompt: An internal research assistant's output is always reviewed by an analyst before use. Which gate fits?
optionA: Step efficiency alone, since humans check outcomes
optionB: pass^k with k of 50, as for customer-facing agents
optionC: pass@k is acceptable, since a human checks the output
optionD: A single-run pass rate, as review removes flakiness
correctAnswerText: pass@k is acceptable, since a human checks the output
explanation: With a human in the loop, an agent that succeeds in some of k tries is useful. pass^k is for unsupervised, customer-facing agents. One run hides flakiness; efficiency alone ignores success.

prompt: Which allocation of simulated users across test tiers is soundest?
optionA: LLM users in CI on every commit; scripted ones nightly
optionB: LLM users everywhere, with no turn cap, for realism
optionC: Scripted users only, since LLM users never repeat
optionD: Scripted in CI; persona LLM users with a turn cap nightly
correctAnswerText: Scripted in CI; persona LLM users with a turn cap nightly
explanation: Scripted users are cheap and deterministic for CI; LLM users find unexpected phrasings and belong in the nightly tier, with a hard turn limit so two models cannot chat forever.

prompt: What should happen when an agent run hits its budget?
optionA: A silent retry with the budget doubled for the user
optionB: The raw exception returned to the client for debugging
optionC: A clear handover or partial answer, never a stack trace
optionD: The run continues, and the overrun is billed later
correctAnswerText: A clear handover or partial answer, never a stack trace
explanation: What happens at the limit is product design: hand over to a human, return what was found, or ask the user to narrow the request. A retry or continuing defeats the budget.

prompt: An incident: the agent e-mailed a customer in the wrong language. Which process is best?
optionA: Fix the prompt quickly and close the incident ticket
optionB: Reproduce it as a scenario, see it fail, fix, keep it
optionC: Add a line to the system prompt and skip the suite
optionD: Roll back the model and wait for another report
correctAnswerText: Reproduce it as a scenario, see it fail, fix, keep it
explanation: Turning every incident into a scenario before fixing it proves the fix and stops the bug returning. A quick prompt edit without the suite can break other cases unnoticed.

prompt: A team wants an LLM judge to verify the refund amount in each run. Your view?
optionA: Use code for the amount; keep the judge for what code can't
optionB: Use the judge without calibration, as amounts are simple
optionC: Fine; judges are as reliable as code on numeric checks
optionD: Fine, provided the judge is larger than the agent model
correctAnswerText: Use code for the amount; keep the judge for what code can't
explanation: Never let a judge grade what code can check: the refund row's amount is exact in the fake or test database. Judges are for qualities with no state, and are calibrated against humans.

prompt: Which rollback plan for agent versions is sound?
optionA: Wait for the next release to fix the regression forward
optionB: Route new threads to the previous version, kept deployable
optionC: Edit the live prompt back by hand from a saved copy
optionD: Delete all threads started on the new version at once
correctAnswerText: Route new threads to the previous version, kept deployable
explanation: Rolling back is a routing change to a version that still deploys. Hand edits are unmeasured, deleting threads destroys users' conversations, and waiting leaves users on a bad version.

prompt: A new version changes the graph's state schema while thousands of threads are open. Which plan is best?
optionA: Keep both schemas in one graph with no version field at all
optionB: Delete the open threads and ask all users to start over
optionC: Switch every open thread now, as checkpoints will adapt
optionD: Let open threads finish on the old version, or migrate them
correctAnswerText: Let open threads finish on the old version, or migrate them
explanation: A checkpoint written by the old graph may not load in the new one. Draining on the old version or migrating explicitly protects open conversations; the others break or discard them.

prompt: After a worker crash mid-run, an engineer proposes re-running the agent from the start. Evaluate it.
optionA: Unsafe only if the run had already streamed an answer
optionB: Unsafe: it repeats side effects; resume from checkpoint
optionC: Safe: agents are stateless, so a re-run is identical
optionD: Safe, if the same prompt and model version are used
correctAnswerText: Unsafe: it repeats side effects; resume from checkpoint
explanation: A half-finished run may already have refunded or e-mailed. Re-running repeats those actions; resuming from the checkpoint and event log does not. Agents are neither stateless nor deterministic.

prompt: Which set of per-version production metrics best reveals an agent's health?
optionA: Total runs per day and the provider's uptime figure
optionB: Success, p95 steps and cost, budget stops, denials
optionC: Average reply length and the share of polite replies
optionD: Server CPU, memory and disk use, and nothing more
correctAnswerText: Success, p95 steps and cost, budget stops, denials
explanation: Task success, steps and cost per run (p95), budget-stop rate, tool errors and gateway denials show whether the agent works and whether it is looping. Infrastructure metrics alone cannot.

prompt: A trained model is a function of which four things?
optionA: Code, tests, docs and the project README
optionB: Code, GPU, team size and cloud provider
optionC: Code, data, configuration and environment
optionD: Data, labels, dashboard and alert rules
correctAnswerText: Code, data, configuration and environment
explanation: Rebuilding a model needs the exact code, data, parameters and library environment. Git versions only the first, which is why data versioning and pinning exist.

prompt: In DVC, what does Git store for a large data file?
optionA: Nothing; history lives in a separate database
optionB: A small pointer file naming its content hash
optionC: The full file, compressed with each commit
optionD: A diff of the file against the last version
correctAnswerText: A small pointer file naming its content hash
explanation: Git keeps a small .dvc pointer with the content hash; the bytes live in the cache and a remote. Identical content is stored once, whatever it is called.

prompt: What structure do a pipeline's stages and their dependencies form?
optionA: A balanced binary tree
optionB: A cyclic state machine
optionC: A doubly linked list
optionD: A directed acyclic graph
correctAnswerText: A directed acyclic graph
explanation: Outputs of one stage feed inputs of the next, with no cycles. The DAG tells the tool what must run, in which order, and what can be skipped.

prompt: What does dvc.lock record after a pipeline run?
