optionA: Hashes of every dependency, parameter and output
optionB: The cloud credentials used to push the outputs
optionC: The wall-clock time each stage took to complete
optionD: The names of everyone who ran the pipeline lately
correctAnswerText: Hashes of every dependency, parameter and output
explanation: The lock file is the exact recipe of this model: what went in and what came out, by hash. Committing it ties a model to its inputs. Credentials never belong in it.

prompt: What does an orchestrator add that a pipeline tool like DVC does not?
optionA: Schedules, retries and alerts for pipeline runs
optionB: Content hashes for each input and output file
optionC: A diff of parameters against the last commit
optionD: A lock file recording the recipe of each run
correctAnswerText: Schedules, retries and alerts for pipeline runs
explanation: DVC knows what is out of date and how to build it; it does not run at 2 a.m., retry a flaky query or alert anyone. Hashes, lock files and params diff are DVC's own features.

prompt: Which three layers of batch data checks did the course use?
optionA: Schema, values and distribution
optionB: Syntax, style and documentation
optionC: Latency, throughput and errors
optionD: Unit, integration and load tests
correctAnswerText: Schema, values and distribution
explanation: Schema (columns, types, uniqueness), values (ranges, allowed sets, cross-field rules) and distribution (does the batch look like training data).

prompt: What is training-serving skew?
optionA: A model that trains slower than it serves predictions
optionB: A gap between the train set and the test set sizes
optionC: Features computed differently in training and serving
optionD: Serving more requests than the model was trained on
correctAnswerText: Features computed differently in training and serving
explanation: The same feature name holds a different number at serving time — a different formula, source or time — so offline metrics do not hold live.

prompt: What is a point-in-time join when building training data?
optionA: Joining each customer's latest available value
optionB: Joining each feature as of the prediction time
optionC: Joining tables at a fixed time every night
optionD: Joining rows that share one calendar date
correctAnswerText: Joining each feature as of the prediction time
explanation: Each training row gets the feature value that was available at its prediction time. Joining the latest value leaks information from the future.

prompt: In a feature store, what are the offline and online stores for?
optionA: Raw data for audits; cleaned data for dashboards
optionB: Development features; production ones after review
optionC: History for training; latest values for fast serving
optionD: Numeric features; text features stored as vectors
correctAnswerText: History for training; latest values for fast serving
explanation: The offline store holds history for point-in-time training sets; the online store holds the latest value per entity, loaded by materialisation, read in milliseconds.

prompt: What pins a Python environment exactly for a training job?
optionA: A README listing the versions used last time
optionB: A committed lock file and a pinned base image
optionC: A requirements file listing package names only
optionD: A global random seed at the top of the script
correctAnswerText: A committed lock file and a pinned base image
explanation: A lock file (uv, pip-tools, poetry) plus the Python version or base image makes the environment part of the commit. Unpinned names install whatever is newest.

prompt: Why is Git alone a poor fit for versioning large, frequently changing data files?
optionA: It changes the bytes of data files on checkout
optionB: It refuses to track files that are not source code
optionC: It cannot store binary files of any size at all
optionD: It keeps every full version, so the repository balloons
correctAnswerText: It keeps every full version, so the repository balloons
explanation: Git keeps full history of every file and diffs text by line, so a weekly 500 MB file makes a repository unusable, and hosts reject very large files. Git can store binaries; that is not the problem.

prompt: Why must a pipeline stage read only the files it declares as dependencies?
optionA: An undeclared input will not trigger a rerun on change
optionB: Reading undeclared files makes stages run in parallel
optionC: Undeclared files are deleted by the tool before runs
optionD: Declared files load faster from cache than others
correctAnswerText: An undeclared input will not trigger a rerun on change
explanation: The tool decides what to rerun from declared dependencies; it does not watch what a script opens. An undeclared config change leaves a stale, cached model.

prompt: Why does a pipeline tool skip a stage whose dependency hashes have not changed?
optionA: Same inputs give the same output, restored from cache
optionB: Skipping is a fallback when the stage failed before
optionC: Stages are skipped to stay within a cloud budget
optionD: Stages with unchanged code are treated as retired
correctAnswerText: Same inputs give the same output, restored from cache
explanation: Caching rests on determinism of the stage: unchanged inputs mean the output already exists. That is why a new threshold reruns only evaluation, not 40 minutes of features.

prompt: Why should parameters live in a params file rather than as constants edited inside scripts?
optionA: Constants in code are reset by every Git checkout
optionB: Scripts with constants cannot be run by orchestrators
optionC: Changes become tracked dependencies that can be diffed
optionD: A params file makes training run faster on GPUs
correctAnswerText: Changes become tracked dependencies that can be diffed
explanation: Parameters in params.yaml are dependencies of the stages that use them, so a change reruns exactly those stages and dvc params diff shows what changed.

prompt: Why does a random seed not by itself guarantee an identical model on rerun?
optionA: Seeds work in deep learning but not in scikit-learn
optionB: Row order, library versions and threads still vary
optionC: Seeds are reset whenever a new process is started
optionD: Seeds only affect the test split, not the training
correctAnswerText: Row order, library versions and threads still vary
explanation: Unordered reads, a changed library default and different thread counts or BLAS all change results under the same seed. Seeds do apply to training and to scikit-learn.

prompt: Why compare rerun predictions with a tolerance rather than with exact equality?
optionA: A tolerance hides real bugs, which keeps CI green
optionB: The serving layer rounds predictions at random
optionC: Float addition order differs across threads and hardware
optionD: Exact comparison of arrays is not possible in numpy
correctAnswerText: Float addition order differs across threads and hardware
explanation: Floating-point addition is not associative, so summing in a different order gives last-digit differences. np.allclose with a small atol separates that from real change.

prompt: Why record a git_dirty flag with each training run?
optionA: The model registry rejects any run that lacks such a flag
optionB: Dirty trees train more slowly, so the flag explains timings
optionC: Uncommitted code means the commit hash does not describe it
optionD: It tells the orchestrator to retry the run one more time
correctAnswerText: Uncommitted code means the commit hash does not describe it
explanation: A commit hash only describes a run if the working tree matched the commit. Many teams refuse to log dirty runs to the shared server for exactly this reason.

prompt: Why do schema and value checks fail hard while distribution checks usually only warn?
optionA: Distribution checks are too slow to run on every batch
optionB: Warnings are cheaper to store than failure reports
optionC: Errors there are plain wrong; a shift may be real data
optionD: Schema checks run only in training, never in scoring
correctAnswerText: Errors there are plain wrong; a shift may be real data
explanation: A null ID or out-of-range score is simply wrong. A distribution shift may be real new customers, so it warns the risk team; only extreme shifts block.

prompt: Why can joining each customer's latest bureau snapshot make offline AUC look brilliant?
optionA: Latest snapshots hold more rows for every customer
optionB: Recent data is always more predictive than old data
optionC: The join drops hard cases and keeps easy examples
optionD: Later values leak the outcome into training features
correctAnswerText: Later values leak the outcome into training features
explanation: Today's snapshot was recorded after the application; defaulters have since missed EMIs, so the feature contains the label. Serving sees only past values, and the gain vanishes.

prompt: Why was coercion deliberately turned off in the batch validation schema?
optionA: Without coercion the schema validates rows faster
optionB: Coercion doubles memory use on large data frames
optionC: Coercion hides an upstream type change behind a pass
optionD: Coercion turns all missing values into zeros
correctAnswerText: Coercion hides an upstream type change behind a pass
explanation: Coercing "45000" to a number makes the check pass while the producer's type has silently changed. Coerce at a boundary you own, never to make a failing check pass.

prompt: Only evaluate.min_auc changed in params.yaml. What happens on the next dvc repro?
optionA: Every stage reruns because the params file changed
optionB: Only the evaluate stage reruns; others are skipped
optionC: Nothing reruns, as thresholds are not dependencies
optionD: Only train reruns, and evaluation comes from cache
correctAnswerText: Only the evaluate stage reruns; others are skipped
explanation: Parameters are tracked per key, and only evaluate depends on min_auc. The rest are unchanged and skipped — the everyday payoff of caching.

prompt: To rebuild last month's model you need last month's data. Which steps restore it?
optionA: Check out the old pointer file, then run dvc checkout
optionB: Run git checkout on the pointer; the bytes follow it
optionC: Copy the newest file and delete its last rows
optionD: Run dvc pull without changing the pointer at all
correctAnswerText: Check out the old pointer file, then run dvc checkout
explanation: Git moves the pointer; dvc checkout makes the workspace bytes match it. Git checkout alone leaves the new file in place and dvc status reports it modified.

prompt: train.py reads features.yaml, but the train stage declares only train.py and the data. What should you do?
optionA: Move the feature list into params or declare it as a dep
optionB: Rename features.yaml so the tool finds it by itself
optionC: Run the train stage by hand when features change
optionD: Clear the cache so every stage reruns on each repro
correctAnswerText: Move the feature list into params or declare it as a dep
explanation: The tool reruns only on declared changes. Declaring the file, or moving the list into params.yaml where params diff shows it, makes the dependency real. Clearing the cache throws away caching.

prompt: Incomes switched from rupees to thousands of rupees; every value is still positive. Which check catches it?
optionA: A uniqueness check on the application id column
optionB: A cross-field rule such as loan within 60× income
optionC: A per-column check that income is greater than 0
optionD: A type check that income is a numeric column
correctAnswerText: A cross-field rule such as loan within 60× income
explanation: Per-column ranges miss unit changes because every value is still plausible on its own. A relationship between columns failed for all 2,000 rows.

prompt: In a nightly scoring batch of 50,000 rows, 3 fail validation. What should the pipeline do?
optionA: Drop the 3 rows silently and score the remainder
optionB: Fail the whole batch until the 3 are fixed upstream
optionC: Quarantine the 3, score the rest, alert past a share
optionD: Score all 50,000, including the 3 that failed
correctAnswerText: Quarantine the 3, score the rest, alert past a share
explanation: In scoring, bad rows go to quarantine for later or manual review, the rest are scored, and an alert fires if the quarantined share passes a threshold such as 1%.

prompt: Building training data from monthly bureau snapshots, which value is right for an application made on 11 May?
optionA: The mean of all snapshots for the customer
optionB: The last snapshot strictly before 11 May
optionC: The newest snapshot in the bureau table
optionD: The first snapshot taken after 11 May
correctAnswerText: The last snapshot strictly before 11 May
explanation: Only values available before the application could have been used. merge_asof with allow_exact_matches=False picks it; later or averaged values leak the future.

prompt: Which is the right way to seed a scikit-learn training script?
optionA: Pass random_state to every splitter, CV object and model
optionB: Set PYTHONHASHSEED in the environment and nothing else
optionC: Seed only the model, since data splits are deterministic
optionD: Call a global random seed once at the top of the script
correctAnswerText: Pass random_state to every splitter, CV object and model
explanation: Each estimator and splitter takes its own random_state. A global seed is shared state other code can disturb, and splits like train_test_split are random unless seeded.

prompt: One team, one repository, runs started by people or CI, no schedule yet. What should run the pipeline?
optionA: A pipeline tool like DVC, with no separate orchestrator
optionB: A new Airflow deployment just for this pipeline
optionC: A cluster orchestrator with a container for each step
optionD: A cron job running the notebook from top to bottom
correctAnswerText: A pipeline tool like DVC, with no separate orchestrator
explanation: Without schedules, retries or varied hardware, a pipeline tool covers the need. Add an orchestrator when runs must be scheduled; a cron-driven notebook loses the DAG and caching.

prompt: A Java service recomputes FOIR for scoring while training used pandas. What is the best first fix?
optionA: Retrain weekly so the model adapts to Java values
optionB: Round FOIR to one decimal place in both code paths
optionC: Put the feature logic inside the model artefact itself
optionD: Ask both teams to follow one wiki page on FOIR
correctAnswerText: Put the feature logic inside the model artefact itself
explanation: One implementation removes skew by construction: the service sends raw fields and the model's pipeline computes features. A wiki page leaves two implementations that drift.

prompt: A legitimately missing CIBIL score makes read_csv turn the column to float, failing an int check. What is the fix?
optionA: Read and validate it as nullable Int64, with an imputer
optionB: Drop the type check from the schema for this column
optionC: Fill missing scores with -1 before running checks
optionD: Turn on coercion so the float passes as an integer
correctAnswerText: Read and validate it as nullable Int64, with an imputer
explanation: Classic int64 cannot hold a missing value. A nullable integer type keeps the contract, and the model needs an imputer for the field. Coercion or a sentinel hides the next change.

prompt: dvc repro refuses to run: stage a outputs the directory out, stage b outputs out/x.txt. Diagnosis?
optionA: The cache is corrupt and must be rebuilt from scratch
optionB: Two stages claim one path; each output needs one producer
optionC: Directories can never be declared as stage outputs
optionD: Stage b runs before a, which reverses the graph
correctAnswerText: Two stages claim one path; each output needs one producer
explanation: With overlapping outputs the tool cannot know which stage rebuilds the file. Give each stage its own directory; reading another stage's output is fine, writing into it is not.

prompt: A teammate clones the repo and dvc pull fails, asking whether the cache is up to date. Most likely cause?
optionA: The author committed the pointer but never pushed data
optionB: The teammate has an older version of Git installed
optionC: The pointer was committed with Windows line endings
optionD: The remote stores files by hash rather than by name
correctAnswerText: The author committed the pointer but never pushed data
explanation: Git has the pointer but the remote has no bytes for it; they exist only in the author's local cache. dvc push fixes it; a pre-push hook and a clean-runner CI prevent it.

prompt: After removing city_tier from features.yaml, every stage reports "didn't change, skipping". Why?
optionA: Removing a feature never changes the trained model
optionB: The lock file must be deleted before each repro
optionC: DVC caches models for a week before retraining
optionD: features.yaml is not a declared dependency of train
correctAnswerText: features.yaml is not a declared dependency of train
explanation: The declared world and the real one differ: the script reads a file the stage never declared, so the tool sees nothing changed. Audit every file a stage opens against its deps.

prompt: Offline AUC is 0.876; on values known at application time it drops to 0.680, and an honest model scores 0.687. Diagnosis?
optionA: Overfitting from too few trees in the forest model
optionB: Concept drift, as the economy changed after training
optionC: Leakage from a latest-snapshot join in training data
optionD: A serving bug that drops half the input features
correctAnswerText: Leakage from a latest-snapshot join in training data
explanation: The naive model's test set leaks too, so its offline score is inflated; live it gets past values and does slightly worse than the point-in-time model. That pattern is leakage, not drift.

prompt: Offline metrics are strong, live approvals poor, and served FOIR runs systematically lower than in training. Cause?
optionA: Serving computes FOIR differently, e.g. declared income
optionB: Applicants learned to game the FOIR feature quickly
optionC: The decision threshold was raised after deployment
optionD: The test set was too small to estimate offline AUC
correctAnswerText: Serving computes FOIR differently, e.g. declared income
explanation: A systematic gap between served and training feature distributions is skew from two implementations. Log served features and compare them with training daily to catch it early.

prompt: Same seed, data and commit, but a colleague's model differs, and their lock file has a different scikit-learn. Most likely reason?
optionA: DVC restored a different data file from its cache
optionB: The seed is ignored when the operating system differs
optionC: A library version changed a default or numeric routine
optionD: The tracking server altered the model while logging
correctAnswerText: A library version changed a default or numeric routine
explanation: A new library version can change a solver, tolerance or routine, legitimately producing a different model under the same seed. That is why the lock file is part of the commit.

prompt: A point-in-time join crashes with "left keys must be sorted". Someone proposes a plain merge on customer. Analysis?
optionA: Run the join in SQL, where row ordering never matters
optionB: Sort both frames by time; a plain merge brings back leakage
optionC: Accept it, since a plain merge on customer is equivalent
optionD: Drop the time keys, so that the join is always sorted
correctAnswerText: Sort both frames by time; a plain merge brings back leakage
explanation: merge_asof needs both frames sorted on their time keys. A plain merge on customer reintroduces the latest-snapshot leak the as-of join exists to prevent.

prompt: The registry shows @champion on v4, but live responses still report model version 3. Most likely cause?
optionA: The alias move failed silently inside the registry
optionB: The service pins v3 or loads the alias only at startup
optionC: Version 4 failed validation and was rolled back
optionD: Its signature differs, so v4 cannot be loaded
correctAnswerText: The service pins v3 or loads the alias only at startup
explanation: Moving an alias changes nothing for a service that loads a fixed version number, or that resolved the alias once at startup. Load by alias, report the resolved version, and reload on promotion.

prompt: A new DSA partner's batch passes schema and range checks, but CIBIL PSI is 0.42. What is it most likely?
optionA: Duplicate rows inflating the share of low scores
optionB: A bug in the PSI code, since all values are in range
optionC: Real applicants unlike training data; warn and monitor
optionD: A unit change in CIBIL scores that must block the run
correctAnswerText: Real applicants unlike training data; warn and monitor
explanation: Every value is valid; the population moved because the partner brings thinner-file applicants. That is a warning for the risk team and closer monitoring, not a pipeline failure.

prompt: Same seed and rows, but the SQL extract has no ORDER BY and SGD coefficients differ between runs. Why?
optionA: The database resets the seed on every query it runs
optionB: SGD ignores random_state in every library version
optionC: Floating-point errors make SGD entirely random
optionD: Row order changed, and SGD depends on visiting order
correctAnswerText: Row order changed, and SGD depends on visiting order
explanation: SGD updates weights row by row, so a different order gives a different model under the same seed. Sort by a stable key before training.

prompt: A team with one batch-scored model wants to adopt a feature store. Your judgement?
optionA: Not yet: a tested feature module and PIT joins suffice
optionB: Yes: a feature store removes the need for validation
optionC: Yes: every ML team needs a feature store from day one
optionD: No: feature stores cannot be used for batch scoring
correctAnswerText: Not yet: a tested feature module and PIT joins suffice
explanation: A feature store is another system to run — materialisation jobs, an online database, definitions to sync. For one batch model, a shared tested module and as-of joins give the benefits without the cost.

prompt: Which situation most justifies adopting a feature store?
optionA: A team wanting a feature-store box on its architecture
optionB: Shared features, fresh online aggregates, repeated skew
optionC: A notebook prototype that is not yet deployed anywhere
optionD: A single model retrained once a quarter, scored in batch
correctAnswerText: Shared features, fresh online aggregates, repeated skew
explanation: It pays when many models share features, online scoring needs fresh aggregates in milliseconds (UPI fraud on the last 10 minutes), or skew incidents keep happening.

prompt: The company data platform already runs Airflow; the ML team prefers Prefect. Which choice is soundest?
optionA: Rewrite every stage as a notebook that cron schedules
optionB: Use the platform's orchestrator; keep stage scripts portable
optionC: Avoid orchestration and run the pipeline by hand daily
optionD: Run Prefect alongside it, as its flows are plain Python
correctAnswerText: Use the platform's orchestrator; keep stage scripts portable
explanation: An existing platform brings its scheduler, alerts and operators; a second one doubles operations. Files-in, files-out stage scripts with YAML parameters keep the choice reversible.

prompt: Storage is limited. Which data should be versioned?
optionA: Only the cleaned data, since raw data is not reused
optionB: Raw extracts you cannot regenerate, and the final model
optionC: Every intermediate file, pushed by hand after each run
optionD: Nothing; the warehouse can always rebuild old data
correctAnswerText: Raw extracts you cannot regenerate, and the final model
explanation: Raw data you cannot recreate must be versioned; intermediate files are regenerated by the pipeline. Warehouses change by row unless you record a snapshot id.

prompt: Which validation policy for a credit-scoring pipeline is soundest?
optionA: Warn on every check so the pipeline never stops
optionB: Block on every check, even small distribution shifts
optionC: Decide in advance which checks block and which warn
optionD: Let the on-call engineer decide each failure live
correctAnswerText: Decide in advance which checks block and which warn
explanation: Deciding beforehand, in writing, makes the gate predictable: schema and value errors block, shifts warn unless extreme. Blocking everything gets the gate disabled; warning only lets bad data in.

prompt: Should the training script refuse to log to the shared tracking server from a dirty working tree?
optionA: No: the commit hash describes the run regardless
optionB: Yes: such runs cannot be traced to committed code
optionC: No: dirty runs are the most useful for exploring
optionD: Yes: dirty trees always produce worse models
correctAnswerText: Yes: such runs cannot be traced to committed code
explanation: A run from uncommitted code carries a commit hash that does not describe it, breaking lineage. Local exploration is fine; the shared record must be reproducible.

prompt: Seed 1 gives AUC 0.771 and seed 2 gives 0.764. A colleague claims a 0.003 gain from one run. Judge the claim.
optionA: Unsupported: report the spread across seeds first
optionB: Unsupported: AUC cannot be compared across runs
optionC: Supported: any positive gain is a real improvement
optionD: Supported: 0.003 is large for a credit risk model
correctAnswerText: Unsupported: report the spread across seeds first
explanation: Seed alone moves AUC by 0.007 here, so a 0.003 difference from one run is within noise. Compare across several seeds before claiming an improvement.

prompt: Which practice best ensures a dependency bump that changes the model is noticed quickly?
optionA: An annual audit where someone tries to rebuild the model
optionB: Exact byte comparison of the model file on each commit
optionC: A README note asking people not to upgrade packages
optionD: CI reruns a sample and compares predictions within tolerance
correctAnswerText: CI reruns a sample and compares predictions within tolerance
explanation: A small CI rerun with a tolerance catches a real change the day it lands. An annual audit finds it too late, a note enforces nothing, and byte equality fails on harmless differences.

prompt: Which ordering of fixes for training-serving skew matches the course's best-first advice?
optionA: Retraining more often so the model absorbs the skew
optionB: One implementation, then a shared library, then a store
optionC: A feature store first, whatever the scale or team count
optionD: Two implementations reviewed jointly every quarter
correctAnswerText: One implementation, then a shared library, then a store
explanation: Putting feature logic in the model artefact removes skew by construction; a shared library is next; a feature store when many teams share features. Retraining does not remove a formula mismatch.

prompt: Which documented build process best protects an NBFC facing a regulator's "how was this model built?"
optionA: A wiki page of the steps someone ran in March
optionB: A notebook kept with all cell outputs visible
optionC: dvc pull and repro as the only path, exercised daily
optionD: A zip of the final model kept on a shared drive
correctAnswerText: dvc pull and repro as the only path, exercised daily
explanation: Making the pinned pull-and-rebuild the only documented way means the rebuild is tested every day. A wiki page, a zip or a notebook cannot reproduce code, data, config and environment together.

prompt: A model is a function of which four things that must all be versioned to rebuild it?
optionA: Code alone, since data is fixed once collected
optionB: Data, the model name, its author and the date
optionC: Code, data, configuration and environment
optionD: Code, metrics, the registry and the GPU type
correctAnswerText: Code, data, configuration and environment
explanation: Git versions only the code. The same code trained on different data, settings or library versions gives a different model, so all four must be pinned.

prompt: After `dvc add data/raw/loans.csv`, what does Git end up tracking for that file?
optionA: A line-by-line diff from the previous version
optionB: The full file, compressed to save some space
optionC: A small pointer file holding the content hash
optionD: A symbolic link to the data scientist's laptop
correctAnswerText: A small pointer file holding the content hash
explanation: DVC writes a small .dvc file with the md5 and size, and adds the data path to .gitignore. The bytes go to the DVC cache and remote, not into Git history.

prompt: Which command uploads tracked data bytes from the local cache to the shared DVC remote?
optionA: dvc push
optionB: dvc add
optionC: git push
optionD: dvc commit
correctAnswerText: dvc push
explanation: git push sends the pointer files; dvc push sends the bytes they name to the remote. dvc add only hashes the file and writes the pointer locally.

prompt: In a model registry, what is an alias such as @champion?
optionA: A second copy of the model stored under a new name
optionB: A permanent number given to each new version
optionC: A movable name that points at one model version
optionD: A tag recording the data hash of the training run
correctAnswerText: A movable name that points at one model version
explanation: Version numbers only go up and record history. An alias is moved deliberately and names a role, such as the model production should load.

prompt: What does lineage mean for a registered model version?
optionA: The order in which versions went to production
optionB: The list of people who have downloaded the model
optionC: The chain from version to run, commit and data hash
optionD: The sequence of hyperparameters tried in tuning
correctAnswerText: The chain from version to run, commit and data hash
explanation: Lineage is the walkable trail: version → run → Git commit and data hash → git checkout and dvc pull → the exact code and rows that built it.

prompt: In a champion/challenger setup, what does the @challenger alias mark?
optionA: The candidate under evaluation, perhaps in shadow
optionB: The last good model, kept for a quick rollback
optionC: The newest version the training job registered
optionD: The model currently serving production traffic
correctAnswerText: The candidate under evaluation, perhaps in shadow
explanation: The challenger is the candidate being judged against the champion. Production loads @champion; the newest version is not automatically a challenger or a champion.

prompt: What is the @previous-champion alias kept for?
optionA: Serving traffic while the champion is retraining
optionB: Comparing each new model with the very first
optionC: Archiving versions that failed the promotion rule
optionD: A one-step rollback to the last good model
correctAnswerText: A one-step rollback to the last good model
explanation: When promotion moves @champion, the old version keeps @previous-champion, so rolling back is a single alias move rather than a search through history.

prompt: How does a DVC remote store two identical files that are tracked under different paths?
optionA: Once, addressed by the hash of the content
optionB: Twice, once for each path that points at it
optionC: As a diff against the first copy it stored
optionD: Only in the local cache, never in the remote
correctAnswerText: Once, addressed by the hash of the content
explanation: DVC is content-addressed: identical bytes produce the same hash and are stored once. It does not store diffs, so a changed file is stored again in full.

prompt: After a fresh `git clone`, which command fetches the data that the .dvc pointers name?
optionA: git fetch
optionB: dvc add
optionC: dvc pull
optionD: dvc gc
correctAnswerText: dvc pull
explanation: dvc pull downloads from the remote exactly the objects the committed pointers name and places them in the workspace. git fetch only brings Git objects.

prompt: For a warehouse table that changes row by row, what plays the role of a DVC pointer?
optionA: The table's snapshot or time-travel version ID
optionB: A CSV export committed straight into Git
optionC: The table name together with today's date
optionD: The row count of the table at training time
correctAnswerText: The table's snapshot or time-travel version ID
explanation: DVC versions files. For tables, the warehouse's own time travel names immutable data; record that snapshot ID with the run. A name and date do not pin the rows.

prompt: Why does a team avoid committing its 2 GB monthly training extract straight to Git?
optionA: Git refuses any file that is not plain UTF-8 text
optionB: Git cannot store binary files of any size at all
optionC: Git would silently alter the bytes of the file
optionD: Every version stays in history and hosts cap file size
correctAnswerText: Every version stays in history and hosts cap file size
explanation: Git can store binaries, but it keeps every full version in history forever and hosts reject large files. DVC keeps only a small hash pointer in Git.

prompt: Why must `git checkout` of an old .dvc pointer be followed by `dvc checkout`?
optionA: DVC must recompute a hash that Git has corrupted
optionB: Git moves only the pointer; the bytes must follow it
optionC: Git locks the data file until DVC releases it
optionD: Git deletes the data and DVC then re-downloads it
correctAnswerText: Git moves only the pointer; the bytes must follow it
explanation: Git versions the pointer, not the data. Until dvc checkout (or dvc pull) runs, the workspace still holds the newer bytes and dvc status reports the file as modified.

prompt: Why should a production service never load "the latest version" of a registered model?
optionA: Loading by number is slower than loading by an alias
optionB: Registries delete older versions when a new one arrives
optionC: Every retrain makes a newer version; approval is separate
optionD: Latest versions have no signature until they are aliased
correctAnswerText: Every retrain makes a newer version; approval is separate
explanation: If production follows the newest version, training becomes deployment. Loading an alias means only a deliberate, approved promotion changes what serves.

prompt: Why is a promotion rule written down before anyone looks at the challenger's metrics?
optionA: Because the registry refuses rules added later
optionB: So the challenger can be trained to meet the rule
optionC: Because metrics expire once the run has finished
optionD: So the decision cannot be bent to fit the result
correctAnswerText: So the decision cannot be bent to fit the result
explanation: "The challenger looks better" is a judgement made after seeing the numbers. A rule fixed in advance, and written as code, makes the decision repeatable and auditable.

prompt: Why does a promotion rule refuse to compare models whose evaluation data hashes differ?
optionA: The registry cannot hold two data hashes at once
optionB: Different hashes mean that one model file is corrupt
optionC: Metrics measured on different data are not comparable
optionD: DVC blocks any evaluation when the hashes disagree
correctAnswerText: Metrics measured on different data are not comparable
explanation: A higher AUC on an easier test window says nothing about which model is better. Both must be scored on the same data before the gain means anything.

prompt: Why can per-slice AUC miss a model that systematically underprices one customer segment?
optionA: AUC ignores every feature that has been dropped
optionB: AUC measures ranking, not whether risk levels are right
optionC: AUC rises automatically when the slice is small
optionD: AUC is only defined on the whole test set at once
correctAnswerText: AUC measures ranking, not whether risk levels are right
explanation: A model can rank a slice correctly while predicting too little risk for all of it. A per-slice calibration gap (mean predicted minus actual rate) catches the shift in level.

prompt: Why should the person who trained a credit model not be the one who approves its promotion?
optionA: Approval needs another person to retrain the model
optionB: Trainers lack permission to read the registry at all
optionC: The registry forbids one user creating two aliases
optionD: Separating proposer and approver gives independent review
correctAnswerText: Separating proposer and approver gives independent review
explanation: In a regulated setting, model-risk governance expects someone outside the project to approve, with permissions enforcing it and every alias move logged.

prompt: Why version the raw extract you cannot regenerate, rather than the cleaned copy?
optionA: Raw data is smaller, so it costs less to store
optionB: The pipeline can rebuild the cleaned copy from raw
optionC: DVC cannot compute hashes of cleaned files
optionD: Cleaned data is too small for DVC to track it
correctAnswerText: The pipeline can rebuild the cleaned copy from raw
explanation: Every version costs full storage. Raw data that cannot be fetched again must be kept; anything derived by the pipeline can be regenerated by dvc repro.

prompt: Why is running `dvc gc --workspace` against the remote dangerous for future audits?
optionA: It rewrites the hashes inside older pointer files
optionB: It encrypts old versions so they cannot be read
optionC: It removes the Git tags that name each release
optionD: It deletes stored versions the workspace no longer uses
correctAnswerText: It deletes stored versions the workspace no longer uses
explanation: Garbage collection keeps only what its scope references. Scoped to the workspace, it removes old release data; keep all tags and commits if gc must run.

prompt: Why does DVC on its own not protect personal data held in old dataset versions?
optionA: DVC strips personal data from older versions itself
optionB: DVC encrypts each version with the committer's key
optionC: DVC keeps data only on the laptop that added it
optionD: Anyone who can read the remote can read every version
correctAnswerText: Anyone who can read the remote can read every version
explanation: DVC is not access control. Personal data needs bucket permissions, encryption and a retention plan; a deleted customer's rows survive in old versions until purged.

prompt: You refresh `data/raw/bureau.parquet` and retrain. What must go into the same commit as the training code?
optionA: A note of the date the data was refreshed
optionB: The parquet file itself, so Git holds the bytes
optionC: The model's AUC, written in the commit message
optionD: The updated .dvc pointer written by dvc add
correctAnswerText: The updated .dvc pointer written by dvc add
explanation: Committing the pointer with the code means one Git SHA names both. Without a new pointer, the trained-on bytes are unrecorded and the run cannot be rebuilt.

prompt: Main has moved on, and you must retrain exactly the model built at tag data-v1. Which sequence restores its data?
optionA: git checkout data-v1, then dvc checkout or dvc pull
optionB: dvc gc --workspace, then git checkout data-v1
optionC: dvc pull on main, then rename the file to data-v1
optionD: git checkout data-v1 alone, then retrain at once
correctAnswerText: git checkout data-v1, then dvc checkout or dvc pull
explanation: The tag restores code and pointer; dvc checkout (or dvc pull if the cache lacks it) brings the bytes the pointer names. Git checkout alone leaves the newer data in place.

prompt: A new teammate clones the credit-risk repository and finds `data/raw/` empty. What should they run?
optionA: git lfs pull, since DVC keeps data in LFS
optionB: dvc pull, to fetch the bytes the pointers name
optionC: dvc init, which restores missing tracked files
optionD: dvc add, to re-hash the empty data directory
correctAnswerText: dvc pull, to fetch the bytes the pointers name
explanation: The data is ignored by Git and lives in the remote. dvc pull downloads exactly what the committed pointers name. dvc add on an empty folder records the wrong thing.

prompt: @champion is on v3. Challenger v5 passes the rule and is approved. Which alias moves complete the promotion?
optionA: challenger to v3 and champion to v5, swapped together
optionB: v5 renamed to v3 so production keeps the same URI
optionC: champion to v5 only, and v3 deleted from the registry
optionD: previous-champion to v3, champion to v5, challenger cleared
correctAnswerText: previous-champion to v3, champion to v5, challenger cleared
explanation: Promotion keeps the old champion as @previous-champion so rollback stays one move. Deleting v3 destroys history; versions are never renamed.

prompt: You register a model from a training run. Which tags should you copy onto the new version?
optionA: A full copy of the training rows, as a tag
optionB: The trainer's name and the registration date
optionC: The test AUC, so versions sort by quality
optionD: The run name, the Git commit and the data hash
correctAnswerText: The run name, the Git commit and the data hash
explanation: Copying commit and data hash onto the version makes lineage visible without opening the run. Names and dates do not identify the code or data that built it.

prompt: A UPI fraud model's decision threshold was tuned on one evaluation week. Where should that threshold live?
optionA: As a tag on the version, travelling with it
optionB: Hard-coded in the serving app's source code
optionC: In the commit message of the training run
optionD: In the trainer's notebook, for reference
correctAnswerText: As a tag on the version, travelling with it
explanation: The threshold belongs to that model. Kept on the version, it moves with promotion and rollback; hard-coded in serving, it silently pairs with whatever model loads.

prompt: A team versions a 2 GB raw extract and a 2 GB cleaned copy every week. How should it cut storage?
optionA: Run dvc gc --workspace every week after each training run
optionB: Version the raw extract and let the pipeline rebuild the clean
optionC: Version only the cleaned copy and delete each raw extract
optionD: Move both into Git LFS, which stores only the differences
correctAnswerText: Version the raw extract and let the pipeline rebuild the clean
explanation: Raw data cannot be regenerated, so it is the version to keep; the cleaned copy is a pipeline output. gc on the workspace deletes history, and LFS does not diff.

prompt: A borrower asks for erasure under the DPDP Act, and their rows appear in old DVC dataset versions. What is the right step?
optionA: Rename the old tags so the rows cannot be found
optionB: Nothing, as archived versions are always exempt
optionC: A deliberate, documented purge of the old versions
optionD: Remove the rows from today's file and re-add it
correctAnswerText: A deliberate, documented purge of the old versions
explanation: Old versions still hold the rows. Erasure means purging them too, as a documented operation; editing only the current file or renaming tags leaves the data in place.

prompt: You set up promotion for a product recommender on a shopping app. Which approach fits its risk?
optionA: Serve the newest version straight from training
optionB: Require a model-risk committee sign-off each week
optionC: Promote automatically when the coded rule passes
optionD: Let any engineer move @champion by hand at will
correctAnswerText: Promote automatically when the coded rule passes
explanation: Low-risk models can promote automatically once a written rule passes. Committee sign-off is for credit or fraud; hand moves and serving the newest skip the rule.

prompt: You tag the dataset commit after a September 2025 credit-bureau refresh. Which tag name follows good practice?
optionA: data-latest-final-version
optionB: loans_final_v3_FIXED_new
optionC: data-2025-09-bureau-refresh
optionD: final2-use-this-one-now
correctAnswerText: data-2025-09-bureau-refresh
explanation: Tags should say what changed and when, so a reader can find the version an audit needs. "final" and "latest" names stop being true the next week.

prompt: For version 7, the run's data_md5 tag differs from the md5 in the .dvc pointer at its git_commit. What does that mean?
optionA: The run trained on uncommitted data; the trail is broken
optionB: The remote corrupted the file and must be restored
optionC: Version 7 was registered in a different registry
optionD: DVC re-hashed the file; both name the same bytes
correctAnswerText: The run trained on uncommitted data; the trail is broken
explanation: The commit should pin the exact data the run used. A mismatch means the run used bytes no commit records, and the audit response should say so plainly.

prompt: After checking out last month's pointer, a colleague's training run still sees 9,000 rows instead of 8,000. Why?
optionA: The remote returns the latest data for any pointer
optionB: dvc checkout was skipped, so the bytes are still the new ones
optionC: DVC merged both months, so the file holds all their rows
optionD: Git restored the bytes but kept the newer row count
correctAnswerText: dvc checkout was skipped, so the bytes are still the new ones
explanation: Git moved the pointer; the workspace still holds the newer file until dvc checkout runs. The post-checkout hook from dvc install automates that step.

prompt: False declines doubled the day after a weekly retrain, though nobody promoted anything. What is the likely cause?
optionA: Serving loaded the latest version rather than an alias
optionB: The previous-champion alias had expired that week
optionC: The registry reordered versions by their test AUC
optionD: DVC had pushed the wrong data to the remote store
correctAnswerText: Serving loaded the latest version rather than an alias
explanation: Loading "latest" means each retrain goes live without a decision. Pin serving to @champion and make promotion the only thing that moves it.

prompt: A promotion rule with a tight per-slice calibration limit rejects even the champion's own retrain. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The slice is too large for its calibration to settle
optionB: The champion was never registered in the registry
optionC: Calibration cannot be measured within a slice at all
optionD: The limit is tighter than the slice's own sampling noise
correctAnswerText: The limit is tighter than the slice's own sampling noise
explanation: A small slice of about 200 rows has noisy rates. A limit below that noise rejects good models; set it with the noise in view or require more data.

prompt: `dvc pull` at last quarter's release tag reports the data object missing from the remote. What most likely happened?
optionA: The release tag was created on a different branch
optionB: DVC remotes expire versions older than a quarter
optionC: Someone ran gc without keeping all tags and commits
optionD: The pointer files were edited and re-hashed by Git
correctAnswerText: Someone ran gc without keeping all tags and commits
explanation: Remotes keep objects until garbage collection removes them. gc scoped to the workspace deletes release data; run it only with all tags and commits kept.

prompt: The challenger shows +0.02 AUC, but it was scored on the Q2 test window and the champion on Q1. What do you conclude?
optionA: The challenger is clearly better and can be promoted
optionB: The champion is overfit, since its window is older
optionC: The gain is not comparable; score both on one window
optionD: Any AUC difference below 0.05 is always just noise
correctAnswerText: The gain is not comparable; score both on one window
explanation: Two windows differ in difficulty and mix. Only scores on the same evaluation data, ideally the same hash, can be compared.

prompt: Version 12 has no run ID and no tags, and an auditor asks how it was built. What is broken?
optionA: Its data is in DVC, so lineage is still fully intact
optionB: Lineage needs only the version number to be found
optionC: The registry lost its tags during a routine upgrade
optionD: It was registered with no lineage, so nothing leads back
correctAnswerText: It was registered with no lineage, so nothing leads back
explanation: Lineage is recorded when the version is created. Without the run link, commit and data hash, nothing leads from the version back to its code and rows.

prompt: During an incident, returning to the old model took two days. What was most likely missing?
optionA: A larger GPU to retrain the old model more quickly
optionB: A rule forcing every version to share one data hash
optionC: A kept @previous-champion and a rehearsed one-step move
optionD: An alias named @latest for the serving app to load
correctAnswerText: A kept @previous-champion and a rehearsed one-step move
explanation: With the last good model always aliased, rollback is a single alias move done in minutes. Retraining is slow and risky; @latest is the cause of incidents, not the cure.

prompt: The DVC remote grew by 40 GB in a month, though the only raw extract is 2 GB. What is the likely cause?
optionA: DVC storing each version as a line-by-line text diff
optionB: Intermediate files pushed by hand each run, not regenerated
optionC: Identical files on two branches being stored twice over
optionD: The pointer files in Git growing larger with each commit
correctAnswerText: Intermediate files pushed by hand each run, not regenerated
explanation: Every pushed version is stored in full. Pushing intermediates each run multiplies storage; identical files are stored once, and pointers are tiny.

prompt: Rebuilt from the right commit and data, the model scores an applicant slightly differently from the logged score. What should you check?
optionA: Library versions, since the environment may differ
optionB: Whether DVC altered the bytes during the pull
optionC: Whether the data hash collided with another file
optionD: Nothing, as rebuilds never match by design
correctAnswerText: Library versions, since the environment may differ
explanation: Code and data are pinned, so the remaining input is the environment. Compare library versions; content hashes do not collide in practice and DVC does not change bytes.

prompt: For an NBFC's credit-risk model, which promotion process would you defend to a regulator?
optionA: Production serves the newest; older ones are archived
optionB: Pipeline proposes; a separate reviewer role moves @champion
optionC: Any version with a better AUC is promoted automatically
optionD: The trainer promotes once the overall AUC looks better
correctAnswerText: Pipeline proposes; a separate reviewer role moves @champion
explanation: A rule run by the pipeline, a separate approver enforced by permissions, and a logged alias move is what model-risk review expects. AUC-only promotion skips slices and comparability.

prompt: A team weighs Git LFS against DVC for its training data. What is the strongest reason to pick DVC?
optionA: It needs no remote storage, keeping data inside Git
optionB: It is the only tool that can store binary files at all
optionC: It is storage-agnostic and ties data to pipeline stages
optionD: It encrypts every version, so no access control is needed
correctAnswerText: It is storage-agnostic and ties data to pipeline stages
explanation: LFS moves bytes to the Git host's storage and knows nothing about pipelines. DVC works with many remotes and links data to the stages that produce and use it.

prompt: Training reads a warehouse table that changes daily by row. Which versioning approach would you choose?
optionA: Record only the table name and the query used
optionB: Commit a daily CSV extract straight into Git
optionC: Record the warehouse snapshot ID with each run
optionD: Export a CSV each day and dvc add every one
correctAnswerText: Record the warehouse snapshot ID with each run
explanation: The warehouse's time travel already names immutable data; logging its snapshot ID pins the rows cheaply. Daily exports multiply storage, and a name plus query does not pin rows.

prompt: Which promotion rule would you choose for a lender's default-risk model?
optionA: Promote when a reviewer judges that the curves look better
optionB: Promote the run with the lowest training loss of the batch
optionC: Minimum overall gain, no slice drop, slice calibration bounds
optionD: Promote whenever the overall test AUC is any amount higher
correctAnswerText: Minimum overall gain, no slice drop, slice calibration bounds
explanation: Overall gain alone can hide a degraded or mis-calibrated segment, and training loss says nothing about new data. A coded rule checks gain, slices and calibration on the same data.

prompt: Is three days of shadow mode worth it before promoting a UPI fraud challenger?
optionA: Yes, live decisions are compared without acting on them
optionB: Yes, because shadow mode retrains it on live traffic
optionC: No, because shadow mode exposes customers to its calls
optionD: No, offline metrics on one week already prove it works
correctAnswerText: Yes, live decisions are compared without acting on them
explanation: In shadow, the challenger scores real traffic and its decisions are logged, not acted on, so live behaviour is compared with the champion's at no customer cost.

prompt: Where would you place the DVC remote for a lender's training data?
optionA: In the training cloud account, with access controls
optionB: On the lead data scientist's laptop, backed up weekly
optionC: Inside the Git repository, next to the pointer files
optionD: In a public bucket so any teammate can pull freely
correctAnswerText: In the training cloud account, with access controls
explanation: The remote holds every version of personal data, so it needs permissions, encryption and retention, close to where training runs. Laptops and public buckets fail on all counts.

prompt: A teammate proposes putting test AUC into version names so the best model sorts first. Your verdict?
optionA: Reject it: version names cannot hold decimal numbers
optionB: Accept it: the registry can then promote it unaided
optionC: Reject it: it invites promotion by sorting, not by a rule
optionD: Accept it: the best model becomes quick to find by eye
correctAnswerText: Reject it: it invites promotion by sorting, not by a rule
explanation: Promotion should follow a written rule on comparable data and slices. A sortable metric in the name invites picking the top line, which is exactly what the rule prevents.

prompt: A dataset version history must also honour erasure requests. Which design is most defensible?
optionA: Delete the whole remote whenever a request comes in
optionB: Rename the people in old versions instead of purging
optionC: A retention plan plus documented purges of old versions
optionD: Keep every version forever, since audits will need them
correctAnswerText: A retention plan plus documented purges of old versions
explanation: Retention limits plus deliberate, recorded purges meet erasure duties while keeping an audit trail of what was removed. Keeping all forever breaches the duty; wiping all destroys lineage.

prompt: Which practice best guarantees a model can still be rebuilt when an audit arrives a year later?
optionA: Make dvc pull and dvc repro the only documented build
optionB: A wiki page describing how the model was first trained
optionC: Keep the final pickle on a shared network drive
optionD: Ask the original author to rebuild it on request
correctAnswerText: Make dvc pull and dvc repro the only documented build
explanation: If the documented build is the reproducible one, it is exercised every day and breaks loudly. A wiki or a stored pickle cannot show how the model was built.

prompt: Which rollback design would you choose for a fraud model that is retrained every week?
optionA: Delete the bad version so serving falls back by itself
optionB: An always-set @previous-champion, one move, practised
optionC: Retrain on last week's data whenever problems appear
optionD: Edit the threshold in serving code until errors drop
correctAnswerText: An always-set @previous-champion, one move, practised
explanation: Rollback must be fast and boring: one alias move to a known-good model, rehearsed. Retraining takes time, deleting a version does not tell serving what to load, and threshold edits mask the cause.

prompt: Which OWASP LLM Top 10 category covers model output passed unchecked to a browser, database or shell?
optionA: Improper output handling
optionB: Misinformation
optionC: Unbounded consumption
optionD: Excessive agency
correctAnswerText: Improper output handling
explanation: Improper output handling is classic injection with the model as the typist: output reaches a sink without the checks given to user input. Excessive agency is about too many tools or rights.

prompt: Which OWASP LLM category describes a model given more functionality, permission or autonomy than its task needs?
optionA: System prompt leakage
optionB: Excessive agency
optionC: Supply chain
optionD: Data and model poisoning
correctAnswerText: Excessive agency
explanation: Excessive agency is damage made possible by too much capability. The fix is narrower tools, the user's own rights, and human approval for irreversible actions.

prompt: What does the OWASP LLM category "unbounded consumption" describe?
optionA: A system prompt that is read back to the end user
optionB: Requests that burn compute or money without any limit
optionC: A model giving confident but false answers to users
optionD: Training data that plants a hidden trigger behaviour
correctAnswerText: Requests that burn compute or money without any limit
explanation: Unbounded consumption covers huge inputs, agent loops, mass querying and public endpoints with no quota — "denial of wallet". The others are misinformation, poisoning and prompt leakage.

prompt: One vector index serves many customers with no tenant filter. Which OWASP LLM category is this?
optionA: Misinformation
optionB: Improper output handling
optionC: Vector and embedding weaknesses
optionD: Unbounded consumption
correctAnswerText: Vector and embedding weaknesses
explanation: Vector and embedding weaknesses are retrieval-specific: shared indexes without filters, chunks without permission metadata, poisoned chunks and leaky embeddings.

prompt: Which weights format stores a JSON header plus raw tensor bytes, with no code path run on load?
optionA: pickle
optionB: joblib
optionC: a PyTorch .bin file
optionD: safetensors
correctAnswerText: safetensors
explanation: safetensors only parses a header and copies bytes. Pickle, joblib and older PyTorch .bin/.pt files are pickle-based and can call functions while loading.

prompt: What is an AI bill of materials?
optionA: An inventory of models, datasets, adapters, packages and servers
optionB: An invoice of the tokens each customer used in the month
optionC: A list of the prompts the assistant is allowed to answer
optionD: A record of each person who approved a model release
correctAnswerText: An inventory of models, datasets, adapters, packages and servers
explanation: You cannot patch what you do not know you run. An AI BOM lists each model's source, revision, hash and licence, plus datasets, adapters, packages, MCP servers and hosted APIs.

prompt: In STRIDE applied to an LLM app, which threat is the signature one, where injection borrows the assistant's access?
optionA: Denial of service
optionB: Tampering
optionC: Elevation of privilege
optionD: Repudiation
correctAnswerText: Elevation of privilege
explanation: The assistant usually holds more access than the person talking to it; injection lets them use it. The fix is effective rights as the intersection of the agent's and the user's.

prompt: Where should the model be drawn in a data-flow diagram of an LLM application?
optionA: Inside the trusted zone, alongside your server code
optionB: Inside the least-trusted zone of any input it reads
optionC: Outside the diagram, as the provider's concern
optionD: As a trust boundary that filters untrusted input
correctAnswerText: Inside the least-trusted zone of any input it reads
explanation: The model's behaviour is shaped by whatever text reached it. If it reads customer emails, its output is as trustworthy as a customer email, so it is not a boundary.

prompt: Under which Indian law is a company processing personal data called a data fiduciary?
optionA: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
optionB: The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
optionC: The Right to Information Act, 2005 as amended
optionD: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 in full
correctAnswerText: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
explanation: The DPDP Act names the processor a data fiduciary, with duties of purpose, minimisation, security, erasure and breach reporting to the Data Protection Board.

prompt: An agent acts for a logged-in user. What should its effective rights be?
optionA: The intersection of its own and the user's rights
optionB: The union of its own and the user's own rights
optionC: Whatever rights the model requests in its call
optionD: Whatever the service account has been granted
correctAnswerText: The intersection of its own and the user's rights
explanation: An agent may be less capable than its user, never more. Intersecting the agent's tool set with the user's permissions stops injection from borrowing extra access.

prompt: Why is "the system prompt says never reveal X" not a security control?
optionA: The rule only holds when temperature is set to zero
optionB: Models ignore system prompts once a chat begins
optionC: It asks the model; X must simply not be in context
optionD: System prompts are visible only to the provider
correctAnswerText: It asks the model; X must simply not be in context
explanation: Assume every system prompt is eventually read by a user. If revealing X would hurt, X must not be in the context; the instruction is a request, not an enforcement point.

prompt: Why must permission checks go into the retrieval query rather than run on the answer?
optionA: The model rewrites answers after they are checked
optionB: A chunk in the context can come out in any form
optionC: Vector stores cannot return chunks in batches
optionD: Answer checks are slower than retrieval checks
correctAnswerText: A chunk in the context can come out in any form
explanation: Once a forbidden chunk reaches the model it can be paraphrased or summarised past any answer check. The model cannot leak what it was never given.

prompt: Why does taking the top-k results and then dropping forbidden chunks fail users?
optionA: Dropping chunks raises the similarity threshold
optionB: The index forgets chunks that were dropped once
optionC: Dropping chunks re-ranks the rest by tenant name
optionD: The nearest hits may all be forbidden, leaving none
correctAnswerText: The nearest hits may all be forbidden, leaving none
explanation: If the closest chunks belong to another tenant, filtering afterwards returns nothing although a permitted chunk exists. Filtering inside the search ranks only permitted chunks.

prompt: Why is a response cache keyed on the prompt text alone a disclosure risk?
optionA: Answers depend on the user, so another user receives them
optionB: Prompt hashes collide whenever two prompts are long
optionC: Cached answers expire and are returned as empty text
optionD: Hashing the prompt reveals the prompt text to others
correctAnswerText: Answers depend on the user, so another user receives them
explanation: Two users asking in the same words get the first user's answer. The key must include everything the answer depends on: tenant, user or permission scope, and the prompt.

prompt: Why is a semantic cache riskier than an exact cache for answers built from user data?
optionA: Semantic caches never expire any of their entries
optionB: Similar questions always need identical answers
optionC: Different users' similar questions can share one entry
optionD: Embeddings cannot be stored inside a cache safely
correctAnswerText: Different users' similar questions can share one entry
explanation: A semantic cache matches on similarity, so a second user's similar question can return the first user's personal answer. Use it only for answers that depend on no user data.

prompt: Why can loading a pickle-based model checkpoint run code on your server?
optionA: Pickle files are compiled binaries run on the GPU
optionB: Pickle imports the original training script to load
optionC: Pickle unpacks weights using a shell command each time
optionD: Pickle stores rebuild steps that can call any function
correctAnswerText: Pickle stores rebuild steps that can call any function
explanation: Pickle records instructions for rebuilding objects, including "call this function with these arguments". Loading an untrusted file can therefore run arbitrary code with the server's credentials.

prompt: Why must a tool take the user's identity from the session rather than from the model's arguments?
optionA: Providers strip tool arguments for user privacy
optionB: The session is quicker to read than an argument
optionC: Models cannot write strings that look like ids
optionD: A steered model could then claim to be anyone
correctAnswerText: A steered model could then claim to be anyone
explanation: Model arguments can be influenced by any text in the context. A tenant or user id taken from them is the spoofing row of the threat model; the authenticated session is the source of truth.

prompt: Why is fine-tuning on raw customer conversations a disclosure risk?
optionA: Fine-tuning makes the training logs visible to users
optionB: Fine-tuned models refuse to answer customer queries
optionC: Models can memorise and repeat rare training strings
optionD: Fine-tuning shares the data with every other tenant
correctAnswerText: Models can memorise and repeat rare training strings
explanation: Training-data extraction research shows models can emit rare strings such as names and numbers. A record also cannot be deleted from weights, so de-identify first or prefer RAG.

prompt: Why does every arrow leaving the model in a threat model need the checks you give user input?
optionA: The provider rewrites model outputs while in transit
optionB: Model outputs are always longer than their inputs
optionC: Outputs are encrypted and must be decoded first
optionD: Text that reached the model can steer what it emits
correctAnswerText: Text that reached the model can steer what it emits
explanation: Anyone who can place text in the context can influence the output, so every output flow — to a tool, a database or a browser — comes from an untrusted source.

prompt: Why should security logs record reason codes and lengths rather than raw prompts?
optionA: Raw prompts cannot be searched after being logged
optionB: Raw prompts are too large for any log store to hold
optionC: Reason codes are required by every model provider
optionD: So logs do not become a second copy of personal data
correctAnswerText: So logs do not become a second copy of personal data
explanation: Purpose limitation and minimisation under the DPDP Act apply to logs too. Keep decisions and ids; any sample kept for investigation is redacted, restricted and short-lived.

prompt: A support bot answers "where is my order?". What should be placed in the model's context?
optionA: The customer profile, with PAN and phone masked
optionB: The full customer row, so the model has context
optionC: Only the status of this user's order, as a field
optionD: All the tenant's orders, for the model to filter
correctAnswerText: Only the status of this user's order, as a field
explanation: Anything in the context can come out in the answer. Retrieve per user and per purpose, and pass the fields the answer needs, not whole records.

prompt: You are fixing a response cache for a multi-tenant loan assistant. What must the cache key include?
optionA: The prompt text and the time of the request
optionB: The prompt text, lower-cased and trimmed
optionC: Tenant, user or permission scope, and the prompt
optionD: The model name and the prompt text together
correctAnswerText: Tenant, user or permission scope, and the prompt
explanation: The key must cover everything the answer depends on. Leaving out tenant and user lets one borrower receive another's balance when they ask in the same words.

prompt: Your tenants share one vector collection with metadata filters. How do you guard against one forgotten filter?
optionA: A step after search that drops other tenants' chunks
optionB: One search wrapper that requires a user, plus a test
optionC: A system prompt telling the model to respect tenants
optionD: A larger top-k so every tenant's chunks come back
correctAnswerText: One search wrapper that requires a user, plus a test
explanation: With one collection, one missing filter leaks everything. A single wrapper that cannot be called without a user, and a test that every path uses it, closes that gap.

prompt: HR restricts the salary document to hr-leads in the source system; the index still says hr-only. What do you do?
optionA: Sync the change into the chunk metadata at once
optionB: Stop answering every HR question until audit
optionC: Leave it, as index metadata is only advisory
optionD: Tell the model salaries are now for leads only
correctAnswerText: Sync the change into the chunk metadata at once
explanation: Metadata copied at ingestion goes stale. Sync permission changes as events (or re-crawl ACLs), update the chunks, and re-check high-sensitivity sources at answer time.

prompt: A pull request loads a downloaded checkpoint with `torch.load(path, weights_only=False)`. What is your review comment?
optionA: Fine, as model hubs scan all uploaded files
optionB: Load it on a laptop first to check it works
optionC: Use safetensors or weights_only=True, never False
optionD: Wrap the load in try/except to catch errors
correctAnswerText: Use safetensors or weights_only=True, never False
explanation: weights_only=False re-enables full unpickling, so a hostile file can run code. A data-only format or the restricted loader closes the hole; error handling does not.

prompt: Code loads a hub model by the name `org/model` with no other argument. What should change?
optionA: Download it fresh on every deploy to stay current
optionB: Pin the exact revision hash and record file hashes
optionC: Add the model name to the requirements.txt file
optionD: Copy the model card into the repo for reference
correctAnswerText: Pin the exact revision hash and record file hashes
explanation: A bare name means whatever is there today. Pinning the revision commit and recording hashes, ideally via an internal mirror, makes the download reviewable and repeatable.

prompt: A cached summary was built from three documents, one of them restricted to HR. What permission does the summary carry?
optionA: The most open permission among its sources
optionB: None, since a summary is newly written text
optionC: The strictest permission among its sources
optionD: Whatever the requesting user happened to hold
correctAnswerText: The strictest permission among its sources
explanation: Derived data inherits the strictest permission of its inputs. Summaries, cached answers, eval cases and memories built from a restricted chunk are restricted too.

prompt: An HR assistant must answer leave questions from a database. How should queries be built?
optionA: The model fills a typed intent; the server writes SQL
optionB: Run the model's SQL as written on the main database
optionC: Ask the model to avoid the salary table in its SQL
optionD: Block any model SQL longer than 200 characters
correctAnswerText: The model fills a typed intent; the server writes SQL
explanation: Model output is untrusted. A validated intent plus server-written, parameterised SQL with the employee id from the session cannot be steered into other tables.

prompt: Security logs must identify users without storing their email addresses. Which pseudonym do you use?
optionA: The raw email, as security logs are internal
optionB: The first four letters of the user's email name
optionC: A keyed hash (HMAC) with a secret from the vault
optionD: A plain SHA-256 hash of the user's email address
correctAnswerText: A keyed hash (HMAC) with a secret from the vault
explanation: A plain hash is reversible by anyone who can hash the staff list. A keyed hash lets only the security team, holding the key, re-identify a user during an incident.

prompt: A nightly agent reconciles invoices with no live user present. Which identity should it use?
optionA: No identity at all, as background jobs are trusted
optionB: Its own narrowly scoped identity, logged per action
optionC: A super-user key, since no user is there to scope
optionD: The identity of whoever last chatted with the agent
correctAnswerText: Its own narrowly scoped identity, logged per action
explanation: Without a user to intersect with, the agent gets its own least-privilege identity, and every action is logged against it for accountability.

prompt: Ravi and Meena both asked "what is my loan balance?" and both saw Ravi's figure. What most likely caused this?
optionA: The two users share one account in the core system
optionB: The retriever searched both users' notes together
optionC: The model invented a balance for the second user
optionD: The cache key left out the user, so answers were shared
correctAnswerText: The cache key left out the user, so answers were shared
explanation: Identical wording produced the same prompt-only key, so Meena received Ravi's cached answer. Adding tenant and user to the key fixes it.

prompt: A Zenith user gets "I could not find that" for Zenith's own policy, though its chunk is in the index. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The answer filter judged the policy to be secret
optionB: The model refused because the policy was so long
optionC: The similarity threshold was set far too low
optionD: Top-k was taken first and then filtered by tenant
correctAnswerText: Top-k was taken first and then filtered by tenant
explanation: The nearest chunks belonged to another tenant, so filtering after the search left nothing. Put the tenant filter inside the search.

prompt: PII redaction is switched on, yet PAN numbers are visible in the external tracing vendor. What went wrong?
optionA: PAN numbers cannot be matched by a pattern
optionB: The vendor re-identifies data by design
optionC: Redaction ran in the viewer, after the export
optionD: Traces were written before the model call
correctAnswerText: Redaction ran in the viewer, after the export
explanation: Redaction must happen before data leaves your systems, in the log handler or exporter. Masking only in a dashboard leaves the raw values in the vendor's store.

prompt: Right after a new model file is loaded, an unknown process appears on the GPU node. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: The GPU driver started its own monitoring daemon
optionB: The tokenizer compiled itself into a new process
optionC: safetensors spawned a helper to parse the header
optionD: The checkpoint was a pickle that ran code on load
correctAnswerText: The checkpoint was a pickle that ran code on load
explanation: Pickle-based checkpoints can call any function while loading. Scan model files, prefer safetensors, and use the restricted loader for any PyTorch checkpoint.

prompt: A summariser has no tools at all, yet customer data reached an outside server. Which path is most likely?
optionA: The vector index copied itself to a public host
optionB: The provider forwarded the chat to a partner company
optionC: The UI rendered a model-written image link carrying it
optionD: The summariser's logs were emailed out overnight
correctAnswerText: The UI rendered a model-written image link carrying it
explanation: If the model can be steered and the UI renders images or links, data can leave in a URL the browser fetches. Render with raw HTML off, sanitise, allow-list hosts and set a CSP.

prompt: An HR user at one company read another company's leave balances through a tool. What is the likely flaw?
optionA: The other company had made its HR files public
optionB: The model memorised the other company's balances
optionC: The cache key held the tenant but not the user
optionD: The tool trusted a tenant id supplied by the model
correctAnswerText: The tool trusted a tenant id supplied by the model
explanation: A tool that accepts identity from model arguments can be pointed anywhere. Tools take tenant and user from the authenticated request context.

prompt: A threat model lists "add a guardrail prompt" as the fix for every threat. What is wrong with it?
optionA: It needs one STRIDE row for each guardrail prompt
optionB: It should have quoted each guardrail prompt in full
optionC: Guardrail prompts belong in code, not in the model
optionD: It never removes reach: narrow tools, filter data, gate
correctAnswerText: It never removes reach: narrow tools, filter data, gate
explanation: Fixes come in order: remove reach, add a human gate, then add detection. A prompt is a request to the model, so a model of only prompt fixes has not been done.

prompt: A team rated injection "low likelihood" for an assistant reading a public support inbox, since the model "usually refuses". The flaw?
optionA: Refusals lower the impact, not the likelihood itself
optionB: Likelihood can only be scored after a full pen test
optionC: Email is plain text, so it cannot carry instructions
optionD: Likelihood depends on who can place text; anyone can here
correctAnswerText: Likelihood depends on who can place text; anyone can here
explanation: Assume injection succeeds for flows that read untrusted text. Likelihood is about whether an attacker can place text — for a public inbox, anyone can.

prompt: An agent took an action and the logs cannot show which prompt, chunk or approving user led to it. Which STRIDE threat is exposed?
optionA: Repudiation
optionB: Tampering
optionC: Spoofing
optionD: Information disclosure
correctAnswerText: Repudiation
explanation: Repudiation is the inability to prove who did what. Log the request, retrieved chunk ids, tool arguments and approver for every action.

prompt: One user has five guard blocks in ten minutes but never hits the rate limit; a batch script hits the limit. How do you read this?
optionA: The user is probing; the script is only volume
optionB: Both are attacks, as both crossed a threshold
optionC: The script is the attacker; blocks are typos
optionD: Neither matters until the rate limit is reached
correctAnswerText: The user is probing; the script is only volume
explanation: Rate limits catch volume, not behaviour. Repeated guard blocks in a short window signal probing and warrant step-up or suspension; the script needs only throttling.

prompt: A large regulated bank joins your multi-tenant assistant. Which isolation would you choose for its documents?
optionA: An answer filter that hides other banks' names
optionB: A system prompt naming the tenant in every session
optionC: A separate database or deployment for that tenant
optionD: One shared collection with a tenant metadata filter
correctAnswerText: A separate database or deployment for that tenant
explanation: For regulated or very large customers, a separate store is the strongest boundary: a missing filter cannot cross it. Prompts and answer filters are not boundaries at all.

prompt: A screening agent reads uploaded résumés and can change a candidate's status. Which defence would you prioritise?
optionA: A firmer system prompt against hidden instructions
optionB: A keyword list of known risky phrases in uploads
optionC: Limit reach: it proposes, a recruiter confirms
optionD: Asking the model to rate each résumé's honesty
correctAnswerText: Limit reach: it proposes, a recruiter confirms
