explanation: Résumés are untrusted text, so assume injection sometimes succeeds. Removing the agent's power to change status, with a human confirming, removes the impact; filters only lower the rate.

prompt: Customer data must stay current and be erasable on request. Fine-tune on it, or use RAG with access control?
optionA: Fine-tune, as weights hide data better than an index
optionB: RAG with access control, as weights cannot forget a row
optionC: Either, as both handle erasure requests the same way
optionD: Fine-tune monthly, then delete rows from the dataset
correctAnswerText: RAG with access control, as weights cannot forget a row
explanation: A record cannot be removed from trained weights and may be memorised. RAG with per-user filters lets data be updated and deleted at the source.

prompt: "We use a large model provider, so the OWASP LLM Top 10 is their problem." Is this a sound position?
optionA: Yes: providers certify their model against the list
optionB: No: you own prompts, retrieval, tools, output and logs
optionC: No, though only supply chain risk remains with you
optionD: Yes: the list covers only model training risks
correctAnswerText: No: you own prompts, retrieval, tools, output and logs
explanation: The provider runs the model. Your prompt, retrieval, tools, output handling and logs carry most of the ten categories.

prompt: An analyst tool genuinely needs free-form model-written SQL. Which containment would you require?
optionA: Allow any SQL but cap each result at one thousand rows
optionB: Instruct the model to write only SELECT statements always
optionC: Read-only replica, narrow role, row-level security, timeouts
optionD: Run it on production but log every query for later review
correctAnswerText: Read-only replica, narrow role, row-level security, timeouts
explanation: When the server cannot write the SQL, the database must enforce limits: a read-only replica, a role that sees permitted views, per-user row security, timeouts and row limits.

prompt: Your team wants to adopt a third-party MCP server. Which approval policy would you set?
optionA: Approve it once, since descriptions never change later
optionB: Trust it outright if its registry downloads are high
optionC: Run it with the developer's own cloud credentials
optionD: Pin its version, review descriptions, re-review on change
correctAnswerText: Pin its version, review descriptions, re-review on change
explanation: An MCP server is code with access, and its tool descriptions enter the model's context. Pin it, read the descriptions, re-review when they change, and run it with least privilege.

prompt: Which rate-limiting design would you defend for a public AI feature with logged-in and anonymous users?
optionA: One global limit shared by all traffic at once
optionB: No limit; review the provider bill each month
optionC: A per-IP limit alone, as user ids can be faked
optionD: Limits per user, per tenant or key, and per IP
correctAnswerText: Limits per user, per tenant or key, and per IP
explanation: Attackers spread across whichever key you forgot. Limiting at several keys, with windows shared by all workers, contains both abuse and denial of wallet.

prompt: A tool calls another internal service for the user. Which credential would you choose?
optionA: The model provider's API key, reused downstream
optionB: A token exchanged for the user, scoped to that service
optionC: The user's original token, passed straight through
optionD: A super-user key held by the tool gateway itself
correctAnswerText: A token exchanged for the user, scoped to that service
explanation: An on-behalf-of or token-exchange flow gives a token scoped to the user and the service, so the downstream system enforces the user's own permissions. Passthrough and super-user keys over-grant.

prompt: A review of a support bot finds three issues. Which do you fix first?
optionA: A guard refusing some real questions at times
optionB: Cross-tenant retrieval of customers' data
optionC: An inconsistent tone in Hinglish answers
optionD: Harmless business rules in the system prompt
correctAnswerText: Cross-tenant retrieval of customers' data
explanation: Rank by likelihood times impact. Another customer's data leaking is the highest impact; a prompt whose leak only embarrasses and some over-blocking come after.

prompt: Developers install packages that a coding assistant suggests. Which policy would you set?
optionA: Install the newest release without pinning a hash
optionB: Verify it exists, is the intended one and is maintained
optionC: Install it into the global Python environment only
optionD: Install it, as assistants only suggest real packages
correctAnswerText: Verify it exists, is the intended one and is maintained
explanation: Assistants sometimes invent package names that others then register. Check the package is real, intended and maintained, then pin it with hashes and scan it.

prompt: In a security test plan for your own AI assistant, what is actually being certified?
optionA: That each control holds when the model misbehaves
optionB: That the prompt was reviewed by the legal team
optionC: That the model never produces a harmful reply
optionD: That the provider has passed its own yearly audit
correctAnswerText: That each control holds when the model misbehaves
explanation: The model will sometimes do the wrong thing; the design assumes it. What you certify is that the retrieval filter, gateway, approvals and output checks hold when it does.

prompt: What is a canary marker in defence testing?
optionA: A real API key put in the prompt to detect its theft
optionB: A user account that receives each new release first
optionC: A harmless planted string whose appearance shows a leak
optionD: A log line printed when the regression suite starts
correctAnswerText: A harmless planted string whose appearance shows a leak
explanation: A meaningless marker such as CANARY-7731 sits where a secret would be. If it ever appears in output, a control failed, and nothing real leaked.

prompt: Which three fixture sets does an AI security test plan name?
optionA: Easy, medium and hard prompt sets
optionB: Production, staging and demo sets
optionC: Training, validation and test sets
optionD: Hostile, benign and held-out sets
correctAnswerText: Hostile, benign and held-out sets
explanation: Hostile fixtures test the controls, benign ones measure over-blocking, and a held-out hostile set, unseen by fixers, catches fixes tuned to the known fixtures.

prompt: For a deterministic control such as a retrieval permission filter, what is the pass criterion?
optionA: Zero failures across the whole fixture set
optionB: A block rate whose lower bound clears 85%
optionC: Fewer failures than the previous release had
optionD: At most one failure per hundred fixtures run
correctAnswerText: Zero failures across the whole fixture set
explanation: A control that does not depend on the model either works or has a bug. Its criterion is absolute; rates with intervals are for probabilistic layers like a guard classifier.

prompt: Which interval should be used for a block rate measured on a small sample?
optionA: A two-sided t-interval
optionB: The Wilson score interval
optionC: The textbook Wald interval
optionD: The interquartile range
correctAnswerText: The Wilson score interval
explanation: The Wald interval breaks near 0% and 100%, exactly where security rates live, even collapsing to zero width. Wilson stays honest at the extremes.

prompt: After zero failures in n trials, what does the "rule of three" give you?
optionA: The number of repeats needed for each fixture
optionB: An approximate 95% upper bound on the rate of 3/n
optionC: The minimum number of reviewers for a High
optionD: The share of fixtures to hold out from fixers
correctAnswerText: An approximate 95% upper bound on the rate of 3/n
explanation: Zero failures do not mean a zero rate. With none in n trials, the 95% upper bound is about 3/n, so 59 clean trials support "below 5%".

prompt: In garak, which component scores the target's responses?
optionA: Orchestrators
optionB: Generators
optionC: Detectors
optionD: Probes
correctAnswerText: Detectors
explanation: Generators connect to the target, probes send test inputs grouped in families, and detectors score the responses. Orchestrators belong to PyRIT.

prompt: What is the over-blocking rate of a guard?
optionA: The share of findings later found to be invalid
optionB: The share of benign questions it wrongly blocks
optionC: The share of hostile fixtures it lets through
optionD: The share of CI runs that fail without changes
correctAnswerText: The share of benign questions it wrongly blocks
explanation: Over-blocking is the cost side, measured on real anonymised questions. A guard that blocks everything has a perfect block rate and an unusable product.

prompt: Where should hostile test fixtures be run?
optionA: Against production, so real conditions are measured
optionB: Against any public chatbot that resembles yours
optionC: Against your own staging deployment, as authorised
optionD: Against a shared test endpoint run by the provider
correctAnswerText: Against your own staging deployment, as authorised
explanation: Testing is scoped and authorised in writing: your own system, a staging tenant with synthetic data, named dates. Never production customers, never systems you do not own.

prompt: In a defence regression suite, what is a positive control?
optionA: A test that the model is reachable before the suite
optionB: A test that a legitimate approved action still works
optionC: A test that the canary marker is spelled correctly
optionD: A test that each hostile fixture is in the repository
correctAnswerText: A test that a legitimate approved action still works
explanation: It fails if someone "fixes" a defence by refusing everything. A defence that breaks the product will be switched off by the product team.

prompt: Why do defence tests script a fake model to misbehave rather than send fixtures to the live model?
optionA: The live model always refuses fixtures during tests
optionB: It proves the control on every run, fast and repeatably
optionC: A scripted model is more accurate than the real one
optionD: The live model is not allowed to see any test fixtures
correctAnswerText: It proves the control on every run, fast and repeatably
explanation: A live model may simply not misbehave this time, so the test is flaky and slow. Scripting the misbehaviour makes the test prove the control every time in milliseconds.

prompt: Why does the hostile fixture text stay in a restricted set, with code and tickets citing only ids?
optionA: Ticket systems cannot hold text longer than ids
optionB: Ids are needed for the Wilson formula to work
optionC: It is hazardous material that should not spread
optionD: Fixture text changes every time the suite runs
correctAnswerText: It is hazardous material that should not spread
explanation: Hostile inputs are access-controlled like any sensitive artefact. An id and a category are enough for code, reports and tickets to be precise.

prompt: Why plant a different canary marker in the system prompt, a staff document and another tenant's chunk?
optionA: One marker would be too easy to guess
optionB: A hit then shows which boundary failed
optionC: Markers expire after one use in a suite
optionD: Each control can read only its own marker
correctAnswerText: A hit then shows which boundary failed
explanation: Distinct markers turn "something leaked" into "this boundary failed", which tells you which control to fix.

prompt: Why does a report quote the lower bound of a guard's block rate rather than the point estimate?
optionA: Point estimates are biased upwards in all tests
optionB: It is the rate the sample can actually defend
optionC: The lower bound is always 5 points below it
optionD: Auditors may not read point estimates at all
correctAnswerText: It is the rate the sample can actually defend
explanation: 19 of 20 blocked is consistent with a true rate as low as 76%. The lower bound for block rates, and the upper bound for failure rates, are what the data supports.

prompt: Why are 60 fixtures each repeated 5 times not 300 independent trials?
optionA: Only the first repeat of each fixture is ever scored
optionB: Repeats of one fixture are correlated with each other
optionC: Temperature resets after each fixture is repeated
optionD: The provider caches replies, so repeats are skipped
correctAnswerText: Repeats of one fixture are correlated with each other
explanation: Repeats of the same fixture tend to fail together. Report the pooled rate and per-fixture results, and do not stretch repeats of a few fixtures into a claim about a category.

prompt: Why is over-blocking measured in the same job, build and settings as the block rate?
optionA: A guard that blocks everything scores 100% on block rate
optionB: Benign questions are needed to compute Wilson bounds
optionC: Over-blocking can be measured only in production
optionD: The CI system requires two metrics for each job
correctAnswerText: A guard that blocks everything scores 100% on block rate
explanation: Block rate alone rewards refusing everything. Measuring both on the same build shows the trade-off the owner must accept.

prompt: Why must a regression test first assert that the scripted misbehaviour really happened?
optionA: The control will not run without that assertion
optionB: A mistyped fixture id would otherwise pass vacuously
optionC: Pytest skips tests that lack it by default
optionD: The assertion makes the scripted model run faster
correctAnswerText: A mistyped fixture id would otherwise pass vacuously
explanation: If the fixture id has no script entry, the fake model replies benignly and "no leak" is true without any control acting. Asserting the precondition makes that a red test.

prompt: Why keep a held-out hostile set that the engineers fixing findings never see?
optionA: To train the guard classifier on fresh examples
optionB: To catch fixes tuned only to the known fixtures
optionC: To cut the token cost of each nightly test run
optionD: To give auditors a set they can publish openly
correctAnswerText: To catch fixes tuned only to the known fixtures
explanation: A patch can make the known fixtures pass without fixing the weakness. Fixtures of the same category that the fixer never saw show whether the fix generalises.

prompt: An approval bypass reproduces in 2% of runs at a bank. Why is that rate not its severity?
optionA: At bank volume, 2% means many customers each day
optionB: Rates vary, so severity is judged from one run
optionC: Rates under 5% are always treated as Low findings
optionD: Severity is assigned by the model provider instead
correctAnswerText: At bank volume, 2% means many customers each day
explanation: Severity comes from impact and reach. Rate tells you how urgent measurement is; a wrong-transaction action is High whether it happens 2% or 60% of the time.

prompt: Why does a scanner sweep reporting zero hits not show the system is secure?
optionA: Scanners report zero hits for almost any target
optionB: It covers only the probes run, at those settings
optionC: Hits stay hidden until a licence is purchased
optionD: Zero hits means the detectors failed to load
correctAnswerText: It covers only the probes run, at those settings
explanation: "0 hits" is a statement about those probes, detectors, settings and that build on that day. It says nothing about categories or controls the sweep did not exercise.

prompt: Which row is a checkable claim for the tool gateway in a test plan?
optionA: The gateway blocks most hostile requests seen
optionB: Customer id from the session only; 0 calls run
optionC: The gateway is secure and was reviewed closely
optionD: The model rarely asks for others' customer data
correctAnswerText: Customer id from the session only; 0 calls run
explanation: A claim names the property, how it is verified and an absolute pass criterion. "Secure" and "most" cannot be checked or failed.

prompt: You want to claim a failure rate below 5% with zero failures observed. About how many trials do you need?
explanation: With zero failures, the 95% upper bound falls below 5% at about 59 trials. 29 supports "below 10%" and 299 "below 1%".

prompt: To know an over-blocking rate near 5% within ±3 points at 95% confidence, about how many benign trials are needed?
optionA: About 20
optionB: About 200
optionC: About 1,800
optionD: About 60
correctAnswerText: About 200
explanation: n ≈ 1.96² × p(1−p) / margin² gives about 203 at p = 0.05 and ±0.03. About 1,800 would be needed for ±1 point.

prompt: A promptfoo test must fail if CANARY-7731 appears in any capitalisation. Which assertion fits?
optionA: is-json on the whole of the reply
optionB: llm-rubric asking about secrets
optionC: a regex anchored at reply start
optionD: not-icontains with the marker
correctAnswerText: not-icontains with the marker
explanation: The marker is a fixed string, so a case-insensitive substring check is exact and deterministic. A model-graded rubric adds noise and an anchored regex misses mid-reply markers.

prompt: You are setting up the environment for live-model defence testing. What do you build?
optionA: A developer laptop holding the production API keys
optionB: A staging tenant with synthetic customers and own keys
optionC: A copy of production data so the tests look realistic
optionD: Production itself, used during quiet night-time hours
correctAnswerText: A staging tenant with synthetic customers and own keys
explanation: Testing never touches production customers or real data. A staging tenant with synthetic data and separate keys and quotas keeps the testing safe and repeatable.

prompt: A new finding has just been confirmed. In what order should the work happen?
optionA: Add the fixture wording to a keyword list
optionB: Reword the prompt and close it the same day
optionC: Merge the fix, then add a test if time allows
optionD: Add a fixture and failing test, then merge the fix
correctAnswerText: Add a fixture and failing test, then merge the fix
explanation: A test added first is seen to fail on the old code and pass on the new, which proves both the fix and the test. Prompt rewording and keyword lists are patches.

prompt: Where in the pipeline would you schedule a broad scanner sweep of your staging assistant?
optionA: Once at launch, and never repeated after
optionB: Before each release, feeding human triage
optionC: On every pull request, failing on any hit
optionD: In production, against live customer chats
correctAnswerText: Before each release, feeding human triage
explanation: A broad sweep is slow and its detectors flag context-dependent things, so it informs triage before release. Testing belongs in staging, and every model or prompt change re-runs it.

prompt: What should the record of a probabilistic finding contain?
optionA: A screenshot of the one reply along with the hostile text
optionB: Fixture id, build, prompt hash, settings, k of n, trace ids
optionC: The tester's own account of what seemed to have happened
optionD: The full hostile input pasted into the ticket for clarity
correctAnswerText: Fixture id, build, prompt hash, settings, k of n, trace ids
explanation: "It happened once" is not reproducible. Ids, versions, settings, counts and trace ids make it reproducible, and the hostile text stays in the restricted set.

prompt: A CI gate decides whether a guard ships. Which numbers should it compare with the plan's thresholds?
optionA: Block point estimate and over-blocking estimate
optionB: Block lower bound and over-blocking upper bound
optionC: Block upper bound and over-blocking lower bound
optionD: The total trial count and the fixture count only
correctAnswerText: Block lower bound and over-blocking upper bound
explanation: The gate applies criteria to the bounds the sample can defend: the lowest plausible block rate and the highest plausible over-blocking rate, plus a minimum-trials check.

prompt: Which change should re-open the security test plan for an AI assistant?
optionA: A rename of the repository on the Git host
optionB: A new model setting, prompt, tool or data source
optionC: A change of colour scheme in the chat widget
optionD: A new engineer joining the assistant team
correctAnswerText: A new model setting, prompt, tool or data source
explanation: AI systems change behaviour without a code change. A new model or setting, prompt, tool, data source or tenant type are the retest triggers the plan names.

prompt: A deliberate one-line weakening of the gateway leaves the whole defence suite green. What does that show?
optionA: Mutation testing always passes on a first attempt
optionB: The CI cache served results from an earlier run
optionC: No test exercises that control; it is decoration
optionD: The weakening was too small to matter in practice
correctAnswerText: No test exercises that control; it is decoration
explanation: A suite that stays green when a control is weakened is not testing it. Proving the suite can fail is part of adding every test.

prompt: A nightly trace shows the canary marker in lower case got past the output check, though its test is green. Why?
optionA: The marker leaked from a different location
optionB: The model is hiding the marker on purpose
optionC: The check is case-sensitive and tested in one case
optionD: Lower-case text is never shown to the user
correctAnswerText: The check is case-sensitive and tested in one case
explanation: The control was tested only against the form the author wrote. Normalise before comparing and test the marker in several case variants.

prompt: After a metadata key was renamed in the query only, the cross-tenant test stays green while users find nothing. Why?
optionA: The filter matched nothing, so no hit was checked
optionB: The renamed key matched only one tenant's chunks
optionC: The store ignored the key and used the old one
optionD: The test was skipped after the store warned
correctAnswerText: The filter matched nothing, so no hit was checked
explanation: A loop over zero hits asserts nothing. Assert that hits exist, require a minimum number checked, and add a positive case that each user gets their own chunk.

prompt: The gate script prints "GATE FAIL" yet the CI step stays green. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The threshold sat too close to the rate
optionB: The message went to stdout, not to stderr
optionC: Its return value never became the exit code
optionD: The gate ran before the results were ready
correctAnswerText: Its return value never became the exit code
explanation: CI reads the exit status. Pass main's result to sys.exit, use pipefail in shell steps, and test the gate with a regressed results file.

prompt: A report says "block rate 100% (95% CI 100–100%), 20 trials", and next week's run shows misses. What went wrong?
optionA: A Wald interval, which collapses at 100%, was used
optionB: The interval was computed on the benign set
optionC: The guard degraded between the two weekly runs
optionD: Twenty trials suffice, so the second run is faulty
correctAnswerText: A Wald interval, which collapses at 100%, was used
explanation: Wald gives zero width at 0% and 100%. Wilson for 20/20 gives a lower bound near 84%, so misses next week were entirely consistent with the data.

prompt: A customer approved a dispute on T1, and the trace shows it executed for T2 while the approval test passes. What is the flaw?
optionA: Approval is bound to the tool name, not its arguments
optionB: The model chose T2 because the fixture was ambiguous
optionC: The approval token expired before the call ran
optionD: The customer approved both transactions by mistake
correctAnswerText: Approval is bound to the tool name, not its arguments
explanation: Name-only approval behaves like exact approval when the arguments match, which is all the test checked. Bind approval to a hash of tool and arguments, and test a mismatch.

prompt: A fix moved a category from 89/100 to 95/100 blocked, and the team announces an improvement. What is the problem?
optionA: The intervals overlap, so it may be only noise
optionB: The fix made things worse by adding variance
optionC: Both runs are void unless n is a thousand
optionD: Nothing, as 95 is above the plan's threshold
correctAnswerText: The intervals overlap, so it may be only noise
explanation: 89/100 and 95/100 have overlapping Wilson intervals. Run more trials or use a two-proportion test before claiming the change, keeping settings like for like.

prompt: A guard's block rate was measured at temperature 0, but production runs at 0.7. How do you judge the result?
optionA: Temperature never affects guards, so it carries
optionB: It holds as long as the prompt is unchanged
optionC: Lower temperature always gives a lower rate
optionD: It may not hold at release settings; re-measure
correctAnswerText: It may not hold at release settings; re-measure
explanation: Rates must be measured at the release settings — model, prompt and temperature. A rate at temperature 0 says little about behaviour at 0.7.

prompt: Pooled block rate passes at 92.7%, but one category is 89% (CI 81–94%). What does the analysis point to?
optionA: Nothing, since the pooled rate passed the gate
optionB: Dropping that category as an outlier from the set
optionC: A deterministic control behind that category
optionD: Raising temperature until that category improves
correctAnswerText: A deterministic control behind that category
explanation: The pooled number hides the weak category. The next control for it is permission and approval, which removes impact, rather than hoping the guard improves.

prompt: A measurement report shows a block rate of 140%. What is the most likely error?
optionA: Pooled repeats were divided by fixtures, not runs
optionB: Some benign questions were blocked twice
optionC: Hits were counted again in the HTML report
optionD: Wilson adds a correction that can exceed one
correctAnswerText: Pooled repeats were divided by fixtures, not runs
explanation: Dividing pooled repeats by the number of fixtures rather than runs gives impossible rates. Sanity-check that k ≤ n before any interval is computed.

prompt: A gateway weakness lets a dispute be raised on the wrong transaction in 2% of runs. Which severity would you assign?
optionA: Medium, since probabilistic issues are capped there
optionB: Informational, until it reproduces on every single run
optionC: High, since impact decides and 2% at volume is many
optionD: Low, since it reproduces in only two runs in a hundred
correctAnswerText: High, since impact decides and 2% at volume is many
explanation: An unapproved money action for a customer is High on impact. The low rate affects how you measure it, not whether it matters at a bank's volume.

prompt: Another customer's note appeared in a reply. Which fix would you accept?
optionA: Add the fixture's wording to the guard's block list
optionB: Lower the guard's threshold until that fixture is caught
optionC: Filter retrieval from the session; test every user and chunk
optionD: Add "never mention other customers" to the system prompt
correctAnswerText: Filter retrieval from the session; test every user and chunk
explanation: Ask which control should have stopped it. The retrieval filter, tested across every user and chunk, removes the cause; prompts and block lists are patches that overfit.

prompt: What evidence would you require before closing a High finding?
optionA: The original tester can no longer reproduce the issue
optionB: The pull request containing the fix has been merged
optionC: The model provider confirms that the issue is fixed
optionD: Old fails, new passes, held-out and benign sets clean
correctAnswerText: Old fails, new passes, held-out and benign sets clean
explanation: A finding closes on evidence: the regression test flips, held-out fixtures pass, no new over-blocking appears, and someone other than the fixer reviews it.

prompt: Should every hit from a generic scanner sweep automatically fail the build?
optionA: No: scanner results are best simply ignored
optionB: No: generic detectors feed human triage first
optionC: Yes: any hit proves an exploitable flaw exists
optionD: Yes: it is the only way findings get noticed
correctAnswerText: No: generic detectors feed human triage first
explanation: Detectors are heuristics that flag many things fine in context. A human decides which hits are findings, which then become fixtures in the deterministic suite.

prompt: A guard's block lower bound is 89% (plan minimum 85%), but its over-blocking upper bound is 12% (plan maximum 8%). Your call?
optionA: Fail the gate, as over-blocking breaches the plan
optionB: Ship it, as block rate is what security cares about
optionC: Fail it, but only because 89% is below 90%
optionD: Ship it, then measure over-blocking in production
correctAnswerText: Fail the gate, as over-blocking breaches the plan
explanation: Both criteria are in the plan for a reason: refusing real customers is a product cost the owner must not absorb silently. Either bound failing fails the gate.

prompt: A fix lowered a finding's rate but did not remove its cause. How should it be recorded?
optionA: Closed, with a new finding for what remains
optionB: Closed, as the rate is now below the threshold
optionC: Kept open at a lower severity, with the numbers
optionD: Reopened only if a customer reports it again
correctAnswerText: Kept open at a lower severity, with the numbers
explanation: Partial fixes recorded as closed are how the same finding returns next quarter. Keep it open, record the retest numbers, and lower severity only as the evidence allows.

prompt: Who should review the retest of a High or Critical finding?
optionA: Someone other than the engineer who wrote the fix
optionB: Nobody, once the regression test passes in CI
optionC: The model provider's support team for that model
optionD: The engineer who wrote the fix, who knows it best
correctAnswerText: Someone other than the engineer who wrote the fix
explanation: An independent reviewer catches fixes tuned to the known fixtures and tests that cannot fail. The fixer is the person least able to see their own blind spot.

prompt: How would you present a finding to the business owner of the assistant?
optionA: Business impact, numbers with intervals, a dated fix
optionB: A live replay of the issue during a sales meeting
optionC: The hostile fixture text, so they can see the risk
optionD: Only a severity label, as owners need no detail
correctAnswerText: Business impact, numbers with intervals, a dated fix
explanation: Owners need what can happen in business terms, how sure you are, and what you recommend by when. The fixture text stays in the restricted set.

prompt: What should remain the core of assurance for a multi-tenant assistant with tools?
optionA: A scanner sweep, since it covers every category
optionB: Manual checks by the developers before release
optionC: Your scripted suite and fixtures; tools add breadth
optionD: The provider's safety evaluation of the model
correctAnswerText: Your scripted suite and fixtures; tools add breadth
explanation: Scanners cannot see cross-tenant authorisation, tool side effects, approval flows or downstream systems. Your own fixtures and scripted suite test those; tools widen coverage.

prompt: With a limited token budget for live-model runs, where would you spend the trials?
optionA: On every fixture once, then extrapolating rates
optionB: On deterministic controls, repeated many times
optionC: On the categories that passed last release only
optionD: On probabilistic layers, sized to the plan's claims
correctAnswerText: On probabilistic layers, sized to the plan's claims
explanation: Deterministic controls are proven by the scripted suite at no token cost. Live trials buy the intervals for probabilistic layers, planned in advance from the claims they must support.

prompt: Which kind of function is designed for storing user passwords?
optionA: Reversible encryption with a key kept on the same server
optionB: A slow, salted password hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt
optionC: A fast general-purpose hash such as SHA-256, applied once
optionD: Base64 encoding applied before the value is written out
correctAnswerText: A slow, salted password hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt
explanation: Password hashes such as Argon2id and bcrypt are slow and salted by design, so each guess against a stolen table is expensive. SHA-256 is built to be fast, which helps the guesser; encryption can be reversed by whoever finds the key; Base64 is not protection at all.

prompt: What does a random per-password salt achieve in a table of stored password hashes?
optionA: Equal passwords produce different stored values
optionB: The salt keeps each hash secret from the database
optionC: The stored hash can be decrypted by an admin later
optionD: The password is shortened to a fixed, safe length
correctAnswerText: Equal passwords produce different stored values
explanation: A fresh salt per hash means two users with the same password get different stored strings, so each must be attacked separately and precomputed tables are useless. Salts are not secret (they sit in the stored string) and nothing about them makes a hash reversible.

prompt: Multi-factor authentication combines factors drawn from which categories?
optionA: A user name, an email address and a mobile number on file
optionB: A password, a security question and a memorable date
optionC: Something you know, something you have, something you are
optionD: A device ID, the source IP address and the browser version
correctAnswerText: Something you know, something you have, something you are
explanation: MFA means two or more different kinds of factor: knowledge (a PIN), possession (a phone or key) and inherence (a fingerprint). A password plus a security question is two things you know, which is still one factor; identifiers and device attributes are not secrets the user proves.

prompt: Which MFA form is phishing-resistant because the browser binds the credential to the real site?
optionA: One-time codes delivered by SMS
optionB: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys
optionC: Codes from a TOTP authenticator app
optionD: Push approval prompts on a phone
correctAnswerText: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys
explanation: With FIDO2 and passkeys the credential is scoped to the origin, so a look-alike domain receives nothing usable. SMS and TOTP codes can be typed into a fake page and relayed, and push prompts can be approved by a tired user.

prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?
optionA: Authentication runs on the client; authorisation runs on the network
optionB: Authentication is for human users; authorisation is only for backend services
optionC: Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do
optionD: Authentication encrypts the request; authorisation signs the response
correctAnswerText: Authentication proves who you are; authorisation decides what you may do
explanation: Authentication establishes identity; authorisation then decides, for each action and object, whether that identity may proceed. Neither is about encryption or where code runs, and both apply to people and services alike.

prompt: Anyone holding a signed JWT can decode and read its claims. What does the signature provide?
optionA: Proof the claims were not altered after issue
optionB: A record of the token kept on the server side
optionC: A way to revoke the token before it expires
optionD: Encryption that hides the claims from readers
correctAnswerText: Proof the claims were not altered after issue
explanation: A signature lets the server detect any change to the claims; it hides nothing, which is why a JWT must not carry secrets. It creates no server-side record, so it gives no way to revoke the token early.

prompt: What does the HttpOnly attribute on a session cookie do?
optionA: Makes the cookie expire when the tab is closed
optionB: Sends the cookie only over HTTPS connections
optionC: Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie
optionD: Stops the cookie being sent on cross-site calls
correctAnswerText: Stops page JavaScript from reading the cookie
explanation: HttpOnly keeps the cookie out of document.cookie, so a script injected by an XSS flaw cannot read the credential. HTTPS-only is the Secure attribute, cross-site sending is governed by SameSite, and lifetime by Expires or Max-Age.

prompt: In role-based access control (RBAC), permissions are granted to what?
optionA: Applications, according to their vendor
optionB: Individual people, one grant at a time
optionC: Roles, which people are then assigned to
optionD: Devices, according to their network zone
correctAnswerText: Roles, which people are then assigned to
explanation: RBAC attaches permissions to roles and assigns people to roles, so thirty roles can be reviewed where three thousand individual grants cannot. Grants per person are what RBAC replaces; device zones and vendors are not the subject of the model.

prompt: Which Windows Security event ID records an account that failed to log on?
explanation: 4625 is a failed logon and carries Logon Type, Status and SubStatus. 4624 is a successful logon, 4740 an account lockout and 4672 special privileges assigned to a new logon.

prompt: What does separation of duties require in a payments workflow?
optionA: The person who raises a payment cannot approve it
optionB: Payments are processed on two separate servers
optionC: Finance staff use separate laptops for payments
optionD: Every payment is approved by the CFO alone
correctAnswerText: The person who raises a payment cannot approve it
explanation: Separation of duties splits a sensitive action so no single person can both initiate and authorise it; bank auditors test this in ERP and core-banking roles. Separate servers or laptops do nothing for it, and one approver for everything concentrates the duty instead.

prompt: Why is a deliberately slow hash preferred over SHA-256 for stored passwords?
optionA: It keeps the stored value secret without needing a salt
optionB: Each offline guess against a stolen table becomes costly
optionC: Its output is longer, which makes it harder to reverse
optionD: It lets the server decrypt passwords users have forgotten
correctAnswerText: Each offline guess against a stolen table becomes costly
explanation: Whoever steals the table guesses offline; bcrypt at cost 12 was hundreds of thousands of times slower per guess than SHA-256 in the course lab, so the same hardware tries far fewer passwords. Output length is irrelevant, nothing is decrypted, and slow hashes still use a salt.

prompt: Why is SMS OTP ranked below a FIDO2 key, even though both add a second factor?
optionA: FIDO2 keys work without the user being present at all
optionB: An SMS code can be relayed by a fake page or lost to SIM swap
optionC: SMS codes are longer, so users mistype them far more often than PINs
optionD: SMS needs a smartphone, which not every user carries
correctAnswerText: An SMS code can be relayed by a fake page or lost to SIM swap
explanation: An SMS code is a value the user can type anywhere, including into a real-time phishing page, and the number itself can be moved by a SIM swap. A FIDO2 key signs only for the genuine origin. SMS still beats a password alone; it is simply not phishing-resistant.

prompt: Why can a server-side session be revoked at once, while a stateless access token cannot?
optionA: Browsers cache tokens and so ignore any later change on the server side
optionB: Sessions are encrypted, while tokens are only Base64 encoded
optionC: Session ids are shorter, so they expire faster than tokens do
optionD: The server deletes the session row; a token has no row to delete
correctAnswerText: The server deletes the session row; a token has no row to delete
explanation: A session is looked up on every request, so deleting the record ends it on the next call. A stateless token is verified by signature alone and stays valid until exp, which is why access tokens are kept short. Encoding, id length and browser caching are not the reason.

prompt: Why pair a short-lived access token with a longer-lived, revocable refresh token?
optionA: Cheap checks on each call, plus a point where access is withdrawn
optionB: The refresh token encrypts the access token while it is in transit
optionC: The access token can then carry secrets the refresh token hides
optionD: Two tokens double the entropy an attacker would have to guess
correctAnswerText: Cheap checks on each call, plus a point where access is withdrawn
explanation: The access token is verified without a lookup and is nearly worthless if leaked because it lives minutes; the refresh token is recorded server-side, so deleting it stops further access. It does not encrypt anything, and entropy was never the problem.

prompt: Why is hiding an admin button in the interface not an authorisation control?
optionA: Screen readers announce hidden buttons to every user anyway
optionB: Hidden buttons slow the page and are removed by browsers
optionC: Hidden elements are still indexed by search engines later
optionD: The API can be called directly, so the server must check it
correctAnswerText: The API can be called directly, so the server must check it
explanation: The interface belongs to whoever holds the browser; any request it could send can be sent without it. Hiding the button is good user experience, but the decision has to be made on the server for every request.

prompt: Why are movers, staff who change team, a common source of excess access?
optionA: Movers receive a fresh account that skips every approval step
optionB: Their manager changes, so their MFA method is reset to SMS
optionC: New access is added but the old access is often never removed
optionD: Their password is reset and then kept in plain text by HR
correctAnswerText: New access is added but the old access is often never removed
explanation: A person who moves Finance to Sales to IT can end up holding all three sets of rights ("access creep") because only the additions are requested. Mover processes must remove the old role, and periodic access reviews catch what they miss.

prompt: Why does an administrator use a separate admin account that has no mailbox?
optionA: Admin accounts need longer passwords than mail accounts allow
optionB: Mail servers refuse to deliver to accounts with admin rights
optionC: Licensing rules forbid administrators from having a mailbox
optionD: A phishing link opened from email cannot then act as admin
correctAnswerText: A phishing link opened from email cannot then act as admin
explanation: Everyday work (email, browsing) is where malicious content arrives. If that account holds no admin rights, a mistake there cannot touch servers; the admin account is used only from an admin workstation. Password length, mail delivery and licensing are not the reason.

prompt: Why is an OAuth 2.0 access token, on its own, not proof of who the user is?
optionA: OAuth delegates API access; identity comes from the OIDC ID token
optionB: Access tokens expire too quickly to identify anyone reliably
optionC: An access token is issued before the user has signed in at all
optionD: OAuth works only for machine clients and never for human users at all
correctAnswerText: OAuth delegates API access; identity comes from the OIDC ID token
explanation: OAuth 2.0 answers "may this client call that API?"; OpenID Connect adds the ID token, meant for the client, that says who signed in. Using an access token as a login proof lets a token minted for another client be replayed. Lifetime and client type are not the issue.

prompt: Why do mobile and single-page apps use PKCE with the OAuth authorization code flow?
optionA: It binds the code to the app that began the flow
optionB: It lets the app hide a client secret in its code
optionC: It turns the access token into a refresh token
optionD: It removes the need to sign in at the provider
correctAnswerText: It binds the code to the app that began the flow
explanation: A public client cannot keep a secret, so PKCE has it send a hash of a one-time verifier at the start and the verifier itself when redeeming the code. An intercepted code is useless without the verifier. Users still sign in at the provider, and PKCE does not change token types.

prompt: Why does a per-account lockout threshold do little against password spraying (T1110.003)?
optionA: Spraying uses valid passwords, so no failures are ever logged
optionB: Spraying targets service accounts, which can never be locked
optionC: Lockout counters reset whenever the source IP address changes
optionD: Spraying makes a few tries per account, under each threshold
correctAnswerText: Spraying makes a few tries per account, under each threshold
explanation: Spraying spreads one or two common passwords across many accounts, so no single account reaches its limit. The defence is detection across accounts from one source (many 4625 or 4771 events, few per name), MFA and banned-password lists. Failures are logged, and counters are per account, not per IP.

prompt: Bharat Mart's legacy user table holds unsalted MD5 password hashes. What is the sound migration?
optionA: Wrap each MD5 value in Argon2id now; rehash cleanly at next login
optionB: Encrypt the MD5 column with AES and keep the key on the server
optionC: Force a reset for all users, still using MD5 for the new values
optionD: Keep MD5 but add one site-wide salt to every new password stored
correctAnswerText: Wrap each MD5 value in Argon2id now; rehash cleanly at next login
explanation: Wrapping (argon2id of the old MD5 value, with the scheme recorded) means no weak value stays at rest from today, and each user is moved to a plain Argon2id hash when they next log in. A site-wide salt and AES leave fast, recoverable values; resetting into MD5 keeps the weak scheme.

prompt: A review of a user table finds stored values beginning $2b$06$. What should the reviewer recommend?
optionA: Raise the bcrypt cost to 10 or more and rehash at next login
optionB: Drop the salt, since the cost is the only setting that matters
optionC: Switch to SHA-512, since its output is longer than bcrypt's
optionD: Nothing; the $2b$ prefix shows the setting is already safe
correctAnswerText: Raise the bcrypt cost to 10 or more and rehash at next login
explanation: The number after $2b$ is the cost (2^6 rounds here), far below the course minimum of 10. Raising it on the next successful login upgrades users without a reset. SHA-512 is fast and therefore worse; the salt is essential; the prefix names the algorithm, not its strength.

prompt: A user reports a stolen laptop. The app uses 10-minute access tokens with refresh tokens. What does "sign out everywhere" do?
optionA: Rotate the signing key, which signs out only that one user
optionB: Delete every access token for the user from the token store
optionC: Nothing until the 30-day refresh token expires by itself
optionD: Revoke all refresh tokens; access tokens lapse within minutes
correctAnswerText: Revoke all refresh tokens; access tokens lapse within minutes
explanation: Refresh tokens are recorded and can be deleted, which stops any new access token being issued; the access tokens already out stay valid for their few remaining minutes, a window the documentation should state. Access tokens have no store, and rotating the key signs out every user.

prompt: A web app keeps its access token in localStorage. Which change best limits what an XSS flaw could take?
optionA: Base64-encode the token a second time before it is saved
optionB: Keep it in a hidden form field that each page re-renders
optionC: Move it to sessionStorage, which page scripts cannot read
optionD: An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, with CSRF protection
correctAnswerText: An HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, with CSRF protection
explanation: Any script on the page can read localStorage, sessionStorage and the DOM, so one XSS anywhere takes the credential. An HttpOnly cookie is not readable by script; because it is sent automatically, SameSite and a CSRF token are added. Encoding hides nothing.

prompt: On Kirana Cloud, GET /api/invoices/{id} returns any invoice to any signed-in user. What is the fix?
optionA: Hide links to other accounts' invoices in the user interface
optionB: Swap the numeric ids for random UUIDs that cannot be guessed
optionC: Rate-limit the endpoint so ids cannot be walked through quickly
optionD: Check on the server that the invoice is in the caller's account
correctAnswerText: Check on the server that the invoice is in the caller's account
explanation: This is broken object-level authorisation: the handler checks login but not ownership. Only a server-side ownership check closes it. UUIDs and rate limits make discovery slower but any leaked id still works, and hiding links changes nothing on the server.

prompt: An access review compares an HR export with an Active Directory export. Which field should the two be joined on?
optionA: The employee ID recorded in both systems
optionB: The display name, lower-cased and trimmed
optionC: The email address as the directory has it
optionD: The department name given in each export
correctAnswerText: The employee ID recorded in both systems
explanation: Names are spelled differently between systems and repeat across people; departments are shared by many; email may be missing or reused. A stable employee ID joins the records reliably, and accounts with no employee ID (service accounts) are flagged for an owner.

prompt: HR shows Sneha exited on 28 Feb; her account is still enabled and logged on on 10 Mar. What comes first?
optionA: Disable it, revoke sessions, and investigate the 10 Mar logon
optionB: Reset her password and email the new one to her old manager
optionC: Move the account to an OU that Group Policy does not touch
optionD: Wait for the next quarterly review to record it as a finding
correctAnswerText: Disable it, revoke sessions, and investigate the 10 Mar logon
explanation: A leaver who can still authenticate is a live risk, and a logon after the last day needs explaining. Disable and revoke now, then investigate. Waiting leaves the door open, a reset password handed to anyone is still a working account, and moving OUs does not stop logons.

prompt: A reporting service account, svc_report, is in Domain Admins and last logged on a year ago. What does least privilege call for?
optionA: Find its owner and need; strip admin rights or disable it
optionB: Leave it alone, since an unused account can do no harm to anyone
optionC: Give it a mailbox so alerts about it reach someone
optionD: Rename it so that it no longer looks like an admin
correctAnswerText: Find its owner and need; strip admin rights or disable it
explanation: Every non-human account needs an owner, the narrowest rights and no interactive use. An unused, highly privileged account is an unmonitored door, not a harmless one. A mailbox or a new name changes nothing about what it can do.

prompt: Hundreds of 4625 events from 192.0.2.40 carry SubStatus 0xC0000064, each for a different user name. What do they show?
optionA: An application using a disabled account
optionB: Logons to accounts that are already locked
optionC: Guessing of passwords for one real account
optionD: Guessing of user names that do not exist
correctAnswerText: Guessing of user names that do not exist
explanation: 0xC0000064 means the user name does not exist; many of them across many names is name guessing. A wrong password for a real account is 0xC000006A, a locked account 0xC0000234 and a disabled one 0xC0000072.

prompt: Kaveri Bank needs an emergency admin account for when single sign-on is down. Which design fits?
optionA: SMS OTP sent to the CIO, with alerting switched off to cut noise
optionB: Shared by the whole IT team, with a password everyone remembers
optionC: Created only during an outage and deleted once SSO is restored
optionD: Outside SSO, long random password sealed away, alert on each use
correctAnswerText: Outside SSO, long random password sealed away, alert on each use
explanation: A break-glass account must not depend on the thing that has failed, must be hard to use casually, and must be visible every time it is used. A shared, memorised password defeats accountability; silencing alerts hides misuse; creating an account mid-outage needs the admin rights you have lost.

prompt: A user removed from the admin role keeps doing admin actions for up to an hour. The API trusts a role claim in a 60-minute JWT. Why?
optionA: The browser cached the admin pages for an hour
optionB: The role claim stays stale until the token expires
optionC: The signing key leaked and new tokens were forged
optionD: The role change was never saved to the database
correctAnswerText: The role claim stays stale until the token expires
explanation: A token carries the claims it was issued with, and the server believes them until exp. The fix is short access tokens, checking sensitive roles server-side, or revoking the refresh token on a role change. Nothing here points to a failed save, a forged token or a cache.

prompt: Two accounts in a bcrypt-protected table have exactly the same stored value. What does this suggest?
optionA: The two accounts were merged by the directory sync
optionB: Two users simply chose the same password by chance
optionC: A fixed salt, or a value copied from one row to another
optionD: The bcrypt cost factor is set too low for the salt to be applied
correctAnswerText: A fixed salt, or a value copied from one row to another
explanation: bcrypt draws a fresh salt for every hash, so even equal passwords give different strings. Identical values mean the salt was fixed or reused, or a value was copied between rows, and both are worth investigating. Cost does not switch salting off.

prompt: A gateway confirms each caller is logged in, and every service behind it then trusts any request it gets. What weakness remains?
optionA: Weak password storage at the shared identity provider service
optionB: Session fixation caused by the gateway cookie
optionC: Broken access control: per-object checks are missing
optionD: Denial of service from the gateway itself
correctAnswerText: Broken access control: per-object checks are missing
explanation: Being logged in says who the caller is, not whether they may touch this order or that record. Checking only at the door leaves every service open to any authenticated user. Password storage, fixation and availability are separate concerns the description gives no sign of.

prompt: Identity logs show 14 push MFA prompts denied, then one approved, for one user at 02:10. Which control addresses this pattern?
optionA: A longer password with more character classes
optionB: A shorter session timeout for that one user
optionC: Moving the user from push approval to SMS OTP
optionD: Number matching on push prompts, or a FIDO2 key
correctAnswerText: Number matching on push prompts, or a FIDO2 key
explanation: Repeated prompts until one is approved is MFA request generation ("MFA fatigue"); the password was already known. Number matching makes a blind tap fail and FIDO2 removes the prompt entirely. A longer password or timeout does not touch it, and SMS is weaker, not stronger.

prompt: svc_print locks out (4740) every 30 minutes since its password change, and the caller computer is always PRN01. Likeliest cause?
optionA: A task or service on PRN01 still using the old password
optionB: A spraying campaign aimed only at the printing service accounts
optionC: A help-desk analyst resetting the account by mistake
optionD: The domain controller clock drifting by half an hour
correctAnswerText: A task or service on PRN01 still using the old password
explanation: A regular cadence from one named caller right after a password change is the classic stored-credential lockout. Check the caller computer before assuming an attack. Spraying spreads across many accounts, clock drift breaks Kerberos rather than causing timed lockouts, and resets are 4724, not 4740.

prompt: After a hypervisor change, Kerberos domain logons fail at one site while every other site works. What should be checked first?
optionA: A site firewall that has started to block HTTPS traffic
optionB: Expired passwords on every account at the affected site
optionC: A change in how the domain stores password hashes
optionD: Clock skew between those hosts and the domain controllers
correctAnswerText: Clock skew between those hosts and the domain controllers
explanation: Kerberos rejects tickets when clocks differ by more than about five minutes, and virtual machines often take their time from the host. One site failing together after a hypervisor change points at time sync. Expired passwords would be spread out, and HTTPS and hash storage play no part in the ticket exchange.

prompt: An authorisation server accepts any redirect_uri that merely starts with the client's domain string. What does a design review flag?
optionA: Redirect URIs must match a registered list exactly
optionB: Redirect URIs should use HTTP so proxies can inspect them
optionC: Redirect URIs should be generated randomly for each login
optionD: Redirect URIs stop mattering once PKCE has been enabled
correctAnswerText: Redirect URIs must match a registered list exactly
explanation: Prefix matching lets a look-alike host or path receive the authorization code. Exact matching against registered URIs is the control, and PKCE complements it rather than replacing it. Plain HTTP would expose the code, and random URIs cannot be registered.

prompt: Under refresh-token rotation, a refresh token that was already exchanged is presented again. What should the server conclude?
optionA: Theft: revoke the whole token family and force sign-in
optionB: Clock skew: accept it within a 30-second tolerance
optionC: A client bug: log it at debug level and carry on
optionD: A retry: issue a fresh token in the same family again
correctAnswerText: Theft: revoke the whole token family and force sign-in
explanation: Each refresh token is single-use, so a second presentation means two parties hold it. The server cannot tell which is genuine, so it revokes the family and both must sign in again. Accepting it as a retry or skew throws away the detection that rotation exists to provide.

prompt: Quarterly access reviews approve 99.8% of grants, and reviewers see group names like GRP_FIN_0173. What is the real problem?
optionA: Reviewers cannot judge access they cannot understand
optionB: Approval rates should be near half to look credible
optionC: The review frequency is too low to find any problems
optionD: Groups must be reviewed by IT rather than by managers
correctAnswerText: Reviewers cannot judge access they cannot understand
explanation: A manager shown an opaque code approves everything, so the review becomes a signature rather than a control. Meaningful role names and descriptions make it work. More frequent rubber stamps change nothing, there is no correct approval rate, and IT does not know who needs what.

prompt: A hospital made a new RBAC role for every ward-and-shift combination and now has 900 roles. Which change addresses the cause?
optionA: Grant permissions to individuals instead of roles
optionB: Review all 900 roles monthly instead of yearly
optionC: Merge every clinical role into one broad clinical role
optionD: Express ward and shift as attributes in ABAC rules
correctAnswerText: Express ward and shift as attributes in ABAC rules
explanation: Role explosion happens when context (which ward, which shift) is baked into role names. Attribute-based rules keep a few roles and evaluate the context at request time. One broad role breaks least privilege, per-person grants are unreviewable, and more reviews of 900 roles treats the symptom.

prompt: A single server-rendered web app with one database must choose between server sessions and JWTs. Which choice is best justified?
optionA: JWTs, because stateless tokens are the modern default
optionB: Sessions: simpler, revocable, and the lookup is cheap
optionC: JWTs plus a server-side blocklist checked on logout
optionD: Sessions held in each instance's memory, no store
correctAnswerText: Sessions: simpler, revocable, and the lookup is cheap
explanation: For one app, sessions give instant revocation and fresh permissions for a cheap lookup. JWTs plus a blocklist rebuild a session with extra steps, "modern" is not a reason, and per-instance memory logs users out whenever a request reaches another server.

prompt: Udaan Logistics can buy FIDO2 keys for only 200 of its 5,000 staff. Who should get them first?
optionA: Staff who complain most often about push MFA prompts
optionB: New joiners, since they are the likeliest to be phished
optionC: Administrators and other high-risk, high-privilege users
optionD: Everyone in alphabetical order until the keys run out
correctAnswerText: Administrators and other high-risk, high-privilege users
explanation: Phishing-resistant MFA is worth most where a compromised account does the most damage: domain and cloud admins, finance approvers, executives. Everyone else keeps their current MFA with number matching. Alphabetical order and complaint volume ignore risk, and joiners are not the highest-impact accounts.

prompt: Which password policy for staff accounts is best supported by current guidance such as NIST SP 800-63B?
optionA: Twelve characters of any kind, changed every 90 days by default
optionB: Long passphrases, a breached-password check, no forced resets
optionC: Short PINs plus security questions, since users remember them
optionD: Eight characters with symbols, changed every 30 days without fail
correctAnswerText: Long passphrases, a breached-password check, no forced resets
explanation: Length and screening against known-breached passwords raise real strength; forced periodic changes push people towards predictable variations, so change is required on evidence of compromise instead. Composition rules with short lengths and security questions are weak.

prompt: An access-token lifetime is being set for a banking API that uses refresh rotation. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Minutes: a leak is brief and refresh keeps users signed in
optionB: Days: fewer refreshes mean fewer chances of theft in transit
optionC: One year: matching the API key lifetime keeps it all simple
optionD: No expiry: revocation is handled by the refresh token anyway
correctAnswerText: Minutes: a leak is brief and refresh keeps users signed in
explanation: An access token cannot be revoked, so its lifetime is the window a leak stays useful; the refresh token restores convenience and revocation. Longer lifetimes widen the window for little gain, and a token that never expires can never be taken back.

prompt: Where should the check "may this user edit this document?" live in a multi-endpoint API?
optionA: In the API gateway, matched on the request URL path pattern alone
optionB: In the React component that renders the edit button
optionC: In one server-side policy layer that every handler calls
optionD: In a nightly job that reverts any unauthorised edits
correctAnswerText: In one server-side policy layer that every handler calls
explanation: One policy function, called by every handler and tested as a matrix of roles and objects, is hard to forget and easy to audit. The client is not under your control, a path pattern cannot know who owns document 42, and reverting later means the damage was already done.

prompt: An SRE team holds permanent production admin rights. Which change gives the biggest risk reduction for the effort?
optionA: Just-in-time elevation tied to a ticket, with session logging
optionB: A longer password on each of the standing admin accounts
optionC: Moving the rights to one shared account the team all uses
optionD: A quarterly reminder email about the acceptable use of admin rights
correctAnswerText: Just-in-time elevation tied to a ticket, with session logging
explanation: Standing privilege is exposure every hour of every day; granting it per ticket for a window shrinks that exposure and leaves a record of who did what. Longer passwords and reminders leave the standing rights in place, and a shared account destroys accountability.

prompt: Recent account takeovers all began with a help-desk MFA reset for a caller. Which control is most effective?
optionA: Verify identity out of band before any reset; alert the user
optionB: Log every reset and have a manager review the log at month end
optionC: Allow resets only in office hours to limit the exposure
optionD: Ask callers for their employee ID and their date of birth
correctAnswerText: Verify identity out of band before any reset; alert the user
explanation: MFA is only as strong as the process that replaces it. A call-back to a known number or the manager, plus a notice to the real user, stops a caller who is not who they claim. Employee IDs and birthdays are easy to find, office hours do not verify anyone, and a monthly review is too late.

prompt: A reviewer must accept one proposed set of OIDC ID-token checks for a web client. Which set should be accepted?
optionA: Signature, issuer, audience, expiry and nonce
optionB: Issuer only, since the token arrived over HTTPS
optionC: Expiry and the email claim, which names the user
optionD: Signature only, since it proves the provider sent it
correctAnswerText: Signature, issuer, audience, expiry and nonce
explanation: The signature proves origin, issuer and audience prove the token was minted by your provider for your client, expiry bounds its life, and the nonce ties it to this login. Dropping audience lets a token issued to another app be replayed; email alone is not a stable identifier.

prompt: Which identity alert gives a SOC the best signal for the analyst time it costs?
optionA: Every password change a user makes through self-service
optionB: Every failed logon anywhere in the domain, one alert each
optionC: Every successful logon made outside 9-to-5 office hours
optionD: A leaver account authenticating after its last working day
correctAnswerText: A leaver account authenticating after its last working day
explanation: A leaver should never authenticate, so the alert is rare and almost always worth a look. Single failed logons, out-of-hours logons and self-service changes are routine and would bury analysts; they become useful only as parts of a pattern.

prompt: A partner integration needs long-lived machine access to an API. Which credential design is best?
optionA: One master key shared by all partners and rotated each year
optionB: A staff member's password saved in the partner's config file
optionC: An unscoped key that never expires, kept in a private repo
optionD: A scoped key, shown once, rotatable, with last use recorded
correctAnswerText: A scoped key, shown once, rotatable, with last use recorded
explanation: Long-lived keys are the most dangerous credentials an API issues, so each gets the narrowest scope, can be rotated without an outage, is shown only once, and records last use so idle keys can be removed. A shared key cannot be revoked for one partner, and a person's password ties a machine to a human.

prompt: In an AWS VPC, what makes a subnet a "public" subnet?
optionA: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway
optionB: Its Name tag contains the word "public" or "dmz"
optionC: It sits in a different Availability Zone from the database
optionD: Every instance in it has a security group allowing 443
correctAnswerText: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway
explanation: A subnet is public only because of its route: a default route to an internet gateway. Tags are labels with no effect, security groups filter traffic but do not create a path, and Availability Zones are about resilience, not exposure.

prompt: What does a NAT gateway let instances in a private subnet do?
optionA: Encrypt the traffic that flows between subnets of one VPC
optionB: Start outbound connections without being reachable inbound
optionC: Resolve the private DNS names of instances in other VPCs
optionD: Accept inbound connections from the internet on chosen ports
correctAnswerText: Start outbound connections without being reachable inbound
explanation: A NAT gateway translates outbound connections (for patches, APIs) so private instances can reach out while nothing on the internet can open a connection to them. It does not publish inbound ports, resolve DNS or encrypt traffic.

prompt: Which description fits an AWS security group?
optionA: Stateless allow-only rules attached to an internet gateway
optionB: Stateless, numbered allow and deny rules attached to a subnet
optionC: Stateful allow and deny rules attached to a route table
optionD: Stateful, allow-only rules attached to a network interface
correctAnswerText: Stateful, allow-only rules attached to a network interface
explanation: Security groups attach to network interfaces (instances, load balancers, databases), track connections so replies are allowed, and have no deny rule. Numbered allow/deny rules on a subnet describe a network ACL; route tables and gateways carry no filter rules.

prompt: How are the rules of an AWS network ACL evaluated?
optionA: Highest rule number first; the last matching rule decides
optionB: All rules are read and any matching deny always wins
optionC: Lowest rule number first; the first matching rule decides
optionD: In alphabetical order of each rule's description text
correctAnswerText: Lowest rule number first; the first matching rule decides
explanation: NACL rules are processed in ascending number order and evaluation stops at the first match, which is why a deny for a bad range must be numbered below the allow it should override. "Any deny wins" describes IAM policy evaluation, not NACLs.

prompt: Which two AWS services are reached through a VPC gateway endpoint rather than an interface endpoint?
optionA: Amazon EC2 and Lambda
optionB: Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon SNS
optionC: Amazon S3 and DynamoDB
optionD: AWS KMS and AWS STS
correctAnswerText: Amazon S3 and DynamoDB
explanation: Gateway endpoints are route-table entries and exist only for S3 and DynamoDB. KMS, STS, CloudWatch, SNS and most other APIs use interface endpoints (PrivateLink), which place a network interface with a private IP in your subnet.

prompt: What does a VPC Flow Log record contain?
optionA: The hostname each instance looked up before connecting
optionB: Addresses, ports, protocol, bytes and ACCEPT or REJECT per flow
optionC: Every API call made to change the VPC's configuration
optionD: The full packet payload of every connection in the VPC
correctAnswerText: Addresses, ports, protocol, bytes and ACCEPT or REJECT per flow
explanation: Flow logs are metadata: source and destination address and port, protocol, packets, bytes, time window and whether the filters accepted or rejected it. Payloads are never captured, DNS names come from resolver query logs, and API changes are in CloudTrail.

prompt: Which Route 53 feature makes a set of DNS names resolvable only from inside chosen VPCs?
optionA: A private hosted zone associated with those VPCs
optionB: A public hosted zone with DNSSEC signing turned on
optionC: An alias record that points at a load balancer
optionD: A health check combined with failover routing
correctAnswerText: A private hosted zone associated with those VPCs
explanation: A private hosted zone answers only for queries from the VPCs it is associated with, so internal names never appear on the public internet. DNSSEC signs public answers, health checks drive failover, and alias records are a record type, not a visibility scope.

prompt: What is the closest Azure equivalent of an AWS security group?
optionA: An Azure Policy assignment
optionB: A Key Vault access policy
optionC: A network security group (NSG)
optionD: An Application Gateway listener
correctAnswerText: A network security group (NSG)
explanation: An Azure NSG filters traffic to subnets or network interfaces, the job a security group does in AWS; unlike a security group it has explicit deny rules and priorities. Azure Policy governs resource settings, a listener receives traffic and Key Vault guards secrets.

prompt: Which AWS load balancer works at layer 7 and routes requests by HTTP path and host header?
optionA: Gateway Load Balancer
optionB: NAT gateway in a public subnet
optionC: Network Load Balancer
optionD: Application Load Balancer
correctAnswerText: Application Load Balancer
explanation: The ALB understands HTTP(S), so it can route /api and /reports to different target groups and pairs with AWS WAF. The NLB forwards TCP/UDP at layer 4, the Gateway Load Balancer steers traffic through appliances, and a NAT gateway is not a load balancer.

prompt: Which statement about AWS VPC peering is true?
optionA: It works only when the two VPCs use overlapping CIDR ranges
optionB: It is transitive, so peering one hub VPC joins every spoke
optionC: Its traffic is routed out through each of the VPCs' internet gateways
optionD: It is not transitive: A-B and B-C peering does not join A and C
correctAnswerText: It is not transitive: A-B and B-C peering does not join A and C
explanation: A peering connection links exactly two VPCs, and traffic cannot hop through a third; that is what a transit gateway is for. Peered VPCs must NOT overlap, and peering traffic stays on the AWS network rather than going via internet gateways.

prompt: A security group allows inbound 443 and has no outbound rule for client ports. Why do the HTTPS replies still get out?
optionA: Outbound traffic is always fully open and cannot be limited
optionB: The subnet's network ACL forwards replies on its behalf
optionC: The group tracks the connection and allows its replies
optionD: Replies travel over ICMP, which groups never filter
correctAnswerText: The group tracks the connection and allows its replies
explanation: Security groups are stateful: once a connection is allowed in, its return traffic is allowed out automatically. Outbound rules can be restricted, the NACL is a separate stateless check rather than a forwarder, and HTTPS replies are TCP, not ICMP.

prompt: Why does a network ACL that allows inbound 443 also need an outbound rule for ports 1024–65535?
optionA: Without it the NACL silently converts every allow into a deny
optionB: It is stateless, so replies to client ephemeral ports are checked too
optionC: Outbound rules decide which TLS versions the web server may offer
optionD: The load balancer health check always arrives on a high port
correctAnswerText: It is stateless, so replies to client ephemeral ports are checked too
explanation: A NACL keeps no connection state, so the reply leaving for the client's ephemeral port is judged as new traffic and must be allowed explicitly. NACLs know nothing of TLS versions, health checks are not the reason, and allows are never converted.

prompt: Why is "allow 5432 from sg-app" a tighter database rule than "allow 5432 from the app subnet's CIDR"?
optionA: Group references also encrypt all of the traffic sent on port 5432
optionB: CIDR sources are ignored by security groups attached to RDS
optionC: Only interfaces carrying sg-app get in, whatever their address
optionD: Group references are stateless, so they are evaluated faster
correctAnswerText: Only interfaces carrying sg-app get in, whatever their address
explanation: A group reference admits exactly the members of that group, so another host dropped into the same subnet is not let in and autoscaled app servers need no rule edits. Security groups are stateful either way, CIDR sources work on RDS, and no rule encrypts anything.

prompt: A bucket policy denies every request unless aws:SourceVpce equals the VPC's endpoint ID. What does this add beyond IAM permissions?
optionA: The bucket becomes visible in the console only to the VPC owner
optionB: IAM users no longer need any permission to read the bucket
optionC: Objects are re-encrypted with a new key on every single request
optionD: A leaked credential cannot read the bucket from outside the VPC
correctAnswerText: A leaked credential cannot read the bucket from outside the VPC
explanation: IAM checks who is asking; the endpoint condition also checks where the request came from, so stolen keys used from a laptop on the internet are refused. The condition does not re-encrypt, does not replace IAM permissions and is not a console visibility switch.

prompt: Why is AWS Systems Manager Session Manager often preferred over SSH for shell access to private instances?
optionA: It replaces the need to patch instances, since the agent blocks exploits
optionB: No inbound port is opened and each session is tied to an IAM identity and logged
optionC: It gives instances a public IP only for the length of each admin session
optionD: It is faster than SSH because it skips authentication for administrators it already knows
correctAnswerText: No inbound port is opened and each session is tied to an IAM identity and logged
explanation: The SSM agent connects outbound to the service, so security groups need no port 22, and access is granted by IAM with sessions recordable to S3 or CloudWatch. It does not skip authentication, never assigns a public IP and is no substitute for patching.

prompt: An investigator asks the flow logs which URL a server requested from 198.51.100.20. Why can they not answer?
optionA: Flow logs drop any record whose destination is outside AWS
optionB: Flow logs store URLs only for plain HTTP, and this one was HTTPS
optionC: Flow logs are only kept for traffic that was REJECTED
optionD: Flow logs keep connection metadata, not the request content
correctAnswerText: Flow logs keep connection metadata, not the request content
explanation: A flow record says this address talked to that address on port 443 and moved so many bytes; it never sees the HTTP request. ACCEPT and REJECT are both logged, external destinations are recorded, and no protocol puts URLs into flow logs; proxy or application logs hold them.

prompt: Why must an exposure check look for ::/0 as well as 0.0.0.0/0 in security group rules?
optionA: ::/0 is shorthand for 0.0.0.0/0, so checking both doubles the noise
optionB: ::/0 is every IPv6 address, and VPC IPv6 is usually internet-routable
optionC: ::/0 means the rule applies only to traffic inside the same VPC
optionD: ::/0 rules stay disabled by default until an administrator turns them on
correctAnswerText: ::/0 is every IPv6 address, and VPC IPv6 is usually internet-routable
explanation: IPv6 addresses in a VPC are typically globally unique and reachable, so a ::/0 source opens the port to the whole IPv6 internet. It is not an alias for the IPv4 rule, not VPC-local and not dormant, which is why IPv4-only scripts miss real exposures.

prompt: Why is a DNS record still pointing at a deleted cloud resource (a "dangling" record) a security risk?
optionA: The record makes the remaining resources in the account run more slowly
optionB: Someone else may claim that resource name and serve content under your domain
optionC: Resolvers will cache it forever, so the domain can never be changed again
optionD: It forces every visitor's browser to downgrade from HTTPS to plain HTTP
correctAnswerText: Someone else may claim that resource name and serve content under your domain
explanation: When the bucket, app or IP behind a record is released, another customer may be able to register the same name or receive the address, and your subdomain then serves their content (subdomain takeover). It has nothing to do with speed, permanent caching or HTTPS downgrade; the fix is removing the record when the resource goes.
