optionB: Decrypt the MD5 values and re-hash all of them in one overnight job
optionC: Re-hash on each successful login, and wrap leftover MD5 values now
optionD: Keep the MD5 rows, since they will expire when users change passwords
correctAnswerText: Re-hash on each successful login, and wrap leftover MD5 values now
explanation: At a successful login you briefly hold the plaintext, so re-hash and overwrite. For accounts that do not log in, store Argon2id(md5_value) so no MD5 stays at rest; force a reset for plaintext rows. Hashes cannot be decrypted.

prompt: Which call should generate a password-reset token in Python?
optionA: hashlib.md5(user_id).hexdigest()
optionB: random.getrandbits(256)
optionC: uuid.uuid1().hex[:32]
optionD: secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
correctAnswerText: secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
explanation: The secrets module uses the operating system's secure generator. random is predictable by design, a hash of a user id is computable by anyone, and uuid1 is built from time and the machine address.

prompt: Secret scanning reports a cloud access key pushed to a public repository 40 minutes ago. What is your first action?
optionA: Ask the developer to delete the commit and force-push
optionB: Have the key deactivated at once, before anything else
optionC: Make the repository private and keep watching for use
optionD: Wait for the provider to confirm misuse before acting
correctAnswerText: Have the key deactivated at once, before anything else
explanation: Public repositories are scraped within minutes, so assume the key was copied and deactivate it first (keeping its last-used data), then scope its use in the audit log. Deleting the commit or hiding the repo does not un-leak it.

prompt: A web server config reads "ssl_protocols TLSv1 TLSv1.1 TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3". What do you recommend?
optionA: Remove TLSv1 and TLSv1.1, keeping 1.2 and 1.3
optionB: Keep only TLSv1, since it is the most compatible
optionC: Remove TLSv1.3, since it hides the certificate
optionD: Keep all four, so the oldest clients still work
correctAnswerText: Remove TLSv1 and TLSv1.1, keeping 1.2 and 1.3
explanation: TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are formally deprecated; accept TLS 1.2 with ECDHE and AEAD suites, and 1.3. Keeping old versions "for old clients" is one of the course's listed findings.

prompt: A company publishes installers with an MD5 file on the same page. Which change gives customers authenticity?
optionA: Sign releases and publish the public key through a separate channel
optionB: Replace the MD5 file with a SHA-512 file on the same download page
optionC: Encrypt the installers with AES so only paying users can open them
optionD: Compress the installers into an archive protected by a passphrase
correctAnswerText: Sign releases and publish the public key through a separate channel
explanation: A signature (Ed25519 or RSA-PSS) proves who produced the file, provided the public key reaches users separately — in the previous installer, documentation or a package manager. A longer hash on the same page fixes nothing.

prompt: After a refactor, every stored KYC document fails with InvalidTag, while new documents work. The refactor changed the associated data from record ID to file name. What is the diagnosis?
optionA: The library caught an error and returned partially decrypted data
optionB: GCM authenticates the associated data, so old ciphertexts now fail
optionC: The nonce length changed, so old documents can no longer be parsed
optionD: The key was rotated by the refactor, so old documents use a lost key
correctAnswerText: GCM authenticates the associated data, so old ciphertexts now fail
explanation: Associated data is covered by the tag, so changing it breaks every old document. Restore the record ID (or re-encrypt in a migration). Never catch InvalidTag and return data — the error is the integrity check working.

prompt: After upgrading the bcrypt library, a few users with long Hindi passphrases get "password cannot be longer than 72 bytes". Why?
optionA: The cost factor rose, so long passwords now take too long to hash
optionB: bcrypt reads 72 bytes; the new library raises instead of truncating
optionC: bcrypt rejects any character outside ASCII in the new library
optionD: The old hashes were stored in UTF-16, so every byte count doubled
correctAnswerText: bcrypt reads 72 bytes; the new library raises instead of truncating
explanation: bcrypt uses only the first 72 bytes; the old library silently truncated and the new one raises ValueError. Devanagari characters take 3 bytes in UTF-8, so passphrases hit the limit sooner. Argon2id has no such limit.

prompt: A Python script calling an internal portal fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate". The portal's chain is complete and issued by the company's private CA. What is the cause?
optionA: The script does not trust the private CA; point it at that CA bundle
optionB: The portal hostname is missing from the SANs of its certificate
optionC: The script needs verify=False, as internal sites cannot be verified
optionD: The portal certificate expired, which openssl reports in this way
correctAnswerText: The script does not trust the private CA; point it at that CA bundle
explanation: The chain did not reach a root the client trusts: the client was never told to trust the private CA. Point it at the CA bundle. Expiry and name mismatch give different errors, and verify=False removes authentication.

prompt: A new alias www.lab.internal fails with a hostname mismatch. The admin had added the name to the certificate's CN only. Why does it still fail?
optionA: The CN accepts only one name, so the original name was removed
optionB: Aliases need a wildcard certificate, whatever the SANs contain
optionC: The server must restart twice before the CN change is noticed
optionD: Clients check the SAN list, which still lacks www.lab.internal
correctAnswerText: Clients check the SAN list, which still lacks www.lab.internal
explanation: Hostname matching uses the Subject Alternative Names; a name in the CN alone does nothing. Reissue the certificate with the alias in the SAN list.

prompt: A site went down on Monday with an expired certificate, although the renewed file on disk shows a valid date. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The server was never reloaded and still serves the old one
optionB: The clocks on client machines all ran a week fast that day
optionC: The CA revoked the new certificate as soon as it was issued
optionD: The renewed file is in PEM, which servers cannot read at all
correctAnswerText: The server was never reloaded and still serves the old one
explanation: The file and the live endpoint differ. Check what the server presents (s_client with -servername, piped to x509 -enddate), make reload part of the renewal job, and monitor the live endpoint.

prompt: The team's secret scanner reports nothing on a repo where another tool finds seven secrets, including in .env. Its AWS pattern is "AKIA[0-9a-z]{16}". What is wrong?
optionA: It scans history, so current files are never checked
optionB: It skips dot-files and its key pattern uses lower case
optionC: It masks findings, so they are hidden from the report
optionD: It needs network access to validate each found key
correctAnswerText: It skips dot-files and its key pattern uses lower case
explanation: Skipping dot-files means .env is never read, and real key IDs are upper case. Scan every file except a short explicit list, and test each rule against a fixture such as AWS's documented example key.

prompt: On one laptop, s_client against your own test server shows the issuer as the laptop's antivirus product, not your lab CA. What is happening?
optionA: Your lab CA was compromised by the antivirus vendor overnight
optionB: The trust store renamed your lab CA after an antivirus update
optionC: The antivirus intercepts TLS and re-signs it with its own root
optionD: The test server is serving the antivirus certificate by mistake
correctAnswerText: The antivirus intercepts TLS and re-signs it with its own root
explanation: Web-shield features and corporate TLS inspection proxies decrypt and re-sign traffic with a root pushed to the device. When an issuer looks wrong, first ask what sits in the path.

prompt: A service builds each AES-GCM nonce from the current Unix time in whole seconds. Why is this a finding?
optionA: Nonces must be counters, and time can never be used
optionB: A time-based nonce is too long for GCM's nonce field
optionC: Two messages in the same second reuse a nonce under one key
optionD: Timestamps are public, and GCM nonces must be kept secret
correctAnswerText: Two messages in the same second reuse a nonce under one key
explanation: GCM needs a unique nonce per message per key; two encryptions within one second repeat it, leaking plaintext relationships and enabling tag forgery. Nonces need not be secret; os.urandom(12) per message is the course's recipe.

prompt: A review lists: reset tokens from a seeded random; AES-128-GCM where policy prefers 256; SHA-256 as a cache key; MD5 in an IOC lookup. Which is most severe?
optionA: The seeded reset tokens, an account takeover today
optionB: SHA-256 as a cache key, since hashes must be salted
optionC: MD5 in the IOC lookup, since MD5 has collisions
optionD: AES-128-GCM, since 128 bits is now considered broken
correctAnswerText: The seeded reset tokens, an account takeover today
explanation: Rank by what an attacker gains now: predictable reset tokens let anyone compute them. AES-128-GCM is a policy preference, SHA-256 is fine as a cache key, and MD5 is acceptable as a lookup key for known samples.

prompt: After rotating a Fernet key, the team removed the old key the same day. Older tokens now fail with InvalidToken. What went wrong?
optionA: The new key was shorter than the one it replaced
optionB: The tokens expired because rotation resets their age
optionC: The old key was removed before data was re-encrypted
optionD: Fernet cannot decrypt anything made before a rotation
correctAnswerText: The old key was removed before data was re-encrypted
explanation: Rotation means decrypt with old and new, encrypt with new only (MultiFernet), then re-encrypt with rotate() before retiring the old key. Dropping it early strands everything written under it.

prompt: A new service must store passwords; one client requires FIPS-validated algorithms. What do you recommend?
optionA: Salted SHA-512 for everyone, since it is FIPS-approved and fast
optionB: bcrypt at cost 4 everywhere, so that login stays as fast as possible
optionC: Argon2id by default; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at high iterations for FIPS
optionD: AES-256-GCM encryption, so support can recover a forgotten password
correctAnswerText: Argon2id by default; PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at high iterations for FIPS
explanation: Argon2id is first choice; PBKDF2 is acceptable where FIPS requires it, at OWASP's high iteration counts (600,000 for SHA-256). Fast hashes and encryption are not acceptable, and bcrypt below cost 10 is too weak.

prompt: Where should a cloud application get its database password from?
optionA: An environment variable baked into the container image at build
optionB: A config file in the repository, so deployments stay reproducible
optionC: A secrets manager, with access by identity and every read logged
optionD: A comment in the source, encoded with Base64 so it is not readable
correctAnswerText: A secrets manager, with access by identity and every read logged
explanation: A secrets manager grants access by workload identity, logs each read and supports rotation. Repositories and images keep secrets forever, environment variables leak into crash reports, and Base64 is not protection.

prompt: KYC documents are encrypted with AES-CBC in a bucket several teams can write to. Which fix addresses the real gap?
optionA: Base64 encoding added after encryption, so the ciphertext looks less obvious
optionB: AES-256-GCM with a random nonce, the document ID as associated data and a KMS key
optionC: AES-CBC kept, but with a 512-bit key so that the documents become stronger
optionD: SHA-512 hashes of each document stored in the same bucket beside each file
correctAnswerText: AES-256-GCM with a random nonce, the document ID as associated data and a KMS key
explanation: CBC gives confidentiality but not integrity, so writers can alter documents undetected. GCM adds integrity, the ID as associated data stops a ciphertext being moved to another record, and the key belongs in a KMS. A longer key fixes none of this.

prompt: The business needs to find applicants who share a PAN, and a developer proposes ECB so equal PANs encrypt equally. What is the better design?
optionA: AES-GCM for storage plus a keyed HMAC of the PAN as a search column
optionB: Plain SHA-256 of each PAN as the search column, with no key at all
optionC: Storing PANs unencrypted in a separate table with stricter access
optionD: ECB for the PAN column only, since one column leaks very little
correctAnswerText: AES-GCM for storage plus a keyed HMAC of the PAN as a search column
explanation: A keyed HMAC gives equal values for equal PANs without the key-less guessability of a plain hash (PANs have a small, structured space), while GCM protects the stored value. ECB leaks patterns and has no integrity.

prompt: Partner Java jobs fail because a server sends only its leaf certificate. Which fix should you recommend?
optionA: Ask partners to use a browser, since browsers already work
optionB: Configure the full chain, leaf then intermediate, on the server
optionC: Import the leaf into every partner's Java trust store manually
optionD: Turn off certificate validation in the partner's Java client
correctAnswerText: Configure the full chain, leaf then intermediate, on the server
explanation: The server should send its intermediates. Importing the leaf breaks at the next renewal, and disabling validation removes authentication altogether. Browsers work only because they cache or fetch missing intermediates.

prompt: Public certificate lifetimes are being cut in steps towards 47 days. How should an organisation respond?
optionA: Automate renewal with ACME and monitor live endpoints for expiry
optionB: Renew by hand each quarter, with a reminder in someone's diary
optionC: Use self-signed certificates on public sites to avoid renewals
optionD: Buy certificates from a CA that still issues three-year lifetimes
correctAnswerText: Automate renewal with ACME and monitor live endpoints for expiry
explanation: With short lifetimes manual renewal becomes a recurring outage, so automation (certbot or another ACME client) plus expiry and chain monitoring is mandatory. No public CA will issue long lifetimes, and self-signed certificates fail in browsers.

prompt: After a contractor leaked a long-lived cloud access key, which corrective action best prevents the next one?
optionA: Making every repository private so leaked keys stay inside the company
optionB: Rotating all long-lived keys once a year on a fixed calendar date
optionC: Short-lived credentials via SSO and roles, plus scanning in pre-commit and CI
optionD: A reminder email asking contractors to be more careful with their keys
correctAnswerText: Short-lived credentials via SSO and roles, plus scanning in pre-commit and CI
explanation: Removing long-lived keys removes the thing that leaks; gitleaks or TruffleHog in pre-commit and CI plus push protection catch the rest. Reminders change little, yearly rotation leaves months of exposure, and private repos still leak.

prompt: Your crypto review has twenty findings. How should the report present them?
optionA: Ranked by what an attacker gains today, each with the library recipe
optionB: In the order found in the code, so they are easy to cross-check
optionC: All at the same severity, so developers do not ignore any of them
optionD: Only the algorithm names, leaving developers to choose the fixes
correctAnswerText: Ranked by what an attacker gains today, each with the library recipe
explanation: A report that lists everything at one severity gets nothing fixed. Rank by exposure now (published secrets, predictable tokens first; policy preferences last) and recommend the recipe, not a parameter tweak, plus a CI check.

prompt: You collect a disk image during an incident and must later prove nothing changed. What should you record?
optionA: Its MD5 only, since most tools still display MD5 by default
optionB: Its file size and timestamp, which change if anything changes
optionC: Nothing, since the image is stored on encrypted media anyway
optionD: Its SHA-256, written in the evidence log at collection time
correctAnswerText: Its SHA-256, written in the evidence log at collection time
explanation: A SHA-256 recorded in an evidence log the attacker cannot touch proves integrity later. MD5 is fine as a lookup key but has collisions, size and timestamps can be preserved while content changes, and encryption is not an integrity record.

prompt: A team wants to encrypt millions of customer records with a cloud KMS. Which design do you recommend?
optionA: Send every record to the KMS to be encrypted byte by byte
optionB: Envelope encryption: a DEK per record, wrapped by a KMS key
optionC: One AES key for all records, kept in the application config
optionD: Hash every record, since hashing protects the customer data
correctAnswerText: Envelope encryption: a DEK per record, wrapped by a KMS key
explanation: The KMS key never leaves the KMS and wraps per-record DEKs; a stolen database holds no usable key, every unwrap is a logged call, and revoking the KEK cuts access. KMS calls per byte do not scale, and hashes cannot be decrypted for use.

prompt: In the joiner, mover, leaver lifecycle, which stage is where access creep usually builds up?
optionA: Joiner, when the first account is made
optionB: Audit, when managers sign the review
optionC: Leaver, when the account is disabled
optionD: Mover, when old access is not removed
correctAnswerText: Mover, when old access is not removed
explanation: A mover gains the new team's access; if the old team's access is not taken away, privilege piles up with every move. Joiners and leavers have their own failures, but creep is a mover problem.

prompt: What is the source of truth for who currently works at a company and in which role?
optionA: The VPN user list for the month
optionB: The Active Directory itself
optionC: The email distribution lists
optionD: The HR system of record
correctAnswerText: The HR system of record
explanation: HR knows who is employed and in what role. The directory is what IAM must keep in step with it, so it cannot be its own reference — an access review compares the directory against HR.

prompt: Which MFA form is phishing-resistant because the credential is bound to the genuine site?
optionA: Push approvals with a single tap
optionB: Six-digit codes from a TOTP app
optionC: SMS one-time passwords to a phone
optionD: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys
correctAnswerText: FIDO2 security keys and passkeys
explanation: With FIDO2 the browser binds the credential to the real origin, so a look-alike domain receives nothing usable. SMS and TOTP codes can be typed into a fake page and relayed; push can be approved by a tired user.

prompt: Number matching on push MFA is mainly a defence against which problem?
optionA: A weak password reused on another site
optionB: Repeated prompts until a user taps Approve
optionC: A stolen session cookie used after login
optionD: A SIM swap moving the phone number away
correctAnswerText: Repeated prompts until a user taps Approve
explanation: MFA request flooding (often called MFA fatigue) relies on a user approving a prompt they did not start. Typing the number shown on the real login screen means a blind tap no longer works. It does nothing for SIM swap or stolen sessions.

prompt: What does Windows LAPS give each domain-joined machine?
optionA: A certificate for logging on to Wi-Fi
optionB: A shared local admin password per OU
optionC: A copy of the Domain Admins group list
optionD: Its own random local admin password
correctAnswerText: Its own random local admin password
explanation: LAPS sets a unique, random local Administrator password on each machine and stores it in the directory, so one recovered password no longer opens every machine built from the same image.

prompt: What is a break-glass account in privileged access management?
optionA: A daily admin account shared by the server team
optionB: An emergency admin account alerted on every use
optionC: A guest account created for visiting auditors
optionD: A test account used to check backups each week
correctAnswerText: An emergency admin account alerted on every use
explanation: Break-glass accounts are one or two emergency admin identities kept for when normal access fails. They are rare by design, so every single use should raise an alert.

prompt: Which statement is an example of separation of duties?
optionA: Whoever raises a payment cannot approve it
optionB: Passwords are changed every ninety days
optionC: Each employee gets one account per system
optionD: Admins log on only from the head office
correctAnswerText: Whoever raises a payment cannot approve it
explanation: Separation of duties splits a sensitive process so that no one person can complete it alone. Bank auditors test it in payment and ERP roles; the other options are different controls.

prompt: In Active Directory, what does a domain controller do?
optionA: Pushes antivirus updates to every laptop
optionB: Holds the directory and answers every logon
optionC: Routes traffic between office subnets
optionD: Stores users' files and home folders only
correctAnswerText: Holds the directory and answers every logon
explanation: Domain controllers hold the directory database and authenticate logons, which is why whoever controls one controls the domain and why DCs are watched more closely than anything else.

prompt: In AWS, an access key ID that begins with AKIA indicates what kind of credential?
optionA: A long-term key belonging to an IAM user
optionB: A key bound to one EC2 instance profile
optionC: A key that only the root user can create
optionD: A temporary key issued by STS for a role
correctAnswerText: A long-term key belonging to an IAM user
explanation: AKIA is a long-term IAM user key that keeps working until someone deactivates it; ASIA marks temporary STS credentials, which expire on their own. That difference drives how urgent a leaked key is.

prompt: What does just-in-time elevation mean for an administrator?
optionA: Admin rights given on the first day of joining
optionB: Admin rights for one ticket and a time window
optionC: Admin rights shared through one team account
optionD: Admin rights held all year for quick response
correctAnswerText: Admin rights for one ticket and a time window
explanation: Just-in-time access grants elevation against a ticket for a limited window and then removes it, so there is no standing privilege for an attacker to borrow between changes.

prompt: Why does IAM grant permissions to roles and then roles to people, instead of granting to people directly?
optionA: Roles remove the need to ever run an access review again
optionB: Thirty roles can be reviewed; thousands of grants cannot
optionC: Roles make each user's password harder to guess online
optionD: Direct grants are not supported by any modern directory
correctAnswerText: Thirty roles can be reviewed; thousands of grants cannot
explanation: RBAC keeps access reviewable: a manager can confirm a handful of meaningful roles, while thousands of individual grants are never really checked. Reviews are still needed — roles make them possible, not unnecessary.

prompt: Why should an administrator have a separate admin account with no mailbox, used only from an admin workstation?
optionA: Mailboxes slow down logons for highly privileged accounts
optionB: A phishing link opened as the daily account cannot reach servers
optionC: Directories limit how many groups one account may belong to
optionD: Admin work is billed to a different cost centre each month
correctAnswerText: A phishing link opened as the daily account cannot reach servers
explanation: Email and browsing are where compromise usually starts. If the account that reads email holds no admin rights, a successful phish lands on an account that cannot touch servers.

prompt: Why is SMS OTP ranked below an authenticator app for MFA, though both send six-digit codes?
optionA: Authenticator apps cannot be used on a stolen phone
optionB: SMS codes are longer and so users mistype them more
optionC: Authenticator apps cannot be phished on a fake page
optionD: SMS codes follow the number, so a SIM swap moves them
correctAnswerText: SMS codes follow the number, so a SIM swap moves them
explanation: SMS delivery depends on the phone number, which a SIM swap can move to an attacker. TOTP apps avoid that, but they are still phishable in real time — the last option is the tempting wrong one.

prompt: Why does a TOTP authenticator app still not stop a real-time phishing page?
optionA: The user types a valid code into the fake page, which relays it
optionB: The app shares its secret with every site the user visits
optionC: TOTP only checks the password and ignores the second factor
optionD: TOTP codes never expire, so an old code works for days
correctAnswerText: The user types a valid code into the fake page, which relays it
explanation: A code is valid for any site it is typed into during its short window. A relay page passes it straight to the real site. Only origin-bound credentials such as FIDO2 close that gap.

prompt: When comparing an HR export with a directory export in an access review, why join on employee ID rather than name?
optionA: The directory does not store any names at all
optionB: Names cannot be read by Python from a CSV file
optionC: Employee IDs are encrypted and names are not
optionD: Names are spelled differently between the two systems
correctAnswerText: Names are spelled differently between the two systems
explanation: Initials, spellings and married names differ between HR and the directory, so a name join silently misses people. A stable employee ID matches records reliably and exposes accounts with no ID at all.

prompt: Why is a 90-day threshold, not a 7-day one, used to find stale accounts from LastLogonDate?
optionA: LastLogonDate is only written once in each calendar month
optionB: The value replicates lazily and can lag by about two weeks
optionC: Seven-day reports are blocked by the default audit policy
optionD: Accounts cannot be disabled until ninety days have passed
correctAnswerText: The value replicates lazily and can lag by about two weeks
explanation: LastLogonDate comes from lastLogonTimestamp, which is replicated only when it is older than a randomised interval of up to about two weeks. A long threshold tolerates that lag; a short one flags people who log on daily.

prompt: Why does MFA not protect an account whose session token was stolen after sign-in?
optionA: MFA turns itself off once the user has signed in once
optionB: MFA only protects accounts that use passkeys or FIDO2 keys
optionC: Session tokens are protected by the password, not by MFA
optionD: The token proves MFA already happened and is replayed as is
correctAnswerText: The token proves MFA already happened and is replayed as is
explanation: MFA is checked at sign-in. The session token issued afterwards carries that result, so whoever presents it is treated as signed in. The response is revoking sessions, not just resetting the password.

prompt: Why do cloud workloads use IAM roles instead of IAM users with stored access keys?
optionA: Roles bypass the explicit deny rules in the account policies
optionB: Roles hand out temporary credentials that expire by themselves
optionC: Roles can perform actions that IAM users are never allowed
optionD: Roles keep their access keys in the code for faster startup
correctAnswerText: Roles hand out temporary credentials that expire by themselves
explanation: A role has no long-term secret; whoever assumes it gets short-lived STS credentials. A leaked user key works until someone deactivates it, which is why long-lived keys are the most dangerous thing to leave on a laptop or in code.

prompt: In AWS policy evaluation, what happens when one policy allows an action and another explicitly denies it?
optionA: The Allow wins because it was added later
optionB: The explicit Deny wins over every Allow
optionC: The more specific policy wins the conflict
optionD: The request is allowed but logged as risky
correctAnswerText: The explicit Deny wins over every Allow
explanation: Everything starts as implicit deny, an Allow is needed to proceed, and an explicit Deny in any applicable policy always wins. Order and specificity do not change that.

prompt: Why do banks record privileged admin sessions into production systems?
optionA: Recordings stop admins from running any commands at all
optionB: Recordings replace the need for any admin password
optionC: Recordings answer the auditor's question of who did what
optionD: Recordings make the admin's network connection faster
correctAnswerText: Recordings answer the auditor's question of who did what
explanation: Regulators such as RBI expect banks to control and monitor privileged access. A recording ties actions to a named person and settles disputes after a change or an incident; it is evidence, not a preventive block.

prompt: HR shows Sneha exited on 28 February; her directory account is still enabled and logged on on 10 March. What do you do first?
optionA: Leave it enabled until her manager confirms at the next review
optionB: Reset her password and email the new one to her personal address
optionC: Disable it, revoke sessions and review the logons after her exit
optionD: Delete the account now, along with its logs, to close the finding
correctAnswerText: Disable it, revoke sessions and review the logons after her exit
explanation: A leaver's account that still authenticates is both an audit finding and a possible incident. Disable and revoke now, then find out who used it after the last day. Deleting logs destroys the evidence you need.

prompt: Arjun moved from Finance to Sales last month; he now holds both Finance-Users and Sales-Users. What is the right change?
optionA: Remove Finance-Users and keep only the Sales role access
optionB: Keep both groups since he may help Finance again someday
optionC: Disable his account until HR sends a fresh joiner form
optionD: Copy a Sales colleague's full access on top of his own
correctAnswerText: Remove Finance-Users and keep only the Sales role access
explanation: A mover gets the new role's access and loses the old. Keeping old groups "just in case" is access creep, and copying a colleague imports whatever creep they have too.

prompt: An access review finds svc_report: no employee ID, member of Domain Admins, last logon nine months ago. What is the sound next step?
optionA: Leave it alone because service accounts are not reviewed
optionB: Give it a mailbox so its owner gets the alert emails
optionC: Find an owner, then remove its admin rights or disable it
optionD: Add it to more groups so the reports keep on working
correctAnswerText: Find an owner, then remove its admin rights or disable it
explanation: Every non-human identity needs an owner and the narrowest rights. An ownerless, unused Domain Admin is an unmonitored door; confirm with an owner, then strip the privilege or disable it.

prompt: A caller tells the help desk they lost their phone and asks for their MFA to be reset right away. What should the procedure require?
optionA: Reset at once if the caller sounds like they are in a hurry
optionB: Reset at once, since the caller already knows the username
optionC: Verify the caller through an independent channel before resetting
optionD: Disable MFA for the account permanently to avoid repeat calls
correctAnswerText: Verify the caller through an independent channel before resetting
explanation: A help desk that resets MFA for anyone who asks undoes MFA entirely. Verification through a separate, trusted channel (manager call-back, in-person check) is the control.

prompt: A reports team only reads files in one bucket, but its policy allows "s3:*" on "*". What should the policy become?
optionA: Read actions on "*" so any future bucket also works
optionB: Every action on "*" with a Deny on deleting buckets
optionC: GetObject and ListBucket on that bucket's ARNs only
optionD: s3:* on that one bucket, so they keep full control
correctAnswerText: GetObject and ListBucket on that bucket's ARNs only
explanation: Least privilege names actions and resources: the reads the team needs, on the bucket they use. Narrowing only the resource or only the actions leaves the other half wide open.

prompt: A monitoring vendor needs to assume a role in your AWS account. What should the role's trust policy specify?
optionA: Your root user as principal so the vendor can use its rights
optionB: The vendor's account as principal plus an sts:ExternalId check
optionC: An IAM user in your account whose key you email to the vendor
optionD: Any AWS principal, since the role name is kept a secret
correctAnswerText: The vendor's account as principal plus an sts:ExternalId check
explanation: A third-party role should trust only the vendor's account and require the agreed external ID, which defends against the confused-deputy problem. A principal of "*" lets any AWS principal try to assume it.

prompt: A co-operative bank is choosing MFA for its twelve domain administrators. Which fits best?
optionA: FIDO2 hardware security keys for each admin
optionB: Push approval without any number matching
optionC: SMS OTP to each admin's registered mobile
optionD: TOTP codes from an app on a shared tablet
correctAnswerText: FIDO2 hardware security keys for each admin
explanation: Admins are the highest-value targets, so they get phishing-resistant FIDO2 keys. SMS is exposed to SIM swap, TOTP to relay, plain push to request flooding — and a shared device breaks accountability.

prompt: All 800 laptops share one local Administrator password because they came from one image. Which control fixes this?
optionA: Add every laptop's local admin to the Domain Admins group
optionB: Change the shared password once and tell the whole IT team
optionC: Deploy Windows LAPS to set a unique password per machine
optionD: Rename the local Administrator account on every laptop
correctAnswerText: Deploy Windows LAPS to set a unique password per machine
explanation: With one shared password, one compromised laptop opens all 800. LAPS gives each machine its own random password stored in AD; changing or renaming the shared one leaves it shared.

prompt: A contractor needs database admin rights in production for a two-hour change tonight. How should access be given?
optionA: Permanent admin rights, removed at the next quarterly review
optionB: The DBA team's shared admin password sent over chat for tonight
optionC: Time-boxed elevation against the ticket, with the session recorded
optionD: Domain Admin membership so nothing blocks the change midway
correctAnswerText: Time-boxed elevation against the ticket, with the session recorded
explanation: Just-in-time elevation tied to a ticket, ending with the window and recorded, gives the access needed and no more. Shared passwords lose accountability; permanent rights outlive the job.

prompt: An AWS credential report shows svc-etl holding an access key 700 days old, unused for the last 400 days. What is the right handling?
optionA: Keep the key because an old key has clearly never been leaked
optionB: Confirm the owner, deactivate the key, then delete if nothing breaks
optionC: Attach an admin policy so the key works if it is ever needed
optionD: Create a second key for svc-etl and keep both active together
correctAnswerText: Confirm the owner, deactivate the key, then delete if nothing breaks
explanation: An unused long-term key is pure risk. Deactivating first is reversible if something depended on it; deleting follows once nothing breaks. Age and disuse are reasons to remove it, not evidence that it is safe.

prompt: Sign-in logs show 14 denied push prompts for Ravi at 02:00, then one approved, then a new MFA method registered. What is most likely?
optionA: His phone lost signal and retried the prompts by itself
optionB: He is travelling and approving sign-ins in a new time zone
optionC: A scheduled job is refreshing his MFA registration nightly
optionD: His password is known and a flooded prompt was approved
correctAnswerText: His password is known and a flooded prompt was approved
explanation: Many denied prompts then an approval, followed by a new MFA method, is the request-flooding pattern followed by persistence. Treat it as a compromised account: revoke sessions, remove the new method, reset the password.

prompt: A DC logs 4771 failures with code 0x18 across 300 accounts from one workstation, two per account within an hour. What does this indicate?
optionA: A clock difference breaking Kerberos for the site
optionB: One user repeatedly mistyping their own password
optionC: Password spraying kept under the lockout threshold
optionD: A service with an old password stored in its config
correctAnswerText: Password spraying kept under the lockout threshold
explanation: A few failures each across many accounts from one source is password spraying (ATT&CK T1110.003). A mistyping user or a stale stored password hits one account many times, not many accounts a few times.

prompt: One user requests 4769 service tickets for forty service accounts in two minutes, all with RC4 encryption. Which hardening addresses the risk?
optionA: A shorter password policy for the forty service accounts
optionB: Turning off Kerberos auditing on the domain controllers
optionC: Long random service passwords or gMSAs, and RC4 disabled
optionD: Moving every service account into the Domain Admins group
correctAnswerText: Long random service passwords or gMSAs, and RC4 disabled
explanation: This is the pattern defenders watch for to catch Kerberoasting (T1558.003), which targets service-account passwords. Long random passwords (or group managed service accounts) and disabling RC4 remove what it depends on.

prompt: A report of accounts not logged on for 14 days lists people who sign in every morning. What is the cause?
optionA: Morning logons are not recorded by the domain controllers
optionB: The report reads the password-last-set date by mistake
optionC: lastLogonTimestamp replicates late, so short thresholds misfire
optionD: Those users log on with cached credentials that skip the DC
correctAnswerText: lastLogonTimestamp replicates late, so short thresholds misfire
explanation: The replicated timestamp only updates after a randomised interval of up to about two weeks. Use a 90-day threshold, or query lastLogon on every DC and take the maximum when exact recency matters.

prompt: A user's identity policy now allows s3:* on the bucket, yet every request still returns AccessDenied. Where do you look first?
optionA: The user's MFA device, which expires after an Allow
optionB: The policy version, which must be today's date
optionC: An explicit Deny or an SCP that caps the account
optionD: The bucket name, which must be written in capitals
correctAnswerText: An explicit Deny or an SCP that caps the account
explanation: An Allow cannot beat an explicit Deny, and guardrails such as SCPs and permission boundaries only take away. When an Allow seems ignored, a Deny or a guardrail is the usual answer.

prompt: A policy reads Allow with NotAction "iam:*" on "*". Why does the reviewer flag it as close to full admin?
optionA: It allows IAM only, which lets the holder edit any policy
optionB: It allows every action except IAM, including new services
optionC: It denies every action except IAM, so nothing works at all
optionD: NotAction is ignored by AWS, so the policy grants nothing
correctAnswerText: It allows every action except IAM, including new services
explanation: Allow plus NotAction grants everything not listed, now and for every service launched later. That is effectively admin outside IAM — the opposite of naming the actions you need.

prompt: Event 4728 shows a user added to Domain Admins at 23:10 with no change ticket. How should the analyst treat it?
optionA: As closed, because the change was made by a domain admin
optionB: As an alert: confirm with the owner and escalate if unexplained
optionC: As noise, because admins often add each other late at night
optionD: As a password issue to be handled by the help desk tomorrow
correctAnswerText: As an alert: confirm with the owner and escalate if unexplained
explanation: A privileged-group change outside a change ticket is always worth an alert. Who made it does not make it safe — an attacker with admin rights would also appear as an admin.

prompt: One account is locked out (4740) every ten minutes, always naming the same caller computer, a report server. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The account was added to a group that blocks all logons
optionB: A spraying run is trying one password against every account
optionC: The domain controller clock is ahead by several hours
optionD: An application on that server holds an old stored password
correctAnswerText: An application on that server holds an old stored password
explanation: Repeated lockouts of one account from one fixed caller is the classic stale-credential pattern after a password change. Spraying spreads across many accounts. Check the caller computer before raising an incident.

prompt: A leaver's directory account was disabled on time, yet the VPN logs show them connecting a week later. What gap does this reveal?
optionA: Disabled accounts can always log on again for one week
optionB: The VPN logs record the time zone wrongly by seven days
optionC: The directory takes a week to disable any account fully
optionD: Their VPN certificate or other credentials were not withdrawn
correctAnswerText: Their VPN certificate or other credentials were not withdrawn
explanation: A leaver process must withdraw every credential — sessions, tokens, keys, VPN certificates — not just the directory account. Anything that authenticates independently of it keeps working.

prompt: An IT engineer holds Finance-Approvers, Sales-Users and IT-Admins. Her HR history shows Finance, then Sales, then IT. What failed?
optionA: Mover steps added new access without removing the old
optionB: The leaver process re-enabled groups she once held
optionC: Her joiner request asked for all three roles at once
optionD: The directory merges groups for staff in the same office
correctAnswerText: Mover steps added new access without removing the old
explanation: Holding every previous team's access matches the job history exactly — access creep from moves. It also breaks separation of duties if she can now raise and approve in Finance.

prompt: With budget for a few hundred security keys and 4,000 staff, which MFA rollout is the strongest choice?
optionA: No MFA until keys can be bought for every member of staff
optionB: SMS OTP for everyone so the whole company is treated equally
optionC: Keys for admins and high-risk users, number-matched push for the rest
optionD: Keys for whoever asks first until the budget runs out
correctAnswerText: Keys for admins and high-risk users, number-matched push for the rest
explanation: Put phishing-resistant keys where compromise costs most and give everyone else a strong, cheap factor. Waiting for perfection leaves everyone on passwords; equal SMS for all leaves admins on the weakest form.

prompt: The server team wants to keep one shared root-style admin login because it is simpler. What is the better design and why?
optionA: Named admin accounts, so every action traces to one person
optionB: The shared login, with its password written in the runbook
optionC: Named accounts that all share the same password for speed
optionD: The shared login, since fewer accounts means fewer targets
correctAnswerText: Named admin accounts, so every action traces to one person
explanation: A shared login makes every privileged action anonymous, so neither an investigation nor an audit can say who did it. Named accounts (with shared secrets vaulted and rotated) keep accountability.

prompt: Should three sysadmins keep permanent Domain Admin, or move to just-in-time elevation with some approval delay?
optionA: Keep permanent rights but share one account among the three
optionB: Move to JIT; less standing privilege outweighs the small delay
optionC: Keep permanent rights; any delay is worse than any exposure
optionD: Move to JIT and also remove the break-glass emergency account
correctAnswerText: Move to JIT; less standing privilege outweighs the small delay
explanation: Standing admin rights are available to anyone who compromises those accounts at any hour. JIT shrinks that window at the cost of some friction — and a break-glass account remains for when the process itself fails.

prompt: Why is it reasonable to keep a break-glass account outside single sign-on, and what must make up for that?
optionA: It is used daily by admins; a shorter password makes that easier
optionB: It must work when SSO fails; a sealed long password and alerts compensate
optionC: It is a test account; it can safely be ignored by monitoring
optionD: It saves licence costs; no further control is needed after that
correctAnswerText: It must work when SSO fails; a sealed long password and alerts compensate
explanation: The emergency account exists for when normal access — often SSO itself — is broken, so it cannot depend on it. The price is a long random password in a sealed process and an alert on every use.

prompt: A firm relies only on quarterly access reviews to remove leavers. What is the better arrangement?
optionA: HR-driven automatic deprovisioning, with reviews as a safety net
optionB: Removing the reviews, since auditors only sample a few accounts
optionC: Monthly reviews instead, still with no link to the HR system
optionD: Letting each leaver disable their own account on the last day
correctAnswerText: HR-driven automatic deprovisioning, with reviews as a safety net
explanation: A quarterly review leaves a leaver's access open for up to three months. Automation from HR removes it on the day; the review then catches what automation missed rather than being the only control.

prompt: Developers ask that service accounts be allowed interactive logon for easier troubleshooting. What should be decided?
optionA: Deny it; an interactive service-account logon then becomes an alert
optionB: Allow it, and share the service passwords with all developers
optionC: Allow it, because service accounts are never targeted at all
optionD: Deny it, but give the service accounts Domain Admin to compensate
correctAnswerText: Deny it; an interactive service-account logon then becomes an alert
explanation: Service accounts should have no interactive logon and the narrowest rights. Keeping that rule turns any interactive logon into a high-signal alert; allowing it hides misuse among routine troubleshooting.

prompt: For forty engineers needing AWS access, which is better: an IAM user each, or sign-in through the company directory?
optionA: One shared IAM user for the team, rotated every single quarter
optionB: Directory sign-in, so offboarding in HR also ends cloud access
optionC: IAM users, with one access key each kept on their own laptops
optionD: IAM users, since separate passwords for AWS add one more layer
correctAnswerText: Directory sign-in, so offboarding in HR also ends cloud access
explanation: Federating through the directory (for example via IAM Identity Center) gives temporary credentials and ties cloud access to the leaver process. Per-person IAM users and laptop keys are what leavers keep.

prompt: On a leaver's last day, is it better to disable the account at once or delete it at once?
optionA: Delete now, because a deleted account cannot ever be misused
optionB: Neither; leave it enabled until the next access review runs
optionC: Delete now and restore from backup if anyone needs its files
optionD: Disable now and delete later, keeping data and evidence available
correctAnswerText: Disable now and delete later, keeping data and evidence available
explanation: Disabling stops use immediately while keeping mail, files and history for handover and any investigation. Deletion follows the retention policy. Deleting at once can destroy what an incident would need.

prompt: Leadership wants NTLM switched off domain-wide tomorrow because it is weaker than Kerberos. What is the better plan?
optionA: Audit NTLM use first, fix those systems, then reduce it in stages
optionB: Switch it off tomorrow and fix whatever breaks in production
optionC: Switch off Kerberos instead so only one protocol is left
optionD: Leave it everywhere, because Kerberos is the weaker protocol
correctAnswerText: Audit NTLM use first, fix those systems, then reduce it in stages
explanation: NTLM is weaker and worth reducing, but old applications, IP-based access and local accounts still use it. Auditing shows what depends on it, so the reduction does not become an outage.

prompt: An AD health review finds fifty Domain Admins, half nested through groups. Which first fix gives the most risk reduction?
optionA: Raise the minimum password length for all ordinary users by one
optionB: Rename the Domain Admins group so it is harder to recognise
optionC: Cut to a handful of named admin accounts used from admin hosts
optionD: Add a banner warning admins about policy at every logon
correctAnswerText: Cut to a handful of named admin accounts used from admin hosts
explanation: Every Domain Admin is a path to the whole domain. Shrinking that set to a few separate, named admin accounts removes the most risk; renaming a group or adding a banner changes nothing an attacker relies on.

prompt: In SOC terms, which description fits an incident rather than an event or an alert?
optionA: Any log entry recording a failed sign-in or a blocked connection
optionB: A confirmed or strongly suspected policy violation needing a response
optionC: An alert that has stayed open in the queue past its response target
optionD: Any event that a detection rule has flagged for an analyst to review
correctAnswerText: A confirmed or strongly suspected policy violation needing a response
explanation: An event is anything observable, an alert is an event a detection flagged, and an incident is a confirmed or strongly suspected violation that needs a coordinated response. An old alert is still an alert; age does not make it an incident.

prompt: Which list gives the four phases of the NIST SP 800-61 incident handling lifecycle in order?
optionA: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
optionB: Detection and Analysis; Preparation; Post-Incident Activity; Containment, Eradication and Recovery
optionC: Identification; Preparation; Eradication and Containment; Recovery and Lessons Learned Review
optionD: Preparation; Containment and Analysis; Detection, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Report
correctAnswerText: Preparation; Detection and Analysis; Containment, Eradication and Recovery; Post-Incident Activity
explanation: NIST's long-standing model is Preparation, Detection and Analysis, Containment/Eradication/Recovery, then Post-Incident Activity, with a loop from phase 3 back to phase 2. The SANS model splits the third phase into three, but nobody contains before detecting.

prompt: During an incident, which named role keeps the timeline and the decision log?
optionA: The communications lead
optionB: The system owner
optionC: The incident commander
optionD: The scribe
correctAnswerText: The scribe
explanation: The scribe records what happened and every decision with its reason and time; it is often a junior analyst's role. The incident commander makes the decisions, communications speaks outside the team, and system owners carry out changes on their systems.

prompt: Following the RFC 3227 order of volatility, which should be collected first from a live, compromised host?
optionA: The physical network topology diagram
optionB: A full forensic image of the system disk
optionC: Memory and the running process list
optionD: Archived backup media for that host
correctAnswerText: Memory and the running process list
explanation: The most volatile evidence goes first, because it vanishes soonest: memory, processes and connections are lost at power-off. Disk comes after live state, and topology and archival media are the least volatile of all.

prompt: What does a chain-of-custody record document for each item of evidence?
optionA: How severe the incident was when it was taken
optionB: Which attacker created it and from which address
optionC: Who held it, when, and what they did with it
optionD: Which detection rule first pointed to the item
correctAnswerText: Who held it, when, and what they did with it
explanation: Chain of custody answers "how do we know nobody changed this?" by recording every holder, time and action, alongside the item's hash. Attribution, severity and the triggering rule belong elsewhere in the case record.

prompt: Which algorithm should be used to fingerprint collected evidence files?
optionA: Base64
optionB: CRC32
optionC: SHA-256
optionD: MD5
correctAnswerText: SHA-256
explanation: SHA-256 is a cryptographic hash with no practical collisions, so matching digests show the bytes are unchanged. MD5 has known collisions, CRC32 is an error check rather than a security hash, and Base64 is an encoding, not a hash at all.

prompt: Which of these is a short-term containment action?
optionA: Writing the lessons-learned action list
optionB: Isolating a laptop from the network through EDR
optionC: Exporting the final report for leadership
optionD: Rebuilding the server from a known-good image
correctAnswerText: Isolating a laptop from the network through EDR
explanation: Short-term containment is fast and reversible: isolate a host, disable an account, revoke sessions, block an indicator. Rebuilding belongs to eradication and recovery, and the action list and report are post-incident work.

prompt: Which element must a usable incident playbook contain?
optionA: The source code of the detection that triggers it
optionB: Forty pages of background on the attack category
optionC: A full history of every past incident of that type
optionD: Decision points saying what each answer leads to
correctAnswerText: Decision points saying what each answer leads to
explanation: A usable playbook has a trigger, steps with owners, decision points, stop conditions, evidence to keep and communication rules, in a page or two. Incident history, rule source and long background are not read during a live incident.

prompt: Which national body, acting under the IT Act, has issued directions requiring Indian organisations to report specified cyber incidents to it?
optionA: The Data Protection Board of India
optionB: NPCI
optionC: NASSCOM
optionD: CERT-In
correctAnswerText: CERT-In
explanation: CERT-In is India's national CERT and its directions require specified incidents to be reported within a short, fixed time. The Data Protection Board receives personal data breach notices under the DPDP Act; NPCI runs payment systems and NASSCOM is an industry body.

prompt: Which MITRE ATT&CK technique does the account-takeover playbook map to?
optionA: T1110 Brute Force
optionB: T1078 Valid Accounts
optionC: T1566 Phishing
optionD: T1486 Data Encrypted for Impact
correctAnswerText: T1078 Valid Accounts
explanation: An attacker signing in with a real user's credentials is T1078 Valid Accounts. T1566 is the phishing playbook's technique and T1486 the ransomware one; brute force is one way credentials may be obtained, not the takeover itself.

prompt: Why is incident severity set from impact and scope rather than from how alarming the alert sounded?
optionA: Severity must stay fixed once set, so it needs the firmest basis
optionB: Impact is the only field the SIEM can sort an incident queue by
optionC: Severity decides who is woken and how fast, which impact justifies
optionD: Alert titles are written by vendors and are not allowed in tickets
correctAnswerText: Severity decides who is woken and how fast, which impact justifies
explanation: Severity drives the response: who is called, how quickly, whether leadership is told. An alarming title can sit on a trivial event and the reverse. Severity is also re-assessed as facts arrive, so it is never fixed once set.

prompt: Why is pulling the power cable on a compromised laptop usually the wrong first step?
optionA: Laptops cannot be re-joined to the domain after an unclean shutdown
optionB: Memory and live connections vanish, while EDR isolation keeps them
optionC: Powering off corrupts the disk so that it can no longer be imaged
optionD: The attacker is alerted the moment any of their hosts loses power
correctAnswerText: Memory and live connections vanish, while EDR isolation keeps them
explanation: Network isolation through EDR cuts the attacker off while the machine stays on, so the forensic team can still capture memory and process state. A power-off rarely ruins the disk, and the other claims are not reasons the course gives.

prompt: Why is a password reset on its own not enough to contain a taken-over cloud account?
optionA: Existing sessions and tokens can stay valid after the reset
optionB: The new password is emailed to the address the attacker reads
optionC: A reset deletes the sign-in logs needed for the investigation
optionD: Cloud providers take a full day to apply a password change
correctAnswerText: Existing sessions and tokens can stay valid after the reset
explanation: Sessions and refresh tokens issued before the reset may keep working, and the attacker may have added their own MFA method or inbox rules. That is why sessions are revoked first. Resets apply quickly and do not erase sign-in logs.

prompt: Why is a compromised endpoint reimaged from a known-good build rather than cleaned by hand?
optionA: Hand-cleaning misses things, and a rebuild costs less than a repeat
optionB: Hand-cleaning a host is not permitted by the CERT-In directions
optionC: A rebuilt host no longer needs an EDR agent or log forwarding
optionD: Reimaging also recovers the user's files exactly as they were before
correctAnswerText: Hand-cleaning misses things, and a rebuild costs less than a repeat
explanation: Nobody can be sure every change an attacker made has been found, so rebuilding from a known-good image is cheaper than a second incident. A rebuild does not restore user files by itself, and rebuilt hosts still need EDR and logging.

prompt: Why is a post-incident review run blamelessly?
optionA: Nobody was really at fault, since attacks cannot be prevented at all
optionB: It shortens the meeting, so actions can be written down sooner
optionC: Regulators forbid naming any employee in an internal review record
optionD: People speak openly, so system conditions behind the failure surface
correctAnswerText: People speak openly, so system conditions behind the failure surface
explanation: Blame teaches people to hide mistakes, which hides the conditions that let the incident happen. Phrasing findings as conditions ("the group was excluded from MFA") leads to fixes. It is not a legal rule, and it does not claim attacks are unpreventable.

prompt: Why should an incident be confirmed with a source independent of the alert that raised it?
optionA: The alert itself cannot be attached to the incident ticket as evidence
optionB: Detections are only allowed to raise alerts, never incidents directly
optionC: Declaring an incident needs a signature from a second analyst first
optionD: One source can be wrong; two from different systems rarely agree wrongly
correctAnswerText: One source can be wrong; two from different systems rarely agree wrongly
explanation: Re-reading the same alert repeats the same evidence; sign-in logs or a call to the user can show it was wrong. Two agreeing sources from different systems are strong grounds for declaring. The alert is still part of the record.

prompt: Why does scoping also pivot on what compromised accounts did, not only on the first indicators?
optionA: Indicators such as IPs may not be stored in the case record by law
optionB: Accounts are easier to block than IP addresses during containment
optionC: Attackers change IPs and domains, so fixed indicators miss later steps
optionD: Pivoting on behaviour is faster, so it can replace the indicator search
correctAnswerText: Attackers change IPs and domains, so fixed indicators miss later steps
explanation: Indicators are brittle; a known-compromised account signing in from a new address reveals a new indicator. Behaviour pivots add to the indicator search rather than replacing it, and storing IPs in the record is normal.

prompt: Why does a watch list on the attacker's indicators stay in place for 30 days or more after recovery?
optionA: Regulators require every alert rule to run for a month before removal
optionB: The SIEM needs a month of data before it can index new watch rules
optionC: Recovered systems are not monitored at all until the watch ends
optionD: Attackers who lose access often try to return through a missed path
correctAnswerText: Attackers who lose access often try to return through a missed path
explanation: A return through the same users, another reused password or an unfound foothold shows that scoping missed something. The watch catches it. The other options describe rules and limits that do not exist.

prompt: Why does the decision log record the exact time an incident was noticed?
optionA: The time is used to work out which analyst is paid overtime
optionB: It sets when the attacker first got in, for the root cause
optionC: It decides the incident number given to the case in the ticket
optionD: Reporting clocks, internal and regulatory, run from that moment
correctAnswerText: Reporting clocks, internal and regulatory, run from that moment
explanation: CERT-In and other reporting duties are measured from when an incident is noticed, so that time must be on record. It is not the time of first attacker access, which the timeline establishes separately from evidence.

prompt: What does a tabletop exercise give an incident response team?
optionA: Proof that every detection rule fires on real attacker activity
optionB: Gaps in the plan, found by talking through a scenario beforehand
optionC: A certified record that satisfies every regulator's audit duty
optionD: Live practice restoring each production system from its backups
correctAnswerText: Gaps in the plan, found by talking through a scenario beforehand
explanation: In a tabletop the team talks a scenario through round by round, finding missing contacts, approvals and logs on a quiet afternoon instead of during an incident. It does not test detections or restore systems, and it is not a certification.

prompt: Tarang Bank's identity provider keeps sign-in logs for 30 days. The incident was 20 days ago and the review is in three weeks. What should the analyst do now?
optionA: Screenshot the key sign-in rows and paste them into the ticket
optionB: Raise the retention setting so the old logs are kept for a year
optionC: Export the relevant sign-in logs now and hash the export files
optionD: Wait for the review, then ask the vendor for any logs still held
correctAnswerText: Export the relevant sign-in logs now and hash the export files
explanation: Logs older than the retention period will be gone before the review, and raising retention usually only keeps new logs longer. Export now, hash the files and log them in the chain of custody. Screenshots lose most fields and cannot be verified.

prompt: A finance user's cloud account at Nilgiri Mutual is confirmed taken over. In which order should containment run?
optionA: Revoke sessions; reset password; review MFA; remove rules and OAuth grants
optionB: Reset password; remove rules and OAuth grants; review MFA; revoke sessions
optionC: Remove rules and OAuth grants; reset password; revoke sessions; review MFA
optionD: Review MFA; revoke sessions; remove rules and OAuth grants; reset password
correctAnswerText: Revoke sessions; reset password; review MFA; remove rules and OAuth grants
explanation: Revoking sessions first cuts the attacker's live access, the reset stops them signing in again, the MFA review removes any method they registered, and then persistence inside the account is removed. Leaving revocation to last gives a live session hours more.

prompt: One user clicked a phishing link but entered no credentials, and EDR shows no download. Using the four-level matrix, which severity fits?
optionA: SEV-3: suspicious and limited, handled by the SOC the same day
optionB: SEV-2: confirmed compromise with contained scope, IR lead in an hour
optionC: SEV-4: policy violation with negligible impact, normal ticket queue
optionD: SEV-1: critical impact, IR lead now and a 24x7 bridge opened
correctAnswerText: SEV-3: suspicious and limited, handled by the SOC the same day
explanation: Nothing is confirmed compromised, but a click is more than a policy matter, so SEV-3 fits. It would be raised if a credential entry or a download turned up. SEV-1 and SEV-2 need confirmed compromise; SEV-4 is for things like unapproved software.

prompt: An analyst needs to filter a hashed mail-gateway export in a spreadsheet. How should the evidence be handled?
optionA: Delete the hash entry, since filtering changes it
optionB: Rename the original so nobody else edits it later
optionC: Open the original, filter it, and rehash it after
optionD: Keep the original read-only and work on a copy
correctAnswerText: Keep the original read-only and work on a copy
explanation: Any save, even one that only changes line endings, alters the hash and makes the original unverifiable. Working on a copy keeps the evidence matching its recorded digest. Rehashing after editing records the change but no longer proves the original.

prompt: At Tarang Bank, neha.v typed her password into the phishing page; her MFA push was refused and no successful attacker sign-in exists. How is she classified?
optionA: Not affected: MFA held, so her account needs no action at all
optionB: Compromised: revoke sessions and isolate her laptop straight away
optionC: Received only: purge the message and send an awareness note
optionD: Credentials exposed: reset the password, no session revocation
correctAnswerText: Credentials exposed: reset the password, no session revocation
explanation: "Compromised" is reserved for a successful attacker sign-in. Her password is now known, so it must change, but there is no attacker session to revoke. Calling her unaffected leaves a known password live; "received only" ignores that she clicked and typed it.

prompt: A proxy log records a click at 14:30:00 in Indian Standard Time, with no zone stored. What goes on the unified UTC timeline?
explanation: IST is UTC+05:30, so 14:30 IST is 09:00 UTC. Adding 5.5 hours gives 20:00, the wrong direction; copying 14:30 treats local time as UTC; 08:30 subtracts six hours instead of five and a half.

prompt: First attacker sign-in 11:20Z, detection 12:15Z, containment complete 12:50Z. What was the time to contain?
optionA: 1 h 50 min
optionB: 1 h 30 min
optionC: 55 min
optionD: 35 min
correctAnswerText: 35 min
explanation: Time to contain runs from detection to containment: 12:15Z to 12:50Z is 35 minutes. 55 minutes is the time to detect, and 1 h 30 min is the attacker's total access, from first sign-in to containment.

prompt: Running the phishing playbook, you find two users clicked and one then had a successful sign-in from an unusual IP. What happens for that user?
optionA: Switch to the account-takeover playbook for that user
optionB: Isolate both users' laptops and close the playbook
optionC: Purge the message and close the case for that user
optionD: Send that user an awareness note and wait a day
correctAnswerText: Switch to the account-takeover playbook for that user
explanation: A risky sign-in after a click is the playbook's decision point for a takeover, which brings session revocation, persistence removal and a review of what the account did. Purging and awareness notes are for users with no follow-on activity.

prompt: During a ransomware response at Vayu Logistics, the backup server is still reachable from the affected network. What should be done with it?
optionA: Run an immediate full backup so the latest data is safely captured
optionB: Confirm offline copies are intact and disconnect the reachable system
optionC: Leave it connected, since backup software cannot be encrypted
optionD: Restore every affected host from it at once to shorten the outage
correctAnswerText: Confirm offline copies are intact and disconnect the reachable system
explanation: Reachable backups can be encrypted or deleted too, so they are cut off and the offline or immutable copies checked. A fresh backup would capture encrypted data, restoring before scoping risks reinfection, and backup systems are a common target.

prompt: The timeline shows first attacker activity on 3 May at 02:10Z. Backups exist from 1 May, 2 May 23:00Z, 3 May 23:00Z and 5 May. Which one is restored?
optionA: 5 May
optionB: 2 May 23:00Z
optionC: 3 May 23:00Z
optionD: 1 May
correctAnswerText: 2 May 23:00Z
explanation: The latest backup taken before the first malicious activity balances a clean state against data lost. The 3 and 5 May backups were taken after the attacker was in and may hold what they planted; 1 May is clean but loses a day more than needed.

prompt: After session revocation and a password reset on a CFO's mailbox, invoices keep reaching an outside address. What was most likely missed?
optionA: Blocking the phishing domain at the web proxy
optionB: A forwarding or inbox rule left inside the account
optionC: Turning on audit logging for the CFO's mailbox
optionD: Searching the gateway for other phish recipients
correctAnswerText: A forwarding or inbox rule left inside the account
explanation: Rules and forwarding live in the account and keep working after a reset and revocation. Blocking the domain protects new victims, audit logging only records, and other recipients widen scope; none stops mail already being forwarded.

prompt: Scope was built from the phishing recipient list and contained. A week later the attacker IP signs in as a user who never got the email. What went wrong?
optionA: The recipient list was purged before it could be read
optionB: The watch list was set to alert on the wrong country
optionC: The user must have forwarded the phish from a home inbox
optionD: Nobody pivoted on the attacker IP across all sign-ins
correctAnswerText: Nobody pivoted on the attacker IP across all sign-ins
explanation: A user can be compromised by password reuse with no link to the email; only a pivot on the attacker IP across successful sign-ins finds them. The watch list did its job by catching the return. Guessing at forwarding ignores the evidence available.

prompt: A unified timeline shows the phishing click five and a half hours after the fraudulent payment it led to. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The attacker altered the proxy clock to mislead
optionB: The click was cached by the browser and sent late
optionC: The proxy's local IST times were labelled as UTC
optionD: The payment system records times in epoch seconds
correctAnswerText: The proxy's local IST times were labelled as UTC
explanation: A gap of exactly 5.5 hours is the IST offset: local times written as UTC appear 5.5 hours late. Epoch seconds are UTC by definition, and the exact offset points to a parsing slip rather than tampering or caching.

prompt: A server was restored from the previous night's backup and was compromised again within hours. Attacker activity began four days before the restore. Why?
optionA: Backups cannot be restored onto the same server name
optionB: The restore reset the server's clock to the backup time
optionC: The backup already held what the attacker had planted
optionD: The EDR agent always needs a day to start after a restore
correctAnswerText: The backup already held what the attacker had planted
explanation: A backup taken after persistence was planted brings it back. The restore point should precede the first attacker activity, and the way in must be removed before recovery. The other options are not how restores behave.

prompt: On day one the SOC blocked one attacker IP. The next day activity came from new IPs and two accounts nobody had linked to the case. What does the review conclude?
optionA: Two separate attackers happened to strike on consecutive days
optionB: The firewall block failed, so the original IP was never stopped
optionC: The block should have been on the domain rather than the IP
optionD: Partial containment warned the attacker before scope was known
correctAnswerText: Partial containment warned the attacker before scope was known
explanation: Blocking one foothold tells a careful intruder they were seen, and they shift to others. Scoping first and then containing everything together avoids that. The new activity came from new IPs, so the block worked; nothing suggests a second actor.

prompt: A custody check reports MISMATCH for a proxy export that grew from 513 to 517 bytes with no visible change. A colleague opened it in an editor. What happened?
optionA: The file was compressed when it was copied over
optionB: The hashing script read the file in text mode
optionC: SHA-256 gives a new digest on every single run
optionD: The editor resaved it with Windows line endings
correctAnswerText: The editor resaved it with Windows line endings
explanation: Four extra bytes with nothing visible is the CRLF change from a resave; the hash cannot tell that innocent change from tampering, so evidence is never opened in an editor. SHA-256 is deterministic, and compression would shrink the file.

prompt: An incident stayed at SEV-3 for two days after the analyst found that money had been redirected. What does the review identify?
optionA: The first SEV-3 rating was a mistake that should be blamed
optionB: Severity should have been set to SEV-1 for every phishing case
optionC: Severity was not re-assessed when the impact became known
optionD: The money transfer was outside the scope of the SOC to judge
correctAnswerText: Severity was not re-assessed when the impact became known
explanation: Upgrading from SEV-3 to SEV-1 when money is found moved is normal and expected; the failure was not doing it. The first rating fitted what was known then, starting every phish at SEV-1 would wake people needlessly, and impact on money is central to severity.

prompt: What makes "a highly sophisticated attacker bypassed our MFA" unsuitable for an incident report?
optionA: It gives no time, source or evidence, only an adjective
optionB: It is too short for the executive summary's half page
optionC: It credits the attacker, which is a legal admission
optionD: It names MFA, which reports must never mention at all
correctAnswerText: It gives no time, source or evidence, only an adjective
explanation: A report row states the exact time, the account, the source and what the evidence shows, for example an approved push after two refusals. "Sophisticated" is an excuse in the making and cannot be checked. Naming the control involved is fine.

prompt: Midway through an incident the team learns the attacker has been reading the responders' email. Which preparation gap does this expose?
optionA: The severity matrix had too few levels for this case
optionB: The playbook did not list the relevant ATT&CK IDs
optionC: No out-of-band contact channel was set up in advance
optionD: The tabletop was run by an external facilitator
correctAnswerText: No out-of-band contact channel was set up in advance
explanation: Preparation includes phone numbers and a channel outside corporate email, so responders can talk where the attacker cannot listen. Severity levels, ATT&CK tags and who facilitates a tabletop have nothing to do with a compromised communication path.

prompt: A timeline row reads "user approved the MFA push", though its only source is two refusals followed by a success. What is wrong with the row?
optionA: It names the user, which a timeline must never do
optionB: It uses UTC rather than the user's own local time zone
optionC: It should be deleted, since inferences have no place here
optionD: It is an inference written as if it were an observation
correctAnswerText: It is an inference written as if it were an observation
explanation: The logs observe refusals and a success; the approval is inferred from them. Both belong in the timeline, marked differently, so a reader knows what is proven. UTC is correct, and naming the account involved is normal.

prompt: At a fintech, vendor payouts are being redirected right now and scoping is only half done. Which approach should the IR lead choose?
optionA: Take the whole payments platform offline until scoping is done
optionB: Contain the known accounts now and keep scoping, noting gaps
optionC: Finish scoping fully first, then contain every foothold at once
optionD: Watch the attacker quietly for a day to learn the full scope
correctAnswerText: Contain the known accounts now and keep scoping, noting gaps
explanation: When money is leaving, the cost of waiting outweighs the risk of tipping the attacker off, so contain what is known and continue scoping, stating what is unscoped. Full-scope-then-contain suits a slow, careful intruder; shutting the platform is out of proportion to what is known.

prompt: Leadership asks for a single report that serves both the board and the engineers. Which response is best?
optionA: Write two: a half-page summary and a full technical report
optionB: Send only the technical timeline, since facts speak for themselves
optionC: Send only the summary, since engineers can read the ticket
optionD: Write one long report with every log line, so nothing is lost
correctAnswerText: Write two: a half-page summary and a full technical report
explanation: The board needs impact, status, data affected and decisions in plain language; engineers need the timeline, scope, root cause, evidence and indicators. One document fails one audience, and a ticket is not a report with owned recommendations.

prompt: A post-incident review ended with twenty actions such as "improve awareness", none with an owner. What would make the output better?
optionA: Keep the list as is but review it again next quarter
optionB: More actions, so that every possible gap is covered
optionC: One owner for all twenty, so accountability is clear
optionD: Fewer actions, each with one owner and a due date
correctAnswerText: Fewer actions, each with one owner and a due date
explanation: Actions are tracked like any other work; five done beat twenty aspirational. One owner each, with a date, makes them happen. A single owner for everything is overloaded, and revisiting an unowned list changes nothing.

prompt: After an MFA-fatigue takeover, which follow-up gives the most lasting value?
optionA: A note in the report that MFA cannot be fully trusted
optionB: Detect repeated MFA refusals followed by an approval
optionC: A training slide telling staff to refuse unknown pushes
optionD: An all-staff email naming the user who approved it
correctAnswerText: Detect repeated MFA refusals followed by an approval
