explanation: A detection catches the pattern next time, whoever is targeted, and goes to the detection backlog with the incident number. A slide relies on tired people, naming the user is blame, and a vague note changes nothing; a policy change such as number matching also helps.

prompt: To save a day, an L2 analyst proposes deleting the malicious files found on a workstation and returning it to the user. How should this be judged?
optionA: Accept, as long as the user changes their password today
optionB: Reject: the workstation must be destroyed and replaced
optionC: Reject: isolate, collect evidence, then reimage the host
optionD: Accept: the files are gone, so the attacker is gone too
correctAnswerText: Reject: isolate, collect evidence, then reimage the host
explanation: Deleting what was found misses what was not found and destroys evidence. Isolating, collecting what the forensic plan needs and reimaging from a known-good build is cheaper than a second incident. Destroying hardware is unnecessary.

prompt: An analyst confirms an attacker read a mailbox holding customer KYC documents. A colleague wants to email the affected customers tonight. Which course is right?
optionA: Email the customers tonight, since early warning is always the priority
optionB: Wait for the post-incident review to decide whether anything is reportable
optionC: Record the noticed time, keep evidence, and hand it to legal and the DPO
optionD: File the CERT-In report personally, since the analyst noticed it first
correctAnswerText: Record the noticed time, keep evidence, and hand it to legal and the DPO
explanation: Notifications to CERT-In, the Data Protection Board and affected people go through legal and the named owner, who know the current rules and wording. The analyst's part is the timestamp and the evidence. Waiting for the review may miss the deadlines.

prompt: Two draft phishing playbooks: one is forty detailed pages, the other two pages with owners, decision points and stop conditions. Which should the SOC adopt?
optionA: The two-page one, since it can be followed at 3 a.m.
optionB: Both, letting each analyst pick whichever they prefer
optionC: The forty-page one, since more detail means fewer gaps
optionD: Neither, since experienced analysts work from memory
correctAnswerText: The two-page one, since it can be followed at 3 a.m.
explanation: A playbook exists so the 2 a.m. response matches the 2 p.m. one; a forty-page document is not read during an incident. Letting analysts choose, or work from memory, removes the consistency a playbook is for.

prompt: During a ransomware incident, an analyst suggests using the address in the ransom note to open contact and learn more. How should this be judged?
optionA: Decline: contact belongs to leadership, legal and police
optionB: Decline: ransom notes should be deleted on sight anyway
optionC: Accept, provided the analyst uses a personal email account
optionD: Accept: early contact may reveal how the attacker got in
correctAnswerText: Decline: contact belongs to leadership, legal and police
explanation: Any contact with the attacker and any decision about a demand belongs to leadership with legal advice and law enforcement, never the SOC. The ransom note is kept as evidence, not deleted, and a personal account would make things worse.

prompt: After an intrusion, the payment switch, the intranet and the HR portal all need restoring. How should the order be decided?
optionA: By the order the systems appeared in the timeline
optionB: All at once, so that no team feels it was put last
optionC: By whichever system restores fastest, to show progress
optionD: By the priority agreed in preparation, payments first
correctAnswerText: By the priority agreed in preparation, payments first
explanation: Restore order is a business decision made calmly in preparation, so the payment switch comes before the intranet. Speed of restore and timeline order say nothing about business need, and restoring everything at once spreads scarce people thin.

prompt: Two weeks after recovery a watch-list alert fires on the same attacker domain. One analyst wants a fresh case, another to reopen the old one. Who is right?
optionA: Neither: alerts on old indicators are expected noise
optionB: New case: the old one was closed, so it cannot be reopened
optionC: New case: a fortnight apart means a different attacker
optionD: Reopen: it is the same incident, and scoping missed something
correctAnswerText: Reopen: it is the same incident, and scoping missed something
explanation: A return within the watch period means a foothold or credential was missed, and its evidence belongs in the same record and timeline. Splitting it into a new case hides that link, and dismissing it repeats the original miss.

prompt: Which file does the OpenSSH server read its main configuration from?
optionA: /etc/sshd/keys.conf
optionB: /etc/ssh/ssh_config
optionC: /var/lib/ssh/sshd.db
optionD: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
correctAnswerText: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
explanation: sshd reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config (plus any files it includes, such as sshd_config.d/*.conf on modern Ubuntu). ssh_config without the d configures the SSH client, not the server.

prompt: On Debian and Ubuntu, which file holds sshd, sudo, su and PAM authentication messages?
optionA: /var/log/auth.log
optionB: /var/log/kern.log
optionC: /var/log/secure
optionD: /var/log/dpkg.log
correctAnswerText: /var/log/auth.log
explanation: Debian and Ubuntu write authentication messages to /var/log/auth.log; the RHEL family uses /var/log/secure. kern.log is kernel messages and dpkg.log is package installs.

prompt: Which command lists failed login attempts recorded in btmp?
optionA: lastlog
optionB: who
optionC: lastb
optionD: last
correctAnswerText: lastb
explanation: lastb reads btmp (failed logins), last reads wtmp (successful logins and reboots), lastlog shows each user's most recent login, and who shows who is logged in now.

prompt: What does file mode 600 mean?
optionA: Everyone read and write; nobody may execute
optionB: Owner read and write; everyone else read
optionC: Owner all; group and others read and execute
optionD: Owner read and write; nobody else anything
correctAnswerText: Owner read and write; nobody else anything
explanation: Read is 4, write 2, execute 1: 6 for the owner is read+write, and 0 for group and others is nothing. That is the mode for secrets and private keys; 755 and 644 are the other two in the course's list.

prompt: Why is sudoers edited with visudo rather than a normal text editor?
optionA: It applies the change to every server in the fleet
optionB: It checks the syntax and refuses to save a broken file
optionC: It encrypts the sudoers file so users cannot read it
optionD: It records the editor's password in the sudo log
correctAnswerText: It checks the syntax and refuses to save a broken file
explanation: A syntax error in sudoers can lock everyone out of sudo. visudo locks the file, validates it and will not save an invalid version.

prompt: In the auditd rule "-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity", what does -k identity do?
optionA: Limits the watch to the user account named identity
optionB: Encrypts the matching events with a key called identity
optionC: Sends matching events to a remote host called identity
optionD: Tags matching events so ausearch -k identity finds them
correctAnswerText: Tags matching events so ausearch -k identity finds them
explanation: -k attaches a search key to events from the rule; ausearch -k identity -i retrieves them with readable names. -w sets the path to watch and -p wa selects writes and attribute changes.

prompt: What does journalctl -u ssh --since "1 hour ago" show?
optionA: Every user who connected over SSH since last boot
optionB: The SSH configuration as it was one hour ago
optionC: Journal entries from the ssh unit in the last hour
optionD: Failed logins for all services in the last hour
correctAnswerText: Journal entries from the ssh unit in the last hour
explanation: -u filters by systemd unit and --since limits the time range. The unit is ssh on Debian and Ubuntu and sshd on RHEL. Adding -o json gives one JSON object per line.

prompt: What does fail2ban do on an SSH server?
optionA: Disables password logins once a user fails one attempt
optionB: Bans an address after repeated failures via a firewall rule
optionC: Resets the password of any account that is attacked
optionD: Encrypts auth.log so attackers cannot read the failures
correctAnswerText: Bans an address after repeated failures via a firewall rule
explanation: fail2ban watches logs for repeated failures and adds a temporary firewall rule against the source address. It complements, not replaces, keys-only SSH and restricting SSH to known ranges.

prompt: What does ss -tlnp list?
optionA: Listening TCP sockets, numeric, with their process
optionB: Login sessions per user with their terminal name
optionC: Every established UDP flow and its byte count
optionD: Firewall rules in the order they are evaluated
correctAnswerText: Listening TCP sockets, numeric, with their process
explanation: -t TCP, -l listening, -n numeric addresses and ports, -p the owning process. It answers "what is listening, on which address, and which program holds it".

prompt: What are the CIS Benchmarks that auditors in Indian banks ask about?
optionA: Standard hardening checklists per OS and distribution
optionB: Speed tests that compare Linux distributions on load
optionC: Government lists of approved Linux distributions
optionD: Certificates that prove an admin passed a Linux exam
correctAnswerText: Standard hardening checklists per OS and distribution
explanation: The CIS Benchmarks are consensus configuration baselines for each operating system and distribution, and the checklist auditors usually expect hardening to be measured against.

prompt: Why does PasswordAuthentication no make an internet-facing SSH server much harder to break into?
optionA: It hides the SSH port from internet-wide scanning tools
optionB: Keys cannot be guessed, so password spraying has nothing to try
optionC: It makes sshd encrypt sessions with a stronger cipher suite
optionD: It stops root from logging in even with a valid key pair
correctAnswerText: Keys cannot be guessed, so password spraying has nothing to try
explanation: Any internet-facing server sees password attempts within minutes of booting; with only keys accepted there is nothing to guess. It does not change ciphers, hide the port, or control root (PermitRootLogin does).

prompt: Why do baselines want a personal account per engineer instead of one shared "admin" login?
optionA: Shared logins send their passwords over SSH without any encryption
optionB: Every log line then names a person, and access is removed per person
optionC: Personal accounts get faster disks and more memory from the kernel
optionD: Shared accounts cannot be given sudo rights on modern distributions
correctAnswerText: Every log line then names a person, and access is removed per person
explanation: With a shared login every action is anonymous and one leaver means changing access for all. Named accounts with sudo make auth.log record who did what, and access can be removed for one person.

prompt: When an engineer leaves, why must their entries in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys be removed as well as their password reset?
optionA: A key keeps working after a password reset
optionB: The key file grows and fills the home disk
optionC: Keys expire only when the server reboots
optionD: Old keys slow every other user's logins
correctAnswerText: A key keeps working after a password reset
explanation: Key authentication does not use the password, so a reset leaves the key valid. Remove leavers' accounts and their authorized keys together.

prompt: Why should a server's auth logs be forwarded to the SIEM rather than kept only on the host?
optionA: Forwarding makes sshd reject failed logins much more quickly
optionB: The SIEM decrypts the logs, which are unreadable on the host
optionC: Local logs are deleted by the kernel after twenty-four hours
optionD: Someone with root can truncate the local log, removing the only copy
correctAnswerText: Someone with root can truncate the local log, removing the only copy
explanation: An attacker who gains root can edit or clear /var/log/auth.log. A copy already shipped to the SIEM survives and can be correlated with other sources.

prompt: If NOPASSWD is used at all, why should it be limited to one specific command?
optionA: NOPASSWD stops sudo from logging the commands it runs
optionB: On ALL, any hijacked session becomes root with no prompt
optionC: Narrow rules make sudo run each command more quickly
optionD: sudo refuses NOPASSWD rules that name more than one user
correctAnswerText: On ALL, any hijacked session becomes root with no prompt
explanation: NOPASSWD: ALL turns any stolen session of that user into root without re-authentication. Scoped to one command, the blast radius is that command. sudo still logs NOPASSWD commands.

prompt: Why should a web service run as its own unprivileged user rather than as root?
optionA: systemd refuses to start services that are owned by root
optionB: If it is compromised, the attacker gets that user, not the machine
optionC: Unprivileged services are given more memory by the kernel
optionD: Root processes cannot bind to any port above number 1024
correctAnswerText: If it is compromised, the attacker gets that user, not the machine
explanation: A compromised root service hands over the whole host. A dedicated user with exactly the files it needs, and no login shell, contains the damage.

prompt: Why keep a second SSH session open while changing and reloading sshd settings?
optionA: Reloading closes the first session, so a spare is needed
optionB: The second session records the change in the audit log
optionC: sshd only reloads its settings when two sessions exist
optionD: A mistake cannot lock you out while one session stays open
correctAnswerText: A mistake cannot lock you out while one session stays open
explanation: Reloading sshd does not drop existing sessions, so an open one lets you fix a bad setting. Test a new login from another window before closing the session you are working in.

prompt: Why can a user get "permission denied" on a file whose own mode is 644?
optionA: Files need execute permission before they can be read
optionB: Mode 644 forbids reading by anyone other than root
optionC: A parent directory lacks execute, so it cannot be entered
optionD: The file was created on another day, so access lapsed
correctAnswerText: A parent directory lacks execute, so it cannot be entered
explanation: On a directory, execute means "may enter". Without it on a parent directory the file cannot be reached, whatever its own mode. 644 lets everyone read.

prompt: Why do identity-file watches in the course use -p wa rather than -p r?
optionA: wa makes auditd block the change, not only log it
optionB: The r flag deletes the watched file after a read
optionC: The aim is to record changes, not every routine read
optionD: auditd cannot record reads on any file in /etc
correctAnswerText: The aim is to record changes, not every routine read
explanation: Writes and attribute changes to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow and sudoers are what matter; logging every read would bury them in noise. Watches record events; they do not block anything.

prompt: Why must __REALTIME_TIMESTAMP from journalctl -o json be converted before it goes on an IST timeline?
optionA: It is milliseconds since midnight in IST
optionB: It is microseconds since the epoch in UTC
optionC: It is the date written as day, month, year
optionD: It is seconds since boot on the local clock
correctAnswerText: It is microseconds since the epoch in UTC
explanation: The value is microseconds since 1970 in UTC; convert with unit="us", utc=True and then to Asia/Kolkata. In the course the same login read 02:12 in a UTC auth.log and 07:42 IST.

prompt: Which auditd rule records writes and attribute changes to /etc/shadow under the key identity?
optionA: -a /etc/shadow -p x -k identity
optionB: -w /etc/shadow -p r -k identity
optionC: -w /etc/shadow -p rx -k identity
optionD: -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
correctAnswerText: -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
explanation: -w sets the watch, -p wa selects writes and attribute changes, and -k names the key. -p r or rx records reads and executions and misses changes; -a adds a syscall rule and does not take a path this way.

prompt: Which sudoers line, added with visudo, gives members of the sysadmins group full sudo with a password prompt?
optionA: %sysadmins ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: ALL
optionB: @sysadmins ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALLOW
optionC: sysadmins ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL
optionD: %sysadmins ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
correctAnswerText: %sysadmins ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL
explanation: The % prefix names a group, and without NOPASSWD sudo asks for the user's password. Without % the line names a user called sysadmins, the NOPASSWD versions skip re-authentication, and @ and ALLOW are not sudoers syntax.

prompt: Only deploy and anita may log in over SSH on a server. Which sshd setting does that?
optionA: AllowUsers deploy anita
optionB: PermitUsers deploy anita
optionC: MaxSessions deploy anita
optionD: DenyUsers !deploy !anita
correctAnswerText: AllowUsers deploy anita
explanation: AllowUsers (or AllowGroups ssh-users) lists who may log in; everyone else is refused. PermitUsers does not exist, MaxSessions takes a number, and DenyUsers lists who is refused.

prompt: Which command shows the events from rules tagged priv_change, with user IDs shown as names?
optionA: aureport --key priv_change -d
optionB: journalctl -k priv_change -r
optionC: auditctl -k priv_change -l
optionD: ausearch -k priv_change -i
correctAnswerText: ausearch -k priv_change -i
explanation: ausearch -k filters by key and -i interprets numeric IDs into names. auditctl -l lists loaded rules, aureport summarises rather than showing events, and journalctl -k shows kernel messages.

prompt: A service running as user payments reads /etc/payments/api.key. How should the file be set?
optionA: Owned by payments, mode 644
optionB: Owned by root, mode 777
optionC: Owned by nobody, mode 666
optionD: Owned by payments, mode 600
correctAnswerText: Owned by payments, mode 600
explanation: Secrets are 600, owned by the user that reads them. 644 lets every local user read the key, and 777 or 666 is not a fix — it is giving up.

prompt: On a RHEL server you have edited sshd_config. Which sequence applies it safely?
optionA: sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
optionB: sudo sshd -T && sudo systemctl disable sshd
optionC: sudo reboot && sudo sshd -t on the next boot
optionD: sudo systemctl stop sshd && sudo sshd -t
correctAnswerText: sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload sshd
explanation: sshd -t checks the syntax and the reload runs only if it passes; the unit is sshd on RHEL (ssh on Ubuntu). Stopping sshd first can lock you out, and rebooting to test is backwards.

prompt: Which pipeline lists the source addresses with the most "Failed password" lines in auth.log?
optionA: grep -c "Failed password" auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort -u | sort -rn
optionB: grep "Failed password" auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
optionC: grep "Failed password" auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | uniq -c | sort | head -n 1
optionD: grep "Accepted password" auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
correctAnswerText: grep "Failed password" auth.log | grep -oE "from [0-9.]+" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
explanation: Extract, sort, count, sort by count. uniq -c only merges adjacent lines, so it must follow sort; Accepted lines are successes, and grep -c prints a single number with nothing left to extract.

prompt: The event you need is a week old and auth.log has rotated into auth.log.2.gz. How do you search it?
optionA: grep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log only
optionB: tail -f /var/log/auth.log.2.gz | less
optionC: zgrep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log.2.gz
optionD: journalctl -u ssh -f to follow the logs
correctAnswerText: zgrep "Accepted" /var/log/auth.log.2.gz
explanation: zgrep searches compressed files directly. grep or tail on the live file never show rotated history, and following the journal shows only new entries.

prompt: A server writing UTC logs records "Accepted password for deploy" at 02:12:10. What time goes in your IST incident note?
explanation: IST is UTC+05:30, so 02:12:10 UTC is 07:42:10 IST. Subtracting gives the wrong day, and adding six hours ignores the half hour. Always state the zone.

prompt: A baseline wants admins to log in by name and then use sudo. Which sshd setting enforces the first half?
optionA: X11Forwarding no
optionB: PermitRootLogin yes
optionC: PermitRootLogin no
optionD: PermitEmptyPasswords no
correctAnswerText: PermitRootLogin no
explanation: PermitRootLogin no stops direct root logins, so every privileged action starts from a named account and goes through sudo. The other settings are worth having but say nothing about root.

prompt: "PasswordAuthentication no" was appended to the end of sshd_config, which already ends with a "Match Address 10.0.0.0/8" block. Passwords still work from the internet. Why?
optionA: The new line falls inside the Match block, so it applies only to 10.x
optionB: Match blocks switch off password settings for every other address
optionC: sshd ignores any setting written below line 100 of the main file
optionD: The setting needs a reboot, as a reload does not re-read the file
correctAnswerText: The new line falls inside the Match block, so it applies only to 10.x
explanation: A Match block runs until the next Match or the end of the file, so anything appended after it applies only to matching connections. Global settings go above the first Match; confirm with sshd -T.

prompt: An Ubuntu server's sshd_config sets PasswordAuthentication no near the bottom, but sshd -T shows yes. What do you check first?
optionA: Whether sshd -T reads only the default compiled settings
optionB: A file in sshd_config.d, included at the top and read first
optionC: Whether the keyword was typed in lower case in the file
optionD: Whether the server needs a reboot before sshd -T is right
correctAnswerText: A file in sshd_config.d, included at the top and read first
explanation: The Include of sshd_config.d/*.conf sits at the top and sshd keeps the first value it reads, so a drop-in such as 50-cloud-init.conf wins. sshd -T is the effective config; keywords are case-insensitive.

prompt: Your auth.log parser counts 6 failures but grep -c "Failed password" counts 12. The regex expects the user name right after "for". What is it missing?
optionA: Lines whose seconds field is 00, which the time pattern rejects
optionB: Lines from IPv4 addresses, which \S+ cannot match with dots in them
optionC: Lines written by sudo, which grep counts as SSH failures as well
optionD: Lines reading "for invalid user <name>", for names that do not exist
correctAnswerText: Lines reading "for invalid user <name>", for names that do not exist
explanation: sshd inserts "invalid user" before unknown names, and those name-guessing lines matter most. Make the prefix optional and always reconcile the parser against a plain count.

prompt: systemctl status shows a service "active (running)" since 40 seconds ago, though it was deployed three hours ago. What is the likely situation?
optionA: It was stopped by a user, and the status is out of date
optionB: It is crash-looping, and systemd keeps restarting it
optionC: It is healthy, as active (running) proves it is fine
optionD: The deploy is still running and has not yet finished
correctAnswerText: It is crash-looping, and systemd keeps restarting it
explanation: A start time far later than the deploy means it has been restarting; systemd will keep doing so and it looks alive from outside. Read the restart count and journalctl -u for the exit reason.

prompt: A service answers curl on the server itself, but not from other machines. ss -tlnp shows 127.0.0.1:8080. What is wrong?
optionA: Port 8080 is reserved for root, so remote clients are refused
optionB: The service has crashed, and ss is showing a stale old socket
optionC: It is bound to localhost, so it only accepts local connections
optionD: Remote clients need IPv6, as 127.0.0.1 is the IPv4 address
correctAnswerText: It is bound to localhost, so it only accepts local connections
explanation: 127.0.0.1 accepts only local connections; 0.0.0.0 (or a specific interface address) accepts remote ones. If it answers locally and not remotely, it is the binding, the firewall or the proxy.

prompt: From 203.0.113.45: 12 failed SSH logins across six user names, then "Accepted password for deploy", then deploy runs sudo cat /etc/shadow. What is this?
optionA: A user who forgot which account to use and finally got it right
optionB: Password guessing that succeeded, then reading password hashes
optionC: A vulnerability scan by IT that touched no data on the server
optionD: Normal key-based automation that logs every attempt as password
correctAnswerText: Password guessing that succeeded, then reading password hashes
explanation: Many names from one source followed by a password success is guessing that worked, and reading /etc/shadow is going after hashes: an incident. Disable password logins, lock deploy, rotate its credentials, block the IP and review its actions.

prompt: Key login to a server fails silently for one user, while password login still works. ~/.ssh on the server is mode 777. Why?
optionA: Mode 777 deletes authorized_keys each time sshd restarts
optionB: sshd ignores keys when ~/.ssh or authorized_keys is too open
optionC: sshd only reads keys for root, whatever the modes are
optionD: Key login needs ~/.ssh at 000 so that no one can read it
correctAnswerText: sshd ignores keys when ~/.ssh or authorized_keys is too open
explanation: With its default StrictModes, sshd refuses keys if the directory or file is writable by others; ~/.ssh should be 700 and authorized_keys 600. This is the case that catches people, because everything else looks correct.

prompt: An analyst says "nothing in auth.log for last Tuesday". It is now the following Monday and logs rotate weekly. What is the likely mistake?
optionA: auth.log never records anything that happens on a Tuesday
optionB: Tuesday's lines are in a rotated file such as auth.log.1
optionC: Rotation deletes every line older than twenty-four hours
optionD: auth.log only stores failures, so successes are elsewhere
correctAnswerText: Tuesday's lines are in a rotated file such as auth.log.1
explanation: After rotation, older events live in auth.log.1 or compressed files that grep on the live file never shows (use zgrep). Also check the log is being written at all before concluding there is nothing.

prompt: Watch rules were saved in /etc/audit/rules.d/hardening.rules, but ausearch -k identity finds nothing after a test change to /etc/passwd. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The rules were never loaded, e.g. augenrules --load was not run
optionB: Watches on /etc/passwd are ignored unless SELinux is disabled
optionC: auditd only records changes made by root, not by test users
optionD: ausearch needs the -i flag before it returns any events
correctAnswerText: The rules were never loaded, e.g. augenrules --load was not run
explanation: Rules in rules.d take effect only once loaded (augenrules --load or a restart of auditd). auditctl -l shows what is actually loaded. -i only formats output, and auditd records changes from any user.

prompt: At 03:00 a sudo line shows "deploy : USER=root ; COMMAND=/usr/sbin/useradd support2". deploy is a service account used only by the CI pipeline. How do you read it?
optionA: A log error, since service accounts are unable to run sudo at all
optionB: A new account made by an account that has no reason to: investigate
optionC: Routine CI work, since pipelines often create users during deploys
optionD: Harmless, since sudo recorded it and so it must have been allowed
correctAnswerText: A new account made by an account that has no reason to: investigate
explanation: Creating a user is outside a deploy account's job and a classic persistence step (Create Account, T1136). That sudo allowed it shows a rule that is too broad, not that it was legitimate.

prompt: Which SSH exposure design best fits the course's baseline for an internet-hosted server?
optionA: Passwords and root login allowed, with fail2ban as the control
optionB: Keys only, no root, SSH allowed only from the VPN or bastion range
optionC: Keys only, with SSH open to the whole internet on port 22
optionD: Passwords kept, but SSH moved to port 2222 so scanners miss it
correctAnswerText: Keys only, no root, SSH allowed only from the VPN or bastion range
explanation: Layer the controls: keys only, PermitRootLogin no, SSH reachable only from the VPN or bastion range, plus fail2ban and logs forwarded. Moving the port hides little, and fail2ban alone does not replace removing passwords.

prompt: A backup job running as user backup must run one script as root unattended. Which sudoers rule is the best choice?
optionA: backup ALL=(ALL:ALL) NOPASSWD: ALL for unattended use
optionB: No sudo at all, by running the backup job itself as root
optionC: %backup ALL=(ALL) ALL, with the password left in the script
optionD: backup ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/run-backup.sh
correctAnswerText: backup ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/bin/run-backup.sh
explanation: NOPASSWD scoped to one root-owned script gives the job exactly what it needs. NOPASSWD: ALL makes any compromise of backup a root compromise, a password in a script is a leaked secret, and running as root widens the blast radius.

prompt: You must report SSH hardening across 200 servers. Which method is soundest?
optionA: Read the main sshd_config on each host, since it is the full picture
optionB: Check five servers by hand and assume the others are set the same way
optionC: Run systemctl status ssh on each host and record whether it is active
optionD: Parse configs for a fast first pass, then confirm with sshd -T per host
correctAnswerText: Parse configs for a fast first pass, then confirm with sshd -T per host
explanation: A parser applying the first-value rule is a quick audit, but includes, Match blocks and defaults are resolved by sshd itself, so sshd -T on each host is the ground truth. The main file alone misses drop-ins.

prompt: Which approach to authentication logs best supports a later investigation?
optionA: Copy them to a USB drive once a month and store it in a drawer
optionB: Keep them only on the host, rotated daily and deleted after a week
optionC: Forward them to the SIEM as written, and keep local copies per policy
optionD: Disable them on busy servers, since they fill the disk too fast
correctAnswerText: Forward them to the SIEM as written, and keep local copies per policy
explanation: Near-real-time forwarding means a root attacker cannot erase the only copy, and central logs can be correlated; CERT-In's 2022 directions also expect logs to be kept. Disk pressure is solved with rotation, not by turning logging off.

prompt: An outside address got in as deploy with a password on a key-only server. Which first response set is best?
optionA: Change only the SSH port, so the same address cannot find the server
optionB: Delete auth.log, so the attacker cannot learn which accounts exist
optionC: Reboot the server, since a reboot ends the attacker's session for good
optionD: Lock deploy, rotate its keys and passwords, block the IP, review its actions
correctAnswerText: Lock deploy, rotate its keys and passwords, block the IP, review its actions
explanation: Contain (lock the account, block the source, rotate credentials), fix the cause (disable password authentication, check sshd -T), then scope what deploy did. Rebooting and port changes do not remove access, and deleting logs destroys evidence.

prompt: A server has PermitRootLogin prohibit-password. Should a baseline accept it?
optionA: No: root can still log in with a key; baselines want no
optionB: No: it lets root log in with an empty password instead
optionC: Yes: it is stronger than no, since keys are required
optionD: Yes: it blocks root entirely, the same as setting no
correctAnswerText: No: root can still log in with a key; baselines want no
explanation: prohibit-password still allows root with a key, so privileged actions are not tied to a named person. The course baseline is PermitRootLogin no, with named accounts and sudo.

prompt: How should a new internal API service be set up on a Linux host?
optionA: Its own user, no login shell, only the files it needs, run by systemd
optionB: Run as an engineer's personal account, so the logs show a name
optionC: Run as root, so it never meets a permission error in production
optionD: Run as nobody, with every file it uses set to mode 777 for ease
correctAnswerText: Its own user, no login shell, only the files it needs, run by systemd
explanation: A dedicated unprivileged user with minimal file access limits what a compromise gives. Root gives away the machine, a personal account mixes people with services, and 777 is not a fix.

prompt: With limited log budget, which auditd watches give the most defensive value?
optionA: Every read of every file under /usr and /lib
optionB: Reads of /tmp files by the web server process
optionC: Writes to passwd, shadow, sudoers and sudoers.d
optionD: Every execution of ls, cat and cd by all users
correctAnswerText: Writes to passwd, shadow, sudoers and sudoers.d
explanation: Changes to identity and privilege files are rare and important: new accounts, changed hashes, new sudo rights. Watching routine reads and common commands floods the log and hides those events.

prompt: Five engineers share an "admin" account with sudo on a payments server. What is the best change?
optionA: Named accounts, sudo through a group, then remove the shared one
optionB: Keep the shared account, but change its password every month
optionC: Keep the shared account, but allow it only during office hours
optionD: Give each engineer the root password and disable the shared one
correctAnswerText: Named accounts, sudo through a group, then remove the shared one
explanation: Named accounts make every action attributable and let access be removed per person; sudo through a group is managed in one place. Rotating a shared password or giving out root keeps everything anonymous.

prompt: How should security updates be handled on a fleet of Linux web servers?
optionA: No updates on servers that work, since updates can break services
optionB: Manual updates once a quarter, during a planned maintenance window
optionC: Updates only after an incident shows a package was vulnerable
optionD: Unattended security updates, with monitoring for failures and reboots
correctAnswerText: Unattended security updates, with monitoring for failures and reboots
explanation: Automatic security updates close known holes quickly; monitor that they apply and that needed reboots happen. Quarterly or reactive patching leaves months of known exposure on internet-facing hosts.

prompt: Which filter language does the -f option of dumpcap expect?
optionA: Wireshark display syntax, such as ip.addr == x
optionB: Zeek script syntax, using event handler blocks
optionC: Suricata rule syntax, with an action and a sid
optionD: BPF capture syntax, such as host 10.10.0.23
correctAnswerText: BPF capture syntax, such as host 10.10.0.23
explanation: dumpcap -f takes a BPF capture filter (words such as host, net, port, and, not) that decides what is saved. Display filters like ip.addr == x are Wireshark's own language for what is shown, used in the filter bar or tshark -Y.

prompt: In Zeek's conn.log, what does a conn_state of S0 record?
optionA: A SYN was seen and no reply ever came back
optionB: Traffic was seen mid-stream without a handshake
optionC: The connection was set up and closed normally
optionD: The responder refused the attempt with a reset
correctAnswerText: A SYN was seen and no reply ever came back
explanation: S0 is an attempt with no answer: dropped by something on the path, or nothing there. SF is a normal setup and close, REJ is a refusal by reset, and OTH is mid-stream traffic with no handshake seen.

prompt: Which open-source tool writes a structured log line for every connection and protocol event, leaving the judging to the analyst?
optionA: Zeek, with conn.log, dns.log, ssl.log and more
optionB: nftables, which logs only the packets it drops
optionC: tshark, which only prints packets to a screen
optionD: Suricata, with an alert for each signature hit
correctAnswerText: Zeek, with conn.log, dns.log, ssl.log and more
explanation: Zeek is a network monitor: it turns traffic into conn.log, dns.log, http.log, ssl.log and others and decides nothing on its own. Suricata is the signature engine that raises alerts on rule matches.

prompt: In a Suricata rule, what is the sid, and which range is set aside for an organisation's own local rules?
optionA: A session id; issued for each connection matched
optionB: A severity score; 1 to 10 with 10 as most severe
optionC: A sensor id; one per interface the sensor watches
optionD: A unique rule id; 1000000 to 1999999 for local rules
correctAnswerText: A unique rule id; 1000000 to 1999999 for local rules
explanation: The sid identifies the rule for its whole life and the 1000000–1999999 range is reserved for local rules. Severity comes from classtype, and rev counts the rule's revisions.

prompt: A DNS answer carries rcode 3. What does it tell the analyst?
optionA: SERVFAIL: the resolver could not finish
optionB: NXDOMAIN: the queried name does not exist
optionC: NOERROR: the name resolved to an address
optionD: REFUSED: the server would not answer it
correctAnswerText: NXDOMAIN: the queried name does not exist
explanation: rcode 3 is NXDOMAIN (filter dns.flags.rcode == 3). A few are normal typos; many from one host, especially for random names, are what makes an analyst look closer.

prompt: What is the SNI field in a TLS ClientHello?
optionA: The session key, wrapped with the server's key
optionB: The server name the client asks for, sent in clear
optionC: The client's username, sent for single sign-on
optionD: The server's certificate, sent before encryption
correctAnswerText: The server name the client asks for, sent in clear
explanation: Server Name Indication carries the hostname so the server can choose a certificate, and it travels unencrypted (unless Encrypted Client Hello is used), which is why sensors can log it for encrypted sessions.

prompt: In a first-match firewall, what should happen to a flow that matches none of the rules?
optionA: It falls to the default action, which must be deny
optionB: It is matched against the most similar rule above
optionC: It is allowed, since no rule has forbidden it yet
optionD: It is queued until an administrator approves it
correctAnswerText: It falls to the default action, which must be deny
explanation: Rules are read top to bottom and the first match acts; anything unmatched falls to the default action. Least privilege means that default is deny, so only flows someone allowed on purpose pass.

prompt: In a segmented network, what is the DMZ for?
optionA: Visitor Wi-Fi that may only reach the internet
optionB: Databases that only the app servers may reach
optionC: Public-facing servers, reachable from the internet
optionD: Admin workstations that may SSH into every zone
correctAnswerText: Public-facing servers, reachable from the internet
explanation: The DMZ holds internet-facing servers: reachable from outside on their service port and allowed to talk only to the app tier. Admin access belongs to the management zone, data stores to the data zone, and visitors to the guest zone.

prompt: What does a ZTNA access layer grant a remote user after checking identity and device?
optionA: A session to one application the role needs
optionB: A permanent pass to every company application
optionC: A route to the whole internal office network
optionD: A copy of the application to run on the laptop
correctAnswerText: A session to one application the role needs
explanation: Zero trust network access brokers a session to an individual application and re-checks per session; the user never gets a route to the subnet behind it, unlike a traditional VPN.

prompt: What is split tunnelling on a remote-access VPN?
optionA: The tunnel is split across two gateways
optionB: Every packet is encrypted by two tunnels
optionC: Two users share one tunnel to save licences
optionD: Only office-bound traffic uses the tunnel
correctAnswerText: Only office-bound traffic uses the tunnel
explanation: With split tunnelling, traffic for office networks goes through the VPN and everything else goes straight to the internet, so the office proxy and sensors never see that internet traffic.

prompt: Why does a SOC treat "capture only on networks you own or are authorised to monitor" as an absolute rule?
optionA: Captures on shared networks are always too large to analyse well
optionB: A capture holds personal data and credentials of everyone on the wire
optionC: Wireshark refuses to start on any network the user is not admin of
optionD: Unauthorised captures contain only encrypted traffic, so are useless
correctAnswerText: A capture holds personal data and credentials of everyone on the wire
explanation: A pcap contains whatever crossed the wire: names, cookies, sometimes clear-text passwords and personal data covered by the DPDP Act. Deleting it afterwards does not undo capturing it. The tool does not enforce authorisation; the analyst must.

prompt: Why is a stateful firewall safer than a stateless ACL when letting replies back in?
optionA: It blocks every inbound packet, so replies never have to be judged
optionB: It admits only packets belonging to connections it already allowed
optionC: It encrypts reply traffic so nobody outside can inject packets in
optionD: It checks each reply against antivirus signatures before allowing it
correctAnswerText: It admits only packets belonging to connections it already allowed
explanation: A stateless filter needs a rule for replies, and that rule admits anything that looks like a reply. A stateful firewall keeps a connection table and drops unsolicited packets that belong to no permitted connection.

prompt: Why is the order of rules part of the policy in most firewalls?
optionA: Rules lower in the list are checked less often and so are less reliable
optionB: Later rules are applied only when the firewall is under heavy traffic load
optionC: Deny rules are evaluated after all allow rules whatever their position is
optionD: The first rule that matches decides, so a broad allow can hide a later deny
correctAnswerText: The first rule that matches decides, so a broad allow can hide a later deny
explanation: In first-match firewalls a deny placed below a broader allow is shadowed: it still looks right in review and never fires. Specific rules and denies go above broad allows.

prompt: Why are DNS logs valuable to a SOC even when most web traffic is encrypted?
optionA: DNS queries carry the full contents of every page a user requested and opened
optionB: Encrypted traffic is always resolved twice, so DNS logs hold a backup of each session
optionC: DNS logs record the passwords users type, which helps with account investigations
optionD: Nearly every connection starts with a lookup, so they map what each host tried to reach
correctAnswerText: Nearly every connection starts with a lookup, so they map what each host tried to reach
explanation: A lookup precedes most connections, so the resolver's log shows what every machine wanted to reach even when the connection itself is TLS. DNS carries names and answers, not page contents or credentials.

prompt: Why is a high-entropy DNS label, on its own, only a weak sign of DNS used as a channel?
optionA: Entropy can only be measured on labels shorter than ten letters
optionB: CDNs and some security products also use long encoded labels
optionC: Entropy measures packet size, which DNS keeps the same anyway
optionD: Channels over DNS always use words, which give a low entropy
correctAnswerText: CDNs and some security products also use long encoded labels
explanation: Legitimate services produce random-looking hex or encoded labels too, so entropy alone gives false positives. It becomes strong combined with length, volume, one host, one parent domain and failure codes.

prompt: Why does tighter egress filtering matter even when inbound rules are already strict?
optionA: It removes the need for email filtering against phishing campaigns
optionB: It stops attackers on the internet opening connections to internal hosts
optionC: It limits what an infected host inside can do: call out and upload data
optionD: It speeds up browsing because fewer outbound rules need to be checked
correctAnswerText: It limits what an infected host inside can do: call out and upload data
explanation: Most organisations filter inbound and allow all outbound, which is how beacons, tool downloads and uploads leave. Egress rules restrict an already-compromised host; inbound connections are an ingress matter.

prompt: Why is a Suricata rule that alerts on every single TCP SYN useless as a scan detection?
optionA: Suricata cannot see SYN packets unless it is running inline as an IPS
optionB: Rules on TCP flags need a sid outside the local range before they load
optionC: SYN packets are encrypted, so the rule can never read their TCP flags
optionD: A lone SYN is normal; only many from one source in a short time is rare
correctAnswerText: A lone SYN is normal; only many from one source in a short time is rare
explanation: Every connection starts with a SYN, so the rule fires on all normal traffic and gets ignored. A threshold (for example 50 SYNs from one source in 10 seconds) separates the rare from the normal.

prompt: Why does "the edge sensor saw nothing" fail to rule out traffic between two laptops on one switch?
optionA: Edge sensors discard internal traffic to save disk once they see it
optionB: That traffic never passes the edge sensor, so its silence proves nothing
optionC: Laptop traffic is always encrypted, so sensors cannot log any of it
optionD: Two laptops on one switch cannot exchange traffic in the first place
correctAnswerText: That traffic never passes the edge sensor, so its silence proves nothing
explanation: Sensors see only what passes them. Traffic inside one switch, unmirrored cloud traffic and VPN traffic that ends beyond the sensor are invisible to it, so endpoint and switch logs are needed.

prompt: Why are VPN gateways and other edge devices patched ahead of most internal servers?
optionA: They hold every user's files, so an outage would lose company data
optionB: They are reachable from the whole internet and lead into the network
optionC: They are the slowest devices, so patches improve remote performance
optionD: They are replaced every year, so patching them later wastes effort
correctAnswerText: They are reachable from the whole internet and lead into the network
explanation: Edge devices face the internet and sit at the door to the internal network, which makes them heavily targeted (External Remote Services, T1133). Watch them for new admin accounts and configuration changes too.

prompt: Why should an analyst require something like ten or more sessions before trusting a low coefficient of variation as a beacon sign?
optionA: The coefficient of variation cannot be computed on fewer sessions
optionB: A handful of gaps can look clock-like by chance; many gaps cannot
optionC: Beacons always connect at least ten times before sending any data
optionD: Fewer sessions mean the traffic is encrypted and timing is hidden
correctAnswerText: A handful of gaps can look clock-like by chance; many gaps cannot
explanation: In the course capture three ordinary browsing sessions scored cv 0.01 by chance, while twelve beacon sessions scored 0.02. Three gaps prove nothing; twelve do. Even then, legitimate agents beacon too, so find the process.

prompt: Which Wireshark display filter shows only new connection attempts to port 3389?
optionA: tcp.flags.syn == 1 || tcp.flags.ack == 0 || tcp.dstport == 3389
optionB: tcp.flags.reset == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 && tcp.port == 3389
optionC: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 && tcp.dstport == 3389
optionD: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 1 && tcp.dstport == 3389
correctAnswerText: tcp.flags.syn == 1 && tcp.flags.ack == 0 && tcp.dstport == 3389
explanation: The first packet of a handshake has SYN set and ACK clear, and dstport limits it to RDP. With ACK set you get the SYN-ACK replies, the || version matches almost everything, and reset matches refusals.

prompt: You must save five minutes of traffic for 192.168.1.10 only, leaving out your own SSH session. Which dumpcap capture filter fits?
optionC: -f "ip.src == 192.168.1.10 and tcp"
optionD: -f "host 192.168.1.10 and not port 22"
correctAnswerText: -f "host 192.168.1.10 and not port 22"
explanation: Capture filters use BPF words: host, port, and, not. The == and ! forms are display-filter syntax and fail with -f; the "or port 22" version adds SSH instead of excluding it.

prompt: Rules, top to bottom: 1 allow 10.20.1.0/24 to 10.20.2.10 tcp 8080; 2 deny 10.20.4.0/24 to 10.20.3.0/24 any; 3 allow 10.20.4.0/24 to 0.0.0.0/0 any; then default deny. What happens to 10.20.4.33 to 10.20.9.5 on tcp 3389?
optionA: Rule 1 allows it, since it is the first rule in the list
optionB: Rule 3 allows it, since 0.0.0.0/0 covers internal hosts
optionC: Rule 2 denies it, since it comes before the broad allow
optionD: The default denies it, since no rule names port 3389
correctAnswerText: Rule 3 allows it, since 0.0.0.0/0 covers internal hosts
explanation: 10.20.9.5 is not in 10.20.3.0/24, so rule 2 does not match; rule 3 matches because 0.0.0.0/0 includes internal ranges. That is the gap: "internet access" written as 0.0.0.0/0 lets users reach admin workstations on RDP.

prompt: A small firm puts its CCTV recorders and printer in an IOT zone. Which rule fits the course's design for that zone?
optionA: IOT to the management zone on 22 and 3389, ALLOW, for remote support
optionB: IOT to any, any protocol, ALLOW, since cameras need cloud viewing apps
optionC: IOT to any, any protocol, DENY and logged, below the few needed allows
optionD: IOT to the internet on 80 and 443 only, ALLOW, as for the staff zone
correctAnswerText: IOT to any, any protocol, DENY and logged, below the few needed allows
explanation: Cameras and printers need no internet or internal access beyond their specific flows (printing from staff to one printer, cameras to their recorder). A logged deny shows the SOC any device trying to reach where it should not.

prompt: An ET Open rule for curl user agents fires thousands of times a day, almost all from build servers in 10.40.8.0/24. Which threshold.config line keeps it useful?
optionA: suppress gen_id 1, sig_id <sid>, track by_dst, ip 0.0.0.0/0
optionB: suppress gen_id 1, sig_id <sid>, track by_src, ip 10.40.8.0/24
optionC: threshold gen_id 1, sig_id <sid>, type limit, count 1, seconds 86400
optionD: disable the sid in suricata-update so the rule is no longer loaded
correctAnswerText: suppress gen_id 1, sig_id <sid>, track by_src, ip 10.40.8.0/24
explanation: Suppressing by source for the build subnet silences only the expected traffic; curl from a finance laptop still alerts. Suppressing for every address or disabling the rule blinds you, and a one-a-day limit hides all but the first.

prompt: A Zeek conn.log row converts to 04:44:20 UTC. The user reported the problem in Mumbai office time. What time do you put on the IST timeline?
optionA: 10:14:20 IST, since IST is UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes
optionB: 09:44:20 IST, since IST is UTC plus exactly five hours
optionC: 04:44:20 IST, since Zeek already writes the sensor's local time
optionD: 23:14:20 IST the previous day, as IST is behind UTC
correctAnswerText: 10:14:20 IST, since IST is UTC plus 5 hours 30 minutes
explanation: Zeek's ts is UTC epoch seconds. IST is UTC+05:30, so 04:44:20 UTC is 10:14:20 IST. State the zone in every note; mixing UTC and local time is a classic timeline error.

prompt: One host sends a stream of 60-character random labels, all under the single parent t.example.net, and every answer is NXDOMAIN. Which reading fits best?
optionA: A failed internal resolver answering NXDOMAIN to everything
optionB: An ordinary browser pre-fetching links on a long news page
optionC: A domain generation algorithm trying many unrelated domains
optionD: Possible DNS used as a channel to one domain's name server
correctAnswerText: Possible DNS used as a channel to one domain's name server
explanation: Many random labels under one parent suggests data carried in the name to that domain's server (T1071.004); the NXDOMAIN answer does not matter to such a channel. A DGA spreads across many domains, and a broken resolver would affect every host.

prompt: An account logs in to the VPN from Pune at 14:05 and from Frankfurt at 14:25. What should the analyst do first?
optionA: Close the case, as VPN exits often show other countries
optionB: End the Pune session, since the foreign one must be real
optionC: Review both sessions and confirm with the user by phone
optionD: Email the user at that account to ask which login it was
correctAnswerText: Review both sessions and confirm with the user by phone
explanation: Two places too far apart for 20 minutes suggest a stolen credential. Check device, IP and activity for both and verify out of band; emailing the possibly compromised account and guessing which session is genuine are both mistakes.

prompt: How do you read this line: "[DROP-USERS-DB] IN=eth2 OUT=eth3 SRC=10.20.4.33 DST=10.20.3.5 PROTO=TCP DPT=5432 SYN"?
optionA: A firewall fault, since denied packets are never written to the log
optionB: An established database session was reset after the transfer was done
optionC: The database server opened a session to a user host and it was allowed
optionD: A user host's new connection to the database port was dropped by that rule
correctAnswerText: A user host's new connection to the database port was dropped by that rule
explanation: The prefix names the rule, IN and OUT the interfaces, SRC and DST the hosts, DPT=5432 the PostgreSQL port, and SYN a new connection attempt. The rule worked; the question is why a user host tried the database.

prompt: You want an alert whenever an internal host starts a TCP connection to the watched address 203.0.113.50. Which rule header is right?
optionA: drop tcp any any -> 203.0.113.50 any offline
optionB: alert tcp 203.0.113.50 any -> $HOME_NET any
optionC: alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 443
optionD: alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> 203.0.113.50 any
correctAnswerText: alert tcp $HOME_NET any -> 203.0.113.50 any
explanation: The traffic flows from inside to the watched address, so the source is $HOME_NET and the destination 203.0.113.50 (with flags:S to catch the start). The reversed headers match the wrong direction, and drop needs inline IPS mode, not an offline read.

prompt: The display filter dns.qry.name == "example.net" shows zero packets, yet a host queried many names under example.net. Why?
optionA: == compares the whole name, and none is exactly example.net
optionB: dns.qry.name only exists for the answers, not for the queries
optionC: Display filters cannot be used on UDP traffic such as DNS
optionD: DNS names are stored in upper case, so the match is missed
correctAnswerText: == compares the whole name, and none is exactly example.net
explanation: Queries like abc.t.example.net never equal "example.net". Use contains ".example.net" or matches, and first confirm with a bare dns filter that the packets you expect are there before narrowing.

prompt: A new sensor's local rules written with $HOME_NET never fire. suricata.yaml sets HOME_NET to 192.168.0.0/16, but the office uses 10.30.0.0/16. What is the diagnosis?
optionA: HOME_NET does not describe the network, so those rules cannot match
optionB: Private 10.x addresses are always ignored by Suricata by design
optionC: Local rules only fire after the ET Open rule set has been loaded too
optionD: Suricata needs a restart for each rule before any of them can fire
correctAnswerText: HOME_NET does not describe the network, so those rules cannot match
explanation: Rules written with $HOME_NET only match traffic involving that range; a wrong HOME_NET silently disables them. Fix the variable, then test each rule against a capture known to contain a match.

prompt: During a review, every rule below position 1 has zero hits for six months. Rule 1 is "any to any, allow", added during an outage last year. What does that show?
optionA: Rule 1 shadows the whole policy; every rule below it is dead
optionB: Hit counters only count the first rule, which is normal
optionC: The firewall is idle, since zero hits mean no traffic passed
optionD: The lower rules are working and simply never needed to fire
correctAnswerText: Rule 1 shadows the whole policy; every rule below it is dead
explanation: A temporary allow-any at the top matches everything first, so nothing beneath it ever decides. Sorting rules by hit count and by date added finds it; remove it through a change request.

prompt: A ticket says "the firewall is blocking 10.10.0.10 on port 23 — we saw resets". The capture shows SYN then RST-ACK from 10.10.0.10. Which correction is accurate?
optionA: The firewall dropped the SYN and then sent the reset on its behalf
optionB: The connection succeeded and closed, so port 23 is open and in use
optionC: The host itself refused: it is up, with nothing listening on 23
optionD: The host is down, so the switch answered the SYN with a reset
correctAnswerText: The host itself refused: it is up, with nothing listening on 23
explanation: A RST-ACK from the server's own address in reply to a SYN is the host refusing a closed port. A dropping firewall shows silence (S0 in Zeek); a rejecting one is checked by source address and TTL.

prompt: Run offline over a hand-built pcap, Suricata produces no alerts at all, while Zeek with -C logs every connection from the same file. What is the likely cause?
optionA: Offline mode disables every alert rule unless the rule action is drop
optionB: Bad checksums: Suricata discards the packets unless run with -k none
optionC: Zeek consumed the packets first, leaving nothing for Suricata to read
optionD: Suricata only reads live interfaces and never processes pcap files
correctAnswerText: Bad checksums: Suricata discards the packets unless run with -k none
explanation: Hand-built captures and captures taken on the sending host often have uncomputed checksums; -k none stops Suricata discarding them, as -C does for Zeek. Suricata reads pcaps with -r and alert rules work offline.

prompt: Host A made 3 sessions to a site with cv 0.01; host B made 40 sessions to one address with cv 0.04. Which is stronger evidence of automated check-ins?
optionA: Host A, because its cv is the lower of the two
optionB: Both equally, since any cv under 0.1 is proof
optionC: Host B, because 40 regular gaps cannot be chance
optionD: Neither, since cv only applies to UDP traffic
correctAnswerText: Host B, because 40 regular gaps cannot be chance
explanation: A low cv over many sessions is strong; over three it can happen by chance. Even host B is a question, not proof: monitoring agents and updaters beacon too, so the next step is identifying the process.

prompt: A host shows long encoded DNS queries under one domain and minute-by-minute HTTPS sessions to one address. Which fact would most weaken the case for escalation?
optionA: The domain belongs to a security product the company runs
optionB: The DNS answers were all NXDOMAIN rather than NOERROR
optionC: The host is a desktop rather than a server in a data zone
optionD: The HTTPS sessions are encrypted, so contents are unknown
correctAnswerText: The domain belongs to a security product the company runs
explanation: Some antivirus and reputation services use long encoded DNS names, so confirming the domain is the company's own product explains the pattern. Encryption, NXDOMAIN answers and the host type do not.

prompt: An analyst closes a case with "the proxy logs show no suspicious connections from that remote laptop". The VPN uses split tunnelling. What is the flaw?
optionA: Proxy logs drop all HTTPS entries for laptops on the VPN
optionB: That laptop's internet traffic never passed the office proxy
optionC: Split tunnelling sends everything through the proxy twice
optionD: Remote laptops cannot make any internet connections at all
correctAnswerText: That laptop's internet traffic never passed the office proxy
explanation: With split tunnelling only office-bound traffic uses the tunnel; browsing goes straight out, so the proxy never saw it. Endpoint telemetry has to cover that laptop before "no suspicious connections" can be said.

prompt: Firewall logs show a database server in the data zone trying to reach an internet address on 443 every five minutes, always denied. What is the right reading?
optionA: Normal behaviour, since every server checks the internet for its time
optionB: A firewall fault, as servers in the data zone cannot generate traffic
optionC: A data-zone server should not start internet connections; find the process
optionD: Harmless, because each attempt was denied and nothing left the zone
correctAnswerText: A data-zone server should not start internet connections; find the process
explanation: Servers that only serve requests rarely need outbound internet access, and a regular, denied call-out is either a misconfigured updater or something beaconing. The deny protected you; the host still needs checking.

prompt: VPN logs show one external address failing a login once or twice against each of 200 different accounts within an hour. What pattern is this?
optionA: One user who has forgotten a password and keeps trying
optionB: Normal start of day, as staff log in at the same hour
optionC: MFA fatigue: repeated push prompts to a single user
optionD: Password spraying: a few guesses across many accounts
correctAnswerText: Password spraying: a few guesses across many accounts
explanation: Few attempts per account across many accounts from one source is password spraying (T1110.003), designed to stay under lockout thresholds. MFA fatigue targets one user with prompts after the password is known.

prompt: A noisy rule floods the SOC. Which handling best keeps the sensor useful?
optionA: Suppress it for the known source, record why, and set a review date
optionB: Raise its priority so the flood is noticed and cleared more quickly
optionC: Disable the rule entirely, since noisy rules train people to ignore it
optionD: Leave it as it is, since every alert must be reviewed by an analyst
correctAnswerText: Suppress it for the known source, record why, and set a review date
explanation: Count, find the expected source, suppress for that source only, record who approved it and when to review it, then verify. Disabling hides the rare true positive; leaving the flood means real alerts get ignored.

prompt: A 300-person company moving to remote work asks: VPN or zero trust? Which recommendation best fits the course?
optionA: ZTNA alone at once, switching off every VPN on the first day
optionB: Neither, since remote staff should work only from the office
optionC: ZTNA for web and SaaS apps, a VPN kept for the few legacy systems
optionD: A VPN for everything, since it already encrypts all remote traffic
correctAnswerText: ZTNA for web and SaaS apps, a VPN kept for the few legacy systems
explanation: Most organisations run both for years: per-application ZTNA with identity and device checks for most apps, a VPN for legacy systems that need network access, and admins through a hardened jump host.

prompt: The SOC has one sensor at the internet edge and budget for one more. Which placement adds the most visibility?
optionA: On the printer subnet, which has the most devices
optionB: On the guest Wi-Fi, which carries visitors' traffic
optionC: Next to the edge sensor, on the same internet link
optionD: Between the user zone and the server and data zones
correctAnswerText: Between the user zone and the server and data zones
explanation: The edge sensor already sees internet traffic; the blind spot is internal movement towards servers and data. A second sensor on the same link adds nothing new, and guest or printer subnets carry the least valuable flows.

prompt: You suspect DNS tunnelling from one host to t.example.net. Should you block the domain yourself right away?
optionA: Escalate with evidence and let the IR lead decide when to block
optionB: Wipe the host first and look at the DNS evidence afterwards
optionC: Block at once and close the case, since the channel is now cut
optionD: Do nothing, since NXDOMAIN answers mean no data has left yet
correctAnswerText: Escalate with evidence and let the IR lead decide when to block
explanation: Blocking tells whoever runs the domain they have been noticed, and the incident lead may want to scope first. Escalate promptly with query names, times and related sessions; regulatory timelines such as CERT-In's six hours make delay costly too.

prompt: A 40-person firm has one flat network for laptops, file servers, CCTV and guest Wi-Fi. Which design best follows least privilege?
optionA: One flat network kept, but with stronger passwords on every server
optionB: Guest Wi-Fi removed, with visitors using the staff network instead
optionC: Separate VLANs for each floor, with every VLAN allowed to reach all
optionD: Zones by trust, default deny between them, each allow with a reason
correctAnswerText: Zones by trust, default deny between them, each allow with a reason
explanation: Group machines by trust and function, deny by default between zones, and write each allow with a source, destination, port and reason. VLANs that can all reach each other are still flat, and passwords do not stop lateral spread.

prompt: Which outbound policy suits an internal application server that only serves requests?
optionA: Allow all outbound traffic, since servers rarely get infected at all
optionB: Block all outbound traffic, including updates and the time servers
optionC: Allow outbound on 80 and 443 to anywhere, as for the staff laptops
optionD: Allow only named update mirrors or the proxy, deny and log the rest
correctAnswerText: Allow only named update mirrors or the proxy, deny and log the rest
explanation: A server that only answers requests rarely needs to start internet connections, so allow its specific needs and log denies; a denied call-out is then a strong signal. Blocking updates and time sync creates its own risk.

prompt: A rule "STAFF to 0.0.0.0/0, any, ALLOW — internet access" lets staff reach internal zones. What is the best fix?
optionA: Change 0.0.0.0/0 to 0.0.0.0/32 so the rule only matches the single internet
optionB: A deny from staff to internal ranges placed above it, or an internet-only object
optionC: Move the rule to the bottom, so that the default deny is checked before it
optionD: Delete the rule and let staff reach the internet through the DMZ servers
correctAnswerText: A deny from staff to internal ranges placed above it, or an internet-only object
explanation: 0.0.0.0/0 includes every internal address. An explicit deny to internal ranges above it, or a destination group meaning internet only, makes the rule say what its comment says. 0.0.0.0/32 matches one address, and default deny is always last.

prompt: You are asked to hunt for beacons across the whole company. Which approach is soundest?
optionA: Reading the full packet capture of every host by hand once each week
optionB: Blocking every outbound connection that happens on a fixed timer at once
optionC: An alert on any host that connects to the same address twice within a day
optionD: Zeek conn logs, periodicity with a minimum count, then known agents allow-listed
correctAnswerText: Zeek conn logs, periodicity with a minimum count, then known agents allow-listed
explanation: Measure gaps per client and server over enough sessions, then remove known software (antivirus, monitoring, chat) by allow-list with owners. Alerting on any repeat floods you, auto-blocking breaks legitimate agents, and reading pcaps by hand does not scale.

prompt: How should administrators reach internal servers in a zero-trust design?
optionA: From any office desk, because the office network is trusted by definition
optionB: Through a hardened jump host in the management zone, with MFA and logging
optionC: From the DMZ, because it already sits in front of every other network zone
optionD: Directly from their usual laptops, over the VPN, with any port allowed open
correctAnswerText: Through a hardened jump host in the management zone, with MFA and logging
explanation: Admin protocols should come only from a small, hardened management path with strong authentication and every session logged. Admin access from ordinary laptops or the DMZ is the lateral path segmentation exists to remove.

prompt: Which logging design best supports building incident timelines across firewalls, sensors and VPN?
optionA: Logs are kept only on the firewall, as it sees every flow on the network
optionB: Clocks synchronised, logs sent centrally, kept per policy, times in one zone
optionC: Only denied traffic is logged, since allowed traffic is not suspicious
optionD: Each device keeps its own local logs in its own time zone for one week
correctAnswerText: Clocks synchronised, logs sent centrally, kept per policy, times in one zone
explanation: Correlation needs synchronised clocks, central collection and a single stated time zone; CERT-In's 2022 directions also expect logs kept (180 days) and clocks synchronised. Allowed flows matter as much as denies, and no single device sees everything.

prompt: Which category sits at A01, the top position, in the 2021 edition of the OWASP Top 10?
optionA: Broken Access Control
optionB: Injection
optionC: Security Misconfiguration
optionD: Cryptographic Failures
correctAnswerText: Broken Access Control
explanation: The 2021 edition moved Broken Access Control to first place because it was found in the largest share of tested applications. Injection, long the top item, dropped to A03; Cryptographic Failures is A02 and Security Misconfiguration A05.

prompt: Which defence removes SQL injection as a category instead of trying to filter it out?
optionA: Escaping single quotes in every user input field
optionB: Wrapping each query inside a database transaction block
optionC: Parameterised queries with values bound separately
optionD: Blocking SQL keywords such as UNION in requests
correctAnswerText: Parameterised queries with values bound separately
explanation: With a bound parameter the value travels apart from the statement and is never parsed as SQL, so there is nothing to break out of. Hand escaping and keyword blocklists are filters that can be defeated (and the blocklist rejects real names); a transaction controls atomicity, not parsing.

prompt: What is the primary fix for cross-site scripting, which the 2021 list files under Injection?
optionA: Store user content in a separate database table
optionB: Encode output for the context it is written into
optionC: Strip script tags from input before saving it
optionD: Reject any input that contains angle brackets
correctAnswerText: Encode output for the context it is written into
explanation: XSS is injection with the browser as the parser, so the fix is escaping at output for the exact context: HTML body, attribute, script or URL. Stripping script tags misses event-handler attributes, and rejecting angle brackets breaks real text while missing non-HTML contexts. Where data is stored changes nothing.

prompt: Which of these flaws belongs in the Cryptographic Failures category?
optionA: An admin page still using its vendor default login
optionB: A library two major versions out of date
optionC: Passwords stored with a fast hash and no salt
optionD: A search box that pastes input into its SQL
correctAnswerText: Passwords stored with a fast hash and no salt
explanation: Cryptographic Failures covers sensitive data protected weakly or not at all: fast unsalted password hashes, plaintext transport, hard-coded keys. The search box is Injection, default credentials are Security Misconfiguration, and the stale library is Vulnerable and Outdated Components.

prompt: What does Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF), A10 in the 2021 list, describe?
optionA: The server fetching a URL a user supplied, reaching hosts it should not
optionB: A script saved in a comment running in other users' browsers later
optionC: The browser sending a forged request that carries the user's cookie
optionD: A user reading another customer's record by changing an id in the URL
correctAnswerText: The server fetching a URL a user supplied, reaching hosts it should not
explanation: In SSRF the application itself makes an outbound request to a destination the user controls, which can reach internal services and cloud metadata the user never could. The forged browser request is CSRF, the changed id is broken access control, and the saved script is stored XSS.

prompt: An app records no failed logins and raises no alert on repeated access denials. Which category is that?
optionA: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
optionB: Software and Data Integrity Failures
optionC: Identification and Authentication Failures
optionD: Security Misconfiguration
correctAnswerText: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
explanation: Not recording or alerting on security-relevant events is A09, Security Logging and Monitoring Failures; it is what turns a quick catch into a breach found months later. Authentication failures are weaknesses in the login itself, and integrity failures concern unverified code and data.

prompt: Which cookie attribute stops the browser attaching the session cookie to a cross-site POST?
optionA: SameSite=Lax
optionB: HttpOnly
optionC: Path=/
optionD: Secure
correctAnswerText: SameSite=Lax
explanation: SameSite=Lax withholds the cookie on cross-site POSTs, which blocks the classic forged form submission. HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts, Secure limits it to HTTPS, and Path scopes it within the site; none of them stops it being sent cross-site.

prompt: Which response header tells the browser which scripts may run, limiting XSS when escaping fails?
optionA: Content-Security-Policy
optionB: X-Frame-Options
optionC: Strict-Transport-Security
optionD: X-Content-Type-Options
correctAnswerText: Content-Security-Policy
explanation: A Content Security Policy declares the allowed script sources, so injected inline script does not run even when an encoding bug slips through. HSTS forces HTTPS, X-Frame-Options limits framing, and X-Content-Type-Options stops MIME sniffing.

prompt: Which kind of tool finds third-party libraries with known vulnerabilities in a build?
optionA: A web application firewall in block mode
optionB: Dynamic scanning of the live app (DAST)
optionC: Static analysis of your own code (SAST)
optionD: Software composition analysis (SCA)
correctAnswerText: Software composition analysis (SCA)
explanation: SCA reads the dependency manifest and lock file and matches each component and version against vulnerability databases, which is how Vulnerable and Outdated Components is found. SAST reads first-party code, DAST probes the running app, and a WAF filters traffic without inventorying anything.

prompt: Which control best defends a login page against credential stuffing?
optionA: Passwords encrypted with one shared server key
optionB: Multi-factor authentication plus login rate limits
optionC: An error message naming which field was wrong
optionD: Longer session timeouts for all returning customers
correctAnswerText: Multi-factor authentication plus login rate limits
explanation: Credential stuffing replays passwords leaked elsewhere, so a second factor makes a correct password insufficient and rate limits slow the replay. Longer sessions do nothing, a field-specific error helps enumerate accounts, and reversible encryption of passwords is itself a cryptographic failure.

prompt: Why do parameterised queries succeed where hand-written escaping keeps failing?
optionA: The statement runs with fewer privileges than an ad hoc SQL string
optionB: The driver escapes characters more thoroughly than hand-written code
optionC: The value travels apart from the statement and is never parsed as SQL
optionD: The database checks every value against a list of dangerous keywords
correctAnswerText: The value travels apart from the statement and is never parsed as SQL
explanation: Binding is not better escaping: the value never becomes part of the statement text, so there is no quoting to escape from. Escaping has to anticipate every character set and quoting rule, which is why it is repeatedly defeated. Keyword checks and privileges are unrelated to how the statement is parsed.

prompt: Why can a web application firewall not fix broken access control?
optionA: The unauthorised request is valid HTTP that only the app can judge
optionB: Access control flaws occur only over encrypted connections
optionC: WAFs inspect only response bodies and never any request parameters
optionD: WAF rules are restricted to injection signatures by design
correctAnswerText: The unauthorised request is valid HTTP that only the app can judge
explanation: A request for another customer's record looks exactly like a request for your own; only the application knows who owns the record. WAFs do inspect requests and run many rule types, and encryption is terminated before the WAF in most designs, so the other reasons are false.

prompt: Why is hiding the admin button in the UI not an access control?
optionA: Server-side checks are needed only to produce an audit trail
optionB: Hidden buttons slow page rendering for every legitimate user
optionC: Any client can send the admin request directly, without the UI
optionD: Browsers cache hidden elements and later display them again
correctAnswerText: Any client can send the admin request directly, without the UI
explanation: The UI is only one client; a script or proxy can call the endpoint without it. Authorisation must be checked in the server on every request, deny by default. The performance, audit and caching reasons are not why it fails.

prompt: Why is encoding at output preferred to sanitising user content at input time?
optionA: Only at output is the context known, and stored data stays intact
optionB: Browsers ignore sanitised input unless it is encoded twice
optionC: Output encoding also prevents SQL injection in the same step
optionD: Sanitising at input is slower because it must run on every request
correctAnswerText: Only at output is the context known, and stored data stays intact
explanation: The same string needs different escaping in HTML, an attribute, a script block or a URL, and at input time you do not know where it will be shown; sanitising there also corrupts the stored data. Output encoding does nothing for SQL, which needs binding, and the other two claims are false.

prompt: Why does requiring a logged-in session do nothing to stop cross-site request forgery?
optionA: The forged request reuses a session id that had expired some time earlier
optionB: The session lookup is skipped for any request from another origin
optionC: The attacker reads the session cookie and copies it into the request
