prompt: A threat model lists 40 risks, each marked "mitigate" with no rank or owner; six months later nothing has changed. What went wrong?
optionA: The model ought to have been written by an external auditor
optionB: The diagram had too many trust boundaries for the team to review
optionC: Question 3 was never really answered: no rank, owner or decision
optionD: Too few STRIDE categories were applied at each of the boundaries
correctAnswerText: Question 3 was never really answered: no rank, owner or decision
explanation: "What are we going to do about it?" is where most models fail: when everything is mitigate and nothing is ranked or owned, nothing is done. Rank, fix the top few, accept or eliminate explicitly. More STRIDE passes or an outside author would produce a longer list with the same outcome.

prompt: A diagram shows no boundary between a web app and a third-party analytics script it loads into its pages. What has the model missed?
optionA: The analytics vendor's own data-centre network
optionB: The CDN cache in front of the static assets
optionC: The read replica used for reporting queries
optionD: Outside code running with the page's full trust
correctAnswerText: Outside code running with the page's full trust
explanation: A script loaded into the page runs with the same access as the app's own code, including to anything JavaScript can read, so it is a crossing from a less-trusted party. The vendor's network, the replica and the CDN may matter, but they are not what this omission hides.

prompt: A finding reads "Spoofing: users can read other users' invoices by changing the id in the URL". What is wrong with it?
optionA: It is denial of service, as invoices get blocked
optionB: It is repudiation, since users can deny reading
optionC: Nothing; changing an id is a form of spoofing
optionD: It is disclosure through a missing access check
correctAnswerText: It is disclosure through a missing access check
explanation: The user is authenticated as themselves, so nobody is impersonated; what fails is the ownership check, and the consequence is information disclosure. The right category points at the right control: a server-side check that the invoice belongs to the caller.

prompt: An incident came in through a webhook added last quarter; the system's threat model is dated two years ago. What does this show?
optionA: The original STRIDE pass was run by the wrong people
optionB: The model was not rerun when a new boundary appeared
optionC: The risk had been accepted and needed no more action
optionD: Webhooks cannot be shown on data-flow diagrams at all
correctAnswerText: The model was not rerun when a new boundary appeared
explanation: A new inbound integration is a new trust boundary, and the model should have been revisited when it was added. Nothing suggests the original authors were wrong, webhooks are ordinary flows on a DFD, and an undocumented risk was never accepted.

prompt: A team ranks a nation-state supply-chain compromise above default admin credentials on an internet-facing panel. What is the flaw?
optionA: Neither risk belongs in an application threat model
optionB: Impact ignored: the supply-chain compromise is minor
optionC: Likelihood ignored: scanners find default passwords first
optionD: Default credentials are configuration, not a risk at all
correctAnswerText: Likelihood ignored: scanners find default passwords first
explanation: Automated scanners probe exposed panels within minutes for default passwords, so that risk is near-certain and cheap to fix. Ranking by the most dramatic scenario puts the rare one first. Both belong in the model, and a configuration weakness is very much a risk.

prompt: A known risk was "accepted" aloud in a meeting, but no record names who decided. After a breach, how should it be classed?
optionA: As eliminated, once the meeting had closed it
optionB: As an unexamined risk, not an accepted one
optionC: As mitigated, since the team was aware of it
optionD: As transferred, since the meeting discussed it
correctAnswerText: As an unexamined risk, not an accepted one
explanation: Acceptance is a decision, and the record is what makes it one: who weighed it, on what basis, when to revisit. Without it the risk was simply left open. Awareness is not mitigation, and talking about a risk transfers or removes nothing.

prompt: A design relies on the mobile app to check a discount code before the order API receives it. Which flawed assumption should the reviewer name?
optionA: "It is behind the VPN"; the app needs a tunnel
optionB: "That id is unguessable"; discounts need UUIDs
optionC: "Nobody knows that endpoint"; the API needs a WAF
optionD: "The client validated it"; the API must check again
correctAnswerText: "The client validated it"; the API must check again
explanation: The client is not yours at the moment of the request, so anything it checks must be checked again by the server that acts on it. The other named assumptions are real but describe different designs, and their suggested fixes would not stop an invalid discount reaching the API.

prompt: A threat model covers outside attackers in depth but says nothing about operators running scripts against production. What is missing?
optionA: Nation states, who target only governments
optionB: Accidents, which typically do the most damage
optionC: Hacktivists, who deface visible web pages
optionD: Opportunists, who scan the whole internet all day
correctAnswerText: Accidents, which typically do the most damage
explanation: A script with a bug or a query run in the wrong window is an accident, and accidents cause more damage than attacks; the model needs controls such as review, least privilege and tested backups. The other sources are deliberate actors already in the spirit of the outside-attacker analysis.

prompt: An AI design draws the model itself as the trust boundary that screens untrusted email before tools run. What is the flaw?
optionA: The model is no boundary; its output stays untrusted
optionB: Tools must be drawn in the same process as email
optionC: Trust boundaries never apply to AI components
optionD: The mail server should be the only trust boundary drawn here
correctAnswerText: The model is no boundary; its output stays untrusted
explanation: A model can be steered by what it reads, so it cannot be relied on to filter that same content. It sits in the untrusted zone, and the boundary is drawn where its output reaches tools, with checks there. The other options either drop boundaries or misplace them.

prompt: Findings read "auth could be bypassed" and "data might leak", and no tickets have been raised from them. Why not?
optionA: They lack a CVSS score, which ticketing systems insist on
optionB: They name no component, field, missing check or consequence
optionC: They are written in plain English rather than STRIDE codes
optionD: They were found by developers rather than by an auditor
correctAnswerText: They name no component, field, missing check or consequence
explanation: Nobody can act on a feeling; an engineer needs to know which endpoint, which field, which check and what happens. Scores and categories are optional, plain English is fine, and who found it does not matter.

prompt: A start-up has half a day for security work before launch. Which threat-modelling approach is best justified?
optionA: Skip modelling and buy a vulnerability scanner subscription
optionB: The four questions on a whiteboard, with the people who know it
optionC: Wait until after launch, so the design is final beforehand
optionD: A week-long formal model with every single component scored in detail
correctAnswerText: The four questions on a whiteboard, with the people who know it
explanation: A half-hour model that finds the three most likely problems is worth far more than a thorough one nobody finishes. A scanner finds known flaws in deployed code but not design gaps, and waiting ships the risks the model would have caught.

prompt: Marketing wants to keep customers' full dates of birth "in case they are useful"; the service only needs to know they are over 18. Best response?
optionA: Transfer: buy insurance against a leak
optionB: Accept: note that the data is low value
optionC: Mitigate: encrypt the birth-date column
optionD: Eliminate: store only an over-18 flag
correctAnswerText: Eliminate: store only an over-18 flag
explanation: Data not held cannot leak, and keeping only what the purpose needs is also what data-minimisation principles (such as those in India's DPDP Act) expect. Encryption still leaves the data to protect, accepting misjudges personal data as low value, and insurance pays out after the harm.

prompt: Which of these four risks should a team fix first?
optionA: A six-month route into an internal test server
optionB: A six-month, insider-only route to all customer data
optionC: A five-minute route to change a public marketing page
optionD: A five-minute, automatable route to all customer data
correctAnswerText: A five-minute, automatable route to all customer data
explanation: The question that beats the matrix is how cheap it is for them and how expensive for us: cheap and highly damaging comes first. The insider route has the same impact but far lower likelihood, and the other two are low impact.

prompt: Two internal services call each other with no authentication "because it is internal". Which mitigation is best justified?
optionA: Rename the endpoints to paths that are hard to guess at
optionB: Authenticate service to service, e.g. mTLS or signed tokens
optionC: Move both onto one VLAN with no other hosts attached to it
optionD: Rely on the VPN, since only staff can reach that network
correctAnswerText: Authenticate service to service, e.g. mTLS or signed tokens
explanation: Each service should prove who it is to the other, so a foothold anywhere inside cannot impersonate a caller (spoofing). Network isolation helps but still trusts location, obscure paths are found in bundles and logs, and the VPN is the weak assumption being questioned.

prompt: A team debates modelling with STRIDE per boundary or by ticking through the OWASP Top 10 list. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: The list alone, since it covers every threat that matters now
optionB: Neither; one penetration test replaces both of them entirely
optionC: STRIDE alone, since any list of attacks is always out of date
optionD: STRIDE per boundary for design gaps; the list then checks code
correctAnswerText: STRIDE per boundary for design gaps; the list then checks code
explanation: STRIDE at each boundary asks what this design lets someone do, which a list of common flaws cannot; the list is then a good check of the implementation. Either alone leaves a gap, and a penetration test comes after the design decisions it could have shaped.

prompt: A control lowers a risk's likelihood from high to medium. What should the threat model now record for it?
optionA: That the risk is closed, since a control now exists
optionB: Nothing more; mitigations do not need to be tracked
optionC: The control, its owner, and the residual risk left
optionD: A transfer of whatever risk remains to the vendor
correctAnswerText: The control, its owner, and the residual risk left
explanation: A mitigation reduces a risk rather than removing it, so the model keeps the control, who owns it and what remains, which someone may then accept explicitly. Closing it hides the remainder, not tracking it loses the control, and nothing has been transferred.

prompt: Who should be in the room for a threat-modelling session on a payments service?
optionA: Only the security team, so the model stays independent
optionB: Only product managers, who know every user journey
optionC: The engineers who built it, plus whoever owns the risk
optionD: Only external auditors, so the findings stay unbiased
correctAnswerText: The engineers who built it, plus whoever owns the risk
explanation: The people who know the system can draw it accurately and name its assumptions, and someone who owns the risk can decide on responses, including acceptance. Security alone draws the wrong diagram, auditors come later, and product managers rarely know the flows in enough detail.

prompt: For a refund feature whose top risk is refund fraud by staff, the team can build one control this sprint. Which is best justified?
optionA: Rate limiting that slows refunds above a threshold
optionB: A CAPTCHA proving a human made each refund request
optionC: An append-only audit trail of staff refund actions
optionD: None until all three controls can ship together
correctAnswerText: An append-only audit trail of staff refund actions
explanation: Staff misuse is about accountability, so a record they cannot edit both deters and detects it; separation of duties would come next. A rate limit slows but still allows fraud, a CAPTCHA proves only that a human acted (staff are human), and waiting delivers nothing.

prompt: A support agent can call refund(order_id, amount). Which mitigation is best justified in the threat model?
optionA: A system prompt telling the model never to over-refund
optionB: Server-side limits and user-rights checks in the tool
optionC: A larger model that is less likely to be manipulated
optionD: A filter blocking any prompt containing the word refund
correctAnswerText: Server-side limits and user-rights checks in the tool
explanation: Controls that do not depend on the model behaving belong where the action happens: the tool checks the caller's rights and enforces amount limits whatever the model asks. Prompt instructions and keyword filters can be bypassed, and no model is immune to manipulation.

prompt: Which risk is the strongest candidate for documented acceptance?
optionA: Likely, low impact, with a cheap configuration fix ready to apply
optionB: Likely and high impact, with a fix already scheduled
optionC: Unlikely but high impact, on regulated personal data
optionD: Unlikely, low impact, and the fix costs more than the loss
correctAnswerText: Unlikely, low impact, and the fix costs more than the loss
explanation: Acceptance fits when the cost of fixing exceeds the risk, and it is written down. A cheap fix should simply be done, high-impact personal data rarely qualifies, and a likely, damaging risk with a planned fix is being mitigated, not accepted.

prompt: In the vulnerability management cycle, which stage comes directly after prioritisation?
optionA: Verification
optionB: Asset inventory
optionC: Discovery
optionD: Remediation
correctAnswerText: Remediation
explanation: The cycle runs asset inventory, discovery, assessment, prioritisation, remediation, verification and reporting, then starts again. Verification checks a fix that remediation made, so it cannot come first; discovery and inventory come before assessment.

prompt: What does a CWE identifier, such as CWE-79, catalogue?
optionA: The class of mistake behind a vulnerability
optionB: One specific, publicly disclosed vulnerability
optionC: The chance a flaw is exploited in the next month
optionD: The list of components inside a software product
correctAnswerText: The class of mistake behind a vulnerability
explanation: CWE names weakness classes (CWE-79 is cross-site scripting); a CVE names one specific public vulnerability. Exploitation probability is EPSS, and a component list is an SBOM.

prompt: In vulnerability management, what counts as one "finding"?
optionA: One vulnerability on one asset
optionB: One vulnerability on every asset
optionC: One patch fixing several flaws
optionD: One scan of one network range
correctAnswerText: One vulnerability on one asset
explanation: A finding is one vulnerability on one asset, so ten servers with the same flaw are ten findings and one fix. A scan produces many findings, and a patch is a fix that may close several.

prompt: In a CVSS v3.1 base vector, what does the PR metric describe?
optionA: Probability of exploitation in 30 days
optionB: Privileges the attacker needs beforehand
optionC: Patch release status published by the vendor
optionD: Priority rank the analyst has assigned
correctAnswerText: Privileges the attacker needs beforehand
explanation: PR is Privileges Required: None, Low or High, meaning whether the attacker must already be logged in. Exploitation probability is EPSS, and neither patch status nor internal priority is part of the CVSS base vector.

prompt: What does EPSS publish for each CVE?
optionA: A severity score computed from the flaw's technical metrics
optionB: A probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days
optionC: A yes-or-no flag showing exploitation is already confirmed
optionD: A count of the assets in your estate that carry the flaw
correctAnswerText: A probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days
explanation: FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System gives a 0-to-1 probability, with a percentile, updated daily. Technical severity is CVSS, confirmed exploitation is what KEV catalogues record, and asset counts come from your own scans.

prompt: What does CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue list?
optionA: CVEs whose CVSS base score is 9.0 or higher in NVD
optionB: CVEs with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild
optionC: CVEs reported in software made by US-based vendors
optionD: CVEs a model predicts will be exploited within the next month
correctAnswerText: CVEs with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild
explanation: KEV is evidence: a CVE is listed when there is reliable proof it is being exploited. It is not a score cut-off and not a forecast, which is what EPSS gives, and it covers products from any vendor.

prompt: Which two formats are the common standards for a software bill of materials?
optionA: STIX and TAXII
optionB: Sigma and YARA
optionC: CycloneDX and SPDX
optionD: CVSS and EPSS
correctAnswerText: CycloneDX and SPDX
explanation: CycloneDX (OWASP) and SPDX (Linux Foundation) are the SBOM formats. CVSS and EPSS score vulnerabilities, STIX and TAXII share threat intelligence, and Sigma and YARA describe detections.

prompt: In a Greenbone (OpenVAS) report, what does the QoD value indicate?
optionA: How soon the fix must be applied
optionB: How reliable the detection test is
optionC: How severe the vulnerability is
optionD: How many hosts share the finding
correctAnswerText: How reliable the detection test is
explanation: Quality of Detection says how far to trust the result; banner-only guesses score low, and the web interface hides QoD below 70 by default. Severity is a separate column, due dates come from your SLA, and host counts from grouping.

prompt: What does a supplier's VEX statement say about a product?
optionA: How the CVSS score of each component was calculated
optionB: Which of its customers have installed the vulnerable version
optionC: Which components and versions the product is built from
optionD: Whether a CVE in one of its components really affects it
correctAnswerText: Whether a CVE in one of its components really affects it
explanation: VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) tells "present" from "exploitable", for example "not affected: the vulnerable function is never called". The component list itself is the SBOM; VEX complements it.

prompt: Which of these is a compensating control for a flaw that cannot be patched yet?
optionA: Lowering the finding's tier so it no longer shows overdue
optionB: Raising the CVSS score so the owner pays more attention
optionC: Removing the host from the scanner's list of scan targets
optionD: Firewall rules so only the hosts that need it can reach it
correctAnswerText: Firewall rules so only the hosts that need it can reach it
explanation: Compensating controls reduce risk another way: restrict reach, disable the affected feature, virtual patching, or extra detection. Re-tiering, unscanning or rescoring changes the paperwork, not the risk.

prompt: Why is a server missing from the asset inventory a bigger risk than a known server with a critical flaw?
optionA: Inventory gaps are reported to regulators as breaches
optionB: Known flaws are already fixed by the time they are found
optionC: Unknown servers always run older operating systems
optionD: Nobody scans, patches, monitors or owns it
correctAnswerText: Nobody scans, patches, monitors or owns it
explanation: A known flaw has an owner and a ticket; an unknown server has no owner, no scan, no patching, no EDR agent and no logs in the SIEM, so it is invisible to every control. Its age and any regulatory angle are beside the point.

prompt: Why does an authenticated scan usually report fewer false positives than an unauthenticated one?
optionA: It reads the real installed package versions, not banners
optionB: It skips every check that could ever produce a false result
optionC: It runs only during the agreed window, when hosts are quiet
optionD: It reports only findings that have a CVSS score above 7.0
correctAnswerText: It reads the real installed package versions, not banners
explanation: Logged in with a read-only account, the scanner reads packages, registry keys and patch levels directly, so it is not misled by banners or backported fixes. It does not skip checks or filter by score, and the window has nothing to do with accuracy.

prompt: Why do banner-based version checks often misfire on Debian or RHEL servers?
optionA: Scanners are not able to connect to Linux hosts over SSH
optionB: Distributions backport fixes without changing the version
optionC: Their package managers refuse to install security updates
optionD: These distributions hide all service banners by default
correctAnswerText: Distributions backport fixes without changing the version
explanation: Debian and RHEL often patch a library while keeping the upstream version number the banner shows, so a version comparison says "vulnerable" when it is fixed. An authenticated check of the distribution's package version settles it.

prompt: Why is a CVSS base score called severity rather than risk?
optionA: It is the same everywhere and ignores your asset and threats
optionB: It changes daily as new exploitation evidence is collected
optionC: It is set by the vendor, who may play down flaws in its own products
optionD: It covers only network flaws and leaves local ones unscored
correctAnswerText: It is the same everywhere and ignores your asset and threats
explanation: A base score describes the flaw on paper and is identical in every organisation; it knows nothing of exploitation, your asset's exposure or your controls. It does not change daily (EPSS does), and it covers local flaws too.

prompt: Why does a KEV listing outrank a high EPSS value when the two are weighed against each other?
optionA: KEV is evidence of exploitation; EPSS is a forecast of it
optionB: KEV entries always carry a higher CVSS score than others
optionC: EPSS covers only Windows flaws, so it misses most servers
optionD: KEV values are updated daily while EPSS changes once a year
correctAnswerText: KEV is evidence of exploitation; EPSS is a forecast of it
explanation: A KEV entry means exploitation has been observed; EPSS predicts how likely it is. Evidence beats prediction. EPSS is updated daily and covers all CVEs, and KEV has no CVSS threshold.

prompt: Why must every vulnerability exception carry an expiry date?
optionA: Auditors count only exceptions that have already ended
optionB: Expiry dates are needed to compute the CVSS score
optionC: Scanners delete findings whose exception has no date
optionD: Without one it becomes a permanent hole with paperwork
correctAnswerText: Without one it becomes a permanent hole with paperwork
explanation: An exception pauses escalation for a reason that should change: a vendor fix, an upgrade project. An end date forces a fresh decision. Scanners do not delete findings, and CVSS has nothing to do with exceptions.

prompt: Why is "we don't use that library" so often wrong when a new library advisory lands?
optionA: Every library is bundled into the operating system image
optionB: Developers rarely know which programming languages their apps use
optionC: Most vulnerable components arrive as transitive dependencies
optionD: Advisories name the wrong libraries more often than not
correctAnswerText: Most vulnerable components arrive as transitive dependencies
explanation: An application lists its direct dependencies, and each pulls in others; most vulnerable components found in real applications are transitive. An SBOM with dependency relationships shows them, and the fix is usually upgrading the direct dependency.

prompt: Why does every vulnerability scan start with a scan plan signed by the asset owners?
optionA: Scanners will not run until a signed PDF is uploaded to them
optionB: Owners must sign before a CVE can be assigned to a finding
optionC: A signature is what makes the results admissible as court evidence
optionD: Scanning systems you are not authorised to assess is an offence
correctAnswerText: Scanning systems you are not authorised to assess is an offence
explanation: Scanning someone else's systems is unauthorised access, an offence under India's IT Act. The plan fixes the scope, exclusions, window, profile and contacts. Scanners do not check paperwork, and CVE ids are assigned publicly, not by owners.

prompt: Why is a vulnerable package in a running container fixed by rebuilding the image rather than patching the container?
optionA: A patched container uses twice the memory of a rebuilt one
optionB: Image scanners refuse to scan containers that were patched
optionC: Containers are replaced from images, so a patch inside is lost
optionD: Container runtimes block package managers from ever running inside
correctAnswerText: Containers are replaced from images, so a patch inside is lost
explanation: Containers are short-lived copies of an image; the next deployment starts from the image again, undoing any change made inside. Rebuilding from an updated base and dependencies, then redeploying, makes the fix stick.

prompt: Why should the SOC suppress alerts from the scanner's source IP only for the scan window, not permanently?
optionA: The scanner changes its IP address after every single run
optionB: An intruder on that host would inherit a permanent allow-list
optionC: Permanent rules make the scanner run twice as slowly
optionD: The IDS licence limits how many suppressions can be active at once
correctAnswerText: An intruder on that host would inherit a permanent allow-list
explanation: A scan looks like reconnaissance, so a documented, time-boxed suppression avoids false alarms. A permanent allow-list for "the scanner" would also hide an attacker who lands on that box. Licences and speed are not the reason.

prompt: Saraswati Insurance's inventory has 20 assets; 15 were scanned in the last 30 days, and 2 more scanned addresses are not in the inventory. What is the coverage?
explanation: Coverage is inventory assets scanned recently over inventory assets: 15 of 20 is 75%. The two unknown addresses are a separate, urgent finding, not extra coverage (17/20 or 17/22 would count them). 25% is the uncovered share.

prompt: Rule: exploited = KEV or EPSS of at least 0.5; exposed = internet-facing or critical; exploited and exposed = P1. A KEV-listed CVSS 5.4 flaw sits on the internet-facing portal. Which tier?
optionA: P3
optionB: P2
optionC: P1
optionD: P4
correctAnswerText: P1
explanation: It is exploited (KEV) and exposed (internet-facing), so the rule gives P1 whatever the base score. Sorting by CVSS would bury it, which is exactly what risk-based ranking exists to prevent.

prompt: Policy: P2 findings are remediated within 15 days. A P2 finding was first seen on 3 November and its ticket raised on 10 November. When is it due?
optionA: 25 November
optionB: 10 November
optionC: 3 December
optionD: 18 November
correctAnswerText: 18 November
explanation: The SLA clock starts when the finding is first seen: 3 + 15 = 18 November. Counting from the ticket (25 November) rewards slow ticketing, and 3 December applies the 30-day P3 window.

prompt: A scan export has 40 rows: 6 are Log rows, 4 have QoD below 70, and 5 of the rest duplicate a host and vulnerability already listed. How many findings are reported?
optionA: 34, after only the Log rows are removed
optionB: 30, keeping the 5 duplicates for context
optionC: 25, with 4 set aside for a manual check
optionD: 40, since every row is a scanner result
correctAnswerText: 25, with 4 set aside for a manual check
explanation: 40 minus 6 Log rows minus 4 low-QoD rows leaves 30; de-duplicating on host plus vulnerability leaves 25. The low-QoD rows are not deleted but confirmed by hand. Counting rows is not counting findings.

prompt: A Python matcher must decide whether installed jsonkit 2.9.0 is below the fixed 2.10.1. How should it compare them?
optionA: Compare only the major numbers, 2 and 2, as integers
optionB: Parse both with packaging.version.Version and compare
optionC: Convert each to a float, such as 2.9 and 2.10, then compare
optionD: Compare the two version strings with the < operator
correctAnswerText: Parse both with packaging.version.Version and compare
explanation: Version parsing compares 9 and 10 as numbers, so 2.9.0 is correctly below 2.10.1. A string compare says "2.9.0" > "2.10.1", floats make 2.10 equal 2.1, and the major numbers alone are equal here, so that check calls it fixed.

prompt: Read the vector CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:N. Which statement is true?
optionA: Causes a total loss of the service's availability
optionB: Needs local access plus a low-privilege login
optionC: Cannot affect anything beyond the flawed component
optionD: Reachable over the network, but a user must act
correctAnswerText: Reachable over the network, but a user must act
explanation: AV:N is network, PR:N needs no login, and UI:R means a user must interact. A:N means no availability impact, and S:C means it can affect components beyond the vulnerable one. This is a typical reflected cross-site scripting vector.

prompt: An end-of-life appliance has a flaw in its admin interface, the vendor offers no fix, and only two admins use the interface. What is the best interim action?
optionA: Mark the finding as a false positive until a fix is released
optionB: Remove the appliance from the scan scope to stop the alerts
optionC: Limit the interface to the admins' subnet and add detection
optionD: Wait for the vendor, since nothing can be done without a patch
correctAnswerText: Limit the interface to the admins' subnet and add detection
explanation: When a patch is impossible, reduce risk another way: restrict reach to the hosts that need it and watch for exploitation behaviour, under a time-boxed exception with a replacement plan. Calling it a false positive or unscanning it hides a real risk.

prompt: A finding on kf-hr-app was closed as fixed a month ago. This week's re-scan, keyed by host and vulnerability, finds it again. How is it classified?
optionA: Reopened
optionB: Still open
optionC: Fixed
optionD: New
correctAnswerText: Reopened
explanation: A finding that was closed and has come back is reopened, which usually means the fix was undone by a rebuild from an old image or a downgrade. "New" would lose that history, and "still open" applies to findings that never closed.

prompt: Kaveri Finserv's web servers call a payment partner's hosted page. How should that page appear in Kaveri's scan plan?
optionA: As an exclusion, since Kaveri does not own it
optionB: Not at all, since plans list only included hosts
optionC: As a target, since Kaveri's servers depend on it
optionD: As a target, but only for the safe-check profile
correctAnswerText: As an exclusion, since Kaveri does not own it
explanation: Kaveri may only scan what it is authorised to assess, and a partner's hosted system is not Kaveri's. Listing it explicitly as an exclusion stops someone adding it later; any assurance comes from the partner, by contract.

prompt: A CI build should fail only when an image has HIGH or CRITICAL findings that already have a fix. Which Trivy options do that?
optionA: --severity CRITICAL --format table --exit-code 0
optionB: --ignore-unfixed --severity LOW,MEDIUM --exit-code 1
optionC: --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1
optionD: --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 0 --format json
correctAnswerText: --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1
explanation: The severity filter picks HIGH and CRITICAL, --ignore-unfixed drops findings with no fix yet, and --exit-code 1 fails the build when anything remains. Exit code 0 never fails, and LOW,MEDIUM is the wrong filter.

prompt: A coverage diff joined on hostname says the jump host was never scanned. The scanner log shows it scanned last night as kf-jump-01; the CMDB has KF-JUMP-01.kaveri.local. Why the miss?
optionA: The scanner log is written before each scan completes
optionB: Jump hosts are excluded from coverage exports by design
optionC: pandas drops rows whose hostname contains a hyphen
optionD: The join is exact, so case and domain suffix break it
correctAnswerText: The join is exact, so case and domain suffix break it
explanation: Exact joins fail on upper case and a domain suffix. Normalise both sides (lower-case, strip the domain) or join on a stable key such as IP plus asset id. The other explanations are not how scanners or pandas behave.

prompt: The weekly report jumped from 9 findings to 17 for the same hosts after the team switched to a new export, though nothing changed on the hosts. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: Hosts were rebuilt from an older golden image
optionB: The scanner switched from CVSS v3.1 to v4.0
optionC: Log rows and per-port repeats are now counted
optionD: Seventeen new CVEs were published that week
correctAnswerText: Log rows and per-port repeats are now counted
explanation: The change was the export: informational Log rows and the same CVE listed once per port inflate a row count. Drop Log rows and de-duplicate on host plus vulnerability. New CVEs or rebuilds would show as real host changes, and a scoring version does not add rows.

prompt: After a second EPSS feed is added, the tiering puts almost every finding into P1, including ones with values like 2.0 and 1.0. What should be checked first?
optionA: Whether the inventory now marks all hosts critical
optionB: Whether the CVSS calculator now rounds all up
optionC: Whether every CVE joined the KEV list overnight
optionD: Whether the new feed gives EPSS as a percentage
correctAnswerText: Whether the new feed gives EPSS as a percentage
explanation: Values above 1 cannot be probabilities: the feed is in percent, so 2.0 passes a 0.5 threshold. Convert on load and assert the range is 0 to 1. The other causes would not coincide with adding the feed.

prompt: A pandas check of expires < today has shown a TLS 1.0 exception as valid for a year. Its expiry cell is blank. Why is it never flagged?
optionA: The blank becomes NaT, and NaT comparisons are False
optionB: An empty string sorts before every date, so it passes
optionC: pandas fills a blank date with the year 2262 instead
optionD: read_csv drops the row, so the check never sees it
correctAnswerText: The blank becomes NaT, and NaT comparisons are False
explanation: Missing dates load as NaT, and every comparison with NaT returns False, so "expired" is never true. Treat a missing expiry as invalid and reject such records at entry. pandas does not substitute a far-future date, and the row is kept.

prompt: One CVE was patched on kf-web-01, yet the re-scan shows four of its six findings gone. Three of them need a local check to detect. What most likely happened?
optionA: The host was rebuilt from a newer image that night
optionB: The patch also fixed three other unrelated flaws
optionC: The re-scan ran without the original scan credentials
optionD: The scanner feed dropped those three tests overnight
correctAnswerText: The re-scan ran without the original scan credentials
explanation: Findings that need a local check vanish when a re-scan has no credentials or its login fails. Verify with the same profile and credentials and check the per-host authentication result before closing anything. One patch rarely fixes unrelated flaws.

prompt: Trivy flags imgtool 9.4.0 (fixed in 10.0.0), but the in-house SBOM matcher reports the app clean. Its check is installed < fixed on the raw strings. Why the miss?
optionA: Version 10.0.0 is a pre-release, not a fix
optionB: As strings "9.4.0" sorts after "10.0.0"
optionC: Trivy reports transitive packages twice
optionD: The SBOM lists imgtool under another name
correctAnswerText: As strings "9.4.0" sorts after "10.0.0"
explanation: String comparison goes character by character, and "9" is greater than "1", so 9.4.0 looks newer than the fix. Parse versions with the ecosystem's rules (packaging.version for Python, Debian's comparison for Debian packages).

prompt: The same CVE reopens on the web servers after every scheduled rebuild, though each time the hosts are patched and verified. What is the root cause?
optionA: Verification is done by an unauthenticated scan
optionB: The patch is rolled back by the EDR agent
optionC: The golden image still holds the old version
optionD: The scanner caches results from earlier scans
correctAnswerText: The golden image still holds the old version
explanation: Rebuilding from an unpatched image brings the flaw back each time. Fix the image or configuration baseline, so the next server is born patched, not only the hosts. The verification step was correct, which is why the reopen is visible.

prompt: A team's CVSS-sorted top five holds one KEV finding; a risk-based top five over the same data holds three. What does that show about the CVSS-only list?
optionA: It is fine, since KEV findings always score above 9.0 anyway
optionB: It ignores exploitation and exposure, so it buries urgent work
optionC: It used CVSS v4.0, which ranks KEV findings lower by design
optionD: It is correct, and the risk-based list overweights old CVEs
correctAnswerText: It ignores exploitation and exposure, so it buries urgent work
explanation: Base scores know nothing of exploitation or the asset, so exploited flaws on exposed hosts can sit below unexploited 9.8s. KEV entries span all scores, which is why a 6.1 can rightly rank first.

prompt: An "authenticated" scan of a Linux server returns only open ports and TLS settings, with no package findings at all. What is the likeliest explanation?
optionA: The server is fully patched and has no packages
optionB: Package checks only run on Windows hosts
optionC: The SSH login failed, so it ran unauthenticated
optionD: TLS findings always hide any package findings
correctAnswerText: The SSH login failed, so it ran unauthenticated
explanation: A credential failure is the commonest reason an authenticated scan silently becomes an unauthenticated one: only the outside view remains. Check the per-host authentication result in the report, not only the findings.

prompt: Kaveri Finserv built its scan target list from the EDR console alone. Which assets does that approach systematically miss?
optionA: Servers that were patched in the last month
optionB: Laptops, which leave the office network often
optionC: Domain controllers, which EDR never covers
optionD: Hosts with no agent, the least protected ones
correctAnswerText: Hosts with no agent, the least protected ones
explanation: An EDR console lists hosts with an agent and by definition misses those without one, which are the least watched. That is why the inventory is reconciled from CMDB, AD, DHCP/DNS, network data, cloud APIs and scanner discovery.

prompt: The IT head asks why a KEV-listed 6.1 on the internet-facing loan portal ranks above three unexploited 9.8s on internal hosts. Which answer is best?
optionA: The ranking is a mistake, and the 9.8s should be moved up
optionB: It was found first, so it keeps its place at the head of the queue
optionC: It is being exploited now and ours is reachable, so it goes first
optionD: Lower scores are quicker to patch, so they are cleared first
correctAnswerText: It is being exploited now and ours is reachable, so it goes first
explanation: Evidence of exploitation plus exposure makes it the likeliest to be used against us this week; the 9.8s matter but are not yet exploited and not reachable from outside. A written, reproducible rule lets anyone check that reasoning.

prompt: An exception request for TLS 1.0 on a web server is approved by the analyst, names no compensating control, and expires "when the vendor upgrades". How should it be judged?
optionA: Accept: the vendor upgrade will close it in good time anyway
optionB: Reject: it needs a risk owner, a control and a fixed end date
optionC: Accept, provided the analyst re-checks it every few months
optionD: Reject: TLS findings can never be accepted as exceptions
correctAnswerText: Reject: it needs a risk owner, a control and a fixed end date
explanation: An exception needs someone with authority to accept the risk (not the analyst), a compensating control, and a dated expiry. "When the vendor upgrades" is no date. Any finding can be excepted if those conditions hold.

prompt: To avoid permission gaps, a colleague proposes running authenticated scans with a domain-admin account. Which judgement is right?
optionA: Accept, since complete results matter more than anything
optionB: Accept, provided the password is changed every year
optionC: Use a dedicated read-only account, vaulted and rotated
optionD: Drop authenticated scanning to avoid any credentials
correctAnswerText: Use a dedicated read-only account, vaulted and rotated
explanation: A scan account only needs to read packages and settings; domain admin rights on it would be a gift to an intruder who reaches the scanner. Dropping authenticated scans loses the real patch state, which is worse.

prompt: A manager wants every available check, including ones that may crash services, run against core banking production at noon. What should the analyst recommend?
optionA: Safe checks in the agreed window; risky ones in test or not at all
optionB: Run them at night, with no change to the set of checks included
optionC: Run them at noon, since problems show up fastest under real load
optionD: Skip core banking entirely, since it is too fragile to be scanned
correctAnswerText: Safe checks in the agreed window; risky ones in test or not at all
explanation: Production scans use safe checks inside the agreed window; anything that could crash a service belongs in a test window or nowhere. Moving the risky checks to night still risks an outage, and skipping core systems leaves them unassessed.

prompt: A new library advisory lands. One option is emailing every development team to ask; the other is keeping an SBOM for every release. Which serves the organisation better?
optionA: SBOMs per release, so "are we affected?" is one search
optionB: Emails, since developers know their own code best
optionC: Emails first, then SBOMs only for critical apps
optionD: Neither, since advisories rarely affect real apps
correctAnswerText: SBOMs per release, so "are we affected?" is one search
explanation: Stored SBOMs, including transitive dependencies, turn the question into a search across every release in minutes. Emails take days and miss transitive components developers do not know they ship.

prompt: A team debates whether to run only unauthenticated scans or only authenticated ones across its servers. What is the best position?
optionA: Whichever finishes faster, since both report the same findings
optionB: Only unauthenticated, since that is how an attacker sees things
optionC: Both: one shows what is reachable, the other what is unpatched
optionD: Only authenticated, since it alone finds every kind of flaw
correctAnswerText: Both: one shows what is reachable, the other what is unpatched
explanation: The outside view shows exposure, especially for internet-facing hosts; the authenticated view shows the real patch state behind closed ports. Each misses what the other sees, so a mature programme runs both.

prompt: Which set of measures best tells leadership whether the vulnerability programme is getting better?
optionA: Count of CVEs published worldwide during the quarter
optionB: Critical-asset coverage, SLA compliance and overdue items
optionC: Total findings this month, sorted from highest CVSS down
optionD: Number of scans run and hours of scanner time consumed
correctAnswerText: Critical-asset coverage, SLA compliance and overdue items
explanation: Coverage shows what is being looked at, SLA compliance and overdue items show whether fixes land on time. Raw finding totals rise with coverage, scanner hours measure effort, and global CVE counts say nothing about this organisation.

prompt: An image scan shows three findings with no fix yet, all in OS packages the application never uses. Which response is best?
optionA: Ignore them for good, since no fix exists for any of the three
optionB: Patch the packages inside the running containers by hand
optionC: Block the release until the upstream fixes are published
optionD: Move to a smaller base image without them, and track the rest
correctAnswerText: Move to a smaller base image without them, and track the rest
explanation: A smaller base image simply does not contain packages the application never uses, removing the findings, while anything left is tracked. Ignoring loses sight of them, patching running containers is undone at the next deploy, and blocking waits on others indefinitely.

prompt: A P1 patch for the loan portal is due in seven days, and the owner wants to skip UAT testing to be sure of meeting it. What should the analyst advise?
optionA: Wait for the next quarterly window to test it thoroughly
optionB: Raise an exception now, since seven days is too short
optionC: Skip UAT, since meeting the SLA due date matters more than anything
optionD: Test briefly in UAT with a rollback plan; add a control if late
correctAnswerText: Test briefly in UAT with a rollback plan; add a control if late
explanation: A patch that breaks the portal gets rolled back and never reapplied, so a short UAT test and a rollback plan protect the fix itself; a compensating control covers any slip. Waiting a quarter or excepting a P1 by default ignores an exploited, exposed flaw.

prompt: Because tickets lag scans by a week, a team proposes starting the SLA clock when the ticket is raised. How should the proposal be judged?
optionA: Accept: owners cannot fix what they have not been told about
optionB: Reject: keep first-seen and fix the ticketing delay instead
optionC: Reject: the clock should start when the CVE is published
optionD: Accept, but only for findings that are P3 and P4 in tier
correctAnswerText: Reject: keep first-seen and fix the ticketing delay instead
explanation: The risk exists from the moment the finding is seen; moving the clock hides a week of exposure in every metric. Fix the delay. Starting at CVE publication would penalise owners for flaws nobody had yet found on their hosts.

prompt: In the EC2 instance type c7g.2xlarge, what does the "g" after the generation number tell you?
optionA: It carries a GPU for graphics or ML work
optionB: It belongs to the general-purpose family
optionC: It uses an AWS Graviton (ARM) processor
optionD: It has local NVMe instance store disks
correctAnswerText: It uses an AWS Graviton (ARM) processor
explanation: The letters after the generation are attributes: "g" means Graviton (ARM), "d" means local instance store, "a" means AMD. The family letter comes first (c = compute optimised), and GPU families have their own letters (g and p at the front, not after the number).

prompt: What is an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) in EC2?
optionA: The image an instance boots from: OS, software and disk layout
optionB: A list of the instance types allowed in a given AWS Region
optionC: The IAM identity an instance uses when it calls other services
optionD: A snapshot of the memory of a running instance for debugging
correctAnswerText: The image an instance boots from: OS, software and disk layout
explanation: An AMI is the template a server starts from — the root volume snapshot with its operating system and installed software. It is not a memory dump; the identity comes from an instance profile, and allowed types are a policy question.

prompt: What is EC2 user data normally used for?
optionA: A script or cloud-init file run at first boot to configure it
optionB: The application data volume that survives instance termination
optionC: A tag set that tells billing which team owns the running server
optionD: A record of which users have logged in to the server over SSH
correctAnswerText: A script or cloud-init file run at first boot to configure it
explanation: User data is handed to cloud-init and run at first boot to install or configure software (Azure calls the same idea custom data). It is not a login record, not storage — that is EBS — and not tagging.

prompt: What does an EC2 launch template hold for an Auto Scaling group?
optionA: Versioned launch settings: AMI, type, security groups, profile, user data
optionB: The list of subnets and Availability Zones the group launches into
optionC: The minimum, maximum and desired instance counts the group aims for
optionD: The scaling policies and CloudWatch alarms that resize the group
correctAnswerText: Versioned launch settings: AMI, type, security groups, profile, user data
explanation: A launch template is everything run_instances would take, and every change makes a new version. Sizes, policies and subnets belong to the Auto Scaling group itself, which points at a template version.

prompt: What defines an EC2 Spot Instance compared with an On-Demand one?
optionA: It guarantees capacity in an AZ without giving any discount at all
optionB: It runs on hardware dedicated to a single customer account only
optionC: It is reserved for one or three years in exchange for a discount
optionD: It uses spare capacity AWS can reclaim with a two-minute warning
correctAnswerText: It uses spare capacity AWS can reclaim with a two-minute warning
explanation: Spot is spare capacity at a large discount that can be reclaimed with a two-minute notice. A term commitment is a Savings Plan or Reserved Instance, dedicated hardware is a Dedicated Host or Instance, and a capacity guarantee without discount is an On-Demand Capacity Reservation.

prompt: What is the longest a single AWS Lambda invocation can be allowed to run?
optionA: 60 minutes
optionB: 24 hours
optionC: 5 minutes
optionD: 15 minutes
correctAnswerText: 15 minutes
explanation: The timeout can be set up to 900 seconds (15 minutes); the default is only 3 seconds. Work longer than that is split with Step Functions or moved to a container task.

prompt: In Amazon ECS, what is a task definition?
optionA: The object that keeps N copies running behind a load balancer
optionB: A versioned recipe: image, CPU and memory, ports, secrets, roles
optionC: A running copy of a container with its own private IP address
optionD: A grouping of capacity in which services are placed and run
correctAnswerText: A versioned recipe: image, CPU and memory, ports, secrets, roles
explanation: A task definition is the immutable, numbered recipe (family:revision). A task is one running copy, a service keeps N tasks running and registered with a target group, and a cluster groups services and capacity.

prompt: Which Azure service is the equivalent of an EC2 Auto Scaling group?
optionA: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
optionB: Azure Container Apps
optionC: An availability set
optionD: An App Service plan slot
correctAnswerText: Virtual Machine Scale Sets
explanation: Virtual Machine Scale Sets (Flexible orchestration for new sets) with Azure Monitor autoscale rules play the ASG role. Container Apps is closer to ECS on Fargate, slots are App Service release copies, and availability sets are the older single-datacentre spreading pattern.

prompt: What exactly does a team commit to when it buys an AWS Compute Savings Plan?
optionA: A capacity guarantee in one Availability Zone for a sale day
optionB: A fixed amount of compute spend per hour for one or three years
optionC: A promise to run only Spot capacity in return for lower rates
optionD: A fixed number of one instance type in one AZ for a single year
correctAnswerText: A fixed amount of compute spend per hour for one or three years
explanation: A Savings Plan is a commitment to spend per hour over a one- or three-year term; a Compute Savings Plan applies across families, sizes, Regions, Fargate and Lambda. A count of one type is closer to a Reserved Instance, and a capacity guarantee is a Capacity Reservation.

prompt: What is a Lambda function's execution role?
optionA: The service role that Lambda uses to bill the owning account
optionB: The IAM role the function's code runs as when it calls AWS
optionC: The role a developer assumes to deploy a new function version
optionD: The policy that decides which services may invoke the function
correctAnswerText: The IAM role the function's code runs as when it calls AWS
explanation: The execution role is what the function can do. Who may call it is a separate resource-based policy (for example letting S3 invoke it). Deployment uses the deployer's own identity, and billing has no role.

prompt: Why does a security review insist that every EC2 instance requires IMDSv2 tokens for its metadata service?
optionA: A session token blocks simple request-forgery reads of role credentials
optionB: IMDSv2 encrypts the instance's root volume with a key held by AWS KMS
optionC: IMDSv1 is billed per call, and token-based requests are not charged
optionD: IMDSv2 stops anyone from opening port 22 on the instance from outside
correctAnswerText: A session token blocks simple request-forgery reads of role credentials
explanation: Credentials for the instance role are served by the metadata service; IMDSv2 requires a session token obtained by a PUT first, which a server-side request forgery bug or an open proxy cannot easily obtain. It has nothing to do with disk encryption, billing or inbound ports.

prompt: Why should a web Auto Scaling group use the ELB health check type rather than the default EC2 check?
optionA: The EC2 check makes the group launch instances in a single AZ only
optionB: The ELB check lets the group skip the health check grace period
optionC: The ELB check is the only type that allows target tracking policies
optionD: The EC2 check sees only the VM, so a crashed app would stay in service
correctAnswerText: The EC2 check sees only the VM, so a crashed app would stay in service
explanation: With the EC2 check a running VM counts as healthy even when the app is down. The ELB type also replaces instances the load balancer marks unhealthy. It does not change AZ placement, still needs a grace period, and has no link to the policy type.

prompt: Why is a boto3 client for a Lambda function created at module level instead of inside the handler?
optionA: Module code runs once per environment and warm calls reuse the client
optionB: Module-level clients are billed at a lower GB-second rate than others
optionC: Lambda rejects handlers that open network connections after they start
optionD: Clients created in the handler cannot see the function's execution role
correctAnswerText: Module code runs once per environment and warm calls reuse the client
explanation: Module-level code runs in the init phase, once per execution environment, and later invocations in that warm environment reuse it. A client in the handler works and has the same role — it is just rebuilt on every call. Billing is not split by where code lives.

prompt: Why can raising a CPU-bound Lambda function's memory setting make it faster without raising its cost much?
optionA: Higher memory moves the function onto dedicated hardware for free
optionB: Memory above a threshold is not counted in the GB-seconds billed
optionC: CPU is allocated in proportion to memory, so duration falls as well
optionD: A larger memory setting turns off cold starts for that function
correctAnswerText: CPU is allocated in proportion to memory, so duration falls as well
explanation: Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory. Cost is memory × duration, so a shorter run at a higher setting can cost about the same — which is why you measure rather than guess. Memory does not remove cold starts, buy dedicated hardware or escape billing.

prompt: Why does the course say to size a Savings Plan to the steady floor of usage, not to the daily peak?
optionA: Savings Plans cannot be applied to instances that run fewer than 12 hours
optionB: AWS sells Savings Plans only in units that match the overnight fleet
optionC: Usage above a Savings Plan commitment is blocked until the next month
optionD: Commitment unused in quiet hours is still paid, wiping out the discount
correctAnswerText: Commitment unused in quiet hours is still paid, wiping out the discount
explanation: Each extra unit of commitment pays off only if usage is at or above it for more than (1 − discount) of the hours. Committing to the peak means paying for idle commitment most of the day. Usage above the commitment is simply billed On-Demand, not blocked.

prompt: Why does an Azure VM shut down from inside its operating system still cost compute money?
optionA: Azure bills a VM for the full month once it has started even once
optionB: It is Stopped, not deallocated, so Azure still holds its hardware
optionC: Shutting down from the OS keeps the temporary disk billed as compute
optionD: The VM keeps running in the background until its scale set removes it
correctAnswerText: It is Stopped, not deallocated, so Azure still holds its hardware
explanation: An OS shutdown leaves the VM Stopped with its host still allocated, so compute is billed. Only Stopped (deallocated) — az vm deallocate or Stop in the portal — releases it, after which disks and any static public IP are what you pay for.

prompt: Why does an ECS task definition carry both an execution role and a separate task role?
optionA: ECS needs pull, logs and secrets; the code gets only what it uses
optionB: Two roles double the API rate limit available to each running task
optionC: The task role is a backup used only when the execution role fails
optionD: One role is for Fargate tasks and the other for EC2-hosted tasks
correctAnswerText: ECS needs pull, logs and secrets; the code gets only what it uses
explanation: The execution role is used by ECS before the container runs (image pull, logs, injecting secrets); the task role is what application code gets. Keeping them apart means a bug in the app cannot read every secret ECS can. Both roles apply on either capacity type, neither is a fallback, and rate limits are unrelated.

prompt: Why does a well-built Spot fleet list several interchangeable instance types instead of one?
optionA: Each extra type adds to the two-minute interruption warning time
optionB: A shortage or reclaim in one capacity pool cannot starve the fleet
optionC: Spot requests naming a single instance type are rejected by EC2
optionD: Mixed types let the fleet keep state when an instance is reclaimed
correctAnswerText: A shortage or reclaim in one capacity pool cannot starve the fleet
explanation: Each instance type in each AZ is a separate Spot pool; spreading across pools (with price-capacity-optimized allocation) means one pool running short does not empty the fleet. Single-type requests are allowed, the warning is fixed, and nothing preserves an instance's local state.

prompt: Why does baking a golden AMI help an Auto Scaling group more than tuning its scaling policy?
optionA: Scaling policies only work when every instance shares one AMI build id
optionB: A golden AMI removes the need for health checks on new instances
optionC: Golden AMIs let the group exceed its maximum size during a sudden spike
optionD: A group adds capacity only as fast as a new instance boots and is ready
correctAnswerText: A group adds capacity only as fast as a new instance boots and is ready
explanation: Scale-out has a speed limit set by boot-to-healthy time; an AMI with everything installed may be ready in under a minute where installing in user data takes several. The maximum still applies, policies do not care about AMI ids, and health checks remain essential.

prompt: Two busy web apps on one Azure App Service plan slow each other down. Why?
optionA: App Service limits each plan to a single request at a time across apps
optionB: The second app on a plan always runs in a lower pricing tier than the first
optionC: Every app on a plan runs on every one of its instances and shares the CPU
optionD: Apps on one plan share one deployment slot and queue each other's releases
correctAnswerText: Every app on a plan runs on every one of its instances and shares the CPU
explanation: The plan is the set of VMs you pay for, and all its apps run on all its instances — a noisy neighbour you created yourself. Plans handle many concurrent requests, tiers apply to the plan as a whole, and each app has its own slots.

prompt: KiranaKart's order-validation function receives 300 requests per second, each taking 0.5 seconds on average. About how many concurrent execution environments does it need?
optionA: About 600
optionB: About 60
optionC: About 300
optionD: About 150
correctAnswerText: About 150
explanation: One environment handles one request at a time, so concurrency ≈ requests per second × average duration = 300 × 0.5 = 150. 600 divides instead of multiplying, and 300 ignores duration altogether.

prompt: A scheduled action with no TimeZone must pre-warm a fleet at 22:30 IST for a midnight sale. Which StartTime is right?
optionA: 16:30 UTC on the same day
optionB: 22:30 UTC on the same day
optionC: 17:00 UTC on the same day
optionD: 04:00 UTC on the next day
correctAnswerText: 17:00 UTC on the same day
explanation: Without a TimeZone, scheduled action times are UTC, and IST is UTC+5:30, so 22:30 IST is 17:00 UTC. Adding instead of subtracting gives 04:00, using the IST clock unchanged fires five and a half hours late, and 16:30 subtracts an extra half hour.

prompt: A report server on r6i.xlarge averaged 4% CPU for two weeks, and you are asked to downsize it. What do you do first?
optionA: Double its size, because low CPU usually means the app is waiting on CPU
optionB: Move it to the smallest t-type at once, since its CPU is almost always idle
optionC: Buy a Savings Plan for it first, so the downsizing is cheaper afterwards
optionD: Check its memory with the CloudWatch agent, since R types are sized for RAM
correctAnswerText: Check its memory with the CloudWatch agent, since R types are sized for RAM
explanation: EC2 does not report memory without the agent, and an R (memory-optimised) instance may be idle on CPU because it is sized for memory. Look at memory and network (or Compute Optimizer), then downsize one step at a time. Committing before right-sizing locks in waste.

prompt: A Lambda function set to 512 MB runs for 400 ms per call. How many GB-seconds does one call use?
optionA: 204.8 GB-seconds
optionB: 2.0 GB-seconds
optionC: 0.02 GB-seconds
optionD: 0.2 GB-seconds
correctAnswerText: 0.2 GB-seconds
explanation: GB-seconds = memory in GB × duration in seconds = 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2. Multiplying 512 by 0.4 forgets to convert MB to GB, and the other two misplace the decimal point.

prompt: StreamNest transcodes uploaded videos overnight in jobs that checkpoint and can be retried. Which EC2 capacity fits best?
optionA: Standard Reserved Instances for one exact type in one AZ
optionB: A single large On-Demand instance with termination protection
optionC: Dedicated Hosts so that no other customer can reclaim them
optionD: Spot in an Auto Scaling group with several instance types
correctAnswerText: Spot in an Auto Scaling group with several instance types
explanation: Interruptible, retryable, checkpointed batch work is exactly what Spot is for, run as a diversified fleet. One big instance is a single point of failure at full price, a three-year RI suits steady 24×7 load, and dedicated hardware is about isolation, not cost.

prompt: Each nightly reconciliation file takes about 40 minutes to process as one indivisible unit. Where should it run?
optionA: A Lambda layer holding the processing code
optionB: A Lambda function with its timeout raised
optionC: A Lambda function with more memory set
optionD: An ECS task on Fargate, started per file
correctAnswerText: An ECS task on Fargate, started per file
explanation: A Lambda invocation cannot exceed 15 minutes, whatever its memory or layers, so a 40-minute indivisible job belongs in a container task (or Batch). If the work could be split, Step Functions orchestrating shorter steps would be the other option.

prompt: An instance refresh runs on a 10-instance group with MinHealthyPercentage 90. How does it proceed?
optionA: Half the group at a time, so the refresh finishes in two short batches
optionB: All ten at once, then the group waits for 90% of them to pass checks
optionC: One instance at a time, each new one healthy and warm before the next
optionD: Nine instances at once, keeping a single old instance until the end
correctAnswerText: One instance at a time, each new one healthy and warm before the next
explanation: Keeping 90% of 10 healthy allows only one instance out of service at a time, so the refresh replaces them one by one and waits for warm-up between batches. Replacing all, nine or half would drop below the minimum healthy percentage.

prompt: A team sets Azure autoscale on a scale set with one rule: CPU above 70% for 5 minutes adds 2 instances. What must they add?
optionA: A separate scale-in rule with a threshold well below 70%
optionB: A deployment slot, since autoscale needs one to scale in
optionC: Nothing: Azure scales in by itself when CPU drops back
optionD: A scale-in rule at 69% so the set returns at once to size
correctAnswerText: A separate scale-in rule with a threshold well below 70%
explanation: Unlike AWS target tracking, Azure autoscale needs separate scale-out and scale-in rules; without the second the set grows and stays large. The thresholds should be well apart (for example below 30%) or the set flaps. Slots belong to App Service, not scale sets.

prompt: Measured from launch, a web instance first passes its target group health check after about 3 minutes. How should HealthCheckGracePeriod be set?
optionA: Comfortably above that, for example 240 to 300 seconds
optionB: At 30 seconds, so that broken instances are found quickly
optionC: At exactly 180 seconds, matching the measured time precisely
optionD: At zero, since the load balancer has its own health check
correctAnswerText: Comfortably above that, for example 240 to 300 seconds
explanation: The grace period must cover boot plus user data plus app start with headroom, or the group terminates instances that are still starting. 30 seconds or zero cause a replacement loop, and an exact match fails whenever a boot runs slightly slow.

prompt: An App Service app has DB_HOST, APP_ENV and FEATURE_PAYSLIP_V2 settings, and releases by swapping staging into production. Which should be slot settings (sticky)?
optionA: FEATURE_PAYSLIP_V2 only, since it ships with the code
optionB: All three, so that nothing at all moves in the swap
optionC: DB_HOST and APP_ENV, which describe the environment
optionD: None of them, since a swap never moves app settings
correctAnswerText: DB_HOST and APP_ENV, which describe the environment
explanation: Settings that belong to the environment must stay with their slot, or production ends up pointed at the staging database. A feature flag released with the code should move with it. Ordinary settings do move in a swap, which is the trap.

prompt: During a deploy, a web group's activity log repeats every two minutes: launch an instance, then terminate it after an ELB health check failure. It never reaches desired capacity. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The group is in two AZs and keeps moving instances between them to balance
optionB: The maximum size is too low, so new launches are cancelled by the group
optionC: The grace period is shorter than the time the app takes to become healthy
optionD: The launch template points at $Latest, which keeps changing the AMI used
correctAnswerText: The grace period is shorter than the time the app takes to become healthy
explanation: The group judges instances by the ELB check before they can answer /healthz, so it kills them and launches more. Fix the grace period (and shorten boot); switching back to the EC2 check would only hide genuinely dead apps. Max size, template version and AZ balance would not produce this pattern.

prompt: At a sale peak, average CPU sits at 95% for twenty minutes, users see errors, and the target-tracking group has stopped adding instances. Which fact explains it best?
optionA: Target tracking pauses during sustained high CPU load
optionB: Desired capacity has reached the group's maximum size
optionC: The instance warm-up hides all metrics during a spike
optionD: The ELB health check stops scaling while targets fail
correctAnswerText: Desired capacity has reached the group's maximum size
explanation: Scaling moves desired between min and max, so a group pinned at max cannot add capacity however high CPU goes. The course fix is a higher max for the window, an alarm when desired equals max, and a confirmed vCPU quota. Target tracking does not pause, and warm-up only excludes booting instances.

prompt: A new function that calls a payment API logs "Task timed out after 3.00 seconds" on slow responses, though nobody set a timeout. What is happening?
optionA: Lambda caps any function that calls the internet at three seconds
optionB: The payment API closes connections after three seconds of waiting
optionC: The function kept Lambda's default timeout, which is three seconds
optionD: The memory setting is too low, which shortens the allowed runtime
correctAnswerText: The function kept Lambda's default timeout, which is three seconds
explanation: An unset timeout is the 3-second default; set one that covers the dependency's realistic latency (and a client timeout shorter than it). The message is Lambda's, not the API's, there is no internet cap, and memory does not change the timeout.

prompt: A Lambda SQS consumer raises an exception on one malformed message, and all ten messages in that batch are processed again. What is missing?
optionA: A larger batch size, so the bad message is diluted among others
optionB: Provisioned concurrency, so retries land in a warm environment
optionC: ReportBatchItemFailures, returning only the failed message ids
optionD: A longer timeout, so the bad message has time to finish parsing
correctAnswerText: ReportBatchItemFailures, returning only the failed message ids
explanation: Without a partial batch response, an exception fails the whole batch and every message returns to the queue. Returning batchItemFailures lets the good nine be deleted while the bad one is retried and eventually reaches the dead-letter queue. Size, timeout and warm environments do not change that.

prompt: Fargate tasks in private subnets stop with "ResourceInitializationError: unable to pull secrets or registry auth". Where should the investigation focus?
optionA: The ALB health check path, which is failing before the app is up
optionB: The task role that the application uses for its own AWS API calls
optionC: The application's Python code that reads the password at startup
optionD: The execution role and the network path to ECR and Secrets Manager
correctAnswerText: The execution role and the network path to ECR and Secrets Manager
explanation: This error happens before the container starts, so it is ECS's own work that failed: the execution role's permissions, or no NAT/endpoints to reach ECR, S3, Secrets Manager and Logs. App code, the task role and health checks only matter once the container is running.

prompt: Attaching a restored data volume to a replacement instance fails with InvalidVolume.ZoneMismatch. The group launched the instance in ap-south-1a. What happened, and what is the fix?
optionA: The volume is still attached elsewhere; force-detach it first
optionB: The volume is in another AZ; snapshot it and restore it in 1a
optionC: The instance type lacks EBS support; pick a type that has it
optionD: The volume is unencrypted; copy it with a KMS key and retry it
correctAnswerText: The volume is in another AZ; snapshot it and restore it in 1a
explanation: EBS volumes attach only within their own AZ, and snapshots are regional, so a snapshot restored in ap-south-1a works. Longer term, state that ties a server to one disk should not live in a group that can place it in any AZ. Encryption, type and multi-attach give different errors.

prompt: A new private instance returns TargetNotConnected in Session Manager and is missing from Fleet Manager. It has no instance profile and its subnet has no NAT route. What is the right diagnosis?
optionA: It lacks an SSM-permitted role and any outbound path to SSM
optionB: Session Manager needs port 22 open from the operator's IP
optionC: The agent works only on instances that have a public IP set
optionD: Session Manager is supported only on Windows instance images
correctAnswerText: It lacks an SSM-permitted role and any outbound path to SSM
explanation: Session Manager needs the agent, an instance profile allowing AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore, and outbound HTTPS to the SSM endpoints (NAT or interface endpoints). It never needs port 22 or a public IP, and it supports Linux — that is the point of using it.

prompt: While a bulk-report function was backfilling a year of data, the checkout function in the same account and Region was throttled with TooManyRequestsException. What explains it, and what prevents a repeat?
optionA: The report job used the execution role; give each a separate account id
optionB: Checkout's memory was too low; raise it so it runs before the report job
optionC: They share the Region's concurrency quota; reserve concurrency for checkout
optionD: Throttling means a cold start; add a layer so checkout starts up faster
correctAnswerText: They share the Region's concurrency quota; reserve concurrency for checkout
explanation: Concurrency is a regional quota shared by all functions in the account, so a burst in one can starve another. Reserved concurrency guarantees checkout its share and can also cap the report job. Memory and layers do not affect throttling, and roles are not counted against concurrency.

prompt: A team bought a Savings Plan matching its evening peak usage, and the compute bill went up. Usage runs at the peak only about a fifth of the hours. Why?
optionA: Peak-hour usage is billed On-Demand even when it is under the commitment
optionB: Savings Plans apply only to Spot capacity, so the fleet got no discount
optionC: Most hours the commitment sits unused, and unused commitment is still paid
optionD: Savings Plans switch off once usage drops below the commitment for an hour
correctAnswerText: Most hours the commitment sits unused, and unused commitment is still paid
explanation: An extra unit of commitment pays off only when usage is at or above it for more than (1 − discount) of the hours; at a fifth of the hours the idle commitment outweighs the discount. The plan does not switch off, covers usage under it, and does not apply to Spot.

prompt: At a traffic spike, a Lambda API backed by PostgreSQL on RDS starts failing with "too many connections", while CPU on the database is modest. What is the cause and the fix the course gives?
optionA: Each concurrent environment opens its own connection; put RDS Proxy in front
optionB: The handler opens connections too slowly; shorten the function timeout
optionC: RDS blocks Lambda after a fixed number of calls; move it to a public subnet
optionD: Lambda shares one connection across all calls; raise the function memory
correctAnswerText: Each concurrent environment opens its own connection; put RDS Proxy in front
explanation: Every concurrent execution environment holds its own connection, so concurrency becomes connection count. RDS Proxy pools them (or the data moves to DynamoDB). Environments do not share a connection, timeouts do not reduce concurrency, and a public subnet is a security problem, not a fix.

prompt: An internal pricing API serves high, steady, predictable traffic around the clock and runs on Lambda. Finance asks whether that is still the right home. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Move it to one large EC2 instance, since steady load needs no scaling
optionB: Model a container fleet against it; at steady volume it may cost less
optionC: Keep Lambda for good, since serverless is always the cheapest option
optionD: Add provisioned concurrency to everything, since that removes the cost
correctAnswerText: Model a container fleet against it; at steady volume it may cost less
explanation: Lambda shines for spiky or low-volume work; at some steady, high volume a container fleet costs less, so you model both with the calculator. Serverless is not always cheapest, a single instance gives up availability, and provisioned concurrency adds cost rather than removing it.

prompt: A company with twelve product teams wants one shared container platform, Helm charts, Argo CD and operators, and may run a second cloud next year. ECS or EKS?
optionA: ECS: it has fewer moving parts, so it is the better fit for every organisation
optionB: EKS: the ecosystem, many-team platform and portability are the deciding needs
optionC: EKS: ECS cannot run more than a handful of services inside any single cluster
optionD: ECS: Helm charts and Argo CD only ever deploy to ECS services on AWS Fargate
correctAnswerText: EKS: the ecosystem, many-team platform and portability are the deciding needs
explanation: The course's rule: choose ECS when the team is small and AWS-only with ordinary services; choose EKS when you need portability, the Kubernetes ecosystem (operators, Helm, Argo CD) and many teams on one platform. Simplicity is not right for every case, Helm and Argo CD target Kubernetes, and ECS has no such service limit.

prompt: An image-resizing service must keep at least two workers at all times and wants Spot savings above that. Which design best balances cost and reliability?
optionA: On-Demand base of 2, Spot above it on several types, capacity rebalancing
optionB: All On-Demand, since any Spot interruption loses the images in progress
optionC: Spot base of 2 and On-Demand above it, so the cheapest part is the floor
optionD: All Spot on one cheap type, since two-minute warnings are always enough
correctAnswerText: On-Demand base of 2, Spot above it on several types, capacity rebalancing
explanation: A mixed instances policy with an On-Demand base protects the minimum, diversified Spot above it with price-capacity-optimized allocation and capacity rebalancing saves money, and idempotent, checkpointed jobs absorb interruptions. One type risks starvation, all On-Demand forgoes the saving, and a Spot floor puts the guarantee on reclaimable capacity.

prompt: A brand-new booking service launches next month with no traffic history. The manager wants a three-year commitment now "to lock in savings". What do you recommend?
optionA: Run it entirely on Spot until the commitment pays for itself later
optionB: Buy a three-year plan now at the forecast peak to get the best rate
optionC: Buy zonal Reserved Instances now, since they also reserve capacity
optionD: Run On-Demand, right-size, then commit to the proven floor in steps
correctAnswerText: Run On-Demand, right-size, then commit to the proven floor in steps
