explanation: Commitment is a calculation on usage you can prove; before right-sizing it locks in waste, and committing to a forecast peak loses money. Spot is wrong for an interactive service floor, and zonal RIs are an even less flexible commitment.

prompt: Traffic will jump tenfold within a minute when a festival sale opens at a known time. Which plan best handles that cliff?
optionA: Target tracking alone at a lower CPU target so it reacts a little sooner
optionB: Larger instance types all month, so the existing fleet absorbs the spike
optionC: Scheduled pre-warm, target tracking kept on, and a fast-booting golden AMI
optionD: Step scaling with very large steps, so each alarm adds many instances
correctAnswerText: Scheduled pre-warm, target tracking kept on, and a fast-booting golden AMI
explanation: A known cliff outruns metric delay plus boot time, so capacity should already be running; target tracking handles what the forecast misses, and a golden AMI shortens every launch. Lower targets and big steps still react after the fact, and oversizing all month pays for the peak every day.

prompt: A team runs Python and Java services on x86 and considers moving to Graviton. One service depends on an old native library with no ARM build. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Stay on x86 for good, since a single library blocks the whole organisation
optionB: Move the ARM-ready services after multi-arch builds and load tests
optionC: Move everything and emulate x86 on ARM, since emulation costs nothing at all
optionD: Move everything at once, since interpreted languages never need any changes
correctAnswerText: Move the ARM-ready services after multi-arch builds and load tests
explanation: Graviton usually gives better price-performance, but the cost is engineering: multi-architecture images, checking native dependencies and load-testing. Moving the ready services and holding back the blocked one captures the benefit without the risk. All-at-once ignores the native library; never moving wastes the gain.

prompt: A team runs a customer-facing checkout function and a nightly SQS report consumer. Both see cold starts. Where is provisioned concurrency worth paying for?
optionA: On neither, since a bigger package would remove cold starts
optionB: On both, since cold starts slow down every kind of function
optionC: On the report consumer only, since it starts cold every night
optionD: On checkout only, where users wait through the init phase
correctAnswerText: On checkout only, where users wait through the init phase
explanation: Provisioned concurrency costs money and pays off where a person waits on the latency. Nobody notices a cold start on a queue consumer or nightly report. Bigger packages make cold starts worse, not better — lean packages and module-level clients help everywhere.

prompt: On Azure, a small team must host a Python web API with a staging copy and releases that can be rolled back in seconds, with no servers to patch. Which choice fits best?
optionA: App Service on a Standard-or-higher plan, releasing by slot swap
optionB: A Virtual Machine Scale Set with a custom image for every release
optionC: Two single VMs behind a load balancer, switched over by editing DNS
optionD: Azure Functions on the Consumption plan, with one function per route
correctAnswerText: App Service on a Standard-or-higher plan, releasing by slot swap
explanation: App Service is the managed web platform; deployment slots give a warm staging copy, and rollback is another swap. Scale sets and VMs leave patching with the team, and DNS switches are slow to roll back. Functions suits event-driven work rather than a whole web API with staged releases.

prompt: A DR plan must be certain that twenty instances of one type can launch in a specific AZ during a regional event, and finance also wants a discount. Which combination meets both?
optionA: An On-Demand Capacity Reservation, paired with a Savings Plan
optionB: A Spot fleet with twenty instances kept stopped until it is needed
optionC: Larger quotas only, since a quota increase guarantees the capacity
optionD: A Compute Savings Plan alone, since it reserves the capacity too
correctAnswerText: An On-Demand Capacity Reservation, paired with a Savings Plan
explanation: A Capacity Reservation guarantees capacity in an AZ without a discount; combining it with a Savings Plan adds the discount. A Savings Plan is a billing commitment and reserves nothing, Spot can be unavailable exactly when needed, and a quota is permission to launch, not capacity.

prompt: A web app must survive the loss of an Availability Zone. One proposal is a single large instance with termination protection and nightly snapshots. Which is the better design?
optionA: The single instance, since termination protection stops it from ever failing
optionB: An Auto Scaling group with at least two instances across two AZs behind an ALB
optionC: The single instance with hourly snapshots, so a restore loses less recent data
optionD: Two instances in one AZ, since spreading across zones adds too much latency
correctAnswerText: An Auto Scaling group with at least two instances across two AZs behind an ALB
explanation: Termination protection only stops deliberate termination; an AZ outage still takes the instance down, and snapshots mean a restore, not survival. A group spread over two AZs (min 2) keeps serving through the loss of one and replaces what failed. Two instances in one AZ share its fate.

prompt: Which Kubernetes component chooses the node for a Pod that has not yet been placed?
optionA: The kube-scheduler
optionB: The ReplicaSet controller
optionC: The kubelet
optionD: The kube-proxy
correctAnswerText: The kube-scheduler
explanation: The scheduler filters out nodes that cannot take the Pod, scores the rest and writes the chosen node into the Pod; it starts nothing itself. The kubelet then starts it, the ReplicaSet controller only creates Pod objects, and kube-proxy programs Service routing.

prompt: What is the job of the kubelet on each Kubernetes node?
optionA: Give each new Pod an IP address and wire Pod-to-Pod networking
optionB: Authenticate and authorise every request made to the cluster
optionC: Start its Pods via the runtime, run probes, report status
optionD: Store every cluster object in a consistent key-value database
correctAnswerText: Start its Pods via the runtime, run probes, report status
explanation: The kubelet watches for Pods bound to its node, asks containerd (through the CRI) to start them, runs their probes and reports back. etcd stores objects, the CNI plugin handles Pod networking, and the API server authenticates and authorises.

prompt: A log-shipping agent must run exactly one copy on every node. Which workload object is meant for that?
optionA: StatefulSet
optionB: Deployment
optionC: DaemonSet
optionD: CronJob
correctAnswerText: DaemonSet
explanation: A DaemonSet runs one Pod per node, including nodes added later. A StatefulSet gives stable identities and storage, a Deployment runs N interchangeable replicas wherever they fit, and a CronJob runs Jobs on a schedule.

prompt: Which Service type is reachable only from inside the cluster?
optionA: ClusterIP
optionB: NodePort
optionC: LoadBalancer
optionD: ExternalIP
correctAnswerText: ClusterIP
explanation: ClusterIP gives a virtual IP that only works inside the cluster — the default for internal services. NodePort opens a port on every node, LoadBalancer creates a cloud load balancer, and external IPs expose a Service on an outside address.

prompt: Every container in a Pod has CPU and memory requests equal to its limits. What QoS class does the Pod get?
optionA: Burstable
optionB: Critical
optionC: Guaranteed
optionD: BestEffort
correctAnswerText: Guaranteed
explanation: Requests equal to limits for CPU and memory in every container makes a Pod Guaranteed. Some requests or limits but not that is Burstable, nothing set is BestEffort, and "Critical" is not a QoS class (priority classes are a separate mechanism).

prompt: What kind of Pod disruption does a PodDisruptionBudget limit?
optionA: Container crashes caused by bugs in the application
optionB: Node failures caused by hardware or a network outage
optionC: Voluntary evictions such as drains and node upgrades
optionD: Out-of-memory kills when a container passes its limit
correctAnswerText: Voluntary evictions such as drains and node upgrades
explanation: A PDB is honoured by the eviction API, which drains, upgrades and node consolidation use. Crashes, node failures and OOM kills are involuntary and happen whatever the budget says.

prompt: In Helm, what is a release?
optionA: An installed instance of a chart in a cluster, with a revision history
optionB: A packaged chart version published to a repository for others to use
optionC: The values.yaml file that sets defaults for every template in a chart
optionD: A container image tag that Helm builds when a chart is first packaged
correctAnswerText: An installed instance of a chart in a cluster, with a revision history
explanation: Installing a chart creates a named release; each upgrade adds a revision, which is what helm rollback returns to. A packaged chart is a chart version, values.yaml holds defaults, and Helm does not build images.

prompt: What is the fully qualified in-cluster DNS name of a Service called api in the namespace clinic?
optionA: api.clinic.svc.cluster.local
optionB: api.svc.clinic.cluster.local
optionC: clinic.api.svc.cluster.local
optionD: api.clinic.pod.cluster.local
correctAnswerText: api.clinic.svc.cluster.local
explanation: CoreDNS names a Service <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. From the same namespace "api" is enough, and from another namespace "api.clinic". The other forms reverse or misplace the parts.

prompt: Which access mode does an EBS-backed PersistentVolumeClaim support?
optionA: ReadOnlyMany, read by many nodes
optionB: ReadWriteMany, many nodes at once
optionC: Any mode the claim asks for at all
optionD: ReadWriteOnce, one node at a time
correctAnswerText: ReadWriteOnce, one node at a time
explanation: An EBS volume attaches to one node, so it supports ReadWriteOnce (or ReadWriteOncePod). Shared read-write access across nodes needs EFS through its CSI driver; asking EBS for ReadWriteMany leaves the claim Pending.

prompt: What does kube-proxy do on each node?
optionA: Forwards kubectl commands from users to the API server
optionB: Caches container images so that Pods start more quickly
optionC: Terminates TLS for Ingress traffic arriving from outside
optionD: Programs rules so a Service's virtual IP reaches its Pods
correctAnswerText: Programs rules so a Service's virtual IP reaches its Pods
explanation: kube-proxy writes iptables or IPVS rules that turn a Service's ClusterIP into one of its ready Pod IPs (some CNIs replace it). It is not a kubectl proxy, an image cache or an Ingress controller.

prompt: Why does a Deployment recover by itself when one of its Pods is deleted by hand?
optionA: The kubelet keeps a backup copy of each Pod and restores it on deletion
optionB: Controllers watch the API server and act to close desired versus actual
optionC: kubectl warns the scheduler, which immediately reschedules the Pod
optionD: etcd refuses deletions of Pods that belong to a running Deployment
correctAnswerText: Controllers watch the API server and act to close desired versus actual
explanation: Nobody calls anybody: the ReplicaSet controller sees fewer Pods than desired and creates another, the scheduler places it and a kubelet starts it. Kubelets keep no backups, etcd accepts the delete, and kubectl talks only to the API server.

prompt: A ConfigMap consumed through envFrom is changed, but running Pods keep the old values. Why?
optionA: ConfigMap changes need an API server restart before they apply
optionB: envFrom copies values into the image the first time it is pulled
optionC: Environment variables are read once, when the container starts
optionD: The kubelet only syncs ConfigMaps for Pods in the default namespace
correctAnswerText: Environment variables are read once, when the container starts
explanation: A process's environment is fixed at start, so a ConfigMap change reaches env vars only after a restart — which is why config changes are made into rollouts. No API server restart is needed, images are untouched, and namespace makes no difference.

prompt: Why is the base64 encoding of a Kubernetes Secret not, by itself, any protection?
optionA: It is applied only when the Secret is created with kubectl directly
optionB: It is a reversible encoding that anyone who reads it can decode
optionC: It is removed by the API server whenever the Secret is listed out
optionD: It is encryption, but the key is printed in every Pod's environment
correctAnswerText: It is a reversible encoding that anyone who reads it can decode
explanation: base64 is an encoding with no key, so anyone with get or list on the Secret, etcd access or exec into the Pod has the value. Real protection is RBAC, encryption at rest (KMS on EKS) and keeping values in an external store, not in Git.

prompt: Why should an EBS StorageClass use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer?
optionA: The disk lives in one AZ, so it should be made where the Pod lands
optionB: It delays the bill for the disk until the Pod has been running a day
optionC: It stops the claim from being deleted while a Pod is still using it
optionD: It lets several Pods on different nodes share the same EBS volume
correctAnswerText: The disk lives in one AZ, so it should be made where the Pod lands
explanation: Binding immediately can create the volume in one AZ while the scheduler later wants the Pod in another, leaving it unschedulable. Waiting creates the disk in the scheduled Pod's AZ. It has no effect on billing, multi-attach or deletion protection.

prompt: Why do HTTP services usually share one Ingress instead of each being a LoadBalancer Service?
optionA: LoadBalancer Services work only on NodePort ranges below port 1024
optionB: Each LoadBalancer Service creates its own cloud load balancer and bill
optionC: LoadBalancer Services cannot route HTTP traffic, only raw TCP or UDP
optionD: An Ingress encrypts traffic between Pods, while Services leave it plain
correctAnswerText: Each LoadBalancer Service creates its own cloud load balancer and bill
explanation: Ten LoadBalancer Services mean ten load balancers and ten hourly charges; one Ingress (one ALB with the AWS controller) routes by host and path to many Services. LoadBalancer Services carry HTTP fine, Ingress does not encrypt Pod-to-Pod traffic, and NodePorts are 30000–32767.

prompt: Why does a Pod have separate readiness and liveness probes rather than a single health check?
optionA: They are the same check, run twice so that one failure is not trusted
optionB: Readiness runs on the node and liveness runs on the control plane instead
optionC: Readiness stops traffic without a restart; liveness restarts the container
optionD: Liveness decides scheduling, while readiness decides the QoS of the Pod
correctAnswerText: Readiness stops traffic without a restart; liveness restarts the container
explanation: A failing readiness probe removes the Pod from Service endpoints until it recovers (warming a cache, a slow dependency); a failing liveness probe kills and restarts it. The kubelet runs both, neither affects scheduling or QoS, and they ask different questions.

prompt: Why does a short preStop sleep reduce 502 errors during rolling deploys?
optionA: The sleep delays the new Pod's start so that two versions never overlap
optionB: preStop hooks run only on new Pods and give them time to warm their caches
optionC: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM start together; the sleep lets routing catch up
optionD: The sleep lowers CPU usage so the load balancer health check passes again
correctAnswerText: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM start together; the sleep lets routing catch up
explanation: When a Pod is deleted, it is removed from endpoints while the kubelet runs preStop then SIGTERM; other nodes and the load balancer take seconds to notice, so a Pod that exits at once still receives requests. preStop runs on terminating Pods, not new ones, and has nothing to do with CPU or version overlap.

prompt: Why do Pods with no resource requests tend to end up packed onto nodes that are already busy?
optionA: The scheduler adds up requests, so a Pod with none looks free to place
optionB: The scheduler sends request-less Pods to the busiest node on purpose
optionC: Pods without requests are pinned to the node that pulled their image
optionD: The kubelet moves request-less Pods to full nodes to free empty ones
correctAnswerText: The scheduler adds up requests, so a Pod with none looks free to place
explanation: Scheduling arithmetic uses requests, not live usage, so a Pod requesting nothing fits anywhere on paper and lands on full nodes, where it is also first to be evicted (BestEffort). There is no deliberate busy-node rule, image pulls do not pin Pods, and kubelets do not move Pods.

prompt: Why do Pods on a node that has just gone NotReady stay there for about five minutes before being replaced?
optionA: Pods are replaced only once the cloud provider has deleted the VM itself
optionB: The scheduler only runs every five minutes, so Pods wait for its next pass
optionC: Default tolerations wait so a brief network blip does not reshuffle Pods
optionD: etcd needs five minutes to elect a new leader after any node is lost
correctAnswerText: Default tolerations wait so a brief network blip does not reshuffle Pods
explanation: Pods get not-ready and unreachable tolerations of 300 seconds by default, a deliberate delay so short outages do not cause churn; after that they are evicted and replaced. The scheduler runs continuously, a worker node is not an etcd member, and VM deletion is not required.

prompt: On EKS, why is each service account given its own IAM role rather than relying on the node's instance role?
optionA: Every Pod on a node would share the node role and all of its permissions
optionB: EKS bills AWS API calls made with the node role at a much higher rate
optionC: Instance roles expire after an hour, while service account roles do not
optionD: The node's instance role cannot be used by any process inside a container
correctAnswerText: Every Pod on a node would share the node role and all of its permissions
explanation: With the node role, any Pod scheduled on that node gets the union of everything its neighbours need. IRSA or Pod Identity scopes permissions to one service account. Containers can reach the node role (that is the danger), both credentials are temporary, and billing is not affected.

prompt: An HPA targets 60% average CPU utilisation. Five api Pods are averaging 90%. How many replicas will it ask for?
explanation: desired = ceil(current × metric ÷ target) = ceil(5 × 90 ÷ 60) = ceil(7.5) = 8. Rounding down gives 7; the HPA always rounds up so the target is met.

prompt: An HPA has two metrics: CPU target 60% and memory target 60%. Six Pods are at 40% CPU and 90% memory. What replica count results?
optionA: 4, the smaller of the two answers
optionB: 9, the larger of the two answers
optionC: 6, since the two metrics disagree
optionD: 7, the average of the two answers
correctAnswerText: 9, the larger of the two answers
explanation: The HPA computes a count per metric — ceil(6 × 40 ÷ 60) = 4 for CPU and ceil(6 × 90 ÷ 60) = 9 for memory — and takes the largest, 9, so no metric is left over target. It never takes the minimum or an average, and disagreement does not freeze it.

prompt: An Ingress sends path /api (pathType Prefix) to the api Service and / to the web Service. Which request goes to web, not api?
optionA: /api
optionB: /api/slots/42
optionC: /api/
optionD: /apis/status
correctAnswerText: /apis/status
explanation: Prefix matches whole path elements, so /api matches /api, /api/ and /api/slots/42, but not /apis/status — that falls through to /. A plain string prefix would wrongly include /apis.

prompt: With the VPC CNI and no prefix delegation, an instance type supports 4 ENIs with 15 IPv4 addresses each. What is its maximum Pods per node?
explanation: max Pods = ENIs × (IPv4 addresses per ENI − 1) + 2 = 4 × 14 + 2 = 58. Each ENI's primary address is not given to Pods, and the + 2 covers host-network Pods. Prefix delegation raises this ceiling considerably.

prompt: The web Deployment runs 3 replicas. Which PodDisruptionBudget protects it while still letting node drains proceed?
optionA: minAvailable: 3
optionB: maxUnavailable: 0
optionC: maxUnavailable: 1
optionD: minAvailable: 100%
correctAnswerText: maxUnavailable: 1
explanation: maxUnavailable: 1 lets a drain evict one Pod at a time and keeps working as replicas change. minAvailable: 3, minAvailable: 100% and maxUnavailable: 0 all forbid every eviction, so node upgrades hang.

prompt: A Pod's preStop hook sleeps 10 seconds and the app needs up to 30 seconds to finish in-flight requests after SIGTERM. Which terminationGracePeriodSeconds is right?
optionA: 30, matching only the drain on its own
optionB: 10, matching only the preStop sleep
optionC: 45, covering both with some headroom
optionD: 0, so the old Pod is gone at once
correctAnswerText: 45, covering both with some headroom
explanation: The grace period counts from the start of termination and must cover preStop plus the drain (40 s here), with headroom; after it the kubelet sends SIGKILL. 30 or 10 cut the drain short, and 0 kills in-flight requests.

prompt: A cleanup CronJob must run daily at 01:30 India time, and the controller runs in UTC. Which spec does that?
optionA: schedule "30 1 * * *" with no timeZone field set
optionB: schedule "30 1 * * *" with concurrencyPolicy Forbid
optionC: schedule "1 30 * * *" with timeZone "Asia/Kolkata"
optionD: schedule "30 1 * * *" with timeZone "Asia/Kolkata"
correctAnswerText: schedule "30 1 * * *" with timeZone "Asia/Kolkata"
explanation: Cron fields are minute then hour, and spec.timeZone makes the schedule read in IST. Without timeZone it runs at 01:30 UTC (07:00 IST), swapping the fields is invalid, and concurrencyPolicy controls overlapping runs, not time.

prompt: A chart's values.yaml sets replicaCount: 2, the release uses -f values-prod.yaml with replicaCount: 4, and the command adds --set replicaCount=6. What is rendered?
optionA: 4, since the -f file overrides --set flags
optionB: 6, since --set overrides the values files
optionC: 12, since Helm adds all three values together
optionD: 2, since chart defaults always take priority
correctAnswerText: 6, since --set overrides the values files
explanation: Helm merges chart defaults, then -f files in order, then --set, with later sources winning: 6. Values files do not beat --set, defaults are the lowest priority, and numbers are replaced, not summed.

prompt: The clinic namespace has a default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy. The api Pods must now accept traffic from the web Pods only. What do you add?
optionA: A policy selecting app: api, allowing ingress from podSelector app: web
optionB: Nothing: Pods in the same namespace are always exempt from the default deny
optionC: A policy selecting all Pods, allowing ingress from anywhere on port 80
optionD: A policy selecting app: web, allowing egress to every Pod in the cluster
correctAnswerText: A policy selecting app: api, allowing ingress from podSelector app: web
explanation: Policies are additive: a policy selecting the api Pods that allows ingress from Pods labelled app: web (on the api port) opens exactly that path. An egress rule on web does not open api's ingress, an allow-all undoes the default deny, and namespaces give no exemption.

prompt: A 4-replica Deployment rolls out with maxSurge: 25% and maxUnavailable: 0. How does the rollout proceed?
optionA: Two new Pods start at once, and two old Pods stop at the same moment
optionB: One old Pod stops first, then a new one starts in its place each time
optionC: One extra new Pod at a time; an old one goes only when it is Ready
optionD: All four old Pods stop first, then four new Pods start together
correctAnswerText: One extra new Pod at a time; an old one goes only when it is Ready
explanation: 25% of 4 allows one Pod above the desired count and 0 unavailable allows none below it, so the controller adds one new Pod, waits for it to be Ready, removes an old one, and repeats. Stopping old Pods first would breach maxUnavailable: 0.

prompt: A report Pod stays Pending with "Insufficient memory", yet dashboards show every node using under half its RAM. What explains it?
optionA: The Pod's memory limit is too low for the scheduler to find any node
optionB: The dashboards lag, and the nodes are really using all of their memory
optionC: Requests already placed leave no node room for this Pod's memory request
optionD: The image is too big to fit in node memory, so it cannot be pulled yet
correctAnswerText: Requests already placed leave no node room for this Pod's memory request
explanation: The scheduler compares the sum of requests on each node, not live usage, so generous requests can fill nodes on paper while RAM sits idle. Right-size requests from measurements or add capacity. Limits do not affect scheduling, and image size causes pull problems, not FailedScheduling.

prompt: Calls to http://api from the web Pods time out. The api Pods are Running and Ready with label app: api-server; the Service selector is app: api. What is wrong?
optionA: ClusterIP addresses cannot be reached from Pods in the same namespace
optionB: The Service needs type LoadBalancer before other Pods can reach it
optionC: The selector matches no Pods, so the Service has no endpoints at all
optionD: The api Pods must be restarted before a new Service can find them
correctAnswerText: The selector matches no Pods, so the Service has no endpoints at all
explanation: A Service sends traffic to the Ready Pods its selector matches; app: api matches nothing, so the endpoint list is empty and traffic goes nowhere. Fix the selector or the labels. ClusterIP works within and across namespaces, Pods need no restart, and LoadBalancer is for outside access.

prompt: After a secrets clean-up, new api Pods show CreateContainerConfigError: "couldn't find key DB_PASSWORD in Secret clinic/api-db". Old Pods are still running. Why?
optionA: The Secret's key was renamed, while secretKeyRef still names DB_PASSWORD
optionB: The new Pods have too little memory to decode the Secret at start-up
optionC: The old Pods have locked the Secret, so new Pods cannot read it yet
optionD: The Secret is encrypted, and only the old Pods hold the decryption key
correctAnswerText: The Secret's key was renamed, while secretKeyRef still names DB_PASSWORD
explanation: The sync now writes a differently named key, and the Deployment asks for one that no longer exists; old Pods are fine because env vars were read when they started. Make the names agree in one reviewed change. Memory, decryption keys and locks play no part.

prompt: A worker restarts every few hours with Reason OOMKilled and exit code 137. Its memory limit is 256Mi, and kubectl top shows peaks near 330Mi while batching. What is the right fix?
optionA: Raise the CPU limit so the batch finishes before memory fills up
optionB: Add a liveness probe so the worker restarts before it is killed
optionC: Set explicit requests and a memory limit above the measured peak
optionD: Remove all resources so the Pod becomes BestEffort and is not capped
correctAnswerText: Set explicit requests and a memory limit above the measured peak
explanation: Exit 137 with OOMKilled means the container passed its memory limit; size from measurements, for example request 256Mi and limit 384Mi. A probe still restarts it, CPU does not cap memory, and dropping resources makes it first to be evicted (or a LimitRange will add a default limit back).

prompt: A claim for shared report storage asks for ReadWriteMany from the gp3 (EBS) StorageClass and has been Pending for a day. What is the cause and fix?
optionA: gp3 needs Retain as its reclaim policy before it will bind any claims
optionB: The claim is too small; ask for more storage so it will be provisioned
optionC: EBS cannot attach to many nodes; use an EFS class for shared storage
optionD: The Pod must be deleted, since claims bind only to Pods yet to start
correctAnswerText: EBS cannot attach to many nodes; use an EFS class for shared storage
explanation: An EBS volume is single-node, so a ReadWriteMany claim against an EBS class never binds. Shared read-write storage across nodes needs EFS through its CSI driver. Size, reclaim policy and deleting the Pod do not change what EBS supports.

prompt: A feature-flag file is mounted from a ConfigMap with subPath, and the app re-reads it every minute. Hours after the ConfigMap changed, the file is still old. Why?
optionA: The kubelet updates mounted ConfigMap files only once every day
optionB: Files mounted with subPath are never updated after the Pod starts
optionC: The app needs read permission granted on the ConfigMap via RBAC
optionD: ConfigMaps larger than one key are never refreshed in a mounted volume
correctAnswerText: Files mounted with subPath are never updated after the Pod starts
explanation: The kubelet refreshes ConfigMap volume files after a short delay, but never for a subPath mount. Mount the whole volume, or treat config changes as rollouts (a checksum annotation or kubectl rollout restart). The refresh is not daily, the app reads a file not the API, and key count does not matter.

prompt: Even with a preStop sleep, a service still drops in-flight requests at every deploy. Its container starts the server from a shell script that runs as PID 1. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The script does not forward SIGTERM, so the server never drains
optionB: PID 1 always ignores SIGKILL, so the grace period never actually ends
optionC: Shell scripts cannot open network ports, so requests fail at random
optionD: The preStop sleep is too long, so the readiness probe begins failing
correctAnswerText: The script does not forward SIGTERM, so the server never drains
explanation: Uvicorn or Gunicorn drain on SIGTERM, but a shell script as PID 1 that does not forward signals means the server is simply killed at the end of the grace period. Use exec in the script or run the server directly. A readiness failure while draining is intended, and SIGKILL cannot be ignored.

prompt: kubectl get hpa shows TARGETS <unknown>/65% for a CPU-based HPA, and it never scales. The metrics server is running. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: The Deployment uses RollingUpdate, which the HPA does not support
optionB: The scale-down stabilisation window is blocking all scaling actions
optionC: The containers set no CPU request, so utilisation cannot be computed
optionD: The maximum replica count is lower than the current number of Pods
correctAnswerText: The containers set no CPU request, so utilisation cannot be computed
explanation: CPU utilisation is usage as a percentage of the request; with no request there is nothing to divide by, so the target shows <unknown>. A low max would show a real value capped at max, the stabilisation window only slows scale-down, and the HPA works with any strategy.

prompt: An Ingress with ingressClassName: alb was applied to a new EKS cluster an hour ago. It has no address and no load balancer exists. What is the most likely reason?
optionA: No controller watches that class; the AWS Load Balancer Controller is missing
optionB: Ingress objects take several hours before AWS creates their load balancer
optionC: The backend Services must be type LoadBalancer before the Ingress can work
optionD: Ingress needs a NetworkPolicy allowing the internet into the namespace first
correctAnswerText: No controller watches that class; the AWS Load Balancer Controller is missing
explanation: An Ingress is only a set of rules; without a controller for its class it does nothing. Install the AWS Load Balancer Controller with its own IAM role. There is no multi-hour delay, backends are normally ClusterIP, and NetworkPolicy does not create load balancers.

prompt: On a growing EKS cluster whose nodes sit in /24 subnets, new Pods stay in ContainerCreating with "failed to assign an IP address to container". What is the underlying problem?
optionA: CoreDNS has failed, so new Pods cannot resolve the API server's address
optionB: The nodes have too little memory to create another network namespace
optionC: The VPC CNI has run out of subnet IPs, since every Pod takes a VPC address
optionD: The Pods need a NodePort Service before the CNI will give them addresses
correctAnswerText: The VPC CNI has run out of subnet IPs, since every Pod takes a VPC address
explanation: The VPC CNI gives each Pod a real subnet IP, so a small subnet runs dry; larger subnets or prefix delegation are the fixes. DNS failures show differently, memory is not the message here, and Services do not hand out Pod IPs.

prompt: An EKS cluster runs Pods of very different sizes, wants Spot where possible, and must scale up quickly at a morning rush. Which way of providing nodes fits best?
optionA: Fargate profiles for everything, since they need no nodes at all
optionB: Karpenter, launching right-sized nodes including Spot as Pods appear
optionC: One managed node group of a single large type, sized for the rush
optionD: Hand-built EC2 nodes joined to the cluster by an engineer each time
correctAnswerText: Karpenter, launching right-sized nodes including Spot as Pods appear
explanation: Karpenter launches nodes sized to pending Pods, mixes Spot and types, and scales up fast. One fixed type wastes capacity when sized for the peak, Fargate on EKS has limits (no DaemonSets, no EBS volumes) and no Spot mixing of this kind, and hand-built nodes do not scale.

prompt: A team wants its database password managed declaratively alongside its manifests. Which approach should it choose?
optionA: Bake the password into the image, so no Secret object exists in the cluster
optionB: Commit the Secret manifest to Git, since base64 hides the value from readers
optionC: Put it in a ConfigMap, since ConfigMaps are easier to update than Secrets
optionD: Keep it in Secrets Manager, synced by External Secrets, with RBAC
correctAnswerText: Keep it in Secrets Manager, synced by External Secrets, with RBAC
explanation: An ExternalSecret in Git names the remote key, so the manifests stay declarative while the value lives in Secrets Manager; RBAC and encryption at rest protect the synced Secret. A Secret in Git is a leak, an image ships the value to everyone who pulls it, and a ConfigMap is not treated as secret at all.

prompt: A chart's ConfigMap changes often, and running Pods keep stale values until someone remembers to restart them. Which change is best?
optionA: Delete all Pods by hand after each helm upgrade to force fresh values
optionB: Add a checksum of the ConfigMap as a Pod annotation, so changes roll out
optionC: Lower the kubelet sync period so env vars refresh inside running Pods
optionD: Tell engineers to run kubectl edit on the live Pods after every change
correctAnswerText: Add a checksum of the ConfigMap as a Pod annotation, so changes roll out
explanation: A checksum annotation changes the Pod template whenever the config changes, so Helm's upgrade becomes a normal, controlled rolling update. Editing Pods by hand is drift, env vars never refresh in place, and mass deletion skips the rollout's safety.

prompt: Four api replicas must survive an AZ outage but should not fail to schedule when one node is busy. Which spreading design best balances the two?
optionA: No spreading at all, since the scheduler already places replicas evenly
optionB: Hard spread across zones, soft spread across nodes (ScheduleAnyway)
optionC: Spread hard across nodes and zones, so no two replicas ever share either
optionD: Pin all four replicas to one large node so they can share a warm cache
correctAnswerText: Hard spread across zones, soft spread across nodes (ScheduleAnyway)
explanation: A hard zone constraint guarantees survival of an AZ loss; a soft node constraint prefers spreading without leaving Pods Pending when nodes are tight. Hard on both can block scheduling, no constraint can stack replicas, and one node makes four replicas one replica for availability.

prompt: A bookings API sees sharp morning spikes followed by noisy, uneven traffic. How should its HPA behaviour block be tuned?
optionA: Scale up slowly to save money; scale down fast as soon as CPU drops
optionB: Scale up fast with no window; scale down slowly after a calm window
optionC: Disable scale-down altogether, so capacity from the spike is never lost
optionD: Scale both directions instantly, so replicas always track the metric
correctAnswerText: Scale up fast with no window; scale down slowly after a calm window
explanation: Fast scale-up meets the spike; a stabilisation window and limited scale-down rate stop the HPA removing Pods on every dip and then adding them back. Slow scale-up drops users, instant both ways flaps, and never scaling down pays for the peak all day.

prompt: MediSlot will expose eight HTTP services on one domain from EKS, with TLS from ACM. Which design is best?
optionA: Eight NodePort Services, with users told the node IP and port of each service
optionB: One LoadBalancer Service in front of an api Pod that proxies to all the others
optionC: Eight LoadBalancer Services, giving each service its own network load balancer
optionD: One Ingress through the AWS Load Balancer Controller, routing by path to an ALB
correctAnswerText: One Ingress through the AWS Load Balancer Controller, routing by path to an ALB
explanation: One Ingress becomes one ALB with the ACM certificate, routing by host and path to eight ClusterIP Services. Eight load balancers multiply cost and certificates, NodePorts expose node addresses that change, and a hand-written proxy Pod reinvents the controller as a single point of failure.

prompt: A latency-critical service loses a third of its capacity for about five minutes whenever a node dies. A proposal is to cut its unreachable tolerationSeconds to 30. How should this be judged?
optionA: Pointless, since tolerationSeconds only affects Pods during a manual drain
optionB: A clear win with no downside, since Pods on a lost node are never coming back
optionC: Dangerous, since a shorter toleration deletes the node from the cluster
optionD: Faster replacement, at the cost of churn on brief network blips; add replicas
correctAnswerText: Faster replacement, at the cost of churn on brief network blips; add replicas
explanation: A shorter toleration evicts sooner, but a node that was only briefly unreachable then sheds its Pods for nothing. Pair any change with enough replicas, spread across nodes and zones, so losing one node's share is survivable. Drains use eviction, not tolerations, and tolerations do not delete nodes.

prompt: A company is building several new EKS clusters on EC2 nodes and wants Pods to reach S3 with one role reused across clusters. Which mechanism suits it best?
optionA: Access keys stored in a Kubernetes Secret and mounted in each Pod
optionB: EKS Pod Identity, with associations made through the EKS API
optionC: IRSA, with a separate OIDC trust written into the role per cluster
optionD: The node instance role, extended with S3 access for all the Pods
correctAnswerText: EKS Pod Identity, with associations made through the EKS API
explanation: Pod Identity needs no OIDC provider per cluster and one role can serve several clusters, so the course prefers it for new EC2-node clusters. IRSA works (and is still needed on Fargate) but ties trust to each cluster's issuer. Stored keys and a shared node role are what both mechanisms replace.

prompt: During an incident an engineer fixed a probe with kubectl edit on the live Deployment. A week later the bug returned after a routine release. What should the team change?
optionA: Give more engineers kubectl edit rights so fixes are made more quickly
optionB: Take a weekly etcd backup so live edits can be restored after releases
optionC: Stop running releases so that live fixes are never overwritten again
optionD: Change the cluster only from Git, via apply or Argo CD, never by hand
correctAnswerText: Change the cluster only from Git, via apply or Argo CD, never by hand
explanation: A hand edit is drift waiting to be overwritten by the next apply from Git. Fixes go through version control (an emergency edit is followed at once by the same change in Git). More edit rights add drift, freezing releases is not a fix, and restoring etcd would roll back everything else too.

prompt: A StorageClass for a production database's volumes is being chosen. Should its reclaimPolicy be Delete or Retain?
optionA: Delete: Retain makes a claim impossible to resize after it is created
optionB: Retain: it also makes the volume readable from many nodes at once
optionC: Delete: it is the default, and defaults are always safest for production
optionD: Retain: one careless claim deletion must not destroy the data volume
correctAnswerText: Retain: one careless claim deletion must not destroy the data volume
explanation: With Delete, removing the claim deletes the disk — one command from data loss. Retain keeps it, at the cost of manual clean-up and paying for it until then. Defaults are not chosen for production data, expansion is a separate setting, and access modes are unaffected.

prompt: What does a declarative infrastructure file such as a Terraform configuration describe?
optionA: The end state that should exist; the tool works out the steps
optionB: A snapshot of the account that is restored on each apply
optionC: A full history of every change, replayed from the beginning
optionD: The ordered list of API calls the tool replays on every run
correctAnswerText: The end state that should exist; the tool works out the steps
explanation: Declarative code states what should exist; the tool reads what does exist and plans only the difference. An ordered list of calls is the imperative style, which breaks when the starting point differs, and neither history replay nor snapshot restore is how Terraform, CloudFormation or Bicep work.

prompt: In terraform plan output, what does the symbol -/+ in front of a resource mean?
optionA: Destroy the existing object, then create a replacement
optionB: Create the replacement first and only then destroy the old
optionC: Update the existing object in place without replacing it
optionD: Read a data source and leave every managed object alone
correctAnswerText: Destroy the existing object, then create a replacement
explanation: -/+ is destroy-then-create: the object is replaced, which for a bucket or database means a new, empty one. ~ is an in-place update, <= reads a data source, and +/- is the create_before_destroy order — so -/+ lines are the ones a reviewer reads first.

prompt: What does Terraform state record?
optionA: The provider credentials that were used for the most recent terraform apply
optionB: The list of engineers allowed to run plan and apply against the configuration
optionC: Which real object each resource address manages, with its last-seen attributes
optionD: A copy of every .tf file, so the configuration can be rebuilt if it is lost
correctAnswerText: Which real object each resource address manages, with its last-seen attributes
explanation: State maps each address (aws_s3_bucket.reports) to the real object and stores its attributes, which is how Terraform tells "create" from "already mine". It holds no provider credentials, is not a backup of the code, and access control lives in IAM on the backend, not in state.

prompt: A required_providers block sets the AWS provider to version = "~> 6.0". Which releases does that allow?
optionA: Any release at or above 6.0, including 7.x
optionB: Any 6.0.x patch, but no 6.1 or later minor
optionC: Exactly 6.0.0 and none of its later patches
optionD: 6.0 and any later 6.x release, but not 7.0
correctAnswerText: 6.0 and any later 6.x release, but not 7.0
explanation: "~> 6.0" lets the rightmost given number grow: minors and patches of 6 are allowed, the next major (which may rename arguments) is not. An exact pin is "= 6.0.0", ">= 6.0" would allow 7.x, and patch-only is "~> 6.0.0".

prompt: Which CloudFormation feature plays the role of terraform plan before a stack update?
optionA: A change set, created and read before it is executed
optionB: Termination protection, which blocks delete-stack calls
optionC: Drift detection, which compares the stack with reality
optionD: A stack policy, which forbids updates to named resources
correctAnswerText: A change set, created and read before it is executed
explanation: A change set lists each Add, Modify or Remove (with Replacement True or False) before anything happens, like a plan. Stack policies and termination protection restrict changes, and drift detection compares reality with the record; none of them previews an update.

prompt: What does the state lock in an S3 backend with use_lockfile = true prevent?
optionA: Terraform from upgrading the provider during terraform init
optionB: Anyone from changing resources by hand in the AWS console
optionC: Engineers without the right IAM role from reading the state
optionD: Two plans or applies writing the same state at the same time
correctAnswerText: Two plans or applies writing the same state at the same time
explanation: The lock lets one operation at a time hold a given state; a second gets "Error acquiring the state lock" and waits. Read access is IAM on the bucket, console edits are drift the lock never sees, and provider upgrades are governed by the dependency lock file.

prompt: What does a moved block tell Terraform?
optionA: A resource should move to another AWS region on next apply
optionB: The state file should be migrated to a different backend key
optionC: An object now has a new address but is the same real object
optionD: A resource should be copied into another configuration's state
correctAnswerText: An object now has a new address but is the same real object
explanation: moved { from, to } records a rename — into for_each, a module or a new name — so the plan shows a move instead of destroy-and-create. It moves nothing in AWS, does not copy into another state, and backend moves are terraform init -migrate-state.

prompt: Where does Bicep keep its record of what it has deployed?
optionA: In a local .bicepstate file committed next to the template file
optionB: Nowhere of its own: Azure Resource Manager itself is the record
optionC: In a state file stored in a Blob Storage container you create
optionD: In a CloudFormation-style stack object kept inside the subscription
correctAnswerText: Nowhere of its own: Azure Resource Manager itself is the record
explanation: Bicep compiles to ARM templates and deploys into a resource group; ARM is the source of truth, so there is no state file to protect. Blob Storage with a lease is where Terraform's azurerm backend keeps state, which is a different tool.

prompt: With terraform plan -detailed-exitcode, what does exit code 2 mean?
optionA: The plan succeeded and has nothing to do
optionB: The plan failed with a configuration error
optionC: The plan succeeded and contains changes
optionD: The plan could not acquire the state lock
correctAnswerText: The plan succeeded and contains changes
explanation: The codes are 0 for no changes, 1 for an error and 2 for a successful, non-empty plan. A scheduled job on an untouched main branch that gets 2 has found drift; a lock failure is an error, reported as 1.

prompt: What is .terraform.lock.hcl, and what should a team do with it?
optionA: It stores the saved plan for CI; upload it as a job artifact
optionB: It records the exact provider builds chosen; commit it to Git
optionC: It caches downloaded provider binaries; add it to .gitignore
optionD: It holds the state lock for the backend; delete it after apply
correctAnswerText: It records the exact provider builds chosen; commit it to Git
explanation: The dependency lock file pins the provider versions and hashes init selected, so every laptop and CI run uses the same build — it belongs in Git. The state lock lives in the backend, binaries live in .terraform/ (ignored), and a saved plan is a separate file.

prompt: Right after a successful apply, an engineer runs terraform plan again on the same code. Why is "No changes." the result a team wants to see?
optionA: It shows the state lock was released properly after the last apply
optionB: It shows the provider cached the result and skipped calling AWS
optionC: It shows the plan role has no write access to the account at all
optionD: It shows the definition is idempotent and matches what now exists
correctAnswerText: It shows the definition is idempotent and matches what now exists
explanation: An idempotent definition converges: applying it again changes nothing, so an empty plan proves the code and reality agree. A plan that is never empty points at two owners of one object or a floating value. Lock release, caching and role permissions are not what the empty plan demonstrates.

prompt: Why is the bucket holding Terraform state treated as a secret store, even when every password variable is marked sensitive = true?
optionA: The S3 backend refuses to encrypt objects unless they are tagged as secrets
optionB: Plan output is copied into the state bucket every time a pipeline job runs
optionC: sensitive variables are written to a second file that sits beside the state
optionD: sensitive only hides values in output; state still stores them in plain text
correctAnswerText: sensitive only hides values in output; state still stores them in plain text
explanation: sensitive redacts plan and apply output, but state records every attribute, so a password, a random_password result or a private key is readable to anyone who can read state. Hence encryption, versioning, tight IAM — and keeping secrets out of state (manage_master_user_password) where possible.

prompt: Why does the course prefer for_each over count when creating one queue for each name in a collection?
optionA: Keys are names, so removing one item does not shift any other address
optionB: for_each resources are excluded from state, so they are faster to plan
optionC: count cannot be combined with variables, only with literal whole numbers
optionD: for_each runs the API calls in parallel, while count creates one by one
correctAnswerText: Keys are names, so removing one item does not shift any other address
explanation: count addresses are positions: delete the middle item and every later item shifts index, so Terraform plans replacements. for_each addresses are keys, so only the removed key is touched. Both run in parallel, count accepts expressions, and both live in state.

prompt: Why should the container image tag of a service released several times a day stay out of the Terraform code?
optionA: Terraform cannot pass a string value into an ECS task definition
optionB: Image tags are secrets and must never appear in any repository
optionC: Every release would then need an infrastructure plan and apply
optionD: The AWS provider rejects tags that do not follow semantic versions
correctAnswerText: Every release would then need an infrastructure plan and apply
explanation: Fast-moving application releases belong to the CI/CD pipeline; if the tag lives in Terraform, each release becomes an infrastructure change with its own plan, lock and review. Terraform can set the value, tags are not secrets, and the provider has no versioning rule for them.

prompt: Why should a reusable child module leave out provider configuration and backend blocks?
optionA: Because Terraform rejects any module that contains a provider block at all
optionB: So the module runs without credentials, which makes it safe to share widely
optionC: Because modules store their own state, and a backend block would duplicate it
optionD: So the root decides the account and region, and one module serves any of them
correctAnswerText: So the root decides the account and region, and one module serves any of them
explanation: Provider settings and the backend belong to the root; the module just uses "aws", so callers can hand it an aliased provider for another region or account. Terraform tolerates legacy in-module providers, the module still runs with the root's credentials, and its resources live in the root's state.

prompt: Why are CLI workspaces a weak way to separate a production environment from dev?
optionA: Each workspace downloads its own provider, so plans are much slower to run
optionB: The selected workspace is invisible in code and shares the same credentials
optionC: Workspaces cannot keep their state in an S3 backend with a lock file at all
optionD: Workspaces force every environment to use exactly the same variable values
correctAnswerText: The selected workspace is invisible in code and shares the same credentials
explanation: One directory, one backend and one set of credentials serve every workspace; which is selected is only in the CLI's memory, so an apply in the wrong one changes prod. Workspaces do work with S3 (under env:/), can read different values via terraform.workspace, and share plugins.

prompt: Why does a production pipeline apply the saved tfplan file rather than run a fresh apply with auto-approve?
optionA: A saved plan carries the credentials, so the job needs no role
optionB: Applying a saved plan skips the state lock and so finishes sooner
optionC: What runs is exactly what the approver read, or it fails as stale
optionD: A fresh apply cannot run in a job that has no terminal attached
correctAnswerText: What runs is exactly what the approver read, or it fails as stale
explanation: auto-approve recomputes a new plan nobody reviewed; a saved plan applies precisely the reviewed changes and Terraform refuses it if state moved in between. Applies run non-interactively either way, the lock is still taken, and a plan file holds no credentials (though it does hold values, so it is guarded).

prompt: Why does a Terraform configuration rarely need depends_on?
optionA: Terraform retries failed creates until all dependencies are ready
optionB: A reference to another resource's attribute already orders the two
optionC: Terraform creates resources in the order they appear in the files
optionD: The provider sorts every resource type into a fixed creation order
correctAnswerText: A reference to another resource's attribute already orders the two
explanation: Using aws_s3_bucket.reports.id in another block adds an edge to the dependency graph, so Terraform waits for the bucket. File order and provider ordering play no part, and retries are not how ordering works; depends_on is for dependencies Terraform cannot see.

prompt: Why does the course set DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy explicitly on CloudFormation resources that hold data?
optionA: So that other stacks can read the resource through !ImportValue calls
optionB: So data survives the resource leaving the template or being replaced
optionC: So CloudFormation encrypts the data with a customer managed KMS key
optionD: So that the stack can be updated without creating a change set first
correctAnswerText: So data survives the resource leaving the template or being replaced
explanation: Retain (or Snapshot for databases and volumes) keeps the physical resource or a final snapshot when it is removed from the stack or replaced by an update. They do not encrypt anything, do not bypass change sets, and exports are a separate feature.

prompt: Why must the role used for pull-request plans be read-only, even though a plan changes nothing?
optionA: AWS refuses plan-style read calls from roles with write access
optionB: A read-only role lets plan skip refreshing resource attributes
optionC: Read-only roles make the posted plan output shorter to review
optionD: Plan runs providers and data sources from the PR's own code
correctAnswerText: Plan runs providers and data sources from the PR's own code
explanation: During plan Terraform executes provider code and data sources such as data "external" from the proposed branch, so a hostile pull request acts with whatever that role allows. AWS has no such rule, refresh still runs, and the role has nothing to do with output size.

prompt: Kavach Logistics has a console-built bucket, kavach-legacy-manifests, that must come under Terraform without being recreated. What should the engineer do?
optionA: Write a new resource with the same bucket name and let apply adopt it
optionB: Write an import block, generate config, and aim for a plan with only the import
optionC: Delete the bucket, then let Terraform create it again with the right settings
optionD: Copy the bucket's JSON into terraform.tfstate by hand and run apply
correctAnswerText: Write an import block, generate config, and aim for a plan with only the import
explanation: An import block (with -generate-config-out for a starting block) brings the object into state; a plan showing "1 to import" and nothing else proves the code matches reality. A plain resource would try to create a duplicate and fail on the global name, deleting loses data, and hand-editing state is unreviewed and error-prone.

prompt: Kavach's dev and prod roots need different state keys, and backend "s3" { key = var.state_key } fails at init. Which setup works?
optionA: An environment variable TF_VAR_state_key exported before running init
optionB: A backend block inside a shared module, with the key passed in as an input
optionC: backend "s3" {} in code, and terraform init -backend-config=backend/prod.hcl
optionD: A locals block holding the key, since locals are resolved before the backend
correctAnswerText: backend "s3" {} in code, and terraform init -backend-config=backend/prod.hcl
explanation: The backend is read before variables or locals exist, so partial configuration supplies the values at init, one small file per environment. TF_VAR_ sets input variables only, and backends cannot be declared in child modules.

prompt: retention_days has default = 7, terraform.tfvars sets 14, and the shell exports TF_VAR_retention_days=30. Running plain terraform plan, which value is used?
optionA: 30, because an exported environment variable always wins
optionB: 7, because the default is used unless -var is on the command
optionC: None: Terraform stops and asks which of the values to keep
optionD: 14, because terraform.tfvars outranks environment variables
correctAnswerText: 14, because terraform.tfvars outranks environment variables
explanation: From lowest to highest: default, TF_VAR_ environment variables, terraform.tfvars, *.auto.tfvars, then -var and -var-file. So terraform.tfvars beats the environment variable. People expect the environment to win; it sits near the bottom, which is why the course prefers one explicit -var-file per run.

prompt: Kavach wants a disaster-recovery replica bucket only in environments where var.enable_dr is true. Which construct fits?
optionA: depends_on = [var.enable_dr] on the replica resource
optionB: count = var.enable_dr ? 1 : 0 on the replica resource
optionC: for_each = var.enable_dr on the replica bucket resource
optionD: A lifecycle ignore_changes block that lists enable_dr
correctAnswerText: count = var.enable_dr ? 1 : 0 on the replica resource
explanation: count with a conditional is the idiom for "zero or one". for_each needs a map or set, not a bool; depends_on orders resources and cannot take a variable to switch one off; ignore_changes only stops Terraform reacting to attribute changes.

prompt: Kavach's prod root calls a shared module from a Git repository. Staging has just tested v2.3.0. How should prod reference the module?
optionA: ?ref=v2.3.0 on the Git source, moved to it by its own pull request
optionB: A version = "2.3.0" argument next to the plain Git source address
optionC: ?ref=main, so prod always gets every fix the moment it is merged
optionD: A relative path to a copy of the module pasted into the prod folder
correctAnswerText: ?ref=v2.3.0 on the Git source, moved to it by its own pull request
explanation: A tag is a fixed version, so prod changes only through a reviewed bump after staging. A branch moves under prod unreviewed, the version argument works only for registry sources (for Git the ref is the version), and a pasted copy drifts from the shared module.

prompt: An imported bucket holds customs records that must never be deleted by a Terraform typo. What should be added to its resource block?
optionA: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
optionB: lifecycle { ignore_changes = [bucket] }
optionC: lifecycle { create_before_destroy = true }
optionD: force_destroy = true on the bucket itself
correctAnswerText: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }
explanation: prevent_destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail with an error. create_before_destroy changes replacement order, ignore_changes stops reacting to attribute changes but still allows a destroy, and force_destroy does the opposite — it empties the bucket so it can be deleted.

prompt: A queue is being handed to another team's configuration. Kavach's root must stop managing it without deleting it. Which reviewed change does that?
optionA: Delete the resource block and run a normal terraform apply on it
optionB: A moved block pointing at the other team's resource address
optionC: Run terraform apply -refresh-only so the queue drops out of state
optionD: A removed block for its address with lifecycle { destroy = false }
correctAnswerText: A removed block for its address with lifecycle { destroy = false }
explanation: A removed block with destroy = false takes the address out of state through code that is reviewed, leaving the queue alone. Deleting the block plans a destroy, moved only works within one configuration, and refresh-only updates attributes rather than dropping resources.

prompt: Kavach wants its pipeline to stop any change that would delete or replace a production database. Where should that check run?
optionA: On the HCL source with a static scanner such as Checkov or Trivy
optionB: In terraform fmt -check, which fails when a resource is removed
optionC: In terraform validate, by adding a custom rule to the provider
optionD: On the plan as JSON, inspecting each resource change's actions
correctAnswerText: On the plan as JSON, inspecting each resource change's actions
explanation: Only the plan knows that a change forces replacement; terraform show -json lists actions such as ["delete","create"] per resource, so a guard or an OPA/conftest policy can block it. A code scan sees settings, not consequences, validate checks syntax and types, and fmt checks formatting.

prompt: A new CloudFormation stack failed on its very first create and shows ROLLBACK_COMPLETE. The template is now fixed. What is the next step?
optionA: Delete the stack, then create it again from the fixed template
optionB: Execute the previous change set again now that it has reset
optionC: Run continue-update-rollback and then update the stack again
optionD: Run update-stack on the existing stack with the fixed template
correctAnswerText: Delete the stack, then create it again from the fixed template
explanation: A stack whose first create rolled back cannot be updated; it is deleted and created afresh. continue-update-rollback is for UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED, and an old change set cannot be executed against this state.

prompt: Of the releases 6.1.0, 6.2.0, 6.2.7 and 6.9.1, which satisfy the constraint "~> 6.2.0"?
optionA: 6.2.0 and 6.2.7 only
optionB: All four of the releases
optionD: 6.2.0 only, as an exact pin
correctAnswerText: 6.2.0 and 6.2.7 only
explanation: With three numbers given, only the last may grow: at least 6.2.0 and below 6.3.0. "~> 6.2" (two numbers) would also allow 6.9.1. 6.1.0 is below the floor, and an exact pin is written "= 6.2.0".

prompt: Plan fails with "Error: Cycle: aws_security_group.api, aws_security_group.cache". Each group has an inline rule naming the other group. What is wrong, and what fixes it?
optionA: An apply was interrupted earlier; run apply twice so the second pass completes
optionB: The provider is too old to handle two groups; upgrade it and re-run terraform init
optionC: Neither group can be created first; move the rules into standalone rule resources
optionD: The groups are in different VPCs; put them in one VPC and the cycle disappears
correctAnswerText: Neither group can be created first; move the rules into standalone rule resources
explanation: Each group's inline rule needs the other's id, so the graph has a loop. Separate aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule resources depend on both groups, so the groups come first and the rules after. A provider upgrade, VPC placement or a second run do not remove the loop.

prompt: On an untouched branch, every plan shows the same change to a route table and every apply "succeeds". The table has inline route blocks and a separate aws_route resource. What is the cause?
optionA: The state lock is released too early, so each apply writes a partial state
optionB: The separate route resource needs depends_on, so it runs before the table
optionC: The route table is drifting because AWS rewrites routes after each deployment
optionD: Two owners: the inline list removes the separate route, which then adds it back
correctAnswerText: Two owners: the inline list removes the separate route, which then adds it back
explanation: Inline blocks say "these are all the routes", so each apply removes the standalone route and the standalone resource puts it back — one object, two owners, a plan that is never empty. Pick one style. AWS does not rewrite routes, the lock is not involved, and ordering does not fix ownership.

prompt: An alarm resource uses for_each = toset(aws_instance.node[*].id) and plan fails with "Invalid for_each argument". What is the cause?
optionA: Instance ids are unknown until apply, so the keys cannot be planned
optionB: The instances are in another state, so their ids are not readable
optionC: toset() cannot be used on a list produced by a splat expression
optionD: Alarms cannot use for_each and must use count for each instance
correctAnswerText: Instance ids are unknown until apply, so the keys cannot be planned
explanation: for_each keys must be known at plan time; ids exist only after apply. Key by names you chose (for_each = aws_instance.node with named keys), and use the id as a value. toset on a splat is legal, alarms support for_each, and the instances are in the same state. Avoid -target workarounds.

prompt: An engineer changed the backend key, ran terraform init -reconfigure, and the next plan reads "Plan: 31 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy." Nothing was deleted in AWS. What happened, and what is the fix?
optionA: The lock file was reset; run init -upgrade and plan once again
optionB: The provider lost its credentials; log in again and re-run plan
optionC: The resources were dropped by AWS; apply to recreate all of them
optionD: The new key is empty; do not apply, re-init with -migrate-state
correctAnswerText: The new key is empty; do not apply, re-init with -migrate-state
explanation: -reconfigure points at the new location without copying state, so Terraform thinks it manages nothing; applying would collide with every named resource and duplicate the rest. -migrate-state copies the state across and the plan returns to "No changes." AWS, the lock file and credentials are not involved.

prompt: Every few weeks, with no code change, a plan proposes -/+ on Kavach's worker instances with "ami ... # forces replacement". The AMI comes from data "aws_ami" with most_recent = true. Why?
optionA: A newer image was published, so the lookup returns a different AMI
optionB: The workers were stopped overnight, and stopped instances are replaced
optionC: The state file expired after a few weeks and lost the old AMI value
optionD: The provider changed its default instance type for these workers
correctAnswerText: A newer image was published, so the lookup returns a different AMI
explanation: most_recent picks the latest matching image at every plan, and changing an instance's AMI forces replacement. Make image changes deliberate: pin the AMI in a variable that a PR bumps, or use an Auto Scaling group with instance refresh. Stopping, state age and provider defaults do not change the AMI.

prompt: A pull request raised the AWS provider constraint to a new major, and CI now fails at init with "Inconsistent dependency lock file". What should the author do?
optionA: Add -lock=false to the CI init step so that it skips this check
optionB: Run init -upgrade locally, lock hashes for each platform, commit it
optionC: Remove .terraform.lock.hcl from Git so CI picks a provider itself
optionD: Retry the CI job, since the registry probably timed out on the run
correctAnswerText: Run init -upgrade locally, lock hashes for each platform, commit it
explanation: The committed lock file still records the old provider, and CI correctly refuses to rewrite it; the author updates it deliberately (with terraform providers lock for every platform the team uses) and commits. Deleting it loses reproducibility, -lock=false is about the state lock, and a retry gets the same error.

prompt: After wrapping aws_sqs_queue.orders into module "queues", the plan shows "1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy" for the same queue name. What is going on?
optionA: The module pins a different provider, which forces a fresh queue
optionB: The queue drifted in AWS, and the module is putting it back in place
optionC: Modules always rebuild resources the first time they are introduced
optionD: The address changed, so Terraform sees a new resource and an orphan
correctAnswerText: The address changed, so Terraform sees a new resource and an orphan
explanation: The queue's address became module.queues.aws_sqs_queue.this, and without a moved block Terraform plans destroy-old, create-new — losing in-flight messages. A moved block (in the root, or inside the module for its callers) turns it into a move. Modules do not force rebuilds, and drift or providers would show different plan lines.

prompt: A Bicep file no longer lists a storage account it used to deploy. The next deployment in the default mode succeeds, yet the account is still there. Why?
optionA: Bicep marks removed resources for deletion after a waiting period
optionB: Incremental mode creates and updates only, and never deletes resources
optionC: The account is locked by its state file until someone unlocks it
optionD: what-if was not run first, so the deployment skipped the removal step
correctAnswerText: Incremental mode creates and updates only, and never deletes resources
explanation: The default Incremental mode never deletes what the template omits; Complete mode would delete everything in the group not listed — including other people's resources — and deployment stacks are the newer answer. There is no deletion timer, what-if only previews, and Bicep has no state file.

prompt: During an incident an engineer widened a security-group rule in the console. Two weeks later an unrelated DNS change was applied and the incident symptoms returned. What happened?
optionA: The apply put the rule back to the coded value, because the drift was never adopted
optionB: The DNS change broke the security group, since they share the same VPC resource
optionC: The console change expired, because AWS reverts manual edits after two weeks
optionD: The state lock from the incident was still held and corrupted the security group
correctAnswerText: The apply put the rule back to the coded value, because the drift was never adopted
explanation: Terraform plans every managed resource on every apply, so the console edit was drift that the next apply reverted — silently, because the reviewer looked only at the DNS line. Drift needs a decision: adopt it in code or revert it on purpose. AWS does not expire edits, and DNS and locks are unrelated.

prompt: A CI apply was cancelled, and every run since fails with "Error acquiring the state lock", the Lock Info naming that CI runner. What is the safe sequence?
optionA: Remove use_lockfile from the backend block and run terraform init again
optionB: Confirm the runner is really gone, then force-unlock using that lock ID
optionC: Delete the state object from S3 so Terraform starts again from scratch
optionD: Run the next apply with -lock=false so it can get past the stale lock
correctAnswerText: Confirm the runner is really gone, then force-unlock using that lock ID
explanation: The lock may belong to a process that is still writing; unlocking under a live apply is how state gets corrupted. Once the holder is confirmed dead, terraform force-unlock with the ID clears it. Disabling or removing locking invites two writers, and deleting state loses track of every resource.

prompt: Sutradhar Media runs only on AWS, its developers write TypeScript, and it has years of working CloudFormation. A new hire proposes rewriting it all in Terraform. Which judgement is best?
optionA: Move every stack to Bicep, since it has no state file for the team to look after
optionB: Run Terraform and CloudFormation together on the same resources to compare them
optionC: Keep the CloudFormation; add CDK for new stacks if the team wants loops and types
optionD: Rewrite everything in Terraform now, because it is the most common tool in job listings
correctAnswerText: Keep the CloudFormation; add CDK for new stacks if the team wants loops and types
explanation: Tool choice follows the team: one cloud, a TypeScript team and working CloudFormation make CDK (which synthesises CloudFormation) a natural addition, and rewriting working stacks is rarely worth the risk. Popularity alone is not a reason, two tools on one resource always fight, and Bicep targets Azure only.

prompt: Sutradhar needs dev, staging and prod in separate AWS accounts, plus short-lived copies for feature testing. Which layout is the strongest?
optionA: One directory and one backend, with CLI workspaces for dev, staging, prod and every feature copy
optionB: A single state for all three accounts, so one apply keeps every environment in step
optionC: A directory per long-lived env with its own key and allowed_account_ids; workspaces for the throwaway copies
optionD: A copy of every module per environment, so prod changes can never leak from dev at all
correctAnswerText: A directory per long-lived env with its own key and allowed_account_ids; workspaces for the throwaway copies
explanation: Directories make the environment explicit in path, backend key and provider guard, so applying prod by mistake fails; workspaces suit identical short-lived copies. Workspaces for prod hide which one is selected behind shared credentials, copied modules drift, and one state for all accounts maximises blast radius.

prompt: Sutradhar splits its estate into network, data and app states. How should the app layer find the VPC it runs in?
optionA: Look up the VPC by tag, or read an SSM parameter the network layer writes
optionB: Put the VPC back in the app state, since layers cannot share any identifiers
optionC: Read the whole network state with terraform_remote_state, since it is simplest
optionD: Hard-code the VPC id in the app layer's tfvars file for each environment
correctAnswerText: Look up the VPC by tag, or read an SSM parameter the network layer writes
explanation: A data-source lookup or a published SSM parameter gives the app layer exactly the identifier it needs. terraform_remote_state works but hands the reader the entire network state, sensitive values included; hard-coded ids break when the VPC is rebuilt; and merging layers undoes the blast-radius benefit.

prompt: Sutradhar's plan guard blocks a database replacement that the team truly intends, as part of a planned migration. How should the pipeline let it through?
optionA: Comment out the guard for this one pull request and restore it straight after
optionB: An explicit override a second approver applies, read by the job and recorded
optionC: Apply the change from a laptop with admin rights, outside the pipeline entirely
optionD: Lower the guard so it only warns on replacements, for every future change too
correctAnswerText: An explicit override a second approver applies, read by the job and recorded
explanation: An intended replacement still deserves a second human look, so the escape hatch is explicit, reviewed and auditable. Commenting out the guard or going around the pipeline leaves no control and no record, and weakening the guard permanently removes protection from every later change.

prompt: The drift job finds a raised Lambda timeout set in the console during last night's incident, and the postmortem says the higher value is correct. What should the team do?
optionA: Revert it: apply the code now, since every console change must be undone
optionB: Run terraform apply -refresh-only, and leave the code with the old value
optionC: Ignore it: the drift job will stop reporting it after a few nightly runs
optionD: Adopt it: a pull request that puts the new value in code, so plans are empty
correctAnswerText: Adopt it: a pull request that puts the new value in code, so plans are empty
explanation: Drift gets a decision. When the change is right, adopting it in code makes the next plan empty and the fix permanent. Reverting would bring the incident back; ignoring it means the next unrelated apply reverts it silently; refresh-only updates state but leaves code that will plan the old value again.

prompt: A team wants to adopt a popular public registry module to build its VPC. Which condition matters most before it goes near production?
optionA: Check its download count, since a widely used module needs no further review
optionB: Fork it into a private repository and stop taking any upstream releases at all
optionC: Pin a version, read what it creates by default, and read the first plan fully
optionD: Set every input it offers explicitly, so none of its defaults can ever apply
correctAnswerText: Pin a version, read what it creates by default, and read the first plan fully
explanation: Registry defaults can create real resources (NAT gateways in every AZ, for instance) and new majors change inputs, so pin, read the defaults and the first plan line by line — a module you cannot read you cannot debug. Popularity is not review, a frozen fork misses fixes, and setting forty inputs does not explain what is built.

prompt: Sutradhar is moving a production DynamoDB table from a CloudFormation stack into Terraform. Which sequence keeps the data and avoids two owners?
optionA: Set DeletionPolicy: Retain, remove it from the stack, then import it into Terraform
optionB: Leave it in the stack and also declare it in Terraform until the move feels safe
optionC: Import it into Terraform first, then delete the stack so only Terraform manages it
optionD: Create a new table with Terraform, copy items across, then delete the old stack
correctAnswerText: Set DeletionPolicy: Retain, remove it from the stack, then import it into Terraform
explanation: Retain makes CloudFormation let go without deleting; once out of the stack, a Terraform import adopts it with no data movement. Deleting the stack while the table lacks Retain deletes the table, a copy is slow and risky for a live table, and two tools on one resource fight over it.

prompt: A team proposes that Terraform also upload the nightly invoice PDFs into the bucket it manages, "so everything is reviewed in one place". What is the best response?
optionA: Agree, as long as the PDF contents are marked sensitive in the configuration
