optionB: Agree: reviewing invoices in pull requests is a stronger control than code
optionC: Decline, because Terraform has no resource able to write any object to S3
optionD: Decline: Terraform owns the bucket, and the application owns what goes in it
correctAnswerText: Decline: Terraform owns the bucket, and the application owns what goes in it
explanation: Infrastructure tools own infrastructure; data belongs to the application, or each new file needs an apply and a destroy could remove business records. Marking values sensitive does not change that, and Terraform technically can manage objects — which is exactly why the boundary has to be a decision.

prompt: Sutradhar is deciding who may apply Terraform to production. Which arrangement does the course recommend?
optionA: Any senior engineer from a laptop, provided they post the plan in the team channel first
optionB: The pipeline using a long-lived access key stored as a repository secret for the job
optionC: Everyone with admin rights, since the state lock already stops conflicting applies
optionD: Only the pipeline, via OIDC and an approved environment; humans read-only plus break-glass
correctAnswerText: Only the pipeline, via OIDC and an approved environment; humans read-only plus break-glass
explanation: When only the pipeline applies, the code that produced prod is known and reviewed, and OIDC removes stored keys; a break-glass role that alerts covers emergencies. Laptop applies make review optional, stored keys are long-lived and leak, and the lock prevents simultaneous writes, not unreviewed ones.

prompt: Sutradhar's instances get surprise replacement plans whenever a new base image appears. Which fix is the best judgement?
optionA: Make image changes deliberate: a pinned AMI variable bumped by PR, or an ASG instance refresh
optionB: Disable the nightly drift job, because replacement plans are expected and harmless
optionC: Apply each replacement as soon as it appears, so instances always stay up to date
optionD: Add ignore_changes = [ami] everywhere, so the plans stop showing the image at all
correctAnswerText: Make image changes deliberate: a pinned AMI variable bumped by PR, or an ASG instance refresh
explanation: An image change is a release and should arrive by review or a controlled rolling refresh. ignore_changes hides the problem unless something else truly owns the AMI, silencing drift detection removes a safety net, and applying surprise replacements turns a data-source update into unplanned downtime.

prompt: In the twelve-factor approach the course follows, where does an application's per-environment configuration live?
optionA: In a branch of the repository kept for each environment
optionB: In the environment the process runs in, outside the build
optionC: In a config file compiled into each environment's image
optionD: In constants declared at the top of the main source code module
correctAnswerText: In the environment the process runs in, outside the build
explanation: Config that varies between deploys is supplied by the environment (environment variables, mounted ConfigMaps, a parameter store), so one build runs everywhere. Baking it into images, constants or per-environment branches means a different artefact per environment — exactly what "one build, three environments" avoids.

prompt: How is the data in a plain Kubernetes Secret stored in its manifest?
optionA: base64-encoded, which anyone with read access can decode
optionB: Not at all: the Secret only points at an external vault
optionC: Hashed one way, so the original value cannot be recovered
optionD: Encrypted with a per-namespace key that only Pods can use
correctAnswerText: base64-encoded, which anyone with read access can decode
explanation: base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Protection comes from RBAC on who may read Secrets and from enabling encryption at rest in etcd. Secrets can be read back in full, and only an operator such as External Secrets links them to an external store.

prompt: During a Secrets Manager rotation, which staging label marks the new value before it is promoted?
optionA: AWSCURRENT
optionB: AWSPENDING
optionC: AWSPREVIOUS
optionD: AWSROTATING
correctAnswerText: AWSPENDING
explanation: The rotation Lambda creates the new version as AWSPENDING, sets and tests it, then finishSecret moves AWSCURRENT to it and the old value becomes AWSPREVIOUS. There is no AWSROTATING label.

prompt: What does "immutable infrastructure" mean for a fleet of application servers?
optionA: Changes ship as new images and new instances; the old ones are removed
optionB: Each server is patched in place by a configuration tool on a fixed weekly schedule
optionC: Servers are never restarted once they are running in production
optionD: The root volume is mounted read-only so no file can ever change
correctAnswerText: Changes ship as new images and new instances; the old ones are removed
explanation: Immutable means replace rather than patch: bake a new AMI or container image, start new instances from it, retire the old ones. Patching in place on a schedule is the mutable model; never restarting and read-only disks are not what the term means.

prompt: What does a feature flag separate?
optionA: Secrets held in the vault from ordinary configuration values
optionB: Deploying code to production from releasing a feature to users
optionC: The staging database connection from the production connection
optionD: Building the container image from running its unit test suite
correctAnswerText: Deploying code to production from releasing a feature to users
explanation: A flag lets code reach production switched off and be turned on for 1%, a city or staff — deploy is an engineering event, release a business event — and it doubles as a fast kill switch. It has nothing to do with builds, secrets or database connections.

prompt: On Azure App Service, what does marking an app setting as a "deployment slot setting" (sticky) do?
optionA: Locks the setting so that only an Owner can change it
optionB: Copies the setting into every slot of the app at once
optionC: Keeps the setting with its slot when the slots are swapped
optionD: Encrypts the setting value with the app's Key Vault key
correctAnswerText: Keeps the setting with its slot when the slots are swapped
explanation: In a swap, code and ordinary settings move between slots, while sticky settings stay put. Environment-specific values (database host, APP_ENV) are made sticky so production keeps its own. Stickiness neither encrypts, copies nor locks anything.

prompt: Which of these values belongs in a plain Parameter Store String parameter?
optionA: The signing secret used to verify partner webhooks
optionB: The maximum order value a new customer may place
optionC: The API key issued by the payment gateway partner
optionD: The password the API uses to log in to its database
correctAnswerText: The maximum order value a new customer may place
explanation: An order limit is configuration, not a credential, so a String parameter is right. Passwords, signing secrets and partner API keys are secrets: Secrets Manager (with rotation where possible) or at least a SecureString.

prompt: Who can read the user data script attached to an EC2 instance?
optionA: Nobody once the instance has booted, since it is deleted after first run
optionB: Only the instance role, because user data is encrypted with its key
optionC: Anyone who can describe that instance attribute or reach its metadata
optionD: Only the root user of the account, after multi-factor authentication
correctAnswerText: Anyone who can describe that instance attribute or reach its metadata
explanation: User data is stored with the instance and readable through the API and the metadata service, so it is configuration, not a secret store. Secrets are fetched at runtime from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store using the instance role.

prompt: What is configuration drift?
optionA: The gap between a feature flag being set and users seeing it
optionB: A slow rise in memory use caused by a leak in the configuration
optionC: Running configuration that differs from what the repository says
optionD: A configuration value that is read later than it was written
correctAnswerText: Running configuration that differs from what the repository says
explanation: Drift is the running state disagreeing with the source of truth — a kubectl edit, a console change, one environment's file updated and not another's. Memory leaks, read delays and flag propagation are other problems.

prompt: Terraform creates the instances. Which kinds of tool configure packages and files inside them?
optionA: The Kubernetes ConfigMap of the account's default VPC
optionB: A second Terraform state that manages each package
optionC: CloudFormation change sets run from inside the server
optionD: cloud-init, a baked image, or a tool such as Ansible
correctAnswerText: cloud-init, a baked image, or a tool such as Ansible
explanation: Terraform-style tools own cloud resources and are poor at what happens inside a server. That is cloud-init (user data) at first boot, an image baked with Packer or Image Builder, or a configuration tool such as Ansible. Change sets and ConfigMaps do not install packages on a VM.

prompt: Why does the course promote one image through dev, staging and prod instead of building a separate image for each?
optionA: A single image needs no configuration, so nothing can be set wrong
optionB: What was tested is then exactly what runs; only configuration differs
optionC: Building three images would require three different Dockerfiles
optionD: Separate images cannot be stored side by side in one container registry repository
correctAnswerText: What was tested is then exactly what runs; only configuration differs
explanation: A rebuild per environment can pick up different dependencies or code, so staging no longer proves prod. One artefact plus per-environment configuration keeps the tested thing and the shipped thing identical. Registries hold many images, the single image still needs configuration, and one Dockerfile can build any number.

prompt: Why do running Pods keep the old value after a ConfigMap they consume through envFrom is edited?
optionA: Kubernetes applies ConfigMap edits only during the nightly maintenance window
optionB: Edits to a ConfigMap in use are rejected unless the Deployment is paused first
optionC: Environment variables are set when the container starts and not refreshed
optionD: envFrom caches values in etcd for a day before it reads the ConfigMap again
correctAnswerText: Environment variables are set when the container starts and not refreshed
explanation: A process's environment is fixed at start; existing containers keep their values until they restart, and a Pod that restarts later reads the new one — so replicas disagree. Kubernetes has no nightly window, no day-long cache, and accepts the edit, which is exactly how drift happens.

prompt: Why should a service validate its settings at start-up and refuse to start when a required value is missing?
optionA: The failed rollout is caught at deploy time, not by users at 2 a.m.
optionB: A missing value would otherwise be filled in by the cloud provider
optionC: Validation at start-up makes every request after that run faster
optionD: Kubernetes cannot schedule a Pod unless its settings are validated
correctAnswerText: The failed rollout is caught at deploy time, not by users at 2 a.m.
explanation: A Pod that fails its start-up stops the rollout before traffic reaches it; a service that starts without its token fails on live requests later. Validation does not speed requests up, Kubernetes knows nothing of app settings, and no provider fills in missing values.

prompt: Why does replacing servers from a baked image reduce configuration drift compared with patching them in place?
optionA: Patching in place is unsupported by AWS for instances behind a load balancer
optionB: Baked images are encrypted, so their configuration files cannot be altered
optionC: Every server starts from the same reviewed image, so hand edits cannot pile up
optionD: Baked images block SSH access, so nobody can ever log in to change a running server
correctAnswerText: Every server starts from the same reviewed image, so hand edits cannot pile up
explanation: With in-place patching, each server accumulates its own history of fixes and becomes a snowflake. Replacing from one image resets every instance to the same known state, and any change has to go through the image. Images do not block SSH by themselves, AWS supports patching, and encryption is unrelated.

prompt: Why does the course give every feature flag an owner and a removal date?
optionA: A flag without an owner is switched on for all users automatically
optionB: Removal dates are needed before a flag can be read by the application
optionC: Flag services delete any flag that has gone unused for a set number of days
optionD: Each live flag doubles the paths to test, so old ones become hidden risk
correctAnswerText: Each live flag doubles the paths to test, so old ones become hidden risk
explanation: Every flag adds a branch that must be tested on and off; forgotten flags multiply combinations nobody checks. An owner and a date make removal someone's job. Flag services do not auto-delete or auto-enable flags, and reading a flag needs no removal date.

prompt: Why does the course keep database passwords out of tfvars files and reference them by name from Secrets Manager instead?
optionA: Terraform refuses to read any variable whose name contains the word password
optionB: tfvars files can only hold numbers and lists, not strings with special characters
optionC: Secrets Manager values load faster than tfvars when the plan is being computed
optionD: tfvars files are committed and their values also land in plan output and state
correctAnswerText: tfvars files are committed and their values also land in plan output and state
explanation: tfvars live in Git alongside the code, so a password there is in the history for good, and values passed in flow into plans and state. Keeping the secret in a store and referencing it by name avoids both. Terraform has no name rule, tfvars hold strings, and speed is not the point.

prompt: An App Service setting holds @Microsoft.KeyVault(SecretUri=...) rather than the password itself. Why is that safer?
optionA: Key Vault references are visible only to subscription Owners in the Azure portal
optionB: The reference encrypts the password with TLS so that it can be committed safely to the repository
optionC: The app reads the password once at creation and Key Vault then deletes its copy
optionD: The value is resolved at runtime by the app's managed identity and never stored in the setting
correctAnswerText: The value is resolved at runtime by the app's managed identity and never stored in the setting
explanation: A Key Vault reference keeps only a pointer in configuration; App Service resolves it with the app's managed identity, which needs a data-plane role such as Key Vault Secrets User. TLS protects transport, not storage; visibility is not limited to Owners; and the vault keeps the secret.

prompt: Why does a Pod on EKS fetch its secret using its own IAM identity (IRSA or Pod Identity) instead of an access key in a Secret?
optionA: Pods using their own identity no longer need any network route to the AWS APIs
optionB: IAM identities make Secrets Manager return values without any KMS decryption
optionC: Access keys stored in Kubernetes Secrets are rejected outright by every AWS API call made
optionD: No long-lived key exists to leak, and access is scoped and audited per workload
correctAnswerText: No long-lived key exists to leak, and access is scoped and audited per workload
explanation: With a workload identity the Pod gets short-lived credentials for one role, scoped to exactly that secret, and CloudTrail shows who read it. A stored key is long-lived and copyable. AWS does accept keys (that is the danger), KMS decryption still happens, and the API must still be reachable.

prompt: Why should a fraud model's decline threshold be changed through a pull request and a canary rather than a quick ConfigMap edit?
optionA: A canary is needed before any ConfigMap edit can reach the cluster API
optionB: Kubernetes refuses any edit to a ConfigMap that a running Deployment is using
optionC: ConfigMaps cannot store decimal numbers, so the value must live in Git
optionD: It changes who gets declined, so it carries the same risk as a new model
correctAnswerText: It changes who gets declined, so it carries the same risk as a new model
explanation: The threshold moves the decline rate as directly as a model does, so it deserves review, a record and a gradual rollout. ConfigMaps store strings the app parses, Kubernetes allows the edit (which is how drift happens), and canaries are a choice, not an API requirement.

prompt: Why must a service that caches a database secret also refetch it when a login fails?
optionA: Login failures clear the KMS key, so the cache can no longer decrypt the value
optionB: Secrets Manager blocks a cached secret once it has been used a fixed number of times in a row
optionC: After a rotation the cached value is stale, and only a fresh read gets the new one
optionD: The database accepts a password only from a client that fetched it just now
correctAnswerText: After a rotation the cached value is stale, and only a fresh read gets the new one
explanation: Caching with a TTL keeps API calls low, but rotation changes the password underneath; a login failure is the signal to refetch immediately instead of failing until restart. There is no use count, KMS keys are not cleared, and the database does not care how recently the client fetched.

prompt: Thalikart wants every change to its checkout ConfigMap to reach all Pods of the Deployment, through a normal rolling update. What should it add?
optionA: A hash of the ConfigMap as an annotation on the Pod template
optionB: A second ConfigMap holding the same keys, mounted as a backup
optionC: An init container that sleeps until the ConfigMap is updated
optionD: A liveness probe that restarts each Pod once every few minutes
correctAnswerText: A hash of the ConfigMap as an annotation on the Pod template
explanation: When the hash annotation changes, the Pod template changes, so Kubernetes rolls every Pod and each reads the new values (Helm and Kustomize can generate it). Restarting via probes is a hack that breaks health semantics, a duplicate ConfigMap changes nothing, and an init container runs only at start.

prompt: Thalikart's App Service has a staging slot. Which setting should be marked as a deployment slot setting before the first swap?
optionA: DB_HOST, which names the database for that environment
optionB: WEB_CONCURRENCY, which the new release has retuned
optionC: FEATURE_NEW_MENU, which ships with this code release
optionD: LOG_FORMAT, which is the same JSON layout everywhere
correctAnswerText: DB_HOST, which names the database for that environment
explanation: Environment-specific values must stay with their slot; if DB_HOST moved in the swap, production would talk to the staging database. A flag that belongs to the release should travel with the code, an identical value does not matter, and a release-tuned setting should move with its release.

prompt: Thalikart's code reads a SecureString with get_parameter(Name="/prod/checkout/gateway_key") and sends a long unreadable string to the partner, which returns 401. What change fixes it?
optionA: Store the key as a String parameter so it comes back plain
optionB: Pass WithDecryption=True, and allow kms:Decrypt on the key
optionC: Request the parameter by its ARN instead of by its name
optionD: Base64-decode the returned value before sending it on
correctAnswerText: Pass WithDecryption=True, and allow kms:Decrypt on the key
explanation: get_parameter returns the encrypted value of a SecureString unless WithDecryption=True is passed, and the role then needs kms:Decrypt on the parameter's key. Downgrading to String exposes the secret, the value is ciphertext rather than base64 text, and the ARN returns the same ciphertext.

prompt: Thalikart moves its ECS service's DB_PASSWORD from a plain environment variable to Secrets Manager. What does the task need?
optionA: A "secrets" entry naming the ARN, with the execution role allowed to read it
optionB: A sidecar container that copies the secret into a file on the host
optionC: The secret value pasted as plain text into the task definition's environment section
optionD: The task role given secretsmanager:* on every secret in the account
correctAnswerText: A "secrets" entry naming the ARN, with the execution role allowed to read it
explanation: The task definition's secrets list names the secret ARN; the execution role needs GetSecretValue on that secret and kms:Decrypt on its key, and the value arrives as an environment variable at start. Pasting the value defeats the purpose, wildcard access breaks least privilege, and no sidecar is needed.

prompt: Settings load base.env (LOG_LEVEL=INFO), then prod.env (LOG_LEVEL=WARNING), and the Pod also sets the real environment variable LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG. Which value does the service use?
optionA: WARNING, because the environment-specific file is read last
optionB: DEBUG, because real environment variables override both files
optionC: INFO, because the base file sets the value every env shares
optionD: None: two sources for one key make the settings fail to load
correctAnswerText: DEBUG, because real environment variables override both files
explanation: The layering is base file, then the environment's file, then real environment variables (from ConfigMaps and Secrets) on top of both. That is why a stray environment variable on a Pod quietly wins, and why the fingerprint of the effective settings is worth logging. Overlapping keys are normal, not an error.

prompt: Thalikart's dev and prod call the same Terraform modules, but prod needs more instances and a longer log retention. Where do those differences go?
optionA: In each environment's tfvars file, with module code left identical
optionB: In TF_VAR_ variables that each engineer sets by hand on a laptop
optionC: In if-prod conditions written into each module that needs a change
optionD: In a second copy of the modules kept only for the prod environment
correctAnswerText: In each environment's tfvars file, with module code left identical
explanation: Environments should differ in values, not code paths: identical modules plus per-environment tfvars keep them comparable and reviewable. Prod-only branches leave prod paths untested in dev, copied modules drift, and hand-set variables are invisible to review.

prompt: Thalikart's app database user needs a password that rotates automatically on a schedule. Where should it live?
optionA: A Parameter Store String parameter, updated by a weekly cron job
optionB: A SecureString parameter, which rotates itself on a fixed schedule
optionC: Secrets Manager, with a rotation function attached to the secret
optionD: The task definition, regenerated with a new value on each deploy
correctAnswerText: Secrets Manager, with a rotation function attached to the secret
explanation: Built-in rotation with a Lambda (AWS provides the RDS ones) is a Secrets Manager feature. A String parameter is unencrypted, SecureString has no rotation of its own, and a value in the task definition is visible to anyone who can describe it.

prompt: Thalikart ships new discount rules a week before a festival sale and wants to switch them off within seconds if totals look wrong. What should it do?
optionA: Ship the rules in a separate image that is started only on the sale day
optionB: Rely on a rollback of the deployment, which reverts the rules in seconds
optionC: Put the rules behind a flag, default off, enabled for a small slice first
optionD: Keep the rules in a ConfigMap and edit it by hand if anything goes wrong
correctAnswerText: Put the rules behind a flag, default off, enabled for a small slice first
explanation: A flag is a kill switch faster than any rollback and lets the business release to 1% or one city first. A rollback is slower and moves all the code, a separate image is an untested launch on the busiest day, and hand-editing a ConfigMap only reaches Pods that restart.

prompt: A Lambda function needs a table name, a log level and a payment gateway key. How should Thalikart supply them?
optionA: All three fetched from Secrets Manager on every invocation, so the values are always the latest
optionB: All three as environment variables in the SAM template, so every value is versioned along with the function code
optionC: The key in the deployment package, and the other two as tags on the Lambda function itself
optionD: Table name and log level as environment variables; the key read from Secrets Manager at init and cached
correctAnswerText: Table name and log level as environment variables; the key read from Secrets Manager at init and cached
explanation: Non-secret settings fit environment variables; the secret is read from Secrets Manager (or a SecureString) during init and cached across invocations. A key in the template or package lands in Git and the console, and fetching everything per invocation adds latency and API calls for no benefit.

prompt: Thalikart wants to see at a glance whether all replicas of a service run the same configuration. What should each replica expose?
optionA: Its Pod start time, since replicas started together share settings
optionB: A hash of its effective non-secret settings, logged and on /readyz
optionC: Its full settings including secrets, so an engineer can compare them
optionD: The Git commit of the application image, which covers configuration
correctAnswerText: A hash of its effective non-secret settings, logged and on /readyz
explanation: Identical configuration gives an identical fingerprint, so a replica with a different hash stands out — and the hash deliberately excludes secrets. Exposing secrets is a leak, the image commit says nothing about injected configuration, and start time does not prove which values were read.

prompt: Nothing was deployed, yet one of three scorer Pods declines far more payments than the others. It restarted after an OOMKill on Saturday; the audit log shows a kubectl edit of its ConfigMap on Friday. What explains it?
optionA: The OOMKill corrupted the Pod's memory, so it now computes scores incorrectly
optionB: The ConfigMap edit failed, and the restarted Pod fell back to built-in defaults
optionC: The restarted Pod read the edited value; the others kept their start-up values
optionD: The edit applied to every Pod, but only one Pod receives the declined traffic
correctAnswerText: The restarted Pod read the edited value; the others kept their start-up values
explanation: Environment values are read at container start: the Friday edit reached only the Pod that restarted. Restore the ConfigMap from Git, restart the rollout so every Pod reads it, and remove human edit rights. A restart clears memory rather than corrupting it, the other Pods never read the edit, and the edit succeeded.

prompt: A month after moving to Secrets Manager with 30-day single-user rotation, every task's database logins fail at once until the service is restarted. What is the cause?
optionA: The app read the secret once at start and kept the old password after rotation
optionB: Secrets Manager deleted the secret after thirty days because nobody renewed it
optionC: The rotation Lambda locked the database for maintenance until the restart
optionD: The KMS key rotated too, so the database can no longer decrypt its own users
correctAnswerText: The app read the secret once at start and kept the old password after rotation
explanation: Single-user rotation changes the password, the old one stops working, and a value held forever is stale; restarting fetched the new one. Fix: cache with a TTL, refetch on authentication failure, and prefer alternating-users rotation. Secrets do not expire unrenewed, KMS rotation keeps old material, and rotation does not lock the database.

prompt: A service's token field is a pydantic SecretStr, yet a start-up validation error in the logs contains the token in plain text. Why?
optionA: The token came from an environment variable, which SecretStr cannot mask
optionB: SecretStr masks values only after the first request, not during start-up
optionC: The error echoes the raw input values unless hide_input_in_errors is set
optionD: The log shipper decodes masked fields before it writes them to storage
correctAnswerText: The error echoes the raw input values unless hide_input_in_errors is set
explanation: SecretStr masks the field when the settings are printed, but the validation error includes the input dictionary — the secret — unless hide_input_in_errors=True. Masking does not wait for requests, the source of the value does not matter, and log shippers do not unmask anything.

prompt: Settings use extra="forbid". An operator sets the real environment variable APP_DECLINE_TRESHOLD=0.85 (misspelt), and the service starts happily with the default 0.92. Why was there no error?
optionA: extra="forbid" only applies in dev, and production silently ignores the rule
optionB: Environment variables are validated only after the first request is served
optionC: The settings library corrected the typo, then rejected 0.85 as out of range
optionD: Unknown process environment variables are simply not read; forbid checks files
correctAnswerText: Unknown process environment variables are simply not read; forbid checks files
explanation: extra="forbid" rejects unknown keys in .env files, but unrelated process environment variables are ignored, so the default applied silently. The lesson: make important values required with no default. There is no environment exemption, no fuzzy matching and no deferred validation.

prompt: Production resolves its Key Vault reference, but the new staging slot shows the same reference as unresolved. Both use system-assigned identities. What is the cause?
optionA: The slot has its own identity, which was never granted a role on the vault
optionB: Key Vault references are supported only in the production slot of an app
optionC: Staging slots need an access key in the setting instead of a reference
optionD: The secret was rotated, and staging still points at the version before it
correctAnswerText: The slot has its own identity, which was never granted a role on the vault
explanation: Each slot is its own app with its own system-assigned identity, so only production's was granted Key Vault Secrets User. Grant the slot's identity too, or use one user-assigned identity for both. References work in every slot, a versionless URI follows rotation, and access keys are what references replace.

prompt: Right after a slot swap, production starts writing orders into the staging database. Nothing in the code changed. What was missed?
optionA: The swap rolled back halfway, leaving both slots on the old code
optionB: DB_HOST was not sticky, so it moved with the swap into production
optionC: The staging database was promoted to primary by the swap itself
optionD: Staging's managed identity replaced production's during the swap
correctAnswerText: DB_HOST was not sticky, so it moved with the swap into production
explanation: Ordinary settings travel with the code in a swap; only settings marked as deployment slot settings stay. Unmarked, staging's DB_HOST arrived in production. A half-done swap or an identity change would not redirect writes this way, and swaps never touch database roles.

prompt: A contractor with a namespace role that can "get" Secrets reported the production API token, though nobody shared it. The team says "Secrets are encrypted". What is the gap?
optionA: The contractor must have guessed the token from its length and prefix
optionB: Etcd encryption failed, which is the only way a token could ever leak
optionC: Kubernetes writes every Secret value in plain text to the cluster audit log
optionD: Secret data is only base64; anyone allowed to read Secrets can decode it
correctAnswerText: Secret data is only base64; anyone allowed to read Secrets can decode it
explanation: Encryption at rest protects etcd's disk, not an API read: anyone RBAC lets read Secrets gets the decoded value. Restrict get/list on Secrets, and prefer a secrets manager with audit. Etcd encryption is irrelevant to API reads, guessing is implausible, and the audit log does not record Secret values.

prompt: Two web servers built from the same AMI two years ago now behave differently under the same request. Both were patched by hand over SSH since. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: The AMI changed underneath them, since an updated AMI also updates its running instances
optionB: The instance types differ in CPU, which changes how the application behaves
optionC: The load balancer gives one server a different version of each HTTP request
optionD: Months of in-place edits left each server with its own unrecorded configuration
correctAnswerText: Months of in-place edits left each server with its own unrecorded configuration
explanation: Mutable servers drift into snowflakes: each hand fix lands on one machine and nowhere in code. Rebuilding from a freshly baked image makes them identical again. An AMI never changes running instances, the load balancer forwards the same request, and CPU speed alters performance, not behaviour.

prompt: A release crashed on start-up in every Pod even though its new feature sat behind a flag that was switched off. Why did the flag not help?
optionA: Flags are evaluated per user, and start-up happens with no user set
optionB: A flag guards a code path at runtime; it cannot stop a crash on start
optionC: Flags take effect only after the Pod has passed its readiness probe
optionD: The flag service was down, so the flag defaulted to on for everyone
correctAnswerText: A flag guards a code path at runtime; it cannot stop a crash on start
explanation: A flag decides which branch runs once the code is up; a start-up crash happens before any flag is read. That is what canaries and automatic rollback are for. Nothing suggests the flag service failed, readiness does not gate flags, and per-user evaluation does not explain a crash.

prompt: Thalikart builds a fresh image per environment with that environment's config file inside. A release passed staging and then failed in prod with a library error. What does the process explain?
optionA: Container registries change library versions inside images over time
optionB: The staging config file was copied into prod and named the wrong library
optionC: Prod has far more traffic, and library errors of this kind only ever appear under heavy load
optionD: The prod image was a separate build, so it could pull a different dependency
correctAnswerText: The prod image was a separate build, so it could pull a different dependency
explanation: A rebuild is a new artefact: unpinned dependencies or a moved base image can differ, so staging never tested what prod runs. Build once, inject configuration per environment. Load does not cause import errors, a config file names values not libraries, and registries do not alter stored images.

prompt: After a drift incident, Thalikart weighs fixes for production configuration. Which combination prevents a repeat best?
optionA: Keep kubectl edit for speed, and run a drift report once each quarter
optionB: Remove human edit rights, change config only via Git and a GitOps controller
optionC: Ask engineers to post in the team channel whenever they edit a ConfigMap
optionD: Restart every Pod each night so that all of the replicas always share the very latest edits
correctAnswerText: Remove human edit rights, change config only via Git and a GitOps controller
explanation: Prevention beats detection: with no direct edit rights, every change is a reviewed commit, and Argo CD or Flux reports any out-of-band difference as OutOfSync. A quarterly report finds drift months late, a channel post is not a control, and nightly restarts just spread unreviewed edits faster.

prompt: Thalikart needs a partner API key (the partner rotates it, Thalikart only stores it) available in the DR region, plus fifty plain URLs and limits. Which split is best?
optionA: Key in a String parameter, since the partner rotates it and not Thalikart
optionB: Everything as Parameter Store SecureStrings, copied to the DR region by hand
optionC: Key in Secrets Manager with a cross-region replica; URLs as String parameters
optionD: Everything in Secrets Manager, since a single store is always simpler to run
correctAnswerText: Key in Secrets Manager with a cross-region replica; URLs as String parameters
explanation: A credential gets Secrets Manager: versioning, audit and replica support for DR, even without automatic rotation. Plain configuration belongs in String parameters, where Secrets Manager is overkill. Hand-copied SecureStrings drift, and who rotates a key does not make it less secret.

prompt: Thalikart's order service cannot tolerate even a minute of failed database logins during rotation. Which rotation design fits?
optionA: Alternating users, so one valid login exists while the other changes
optionB: Single-user rotation every day, so a failure window is short and known
optionC: Rotate the KMS key instead, which changes the password with no downtime
optionD: Turn rotation off for this service and change the password by hand yearly
correctAnswerText: Alternating users, so one valid login exists while the other changes
explanation: With alternating users, the rotation changes the user that is not current and then switches, so a working credential always exists; apps still refetch on failure. Single-user rotation breaks old logins at once, however often it runs; disabling rotation trades outage risk for long-lived secrets; KMS rotation does not change any password.

prompt: Thalikart's Auto Scaling group must add instances quickly during sale spikes, and each needs an agent stack that takes minutes to install. Which approach is best?
optionA: Run an Ansible job against each new instance after it joins the pool
optionB: Install everything from user data at boot, so the AMI stays generic
optionC: Bake the agents into a golden AMI, and inject only env config at boot
optionD: Keep a few servers running forever and patch them in place by hand
correctAnswerText: Bake the agents into a golden AMI, and inject only env config at boot
explanation: Baking slow, stable parts into an image makes boot fast and every instance identical; only per-environment values and secrets are supplied at start. Long installs in user data delay scaling exactly when it matters, hand-patched pets drift, and post-join Ansible serves traffic from half-configured servers.

prompt: During a sale-day deploy freeze, Thalikart still wants to react to problems. Which policy is the strongest?
optionA: Freeze deploys; allow only flag flips by named people, posted in the incident channel
optionB: Allow any deploy that has passed its tests, since a freeze only slows down the response
optionC: Ban flag changes too, and handle every problem by rolling back the last deploy
optionD: Allow anyone to flip any flag at any time, since flags are safer than a deploy
correctAnswerText: Freeze deploys; allow only flag flips by named people, posted in the incident channel
explanation: Flags give a fast, narrow response while the freeze keeps code steady; naming who may flip them and announcing each flip keeps changes accountable. Lifting the freeze adds risk at peak, unrestricted flipping is uncontrolled change, and banning flags removes the fastest kill switch.

prompt: On EKS, Thalikart compares External Secrets syncing into a Kubernetes Secret with the app fetching from Secrets Manager at runtime via its own identity. Which judgement is fair?
optionA: Runtime fetch is always worse, because each request then calls the secrets manager directly
optionB: Runtime fetch keeps the value out of the cluster; ESO is simpler for apps but needs Secret RBAC
optionC: They are identical in risk, so the choice can be made purely on which one is cheaper to run
optionD: ESO is always more secure, because Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted by default in every cluster
correctAnswerText: Runtime fetch keeps the value out of the cluster; ESO is simpler for apps but needs Secret RBAC
explanation: Fetching at runtime with a workload identity means the value never lands in etcd; ESO lets unchanged apps read an env var or file, at the cost of a copy in a Secret that RBAC and encryption at rest must protect. Secrets are not encrypted by default, runtime fetch caches rather than calling per request, and the risks differ.

prompt: The risk team asks to change a credit-limit multiplier directly in production during office hours "because it is only config". What is the best response?
optionA: Route it through a reviewed change and a gradual rollout, like a code release
optionB: Refuse all changes to it, and hard-code the multiplier in the source instead
optionC: Agree, since configuration changes carry almost no risk when compared with code changes
optionD: Agree, but restart all Pods at once so every replica picks the value up
correctAnswerText: Route it through a reviewed change and a gradual rollout, like a code release
explanation: A business value that changes who gets credit is as risky as code: it needs review, a record and a canary-style rollout, while staying configurable. "Only config" is how drift and incidents start, restarting everything at once skips the gradual check, and hard-coding forces a rebuild for every business decision.

prompt: Thalikart debates whether the payment timeout setting should have a safe-looking default or be required with no default. Which is the better design?
optionA: Required: a missing or misspelt value then stops start-up instead of hiding
optionB: A default in dev and staging, and no setting at all in prod to avoid typos
optionC: A default, because a service that always starts is more reliable than one that fails
optionD: A default, plus a dashboard that alerts if the default is ever being used
correctAnswerText: Required: a missing or misspelt value then stops start-up instead of hiding
explanation: A default silently covers a missing or misspelt variable, so the service runs with a value nobody chose; a required value fails fast at deploy time. "Always starts" is not reliability if it starts wrong, removing the setting in prod hides it entirely, and an alert after the fact is weaker than refusing to start.

prompt: A team wants to bake prod.env, including the database password, into the prod image "so the container is self-contained". Which judgement is best?
optionA: Accept it, as long as the image repository is private to the company
optionB: Accept it for the password only, and inject the other settings at runtime
optionC: Accept it, but rebuild the image whenever the password is rotated
optionD: Reject: inject settings per environment and pull the secret from a store
correctAnswerText: Reject: inject settings per environment and pull the secret from a store
explanation: Baking config makes a different artefact per environment, and a secret in an image layer is readable by anyone who can pull it, forever. Inject non-secret settings and fetch secrets at runtime. A private registry still exposes layers to every puller, and rebuilding per rotation couples releases to secrets.

prompt: Thalikart's prod and dev Terraform must never be applied with each other's credentials. Which setup gives the strongest guarantee?
optionA: A README section reminding engineers to check their AWS profile first
optionB: One root for both, with a variable named env that defaults to dev
optionC: default_tags on every resource marking which environment it is in
optionD: Separate accounts and roots, each provider with allowed_account_ids
correctAnswerText: Separate accounts and roots, each provider with allowed_account_ids
explanation: allowed_account_ids makes the provider fail at plan time if its credentials belong to another account, and separate roots keep backends and values apart. A defaulted env variable invites mistakes, a README stops nothing, and tags label resources after the damage is done.

prompt: Which of the three signals shows where one request spent its time as it crossed several services?
optionA: A metric, summed per minute
optionB: A trace, made of timed spans
optionC: A log group, one per service
optionD: A dashboard, one per service
correctAnswerText: A trace, made of timed spans
explanation: A trace is a tree of timed spans for one request, so it shows which call inside it took the time. Metrics are aggregates over many requests, logs are separate records per event, and a dashboard only displays what those signals already hold.

prompt: What do the three letters of the RED method stand for when watching a request-serving service?
optionA: Rate, Errors, Duration
optionB: Retries, Exits, Delays
optionC: Reads, Egress, Demand
optionD: Requests, Events, Disk
correctAnswerText: Rate, Errors, Duration
explanation: RED is Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests, read as a ratio) and Duration (a latency distribution read as percentiles). It describes what users of a service experience; USE is the companion checklist for resources.

prompt: In the USE method, what does Saturation describe for a resource such as a database connection pool?
optionA: The total capacity the resource was provisioned with
optionB: Work that is waiting because the resource is busy
optionC: Errors the resource itself reported while running
optionD: The share of time the resource was doing any work
correctAnswerText: Work that is waiting because the resource is busy
explanation: Saturation is queued work: pool waiters, run-queue length, queue depth. The busy share of time is Utilisation and device errors are the E. Capacity is a configuration fact, not one of the three USE signals.

prompt: Which parts together identify one CloudWatch metric, so that a query or alarm finds its data?
optionA: Metric name, statistic and the alarm period
optionB: Namespace and the unit attached to the data
optionC: Metric name and the AWS Region it lives in
optionD: Namespace, metric name and every dimension
correctAnswerText: Namespace, metric name and every dimension
explanation: A CloudWatch metric is namespace + name + the full set of dimensions; the same name with different dimensions is a different metric. Units, statistics and periods describe how data is read, not which metric it is.

prompt: What are the three states a CloudWatch metric alarm can be in?
optionA: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA
optionB: ACTIVE, MUTED and EXPIRED states
optionC: OK, WARNING and CRITICAL states
optionD: PENDING, FIRING and RESOLVED
correctAnswerText: OK, ALARM and INSUFFICIENT_DATA
explanation: A CloudWatch alarm is OK, ALARM or INSUFFICIENT_DATA; a new alarm starts in INSUFFICIENT_DATA until it has data. Pending/firing/resolved is the lifecycle of a Prometheus alert, and active/muted/expired describes Alertmanager silences.

prompt: Which Prometheus metric type only ever increases, except when the process restarts and it resets to zero?
optionA: Summary
optionB: Gauge
optionC: Counter
optionD: Info
correctAnswerText: Counter
explanation: A counter is cumulative (requests served, payouts sent) and resets only on restart, which rate() and increase() detect. A gauge goes up and down (queue depth), a summary exports count and sum (and quantiles in some clients), and info carries constant labels.

prompt: In a Prometheus set-up, which component groups firing alerts, routes them to receivers and applies silences?
optionA: Alertmanager
optionB: kube-state-metrics
optionC: node-exporter
optionD: Grafana Loki
correctAnswerText: Alertmanager
explanation: Prometheus evaluates the alerting rules; Alertmanager receives the firing alerts and groups, inhibits, silences and routes them. node-exporter and kube-state-metrics are exporters that produce metrics, and Loki stores logs.

prompt: In OpenTelemetry tracing, what is a span?
optionA: A label set that identifies a time series in a metric
optionB: The full set of requests a service handled in a minute
optionC: A JSON log line that has been sent to the Collector
optionD: One timed unit of work with attributes and a parent
correctAnswerText: One timed unit of work with attributes and a parent
explanation: A span records one piece of work (an HTTP handler, a database insert, an outbound call) with a start, a duration, attributes and its parent span; spans sharing a trace id form the trace. Label sets identify metric series, and log lines are a separate signal.

prompt: Which W3C HTTP header carries the trace context from one service to the next so their spans join one trace?
optionA: authorization
optionB: content-type
optionC: traceparent
optionD: x-request-id
correctAnswerText: traceparent
explanation: The W3C Trace Context header traceparent carries the trace id and parent span id; OpenTelemetry propagators read and write it. A request id header is an application convention that OTel does not use to link spans, and the other two headers are unrelated.

prompt: What is the default retention of a newly created CloudWatch Logs log group?
optionA: Thirty days, then the events are deleted
optionB: Never expire, until a retention is set
optionC: One year, matching the CloudTrail default
optionD: Seven days, unless a budget alarm exists
correctAnswerText: Never expire, until a retention is set
explanation: Log groups keep events forever by default and storage is billed per GB-month, which is why setting retention is a day-one task. The other durations are not defaults; they are values a team might choose.

prompt: Why is a JSON log line with a numeric status field more useful in an incident than the sentence "Payment failed with 502 from psp-a"?
optionA: JSON lines are always smaller than the same text as a sentence
optionB: JSON lines are encrypted at rest and plain sentences are not
optionC: Plain sentences are rejected by CloudWatch Logs at ingestion
optionD: Queries can filter and count on fields such as status >= 500
correctAnswerText: Queries can filter and count on fields such as status >= 500
explanation: Fixed fields let Logs Insights, metric filters and other tools filter, group and count (status >= 500, by psp) instead of text-searching. JSON is often larger, not smaller; plain text is accepted; and encryption at rest does not depend on the line format.

prompt: Why does a well-instrumented service write the active trace id into every structured log line?
optionA: So log lines can be deduplicated when two Pods write at the same time
optionB: So one slow trace can be joined to exactly the log lines it produced
optionC: So the log line is sampled at the same rate as the trace it belongs to
optionD: So the logging library can compute latency percentiles from the lines
correctAnswerText: So one slow trace can be joined to exactly the log lines it produced
explanation: A shared identifier is what correlates signals: from a slow trace you query its logs by trace id, and from an error log you open its trace. Timestamps cannot do this because many requests run at once. Sampling, percentiles and deduplication are unrelated to the field.

prompt: Why is a merchant id fine as a field in a structured log line but harmful as a metric label?
optionA: Metric labels must be numbers, and merchant ids usually contain letters and digits
optionB: Log fields are not indexed at all, so their values cannot be searched by an engineer
optionC: Each label value makes a new series, while a log line is one record per event anyway
optionD: Metrics are kept for longer than logs, so ids in labels breach data retention rules
correctAnswerText: Each label value makes a new series, while a log line is one record per event anyway
explanation: Every distinct label combination is a separately stored and indexed series, so an unbounded id multiplies the series count by the number of ids. A log line already costs one record per event, so an id in it adds almost nothing. Label values may be strings, and log fields are queryable.

prompt: Why is a histogram preferred to a client-side quantile summary for the latency of a service running on many Pods?
optionA: Summaries can only record values above one second, which misses fast requests
optionB: Histograms are computed by Grafana, so the Pods do no work for them at all
optionC: Bucket counters add up across Pods, so one p99 can be computed for the service
optionD: Histograms create fewer time series than summaries for the same latency metric
correctAnswerText: Bucket counters add up across Pods, so one p99 can be computed for the service
explanation: Buckets are counters, and counters sum across Pods; histogram_quantile then estimates the service-wide p99. Quantiles computed on each Pod cannot be averaged into a true overall quantile. Histograms usually create more series (one per bucket), summaries take any value, and the Pods do count the buckets.

prompt: Why is the PromQL rule "rate, then sum" — sum(rate(x[5m])) — and not the other way round?
optionA: rate() must see each Pod's own counter to detect that Pod's reset
optionB: Summing first loses the job label that rate() requires to find targets
optionC: sum() can only take instant vectors, so it cannot run before rate()
optionD: rate() is faster to evaluate on many series than on one summed series
correctAnswerText: rate() must see each Pod's own counter to detect that Pod's reset
explanation: A Pod restart resets its counter; rate() handles that per series. If the counters are summed first, a vanished Pod makes the total fall, rate() reads the fall as a reset and the graph spikes. Speed and labels are not the reason, and a subquery would let sum run first — wrongly.

prompt: Why should the on-call pager fire on error ratio and latency rather than on high CPU utilisation?
optionA: Users feel failures and slowness, while busy CPU may hurt nobody at all
optionB: Error ratio and latency are free metrics, while CPU metrics are billed
optionC: High CPU only matters on EC2, and modern services run on containers
optionD: CPU metrics are reported too rarely by cloud providers to be alarmed on
correctAnswerText: Users feel failures and slowness, while busy CPU may hurt nobody at all
explanation: Pages should mean users are being hurt now. A service can run at 85% CPU and serve perfectly, or fail at 30% CPU because a dependency is down; CPU is a cause to show on dashboards and tickets. Reporting frequency, billing and the compute type are not the reason.

prompt: Why does tail sampling keep better evidence than head sampling, and what does it cost?
optionA: It decides before the trace starts, so it is cheaper, but loses every slow trace
optionB: It samples log lines instead of spans, so traces have gaps but cost almost nothing
optionC: It keeps every span of every request, so storage grows with traffic without limit
optionD: It decides after the trace ends, so it can keep errors, but must hold whole traces
correctAnswerText: It decides after the trace ends, so it can keep errors, but must hold whole traces
explanation: Head sampling decides at the start, before anyone knows whether the request will fail or be slow. Tail sampling waits for the trace to complete, keeps all errors and slow traces plus a few healthy ones, and therefore needs the Collector to buffer whole traces in memory.

prompt: What does a team gain by instrumenting code with OpenTelemetry instead of one vendor's tracing SDK?
optionA: Traces no longer need sampling, because OTel compresses every span
optionB: Context propagation is no longer required between the services
optionC: Metrics and logs stop being needed, because traces carry all of it
optionD: The back end becomes a configuration choice rather than a code change
correctAnswerText: The back end becomes a configuration choice rather than a code change
explanation: OTel is a vendor-neutral API, SDK and protocol; the Collector can export to X-Ray, Prometheus or a vendor, so switching back ends is configuration. Sampling, the other two signals and propagation are all still needed.

prompt: What does setting a CloudWatch alarm to "3 out of 5 datapoints" achieve compared with "1 out of 1"?
optionA: It keeps the alarm in ALARM for five periods after recovery ends
optionB: It ignores one noisy minute yet still fires within a few minutes
optionC: It lets the alarm fire before the first datapoint has been stored
optionD: It halves the alarm's cost because fewer datapoints are evaluated
correctAnswerText: It ignores one noisy minute yet still fires within a few minutes
explanation: M out of N tolerates an isolated spike without waiting for N breaches in a row, so it filters noise at little cost in speed. It does not change pricing, does not hold the alarm open artificially, and cannot fire without data.

prompt: Why does EC2 report CPU utilisation by itself but need the CloudWatch agent to report memory use?
optionA: The hypervisor sees CPU time but not how the guest OS uses its memory
optionB: AWS hides memory figures by default to keep instance data more private
optionC: Memory metrics are only produced when detailed monitoring is switched on
optionD: Memory changes too quickly to be sampled at the one-minute resolution
correctAnswerText: The hypervisor sees CPU time but not how the guest OS uses its memory
explanation: CPU time is visible from outside the instance; memory use is known only inside the operating system, so an agent must read and publish it. Detailed monitoring makes existing metrics one-minute but adds no memory metric, and privacy and sampling speed are not the reason.

prompt: Tarang Logistics counts orders-api requests with labels route (10 values), method (4), status code (5) and pod (3), and every combination occurs. How many counter series is that?
explanation: Each unique label combination is one series, so the counts multiply: 10 × 4 × 5 × 3 = 600. Adding them (22) is the common slip; 200 forgets the pods, and 1,800 multiplies by three a second time.

prompt: A latency histogram has 8 bucket series per label set (including le="+Inf"), plus _sum and _count, labelled by route (5 values) on 2 Pods. How many series does it create?
explanation: Each route-and-Pod combination (5 × 2 = 10) carries 8 bucket series + _sum + _count = 10 series, so 10 × 10 = 100. 80 leaves out _sum and _count, 120 assumes ten buckets plus _sum and _count, and 16 ignores routes and Pods.

prompt: A counter is scraped as 500, 620, 30, 90, with the Pod restarting between the second and third samples. What increase does Prometheus's reset handling count over these samples?
explanation: Prometheus treats the drop to 30 as a reset and counts the new value from zero: 120 (500→620) + 30 (0→30) + 60 (30→90) = 210. Last minus first gives −410; 180 forgets the 30 counted after the restart.

prompt: A nightly reconciliation job publishes a JobHeartbeat metric once a minute while it runs. How should the alarm on it treat missing data?
optionA: As ignore, so that the alarm keeps whatever state it was last in
optionB: As not breaching, because a missing point means nothing went wrong
optionC: As missing, so that the alarm stays in OK until new data arrives
optionD: As breaching, because a heartbeat that stops is the failure itself
correctAnswerText: As breaching, because a heartbeat that stops is the failure itself
explanation: For a heartbeat, absence is the signal: a crashed job sends nothing. notBreaching suits a failure count that is simply absent when nothing failed; ignore and missing would leave a dead job looking healthy or undecided.

prompt: An API serves a steady 2,000 requests per second and uses head sampling that keeps 5% of requests. About how many traces per second are recorded?
explanation: 5% of 2,000 is 0.05 × 2,000 = 100 traces per second, chosen at random at the start of each request. 40 would be 2%, 1,000 is half the traffic, and 5 confuses the percentage with a count.

prompt: The JSON logs of Tarang Logistics' orders-api carry route and duration_ms. Which Logs Insights line gives the p99 duration of each route?
optionA: filter duration_ms > 99 | stats count(*) by route
optionB: sort duration_ms desc | limit 99 | display route
optionC: stats pct(duration_ms, 99) as p99 by route
optionD: stats avg(duration_ms) * 0.99 as p99 by route
correctAnswerText: stats pct(duration_ms, 99) as p99 by route
explanation: pct(field, 99) computes the 99th percentile and "by route" groups it. Scaling an average is not a percentile, counting lines over 99 ms answers a different question, and the top 99 lines are just the slowest few, not a percentile.

prompt: A settlement worker takes jobs from an SQS queue and serves no HTTP requests. Which signals best show it is falling behind?
optionA: Request rate, error ratio and p99 duration of its HTTP health-check route
optionB: CPU utilisation of the worker alone, since busy CPU means a growing queue
optionC: Queue depth and age of oldest message, with the jobs completed per second
optionD: The number of log lines it writes per minute, compared with last week's
correctAnswerText: Queue depth and age of oldest message, with the jobs completed per second
explanation: A queue worker is a USE case: saturation is work waiting (depth, ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage), set against throughput. Its health-check route says little about the jobs, CPU can be low while it is stuck, and log volume is not a measure of progress.

prompt: A Prometheus alert has "for: 5m". Its expression is true from 10:00 to 10:03 and then false. What reaches Alertmanager?
optionA: A firing alert at 10:00 and a resolved one at 10:03
optionB: Nothing; the alert was pending and never fired
optionC: A firing alert at 10:05, once the timer has run out
optionD: A pending notice for the on-call engineer to confirm
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the alert was pending and never fired
explanation: With for, an alert stays pending until the condition has held for the whole duration. It cleared after three minutes, so it never fired; pending alerts are not sent to Alertmanager at all.

prompt: Tarang Logistics will fail over its database between 23:00 and 23:30 tonight and expects orders-api errors. How should the alerting be handled?
optionA: Add an Alertmanager silence for that window, with an expiry and a reason
optionB: Raise the alert's for duration to 45 minutes permanently for safety
optionC: Scale Prometheus to zero for the window so that no rule is evaluated
optionD: Delete the error alert rule now and re-apply it from Git in the morning
correctAnswerText: Add an Alertmanager silence for that window, with an expiry and a reason
explanation: A silence mutes matching notifications for a bounded, documented time while Prometheus keeps evaluating and recording. Deleted rules get forgotten, a permanent long for delays every real page, and stopping Prometheus loses the data from the window.

prompt: X-Ray's default sampling rule records the first request each second and 5% of the rest. A service gets a steady 101 requests a second. About how many are traced each second?
explanation: The reservoir takes the first request (1), and 5% of the remaining 100 adds 5, so about 6 per second. 5 forgets the reservoir, 1 forgets the percentage, and 101 would be tracing everything.

prompt: An alarm on Tarang/Orders OrdersFailed has been INSUFFICIENT_DATA since it was made from a template, yet the console graph shows data each minute. The code publishes it with Service=orders-api. What is wrong?
optionA: TreatMissingData is notBreaching, which hides every real datapoint
optionB: The alarm's period is shorter than the one-minute metric resolution
optionC: Custom metrics only become alarmable after a full day of history
optionD: The alarm omits the Service dimension, so it watches an empty metric
correctAnswerText: The alarm omits the Service dimension, so it watches an empty metric
explanation: Namespace, name and all dimensions identify a metric, so an alarm without Service=orders-api is watching a metric that has never had data. A short period still sees data, TreatMissingData only judges gaps, and custom metrics can be alarmed on at once.

prompt: A Grafana panel built on rate(sum(http_requests_total)[5m:]) jumps to many times real traffic on every rollout, while the load balancer shows nothing unusual. Why?
optionA: When old Pods leave the sum it falls, and rate() reads the fall as a reset
optionB: New Pods replay their old requests on start-up, which doubles the counter
optionC: The 5-minute window is too short, so any restart looks like a traffic burst
optionD: The load balancer samples requests during rollouts, so it under-reports
correctAnswerText: When old Pods leave the sum it falls, and rate() reads the fall as a reset
explanation: Summing first hides each Pod's own reset; the total drops when a Pod disappears, and rate() counts the whole new total as fresh increase. sum(rate(...)) fixes it. Window length does not cause it, Pods do not replay requests, and the ALB count is complete.

prompt: A week after a new HTTP middleware shipped, Prometheus is OOMKilled every few hours and its head series rose from about 300,000 to 8 million. What most likely changed?
optionA: A label now holds raw URL paths that include order ids
optionB: The scrape interval was cut from 30 seconds to 15 seconds
optionC: Grafana dashboards started refreshing every ten seconds
optionD: The autoscaler added three more replicas of orders-api
correctAnswerText: A label now holds raw URL paths that include order ids
explanation: Only unbounded label values grow series by millions: each id in a path is a new series, multiplied by the other labels. A shorter interval adds samples, not series; three Pods add a small bounded number; and queries create no series. Label by the route template instead.

prompt: A ServiceMonitor for a new worker is applied with kube-prometheus-stack, but the target never appears — not even as down — and nothing logs an error. What should be checked?
optionA: The worker's Pods have a liveness probe that is passing at the moment
optionB: The scrape interval is under fifteen seconds, or the target is ignored
optionC: Its labels match the Prometheus selector and its port names a Service port
optionD: The worker runs at least two replicas, since single Pods are not scraped
correctAnswerText: Its labels match the Prometheus selector and its port names a Service port
explanation: The operator only loads ServiceMonitors whose labels match serviceMonitorSelector (the chart release label by default), and endpoints refer to a named port; either mismatch silently yields no target. Probes and replica counts do not gate discovery, and 30-second intervals are normal.

prompt: Customers say checkout takes eight seconds, but the service-wide p99 panel for a twelve-route API looks normal. What is the most likely explanation and next step?
optionA: Latency histograms cannot measure eight seconds; add a log line for each
optionB: The p99 panel is cached by Grafana for hours; reload the dashboard first
optionC: Customers measure on slow phones; nothing in the service needs looking at
optionD: One busy-but-small route is slow inside the total; split duration by route
correctAnswerText: One busy-but-small route is slow inside the total; split duration by route
explanation: An aggregate over many routes can hide one slow route, so break the duration histogram down by route, then use traces for the slow one. Grafana does not cache for hours, dismissing reports skips the evidence, and histograms have a +Inf bucket so long durations are still counted.

prompt: An error-ratio alarm at 2% pages most nights between 02:00 and 05:00, each time on 1 failure in about 3 requests. Which change keeps its daytime sensitivity?
optionA: Turn off the alarm's actions from 01:00 to 06:00 every night
optionB: Raise the threshold from 2% to 40% for every hour of the day
optionC: Alarm on the raw count of failures instead of on their ratio
optionD: Let the ratio alarm only when request volume is above a minimum
correctAnswerText: Let the ratio alarm only when request volume is above a minimum
explanation: Tiny samples make huge ratios; a volume guard (IF(total > N, ...) in metric math, or "and" a minimum rate in PromQL) drops those while keeping the 2% daytime threshold, and long-window rules cover quiet hours. A 40% threshold misses real incidents, raw counts break at peak, and muting nights misses night outages.

prompt: A payment provider declined orders for 20 minutes and orders-api returned HTTP 200 with "status": "failed" each time. The ALB 5xx alarm stayed OK. What gap does this reveal?
optionA: The ALB samples 5% of responses, so a short incident was missed by chance
optionB: The ALB 5xx alarm needed TreatMissingData set to breaching to catch it
optionC: The ALB only sees HTTP codes; a business metric of failed orders is needed
optionD: The ALB alarm period was one minute, and incidents need five-minute periods
correctAnswerText: The ALB only sees HTTP codes; a business metric of failed orders is needed
explanation: A failure returned as 200 is invisible to load-balancer status-code metrics; only the application knows, so it should publish OrdersFailed and OrdersTotal (for example via EMF) and alarm on their ratio. Missing-data handling, sampling and period length do not reveal a code the ALB never saw.

prompt: Since a hand-written HTTP client replaced the instrumented one in orders-api, each request shows up as two separate traces, one per service. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The new client does not send the traceparent header to the next service
optionB: The Collector's tail sampler now drops every span from the second service
optionC: The span names in the two services differ, so the back end cannot match
optionD: The two services export to different Regions, which splits every trace
correctAnswerText: The new client does not send the traceparent header to the next service
explanation: Spans join one trace only when the trace context is propagated; without traceparent the downstream service starts a new trace. Dropping spans would lose data rather than split it, and Region and span names do not decide trace membership.

prompt: Log ingestion for orders-api grew about tenfold overnight while request traffic stayed flat. The only deploy changed configuration. What is the first thing to check?
optionA: Whether the log group retention was raised to a year
optionB: Whether a Logs Insights query is running every minute
optionC: Whether the log level was left at DEBUG in production
optionD: Whether the ALB access logs were switched off by mistake
correctAnswerText: Whether the log level was left at DEBUG in production
explanation: Ingestion volume tracks what the service writes; a DEBUG level left on multiplies lines per request without any traffic change. Retention affects stored volume, not ingestion; Insights queries are billed by data scanned, not ingested; and switching logs off would reduce volume.

prompt: A worker's Deployment was deleted by mistake, yet the alert on up{job="settlement"} == 0 never fired. Why, and what catches it?
optionA: With no target there is no up series at all; alert on absent(up{...})
optionB: The up metric needs a for clause of an hour; lengthen the for duration
optionC: Alertmanager drops alerts for deleted objects; add an inhibition rule
optionD: up only covers node-exporter targets; alert on kube-state-metrics only
correctAnswerText: With no target there is no up series at all; alert on absent(up{...})
explanation: up == 0 needs a target that exists but cannot be scraped; a vanished target produces no series, so the comparison returns nothing. absent() fires when no series matches. A longer for, other exporters and inhibition rules do not create the missing series.

prompt: Tarang Logistics wants traces of every failed and every slow order on a busy API, but 100% tracing would be costly. Which approach is best?
optionA: Skip traces and log each span as a JSON line, since logs are always cheaper
optionB: Trace every request but keep the spans for one day only, then delete them all
optionC: Head sampling at 1%, and raise it to 100% by hand whenever an incident starts
optionD: Tail sampling in the Collector: keep all errors and slow traces, a few healthy
correctAnswerText: Tail sampling in the Collector: keep all errors and slow traces, a few healthy
explanation: Tail sampling decides after the trace completes, so it keeps exactly the interesting traces at a fraction of the volume, at the cost of Collector memory. 1% head sampling misses most failures and evidence of the incident that already happened, short retention still pays for recording everything, and span-per-log-line is not cheaper and loses the trace view.

prompt: Support at Tarang Logistics wants each of its 50,000 shippers' failed orders visible, and proposes a shipper_id label on the failures counter. What should the engineer recommend?
optionA: Keep shipper_id in structured logs and query failures per shipper there
optionB: Use shipper_id as a histogram bucket edge so it adds no new series
optionC: Add the label and drop the route label so the series total stays level
optionD: Add the label, but scrape that counter only once every five minutes
correctAnswerText: Keep shipper_id in structured logs and query failures per shipper there
explanation: An unbounded label multiplies series by 50,000 whatever the scrape interval; trading away a bounded, useful label does not fix it; and buckets are numeric thresholds, not identifiers. Per-entity detail belongs in logs (or traces), where one record per event is the normal cost.

prompt: A team's only page is "ECS CPU above 80%", and a 25-minute outage at 30% CPU went unnoticed until customers complained. Which redesign is best?
optionA: Page on error ratio and p99 latency; keep CPU as a panel and a ticket
optionB: Page on every log line at ERROR level so no failure can go unseen
optionC: Add memory and disk pages next to CPU so every resource is covered
optionD: Lower the CPU page to 50% so that it fires earlier in such incidents
correctAnswerText: Page on error ratio and p99 latency; keep CPU as a panel and a ticket
explanation: Symptom alerts on what users feel catch failures whatever their cause; CPU stays visible as a cause metric and a ticket when sustained. A lower CPU threshold still misses dependency failures and adds noise, more resource pages repeat the mistake, and paging per ERROR line floods the on-call.

prompt: Separate CloudWatch alarms on error ratio and p99 latency both page, so one incident wakes the on-call twice. Which change best keeps both signals but pages once?
optionA: A composite alarm "errors OR latency" holds the action; components stay silent
optionB: Delete the latency alarm, because errors and latency always rise together
optionC: Set both alarms to TreatMissingData breaching so their states move together
optionD: Raise both thresholds so that only one of the two alarms can breach at a time
correctAnswerText: A composite alarm "errors OR latency" holds the action; components stay silent
explanation: A composite alarm pages once when either condition holds, and the component alarms keep their states for diagnosis. Slow-but-successful incidents exist, so latency must stay; higher thresholds hide real incidents; and missing-data handling does not merge alarms.

prompt: An auditor needs a year of order logs, while engineers query only the last few weeks. The team proposes keeping every log group set to never expire. What is the better design?
optionA: Short retention in CloudWatch, plus a subscription to cheaper archive storage
optionB: Seven-day retention only, and ask the auditor to accept the shorter period
optionC: Export the logs to each engineer's laptop weekly and delete them in AWS
optionD: Never-expire as proposed, since retention rules risk failing the audit later
correctAnswerText: Short retention in CloudWatch, plus a subscription to cheaper archive storage
explanation: Keep the searchable copy as long as engineers use it and stream logs (via a subscription filter to Firehose and S3, for example) to cheaper long-term storage for the audit. Never-expire pays search-tier storage for a year of rarely read data, seven days fails the requirement, and laptops are neither safe nor auditable.

prompt: A three-person platform team runs several EKS clusters and keeps losing Prometheus data when its in-cluster volume fills. Which option fits best, and at what cost?
optionA: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, trading control for less operations work
optionB: One shared Prometheus Pod per cluster with no volume, restarted each night
optionC: Stop collecting metrics in the cluster and use only CloudWatch Logs instead
optionD: A larger in-cluster volume, since managed services cannot run PromQL queries
correctAnswerText: Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus, trading control for less operations work
explanation: A small team gains most from handing storage, scaling and upgrades to a managed service that still speaks PromQL; the trade-off is less control and a usage-based bill to watch. A bigger volume postpones the same failure, logs are no substitute for metrics, and a volume-less Pod loses everything on restart.

prompt: To debug failed payments faster, a developer wants to log each customer's full phone number and UPI id. What is the best response?
optionA: Log them in full but at DEBUG level, which is never stored by default
optionB: Log them in full, since only engineers can read the production logs
optionC: Log them in a separate group whose retention is set to never expire
optionD: Log the order id and trace id, and mask or omit the personal identifiers
correctAnswerText: Log the order id and trace id, and mask or omit the personal identifiers
explanation: Personal data in logs is still personal data under the DPDP Act, and logs are copied widely; internal ids and the trace id give the same debugging path without it. Access controls do not remove the obligation, DEBUG lines are stored if enabled, and keeping them forever makes it worse.

prompt: Which on-call dashboard design for orders-api will serve an engineer best at 3 a.m.?
optionA: A single panel of average latency, kept simple so there is nothing to misread
optionB: One panel per Pod for every metric, copied for each environment separately
optionC: RED panels per main route on top, USE for its resources below, runbook linked
optionD: Every metric the service exports, in alphabetical order, for full coverage
correctAnswerText: RED panels per main route on top, USE for its resources below, runbook linked
explanation: Top-down layout answers "are users hurting?" first (RED), then "which resource?" (USE), with the runbook a click away; variables and dashboards-as-code avoid copies. A wall of every metric hides the signal, per-Pod copies drift, and a single average hides the tail and the cause.

prompt: An engineer writes an error-rate alert with irate() "so it reacts faster". Which judgement is right?
optionA: Use rate() over a window; irate() uses two samples and flaps in alerts
optionB: Use increase() without a window, since alerts need no range at all
optionC: Keep irate(), but add a for of one hour to make it react more quickly
optionD: Keep irate(); it averages over the whole window and is the steadier one
correctAnswerText: Use rate() over a window; irate() uses two samples and flaps in alerts
