explanation: irate() looks only at the last two samples, so it swings on every blip — fine for a zoomed-in graph, poor for paging. rate() averages over the window and, with a sensible for, gives stable alerts. increase() needs a range too, and a long for makes the alert slower, not faster.

prompt: Order traffic is ten times higher at noon than at 4 a.m. Which alerting choice fits a "traffic dropped unexpectedly" alarm?
optionA: No alarm on traffic, since a drop in requests can never mean a failure
optionB: An anomaly-detection band learnt from history, which follows the daily shape
optionC: A fixed threshold at the 4 a.m. level, so it never fires falsely at night
optionD: A fixed threshold at the noon level, so a drop is caught at peak hours
correctAnswerText: An anomaly-detection band learnt from history, which follows the daily shape
explanation: A daily-shaped metric needs a threshold that moves with the time of day, which an anomaly band provides. A night-level threshold misses a daytime collapse, a noon-level one fires every night, and a sudden drop often means users cannot reach the service at all.

prompt: How is a service level indicator (SLI) usually expressed?
optionA: Peak CPU utilisation of the service across its Pods
optionB: Good events divided by valid events, as a percentage
optionC: Number of incidents the service had in the quarter
optionD: Average response time of all requests over a day
correctAnswerText: Good events divided by valid events, as a percentage
explanation: An SLI is a ratio — the share of valid events that were good — so it can be compared directly with a target. Averages hide the tail, CPU is a cause rather than what users feel, and an incident count says nothing about how many users were affected.

prompt: What is an error budget for a service with an SLO?
optionA: The number of bugs a team may leave open before a release is blocked
optionB: The money set aside each quarter to pay for incident response overtime
optionC: The share of events allowed to fail: 100% minus the SLO, over its window
optionD: The total downtime written into the customer contract as a penalty
correctAnswerText: The share of events allowed to fail: 100% minus the SLO, over its window
explanation: The error budget is the unreliability the SLO allows — 0.1% of requests for a 99.9% SLO over the window. It is not money, a bug count, or a contract term; contract penalties belong to the SLA.

prompt: What does a burn rate of exactly 1 mean for an error budget?
optionA: The budget would be used up exactly at the end of the window
optionB: The budget is spent in one day, whatever the window length is
optionC: One per cent of the budget is being spent in every single hour
optionD: The service has had exactly one failed request in the window
correctAnswerText: The budget would be used up exactly at the end of the window
explanation: Burn rate compares the actual error ratio with the ratio the SLO allows; at 1 the budget lasts exactly the window, at 2 it lasts half the window. It is not a fixed percentage per hour or a count of failures.

prompt: How does an SLA differ from an SLO?
optionA: An SLA is a contract with consequences such as credits; an SLO is internal
optionB: An SLA is measured by the provider; an SLO is measured by the customer
optionC: An SLA is a monthly target; an SLO is a target for a single request only
optionD: An SLA covers latency only; an SLO covers availability and nothing else
correctAnswerText: An SLA is a contract with consequences such as credits; an SLO is internal
explanation: The SLA is the agreement with customers and carries penalties or credits; the SLO is the team's own target, usually stricter, so it warns before the contract is at risk. Neither is limited to one SLI type or defined by who measures it.

prompt: Which of these is a freshness SLI?
optionA: Share of ledger reconciliations whose totals match up
optionB: Share of requests answered in under half a second each
optionC: Share of payment requests that did not return a 5xx code
optionD: Share of payouts settled within 10 minutes of being due
correctAnswerText: Share of payouts settled within 10 minutes of being due
explanation: Freshness measures how up to date the output is — work done within a time of being due. The others are availability, correctness and latency SLIs respectively.

prompt: In a multiwindow burn-rate alert, how long is the short window compared with the long one?
optionA: About one-twelfth as long, such as 5 minutes with 1 hour
optionB: About twice as long, such as 2 hours paired with 1 hour
optionC: Exactly as long, but offset by one evaluation period
optionD: About half as long, such as 30 minutes with 1 hour
correctAnswerText: About one-twelfth as long, such as 5 minutes with 1 hour
explanation: The recommended pairs are 1 h with 5 m and 6 h with 30 m — the short window is one-twelfth of the long. It confirms the burn is still happening, so the alert also clears soon after recovery.

prompt: For a 30-day SLO, which burn-rate rule does the SRE Workbook recommend as the fast-burn page?
optionA: 14.4x over 1 hour, confirmed over 5 minutes
optionB: 1x over 30 days, confirmed over 3 days
optionC: 100x over 1 minute, with no second window
optionD: 2x over 5 minutes, confirmed over 1 minute
correctAnswerText: 14.4x over 1 hour, confirmed over 5 minutes
explanation: 14.4x for an hour spends 2% of a 30-day budget, which is worth waking someone; the 5-minute window confirms it is still happening. 1x over the window is merely on plan, and very short windows page on noise.

prompt: Which kind of SLO window does the course recommend for day-to-day operations?
optionA: A single day, reset at midnight IST
optionB: A rolling window of 28 or 30 days
optionC: A calendar year, reviewed in March
optionD: A calendar month, reset on the 1st
correctAnswerText: A rolling window of 28 or 30 days
explanation: A rolling window always reflects the last four weeks or so, so an outage on the 30th still counts on the 2nd. A calendar month forgives it at midnight on the 1st, a day is too short to be stable, and a year is too slow to act on.

prompt: When should an error budget policy be agreed, and with whom?
optionA: After each quarter ends, by the finance team alone, privately
optionB: During the first incident that exhausts the budget, by on-call
optionC: Only when a customer asks, by the account manager in an email
optionD: In advance and in writing, between engineering and product
correctAnswerText: In advance and in writing, between engineering and product
explanation: A policy agreed before it is needed — what happens at 25% remaining, at zero, after a big incident — removes the argument when the budget runs out. Deciding mid-incident or alone invites pressure to bend it.

prompt: What is the usual form of a latency SLI?
optionA: The average response time of all requests over the window
optionB: The share of valid requests answered within a set threshold
optionC: The number of Pods needed to keep response times stable
optionD: The fastest response time recorded during the busiest hour
correctAnswerText: The share of valid requests answered within a set threshold
explanation: A latency SLI counts requests answered within a threshold (say 0.5 s) as good, giving a ratio like any other SLI. An average hides the slow tail, the fastest response describes nobody's bad experience, and a Pod count is capacity, not latency.

prompt: Why is 100% availability the wrong SLO for almost every user-facing service?
optionA: Cloud providers forbid customers from promising full availability
optionB: It leaves no budget for change, and users cannot tell it from 99.99%
optionC: A 100% target makes burn-rate arithmetic divide by a negative number
optionD: Monitoring tools cannot display any figure above 99.99% on a graph
correctAnswerText: It leaves no budget for change, and users cannot tell it from 99.99%
explanation: Each extra nine costs far more than the last, a 100% target forbids every risky change, and users' own networks fail more often than the difference. Tools and providers impose no such limit; the arithmetic breaks because the budget is zero, not negative.

prompt: Why should a service's external SLA be looser than its internal SLO?
optionA: So the SLO can be changed freely without informing the product owner
optionB: So customers receive credits more often, which builds their goodwill
optionC: So the team is warned and can react before the contract is breached
optionD: So the SLA can be measured with a cheaper and less precise SLI tool
correctAnswerText: So the team is warned and can react before the contract is breached
explanation: With the SLO stricter, missing it is an internal alarm that leaves room to recover before penalties apply. The SLI is the same measurement either way, frequent credits are a cost not a goal, and the SLO is still agreed with product.

prompt: Why is an availability SLI better measured at the load balancer than from the application's own request metrics?
optionA: Applications report only averages, and SLIs need exact percentiles
optionB: Load balancers retry failed requests, so they show fewer failures
optionC: The application never records requests that failed before reaching it
optionD: Load balancer metrics are cheaper to store than the application metrics
correctAnswerText: The application never records requests that failed before reaching it
explanation: Measuring as close to the user as possible counts failures the service cannot see — crashed tasks, refused connections, gateway timeouts. Cost and averaging are not the reason, and a measurement point that hid failures by retrying would be worse, not better.

prompt: Why is a 400 response to a request with an invalid payment address left out of the valid events of an availability SLI?
optionA: Counting them would make the SLI exceed 100% on busy days
optionB: Rejecting bad input correctly is the service working, not failing
optionC: Client errors are rare enough that including them changes nothing
optionD: A 400 is never logged by the load balancer, so it cannot be counted
correctAnswerText: Rejecting bad input correctly is the service working, not failing
explanation: An SLI should measure the service's own failures; counting correct rejections as bad punishes the team for callers' mistakes. Load balancers do record 4xx, client errors can be common, and a ratio of good to valid cannot exceed 100%.

prompt: Why does a fast-burn alert require both the 1-hour and the 5-minute error ratios to be high, rather than the 1-hour ratio alone?
optionA: Prometheus cannot keep data longer than an hour without the pair
optionB: The pair halves the number of series that Prometheus has to store
optionC: The 5-minute check lets the alert clear soon after errors stop
optionD: The 5-minute check makes the alert fire well before an hour passes
correctAnswerText: The 5-minute check lets the alert clear soon after errors stop
explanation: A 1-hour ratio stays high for up to an hour after recovery; requiring the 5-minute ratio too resolves the alert within minutes. The long window still decides when it fires, retention is unrelated, and the pair adds recording rules rather than removing series.

prompt: Why do burn-rate alerts produce fewer false pages than "error ratio above the SLO for five minutes"?
optionA: They ignore every error that happens outside normal office hours
optionB: They fire only when a meaningful share of the budget is being spent
optionC: They use a lower threshold, so they need far fewer errors to trigger
optionD: They are evaluated once a day, so brief noise is never noticed
correctAnswerText: They fire only when a meaningful share of the budget is being spent
explanation: A burn-rate page ties the threshold to budget impact (for example 2% of the month in an hour), so a few noisy minutes cannot trigger it. In the course simulation the naive rule fired on ten quiet minutes; the fast-burn rule had none. Burn alerts are not time-of-day filters, lower thresholds or daily jobs.

prompt: Why is a rolling 30-day SLO window better for operations than a calendar month?
optionA: A rolling window lets the team pick which incidents should count
optionB: A big outage on the 30th still counts against the budget on the 2nd
optionC: A rolling window always holds exactly the same number of requests
optionD: Calendar months have different lengths, which breaks the alerting
correctAnswerText: A big outage on the 30th still counts against the budget on the 2nd
explanation: A calendar month resets the budget at midnight on the 1st whatever happened the day before; a rolling window keeps recent failures in view until they age out. Request counts vary in any window, month lengths are a minor issue, and no window lets a team choose its incidents.

prompt: Why is a new SLO set a little below what the service achieves today rather than at an aspirational level?
optionA: Monitoring tools need a target below the current level to work
optionB: A lower target lets the team skip writing postmortems for its incidents
optionC: Aspirational targets cost more because they create extra series
optionD: An unreachable target is always breached and soon ignored by everyone
correctAnswerText: An unreachable target is always breached and soon ignored by everyone
explanation: A target the service already meets, and that users accept, leaves a real budget to ship with; an aspiration that is always missed teaches people to ignore it. Postmortems still happen, tools have no such need, and the target value creates no series.

prompt: Why are SLIs on a low-traffic service jumpy, and what keeps them meaningful?
optionA: Quiet services fail more often; raising their SLO target to 99.99% fixes that
optionB: One failure is a big share of few requests; longer windows or minimum counts help
optionC: Low traffic hides latency; switching the SLI to average response time fixes it
optionD: Few requests mean few metrics are stored; a shorter scrape interval fixes that
correctAnswerText: One failure is a big share of few requests; longer windows or minimum counts help
explanation: 2 failures in 40 night-time requests is 5%, so ratios swing wildly on small samples. Longer windows, a minimum request count before alerting, or synthetic traffic make the SLI stable. Scrape interval, averages and a stricter target do not address the small denominator.

prompt: Why does an error budget help product owners and engineers agree on how fast to ship?
optionA: It moves the decision about releases to the cloud provider's support team
optionB: It turns "move fast" against "be careful" into one number both can see
optionC: It lets engineers refuse every feature request until the budget is full
optionD: It guarantees that releases will never cause an incident in production
correctAnswerText: It turns "move fast" against "be careful" into one number both can see
explanation: While budget remains, risk is affordable and shipping continues; when it is spent, reliability work comes first. That shared, measured number replaces opinion. It does not prevent incidents, is not a veto on features, and stays with the team.

prompt: Meghdoot Travel's booking API has a 99.9% availability SLO over a rolling 30 days. How many minutes of full outage does the budget allow?
optionA: 432 minutes
optionB: 4.3 minutes
optionC: 43.2 minutes
optionD: 72 minutes
correctAnswerText: 43.2 minutes
explanation: 30 days is 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is 43.2 minutes. 4.3 minutes is the 99.99% figure, 432 minutes the 99% figure, and 72 minutes comes from using 0.1% of 72,000 by mistake.

prompt: Meghdoot Travel's search API serves 12 million valid requests in a 30-day window with a 99.5% SLO. How many failed requests is the error budget?
explanation: The budget is 0.5% of 12,000,000 = 60,000 failed requests. 6,000 would be 0.05%, 600,000 would be 5%, and 11,940,000 is the number of requests that must succeed, not the budget.

prompt: A service with a 99.9% SLO is failing 0.5% of its requests right now. What is its current burn rate?
explanation: Burn rate = observed error ratio ÷ allowed error ratio = 0.5% ÷ 0.1% = 5, so the budget would last a fifth of the window. 0.5 confuses the error ratio with the rate, 50 slips a decimal place, and 99.5 is the success ratio.

prompt: For an SLO over 30 days (720 hours), what share of the error budget does a burn rate of 14.4 spend in one hour?
explanation: Budget consumed = burn rate × time ÷ window = 14.4 × 1 ÷ 720 = 0.02, or 2%. That is why 14.4x over an hour is the fast-burn page. 14.4% treats the rate as a percentage, and the others misplace the decimal.

prompt: A 30-day error budget is being burnt at a steady rate of 10, starting from full. How long until it is exhausted?
optionA: 72 hours
optionB: 7.2 hours
optionC: 300 hours
optionD: 10 hours
correctAnswerText: 72 hours
explanation: At burn rate 10 the budget lasts one-tenth of the window: 720 h ÷ 10 = 72 hours, or three days. 10 hours confuses the rate with a duration, 300 hours multiplies days by the rate, and 7.2 hours divides by a hundred.

prompt: Out of 100,000 booking requests, 2,000 got a 400 for invalid traveller details and 490 got a 5xx. With client-input errors excluded from valid events, what is the availability SLI?
explanation: Valid = 100,000 − 2,000 = 98,000; good = 98,000 − 490 = 97,510; 97,510 ÷ 98,000 = 99.5%. 97.51% counts the 400s as failures, 99.51% keeps them in the denominator as good, and 98.0% ignores the 5xx entirely.

prompt: A service has a 99.5% SLO. Above what error ratio should its 6x slow-burn page fire?
explanation: Threshold = burn rate × allowed error ratio = 6 × 0.5% = 3%. 0.6% is the 6x threshold for a 99.9% SLO, 6% treats the burn rate as a percentage, and 0.3% would be 3x at 99.9%.

prompt: An API expects 50 million valid requests in its 30-day window and has a 99.9% SLO. So far 20,000 requests have failed. How much of the error budget remains?
explanation: The budget is 0.1% of 50,000,000 = 50,000 failures; 20,000 spent is 40%, so 60% remains. 40% is the share spent, 99.96% is an SLI-style figure, and 20% reads the failure count as a percentage.

prompt: A latency SLO says 99% of valid requests finish within 0.8 s. This window had 1,200,000 valid requests, of which 18,000 took longer. Is the SLO met?
optionA: Yes: only 1.8% were slow, inside the 2% allowance
optionB: Yes: 99.85% were within 0.8 s, above the 99% target
optionC: No: 18,000 slow requests always breach any latency SLO
optionD: No: 98.5% were within 0.8 s, below the 99% target
correctAnswerText: No: 98.5% were within 0.8 s, below the 99% target
explanation: 18,000 ÷ 1,200,000 = 1.5% slow, so 98.5% were good — below 99%, and 1.5% slow exceeds the 1% budget. 99.85% and 1.8% are arithmetic slips, and the judgement depends on the ratio, not the raw count.

prompt: The policy says: below 25% budget remaining, risky releases need sign-off; at zero, feature releases pause. With 20% left, a team wants to ship a database schema migration. What applies?
optionA: Nothing applies until the budget actually reaches zero
optionB: All releases stop until the next rolling window is clean
optionC: The migration can go ahead only with the agreed sign-off
optionD: The SLO is lowered first so that more budget is available
correctAnswerText: The migration can go ahead only with the agreed sign-off
explanation: At 20% remaining the "below 25%" rule is in force: risky changes need sign-off, and features still ship. The freeze is for an exhausted budget, the 25% rule exists precisely to act before zero, and moving the target defeats the policy.

prompt: A 30-minute full outage hits a service with a 99.9% SLO over 30 days. The policy asks for a postmortem when one incident spends over 20% of the budget. What follows?
optionA: The whole budget is gone, so feature releases stop immediately
optionB: About 69% of the budget is gone, so a postmortem is required
optionC: About 30% of the budget is gone, so it is left to the on-call
optionD: About 3% of the budget is gone, so no postmortem is required
correctAnswerText: About 69% of the budget is gone, so a postmortem is required
explanation: The budget is 43.2 minutes; 30 ÷ 43.2 ≈ 69%, far above the 20% trigger, leaving about 31%. 3% and 30% misread the minutes as a share, and 69% spent is not 100%, so the exhausted-budget freeze does not yet apply.

prompt: With a 99.9% SLO, a slow leak keeps errors at 0.4% for two days. Alerts are: page 14.4x (1 h & 5 m), page 6x (6 h & 30 m), ticket 3x (1 d & 2 h). What happens?
optionA: Nothing fires, since a 0.4% error ratio is inside the 99.9% SLO
optionB: The 14.4x page fires, since 0.4% is four times higher than the SLO
optionC: The 6x page fires within six hours, since the leak lasts for two days
optionD: Neither page fires; the 3x ticket catches it after about 27% is spent
correctAnswerText: Neither page fires; the 3x ticket catches it after about 27% is spent
explanation: 0.4% ÷ 0.1% is a burn of 4: below both page thresholds but above the 3x ticket. Over 48 hours it spends 4 × 48 ÷ 720 ≈ 27% of the budget — serious, but slow enough for working hours. 0.4% is four times the allowed ratio, not inside the SLO.

prompt: The availability SLI computed from the application's own metrics shows 99.99%, yet customers report failed bookings and the load balancer logged many 502s. What is wrong?
optionA: A 99.99% SLI means four failures a month, which matches reports
optionB: The SLI only counts requests that reached the app, missing the 502s
optionC: Customers count their own retries as separate failed bookings
optionD: The load balancer double-counts every request it retries upstream
correctAnswerText: The SLI only counts requests that reached the app, missing the 502s
explanation: A 502 from the load balancer often means the target never answered — those requests never appear in the app's metrics, so the SLI looks perfect. Measure where the user is. The other options explain away real evidence; 99.99% is a ratio, not a count of four.

prompt: During a sale, the team's own rate limiter returned 429 to many well-behaved partners, but the availability SLI stayed at 99.95%. The SLI counts every non-5xx as good. What is the flaw?
optionA: Rate limiting is a client problem, so the SLI behaved correctly here
optionB: The SLI should use average latency, which would have shown the problem
optionC: 429s should be excluded entirely, so the SLI should have been higher
optionD: 429s from its own limiter to valid callers should count as bad events
correctAnswerText: 429s from its own limiter to valid callers should count as bad events
explanation: A well-behaved caller refused by the service's own limiter has had a failed request, even though the code is 4xx. Counting it as good (or excluding it) hides real user pain; average latency would not reveal refusals either.

prompt: A burn-rate page keeps firing for almost an hour after a fix has brought errors back to normal. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The 5-minute window is too long and should be made 1 minute instead
optionB: Alertmanager repeats every alert until a human closes it in the tool
optionC: The rule checks only the 1-hour ratio, with no short-window condition
optionD: The SLO target is too loose, so recovery is not counted as recovery
correctAnswerText: The rule checks only the 1-hour ratio, with no short-window condition
explanation: A 1-hour error ratio stays above threshold until the bad minutes age out of the window. Adding "and the 5-minute ratio is also high" makes the alert resolve within minutes of recovery. A 5-minute window is already short, the target does not cause this, and Alertmanager resolves alerts when they stop firing.

prompt: A latency SLI is "requests within 0.5 s", but the histogram's nearest bucket edges are 0.25 s and 1.0 s. Why can't the SLI be computed exactly, and what fixes it?
optionA: Histograms only store averages; switch to a gauge for the latency
optionB: Prometheus cannot divide two counters; compute the SLI in Grafana
optionC: The 1.0 s bucket double-counts requests; delete it from the metric
optionD: No bucket counts requests up to 0.5 s; add a bucket edge at 0.5 s
correctAnswerText: No bucket counts requests up to 0.5 s; add a bucket edge at 0.5 s
explanation: Good events are read from the bucket le="0.5", which does not exist, so the ratio would be estimated between 0.25 and 1.0. Placing an edge exactly at the threshold makes it exact. Histograms store cumulative bucket counts, buckets are cumulative by design, and PromQL divides counters freely.

prompt: A checkout service needs both a payment provider and an inventory service on every request; each achieves 99.9%. Product proposes a 99.95% SLO for checkout. What is the problem?
optionA: Dependencies never affect an SLO, which measures only checkout's own code
optionB: Two dependencies at 99.9% give checkout 99.99%, so the target is too low
optionC: With both needed, checkout can expect only about 99.8%, below the target
optionD: Checkout can reach 99.95% easily, since it averages its two dependencies
correctAnswerText: With both needed, checkout can expect only about 99.8%, below the target
explanation: Serial hard dependencies multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, about 99.8%, before checkout's own failures. A 99.95% target is unreachable without fallbacks or retries that change the maths. Availabilities are not averaged or improved by adding dependencies, and users feel dependency failures.

prompt: A service has a 99% SLO and has achieved 99.97% every month for a year, but customers still complain about failures in busy hours. What does the review suggest?
optionA: The SLI should switch to a calendar month so that busy hours count less
optionB: The SLO is working perfectly, since the budget has never once been at risk
optionC: The target is too loose to reflect what users need; revisit it with product
optionD: The customers are mistaken, because the measured SLI is well above target
correctAnswerText: The target is too loose to reflect what users need; revisit it with product
explanation: A target never at risk while users are unhappy is too loose, or the SLI misses what users feel (busy-hour failures diluted over a month). Review both with product. Reading a met SLO as proof, dismissing complaints, or diluting busy hours further all ignore the evidence.

prompt: An internal admin API gets about 40 requests an hour at night, and its 5-minute burn-rate condition fires on a single failed request. Which diagnosis and fix fit?
optionA: Night traffic is not real traffic; exclude every request after 22:00
optionB: The burn rule is broken; replace it with a CPU alarm for night hours
optionC: Too few events per window; use longer windows or a minimum request count
optionD: The SLO is too strict; set it to 90% so that single failures no longer matter
correctAnswerText: Too few events per window; use longer windows or a minimum request count
explanation: With a handful of requests per window one failure is a huge ratio. Longer windows, a minimum volume guard or synthetic probes make the signal meaningful. Gutting the target, excluding real night users, or paging on CPU all trade the noise for blindness.

prompt: After the budget ran out mid-month, a team lowered its SLO from 99.9% to 99.5% "for the rest of the month" so releases could continue. What is wrong with this?
optionA: Nothing; the policy is only a guide and can be bent when needed
optionB: A 99.5% SLO cannot be represented in CloudWatch or Prometheus
optionC: Moving the target after missing it empties the SLO of meaning
optionD: Lowering an SLO always breaches the customer SLA immediately
correctAnswerText: Moving the target after missing it empties the SLO of meaning
explanation: An SLO that bends whenever it is missed constrains nothing, and the policy agreed in advance said what happens at zero: features pause, reliability first. Targets are reviewed on a schedule with evidence, not mid-window to escape the policy. Any percentage can be represented, and the SLA may or may not be affected.

prompt: Meghdoot Travel's refund worker reads a queue and pays refunds; customers only care that money arrives soon. Which SLI is the best primary choice?
optionA: Share of HTTP health checks on the worker that return a 200 code
optionB: Share of due refunds paid within the promised time of becoming due
optionC: Average CPU utilisation of the worker Pods over each hour of the day
optionD: Number of messages received from the queue per minute by the worker
correctAnswerText: Share of due refunds paid within the promised time of becoming due
explanation: A freshness SLI measures what customers feel — refunds arriving on time — and counts good over valid events. Health checks show the process is up, not that refunds flow; CPU is a cause; and throughput says nothing about lateness.

prompt: A booking API achieved 99.95% over 90 days, users have been satisfied, and its payment provider offers 99.9%. Product asks for 99.99%. Which SLO should the team propose?
optionA: 100%, since a payment flow should never be allowed to fail at all
optionB: 99.9%, reachable with room to ship and in line with the dependency
optionC: 99.0%, the loosest target, so the budget can never be exhausted
optionD: 99.99%, as asked, since a stricter target always drives quality up
correctAnswerText: 99.9%, reachable with room to ship and in line with the dependency
explanation: A target just below achieved performance that users accept, and no stricter than a hard dependency allows, leaves a real budget. 99.99% would be breached by the provider alone, 100% leaves no budget, and 99% is far looser than users are used to.

prompt: A team must choose an SLO alerting design for its availability SLI. Which is best?
optionA: Pages at 14.4x (1 h & 5 m) and 6x (6 h & 30 m); slower burns as tickets
optionB: Pages on CPU and memory at 80%, since these predict every SLO breach
optionC: One page whenever the 5-minute error ratio exceeds the SLO's allowance
optionD: A daily email of the SLI, with no pages, so nobody is woken for errors
correctAnswerText: Pages at 14.4x (1 h & 5 m) and 6x (6 h & 30 m); slower burns as tickets
explanation: Multiwindow burn rules page for fast, significant burns, clear quickly after recovery and send slow leaks to working hours. The naive 5-minute rule pages on noise, a daily email reacts far too slowly to an outage, and resource pages miss dependency failures.

prompt: The error budget is exhausted and feature releases are paused under the policy. A tested fix for a security vulnerability is ready. What should happen?
optionA: Ship it; the freeze covers features, while security and reliability fixes go on
optionB: Lower the SLO first so that the budget is positive and the freeze is lifted
optionC: Hold it until the rolling window recovers, since the freeze covers every change
optionD: Ship it with three new features in the same release to save deployment effort
correctAnswerText: Ship it; the freeze covers features, while security and reliability fixes go on
explanation: A typical policy pauses feature work but lets security fixes and reliability work continue — they reduce risk. Holding a security fix increases exposure, bundling features defeats the freeze, and moving the target to escape the policy makes it meaningless.

prompt: A team's internal SLO is 99.9%. Sales wants to sign an SLA promising 99.95% with service credits. What should engineering advise?
optionA: Sign 99.95% and quietly raise the internal SLO to 99.99% to match it
optionB: Refuse any SLA at all, since cloud services cannot be measured accurately
optionC: Sign 99.95%, since a stricter promise will push the team to improve
optionD: Offer an SLA looser than the SLO, such as 99.5%, so warnings come first
correctAnswerText: Offer an SLA looser than the SLO, such as 99.5%, so warnings come first
explanation: An SLA stricter than the SLO means credits are owed before the team's own alarm sounds. Keep the SLA looser so the SLO warns first. Raising the SLO on paper does not make the service more reliable, and the SLI is perfectly measurable.

prompt: A rarely used partner API matters a lot when it is called, but sees only a few hundred requests a day. Which SLO approach is best?
optionA: Drop the SLO, since services with low traffic cannot have meaningful ones
optionB: Keep 5-minute burn alerts unchanged, accepting pages on single failures
optionC: Add synthetic probes and use longer windows so the SLI has enough events
optionD: Measure its CPU instead, since CPU never depends on how busy traffic is
correctAnswerText: Add synthetic probes and use longer windows so the SLI has enough events
explanation: Synthetic traffic supplies a steady stream of events and longer windows smooth small samples, keeping the SLI meaningful without noise. Dropping the SLO leaves an important service unmeasured, single-failure pages train people to ignore them, and CPU does not measure user experience.

prompt: Which pair of SLIs best represents what merchants feel from a payments API?
optionA: Number of deploys a week and number of open bugs, from the team's tools
optionB: Average response time and peak CPU, both measured inside the application
optionC: Non-5xx share and share within 0.8 s, both measured at the load balancer
optionD: Database connection count and disk usage, both measured on the database
correctAnswerText: Non-5xx share and share within 0.8 s, both measured at the load balancer
explanation: Availability and latency ratios measured near the user describe the merchant's experience directly. Averages and CPU hide the tail and measure causes, delivery metrics describe the team, and database resources are USE signals for diagnosis.

prompt: An API's traffic at midday is ten times its traffic at 4 a.m. Should its error budget be counted in failed requests or in minutes of downtime?
optionA: In requests, since that lets night outages be left out of the budget
optionB: In requests, since an outage at midday hurts ten times more users
optionC: In minutes, since request counts cannot be measured on a load balancer
optionD: In minutes, since every minute of the day matters equally to users
correctAnswerText: In requests, since an outage at midday hurts ten times more users
explanation: A request-based budget weights each failure by the users it hit, so a busy-hour outage spends more budget than a quiet-hour one. Minutes treat both alike. Load balancers do count requests, and night failures still count — just by how many requests they affected.

prompt: With 70% of the budget left, a team plans a database migration it estimates may spend about 15% of the budget. The policy's sign-off line is 25% remaining. What is the sound call?
optionA: Postpone it until the budget is back at 100%, whatever the business need
optionB: Cancel it, since any planned spending of the budget is a policy breach
optionC: Go ahead, but stop counting failures during the migration window itself
optionD: Go ahead with a rollback plan; about 55% would remain, above the line
correctAnswerText: Go ahead with a rollback plan; about 55% would remain, above the line
explanation: Spending budget on a deliberate, valuable change is what it is for: 70% − 15% leaves about 55%, still above the 25% line, so it proceeds with mitigations. The budget is not meant to stay untouched, a rolling budget rarely sits at 100%, and hiding failures falsifies the SLI.

prompt: A team wants its latency objective to catch both "most requests are slower than usual" and "a long tail is timing out". Which latency SLOs fit best?
optionA: One SLO on the median, since half the requests describe the rest
optionB: One SLO on the maximum latency seen, which must stay under 2 s
optionC: One SLO on the daily average latency, which covers both cases
optionD: Two threshold SLOs, such as 95% within 0.5 s and 99% within 2 s
correctAnswerText: Two threshold SLOs, such as 95% within 0.5 s and 99% within 2 s
explanation: A threshold for the typical request and a looser one for the tail each give a good-over-valid ratio and a budget. An average hides the tail, a maximum is set by a single outlier and is always breached, and a median ignores the slowest half entirely.

prompt: Besides an overall deadline, which two timeouts should a client set on every call to a dependency?
optionA: A DNS cache timeout and a record TTL
optionB: A connect timeout and a read timeout
optionC: An idle timeout and a session timeout
optionD: A keep-alive timeout and a lock timeout
correctAnswerText: A connect timeout and a read timeout
explanation: The connect timeout is short (a host that will not accept a connection is down) and the read timeout follows the dependency's real p99 plus margin. DNS TTLs, idle sessions and locks are real settings but do not bound how long one call can hold the caller.

prompt: Which kind of failure is suitable for an automatic retry?
optionA: Client errors such as a 400 for a malformed body
optionB: Validation failures such as a missing required field
optionC: Authorisation failures such as a 403 on a role
optionD: Transient ones such as timeouts, 503s and throttling
correctAnswerText: Transient ones such as timeouts, 503s and throttling
explanation: A transient failure may succeed a moment later, so a retry can help. A 400, a 403 or a validation error will fail identically every time, so retrying only adds load and delay.

prompt: What does exponential backoff do between retry attempts?
optionA: Keeps the same fixed wait before every retry
optionB: Grows the wait after each failure, up to a cap
optionC: Shrinks the wait as the dependency recovers
optionD: Retries at once, and waits only after the last
correctAnswerText: Grows the wait after each failure, up to a cap
explanation: Exponential backoff multiplies the wait after each failure (0.1 s, 0.2 s, 0.4 s …) and caps it so a client never waits absurdly long. A fixed wait gives a struggling service no extra room, and shrinking or skipping the wait does the opposite of backing off.

prompt: With full jitter, how long does a client sleep before a retry?
optionA: A fixed one second, whichever attempt it happens to be
optionB: The backoff value plus the dependency's p99 latency
optionC: Exactly the backoff value, doubled at every attempt
optionD: A random time between zero and the backoff value
correctAnswerText: A random time between zero and the backoff value
explanation: Full jitter picks a random sleep in [0, backoff], so clients that failed together spread out. Sleeping exactly the backoff keeps them synchronised, a fixed second is not backoff at all, and adding the p99 is not a jitter scheme.

prompt: Which three states does a circuit breaker move between?
optionA: Healthy, degraded and failed
optionB: Closed, open and half-open
optionC: Active, standby and draining
optionD: Pending, running and stopped
correctAnswerText: Closed, open and half-open
explanation: Closed lets calls through and counts failures, open fails calls immediately, and half-open lets one trial call through after the cool-down. The other triples describe deployments, health checks and task lifecycles.

prompt: What is a bulkhead in a service that calls several dependencies?
optionA: A separate pool per dependency, so one cannot use them all
optionB: A firewall rule that blocks all calls to a failing dependency
optionC: A shared pool that every dependency borrows from in turn
optionD: A cache that answers whenever every dependency is down
correctAnswerText: A separate pool per dependency, so one cannot use them all
explanation: Like the watertight compartments of a ship, a bulkhead gives each dependency its own threads or connections, so a slow one exhausts only its own pool. A shared pool is the problem bulkheads solve; blocking calls is closer to a breaker, and a cache is a fallback.

prompt: What does an idempotency key let a payment API do?
optionA: Encrypt the request body so that it cannot be replayed
optionB: Reject any request that arrives more than once a minute
optionC: Route the request to the least busy instance in the pool
optionD: Return the first result when the same request is repeated
correctAnswerText: Return the first result when the same request is repeated
explanation: The client sends a key and the server stores it with the outcome; a repeat with the same key returns the stored result instead of acting twice. It has nothing to do with encryption or routing, and rate limiting would reject legitimate distinct requests.

prompt: In disaster recovery planning, what does the RTO state?
optionA: How long the service may be down before it is back
optionB: How long backups are kept before they are deleted
optionC: How much data, measured in time, the business may lose
optionD: How often snapshots are copied to the second region
correctAnswerText: How long the service may be down before it is back
explanation: The recovery time objective bounds downtime. Data loss measured in time is the RPO, the usual slip; retention and copy frequency are settings chosen to meet the objectives, not the objectives themselves.

prompt: Which regional DR strategy keeps a cross-region database replica running but the application switched off?
optionA: Backup and restore
optionB: Warm standby
optionC: Active-active
optionD: Pilot light
correctAnswerText: Pilot light
explanation: Pilot light keeps the data warm (a replica) and the compute off, so RPO is seconds to minutes and RTO tens of minutes. Warm standby also runs a small copy of the app; backup and restore keeps only snapshot copies; active-active serves traffic in both regions.

prompt: Which kind of load test holds the expected peak for hours to find leaks and pool exhaustion?
optionA: A smoke test
optionB: A ramp test
optionC: A spike test
optionD: A soak test
correctAnswerText: A soak test
explanation: A soak runs at expected peak for a long time, which is when slow leaks and exhausted pools show. A spike tests a sudden jump, a ramp finds the knee where latency leaves the SLO, and a smoke test only checks that things work at all.

prompt: Why does a call with no timeout endanger the calling service, not just the waiting user?
optionA: It makes the far side drop the request after its own default time
optionB: It holds a thread and a connection for as long as the far side likes
optionC: It forces the SDK to retry the call with no backoff in between
optionD: It disables TLS so that the connection can stay open for longer
correctAnswerText: It holds a thread and a connection for as long as the far side likes
explanation: Every waiting call pins caller resources; enough of them and the caller runs out of threads or connections and fails for everyone. The far side need not drop anything, and timeouts have nothing to do with retry behaviour or TLS.

prompt: Why do retries help so little when a dependency is completely down?
optionA: The SDK stops retrying as soon as the dependency returns a 503
optionB: Its failures are not independent, so each retry fails the same way
optionC: Every retry goes to the same IP, which the load balancer blocks
optionD: Retries are only permitted for reads, never for any kind of write
correctAnswerText: Its failures are not independent, so each retry fails the same way
explanation: Retries cut failure sharply only when attempts fail independently (0.2, 0.04, 0.008 …). A dependency that is down fails every attempt, so retries only add load and delay. Writes can be retried with idempotency keys, SDKs do retry 503s, and load balancers do not block retries.

prompt: Why should retries live at one layer of a call chain rather than at every layer?
optionA: Each layer has its own deadline, so retries can never overlap
optionB: Retries at each layer multiply, flooding the failing service
optionC: Only the outermost layer can ever see the HTTP status code
optionD: Lower layers are unable to use exponential backoff at all
correctAnswerText: Retries at each layer multiply, flooding the failing service
explanation: Each layer multiplies the attempts of the one below — three layers of three attempts is 27 calls at the bottom per user request — which keeps an overloaded service down. Every layer can see status codes and use backoff; separate deadlines do not stop the multiplication.

prompt: Why can synchronised retries keep a recovering service down even when every client uses exponential backoff?
optionA: A recovering service rejects any request marked as a retry
optionB: Backoff resets to zero once a single retry has succeeded
optionC: Clients that failed together come back together, in waves
optionD: Exponential backoff makes the gap between retries shrink
correctAnswerText: Clients that failed together come back together, in waves
explanation: Identical backoff schedules keep clients in step: in the course simulation all 1,000 retries landed in one 10 ms slot, three times over. Backoff grows the gap rather than shrinking it, services do not reject retries as such, and a reset after success is not the problem.

prompt: Why does an open circuit breaker help the caller, and not only the failing dependency?
optionA: Requests are logged so that the postmortem can replay them later
optionB: Requests fail at once instead of holding resources for a timeout
optionC: Requests are queued until the breaker closes, so none are lost
optionD: Requests are retried in the background with a longer timeout
correctAnswerText: Requests fail at once instead of holding resources for a timeout
explanation: Failing fast frees the thread, the connection and the user at once, and lets a fallback act. A breaker does not queue or retry the calls it rejects — that would recreate the load it exists to stop — and logging is incidental.

prompt: Why can a timed-out "debit ₹499" request not simply be retried as it stands?
optionA: The PSP blocks any client that sends the same body twice
optionB: The timeout does not say whether the first debit went through
optionC: Payment APIs reject every request sent again within a minute
optionD: A retry needs a fresh TLS session, which takes far too long
correctAnswerText: The timeout does not say whether the first debit went through
explanation: A timeout means "no answer", not "nothing happened"; the first debit may have succeeded, so a blind retry can debit twice. An idempotency key makes the repeat safe. The other options invent behaviours that payment APIs do not have.

prompt: Why does rejecting excess requests early with 429 or 503 protect an overloaded service?
optionA: The load balancer adds capacity each time it sees a 503 reply
optionB: Clients never retry a 429, so that traffic disappears for good
optionC: Rejected requests are stored and replayed once the load falls
optionD: A quick rejection is cheap; accepting then timing out is costly
correctAnswerText: A quick rejection is cheap; accepting then timing out is costly
explanation: Accepting everything means every request queues, holds resources and times out, so nobody is served; rejecting some early keeps the rest inside the SLO. Clients may well retry a 429, load balancers do not scale on 503s, and shed requests are not replayed.

prompt: Why is a Multi-AZ standby database no substitute for backups?
optionA: It is promoted only during a planned maintenance window each week
optionB: It keeps its data in another region, which makes restores slower
optionC: It is read-only, so it cannot be restored to a point in time
optionD: It copies a bad DROP TABLE within moments, so both lose the data
correctAnswerText: It copies a bad DROP TABLE within moments, so both lose the data
explanation: A synchronous standby replicates every change faithfully, including destructive ones, so it protects against host and AZ failure but not against a bad migration or a corrupting bug. It fails over automatically, sits in the same region, and is not a read endpoint.

prompt: Why is a database backup that has never been restored treated as unproven?
optionA: An unrestored snapshot stays unencrypted until the first time it is used
optionB: Only a timed restore measures the real RTO and RPO and checks the data
optionC: Restoring is the step that copies the snapshot into the DR region
optionD: Backups expire if they are not restored within their first seven days
correctAnswerText: Only a timed restore measures the real RTO and RPO and checks the data
explanation: A drill shows how long recovery really takes, how fresh the newest data is, and whether the data is usable — none of which a "backup succeeded" status proves. Expiry follows retention, encryption is set at creation, and cross-region copy is a separate step.

prompt: Why is throughput per instance at the latency SLO the useful load-test result, rather than the maximum reached before errors?
optionA: The maximum before errors is identical in every test that runs
optionB: Autoscaling reads that figure directly from the load-test tool
optionC: Capacity must be planned at a load that still meets the SLO
optionD: Errors seen in load tests never occur under production traffic
correctAnswerText: Capacity must be planned at a load that still meets the SLO
explanation: Well before errors appear, latency has usually left the SLO, so sizing on the error point plans for a service users already find too slow. The other options are false claims about test repeatability, production and autoscaling.

prompt: A merchant client gives up after 10 s. payments-api calls the PSP with a 4 s read timeout and up to 3 attempts. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing; three attempts are bounded by 4 s in total anyway
optionB: Three 4 s attempts can take 12 s, beyond the 10 s deadline
optionC: The read timeout must equal the deadline, so it should be 10 s
optionD: The connect timeout should be raised to 10 s to match the client
correctAnswerText: Three 4 s attempts can take 12 s, beyond the 10 s deadline
explanation: Worst case is 3 × 4 = 12 s plus backoff, so the client has given up while payments-api is still retrying — wasted work, and a payment whose outcome the merchant never sees. Timeouts apply per attempt, and setting either to the full deadline leaves no room for a retry.

prompt: At Kirana Cloud, an API gateway and the order service behind it each make up to 4 attempts. The inventory service is failing. With 500 user requests a second, what can inventory receive in the worst case?
optionA: 4,000 requests a second
optionB: 2,000 requests a second
optionC: 1,000 requests a second
optionD: 8,000 requests a second
correctAnswerText: 8,000 requests a second
explanation: Attempts multiply: 4 at the gateway × 4 at the order service = 16 calls per user request, and 500 × 16 = 8,000. 4,000 adds the attempts instead of multiplying them, 2,000 counts only one layer, and 1,000 assumes a single retry.

prompt: A dependency fails 10% of calls, independently and at random. With up to three attempts per request, what share of requests still fail?
explanation: All three attempts must fail: 0.1 × 0.1 × 0.1 = 0.001, or 0.1%. 1% is two attempts, 10% ignores the retries, and 30% adds probabilities that should be multiplied. This only holds because the failures are independent.

prompt: Backoff starts at 0.2 s, doubles after each failure and is capped at 2 s. Before jitter, what are the first five waits?
explanation: Doubling gives 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 and then 3.2, which the cap brings down to 2.0. The second option forgets the cap, the third grows linearly, and the fourth is a fixed wait.

prompt: Rupayo's mobile app retries POST /v1/payouts after a timeout. Which design makes that retry safe?
optionA: The app waits twice as long before each retry of the payout request
optionB: The server rejects any payout whose body matches an earlier one
optionC: One idempotency key per payout, stored by the server with its result
optionD: A circuit breaker on the server in front of the payout endpoint
correctAnswerText: One idempotency key per payout, stored by the server with its result
explanation: With a key per payout, a repeat returns the stored outcome and money moves once. Waiting longer does not stop a double payout, a breaker limits load rather than duplicates, and matching on body would wrongly reject two genuine payouts of the same amount to the same account.

prompt: payments-api shares one pool of 200 threads across all outbound calls. PSP-A slows to 20 s per call while receiving 10 calls a second. What happens?
optionA: PSP-A calls use 10 threads, one for each call every second
optionB: PSP-A calls fill all 200 threads and starve every other call
optionC: PSP-A calls use 2 threads, since 20 divided by 10 is two
optionD: PSP-A calls use 20 threads, leaving 180 for the other work
correctAnswerText: PSP-A calls fill all 200 threads and starve every other call
explanation: By Little's law, calls in flight = 10 a second × 20 s = 200, the whole pool, so the health check and refunds have no threads. A separate pool per dependency (a bulkhead) plus a sane timeout would have contained it. The distractors confuse rate with concurrency.

prompt: A breaker with a 30 s cool-down opened at 10:00:05. At 10:00:35 its single trial call succeeds. Which state is it in now?
optionA: Half-open, until ten calls succeed
optionB: Open, until an operator resets it
optionC: Open, until a second cool-down ends
optionD: Closed, so normal calls flow again
correctAnswerText: Closed, so normal calls flow again
explanation: After the cool-down the breaker goes half-open and lets one trial through; success closes it, failure would open it again for another cool-down. No manual reset or batch of successes is needed in the pattern as taught.

prompt: A service needs 40 tasks of capacity at peak and runs across two AZs. To survive losing either AZ without waiting for scaling, how many tasks should run?
optionA: 40, with 20 in each AZ
optionB: 120, with 60 in each AZ
optionC: 80, with 40 in each AZ
optionD: 60, with 30 in each AZ
correctAnswerText: 80, with 40 in each AZ
explanation: Either AZ alone must carry the full 40, so each needs 40: 80 in total. 40 halves capacity on an AZ loss, 60 leaves 30 (short by 10), and 120 is the three-AZ figure applied to two.

prompt: A ledger in ap-south-1 needs RPO 5 minutes and RTO 1 hour even if the whole region fails. Which design fits?
optionA: Point-in-time restore from the ap-south-1 automated backups
optionB: Daily snapshots copied to ap-south-2 and restored on failure
optionC: A Multi-AZ standby in ap-south-1 with automatic failover
optionD: A cross-region read replica in ap-south-2, promoted on failure
correctAnswerText: A cross-region read replica in ap-south-2, promoted on failure
explanation: A cross-region replica keeps data seconds to minutes behind and can be promoted well inside an hour — pilot light. Daily snapshots lose up to a day, and both Multi-AZ and in-region PITR are lost with the region.

prompt: A festive sale opens at midnight and traffic jumps sixfold within a minute. Which test shows how autoscaling copes?
optionA: A soak test held at normal load for eight hours
optionB: A ramp test that stops at the very first error seen
optionC: A spike test from normal load to the expected jump
optionD: A unit test of the scaling policy definition file
correctAnswerText: A spike test from normal load to the expected jump
explanation: A spike reproduces the step change and shows scaling lag and whether the SLO holds meanwhile (often the answer is to scale ahead on a schedule). A soak tests duration, a unit test checks syntax, and a ramp finds the knee rather than the reaction to a jump.

prompt: A worker using boto3 with no Config hangs for about a minute on SQS calls whenever a network path drops packets. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: SQS throttles any client sending more than one call a second
optionB: The worker's IAM role credentials expire after a minute idle
optionC: Library default timeouts are long, and nobody set shorter ones
optionD: DNS caching makes every call wait for a fresh lookup first
correctAnswerText: Library default timeouts are long, and nobody set shorter ones
explanation: boto3's connect and read timeouts default to 60 seconds each, so a lost packet costs a minute per attempt; set them in a Config from the dependency's real latency. Throttling returns an error quickly, role credentials last far longer and refresh, and DNS caching shortens rather than lengthens calls.

prompt: A team set retries={'mode': 'standard', 'max_attempts': 3} in a botocore Config, expecting three calls in total, and logs show four. Why?
optionA: The SDK adds one extra attempt whenever jitter has been switched on
optionB: Standard mode always makes exactly one more attempt than configured
optionC: The fourth call is a health probe sent by the SDK, not a real retry
optionD: In that retries config, max_attempts counts retries, so four in all
correctAnswerText: In that retries config, max_attempts counts retries, so four in all
explanation: In botocore's retries dictionary, max_attempts is the number of retries, and the client reports total_max_attempts as 4. The lesson is to read what a library means by its numbers before reasoning about load. Jitter does not add attempts, and the SDK sends no health probes.

prompt: After a five-minute outage, a PSP comes back and falls over again within seconds, three times running. Clients retry at three layers with fixed 1 s waits. What is happening?
optionA: Its own recovery takes longer than the clients' fixed one-second wait
optionB: It cannot accept any connection until every client has restarted
optionC: Multiplied, synchronised retries hit it at once and knock it back down
optionD: The clients' DNS still points at the PSP's old, failed endpoint
correctAnswerText: Multiplied, synchronised retries hit it at once and knock it back down
explanation: Three layers multiply the attempts and fixed waits keep every client in step, so the backlog lands in one burst the moment the PSP returns. One retrying layer, capped exponential backoff, full jitter and a retry budget prevent the storm. A stale DNS entry would fail constantly rather than knock the PSP over.

prompt: On a day the PSP was slow, several customers were debited twice for one order. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: Timed-out debits were retried without any idempotency key
optionB: Full jitter made two debits land at exactly the same moment
optionC: The circuit breaker opened and sent each debit to both PSPs
optionD: The read timeout was too long, so each debit was held twice
correctAnswerText: Timed-out debits were retried without any idempotency key
explanation: A slow PSP produces timeouts on debits that actually succeeded; retrying them without a key repeats the money movement. An open breaker fails fast rather than duplicating, a long timeout reduces retries, and jitter spreads retries but does not create them.

prompt: When PSP-A slows down, payments-api's health check and its refund API fail too, and the load balancer replaces tasks. What design gap explains it?
optionA: All calls share one pool, and the slow PSP has taken every thread
optionB: The refund API retries too fast, which overloads PSP-A once more
optionC: The health check is wired to PSP-A, so it must fail along with it
optionD: The load balancer health check interval is set much too short
correctAnswerText: All calls share one pool, and the slow PSP has taken every thread
explanation: With no bulkhead, slow PSP-A calls pile up until nothing is left for refunds or the health check, and the load balancer then kills tasks that are only starved. A health check wired to PSP-A would not explain refunds failing too, and a short interval or refund retries do not exhaust threads on their own.

prompt: A circuit breaker opens on every brief blip, so payments fail fast even though the PSP answers 99.9% of calls well within the timeout. What is most likely misconfigured?
optionA: Its read timeout is far shorter than the PSP's p99 latency
optionB: Its cool-down is far too long for the PSP's recovery time
optionC: Its failure threshold is far too low for the call volume
optionD: Its half-open trial lets far too many calls through to the PSP
correctAnswerText: Its failure threshold is far too low for the call volume
explanation: A threshold of one or two failures trips on the normal 0.1% at high volume; the threshold should reflect a real outage. A long cool-down prolongs an open state but does not cause the opening, a half-open trial is one call, and the stem rules out a short timeout.

prompt: A service spread evenly over three AZs ran its tasks at 85% utilisation. When one AZ failed, the whole service fell over. Why?
optionA: The surviving tasks needed exactly 100% of their capacity
optionB: The surviving tasks needed about 128% of their capacity
optionC: The surviving tasks needed about 118% of their capacity
optionD: The surviving tasks needed about 92% of their capacity
correctAnswerText: The surviving tasks needed about 128% of their capacity
explanation: Losing one of three AZs moves the load onto two-thirds of the tasks: 85% × 3 ÷ 2 = 127.5%, so they overload. 118% adds 33 percentage points instead of scaling by three-halves, and 100% or 92% understate the jump. Running near 60% (or adding AZ headroom) keeps the survivors under 100%.

prompt: A quarterly DR drill restores the ledger and the app connects, but the newest entry is three hours old against an RPO of five minutes. What does this show?
optionA: The measured RPO is about three hours, so the design misses its target
optionB: The drill passed, because the application connected to the restored copy
optionC: The restored instance's clock is set three hours behind the original
optionD: The RTO was missed, because the restore itself took over three hours
correctAnswerText: The measured RPO is about three hours, so the design misses its target
explanation: The age of the newest record is the measured RPO, and three hours against five minutes is a failed objective to fix (PITR, replication, or copy frequency). Connecting proves nothing about data loss, the stem says nothing about restore duration, and clock skew is not the plain reading.

prompt: After a point-in-time restore of ledger-prod to a minute before a bad UPDATE, the application still shows the corrupted rows. What was missed?
optionA: The restore time was given in IST while the service expects local time
optionB: The restore overwrote the data, but a cache kept the corrupted rows
optionC: Point-in-time restore brings back the schema only, never the rows
optionD: The restore made a new instance, and the app still uses the old one
correctAnswerText: The restore made a new instance, and the app still uses the old one
explanation: RDS restores never overwrite: they create a new instance with a new endpoint, which the app must be pointed at (or rows copied back). There was no overwrite for a cache to mask, PITR restores data, and the time-zone option does not explain unchanged rows on the original.

prompt: A load test reported 400 rps per task, yet in production the service breaches its p99 SLO at 250 rps per task. What is the likeliest flaw in the test?
optionA: It used too few virtual users to reach the real production peak load
optionB: It reported the maximum before errors, not throughput within the SLO
optionC: It used k6, which cannot measure any latency percentiles at all
optionD: It ran against production, which always gives higher figures
correctAnswerText: It reported the maximum before errors, not throughput within the SLO
explanation: Latency leaves the SLO well before errors begin, so the error point overstates usable capacity. k6 does report percentiles, testing production is not implied, and too few virtual users would understate the figure rather than inflate it.

prompt: A request passes gateway → orders → inventory → database client, and today every layer retries. Which retry policy should replace it?
optionA: Retry at the call nearest the failure, capped, within a retry budget
optionB: Retry only at the gateway, without a limit, until the client gives up
optionC: Retry at every layer, three times each, so each recovers on its own
optionD: Never retry anywhere, since retries always make an outage much worse
correctAnswerText: Retry at the call nearest the failure, capped, within a retry budget
explanation: One layer, closest to the failing call, with capped jittered attempts and a budget keeps the benefit for independent failures without multiplying load. Retrying everywhere is the 27× storm, unlimited retries are worse still, and banning retries throws away cheap recovery from transient faults.

prompt: PSP-A's breaker opens during a sale while PSP-B is healthy. What should happen to new payments that would have used PSP-A?
optionA: Hold each request open until the breaker's cool-down has ended
optionB: Route them to PSP-B, with the idempotency key kept per payment
optionC: Retry them against PSP-A with a doubled read timeout instead
optionD: Queue them and tell each customer at once that payment succeeded
correctAnswerText: Route them to PSP-B, with the idempotency key kept per payment
explanation: The breaker's fast failure is what makes a fallback possible: the second PSP takes the payment and the key prevents duplicates. Confirming an unprocessed payment misleads the customer, holding requests recreates the thread exhaustion, and retrying the open dependency defeats the breaker.

prompt: A payments platform is overloaded on a sale night and must shed load. Which shedding policy is best?
optionA: Shed payments first, as they cost the most to serve
optionB: Shed requests at random, so every feature is treated alike
optionC: Shed nothing; accept every request and wait for scaling
optionD: Shed reporting and analytics first, and payments last
correctAnswerText: Shed reporting and analytics first, and payments last
explanation: Load shedding is a priority decision: protect the money path and drop what can wait. Shedding payments first inverts the priority, random shedding hurts the critical path as much as the trivial one, and accepting everything means everything times out.

prompt: A marketing database has an agreed RPO of 24 hours and RTO of one day. A regional DR design is needed. Which is best?
optionA: Active-active, with a global database serving both regions
optionB: Backup and restore, with snapshot copies in the second region
optionC: Warm standby, with a scaled-down app always running in DR
optionD: No regional plan, as such long targets need no design at all
correctAnswerText: Backup and restore, with snapshot copies in the second region
explanation: Hours of RPO and RTO are exactly what backup and restore delivers, at the lowest cost and complexity. Active-active and warm standby buy seconds and minutes the business did not ask for, and a long target still needs copies outside the region to be met at all.

prompt: A ledger needs RPO of seconds to minutes and RTO of minutes for a regional failure. An engineer proposes active-active writes in two regions. Which judgement is best?
optionA: Pilot light with the app switched off meets an RTO of a few minutes
optionB: Backup and restore meets them if snapshots are copied every hour
optionC: Active-active is required whenever an RPO is measured in seconds
optionD: Warm standby meets these targets without two-region write conflicts
correctAnswerText: Warm standby meets these targets without two-region write conflicts
explanation: Warm standby (replica plus a small running app) gives RPO of seconds to minutes and RTO of minutes, without the conflict handling active-active writes demand. Hourly snapshots lose up to an hour, and pilot light needs tens of minutes to start the app.

prompt: Timeouts, breakers and bulkheads are configured for the sale but have never been exercised. What best shows they work beforehand?
optionA: A code review checking every setting against the design document
optionB: Waiting for the next real outage and studying the dashboards then
optionC: Switching the breakers off in production to compare the results
optionD: A game day in staging that blocks the PSP while SLIs are watched
correctAnswerText: A game day in staging that blocks the PSP while SLIs are watched
explanation: Breaking the dependency on purpose, at sale-like load and with pass criteria on the SLIs, is the only evidence the patterns behave as designed. A review checks intent rather than behaviour, removing protection in production is reckless, and waiting learns the answer at the worst time.

prompt: A PSP's p99 latency is 1.2 s and the merchant client's deadline is 10 s. Which timeout plan is best?
optionA: No read timeout at all, relying on a breaker to catch slow calls
optionB: Connect 60 s, read 60 s, the library defaults, with three retries
optionC: Read timeout 1 s, below the p99, with five quick retries after it
optionD: Connect 1 s, read 3 s, one jittered retry, all within the deadline
correctAnswerText: Connect 1 s, read 3 s, one jittered retry, all within the deadline
explanation: A read timeout above the p99 with margin, and a worst case of 2 × (1 + 3) = 8 s plus a short jittered wait, fits inside 10 s. Defaults blow the deadline, a timeout below p99 fails healthy calls and five retries multiply load, and a breaker counts failures but does not bound a single call.

prompt: A young startup agrees an RTO of four hours for a regional outage, yet proposes active-active across two regions from day one. Which judgement is best?
optionA: Active-active is the only design that survives losing a single AZ
optionB: Multi-AZ in one region plus cross-region backups fits the targets
optionC: Two regions with writes split by customer is simpler than one AZ
optionD: A single AZ is enough, since whole regions so rarely fail at all
correctAnswerText: Multi-AZ in one region plus cross-region backups fits the targets
explanation: Multi-AZ handles the common failure (an AZ), and backups copied to a second region meet a four-hour regional RTO at a fraction of the complexity. Surviving an AZ needs only Multi-AZ, a single AZ fails at the first AZ incident, and splitting writes across regions is not simpler.

prompt: Which single control best stops retries from turning a partial outage into a full one?
optionA: A longer backoff cap so that retries arrive somewhat later
optionB: A shorter connect timeout so that failed attempts end sooner
optionC: A higher attempt limit so that more requests end up succeeding
optionD: A retry budget that caps retries at a small share of requests
correctAnswerText: A retry budget that caps retries at a small share of requests
explanation: A budget (for example retries at most 10% of requests) bounds the extra load however bad things get, so retries cannot multiply traffic. A longer cap only delays the load, more attempts add to it, and a shorter connect timeout makes failed attempts cheaper but not fewer.

prompt: Designing idempotency for POST /v1/payments, where should the keys and results be kept?
optionA: In the load balancer's access logs, searched on every new request
optionB: In the client only, trusted by the server whenever it resends the key
optionC: In an in-memory map on each task, cleared at every deployment
optionD: Server-side in a durable store, for at least the client retry window
correctAnswerText: Server-side in a durable store, for at least the client retry window
explanation: The server must find a key whichever task the retry reaches and after restarts, so it belongs in a shared durable store kept at least as long as clients may retry. A client-only key gives the server nothing to compare, a per-task memory map misses retries routed elsewhere or after a deploy, and logs are not a lookup store.

prompt: In an on-call rotation, what happens when the primary does not acknowledge a page within the escalation window?
optionA: The secondary is paged, then the team lead
optionB: The alert is silenced until the next shift
optionC: The page is resent to the same person only
optionD: The page is closed and logged as resolved
correctAnswerText: The secondary is paged, then the team lead
explanation: Escalation, enforced by the paging tool, makes sure an unacknowledged page reaches someone: secondary, then lead. Closing, silencing or endlessly resending to one person all leave an incident with nobody responding.

prompt: In PaySetu's four-level operational severity table, which description fits SEV4?
optionA: A major function degraded, with a workaround
optionB: No user impact yet, but a risk has been found
optionC: Minor or internal impact, such as late reports
optionD: Payments failing for many merchants at once
correctAnswerText: No user impact yet, but a risk has been found
explanation: SEV4 is a risk with no impact yet, such as a certificate expiring in ten days. A degraded function with a workaround is SEV2, minor or internal impact is SEV3, and widespread payment failure is SEV1.

prompt: What is the Incident Commander's job during a major outage?
optionA: Publish: post every update to the public status page
optionB: Steer: set priorities, assign work and make the calls
optionC: Write: draft the postmortem while the incident runs
optionD: Debug: read the logs and find the faulty line of code
correctAnswerText: Steer: set priorities, assign work and make the calls
explanation: The IC owns the incident — priorities, assignments, decisions such as "roll back now" — and does not debug. Investigation is the operations lead's, updates and the status page are the communications lead's, and the postmortem comes afterwards.

prompt: Which incident role posts updates on a fixed cadence and deals with the business and support teams?
optionA: The communications lead
optionB: The Incident Commander
optionC: The secondary on-call
optionD: The operations lead
correctAnswerText: The communications lead
explanation: The communications lead writes internal updates and the status page and fields stakeholders so engineers are not interrupted. The operations lead changes systems, the IC steers, and the secondary usually works the problem.

prompt: In what order do the stages of an operational outage run, as the SRE lesson teaches them?
optionA: Detect, mitigate, declare, resolve, triage, follow up
optionB: Detect, declare, triage, mitigate, resolve, follow up
optionC: Detect, triage, find root cause, fix, declare, follow up
optionD: Declare, detect, mitigate, triage, follow up, resolve
correctAnswerText: Detect, declare, triage, mitigate, resolve, follow up
explanation: Declaring early brings in roles and help; triage establishes impact and what changed; mitigation stops the bleeding before the cause is understood; resolution is confirmed on the SLI; follow-up is the postmortem. Finding root cause before mitigating is the classic mistake.

prompt: What belongs on a public status page during an outage?
optionA: Impact and progress in the customers' own words
optionB: The on-call engineer's name and phone number
optionC: The raw error logs, so customers see the detail
optionD: Internal service names and the suspected cause
correctAnswerText: Impact and progress in the customers' own words
explanation: The status page says what customers experience and what is being done, in their language. Internal names, guesses at cause, staff contact details and raw logs confuse or mislead customers and can leak information.

prompt: Where should an alert's runbook be reachable from?
optionA: The postmortem of the last similar incident
optionB: A wiki page found by searching on the night
optionC: A runbook_url link carried in the alert itself
optionD: The on-call engineer's own personal notes file
correctAnswerText: A runbook_url link carried in the alert itself
explanation: Linking the runbook from the alert means the person paged is one click from what it means and what to do. Searching a wiki at 3am, digging through old postmortems or relying on personal notes all cost minutes and fail for whoever is new.

prompt: In incident response metrics, what does MTTA measure?
optionA: Time from resolution to the postmortem
optionB: Time from detection to full restoration
optionC: Time from a page to its acknowledgement
optionD: Time from the first impact to detection
correctAnswerText: Time from a page to its acknowledgement
explanation: Mean time to acknowledge runs from the page to someone accepting it. Impact to detection is MTTD, restoration is MTTR, and the postmortem gap is not one of the standard trio.

prompt: Which content belongs in the impact section of an outage postmortem?
optionA: Users affected, duration and error budget consumed
optionB: The action items with owners and their due dates
optionC: A copy of the scribe's notes, minute by minute
optionD: The names of the engineers who made the change
correctAnswerText: Users affected, duration and error budget consumed
explanation: Impact quantifies the harm: who and how many, for how long, money delayed and the share of the error budget spent. Action items and the timeline have their own sections, and naming people is not what a blameless review records as impact.

prompt: Which four things should every postmortem action item carry?
optionA: An owner, a priority, a due date and a ticket link
optionB: A summary, a timeline, an impact and a lesson
optionC: A root cause, a culprit, a deadline and a reviewer
optionD: A severity, a pager, a status page and a runbook
correctAnswerText: An owner, a priority, a due date and a ticket link
explanation: Owner, priority, date and a ticket in the normal backlog are what make an action get done and be tracked. A culprit has no place in a blameless review, and the other lists are parts of the incident or the document, not of an action.

prompt: Why should an alert that the on-call engineer reads and then ignores be made a ticket or deleted?
optionA: Ignored pages are retried until someone acknowledges
optionB: Noisy pages teach people to stop reading pages at all
optionC: Tickets are resolved faster than pages during a shift
optionD: Deleting alerts lowers the measured MTTD of the team
correctAnswerText: Noisy pages teach people to stop reading pages at all
explanation: Every page should need action; pages that do not erode attention until a real one is missed, and they burn people out. Retry behaviour, ticket speed and MTTD are not the reason — removing an alert can even hide real detection.

prompt: Why is the advice, when unsure, to declare the higher severity and downgrade later?
optionA: Declaring is cheap, while a late declaration costs time
optionB: Downgrading resets the incident clock back to zero
optionC: Postmortems are written only for the lower severities
optionD: Higher severities are closed sooner by the paging tool
correctAnswerText: Declaring is cheap, while a late declaration costs time
explanation: Over-declaring costs a few people some minutes; under-declaring leaves a real outage without roles, help or communication while it grows. Paging tools do not close incidents by severity, SEV1 and SEV2 always get postmortems, and downgrading changes no clock.

prompt: Why must the Incident Commander stay out of hands-on debugging during a SEV1?
optionA: Once deep in the logs, nobody is steering the response
optionB: Logs may be read only after the incident is resolved
optionC: The IC lacks the access rights to read production logs
optionD: Debugging is the job of the communications lead alone
correctAnswerText: Once deep in the logs, nobody is steering the response
explanation: Debugging absorbs attention, so priorities, decisions and communication stop. Diagnosis continues, but by the operations lead. Access rights are not the point, logs are read during incidents, and the communications lead does not debug.
