prompt: Why does an on-call team roll back a suspect release before it understands the bug?
optionA: Root causes can only be found in an older, stable release
optionB: Rollbacks are mandatory by policy before any investigation
optionC: Rollback restores service fast; the cause can be found later
optionD: A rollback removes the evidence the postmortem would need
correctAnswerText: Rollback restores service fast; the cause can be found later
explanation: Users are hurt every minute the outage runs; a rollback usually restores service in minutes, and the bad release can still be studied afterwards. Rolling back does not destroy evidence, the cause lives in the new release, and the reason is impact rather than a rule.

prompt: Why does triage ask "what changed?" — deploys, config, flags, dependencies — so early?
optionA: A config change is always the root cause of any production outage
optionB: A rollback becomes impossible once more than an hour has passed
optionC: Changes are the only events that dashboards keep any record of
optionD: Most incidents follow a change, so recent ones are prime suspects
correctAnswerText: Most incidents follow a change, so recent ones are prime suspects
explanation: Recent changes explain most outages and are usually reversible, which points straight at a mitigation. Dashboards record far more than changes, rollbacks do not expire after an hour, and "always" is false — dependencies and traffic cause outages too.

prompt: Why does a SEV1 update go out every 30 minutes even when nothing has changed?
optionA: The paging tool closes incidents that go quiet too long
optionB: Each update resets the error budget for the month again
optionC: The status page goes offline without regular new posts
optionD: Silence makes stakeholders chase the engineers for news
correctAnswerText: Silence makes stakeholders chase the engineers for news
explanation: "Still investigating, next update 22:30" keeps people informed and away from the responders, and a promised next time stops them asking. Status pages, error budgets and paging tools do not behave as the distractors claim.

prompt: Why does a public status page avoid naming a suspected cause while the outage is still running?
optionA: Customers are never permitted to learn the cause of any outage
optionB: Every cause must be approved by a regulator before it is published
optionC: Status pages can only show green, amber or red, never any text
optionD: Early guesses are often wrong, and internal detail confuses users
correctAnswerText: Early guesses are often wrong, and internal detail confuses users
explanation: A guess that turns out wrong has to be retracted publicly, and internal names mean nothing to merchants; impact and progress are what they need. Causes can be shared later, regulators do not pre-approve status text, and status pages do carry text.

prompt: Why does a blameless postmortem still record exactly what each person did and when?
optionA: The record feeds into each engineer's performance review
optionB: The details reveal the conditions that made the error easy
optionC: Auditors need the name of every engineer who was involved
optionD: Blameless reviews only apply when nobody made a mistake
correctAnswerText: The details reveal the conditions that made the error easy
explanation: Blameless does not mean nobody acted; it asks why the action made sense at the time and what made the mistake easy, which needs the facts. Using the record for appraisal is exactly what makes people hide details, and blamelessness applies most when someone did err.

prompt: Why is "human error" never accepted as the root cause in an outage postmortem?
optionA: It stops the analysis before the system gap that allowed it
optionB: Only software defects count as causes of a production outage
optionC: Human error cannot be measured, so it cannot be reported
optionD: Company policy protects engineers from being named at all
correctAnswerText: It stops the analysis before the system gap that allowed it
explanation: Someone will make the same mistake again unless the review finds what made it easy — no dry run, no review, no guard. Naming is not forbidden, measurability is not the issue, and process gaps are valid contributing factors alongside defects.

prompt: Why are postmortem actions balanced across prevent, detect and mitigate?
optionA: So that no section of the template is left standing empty
optionB: So that every action can be closed in under one week
optionC: So that three teams each get an equal share of the work
optionD: So recurrence is rarer, caught sooner and less harmful
correctAnswerText: So recurrence is rarer, caught sooner and less harmful
explanation: No prevention is perfect, so the review also shortens detection and limits harm next time. Fair division of work, tidy templates and short deadlines are not why the balance exists.

prompt: One merchant's integration with PaySetu is failing after a change on their side; every other merchant is fine. Which severity fits the table?
optionA: SEV2, because no workaround is in place
optionB: SEV1, because a payment path is failing
optionC: SEV4, since the fault is on the merchant's side
optionD: SEV3, minor impact limited to one merchant
correctAnswerText: SEV3, minor impact limited to one merchant
explanation: The table puts one merchant's integration failing at SEV3: real but limited impact. SEV1 needs many merchants affected, SEV2 is a major function degraded, and SEV4 means no impact yet — the merchant is already affected, whoever caused it.

prompt: Errors began at 21:38, the page fired at 21:54, it was acknowledged at 21:55 and service was restored at 22:20. How long did detection take, and how long after errors began was service restored?
optionA: 17 minutes to detect; restored after 26 minutes
optionB: 16 minutes to detect; restored after 26 minutes
optionC: 1 minute to detect; restored after 25 minutes
optionD: 16 minutes to detect; restored after 42 minutes
correctAnswerText: 16 minutes to detect; restored after 42 minutes
explanation: Detection is impact start to page: 21:38 → 21:54 = 16 minutes. Users were affected from 21:38 to 22:20 = 42 minutes. 26 minutes measures from the page, 1 minute and 25 minutes are measured from the acknowledgement, and 17 runs to the acknowledgement rather than the page.

prompt: A SEV1 update is posted at 22:05 IST on a 30-minute cadence. How should its last line read?
optionA: Next update when it is resolved
optionB: Next update 22:35, or sooner
optionC: Next update once root cause is known
optionD: Next update by 23:05 at the latest
correctAnswerText: Next update 22:35, or sooner
explanation: Every update promises a concrete time on the cadence: 22:05 + 30 minutes = 22:35, sooner if something changes. Tying the next update to an event leaves stakeholders guessing, and 23:05 doubles the cadence.

prompt: At 3,000 requests a minute, an outage fails 6% of requests for 20 minutes. How many failed, and what share of an 18,000-failure monthly error budget is that?
optionA: 180 failures, 1% of the budget
optionB: 60,000 failures, over three budgets
optionC: 1,200 failures, about 6.7% of the budget
optionD: 3,600 failures, 20% of the budget
correctAnswerText: 3,600 failures, 20% of the budget
explanation: 3,000 × 20 × 0.06 = 3,600 failures, and 3,600 ÷ 18,000 = 20%. 180 is a single minute, 60,000 counts every request rather than the failing 6%, and 1,200 applies the wrong rate.

prompt: Checkout errors at Sundari Retail jumped eight minutes after a feature flag on the cart page was switched on. The cause is unproven. What should the IC direct?
optionA: Turn the flag off now and keep investigating in parallel
optionB: Leave the flag on until profiling proves it is the cause
optionC: Fail the database over to its standby to clear the load
optionD: Restart every checkout task to clear in-memory state
correctAnswerText: Turn the flag off now and keep investigating in parallel
explanation: The flag is the change closest in time to the symptom and switching it off is reversible in seconds, so it goes first; evidence gathering continues meanwhile. Waiting for proof prolongs the outage, and failover or restarts are changes with no evidence behind them.

prompt: Only two engineers are awake when a SEV2 starts at night. How should the incident roles be handled?
optionA: Wait to wake a full team so every role has its own owner
optionB: Both debug together and skip naming roles until it is over
optionC: One says aloud "I am IC and comms"; the other leads operations
optionD: The first to join is the scribe; the other runs comms and ops
correctAnswerText: One says aloud "I am IC and comms"; the other leads operations
explanation: On a small team one person may hold two roles, provided it is said out loud so everyone knows who steers and who talks to stakeholders. Skipping roles leaves nobody steering, waiting for a full team delays mitigation, and a scribe-only role wastes half the team.

prompt: You are writing the runbook for the PaymentsBudgetFastBurn alert. What must it contain?
optionA: A history of every past page and who acknowledged each one
optionB: Only the alert's query expression, with nothing else beside it
optionC: The full source code of payments-api and all its unit tests
optionD: Meaning, how to confirm impact, first safe actions, escalation
correctAnswerText: Meaning, how to confirm impact, first safe actions, escalation
explanation: A runbook answers, for that alert: what it means, how to confirm impact (dashboard and query), the first safe actions (rollback, failover, scale) and when to escalate to whom, written as a checklist. Source code, page history and a bare query do not tell a tired engineer what to do.

prompt: Escalation gives the primary 5 minutes to acknowledge, then the secondary 5 minutes, then pages the team lead. A page fires at 03:10 and nobody acknowledges. When is the lead paged?
explanation: The primary's window ends at 03:15, when the secondary is paged; the secondary's ends at 03:20, when the lead is paged. 03:15 is the secondary's page, and 03:25 adds a window that does not exist.

prompt: Asha wants to declare resolved because the rollback command reported success. What should she check before doing so?
optionA: That the rollback pipeline logged no warnings at all
optionB: That the postmortem document has already been created
optionC: That the SLI is back inside the SLO on the dashboard
optionD: That every engineer has left the incident call by now
correctAnswerText: That the SLI is back inside the SLO on the dashboard
explanation: Resolved means the user-facing measure is back inside the SLO, confirmed and stable, not assumed from a command's exit status. Pipeline warnings, the postmortem draft and who is still on the call say nothing about whether users are served.

prompt: Which rewrite turns the postmortem action "improve monitoring" into one that will get done?
optionA: Everyone should watch the dashboards more closely from now
optionB: Alert on orders-db connections at 80% — Kiran, P2, 1 week
optionC: Monitoring should be reviewed by someone when time allows
optionD: Improve monitoring across all of the orders services soon
correctAnswerText: Alert on orders-db connections at 80% — Kiran, P2, 1 week
explanation: A good action is specific and testable, with an owner, a priority and a date. The others are vague, unowned or rely on people trying harder, which is why such actions are never closed.

prompt: A rotation averages eight pages a shift, most acknowledged and closed with no action, and response to real outages is getting slower. What is the diagnosis?
optionA: The rotation has too few people, so every shift runs too long
optionB: The paging tool is delaying delivery during the busiest shifts
optionC: Non-actionable pages are training people to ignore all pages
optionD: The escalation window is too short for pages sent at night
correctAnswerText: Non-actionable pages are training people to ignore all pages
explanation: Pages that need no action dull the response to the ones that do, and burn people out. The fix is to make each page actionable or turn it into a ticket, reviewed weekly. Rotation size, tool delays and escalation windows would not produce mostly no-action pages.

prompt: A SEV1-sized outage ran for 40 minutes before anyone declared it, while the on-call engineer worked alone hoping to fix it quietly. What failed?
optionA: No declaration, so no roles, help or communication arrived
optionB: The status page was updated far too often during the outage
optionC: The alert threshold was so sensitive that it fired too early
optionD: The runbook listed too many first actions for that alert
correctAnswerText: No declaration, so no roles, help or communication arrived
explanation: Declaring is what brings in an IC, an operations lead and a communications lead; working alone leaves stakeholders blind and the fix to one tired person. An early alert, a full runbook or frequent updates would all have helped rather than hurt.

prompt: Two SEV1s each took 45 minutes to restore. In the first, detection took 35 minutes; in the second, the rollback itself took 35. What does comparing the timelines show?
optionA: They are equivalent, because both restore times came out the same
optionB: They need different fixes: alerting for one, deploy speed for the other
optionC: Both show that each IC was too slow to declare their incident
optionD: Both need a faster paging tool to cut the time to acknowledgement
correctAnswerText: They need different fixes: alerting for one, deploy speed for the other
explanation: Identical MTTR hides opposite problems: a slow alert in one, a slow rollback path in the other. That is why each SEV1's timeline is read for where the minutes went. Neither timeline points at paging or the declaration.

prompt: Five incidents were restored in 10, 12, 15, 18 and 240 minutes. A quarterly report says "MTTR 59 minutes". What is misleading about it?
optionA: Nothing; 59 minutes describes a typical incident well
optionB: The arithmetic is wrong; the correct mean is 15 minutes
optionC: The figure should be 240, since the worst incident counts
optionD: One long outage drags the mean; the median is 15 minutes
correctAnswerText: One long outage drags the mean; the median is 15 minutes
explanation: The mean is right — 295 ÷ 5 = 59 — but it describes no actual incident: four took under 20 minutes and one took four hours. The median (15) plus a look at the outlier's timeline tells the real story. 15 is the median, not the mean.

prompt: Database connections were pinned by client retries, so the team failed RDS over to its standby. Checkout went fully down, then the standby filled up too. What was wrong with the decision?
optionA: Failover moved the same retry load and added an outage of its own
optionB: The standby was lagging behind, so it refused every connection
optionC: The standby sat in another region, so latency rose sharply
optionD: Failover should have been done before the flag was turned off
correctAnswerText: Failover moved the same retry load and added an outage of its own
explanation: The cause was clients retrying, not a broken instance, so a copy of the same database received the same storm, plus a short total outage during failover. Capping retries and shedding load was the mitigation that fitted the evidence. A Multi-AZ standby is in-region and synchronous.

prompt: After a rollback, errors drop from 18% to 4% and the IC declares the incident resolved. An hour later merchants are still reporting failures. What was missed?
optionA: A partial recovery was taken as full; 4% is still real impact
optionB: The status page was updated before the rollback had finished
optionC: The rollback was slow, so it should have been run a second time
optionD: The postmortem should have begun before the incident was closed
correctAnswerText: A partial recovery was taken as full; 4% is still real impact
explanation: Resolution is the SLI back inside the SLO for a stable period. A big drop that leaves 4% failing means a second problem — retries, another component — still needs working. Repeating the rollback, status-page timing and postmortem timing do not explain the remaining errors.

prompt: At a company whose past postmortems named culprits, engineers now give vague accounts in reviews and timelines have gaps. What does this show?
optionA: The engineers involved lack training in writing timelines
optionB: The postmortem template has too few fields to hold detail
optionC: Reviews are being held too long after each incident date
optionD: Fear of blame is hiding the very details the review needs
correctAnswerText: Fear of blame is hiding the very details the review needs
explanation: People who expect blame protect themselves by saying less, and a postmortem without details fixes nothing. Templates, timing and training may matter, but the pattern follows the naming of culprits.

prompt: A team's last four postmortems each listed twelve actions, and the same outage has recurred twice since. What is the likeliest gap?
optionA: Too few people from other teams invited to the reviews
optionB: Postmortems written too soon after each of the outages
optionC: Timelines kept in IST rather than in UTC for every event
optionD: Vague, unowned actions that were never tracked to closure
correctAnswerText: Vague, unowned actions that were never tracked to closure
explanation: Twelve actions per review is the warning sign: long lists of vague items with no owner or tracking are where postmortems fail. Three to five specific, owned actions in the normal backlog, reviewed weekly, get done. Timing, time zones and attendance do not explain recurrence.

prompt: An internal update reads: "Looking at pgbouncer pool on orders-db-2, maybe GC pauses?" What is wrong with it as a stakeholder update?
optionA: It is too short, as an update must run to a full page or more
optionB: It gives no impact, no action taken and no next-update time
optionC: It should only have been sent once the cause was confirmed
optionD: It names a database, which breaks the blameless principle
correctAnswerText: It gives no impact, no action taken and no next-update time
explanation: A useful update states impact, what is being done and when the next one comes; this one offers internal jargon and a guess. Length is not the test, updates go out before the cause is known, and naming a system is not blame.

prompt: At 03:00 the runbook's PSP failover command fails because the switch was renamed months ago. Which practice would have caught this?
optionA: Letting only the team lead ever edit any runbook page
optionB: Testing runbooks in game days and fixing them in postmortems
optionC: Printing every runbook so that it can be read while offline
optionD: Writing the runbooks as prose rather than as checklists
correctAnswerText: Testing runbooks in game days and fixing them in postmortems
explanation: Runbooks rot as systems change; exercising them in game days and updating them whenever a postmortem finds one wrong keeps them true. Printing preserves the stale text, prose is harder to follow under stress, and restricting edits slows corrections.

prompt: At the 11:00 peak, payments start failing for many merchants. The responder thinks it might be only a SEV2 and is unsure. Which call is best?
optionA: Hold off declaring until a second alert confirms the problem
optionB: Declare SEV3 until the cause is understood, then raise it
optionC: Declare SEV2 and wait to see whether more merchants fail
optionD: Declare SEV1 now and downgrade if the impact proves smaller
correctAnswerText: Declare SEV1 now and downgrade if the impact proves smaller
explanation: Payments failing for many merchants matches SEV1, and when in doubt the higher level is declared — it is cheap to downgrade and costly to escalate late. Waiting for cause or a second alert lets the impact grow without roles or communication.

prompt: A VP joins the incident call and orders a database failover that the IC expects will not help. Which IC response is best?
optionA: State the expected outcome, offer a faster option, log any override
optionB: Pause every action until the VP and the IC agree on it in writing
optionC: Comply at once, since the most senior person on the call decides
optionD: Refuse, and remove the VP from the call to protect the team
correctAnswerText: State the expected outcome, offer a faster option, log any override
explanation: The IC engages with the suggestion, tests it against the signals, proposes a quicker reversible step with a time-box, and if overridden records it in the timeline while making sure the needed mitigation still happens. Caving, fighting and freezing all cost the users time.

prompt: A release caused a SEV1. An engineer says a forward fix could be ready in about 20 minutes; a rollback takes 5. Which is better?
optionA: Do both at once, so whichever finishes first restores service
optionB: Ship the fix straight to production, since it targets the cause
optionC: Roll back now, then ship the fix through the normal pipeline
optionD: Wait for a review of the fix while the bad release keeps running
correctAnswerText: Roll back now, then ship the fix through the normal pipeline
explanation: The rollback is known, quick and reversible; an estimated fix written under pressure is none of those and skips the checks that would have caught the bug. Doing both at once collides two changes, and waiting keeps users failing.

prompt: The month's error budget is spent and two P1 postmortem actions are open. A product manager wants this sprint's feature first. Which is right?
optionA: A team vote each sprint decides between the two of them
optionB: The feature comes first; actions wait until time allows
optionC: Both are dropped until the budget resets next month
optionD: The P1 actions come first under the error budget policy
correctAnswerText: The P1 actions come first under the error budget policy
explanation: With the budget exhausted, the agreed policy puts reliability work ahead of features — that is what the budget is for. Deferring actions is how outages recur, dropping both helps nobody, and a vote replaces an agreement made in advance.

prompt: Leadership wants one MTTR target per team, ranked every quarter. Which approach to measuring incident response is best?
optionA: Count the pages per engineer and reward whoever has the fewest
optionB: Set a strict MTTR target for each team and rank the teams on it
optionC: Read each SEV1 timeline for where time went; keep trends secondary
optionD: Drop all measurement, as no two incidents are ever alike
correctAnswerText: Read each SEV1 timeline for where time went; keep trends secondary
explanation: MTTR averages very different incidents and is easy to game (declare late, resolve early), so a ranking target invites gaming. Timelines show whether detection, the decision or the mitigation was slow, with MTTD/MTTA/MTTR kept as trends. Dropping measurement or rewarding fewer pages invites hiding problems.

prompt: A team split between Bengaluru and Toronto pages its Bengaluru engineers at 3am every week. Which change is best?
optionA: Raise the alert thresholds so that fewer pages fire at night
optionB: Send the night pages by email to be read the next morning
optionC: Keep the rotation as it is and add one extra rest day a month
optionD: Follow-the-sun handover, so each site covers its own daytime
correctAnswerText: Follow-the-sun handover, so each site covers its own daytime
explanation: With two time zones, handing over between sites means nobody is routinely woken while real pages are still answered at once. Raising thresholds or emailing pages hides real incidents, and a rest day leaves the sustainability problem in place.

prompt: Once a postmortem is written, which handling of it does most for the wider engineering organisation?
optionA: Read it in a review meeting, then publish it to all engineering
optionB: Keep it within the team so that its mistakes stay private
optionC: Archive it unread once the action items have been created
optionD: Send it to management only, for use in performance reviews
correctAnswerText: Read it in a review meeting, then publish it to all engineering
explanation: Reviewing it together tests the analysis, and publishing it lets other teams find the same weakness before it bites them. Keeping it private wastes the lesson, using it for appraisal destroys blamelessness, and an unread document changes nothing.

prompt: A clean-up job almost deleted a production table; it was caught by chance and no user noticed. It was logged as a SEV3. Should there be a postmortem?
optionA: Yes, but only to record which engineer ran the job
optionB: No; nothing failed, so there is nothing at all to learn
optionC: No; postmortems are only mandatory for SEV1 and SEV2
optionD: Yes; a near miss with severe potential impact earns one
correctAnswerText: Yes; a near miss with severe potential impact earns one
explanation: The mandatory rule sets a floor, not a ceiling: a lucky escape from serious harm is a cheap chance to fix the gap before it costs anything. "Nothing failed" ignores that luck was the only control, and a postmortem that records a culprit is not blameless.

prompt: Of these on-call handover checks, which most reduces the risk of a slow first response at 3am?
optionA: Check that the pager app's notification sound is loud enough
optionB: Read the previous week's postmortems in full before starting
optionC: Confirm break-glass access, runbook links and rollback rights
optionD: Share each engineer's personal phone number with the team
correctAnswerText: Confirm break-glass access, runbook links and rollback rights
explanation: Discovering at 3am that you cannot assume the break-glass role, reach the runbooks or roll back is what turns minutes into an hour, so access is checked at handover. The other checks help a little or not at all with acting quickly.

prompt: A release changed the PSP client's TLS settings and one PSP rejected the handshake; staging used a sandbox with different TLS. Which action set is best?
optionA: Canary with alarm rollback; per-PSP TLS check; deploy markers
optionB: Improve testing; improve monitoring; be more careful in future
optionC: Freeze all deploys for a month while all the code is reviewed
optionD: Retrain the engineer; require two senior sign-offs per deploy
correctAnswerText: Canary with alarm rollback; per-PSP TLS check; deploy markers
explanation: The chosen set changes the system across prevent (a TLS check against each production PSP), mitigate (a canary that rolls back on alarm) and detect (deploy markers on the dashboard). Retraining blames a person, a freeze stops all delivery without fixing the gap, and the last set is vague and unowned.

prompt: In an ELT pipeline, where and when does the transformation of the data happen?
optionA: In the dashboard tool, at the moment an analyst opens a report
optionB: On a separate ETL server, before anything reaches the warehouse
optionC: Inside the warehouse, with SQL, after the raw data is loaded
optionD: In the source database, through triggers, before it is extracted
correctAnswerText: Inside the warehouse, with SQL, after the raw data is loaded
explanation: ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse, so raw stays available for replay and one engine does the work. Transforming on a separate server before the load is the older ETL order; triggers and dashboards are not where a pipeline transforms.

prompt: In an incremental database extract, what is the watermark?
optionA: The highest change marker, such as updated_at, already loaded
optionB: A hash of the whole table used to decide whether it has changed
optionC: The time of day at which the scheduler is allowed to run the job
optionD: The total number of rows the source table held at the last run
correctAnswerText: The highest change marker, such as updated_at, already loaded
explanation: A watermark records how far you have read: the largest updated_at (or append-only id) already loaded. The next run reads rows beyond it. A row count or table hash cannot say which rows changed, and the schedule time is not a position in the data.

prompt: What does change data capture (for example Debezium on PostgreSQL) read to find changes?
optionA: The application's HTTP access logs for insert and update calls
optionB: Nightly full dumps of each table, compared with the previous one
optionC: The database's own change log, such as the WAL or the binlog
optionD: An updated_at column, queried on every table every few minutes
correctAnswerText: The database's own change log, such as the WAL or the binlog
explanation: CDC reads the change log the database already writes (PostgreSQL WAL via logical replication, the MySQL binlog), so it sees every insert, update and delete in commit order with little load on the tables. Querying updated_at is the watermark approach; dumps and access logs are not CDC.

prompt: Which file format stores data by column in row groups, with the schema and min/max statistics in its footer?
optionA: Parquet
optionB: Avro
optionC: JSON lines
optionD: Gzipped CSV
correctAnswerText: Parquet
explanation: Parquet is columnar: each row group stores every column as an encoded, compressed chunk, and the footer carries the schema plus per-chunk statistics. Avro also carries a schema but stores rows; JSON lines and CSV have no stored schema at all.

prompt: Which dbt materialisation creates no object in the warehouse and is inlined as a CTE into the models that ref it?
optionA: snapshot
optionB: incremental
optionC: ephemeral
optionD: view
correctAnswerText: ephemeral
explanation: An ephemeral model is compiled into a CTE (with __dbt__cte__name as ...) inside each model that refs it, so nothing is created and it cannot be queried or tested on its own. A view and an incremental model both create objects, and a snapshot is a separate resource that builds a history table.

prompt: In dbt, which function should a model use to read another model, so that dbt records the dependency?
optionA: ref(), for example ref('stg_orders')
optionB: var(), for example var('stg_orders')
optionC: this, for example select * from this
optionD: source(), for example source('raw', 'orders')
correctAnswerText: ref(), for example ref('stg_orders')
explanation: ref() compiles to the right schema for whoever runs it and adds an edge to dbt's DAG, so models build in order. source() is for raw tables declared in YAML, {{ this }} is the model's own existing table, and var() reads a project variable.

prompt: When does is_incremental() evaluate to true inside a dbt incremental model?
optionA: On every run after the project's first successful dbt run at all
optionB: When the target table exists and --full-refresh was not passed
optionC: Only when the model is run with the --incremental command flag
optionD: Whenever the model's source has new rows since the last build
correctAnswerText: When the target table exists and --full-refresh was not passed
explanation: is_incremental() is true when the model's table already exists, it is materialised incrementally, and --full-refresh is not set. dbt does not look at the source for new rows, and there is no --incremental flag; the first build and full refreshes skip the filter.

prompt: Which pair of columns does a dbt snapshot add to show when each version of a row was in force?
optionA: dbt_loaded_at and dbt_deleted_at
optionB: dbt_first_seen and dbt_last_seen
optionC: dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to
optionD: dbt_created_on and dbt_expired_on
correctAnswerText: dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to
explanation: A snapshot adds dbt_scd_id, dbt_updated_at, dbt_valid_from and dbt_valid_to; the current version has a null dbt_valid_to. That is Type 2 history: a closed row and a new open row for each change. The other names are not columns dbt generates.

prompt: What does a full extract of a source table capture that an updated_at watermark extract cannot?
optionA: Rows that were hard-deleted from the source since the last run
optionB: Rows whose amount column changed and whose updated_at moved on
optionC: Rows that were updated twice in quick succession since the run
optionD: Rows inserted since the last run that have a fresh updated_at
correctAnswerText: Rows that were hard-deleted from the source since the last run
explanation: A hard-deleted row has no updated_at left to find, so a watermark extract never sees it; a full extract simply no longer contains it. Inserts and updates that move updated_at are exactly what a watermark does capture, including a row changed twice (you get its latest state).

prompt: An API returns a next_cursor value with each page of results. How should an extract page through it?
optionA: Send the cursor from each response to fetch the next page
optionB: Add the page size to an offset it keeps on its own each time
optionC: Request pages 1, 2, 3 in parallel until one comes back empty
optionD: Sort by id and ask for ids above the largest one it has seen
correctAnswerText: Send the cursor from each response to fetch the next page
explanation: With cursor pagination the server tells you where the next page starts; following it is stable even while rows are being added. An offset you compute yourself, guessed page numbers or your own id ranges can skip or repeat rows when the data shifts under you.

prompt: Why did columnar cloud warehouses move most teams from ETL to ELT?
optionA: Warehouses refuse raw data, so it must be cleaned before it can be loaded
optionB: Storage is cheap and SQL scales there, so raw can land first and be replayed
optionC: ETL tools cannot read from APIs, so loading raw was the only option left
optionD: ELT needs no tests or code review, so it is faster for a team to deliver
correctAnswerText: Storage is cheap and SQL scales there, so raw can land first and be replayed
explanation: Cheap storage and on-demand compute made it sensible to load raw data as it is and transform it in the warehouse with SQL: raw stays available for replay and the logic is readable. Warehouses accept raw data, ETL tools do read APIs, and ELT needs more discipline (tests, review), which is what dbt adds.

prompt: Why does a watermark extract on updated_at need a lookback window to avoid missing rows?
optionA: Rows inserted in bulk are given an updated_at of the previous midnight
optionB: The database reuses old updated_at values once a row has been deleted
optionC: Clocks on the database server drift backwards by a few minutes daily
optionD: A slow transaction can commit a row stamped before the last watermark
correctAnswerText: A slow transaction can commit a row stamped before the last watermark
explanation: updated_at is set when the statement runs but the row becomes visible at commit. A transaction that stamped 08:59 and committed at 09:01 sits below a 09:00 watermark taken in between, so the next run skips it. Reading from watermark minus a safety window and deduplicating catches it.

prompt: Why does an outlet code like "004512" come back as 4512 after a round trip through CSV and pandas?
optionA: pandas always strips leading zeros from text to save memory on reading
optionB: CSV files are compressed on write and leading zeros compress to nothing
optionC: CSV stores no schema, so the reader guesses a number and drops the zeros
optionD: The writer converted the column to integers before writing the file out
correctAnswerText: CSV stores no schema, so the reader guesses a number and drops the zeros
explanation: A CSV carries no types, so every reader re-guesses them; digits look like an integer, and the zeros vanish. Passing dtype={"outlet_code": "string"} fixes it, and Parquet avoids it because the schema travels in the file. CSV is not compressed by default and pandas does not strip text.

prompt: Why should a dbt incremental model select new rows by a load timestamp rather than by event time?
optionA: Event timestamps are stored as text in most sources and cannot compare
optionB: Load timestamps are indexed by every warehouse, while event times are not
optionC: dbt can only compare columns that it added itself during an earlier run
optionD: A late event can be older than the newest event already in the table
correctAnswerText: A late event can be older than the newest event already in the table
explanation: Events buffered on an offline phone arrive after newer ones; an event_ts > max(event_ts) filter skips them for ever. A load timestamp (or sequence) says when the row arrived, which is what "new" means for a run. The other reasons are not true in general.

prompt: Why is writing analytics.stg_orders directly in a dbt model, instead of ref(), a mistake?
optionA: dbt refuses to compile any model that contains a schema-qualified name
optionB: A hard-coded name makes the model a view even if configured as a table
optionC: dbt cannot see the dependency, so it may build the two in the wrong order
optionD: The warehouse rejects queries that read across two different schemas
correctAnswerText: dbt cannot see the dependency, so it may build the two in the wrong order
explanation: ref() is how dbt learns the DAG and resolves the right schema for dev, CI or production. A literal name compiles fine but hides the edge, so the model can run before its input is rebuilt, and in dev it reads production. dbt does not refuse it, and materialisation is unaffected.

prompt: Why should the delete and the insert of a partition-replace load run in one transaction?
optionA: Two statements in one transaction run in parallel and finish sooner
optionB: A crash between them rolls back, so the old day stays instead of a gap
optionC: Without a transaction the insert would be blocked by the delete's lock
optionD: A transaction removes duplicate rows from the batch before inserting
correctAnswerText: A crash between them rolls back, so the old day stays instead of a gap
explanation: If the worker dies after DELETE and before INSERT, a transaction rolls back and the dashboard still shows the old day; without it, the day is empty. A transaction does not parallelise, the delete does not block its own transaction, and it does not deduplicate anything.

prompt: Why deduplicate a change batch to the latest version per key before upserting it into a table?
optionA: An upsert of a duplicated key always inserts both rows into the table
optionB: With two versions of a key, which one wins depends on engine and row order
optionC: Unique constraints are dropped for the duration of every upsert run
optionD: Deduplicating first is only needed to make the upsert statement faster
correctAnswerText: With two versions of a key, which one wins depends on engine and row order
explanation: If order 5 appears as OUT_FOR_DELIVERY and REFUNDED in one batch, one engine silently keeps whichever row it met first and PostgreSQL refuses ("cannot affect row a second time"). Keeping row_number() = 1 by updated_at desc makes the result defined. It is about correctness, not speed.

prompt: An extract filters WHERE date(updated_at) > ? instead of WHERE updated_at > ?. Why does that matter on a large orders table?
optionA: Wrapping the column in a function stops the index being used, so it scans
optionB: The index on updated_at is dropped whenever a query uses date() on it
optionC: Functions in WHERE are evaluated once, so only one row is ever returned
optionD: date() rounds every timestamp to UTC, so the rows it returns are wrong
correctAnswerText: Wrapping the column in a function stops the index being used, so it scans
explanation: An index on updated_at can serve a range on the bare column; once the column is wrapped in date(), the plan becomes a scan of every row. On tens of millions of rows that is the difference between milliseconds and slowing the production database. The other claims are false.

prompt: Why should an API extract retry a 503 or 429 response but not a 401 or 400 response?
optionA: The first pair are client errors that a new request always corrects
optionB: The second pair are cached by the server, so a retry returns nothing
optionC: Retrying a 401 or 400 is blocked by the HTTP library by default anyway
optionD: The first pair are temporary conditions; the second will fail again
correctAnswerText: The first pair are temporary conditions; the second will fail again
explanation: 503 (unavailable) and 429 (rate limited) describe a passing state, so a retry with backoff usually succeeds. A 401 (bad credentials) or 400 (bad request) will fail the same way every time; retrying only delays the alert. 503 is a server error, not a client one, and libraries do not block retries.

prompt: Why are dbt snapshots taken on raw or staging data rather than on a finished mart?
optionA: Marts change too rarely for a snapshot to detect any difference at all
optionB: dbt deletes a mart's history whenever its downstream models are rebuilt
optionC: Snapshots only work on views, and marts are always built as tables
optionD: History not captured cannot be rebuilt, so capture it before any logic
correctAnswerText: History not captured cannot be rebuilt, so capture it before any logic
explanation: A snapshot is the only record of past values once the source overwrites them. Taking it before transformation keeps the facts themselves, so a bug in mart logic can be fixed and replayed; history of a buggy mart cannot be corrected. Snapshots work on tables too, and dbt does not delete history.

prompt: DabbaDrop extracts orders hourly by updated_at. Which read window follows the course's advice for both late commits and rows still being written?
optionA: From the watermark plus one second, up to now plus a few minutes
optionB: From the watermark minus ten minutes, up to now minus a few minutes
optionC: From midnight today, up to now, so every run re-reads the whole day
optionD: From the watermark exactly, up to now, ordered by the order id only
correctAnswerText: From the watermark minus ten minutes, up to now minus a few minutes
explanation: A lookback below the watermark catches rows committed late with an older stamp (deduplicated downstream), and an upper bound a little before now leaves rows still being written for the next run. Starting exactly at or after the watermark misses late commits; re-reading the whole day wastes load on the source.

prompt: A payments partner drops one settlements CSV per day into a folder, and the loader scans the whole folder each run. Which load design stops a file being loaded twice?
optionA: Append every file found in the folder, then run a weekly job to remove duplicates
optionB: Delete the folder after each run so that any file seen there must be a new one
optionC: Load only files whose modified time is later than the time the loader last ran
optionD: Record each file in a processed-files table, in the same transaction as its rows
correctAnswerText: Record each file in a processed-files table, in the same transaction as its rows
explanation: A processed-files table lets the loader skip what it has done, and writing the file's row with its data in one transaction means "loaded" and "recorded as loaded" cannot disagree. Appending then cleaning lets duplicates reach users, deleting the folder loses the replay source, and modified times change when files are re-sent or copied.

prompt: A dbt project has light staging models that rename and cast columns, and marts that dashboards read heavily. Which materialisations fit?
optionA: Both as snapshots, to keep history
optionB: Both as ephemeral, to save storage
optionC: Staging as tables, marts as views
optionD: Staging as views, marts as tables
correctAnswerText: Staging as views, marts as tables
explanation: Staging that only renames and casts is cheap to recompute, so a view stays current at no storage cost; a heavily read mart is built once per run as a table so dashboards read it fast. Ephemeral models cannot be queried by a dashboard, and snapshots record history rather than serve marts.

prompt: A partner sends menus as CSV with outlet_code like "004512", a tip column that is often empty and a placed_at timestamp. How should the pandas read be written?
optionA: dtype outlet_code "float64" and tip "int64", with placed_at as category
optionB: dtype outlet_code "string" and tip "Int64", and parse_dates for placed_at
optionC: No dtypes at all, then cast every column to str once the file is read
optionD: dtype outlet_code "int64" and tip "float64", leaving placed_at as text
correctAnswerText: dtype outlet_code "string" and tip "Int64", and parse_dates for placed_at
explanation: A code is text, so reading it as a string keeps its zeros; the nullable Int64 keeps a mostly-empty integer from becoming float; parse_dates makes placed_at a timestamp. Reading the code as a number loses the zeros before any later cast can help, and int64 cannot hold missing tips.

prompt: An API client retries up to 4 times with exponential backoff starting at 2 seconds and doubling, with no jitter. If every attempt fails, how long does it spend waiting in total?
optionA: 8 seconds
optionB: 30 seconds
optionC: 62 seconds
optionD: 16 seconds
correctAnswerText: 30 seconds
explanation: The four waits are 2, 4, 8 and 16 seconds, which sum to 30. 16 is only the last wait, 8 counts three waits' worth wrongly, and 62 adds a fifth wait of 32 that a client limited to four retries never makes. In practice jitter is added so many clients do not retry in step.

prompt: A restaurants table has no reliable updated_at, but finance needs history of city and commission_pct. How should the dbt snapshot be configured?
optionA: An incremental model with unique_key restaurant_id and append
optionB: A table model rebuilt nightly, with a dbt_valid_to column added
optionC: strategy timestamp, with updated_at set to the current run time
optionD: strategy check, with check_cols listing city and commission_pct
correctAnswerText: strategy check, with check_cols listing city and commission_pct
explanation: The check strategy compares the listed columns with the current snapshot row and opens a new version when any differ, which is what you need without a trustworthy change timestamp. A timestamp strategy on run time is meaningless, an append model is not Type 2, and a nightly table keeps no history.

prompt: stg_orders was fixed and everything that reads it must be rebuilt, nothing else. Which dbt command does that?
optionA: dbt run --select stg_orders+
optionB: dbt run --exclude stg_orders
optionC: dbt run --select +stg_orders
optionD: dbt run --select stg_orders
correctAnswerText: dbt run --select stg_orders+
explanation: A trailing + selects the model and all its descendants, which ref() recorded in the DAG. A leading + selects its ancestors, --exclude builds everything but it, and the bare name rebuilds only stg_orders while its marts keep stale data.

prompt: An incremental model with the append strategy has no is_incremental() block. Its source holds 9 events and nothing new arrives. How many rows does the table hold after the third dbt run?
explanation: The first run builds the table with 9 rows; each later run appends the whole unfiltered source again, so 9, 18, 27. Nothing errors, which is why a unique test on event_id is the guard. 9 would need a filter, and 81 would mean each run multiplied rather than added.

prompt: A cities reference table has about 400 rows, rows are sometimes hard-deleted, and it has no updated_at. How should it be extracted and loaded?
optionA: A full extract each run that replaces the whole target table
optionB: A watermark extract on the primary key, appending new ids only
optionC: A one-off extract, since a table that small rarely changes
optionD: Change data capture with a dedicated replication slot for it
correctAnswerText: A full extract each run that replaces the whole target table
explanation: For a small table a full extract is cheap, always correct and reflects deletes; replacing the target keeps it identical to the source. An id watermark misses updates and deletes, CDC is heavy machinery for 400 rows, and a one-off copy goes stale silently.

prompt: A staging model for orders must keep amounts exact and make times comparable across sources. Which pair of transformations fits?
optionA: Cast amounts to integer paise, and timestamps to timezone-aware UTC
optionB: Round amounts to whole rupees, and drop the time part of timestamps
optionC: Cast amounts to float rupees, and timestamps to local text strings
optionD: Keep amounts as text, and convert timestamps to the server's zone
correctAnswerText: Cast amounts to integer paise, and timestamps to timezone-aware UTC
explanation: Integer minor units add up exactly where floats accumulate rounding error, and timezone-aware timestamps in one zone compare correctly whatever zone each source used. Text strings, rounding and server-local times each lose information or comparability.

prompt: An hourly extract with WHERE updated_at > :watermark misses about one refund a week. Each missed row has updated_at a minute or two before the watermark recorded by the run that should have read it. What explains it?
optionA: Those rows committed after the extract ran, with stamps from before it
optionB: The index on updated_at is corrupt and skips some rows in each range
optionC: The extract sorted by updated_at, which reorders rows with equal stamps
optionD: The refunds were hard-deleted and then reinserted with their old stamp
correctAnswerText: Those rows committed after the extract ran, with stamps from before it
explanation: A long transaction stamped the refund at 08:59 but committed at 09:01, after a run that read up to 09:00 and set the watermark there. The next run asks for > 09:00 and never sees it. A lookback window plus downstream dedup fixes it; the index, deletes and sort order do not explain stamps just below the watermark.

prompt: After adding a lookback to an extract, some orders in the target flip from DELIVERED back to OUT_FOR_DELIVERY. The upsert updates on key match. What is missing?
optionA: An is-newer guard so an older version never overwrites a newer one
optionB: A full refresh after every run so the table matches the source again
optionC: A larger lookback window so that the newer versions are re-read too
optionD: A unique index on order_id in the target to stop duplicate inserts
correctAnswerText: An is-newer guard so an older version never overwrites a newer one
explanation: The lookback re-reads older versions, and an unconditional update applies them over newer state. WHERE excluded.updated_at >= target.updated_at keeps state from going backwards. The table has no duplicates to block, a wider lookback re-reads more stale rows, and full refreshes defeat incremental loading.

prompt: A source stores updated_at as naive IST times, and the pipeline saves its watermark as a naive UTC time. Which symptom follows on each run?
optionA: The run reads only rows from the future and always returns zero rows
optionB: The run fails with a type error as soon as the two values are compared
optionC: The run re-reads about five and a half hours of rows it already loaded
optionD: The run reads the right rows but stores them with the wrong time zone
correctAnswerText: The run re-reads about five and a half hours of rows it already loaded
explanation: A naive UTC watermark is 5:30 hours behind the same instant written in IST, so "updated_at > watermark" reaches back that far each run (and the reverse mistake would skip rows instead). Naive values compare without error, which is why the bug is silent. Keep both sides timezone-aware.

prompt: A day's Parquet files will not read together as one dataset: the error says a column is int64 in some files and string in others. What most likely caused it?
optionA: Parquet files written on different days cannot share one folder
optionB: Each writer let pandas infer types from its own chunk of the input
optionC: Parquet cannot store more than one row group for a single column
optionD: The files were compressed with different codecs, snappy and zstd
correctAnswerText: Each writer let pandas infer types from its own chunk of the input
explanation: When types are inferred per chunk, a chunk where every code happens to be numeric writes int64 and another writes string, and a dataset needs one schema. Declare the schema explicitly on write. Mixed codecs and many row groups read fine, and folders can hold any number of days.

prompt: A load deletes order_date = 25 Oct and inserts the batch, in one transaction. The batch for the 25th also held three late orders dated the 24th. What is the effect after a rerun of the 25th?
optionA: The 25th is left empty because the delete removed rows from both days
optionB: The 24th gains the three late orders again on every rerun of the 25th
optionC: The transaction fails because the batch spans two partition values
optionD: Nothing changes, because rows are always filed by the batch's date
correctAnswerText: The 24th gains the three late orders again on every rerun of the 25th
explanation: The delete only clears the 25th, but the insert writes rows into both days; each rerun adds the late 24th rows again, so that day is overcounted. The partition key of the delete must match the batch exactly. Nothing fails or empties the 25th; rows land by their own order_date.

prompt: A status_code column was added to an incremental dbt model's SELECT. dbt run says OK, yet the column is not in the table. What explains it?
optionA: dbt only adds columns to incremental models on the first of a month
optionB: on_schema_change defaults to ignore, so new columns are not added
optionC: The column was added to the model but the source has no such field
optionD: Incremental models can never gain columns, even with --full-refresh
correctAnswerText: on_schema_change defaults to ignore, so new columns are not added
explanation: By default dbt ignores schema changes on an existing incremental table. append_new_columns adds it (NULL on old rows), fail stops the run, and --full-refresh rebuilds with history filled. A missing source field would fail compilation, not run OK.

prompt: A restaurant left the platform and vanished from the source extract weeks ago, but the dbt snapshot still shows it as current with a null dbt_valid_to. Why?
optionA: The unique_key changed when the restaurant left, so a new row was opened
optionB: hard_deletes was left at its default, which ignores rows that disappear
optionC: Snapshots record deletes only after the snapshot is run with --full-refresh
optionD: The snapshot's timestamp strategy only closes rows when updated_at falls
correctAnswerText: hard_deletes was left at its default, which ignores rows that disappear
explanation: With the default the snapshot never closes a row whose key stops appearing; hard_deletes: invalidate sets its dbt_valid_to at snapshot time. The timestamp strategy reacts to updated_at moving forward, snapshots are not full-refreshed, and a vanished row has no new key.

prompt: The lake has 412 more customers than the source app database, and the gap grows each week. The extract is a watermark on updated_at. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The upsert in the lake inserts a new row for every customer update
optionB: The watermark is read in UTC, so new customers are loaded twice a day
optionC: Customers deleted in the app leave no row for the watermark to find
optionD: The extract reads from a replica, which keeps deleted rows for a week
correctAnswerText: Customers deleted in the app leave no row for the watermark to find
explanation: A hard delete removes the row and its updated_at, so the lake keeps it for ever and the surplus grows. Soft deletes, a periodic key comparison or CDC fix it. A replica mirrors deletes, and duplicate inserts from an upsert would contradict its unique key.

prompt: An incremental order_status model takes new events by _loaded_at and keeps the latest event per order within that batch. A resent old "picked_up" event moved a delivered order backwards. What fix does the course give?
optionA: Filter the batch on event_ts greater than the table's newest event
optionB: Change the strategy to append so that each event keeps its own row
optionC: Drop the unique_key so that dbt stops replacing rows that already exist
optionD: Find touched orders by load time, then rank each over all its events
correctAnswerText: Find touched orders by load time, then rank each over all its events
explanation: Ranking only the batch lets a stale resend win. Selecting the orders touched since the last load and recomputing their latest state from their full history keeps state from going backwards. An event_ts filter misses late events, and append or no unique_key duplicates orders.

prompt: A backfill pages through a busy orders table with LIMIT 40000 OFFSET n. Some orders are missing and others appear twice. What explains it?
optionA: Rows changing during the paging shift which rows each offset points to
optionB: The LIMIT is too large, so the database truncates the last page silently
optionC: OFFSET is not supported on indexed columns, so it returns random rows
optionD: Pages read in order always overlap by one row at their boundary in SQL
correctAnswerText: Rows changing during the paging shift which rows each offset points to
explanation: An offset counts positions, so inserts, updates and deletes between pages slide rows across page boundaries: some are skipped, some read twice. It is also slower as n grows. Keyset pagination, WHERE (updated_at, order_id) > (last values), is stable and uses the index.

prompt: A lender's data team runs ELT, but a new feed carries full card numbers that policy says must never be stored in the warehouse. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Mask or tokenise that field in flight, before the load; ELT for the rest
optionB: Move the whole platform back to ETL so every feed is cleaned first
optionC: Load it raw but restrict the raw schema so only engineers can read it
optionD: Load it raw as usual, then mask it in a staging model on the first run
correctAnswerText: Mask or tokenise that field in flight, before the load; ELT for the rest
explanation: ELT's "land raw first" stops being acceptable when raw itself breaks policy, so that one field is transformed before the load while everything else keeps the benefits of ELT. Masking in staging still stores the numbers raw, access controls do not satisfy "never stored", and moving every feed to ETL is out of proportion.

prompt: A team with hourly watermark extracts proposes moving every table to CDC with Debezium. Which judgement fits the course's advice?
optionA: Use CDC only where deletes, sub-minute latency or table size demand it
optionB: Avoid CDC entirely, since it adds load to every table it reads from
optionC: Use CDC for small reference tables only and keep watermarks for the rest
optionD: Move all tables now, since CDC has no operational cost over watermarks
correctAnswerText: Use CDC only where deletes, sub-minute latency or table size demand it
explanation: CDC captures deletes and ordered changes with little table load, but adds a system to run: replication slots to monitor (an abandoned one keeps WAL until the disk fills) and schema changes to handle. Watermarks first, CDC where the need is real. It does not load tables heavily, and small tables are the ones that need it least.

prompt: A payments partner streams settlement records one at a time with a schema, and analysts later scan a few columns over months of them. Which format plan is best?
optionA: Avro for the record stream, then Parquet in the lake for analysis
optionB: Gzipped CSV throughout, since it is about as small as Parquet files
optionC: Parquet for each record as it arrives, and keep it as the lake copy
optionD: JSON lines throughout, since it is readable and keeps the timezone
correctAnswerText: Avro for the record stream, then Parquet in the lake for analysis
explanation: Avro is row-oriented with an embedded schema, suited to writing one record at a time; Parquet is columnar with statistics, suited to scanning a few columns over many rows. One Parquet file per record defeats its design, JSON lines is large and moves offsets to UTC, and a .csv.gz cannot be split or read by column.

prompt: A dbt model holds one row per payment whose status changes over days, and the filter uses a three-day lookback. Which incremental set-up is soundest?
optionA: microbatch with no lookback, since each day's slice is computed once
optionB: append with no unique_key, since the lookback already limits the rows
optionC: merge or delete+insert on payment_id, with the strategy set explicitly
optionD: table materialisation instead, rebuilt fully every run for correctness
correctAnswerText: merge or delete+insert on payment_id, with the strategy set explicitly
explanation: Overlapping lookback reads are harmless only when a unique_key replaces matching rows, and setting the strategy explicitly avoids adapter defaults. Append duplicates every re-read payment, a full rebuild throws away the reason for incremental, and microbatch without lookback misses status changes on earlier days.

prompt: One engineer wants a two-minute lookback to keep extracts light; another wants two hours to be safe. The longest transactions on the source run about five minutes. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Two minutes, since a lookback only ever adds cost and dedup is optional
optionB: No lookback, but run the extract twice an hour to make up the difference
optionC: A window above the longest commit delay, such as ten minutes, with dedup
optionD: Two hours, since extra re-reads are free whenever the target dedups
correctAnswerText: A window above the longest commit delay, such as ten minutes, with dedup
explanation: The window must exceed how late a commit can be relative to its stamp, so two minutes still misses rows; two hours re-reads far more than needed from a production database. A margin over the observed delay plus downstream dedup is the balance. Running more often does not catch a row below the watermark.

prompt: A source has an application-maintained updated_at that is reliable. Should its dbt snapshot use the timestamp or the check strategy?
optionA: Timestamp: check snapshots need a full refresh on each run to work
optionB: Check: timestamp snapshots cannot close rows when a source changes
optionC: Timestamp: valid_from records when the change happened at the source
optionD: Check: it compares every column, so no change can ever be missed
correctAnswerText: Timestamp: valid_from records when the change happened at the source
explanation: With a trustworthy updated_at, the timestamp strategy dates each version by when the source changed, not when the snapshot happened to run, and needs no column list. Check is the fallback without one; it dates changes at snapshot time and only watches listed columns. Both strategies close rows, and neither needs a full refresh.

prompt: An extract returns orders changed in the last hour, across many order dates. A colleague proposes loading it by deleting and reinserting "today's partition". Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Accept it, because partition replacement is always idempotent anyway
optionB: Use a bare INSERT, then remove duplicates in the reporting views
optionC: Accept it, but widen the partition to the whole month to be safe
optionD: Use a deduplicated upsert on order_id with an is-newer guard instead
correctAnswerText: Use a deduplicated upsert on order_id with an is-newer guard instead
explanation: Partition replace fits a batch that is exactly one partition; a change batch spans many dates, so replacing one day both loses and duplicates rows. Changed rows with a key call for dedup then MERGE/ON CONFLICT with a newer-wins guard. A month-wide replace still mismatches the batch, and a bare INSERT is never acceptable for a production table.

prompt: An hourly API ingest parses each JSON page straight into typed warehouse columns and discards the response. A reviewer suggests landing raw responses first. Is that worth it?
optionA: Yes: raw landing makes the API calls faster and avoids rate limits
optionB: No: once typed, data can always be converted back to the raw JSON
optionC: No: raw responses double storage and add nothing a retry cannot redo
optionD: Yes: a parsing bug can be fixed and replayed without calling the API
correctAnswerText: Yes: a parsing bug can be fixed and replayed without calling the API
explanation: Raw responses are the replay source: when parsing drops or mistypes a field, you reparse what you already have, which matters when the API only serves recent data or rate-limits a backfill. Re-calling may not return the same data, landing does not speed the API, and typed columns cannot recreate fields that were dropped.

prompt: A team full-extracts a 40-million-row orders table from the primary database every hour "because it is always correct". Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Keep it, because correctness outweighs any load on the source database
optionB: Keep it, but run it on the primary with more parallel reader threads
optionC: Switch to a daily full extract, accepting a day of staleness for safety
optionD: Switch to an incremental extract from a replica, and handle deletes apart
correctAnswerText: Switch to an incremental extract from a replica, and handle deletes apart
explanation: A full scan every hour on the primary competes with customers; the production database belongs to them. A watermark extract with a lookback, from a read replica, with soft deletes, a key comparison or CDC for deletes, stays correct at a fraction of the load. More threads add load, and a daily extract trades away freshness the team needed.

prompt: An expensive intermediate dbt model joins orders to payments and is ref'd by six marts. A colleague wants it ephemeral to avoid clutter. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Make it a view, since a view stores the join result for all six readers
optionB: Build it as a table, since ephemeral recomputes it inside all six marts
optionC: Make it ephemeral, since it can still be tested and queried on its own
optionD: Make it ephemeral, since CTEs are computed once and shared by all marts
correctAnswerText: Build it as a table, since ephemeral recomputes it inside all six marts
explanation: An ephemeral model is inlined into each model that refs it, so an expensive join runs six times and cannot be tested or queried directly. Built once as a table, the marts read the result. A view stores no result and is recomputed on every read; ephemeral suits small helper steps.

prompt: Which of these does an orchestrator such as Airflow provide that a crontab of scripts does not?
optionA: Writing a script's printed output to a file on the local disk
optionB: Starting a command at a fixed time of day on one single machine
optionC: Starting a task only after the tasks it depends on have succeeded
optionD: Running a Python script with the interpreter of a virtual env
correctAnswerText: Starting a task only after the tasks it depends on have succeeded
explanation: Cron only knows "start this command at this time", so dependencies become timing guesses. An orchestrator runs a task when its upstream tasks succeed, along with retries, per-interval runs, history and backfills. The other three are things cron already does.

prompt: With an Airflow 2 interval schedule, when is a daily run created and what is its logical date?
optionA: At the moment of deploy; the logical date is the deployment time
optionB: After its interval ends; the logical date is the interval's start
optionC: At its interval's start; the logical date is then the interval's end
optionD: After its interval ends; the logical date is the time it started
correctAnswerText: After its interval ends; the logical date is the interval's start
explanation: Interval semantics run a period once it is complete, and label the run with the start of that period. That is why the run that fires on 27 October processes 26 October. The logical date is neither the deploy time nor the wall-clock start.

prompt: Which Airflow sensor mode releases the worker slot between checks rather than holding it for the whole wait?
optionA: mode="block"
optionB: mode="reschedule"
optionC: mode="wait"
optionD: mode="poke"
correctAnswerText: mode="reschedule"
explanation: Poke mode keeps the worker slot for the whole wait; reschedule frees it between checks. Deferrable sensors go further and hand the wait to the triggerer process. "wait" and "block" are not sensor modes.

prompt: Where is an Airflow XCom, such as a @task's return value, stored, and what should it hold?
optionA: In the metadata database; small values such as paths and counts
optionB: In object storage; the raw files that each extract task produces
optionC: In the DAG folder; configuration that every task reads at start
optionD: In the worker's memory; whole DataFrames passed between tasks
correctAnswerText: In the metadata database; small values such as paths and counts
explanation: XComs live in the metadata database, so they suit small things: an S3 path, a row count, a batch id. Large data goes to S3 or a table and the path is passed. Worker memory is gone after the task, and the DAG folder holds code.

prompt: In Airflow, how does a task fail at once on a permanent error even though its retries setting is 3?
optionA: It raises AirflowFailException
optionB: It sets retries=0 in its XCom
optionC: It returns None from the task
optionD: It calls sys.exit(0) to finish
correctAnswerText: It raises AirflowFailException
explanation: AirflowFailException fails the task immediately whatever retries says, which suits an expired token or a wrong schema. Returning None or exiting with code 0 is success, and an XCom cannot change the task's retry setting.

prompt: What does catchup=True make the Airflow scheduler do when a DAG is switched on?
optionA: Rerun every failed task in the DAG's history before new intervals
optionB: Create a run for every past interval since start_date with no run
optionC: Run the latest interval twice to catch rows that arrived late
optionD: Skip the past and wait for the next scheduled tick to come round
correctAnswerText: Create a run for every past interval since start_date with no run
explanation: Catchup fills every interval between start_date and now that has no run, which can queue hundreds at once. Its default is True in Airflow 2 and False in Airflow 3. It does not rerun failures or duplicate the latest run; skipping the past is what catchup=False does.

prompt: What is the main unit of work in Dagster, as opposed to a task in an Airflow DAG?
optionA: A sensor: a step that waits until some condition becomes true
optionB: A flow: a plain Python function decorated to run with retries
optionC: A software-defined asset: a table or file and how it is made
optionD: An operator: a template that runs one kind of external system
correctAnswerText: A software-defined asset: a table or file and how it is made
explanation: Dagster describes the tables, not the steps: each asset is a function that produces a table or file, with upstream assets as dependencies and partitions in place of intervals. Flows are Prefect's unit, operators are Airflow templates, and sensors exist in several tools.

prompt: In Airflow terms, what is a task instance?
optionA: One operator class, such as the BashOperator
optionB: One DAG file, as parsed by the DAG processor
optionC: One worker process, with its own pool of slots
optionD: One task of a DAG, for one particular DAG run
correctAnswerText: One task of a DAG, for one particular DAG run
explanation: An operator is a template, a task is one use of it in a DAG, and a task instance is that task for one run (one interval), with its own state, attempts and log. A DAG file and a worker are different things again.

prompt: A DAG is scheduled on an Airflow Asset (a Dataset in 2.x). When is the asset event that triggers it recorded?
optionA: When a task listing the asset in its outlets starts
optionB: When any file is written under the asset's S3 prefix
optionC: When a task listing the asset in its outlets succeeds
optionD: When the scheduler next parses the producing DAG file
correctAnswerText: When a task listing the asset in its outlets succeeds
explanation: An asset event is recorded only when the producing task succeeds, so a failed load never triggers its consumers. Airflow does not watch S3 itself; it knows about updates made by its own tasks or posted to its API. Starting a task or parsing a file records nothing.

prompt: By default, when an upstream task in an Airflow DAG fails for good, what state do its downstream tasks get?
optionA: running, with the upstream data so far
optionB: success, as they were not asked to run
optionC: queued, until someone clears the DAG
optionD: upstream_failed, and they do not run
correctAnswerText: upstream_failed, and they do not run
explanation: The default rule is that a task runs only when all upstream tasks succeeded; otherwise it is marked upstream_failed, which is what stops a dashboard refreshing on stale data. After a fix, clearing the failed task reruns it and what depends on it.

prompt: Why does the daily Airflow 2 run that fires at 02:00 on 27 October process 26 October's data?
optionA: The scheduler starts each run a full day late to leave time for late data
optionB: The run is still waiting on a sensor for the 27th, so it loads the 26th
optionC: Airflow subtracts a day from every date to convert it into UTC first
optionD: A run covers a completed interval, and that interval began a day earlier
correctAnswerText: A run covers a completed interval, and that interval began a day earlier
explanation: With interval semantics a run is created after its interval ends and processes that interval, so "today's run loads yesterday" is the design. There is no built-in day of delay, the UTC offset is a separate trap with ds, and sensors are not involved.

prompt: Why can many poke-mode sensors stall a whole Airflow installation during a backfill?
optionA: They retry forever by default because sensors ignore any timeout setting
optionB: They lock the S3 key they watch, so that no producer can write the file there
optionC: They hold every worker slot, so the task that makes their file never starts
optionD: They poll so often that the metadata database rejects all other queries
correctAnswerText: They hold every worker slot, so the task that makes their file never starts
explanation: A poking sensor occupies a slot for its whole wait. If sensors take every slot, the producing task cannot run, so they wait until they time out: a deadlock. Reschedule or deferrable mode, a pool for sensors and a timeout prevent it. Sensors do honour timeouts and do not lock S3 keys.

prompt: Why should an Airflow @task write its DataFrame to S3 and return the path, rather than return the DataFrame itself?
optionA: TaskFlow tasks cannot return any value other than a plain string or an int
optionB: A returned DataFrame is silently converted to CSV and loses its dtypes
optionC: The return value lands in the metadata database, which large values slow
optionD: Returning a DataFrame makes the task run in poke mode until it is read
correctAnswerText: The return value lands in the metadata database, which large values slow
explanation: A return value becomes an XCom in the metadata database, which is not a data store; large XComs slow the whole installation. Write data to S3 or a table and pass the path. TaskFlow does allow other return types, and poke mode is a sensor setting.

prompt: Why must a DAG file never call an API or a database at the top level of the module?
optionA: Top-level code runs on the worker, which has no network access at all
optionB: Top-level code runs after every task, so the call repeats for each one
optionC: Top-level code runs only once at install, so its result goes out of date
optionD: Top-level code runs on every parse of the file, every half-minute or so
correctAnswerText: Top-level code runs on every parse of the file, every half-minute or so
explanation: The DAG processor re-imports each file roughly every 30 seconds, so module-level calls hammer the API, slow the scheduler and can exceed the import timeout. Do the work inside tasks. The other options misdescribe when parse-time code runs.

prompt: Why must a load task be idempotent for its interval even when every retry eventually succeeds?
optionA: A failure can come after the write committed, so the retry writes again
optionB: Retries always run against the next interval instead of the one that failed
optionC: The scheduler deletes a task's output before each retry by default
optionD: Retries run on a different worker, which cannot see the earlier rows
correctAnswerText: A failure can come after the write committed, so the retry writes again
explanation: A worker can lose its heartbeat after its insert commits; the task is marked failed and the retry appends the interval again, doubling it with no error. Replacing the interval (delete and insert in one transaction) makes any number of runs give the source's numbers. Airflow does not clean up output or change the interval.

prompt: Why does an interval-safe load filter txn_ts >= data_interval_start AND txn_ts < data_interval_end, rather than BETWEEN the two?
optionA: BETWEEN excludes both ends, so rows at either boundary are lost
optionB: The half-open form lets the database skip the index and run faster
optionC: A row at exactly midnight then belongs to one interval, not to two
optionD: BETWEEN cannot be used with Jinja templates in Airflow SQL fields
correctAnswerText: A row at exactly midnight then belongs to one interval, not to two
explanation: BETWEEN includes both ends, so a transaction at exactly 00:00 would be loaded by two consecutive days. The half-open interval gives every instant exactly one interval. Templates render inside BETWEEN just as well, and a half-open range uses the index the same way.

prompt: Why keep a freshness check such as "is max(loaded_at) newer than 08:00?" outside the orchestrator, in addition to failure callbacks?
optionA: Failure callbacks fire only for sensors, not for ordinary tasks
optionB: A check inside Airflow would be counted as a task and slow down runs
optionC: If the scheduler itself is down, its callbacks never fire at all
optionD: Freshness can only be measured by tools that read the raw files
correctAnswerText: If the scheduler itself is down, its callbacks never fire at all
explanation: Callbacks run inside the scheduler; when it is down or a run is never created, nothing fires and nobody is told. An independent check of the data's freshness still alerts. Callbacks work for every task, and freshness is read from the loaded tables.

prompt: Why should the on-call engineer be paged on a task's final failure rather than on each failed attempt?
optionA: Paging on each attempt cancels all of the remaining retries for that task instance
optionB: Airflow can only send an alert once per DAG run, so it must wait for the last
optionC: A final failure is the only state whose log is kept by the metadata database
optionD: Most attempt failures heal on retry, so paging on them trains people to ignore
correctAnswerText: Most attempt failures heal on retry, so paging on them trains people to ignore
explanation: Transient errors are expected and mostly recover on retry; paging on them creates noise until real pages are ignored. Page on the final failure (on_failure_callback) and send retries to a quieter channel if anywhere. Alerts do not cancel retries, and every attempt keeps its log.

prompt: Why keep pipeline work in plain functions and CLIs (extract.py, dbt build) with the orchestrator as a thin layer that calls them?
