explanation: 401 means the server does not know who is calling; a valid customer token is known, so the role refusal should be 403. It is a wrong code rather than a leak (nothing was returned), and the customer cell of the matrix is testable on its own.

prompt: How should a tester check that POST /orders cannot be used to set an order's status or total directly?
optionA: Send an empty body and assert the defaults are applied
optionB: Call PATCH with those fields and expect a 405 response
optionC: Send those fields in the body and assert they were ignored
optionD: Read the source code to confirm the fields are never copied
correctAnswerText: Send those fields in the body and assert they were ignored
explanation: The test sends status PAID and total_paise 1 and asserts the created order is PLACED with the real total, so a later refactor that copies the body is caught. Reading code is not a regression test, an empty body tests validation, and PATCH is a different endpoint.

prompt: A tester wants to check every quantity from -1000 to 1000 against the rule "accepted only if 1 to 20" without listing cases. What fits?
optionA: A load test sending random quantities at 100 req/s
optionB: A hypothesis test that asserts the rule for any integer
optionC: A Postman data file with one random value on each row
optionD: A parametrize list with all 2,001 values typed by hand
correctAnswerText: A hypothesis test that asserts the rule for any integer
explanation: A property-based test states the rule once and lets hypothesis generate integers, then shrinks any failure to the simplest one (qty=0). Typing 2,001 rows is unmaintainable, random rows are not repeatable, and a load test does not check validation.

prompt: API tests in CI fail because a field added this week is missing, and the health endpoint they reach reports last week's version. What is the first suspicion?
optionA: The CI runner's clock is a week behind
optionB: base_url points at a different environment
optionC: The schema validator caches old responses
optionD: The new field was removed by a later commit
correctAnswerText: base_url points at a different environment
explanation: An old version number means the tests are talking to an old deployment: a stale base_url, a teammate's server or the wrong environment. Read that evidence before the code. A removed field would not change the reported version, and neither validators nor clocks explain it.

prompt: Each test file passes alone, but the full run gives many 401 TOKEN_EXPIRED and the login fixture is session-scoped. Which test most likely set it off?
optionA: A schema test that validated every order in the list
optionB: A pagination test that walked every page of the whole menu
optionC: An expiry test that moved the shared fake clock forward
optionD: A mock test that patched the payment provider call
correctAnswerText: An expiry test that moved the shared fake clock forward
explanation: A session-scoped token is reused by every later test; once the expiry test advances the shared clock past the lifetime, all of them get TOKEN_EXPIRED. Function-scoped logins or resetting the clock in teardown fix it. The other tests do not change time.

prompt: A response schema passed for months, even when a number field arrived as a string. A teammate finds "propertes" in it. Why did it pass?
optionA: jsonschema corrects common misspellings by itself
optionB: Unknown keywords are ignored, so no field was checked
optionC: jsonschema only checks the required list of a schema
optionD: A string is accepted wherever an integer is declared
correctAnswerText: Unknown keywords are ignored, so no field was checked
explanation: JSON Schema ignores keywords it does not know, so the misspelt block declared nothing and every body passed. One test that validates a known-bad body and expects ValidationError proves a schema can fail. jsonschema does not autocorrect and does reject strings for integer.

prompt: A test "provider timeout gives 503" passes, yet the URL recorded in responses.calls matches no registered mock. What really produced the 503?
optionA: The real provider was reached and was slow at that moment by chance
optionB: The mock matched by host name only, so the timeout was still raised
optionC: responses refused the unmatched call, and the app maps that to 503
optionD: The test client retried, and its second attempt matched the mock
correctAnswerText: responses refused the unmatched call, and the app maps that to 503
explanation: responses raises its own ConnectionError for unmatched requests, and the app turns any ConnectionError into 503, so the expected outcome appeared for the wrong reason. assert_all_requests_are_fired or a check on calls[0].request.url exposes it. responses matches the full URL and blocks real calls.

prompt: The web app shows order totals correctly; the Android app shows "Rs NaN" on the order detail screen only. What should the tester suspect and do?
optionA: The Android app rounds wrongly; compare totals on the two screens
optionB: Detail sends the total as another type; check both on one schema
optionC: The list endpoint is cached; clear the cache and try it again
optionD: The detail call is slow; measure its response time under load
correctAnswerText: Detail sends the total as another type; check both on one schema
explanation: One screen breaking points at one endpoint's shape: a total sent as "21000" instead of 21000 still works in loose JavaScript but fails a strict Android parser. Validating the create, detail and list items against one schema finds it and guards every field. Speed and caching do not produce NaN.

prompt: On a test database nobody else writes to, per_page=10 gives page 1 ids 11 to 20 and page 2 ids 22 to 31, and GET /items/21 returns the item. What does that show?
optionA: per_page is applied twice on the second page only
optionB: Page 2 starts one item late, so item 21 is never listed
optionC: Nothing: small gaps are normal when a list is sorted by id
optionD: Item 21 was deleted between the two page requests
correctAnswerText: Page 2 starts one item late, so item 21 is never listed
explanation: Page 2 should begin right after page 1 ends; skipping 21 is an offset defect, and the walk across pages is what shows it. Nobody else writes to the database and item 21 still exists, so it was not deleted, and a doubled per_page would skip ten items, not one.

prompt: Two different customers send POST /orders with the same Idempotency-Key, and the second receives the first customer's order. What is wrong?
optionA: Nothing: a repeated key must always replay the order
optionB: The server cache is stale and needs a shorter expiry
optionC: Keys are not scoped to the user, which leaks an order
optionD: Clients should build keys from timestamps, not UUIDs
correctAnswerText: Keys are not scoped to the user, which leaks an order
explanation: An idempotency key must be matched per caller; replaying across users hands one customer another's order and address. Replay is correct only for the same user (and the same body). Key format and cache expiry do not explain a cross-user answer.

prompt: Sending qty as a JSON array instead of a number gets a 500 with a Python traceback in the body. How should the tester read this?
optionA: A 500 is the right answer to any input the API does not support
optionB: An array is invalid JSON, so the test request itself is broken
optionC: The server is overloaded, and the request should be retried
optionD: Input reached code that did not expect it, and internals leaked
correctAnswerText: Input reached code that did not expect it, and internals leaked
explanation: Bad input should give a 400 with the error envelope; a 500 means validation was missing, and a traceback exposes internals. Both are defects. Load is not involved, an array is valid JSON, and a 500 blames the server for a client mistake.

prompt: A Postman smoke check "status is 2xx" passes on POST /orders, while the pytest suite fails with "assert 200 == 201". The contract promises 201. Which is right?
optionA: Postman: 200 and 201 mean the same on a create
optionB: Neither: the code depends on the client tool used
optionC: Postman: requests reads status codes wrongly
optionD: pytest: the Postman check is too loose to see it
correctAnswerText: pytest: the Postman check is too loose to see it
explanation: A test asserts the exact code the contract promises; "2xx" or "not 500" is not a test of it. The server sends the same status to every client, and requests reports it faithfully, so the pytest failure is the real defect.

prompt: Provider verification of the Android pact fails with "body.total_paise: expected int like 22000, got '22000'". Where must the fix go?
optionA: The pact file, by making the example value a string
optionB: The provider's serializer, which changed the type
optionC: The broker, by marking the interaction pending
optionD: The Android mock, so it sends strings as well
correctAnswerText: The provider's serializer, which changed the type
explanation: The consumer needs an integer and the provider started sending a string; verification caught the drift in the provider's pipeline, which is where it belongs. Editing the pact or the mock to match the bug hides it, and marking it pending ships it.

prompt: A team's API test pack is growing fast. Which split of tooling holds up best as it grows?
optionA: Code for exploring, Postman for the regression pack
optionB: Manual checks only, since API suites go stale fast
optionC: Postman for everything, with a folder per endpoint
optionD: Postman for exploring and smoke, code for regression
correctAnswerText: Postman for exploring and smoke, code for regression
explanation: Postman is excellent for exploring, sharing and a small smoke pack run by Newman; factories, shared helpers and code review make a code suite (pytest or REST Assured) better for hundreds of regression tests. The reverse split wastes both, and manual-only loses regression safety.

prompt: An orders service and a mobile app are built and deployed by separate teams. Which mix of API tests is strongest?
optionA: End-to-end tests only, run on a shared staging environment
optionB: Mocks only, refreshed by hand when someone remembers
optionC: Mocks for failures, a verified contract, a few e2e smokes
optionD: A contract only, since it replaces every other test
correctAnswerText: Mocks for failures, a verified contract, a few e2e smokes
explanation: Mocks cover many failure paths quickly, a contract verified in the provider's pipeline catches drift before either side deploys, and a handful of end-to-end smoke tests check the wiring neither can see. E2E-only is slow and fragile, mocks alone go stale, and a contract does not test behaviour.

prompt: You have one day to test a new wallet top-up API before release. Which order of work is best?
optionA: Response times first, since speed is what users notice
optionB: Every field's format first, then auth, then money if time
optionC: The happy path only, leaving negatives to the developers
optionD: Money and other users' data first, then the busiest flows
correctAnswerText: Money and other users' data first, then the busiest flows
explanation: Risk-based ordering puts the costliest failures first: wrong or negative amounts and one user touching another's wallet, then the flows used most. Formats matter but cost less, speed is a separate test, and happy-path-only misses the defects that hurt.

prompt: A team debates whether another user's object should give 403 or 404. What is the best position for the tester to take?
optionA: Either, if the contract says so and it is applied everywhere
optionB: Whatever each developer chose, as long as it is some 4xx
optionC: Always 403, because a 404 hides a real authorisation choice
optionD: Always 404, and file a defect against any endpoint using 403
correctAnswerText: Either, if the contract says so and it is applied everywhere
explanation: Both are defensible; what matters is that the contract states one, every endpoint applies it, and the test checks it (and that 200 never appears). Insisting on one code is a design preference, and per-developer choices give clients inconsistent behaviour.

prompt: A 31-test API suite takes 7 seconds serially and 20 seconds with pytest-xdist -n 4, because each worker starts its own server. What is the right call?
optionA: Stay serial for now; at this size start-up costs more than it saves
optionB: Keep -n 4, since parallel runs are always faster on bigger machines
optionC: Raise it to -n 8, so the start-up cost is shared by more workers
optionD: Drop the server fixture and point every test at production instead
correctAnswerText: Stay serial for now; at this size start-up costs more than it saves
explanation: Measured, parallelism made this suite slower; the right call is to stay serial and revisit when the suite grows. More workers multiply the start-up cost rather than share it, and testing against production is not an option for a regression suite.

prompt: A single isinstance assert caught one field's type drift. Why is it still worth validating every order-returning endpoint against one shared schema?
optionA: Type assertions are not allowed in pytest test functions
optionB: It also catches the next drift, in a field nobody thought of
optionC: A schema lets the test skip checking the status code
optionD: A schema check always runs faster than a Python isinstance check
correctAnswerText: It also catches the next drift, in a field nobody thought of
explanation: One assert guards one field; a schema guards every field's presence, type and extras on every endpoint that returns the object. Speed is not the reason, pytest allows any assertion, and the status code is still checked first.

prompt: For a service that calls a payment provider, which split of provider tests gives the most confidence for the time spent?
optionA: responses for each failure case, one stub test for the real timeout
optionB: Stub-server tests for every case, since mocks are never really realistic
optionC: The provider's sandbox for every case, run on every commit
optionD: responses for every case, including proof the timeout is set
correctAnswerText: responses for each failure case, one stub test for the real timeout
explanation: In-process mocks cover declines, 500s, HTML bodies and refused connections in milliseconds, but only a stub that really waits proves the timeout is configured. Stubs for everything are slower for no gain, mocks cannot prove a timeout, and a sandbox cannot produce failures on demand.

prompt: When is it right for an API test to check a field by its type or pattern rather than by a literal value?
optionA: When the field is optional and only sometimes sent back
optionB: When it changes by design, such as ids and timestamps
optionC: When a literal value would make the test too long
optionD: When it is money, so that rounding cannot break it
correctAnswerText: When it changes by design, such as ids and timestamps
explanation: Ids and created_at change every run, so their shape is the claim; everything that matters to the case (totals, status, items) gets a literal. Money especially needs literal values, optional fields need presence rules, and test length is no reason to weaken a check.

prompt: A bank's QA team runs Selenium with TestNG in Java. A new SDET prefers pytest for the API tests. What is the better choice?
optionA: Postman only, since it needs no programming language of any kind
optionB: pytest, because Python is always quicker to write tests in
optionC: REST Assured with TestNG, so one framework and report serve all
optionD: Both, each covering half of the endpoints chosen at random
correctAnswerText: REST Assured with TestNG, so one framework and report serve all
explanation: The test design is identical in either language; sharing the team's framework means one set of helpers, one report and one CI setup. Personal preference does not outweigh that, splitting endpoints doubles the upkeep, and Postman alone does not scale to a regression suite.

prompt: After a provider timeout, the app answers 503 and leaves the order PLACED, and the tests prove it. What further test should a careful tester ask for?
optionA: A load test of the provider at ten times the expected peak
optionB: A UI test that the error page shows the brand colours
optionC: A retry loop in the app that pays until the provider answers
optionD: A reconciliation check for money taken after the app gave up
correctAnswerText: A reconciliation check for money taken after the app gave up
explanation: The provider may still collect the money after the app stops waiting, so a reconciliation job must find and settle those payments, and it needs its own tests. Load-testing a third party is not ours to do, colours are cosmetic, and blind retries risk charging twice.

prompt: Which kind of performance test answers the question "Is this build slower than the last one?"
optionA: A spike test with a fast ramp
optionB: A soak test held for hours
optionC: A stress test run in steps
optionD: A baseline (regression) test
correctAnswerText: A baseline (regression) test
explanation: A baseline or regression test runs the same small load on every release and compares with the previous result, catching changes such as a new N+1 query. Spike, soak and stress tests ask about sudden jumps, slow degradation and the breaking point.

prompt: What does "p95 = 800 ms" mean for the booking requests in a load test?
optionA: 95% finished in 800 ms or less; 5% took longer
optionB: 95 bookings per second finished within 800 ms
optionC: The run met its 800 ms target 95% of the time
optionD: The slowest 5% of bookings averaged 800 ms each
correctAnswerText: 95% finished in 800 ms or less; 5% took longer
explanation: p95 is the value 95% of requests were at or below; the slowest 5% took longer. It is not an average of the tail, not a rate, and not a share of time the target was met.

prompt: With N concurrent users, throughput X, response time R and think time Z, which form of Little's law is used to build a load model?
optionA: R = N x X + Z
optionB: X = N x (R + Z)
optionC: N = X / (R + Z)
optionD: N = X x (R + Z)
correctAnswerText: N = X x (R + Z)
explanation: Users in the system equal the rate times the time each spends per request cycle (response plus think time). It turns "2,400 people on the site" into a request rate and back. The other forms invert or misplace the terms.

prompt: In a Locust user class, what does the decorator @task(6) on a method set?
optionA: The number of users who only run that task
optionB: The number of times it runs in a row
optionC: Its wait time in seconds after it has run
optionD: Its relative chance of being picked next
correctAnswerText: Its relative chance of being picked next
explanation: Task weights are relative probabilities: 6, 3 and 1 give roughly a 60/30/10 mix. They are not sequences or separate user groups, and think time is set by wait_time, not by the task weight.

prompt: Which k6 executors start iterations on a schedule, whatever the server is doing?
optionA: constant-vus and ramping-vus executors
optionB: externally-controlled and constant-vus
optionC: shared-iterations and per-vu-iterations
optionD: constant-arrival-rate, ramping-arrival-rate
correctAnswerText: constant-arrival-rate, ramping-arrival-rate
explanation: Arrival-rate executors are an open model: iterations start at the configured rate, and k6 adds VUs up to maxVUs to keep it. VU-based and iteration-count executors are closed: a VU waits for its reply before starting again.

prompt: Which JMeter command-line option runs a test plan without the GUI, as every real load run should?
optionA: -g, with -t for the plan and -o for the results
optionB: -n, with -t for the plan and -l for the results
optionC: -e, with -j for the plan and -l for the results
optionD: -r, with -t for the plan and -q for the results
correctAnswerText: -n, with -t for the plan and -l for the results
explanation: jmeter -n -t plan.jmx -l results.jtl runs non-GUI; -e -o builds the HTML dashboard and -J sets properties. A load run from the GUI measures the GUI, so the GUI is for building and debugging with a few threads.

prompt: In JMeter, what is the name for extracting a token from one response and sending it in later requests?
optionA: Pacing
optionB: Correlation
optionC: Assertion
optionD: Ramp-up
correctAnswerText: Correlation
explanation: Correlation uses a post-processor such as a JSON Extractor to capture a dynamic value (a token, a session id) for later samplers. Ramp-up spreads thread starts, assertions judge responses, and pacing controls the rate.

prompt: Of the four things read in a load test, which one is measured on the server and never by the load tool?
optionA: Latency percentiles per endpoint
optionB: Throughput in requests per second overall
optionC: Saturation of resources such as pools
optionD: Error rate split by type of error
correctAnswerText: Saturation of resources such as pools
explanation: How full CPU, worker threads, connection pools and queues are can only be seen from the server. Throughput, latency and errors are what the load tool observes from the client side.

prompt: What is coordinated omission in a closed-loop load test?
optionA: The tool stops sending while the server stalls, so stalls are under-recorded
optionB: Failed requests are dropped from the percentiles so the results look clean
optionC: The tool leaves out think time whenever the server answers very quickly
optionD: Several generators agree to skip the same requests to avoid overloading a server
correctAnswerText: The tool stops sending while the server stalls, so stalls are under-recorded
explanation: A closed-loop user waits for each reply, so during a stall it sends nothing and records one slow request instead of the many real users who would have arrived and waited. The result is flattering percentiles.

prompt: In a Locust quitting listener that checks thresholds, which attribute sets the exit code a CI job sees?
optionA: environment.runner.exit_status
optionB: environment.process_exit_code
optionC: environment.parsed_options.exit
optionD: environment.stats.fail_ratio
correctAnswerText: environment.process_exit_code
explanation: Locust has no threshold syntax; the listener reads the stats and sets environment.process_exit_code, which the CI step uses. fail_ratio is a statistic to compare against, not the exit code.

prompt: Why can a requirement of "average booking time under 300 ms" pass while some customers wait several seconds?
optionA: The average leaves out failed requests, which are usually the slow ones
optionB: A small slow group barely moves the mean but is the tail users feel
optionC: Averages are computed per minute and then rounded down by tools
optionD: Averages include the ramp-up, so they always come out too high
correctAnswerText: A small slow group barely moves the mean but is the tail users feel
explanation: Latency is skewed: if 5% of bookings take 1.6 s, the mean can still be about 220 ms while one booking in twenty is slow. Requirements are written on per-endpoint percentiles plus an error rate. The other options invent tool behaviour.

prompt: Why must percentiles be reported per endpoint, and not only aggregated across every request in the run?
optionA: A rare endpoint's slow tail vanishes among many fast requests
optionB: Aggregates count every failed request twice in the total
optionC: Load tools are unable to compute an aggregated percentile at all
optionD: Per-endpoint numbers are smaller and easier to present
correctAnswerText: A rare endpoint's slow tail vanishes among many fast requests
explanation: If bookings are 9% of requests and 5% of them are slow, that is under 0.5% of the total, so the aggregated p99 can look fine while bookings suffer. Tools do compute aggregates; they just answer the wrong question.

prompt: Why can the sixty per-minute p95 values from a one-hour test not simply be averaged to give the hour's p95?
optionA: They depend on each minute's distribution; merge and recompute
optionB: Averaging only works when every minute contained some errors
optionC: The hour's p95 is always the highest of the minute values
optionD: Per-minute values are rounded, so their average is too low
correctAnswerText: They depend on each minute's distribution; merge and recompute
explanation: A percentile depends on the counts and shape of the samples behind it; to combine, merge raw samples or histogram buckets and compute again. Errors and rounding are irrelevant, and the overall p95 is not simply the maximum.

prompt: Why does a load test need think time between each virtual user's requests?
optionA: Without it, each user sends far more than a real person
optionB: Think time hides network jitter from the measurements
optionC: Servers reject clients that send with no delay at all
optionD: Load tools crash when requests are sent straight back to back
correctAnswerText: Without it, each user sends far more than a real person
explanation: Real people read and choose between actions; a virtual user with no pause fires again the moment a reply arrives, so 100 of them can act like thousands of people and the rate is invented. Tools and servers run fine without pauses.

prompt: In a step test, why is throughput that stays flat while latency keeps rising read as saturation?
optionA: The load tool stopped sending, so the latency is not real
optionB: Extra work cannot be done any faster, so it waits in a queue
optionC: Flat throughput means the test ran out of rows in its data
optionD: Rising latency always means the network is dropping packets
correctAnswerText: Extra work cannot be done any faster, so it waits in a queue
explanation: Once some resource is doing all it can per second, added users only join a queue: the rate stays at the capacity and time in the system grows. That point is the knee. The other readings would need evidence of their own.

prompt: Why does low server CPU together with rising latency point at a pool, a lock or a slow dependency rather than at slow code?
optionA: CPU readings lag behind latency by several minutes
optionB: Slow code always shows as low CPU when under load
optionC: Requests are waiting for something rather than working
optionD: Low CPU means that the server process has already crashed
correctAnswerText: Requests are waiting for something rather than working
explanation: Busy code burns CPU; time that passes without CPU is time spent waiting for a connection, a lock, a thread or another service. A crashed process answers nothing, and CPU sampled every few seconds does not lag by minutes.

prompt: Why must the load generator's own CPU be watched during a run?
optionA: Load tools stop recording percentiles above 50% CPU
optionB: A busy generator reports its own delays as server latency
optionC: The generator always shares its CPU with the system tested
optionD: High generator CPU means the server is coping very well
correctAnswerText: A busy generator reports its own delays as server latency
explanation: A generator near its CPU limit sends late and times late, so its own slowness appears as the server's. Locust warns above about 90% CPU and is spread over workers for more load. The other options describe things that do not happen.

prompt: Why can an endpoint that never touches the database slow down when the database connection pool saturates?
optionA: Every endpoint quietly opens a database connection when it starts
optionB: The load tool delays every other endpoint as soon as one becomes slow
optionC: It waits for worker threads that are stuck waiting for connections
optionD: Its in-memory cache is flushed whenever the pool becomes full
correctAnswerText: It waits for worker threads that are stuck waiting for connections
explanation: All endpoints share the server's worker threads; when most are blocked waiting for the pool, a fast request queues for a thread. One slow resource slows unrelated endpoints. Load tools time each request independently.

prompt: Why are the first seconds of a load run usually left out before percentiles are read?
optionA: Servers refuse all requests for a minute after start
optionB: Early requests are counted twice by most load tools
optionC: They mix ramp-up, cold caches and connection set-up
optionD: Load tools record no samples in the first minute
correctAnswerText: They mix ramp-up, cold caches and connection set-up
explanation: The start of a run is not the steady state being judged; Locust's --reset-stats and dropping the first minute of a JTL both remove it. Tools do record early samples, once each, and servers do not refuse them.

prompt: In k6, why does a failing check not turn the CI job red on its own?
optionA: Checks only record pass rates; thresholds set the exit code
optionB: Checks only run after the test has ended, too late to matter
optionC: CI ignores k6 output unless it is written out as JUnit
optionD: A check fails only if every single response has failed
correctAnswerText: Checks only record pass rates; thresholds set the exit code
explanation: A check counts results in the checks metric but leaves the exit code alone; a threshold (for example checks: ["rate>0.99"] or http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"]) ends k6 with a non-zero code when crossed. Checks run per response during the test.

prompt: A load test for a ticketing API must produce 150 req/s. Think time is 3.0 s and the expected response time is 0.2 s. How many virtual users does Little's law give?
optionA: 750 users, from 150 / 0.2 seconds
optionB: 150 users, one per request per second
explanation: N = X x (R + Z) = 150 x 3.2 = 480. One user per req/s holds only when R + Z is exactly 1 s, 150 / 0.2 ignores think time, and dividing by (R + Z) inverts the law.

prompt: Analytics show 1,200 people active on a booking site, with an average think time of 5.5 s and response time of 0.5 s. What request rate do they produce?
optionB: About 7,200 req/s, from 1,200 x 6.0
optionC: About 2,400 req/s, from 1,200 / 0.5 s only
optionD: About 218 req/s, from 1,200 / 5.5
explanation: X = N / (R + Z) = 1,200 / 6.0 = 200 req/s. Dividing by the response time alone ignores the pauses, multiplying inverts the law, and dividing by think time alone drops the response time.

prompt: A checkout journey makes 10 API calls, each with an independent 5% chance of being slower than p95. About what share of journeys meet at least one such call?
optionA: About 40%, from 1 - 0.95 to the power 10
optionB: About 60%, from 0.95 to the power 10
optionC: About 50%, from 10 calls x 5% per call
optionD: About 5%, the same as for a single call
correctAnswerText: About 40%, from 1 - 0.95 to the power 10
explanation: 0.95^10 is about 0.599, so about 40% of journeys contain a slower-than-p95 call. 5% is per call, adding 10 x 5% overcounts overlaps, and 0.95^10 is the share of journeys that avoid the tail.

prompt: A mix is 40% seat lookups (40 ms of database time), 20% bookings (120 ms) and 40% searches (none). The pool has 3 connections. What is its ceiling?
optionA: About 38 req/s, from 3 / 0.080
optionB: About 75 req/s, from 3 / 0.040
optionC: About 120 req/s, from 3 x 40
optionD: About 25 req/s, from 1 / 0.040
correctAnswerText: About 75 req/s, from 3 / 0.040
explanation: Average hold = 0.4 x 40 + 0.2 x 120 = 40 ms per request; 3 connections serve 3 / 0.040 = 75 req/s. 1 / 0.040 counts one connection, 0.080 s averages 40 and 120 ms while ignoring the mix and the searches, and 3 x 40 multiplies the wrong way.

prompt: Last festival's busiest hour had 72,000 sessions of 5 requests each. The peak minute runs at twice the hour average and 20% growth is expected. What rate should the load test target?
optionA: About 240 req/s, from 100 x 2 x 1.2
optionB: About 100 req/s, the hour average
optionC: About 120 req/s, the average plus growth
optionD: About 200 req/s, the peak with no growth
correctAnswerText: About 240 req/s, from 100 x 2 x 1.2
explanation: 72,000 x 5 / 3,600 = 100 req/s on average; the peak minute is 200 and 20% growth makes 240. The hour average misses the peak, 200 forgets growth, and 120 applies growth but not the peak.

prompt: Ten response times in ms: 80, 85, 90, 92, 95, 100, 110, 120, 900, 1500. What is the p90 by the nearest-rank method (sorted value at position ceil(0.9 x n))?
optionA: 1,500 ms, the largest value
optionB: 317 ms, the mean of the ten
optionC: 900 ms, the 9th sorted value
optionD: 120 ms, the 8th sorted value
correctAnswerText: 900 ms, the 9th sorted value
explanation: ceil(0.9 x 10) = 9, and the 9th sorted value is 900 ms. 1,500 is the maximum (the nearest-rank p95 and p99 here), 120 is one position too early, and 317.2 ms is the mean, which describes none of the requests.

prompt: The requirement is "errors under 1% and p95 under 800 ms". Which k6 thresholds block expresses it?
optionA: http_req_duration: ['p(95)<0.8'], vus: ['max<1'] on every run
optionB: http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'], http_req_duration: ['p(95)<800']
optionC: checks: ['rate<0.01'], http_req_duration: ['avg<800'] for all runs
optionD: http_req_failed: ['count<1'], http_reqs: ['p(95)<800'] in all
correctAnswerText: http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'], http_req_duration: ['p(95)<800']
explanation: http_req_failed is the failed-request rate and http_req_duration is in milliseconds, so rate<0.01 and p(95)<800 state the requirement. checks rate<0.01 would demand that almost every check fails, avg is not p95, http_reqs is a count, and 0.8 would mean 0.8 ms.

prompt: A locustfile requests /buses/{id}/seats with many different ids, and the stats show 40 rows of a few samples each. What change fixes the report?
optionA: Use only one bus id so that the URL never changes
optionB: Set catch_response=True on that request
optionC: Pass name="/buses/[id]/seats" on that request
optionD: Run with more users so each row fills up
correctAnswerText: Pass name="/buses/[id]/seats" on that request
explanation: Locust groups statistics by request name, which defaults to the URL; name= puts every seat lookup in one row with a meaningful p95 and allows a per-endpoint threshold. catch_response marks failures, more users still split rows, and one id makes the data unrealistic.

prompt: A JMeter thread group has three samplers and a Uniform Random Timer at group level, but the model says one pause per journey. What is the fix?
optionA: Move the timer under one sampler, so it runs once a journey
optionB: Leave it, since group-level timers run once per thread iteration
optionC: Put the timer inside a listener so it runs after each loop
optionD: Add a second timer at test-plan level to balance it out
correctAnswerText: Move the timer under one sampler, so it runs once a journey
explanation: Timers apply before every sampler in their scope, so at group level the pause happens three times per journey. Under one sampler (or as a Flow Control Action) it happens once. Listeners do not hold timers, and another timer only adds more pauses.

prompt: A concert-ticket site opens sales at 10:00 and traffic jumps from 50 to 600 req/s within a minute. Which test should be planned?
optionA: A soak test at normal load for eight hours
optionB: A capacity test of one instance at target
optionC: A baseline test compared with the last build
optionD: A spike test that jumps the load in seconds
correctAnswerText: A spike test that jumps the load in seconds
explanation: A sudden jump is a spike, and the question is whether queues and scaling cope in seconds. Soak finds slow degradation, capacity finds one instance's limit at target, and baseline compares builds at low load.

prompt: A step test gives: 50 users 45 req/s p95 180 ms; 100 users 88 req/s p95 220 ms; 150 users 92 req/s p95 900 ms; 200 users 91 req/s p95 1,900 ms; no errors. The target is p95 under 800 ms. What capacity should be reported?
optionA: 200 users, since no step returned any errors at all
optionB: About 88 req/s, the last step that met the target
optionC: About 92 req/s, the highest throughput that it reached
optionD: 150 users, because its p95 was fairly close to 800
correctAnswerText: About 88 req/s, the last step that met the target
explanation: Capacity is the highest rate that still meets the target, stated as a rate because user counts depend on think time. 92 req/s came with a 900 ms p95, and the system fails by getting slow, so the absence of errors proves nothing.

prompt: From 200 to 400 users throughput stays near 110 req/s, the errors are "connection refused", the database pool always has free connections and CPU is 30%. Where is the limit?
optionA: The test data file, which has run out of rows
optionB: The server's limit on open client connections
optionC: The CPU, which is about to reach its maximum
optionD: The database pool, which is too small for the load
correctAnswerText: The server's limit on open client connections
explanation: Refused connections with flat throughput and idle resources mean new connections are not being accepted at all: a server, load-balancer or file-descriptor connection limit. The pool has free connections, CPU has headroom, and running out of data does not refuse connections.

prompt: Users report 3-second freezes every few minutes. A closed-loop Locust test reports p99 = 40 ms, but its req/s chart dips every few minutes. What is the reading?
optionA: The dips are normal noise in any load test and can be ignored
optionB: Locust is overloaded and simply needs a few more worker processes
optionC: The freezes are on the client side, since the server p99 is perfectly fine
optionD: The tool stopped sending during stalls, so freezes went unrecorded
correctAnswerText: The tool stopped sending during stalls, so freezes went unrecorded
explanation: A closed-loop user waits during a stall, so the achieved rate dips and only one slow sample is recorded per user: coordinated omission. An open model (k6 arrival-rate) would measure the freezes. A busy generator would show its own CPU warning, not periodic dips matching complaints.

prompt: A Locust gate prints "performance gate passed", yet CI is red. 12 requests failed, and the listener sets the exit code only when a limit is broken. Why is it red?
optionA: CI treats any failed request in the log as a failing step
optionB: The p95 was compared in seconds, so the check failed quietly
optionC: Locust always exits with 1 when a listener has printed any text
optionD: With no code set, Locust used its default for runs with errors
correctAnswerText: With no code set, Locust used its default for runs with errors
explanation: If environment.process_exit_code is never set, Locust uses --exit-code-on-error (1 by default) whenever any request failed. Set it in both branches, then decide deliberately whether those errors should pass. Printing does not change the code, and CI only sees the exit code.

prompt: At 350 req/s, app CPU is 97% on all cores, nobody waits for the pool, database CPU is 15% and the generator's CPU is 30%. What should the tester ask for?
optionA: A bigger database instance, since queries must be slow
optionB: More Locust workers, since the generator is the limit
optionC: A CPU profile of the app under load to find the hot code
optionD: A larger connection pool so queries can run in parallel
correctAnswerText: A CPU profile of the app under load to find the hot code
explanation: The application CPU is the full resource and nothing queues elsewhere, so the question is which code burns it; a profile under load (py-spy, a flame graph) answers it. The pool, the database and the generator all have headroom.

prompt: A stress run holds each step for 15 seconds and spawns 25 users a second. Its p95 is highest just after each step change and lowest at the end of each step. What is wrong?
optionA: The spawn rate is too slow, so the steps should be shortened
optionB: The steps are too short, so readings mix the ramp with the load
optionC: The server has a defect that slows it down whenever users connect to it
optionD: Locust cannot report percentiles for a shaped load test run
correctAnswerText: The steps are too short, so readings mix the ramp with the load
explanation: Locust's current percentiles cover roughly the last few seconds, so short steps measure the burst of starting users as much as the step. Hold each step for minutes and judge the steady part. The evidence does not show a server defect, and shaped runs report percentiles normally.

prompt: A load test passed with every user searching the same route and date. On sale day, with searches spread over many routes, search was slow. What was the gap?
optionA: Varied routes trigger a defect in the mobile app rather than the API
optionB: One hot query was served from cache; varied searches hit the database
optionC: Production servers are always slower than the ones used for testing
optionD: The test load was too high, so it overstated the search latency on sale day
correctAnswerText: One hot query was served from cache; varied searches hit the database
explanation: With identical requests a cache or the database's buffer answers almost everything, so the slow paths real traffic takes were never exercised. Realistic data (many users, routes and dates) belongs in the workload model. The other options do not match a test that was too optimistic.

prompt: A run has 300 users with 1.0 s think time and achieves 100 req/s, yet the tool reports an average response time of 0.4 s. What does Little's law say?
optionA: R should be about 0.4 s, so the law confirms the reading from the tool
optionB: R should be about 2.0 s, so the 0.4 s reading and the test are suspect
optionC: R should be about 3.0 s, from 300 users divided by 100 req/s exactly
optionD: The law cannot be applied to any test with more than 100 users in it
correctAnswerText: R should be about 2.0 s, so the 0.4 s reading and the test are suspect
explanation: R = N / X - Z = 300 / 100 - 1.0 = 2.0 s. A large gap between the law and the tool means the test is not doing what it claims (real think time, an overloaded generator, a stalled ramp). 3.0 s forgets to subtract think time, and the law holds at any size.

prompt: 240 closed-loop users with 1.0 s think time produce 200 req/s while responses take 0.2 s. Under load the response time rises to 1.0 s. What rate do they produce now?
optionA: About 120 req/s, as a closed model sends less when it slows
optionB: About 240 req/s, one request per user every single second
optionC: Still 200 req/s, since the number of users has not changed at all
optionD: About 40 req/s, since response time rose five times over
correctAnswerText: About 120 req/s, as a closed model sends less when it slows
explanation: X = N / (R + Z) = 240 / 2.0 = 120 req/s. In a closed model the rate falls as the server slows, which is why a user count alone is never the load. The rate does not stay fixed, and it falls with R + Z (1.2 s to 2.0 s), not with R alone.

prompt: A JMeter script recorded from a browser works on its first replay; on the next day every booking sampler returns 401. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: The recorded token is replayed as-is; it needs correlating
optionB: The CSV Data Set Config has run out of rows of route data
optionC: Listeners are using too much memory on the load generator
optionD: The thread group ramp-up is too short for the server today
correctAnswerText: The recorded token is replayed as-is; it needs correlating
explanation: A recording hard-codes the session token it saw; once that expires, every request is unauthenticated. A JSON Extractor after login stores a fresh token per thread. Ramp-up, listener memory and data rows do not produce 401.

prompt: Which performance requirement for a booking API is the most useful to test against?
optionA: No errors at all with 1,000 concurrent users for one minute
optionB: At 200 req/s, real mix: p95 < 800 ms, errors < 1%, 30 min
optionC: Pages feel fast for every customer on the peak evening
optionD: Average booking under 300 ms with 1,000 users for an hour
correctAnswerText: At 200 req/s, real mix: p95 < 800 ms, errors < 1%, 30 min
explanation: A testable requirement names the rate and mix, the percentile limits, the error rate and the duration. An average hides the tail, a user count without think time is not a load, one minute is not steady state and "no errors" misses slowness, and "feel fast" cannot fail.

prompt: How should a tester decide the load for a sale-day test of a shopping API?
optionA: From last year's peak-minute rate, mix and think time, plus growth
optionB: From the number of registered users, all assumed to be active at once
optionC: From the largest number of users the load tool can generate
optionD: From the developers' own estimate of what the server can take
correctAnswerText: From last year's peak-minute rate, mix and think time, plus growth
explanation: Real access logs give the busiest minute, the request mix and the pauses; growth comes from the business. Registered users are never all active, the tool's maximum measures the tool, and a developer's guess is what the test is meant to check.

prompt: A team needs to keep a fixed arrival rate even when the server slows, with low generator cost and results going to Grafana. Which choice fits best?
optionA: A browser test suite run in parallel
optionB: JMeter, run in its GUI with listeners
optionC: Locust, with between(0, 0) wait time
optionD: k6, with an arrival-rate executor
correctAnswerText: k6, with an arrival-rate executor
explanation: k6's arrival-rate executors give an open model out of the box, its runner is a light Go binary, and it suits teams on Grafana. JMeter must not be run from the GUI for load, Locust with no wait is still a closed model, and browsers are far too heavy as load.

prompt: Ten nightly runs gave the seat-lookup p95 between 180 and 240 ms. Where should the nightly performance gate be set?
optionA: Above the noise, near 300 ms, with one rerun before a defect
optionB: At 1,000 ms, so that the gate never fails the nightly build
optionC: At 180 ms, the best run, so that any slowdown fails the build
optionD: At 210 ms, the average of the ten nightly runs it has seen
correctAnswerText: Above the noise, near 300 ms, with one rerun before a defect
explanation: A gate inside the normal spread fails on noise and gets ignored; one far above it never fires. Setting it just above the observed range and rerunning once before raising a defect keeps it trusted. The environment must also be the same size every night.

prompt: Raising one instance's pool from 2 to 8 lifted throughput in a rerun. Production runs 6 instances and the database allows 40 connections. What should the tester recommend?
optionA: Size them together: 6 x 8 = 48 exceeds the database's 40
optionB: Go back to pool 2, because a larger pool never really helps
optionC: Raise the pool to 32, since more connections gave more speed
optionD: Ship pool 8 at once, because the rerun has already proved it
correctAnswerText: Size them together: 6 x 8 = 48 exceeds the database's 40
explanation: The rerun proves the pool was the bottleneck on one instance, but every instance multiplies it; 48 connections against a limit of 40 moves the failure into the database. Raising further makes it worse, and reverting throws away a proven fix.

prompt: A third-party payment API sits in the booking path. How should the load test treat it?
optionA: Remove the payment step and its delay from the flow
optionB: Send the full load to the real provider for realism
optionC: Call the provider's live API at a lower request rate
optionD: Replace it with a stub that has a realistic delay
correctAnswerText: Replace it with a stub that has a realistic delay
explanation: A stub with a realistic delay keeps the timing of the journey without load-testing a system the team does not own or have permission to test. Removing the step makes bookings unrealistically fast, and any load on the real provider needs its written agreement.

prompt: Autoscaling adds capacity in about three minutes, and the expected spike lasts ninety seconds. What does that mean for the release decision?
optionA: The spike test should be stretched to three minutes to pass
optionB: Scaling will not help in time; capacity must already be in place
optionC: The spike is covered, because autoscaling always reacts to rising load
optionD: Spike tests are unnecessary once any autoscaling is configured
correctAnswerText: Scaling will not help in time; capacity must already be in place
explanation: Capacity that arrives after the spike is over does nothing for it, so the system must be pre-scaled or shed load cleanly during the spike. Stretching the test changes the question, and autoscaling does not remove the need to test sudden jumps.

prompt: What belongs in the "limits of this test" section of a performance report, so that readers do not over-trust the verdict?
optionA: The names of the team members who ran each of the steps
optionB: The tools considered for the test and why they lost out
optionC: What was stubbed or untested, and how often runs repeated
optionD: The full raw console output from every run in the test
correctAnswerText: What was stubbed or untested, and how often runs repeated
explanation: Stubbed dependencies, simulated data, untested paths and single runs all bound what the verdict can claim. Tool history and raw output belong elsewhere (an appendix or artefacts), and names do not change what the result means.

prompt: A single load run shows a p95 of 690 ms against an 800 ms target, two days before release. Should the team sign off on it?
optionA: Yes, provided the average was also under the 800 ms
optionB: No, because p95 must be well under half of the target value
optionC: Repeat the run and report the spread before signing off
optionD: Yes, because the number is already below the target
correctAnswerText: Repeat the run and report the spread before signing off
explanation: Results vary between runs, and one reading with a modest margin is weak evidence; repeating it shows whether 690 ms is typical. A pass from one run can be noise, there is no half-target rule, and an average adds nothing to a percentile target.

prompt: A service never returns errors under overload; it only gets slower. Which pass/fail gate catches that failure?
optionA: An error-rate limit only, since errors are the failures
optionB: A minimum throughput limit on aggregated requests per second
optionC: Per-endpoint p95 and p99 limits alongside the error rate
optionD: A limit on the single slowest request seen in the run
correctAnswerText: Per-endpoint p95 and p99 limits alongside the error rate
explanation: A system that degrades by slowness passes any error-only gate; percentile limits per endpoint catch it while the error limit still catches the other failure mode. One maximum is a single noisy sample, and an aggregate rate can stay flat while latency climbs.

prompt: In an Expo project, which command type-checks every file the tsconfig includes and writes no output files?
optionA: npx expo export
optionB: npx tsc --noEmit
optionC: npx expo start -c
optionD: npx expo install
correctAnswerText: npx tsc --noEmit
explanation: tsc is the TypeScript compiler, and --noEmit makes it check without writing JavaScript. expo start -c clears Metro's cache, expo export bundles through Babel (which strips types without checking them), and expo install adds SDK-matched packages.

prompt: Which TypeScript type has no values at all, and is what a union narrows to once every member has been handled?
optionA: void
optionB: never
optionC: undefined
optionD: unknown
correctAnswerText: never
explanation: never is the empty type: nothing can be assigned to it, which is why "const unreachable: never = p" compiles only when every case is handled. void is the return type of a function that returns nothing, unknown holds any value, and undefined is a value of its own.

prompt: Which built-in utility type produces an object type with the listed keys removed, such as an Order without id?
optionA: Exclude<T, K>
optionB: Omit<T, K>
optionC: Pick<T, K>
optionD: Partial<T>
correctAnswerText: Omit<T, K>
explanation: Omit<Order, 'id'> keeps every field except id. Pick does the opposite and keeps only the listed keys, Partial makes every field optional, and Exclude removes members from a union type rather than keys from an object type.

prompt: Which check, switched on by strict: true, makes tsc report errors such as "'vada' is possibly 'undefined'"?
optionA: noUnusedParameters
optionB: isolatedModules
optionC: noImplicitAny
optionD: strictNullChecks
correctAnswerText: strictNullChecks
explanation: strictNullChecks makes null and undefined their own types, so a value that may be missing must be checked before use. noImplicitAny reports values whose type cannot be worked out, noUnusedParameters is not part of strict, and isolatedModules is about per-file compilation.

prompt: What does a return type written as "x is MenuItem" declare about the function it belongs to?
optionA: It throws a TypeError at runtime when x is not a MenuItem
optionB: It tells the compiler to skip all checks on x in the body
optionC: It converts x into a MenuItem before the function returns
optionD: It is a type guard: a true result narrows x to MenuItem
correctAnswerText: It is a type guard: a true result narrows x to MenuItem
explanation: A type predicate tells TypeScript that wherever the function returns true, the argument may be treated as that type. It converts nothing and throws nothing on its own, and the compiler still checks the body; it simply trusts the boolean the body returns.

prompt: Which zod method checks a value and returns { success: true, data } or { success: false, error } without throwing?
optionA: parseAsync
optionB: safeParse
optionC: infer
optionD: coerce
correctAnswerText: safeParse
explanation: safeParse never throws; it returns a result to branch on, which suits validating items one by one. parseAsync returns a promise of the data and rejects on failure, z.infer is a compile-time type helper, and z.coerce converts input with Number(), String() and so on before checking it.

prompt: Which type does react-native export for the event object that a Pressable passes to onPress?
optionA: GestureResponderEvent
optionB: React.MouseEvent<Element>
optionC: React.ChangeEvent
optionD: KeyboardEvent
correctAnswerText: GestureResponderEvent
explanation: Presses and long presses deliver a GestureResponderEvent, with coordinates under nativeEvent. MouseEvent and ChangeEvent are web DOM event types, which tsc rejects on onPress, and KeyboardEvent is also a browser type.

prompt: Given type Order = { id: string; total: number }, what is the type keyof Order?
optionA: Order[keyof Order]
optionB: ["id", "total"]
optionC: string | number
optionD: "id" | "total"
correctAnswerText: "id" | "total"
explanation: keyof gives the union of the key names. string | number is the union of the value types, which is what Order[keyof Order] means; a tuple of names is an array type, not a union of keys.

prompt: Which type from React describes anything a component can render, and so is the usual type for a children prop?
optionA: PressableProps
optionB: ViewStyle
optionC: ComponentType
optionD: ReactNode
correctAnswerText: ReactNode
explanation: ReactNode covers elements, strings, numbers, arrays, null and the rest of what React can render. ViewStyle describes styles, ComponentType is a component rather than rendered output, and PressableProps is the props object of one component.

prompt: A schema transforms placedAt from an ISO string into a Date. What does z.input<typeof OrderSchema> describe?
optionA: The data after parsing, with placedAt as a Date
optionB: The function that parses a value at runtime
optionC: The schema object itself, with parse methods
optionD: The data as it arrives, before transforms run
correctAnswerText: The data as it arrives, before transforms run
explanation: z.input is the wire shape, so placedAt is a string there; z.infer (the output) has the Date. Runtime checking is done by parse and safeParse, and typeof OrderSchema on its own is the schema object's type.

prompt: Why do careful teams write const body: unknown = await res.json() instead of leaving the result typed any?
optionA: unknown makes Hermes check the shape of the response when it is parsed
optionB: unknown makes the parsed body smaller in memory on budget Android phones
optionC: any is refused by strict mode wherever a developer writes it explicitly
optionD: unknown must be narrowed or validated before use; any flows on unchecked
correctAnswerText: unknown must be narrowed or validated before use; any flows on unchecked
explanation: any switches checking off for the value and everything it touches, so a wrong shape travels until it crashes; unknown blocks use until a check or schema proves the shape. Types are erased, so neither changes runtime behaviour or memory, and strict mode forbids implicit any, not an explicit one.

prompt: With type Slot = { id: string; label: string }, bookSlot({ id: "s1", label: "7-8 pm", fee: 20 }) fails, yet passing a const that holds the same object compiles. Why?
optionA: TypeScript checks argument types only when the object is written inline
optionB: Types are structural; the extra-key check runs only on fresh object literals
optionC: A const is widened to any when it is passed, so the call is not checked at all
optionD: Assigning the object to a const strips the fee key before the call is made
correctAnswerText: Types are structural; the extra-key check runs only on fresh object literals
explanation: Any value with at least id and label is a Slot, so a wider object fits; the excess-property check (TS2353) is an extra rule for literals, where a stray key is probably a typo. The const keeps its precise type, nothing is stripped at runtime, and a variable argument is still checked for the required fields.

prompt: Why can a DabbaKart screen open normally in Expo Go while npx tsc --noEmit reports six errors in the same file?
optionA: Metro bundles through Babel, which strips types without checking them
optionB: The phone keeps the last good bundle until every type error is fixed
optionC: Expo Go runs its own older compiler that does not apply strict mode
optionD: tsc checks only the test files, never the app source that Metro bundles
correctAnswerText: Metro bundles through Babel, which strips types without checking them
explanation: Babel removes annotations and bundles what is left, so type errors never stop an app from running; only tsc checks types, which is why CI must run it. Expo Go has no type checker, tsc checks every included file, and a fresh bundle is served whatever its types say.

prompt: Why write export type MenuItem = z.infer<typeof MenuItemSchema> instead of a hand-written MenuItem interface beside the schema?
optionA: The type is derived from the schema, so the two can never drift apart
optionB: A hand-written interface makes zod skip fields it does not recognise
optionC: z.infer adds a runtime check to every place the MenuItem type is used
optionD: Interfaces cannot describe objects that came from a network response
correctAnswerText: The type is derived from the schema, so the two can never drift apart
explanation: With the type derived from the schema there is one definition: add a field to the schema and the type follows. z.infer is compile-time only, interfaces can describe any object shape, and zod's behaviour does not depend on whether an interface exists.

prompt: const [selected, setSelected] = useState(null); then setSelected(store) fails with "not assignable to SetStateAction<null>". Why?
optionA: setSelected can only be called inside an effect, never in a handler
optionB: Objects in state must be wrapped in a ref before they can be stored
optionC: useState refuses null as a start value whenever strict mode is switched on
optionD: The state type was inferred from null alone, so null is all it can hold
correctAnswerText: The state type was inferred from null alone, so null is all it can hold
explanation: useState infers its type from the initial value, and null tells it only "null"; useState<Store | null>(null) states what it will hold. null is a fine start value once the type says so, setters can be called anywhere, and objects are ordinary state.

prompt: A reviewer says function logValue<T>(x: T): void "gains nothing from being generic". What is the reasoning?
optionA: A type parameter must always carry a constraint such as T extends object
optionB: Generic functions are slower on Hermes, so they belong in hot paths only
optionC: T is used once, so it links no input to any output; unknown says the same
optionD: Functions returning void are not allowed to declare type parameters at all
correctAnswerText: T is used once, so it links no input to any output; unknown says the same
explanation: A type parameter earns its place when it appears at least twice, tying an input to an output (T[] in, T out). Types are erased, so speed is unaffected, constraints are optional, and void functions may be generic; this one simply gains nothing.

prompt: A useToggle hook ends with return [on, toggle] and callers cannot pass toggle to onPress. Why does return [on, toggle] as const fix it?
optionA: It makes a readonly tuple, so each position keeps its own type
optionB: It freezes the array at runtime, so toggle can no longer change
optionC: It turns toggle into a stable function, like wrapping useCallback
optionD: It tells React to skip re-rendering when the hook is called again
correctAnswerText: It makes a readonly tuple, so each position keeps its own type
explanation: An array literal is inferred as (boolean | (() => void))[], so each element might be either and onPress rejects it; as const infers readonly [boolean, () => void]. It is compile-time only: nothing is frozen, no identity is stabilised and rendering is unchanged.

prompt: MenuItem declares readonly id, and tsc rejects dosa.id = "m2". Why can an id still change while the app runs?
optionA: readonly protects nested objects but leaves top-level fields writable
optionB: readonly is a compile-time rule on this type only; nothing is frozen
optionC: Hermes ignores readonly only for string fields, not for numeric ones
optionD: readonly applies only in development builds and is dropped in release
correctAnswerText: readonly is a compile-time rule on this type only; nothing is frozen
explanation: readonly stops assignment through that type (TS2540) but is erased like every type, so code that reaches the object another way, or plain JavaScript, can still change it. It is the same in every build, Hermes knows nothing of it, and it is shallow rather than deep.

prompt: Why does theme.primry compile when theme is annotated : Record<string, string>, but fail when the object ends with satisfies Record<string, string>?
optionA: Record types reject misspelt keys only when declared with interface
optionB: satisfies checks the values but keeps the inferred keys of the object
optionC: satisfies converts the object into an enum whose keys are fixed for good
optionD: The annotation is checked only at runtime, while satisfies is not
correctAnswerText: satisfies checks the values but keeps the inferred keys of the object
explanation: An annotation replaces the inferred type with Record<string, string>, which allows any key; satisfies validates the object against it while keeping { primary: string }, so primry is TS2551. Nothing becomes an enum, neither check exists at runtime, and Record is not declared with interface.

prompt: Under strict mode, outlets[5].length compiles for a two-element string array and crashes. Why did the compiler allow it?
optionA: strict mode checks array indexes only inside for...of loops
optionB: String arrays are typed any[] until an element is assigned
optionC: Array lengths are checked only for tuples, and only when declared readonly
optionD: Index reads are assumed in range unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on
correctAnswerText: Index reads are assumed in range unless noUncheckedIndexedAccess is on
explanation: Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, outlets[5] is typed string; with it, string | undefined, and tsc reports the read. Tuples have fixed lengths but this is a plain array, loops are irrelevant, and a string[] is never any[].

prompt: Payment is { method: "UPI"; vpa: string } | { method: "CARD"; last4: string } | { method: "COD" }. Inside case "CARD": of switch (p.method), which expression compiles?
optionA: p.card.last4
optionB: p.vpa
optionC: p.last4
optionD: p.method.last4
correctAnswerText: p.last4
explanation: The discriminant narrows p to the CARD member, which has last4. p.vpa belongs only to UPI and gives TS2339 there, there is no nested card object, and method is a string literal with no last4 property.

prompt: A list row needs only id, name and rating from Restaurant, and must follow Restaurant if those fields change type. Which type fits?
optionA: Record<'id' | 'name' | 'rating', string>
optionB: Omit<Restaurant, 'id' | 'name' | 'rating'>
optionC: Partial<Restaurant> & { id: string }
optionD: Pick<Restaurant, 'id' | 'name' | 'rating'>
correctAnswerText: Pick<Restaurant, 'id' | 'name' | 'rating'>
explanation: Pick derives exactly those three fields from Restaurant, so a type change flows through. Omit keeps everything except them, the Partial version makes every field optional and keeps them all, and the Record hard-codes string for a rating that is a number or null.

prompt: A PincodeInput accepts every TextInput prop except onChangeText, which it replaces with onPincode(code: string). Which props type fits?
optionA: TextInputProps & { onPincode: (code: string) => void }
optionB: Omit<TextInputProps, 'onChangeText'> & { onPincode: (code: string) => void }
optionC: Pick<TextInputProps, 'onChangeText'> & { onPincode: (code: string) => void }
optionD: { onPincode: (code: string) => void; [prop: string]: any } & TextInputProps
correctAnswerText: Omit<TextInputProps, 'onChangeText'> & { onPincode: (code: string) => void }
explanation: Omit removes the replaced prop and the intersection adds the new one, so placeholder, maxLength and the rest keep their real types and passing onChangeText is a compile error. The plain intersection still accepts onChangeText, so callers can pass the prop the component overrides; Pick keeps only onChangeText; and an any index signature accepts misspelt props.

prompt: Which signature returns the last element of any array and gives the caller back the element type it passed in?
optionA: function lastOf<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined
optionB: function lastOf<T>(items: T): T[] | undefined
optionC: function lastOf(items: any[]): any
optionD: function lastOf(items: unknown[]): unknown | undefined
correctAnswerText: function lastOf<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined
explanation: T links the array's element type to the result, and | undefined covers an empty array, so lastOf(['a']) is string | undefined. The any version loses the type, the third takes T as the whole array and returns an array, and the unknown version forces every caller to narrow again.

prompt: fetchMenu is an async function that resolves to MenuItem[]. Which type names that resolved value without restating it by hand?
optionA: ReturnType<typeof fetchMenu>
optionB: Awaited<typeof fetchMenu>
optionC: Parameters<typeof fetchMenu>[0]
optionD: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchMenu>>
correctAnswerText: Awaited<ReturnType<typeof fetchMenu>>
explanation: ReturnType gives Promise<MenuItem[]> and Awaited unwraps the promise. ReturnType alone is still the promise (assigning it to MenuItem[] fails with TS2740), Parameters describes the arguments, and Awaited of the function type is just the function type.

prompt: An API leaves the offerText key out when a restaurant has no offer and sends a string otherwise. Which zod field describes it?
optionA: offerText: z.string().min(0)
optionB: offerText: z.string().nullable()
optionC: offerText: z.string().optional()
optionD: offerText: z.coerce.string()
correctAnswerText: offerText: z.string().optional()
explanation: optional() accepts a missing key (it parsed {} successfully) and gives string | undefined. nullable() accepts null but rejects a missing key, and both coerce.string() and string().min(0) still fail when the key is absent; coercing also turns other values into text it should not accept.

prompt: CartAction is { type: "add"; item: MenuItem } | { type: "remove"; id: string } | { type: "clear" }. Which dispatch compiles?
optionA: dispatch({ type: 'add', id: 'm1' })
optionB: dispatch({ type: 'remove', itemId: 'm1' })
optionC: dispatch({ type: 'clear', id: 'm1' })
optionD: dispatch({ type: 'remove', id: 'm1' })
correctAnswerText: dispatch({ type: 'remove', id: 'm1' })
explanation: The type literal selects one member and the object must match it. itemId is not a field of remove, add needs an item rather than an id, and clear takes no fields; tsc rejects all three with TS2353.

prompt: <FlatList data={dishes} renderItem={({ item }) => ...} />, where dishes is Dish[]. What type does item get with no annotation?
optionA: Dish, inferred from the data prop
optionB: Dish[], the whole array each time
optionC: any, because renderItem is untyped
optionD: unknown, until item is narrowed
correctAnswerText: Dish, inferred from the data prop
explanation: FlatList is generic and infers its item type from data, so item is a Dish and keyExtractor is checked too. If item ever comes out as any, the data is untyped upstream. renderItem receives one item at a time, not the array.

prompt: const METHODS = ["UPI", "CARD", "COD"] as const; What is the type (typeof METHODS)[number]?
optionA: "UPI" | "CARD" | "COD"
optionB: number, from the index
optionC: readonly string[] again
optionD: string, the element type
correctAnswerText: "UPI" | "CARD" | "COD"
explanation: as const makes a readonly tuple of literals, and indexing it with number gives the union of its elements, so a list you can loop over and a type you can check come from one line ("NETBANKING" is then rejected). Without as const the elements widen to string.

prompt: res is ApiOk | ApiError, where only ApiError has an error key and only ApiOk has data. Which check lets res.data.length compile inside it?
optionA: if (res.data !== undefined) { ... }
optionB: if (!('error' in res)) { ... }
optionC: if (typeof res === 'object') { ... }
optionD: if (res instanceof Object) { ... }
correctAnswerText: if (!('error' in res)) { ... }
explanation: The in operator narrows a union to the members with that key, so its negation leaves ApiOk. Both members are objects, so typeof and instanceof Object narrow nothing, and reading res.data before narrowing is itself TS2339, because ApiError has no data.

prompt: A hand-written isMenuItem(x): x is MenuItem was not updated when spiceLevel: number was added to MenuItem. Spice badges now show "undefined". What happened?
optionA: tsc stopped narrowing with the guard, so MenuItem became any in every screen using it
optionB: TypeScript widened spiceLevel to number | undefined when the guard was compiled
optionC: It still compiles and lets items without spiceLevel through, so code reads undefined
optionD: The guard now throws for items that do carry the spiceLevel field from the API
correctAnswerText: It still compiles and lets items without spiceLevel through, so code reads undefined
explanation: The compiler trusts a type predicate's boolean and never compares its body with the type, so the guard and the type drift apart silently. Narrowing still works, nothing throws, and the declared type stays number, which is exactly why the undefined is a surprise. A schema with z.infer cannot drift this way.

prompt: groupBy returns Record<K, T[]> and starts with const out = {} as Record<K, T[]>. groups.DESSERTS.length crashes for a menu with no desserts, and tsc is silent. Where is the fault?
optionA: PropertyKey should be narrowed to string so that missing keys are checked
optionB: The as lets the signature promise a list for every key it never created
optionC: The ??= operator is unsupported on Hermes and skips the key creation
optionD: Record types are erased in release builds, so they work in debug only
correctAnswerText: The as lets the signature promise a list for every key it never created
explanation: The assertion is where checking stopped: the body only creates keys it meets, yet the return type claims all of them. Returning Partial<Record<K, T[]>> needs no as and makes callers handle a missing group. Narrowing K changes nothing, types are erased in every build, and ??= works.

prompt: After WALLET joined the Payment union, the receipt screen showed a blank payment line with no compiler error. Its switch ends with default: return ''. Why was nothing reported?
optionA: Adding a member to an existing union is only checked when the app is rebuilt from scratch
optionB: Switch statements on string literals are not type-checked in .tsx files
optionC: The default branch accepts any member, so a missing case is never a type error
optionD: The WALLET member needs to be exported before switches can see that it exists
correctAnswerText: The default branch accepts any member, so a missing case is never a type error
explanation: A default that returns a value handles every unknown member quietly. Replacing it with const unreachable: never = p turns the gap into TS2322 at that switch. tsc checks on every run, .tsx files are checked like .ts, and union members need no separate export.

prompt: for (const k of Object.keys(prices)) total += prices[k]; fails with TS7053, where prices is { idli: number; dosa: number }. What is the compiler pointing at?
optionA: Object.keys returns string[], as the object may hold more keys than its type
optionB: prices must be declared with let before its fields can be read inside a loop
optionC: Number values cannot be read with bracket syntax once strict is on
optionD: for...of cannot iterate over the array that Object.keys gives back
correctAnswerText: Object.keys returns string[], as the object may hold more keys than its type
explanation: Types are structural, so a value typed { idli; dosa } may carry extra keys, and Object.keys is honestly string[]; a plain string cannot index the type. Loop over a typed list of keys or use Object.entries. let changes nothing, for...of works on any array, and bracket reads with a valid key are fine.

prompt: A bill showed Rs 0 when the API sent "total": "". The schema has total: z.coerce.number(). Why did parsing succeed?
optionA: z.coerce.number() skips empty strings and leaves the field at its default
optionB: coerce calls Number() first, and Number("") is 0, which is a valid number
optionC: The parse failed, but the screen caught the error and displayed a zero
optionD: Empty strings are treated as missing keys, and missing keys default to 0
correctAnswerText: coerce calls Number() first, and Number("") is 0, which is a valid number
explanation: z.coerce.number() converts with Number() before checking; in the run, "" and null both became 0 while "abc" failed. A strict rule such as z.string().regex(/^\d+(\.\d{1,2})?$/).transform(Number) rejects "" for money. zod has no implicit default, and the parse really did succeed.

prompt: const [state, setState] = useState({ status: 'loading' }); later setState({ status: 'success', data }) fails with TS2353 on data. What is the cause?
optionA: data must be wrapped in useMemo before it can be stored in React state
optionB: The state type was inferred from the first value, which has no data field
optionC: setState cannot accept an object that has more than one field in it
optionD: A status field must be declared as an enum before useState can use it at all
correctAnswerText: The state type was inferred from the first value, which has no data field
explanation: useState inferred { status: string } from the initial object, so data is an unknown property. useState<AsyncState<T>>({ status: 'loading' }) with a discriminated union fixes it. setState takes objects of any size, literal unions work without enums, and memoising data is irrelevant to the type.

prompt: const fee = feeByZone.get(zone)!.amount; compiles, then crashes for a shopper in a zone added last week. What went wrong?
optionA: The ! silenced a correct "possibly undefined": Map.get misses unknown keys
optionB: Map.get returns null instead of undefined, which ! does not cover at all
optionC: The ! assertion is removed only in release builds, so debug never crashed
optionD: Map keys must be numbers for get to find an entry that was set as a string
correctAnswerText: The ! silenced a correct "possibly undefined": Map.get misses unknown keys
explanation: Without the !, tsc reports TS2532 because get returns undefined for a missing key; the ! promised otherwise and nothing checked it. Handle the missing zone as a state of the screen. Map.get returns undefined, assertions are erased in every build, and string keys work.

prompt: seatLabel(s: Seat): string switched on s.state with no default and compiled. After "HELD" was added to the state union it reports TS2366, "Function lacks ending return statement". What does that mean?
optionA: string return types need an explicit return undefined after each switch
optionB: The new member must be listed first in the union for the switch to see it
optionC: The switch no longer covers every member, so a call can fall off the end
optionD: Every switch must have a default branch once a union has three members
correctAnswerText: The switch no longer covers every member, so a call can fall off the end
explanation: While every state had a case, TypeScript knew control could not reach the end; an unhandled HELD makes that path real, and the function would return undefined. Add the case. Defaults are optional, member order is irrelevant, and returning undefined from a string function is itself an error.

prompt: The server began sending status "READY_FOR_PICKUP". Users on last month's build see "could not load" on every active order; this week's build is fine. What is the cause?
optionA: The new status is too long for the string type the old build declared
optionB: The old build's strict z.enum rejects a value it was never told about
optionC: Old builds cache the previous API responses until the phone restarts
optionD: tsc on the server rejected the old build's request for the new field
correctAnswerText: The old build's strict z.enum rejects a value it was never told about
explanation: Installed builds keep running against today's API, and an old schema fails every order carrying the unknown value. The fix is a contract (new values ship after the app handles them) or a tested tolerant fallback. Caching would not fail every order, tsc never runs on requests, and string types have no length.

prompt: useRef<AppStateStatus>(AppState.currentState) fails with TS2769 under strict mode; currentState is declared string | null | undefined. Which fix is honest?
optionA: Cast the argument with as AppStateStatus so that the overload matches
optionB: Use useRef<any> so that any value from AppState can be stored in it
optionC: Turn off strictNullChecks for this file with a comment at the top
optionD: Type the ref as string | null | undefined, matching the declared value
correctAnswerText: Type the ref as string | null | undefined, matching the declared value
explanation: The error says the value may be null or undefined, which is true before the first change event; a ref typed to match (or a defaulted value) handles it. A cast hides that case, per-file strict switches are not a TypeScript feature, and any removes checking for every later use of the ref.

prompt: A team argues about interface versus type alias for object shapes in its React Native app. Which policy is soundest?
