optionA: One consistent rule, such as interface for shapes and type for the rest
optionB: No rule, because neither form can be checked by tsc or by any lint
optionC: Type aliases only, because interfaces cannot be exported from modules
optionD: Interfaces only, because only interfaces are able to describe unions
correctAnswerText: One consistent rule, such as interface for shapes and type for the rest
explanation: For object shapes the two are nearly interchangeable; aliases also name unions and tuples, and interfaces extend and merge. Consistency matters more than the choice, and some teams pick type everywhere because a duplicate alias is an error (TS2300) while a duplicate interface merges. Both export, only aliases express unions, and both are checked.

prompt: Order statuses arrive from the API as plain strings, and the project enables erasableSyntaxOnly. How should OrderStatus be declared?
optionA: As a union of string literals, perhaps derived from an as const array
optionB: As a numeric enum, so statuses compare faster on budget phones
optionC: As plain string, so any value the server sends is always accepted
optionD: As a string enum, which erasableSyntaxOnly was designed to allow through
correctAnswerText: As a union of string literals, perhaps derived from an as const array
explanation: A literal union erases to the same strings the JSON carries and works with tools that only strip types; enum declarations fail with TS1294 under erasableSyntaxOnly, string enums included. Types do not change speed, and plain string gives up every check the union provides.

prompt: Three screens read the same orders endpoint. A teammate proposes each screen validates the response "close to where it is used". What is the better design?
optionA: Validate nowhere, since the backend team already tests the response
optionB: Validate in each screen, since each one knows which fields it needs
optionC: Validate once in the API module, so screens only ever see typed data
optionD: Validate in a Babel plugin, so that bundling rejects a bad response
correctAnswerText: Validate once in the API module, so screens only ever see typed data
explanation: One schema per endpoint at the boundary means unknown never reaches a screen and nothing is checked three times or missed once. The server cannot protect an old installed build from a new response, and Babel runs at build time, long before any response exists.

prompt: A menu response of 80 dishes has one malformed imageUrl and, on another dish, a null price. Which validation policy serves users best?
optionA: Coerce both to defaults: an empty image URL and a price of zero rupees
optionB: Fall back to no image for the bad URL; drop the priceless dish and report it
optionC: Skip validation for menus entirely and validate only payment responses
optionD: Reject the whole menu, since any invalid field proves that the server is broken
correctAnswerText: Fall back to no image for the bad URL; drop the priceless dish and report it
explanation: Decide per field: a non-essential image can fall back (.catch(undefined) shows a placeholder), and an item missing a price is dropped from the list and reported rather than blanking 79 good dishes. Rejecting everything hides the menu, a zero price lists a dish as free, and no validation lets the null crash a label.

prompt: A 300-file app considers noUncheckedIndexedAccess, which reports several hundred new errors at once. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Turn it on only for release builds, where a crash would cost the most
optionB: Never use it, since strict mode already reports out-of-range index reads
optionC: Turn it on today and silence each new error with ! to keep the build green
optionD: Turn it on for new projects or packages first, not mid-way through this one
correctAnswerText: Turn it on for new projects or packages first, not mid-way through this one
explanation: The option is valuable but noisy, which is why the course advises starting with it on new code rather than flooding a large codebase. Hundreds of ! assertions would bury the real reports, strict does not include it, and tsc has no separate release mode.

prompt: A helper formats one OrderSummary for one screen. A teammate rewrites it as format<T extends object, K extends keyof T>(...) "for reuse". Your judgement?
optionA: Keep it concrete; generics pay off in shared utilities, hooks and API clients
optionB: Accept it, since generic functions run faster once Hermes has compiled them to bytecode
optionC: Accept it, since generic code is checked more strictly than concrete code
optionD: Reject it and type the helper's parameter as any so it fits every screen
correctAnswerText: Keep it concrete; generics pay off in shared utilities, hooks and API clients
explanation: Generics make shared code safer and one-off code harder to read; one concrete type handled once does not need a type parameter. Generic code is not checked more strictly, types are erased before Hermes runs anything, and any would remove the checks altogether.

prompt: The backend publishes an OpenAPI spec and the team now generates its TypeScript types from it. Is runtime validation of responses still worth keeping?
optionA: No: the spec guarantees that old builds will receive the old shape
optionB: No: types generated from the spec are checked when responses arrive
optionC: Yes: generated types are still erased, so pair them with schemas
optionD: Yes, but only in development builds, where the bugs are first found
correctAnswerText: Yes: generated types are still erased, so pair them with schemas
explanation: Generating types keeps them in step with the documentation, but they are still only types, so a server that changes or misbehaves is caught only by a runtime check (or by generating schemas too). Nothing checks generated types at runtime, a spec does not freeze what old builds receive, and production is where unexpected data arrives.

prompt: A rupee total arrives as a string such as "240.00". Which schema choice is safest for money, and why?
optionA: z.string() kept as text, since screens can convert totals when they show them
optionB: z.number(), since the server will switch back to numbers before long
optionC: z.coerce.number(), since it accepts every format the server might send
optionD: A strict decimal pattern with transform(Number), since bad input then fails
correctAnswerText: A strict decimal pattern with transform(Number), since bad input then fails
explanation: The pattern-and-transform rule turned "240.00" into 240 and failed for "" and null, so a missing total becomes an error rather than a bill. coerce accepts too much (it made "" and null into 0), z.number() rejects the real response, and leaving text pushes conversion and its bugs into every screen.

prompt: An interviewer asks whether validating every API response will slow the app on budget Android phones. Which answer shows the best judgement?
optionA: Yes, so replace each schema with an as cast once the API is stable
optionB: No, because Hermes compiles zod schemas into native code at build time
optionC: Yes, so validate only in development and remove the schemas in release builds
optionD: Parsing is small beside the network call; measure, then trim if it shows up
correctAnswerText: Parsing is small beside the network call; measure, then trim if it shows up
explanation: Validation costs little next to a round trip, and the honest answer is to profile a huge list on a low-end phone before changing anything, then validate only the fields the screen uses if it matters. Removing checks in release drops them where bad data arrives, Hermes does not compile zod natively, and a cast checks nothing.

prompt: A tracking screen's state is { loading: boolean; rider?: Rider; error?: string }. A pull request silences "s.rider is possibly undefined" with s.rider!.name. Best review response?
optionA: Approve it, because the API always sends a rider once loading becomes false
optionB: Model the screen as a discriminated union so rider exists only where it is real
optionC: Replace the ! with ?. so that an absent rider shows as an empty name instead
optionD: Mark rider as required in the type so that the warning can never appear on that line again
correctAnswerText: Model the screen as a discriminated union so rider exists only where it is real
explanation: The warning points at real states the loose type allows: no rider assigned yet, or already delivered. A union of loading, searching, on-the-way (with rider), delivered and failed lets narrowing supply the rider only where it exists. Trusting the API is the next crash, ?. shows a blank instead of the right message, and a required rider lies about the data.

prompt: In React Native's new architecture, which part lets JavaScript hold and call native C++ objects directly, with no JSON messages?
optionA: Yoga
optionB: Codegen
optionC: JSI
optionD: Metro
correctAnswerText: JSI
explanation: JSI (the JavaScript Interface) replaced the old bridge's serialised, batched messages with direct calls. Yoga is the Flexbox layout engine, Metro is the bundler, and Codegen generates native glue from typed TurboModule specs.

prompt: What does Hermes, React Native's default engine, do with an app's JavaScript in a release build?
optionA: Loads it into a WebView with its own browser engine
optionB: Runs it, compiled ahead of time to Hermes bytecode
optionC: Translates it into Kotlin and Swift source to build
optionD: Checks its TypeScript types each time the app opens
correctAnswerText: Runs it, compiled ahead of time to Hermes bytecode
explanation: Hermes is the JavaScript engine; release bundles are compiled to bytecode at build time, so the phone does not parse source at launch, which helps startup and memory on budget phones. Nothing is translated to Kotlin or Swift, there is no WebView, and types were erased long before.

prompt: Which flexDirection does a React Native View use when the style does not set one?
optionA: the parent's value
optionB: row
optionC: column
optionD: row-reverse
correctAnswerText: column
explanation: Every View is a flex container whose children stack vertically by default, unlike the web's row default. Styles do not cascade in React Native, so nothing is inherited from the parent either.

prompt: Which API returns the current window width and re-renders the component when it changes, as on rotation or a foldable opening?
optionA: useWindowDimensions()
optionB: Dimensions.get('screen')
optionC: PixelRatio.get()
optionD: Platform.Version
correctAnswerText: useWindowDimensions()
explanation: useWindowDimensions is a hook that updates on every window change and also reports scale and fontScale. Dimensions.get is a one-time read that goes stale, PixelRatio.get is the density, and Platform.Version is the OS version.

prompt: Which core component shows a long, virtualised list of orders grouped under month headers?
optionA: SectionList
optionB: ScrollView
optionC: GroupedView
optionD: ListView
correctAnswerText: SectionList
explanation: SectionList virtualises like FlatList and adds section headers (sticky by default on iOS, off on Android). ScrollView renders every child at once; GroupedView does not exist, and ListView was removed from React Native long ago.

prompt: In Expo Router, what does putting screens inside a folder named (tabs) do to their URLs?
optionA: It adds /tabs to the start of each URL path
optionB: It hides those screens from every deep link
optionC: Nothing: a group folder adds no URL segment
optionD: It makes each file's URL a query parameter
correctAnswerText: Nothing: a group folder adds no URL segment
explanation: Parenthesised folders organise files (and hold a _layout that picks the navigator) without appearing in the path, so app/(tabs)/orders is /orders. Group folders do not block links or turn paths into query strings.

prompt: Which field of an Expo permission response tells the app whether the system dialog can still be shown?
optionA: canAskAgain
optionB: expires
optionC: granted
optionD: accuracyLevel
correctAnswerText: canAskAgain
explanation: When canAskAgain is false the system will not show its dialog again, so request() silently resolves "denied" and the app must offer Open settings. granted says whether access is allowed now, expires says how long, and accuracyLevel is not a field of the response (location precision lives under android.accuracy and ios.accuracy).

prompt: Which AppState value means another app or the home screen is now in front of yours?
optionA: 'foreground'
optionB: 'inactive'
optionC: 'suspended'
optionD: 'background'
correctAnswerText: 'background'
explanation: The states are active, background and, on iOS only, inactive: the brief state while the app switcher opens or a call arrives. suspended and foreground are not AppState values.

prompt: Which Reanimated hook creates a value that lives on the UI thread and does not re-render the component when it changes?
optionA: useSharedValue
optionB: useState
optionC: useRef
optionD: useAnimatedStyle
correctAnswerText: useSharedValue
explanation: A shared value is read and written by worklets on the UI thread; changing it re-runs animated styles, not the component. useAnimatedStyle derives a style from shared values, useState re-renders on change, and useRef lives on the JavaScript thread.

prompt: Behind Expo's push service, which platform services deliver a push notification to Android and to iOS phones?
optionA: WorkManager and BGTaskScheduler
optionB: Play Integrity and App Attest
optionC: FCM for Android and APNs for iOS
optionD: APNs for Android and FCM for iOS
correctAnswerText: FCM for Android and APNs for iOS
explanation: The path is your API, Expo's push service, then Firebase Cloud Messaging or the Apple Push Notification service, then the phone. WorkManager and BGTaskScheduler run background tasks, and Play Integrity and App Attest vouch for genuine app copies.

prompt: A product list scrolls smoothly, but Add buttons respond late while a search filter runs. Why does that pattern point at the JavaScript thread?
optionA: Native scrolling needs no JavaScript, but every onPress and setState does
optionB: The UI thread queues every tap behind scrolling, so taps always come last
optionC: Hermes pauses while a list scrolls to save battery, so taps wait for it
optionD: Yoga runs layout on the JavaScript thread, so a filter stops all drawing
correctAnswerText: Native scrolling needs no JavaScript, but every onPress and setState does
explanation: A native ScrollView keeps moving on the UI thread while JavaScript is busy, but a tap must run onPress and a state update on the JavaScript thread. A busy UI thread would make scrolling janky too, layout is not computed on the JS thread in that way, and Hermes does not pause for scrolling.

prompt: Why can a barcode library that ships its own native code never work inside Expo Go, however often node_modules is reinstalled?
optionA: Metro refuses to bundle any package that includes Kotlin or Swift files
optionB: Native libraries load on emulators only, never on a phone over Wi-Fi
optionC: Expo Go only loads libraries that the Expo team has reviewed for its store
optionD: Native code must be compiled into the binary, and Expo Go's set is fixed
correctAnswerText: Native code must be compiled into the binary, and Expo Go's set is fixed
explanation: Metro ships JavaScript; native code is part of the installed app, and Expo Go is a prebuilt app with one SDK's modules. A development build containing the library (or an Expo module such as expo-camera that Expo Go includes) is the fix. Metro simply ignores native sources, and there is no review gate or emulator-only rule.

prompt: Why does <Image source={{ uri: product.thumbnailUrl }} /> with no style show nothing on screen, and raise no error?
optionA: Remote images load only after the user grants the photo library permission
optionB: A remote image has no size until given one, so it is drawn at zero by zero
optionC: Remote URIs must be passed through require(), or the request is dropped
optionD: An Image must be wrapped in a Text component before it can be drawn at all
correctAnswerText: A remote image has no size until given one, so it is drawn at zero by zero
explanation: A local require()d image knows its size; a network image does not, so it needs a width and height or a width with aspectRatio. TypeScript cannot catch this and nothing throws. Showing images needs no permission, Text is for strings, and require() is for bundled files only.

prompt: After changing app.json to "userInterfaceStyle": "automatic", the development build is still always light after pressing r. Why?
optionA: useColorScheme reads the setting only once a day, to save on battery use
optionB: Dark mode works only in release builds, and never in any development build
optionC: The r key reloads styles but not the theme hook, which needs the j key
optionD: It is native configuration, so it needs a new build; a reload is not enough
correctAnswerText: It is native configuration, so it needs a new build; a reload is not enough
explanation: app.json is read at build time and feeds the native projects; a JavaScript reload runs new JavaScript inside the same binary. The blank template ships "light", which locks useColorScheme to light until the app is rebuilt. The other options describe behaviour that does not exist.

prompt: Why does an Orders screen's polling interval, started in useEffect, keep running after Order Detail is pushed on top of it?
optionA: Native stacks re-run the effects of every screen in the stack on each frame
optionB: Intervals ignore effect clean-up in React Native and must be paused by hand
optionC: The screen below stays mounted in the stack, so its effect is never cleaned up
optionD: Pushed screens share a timer queue with the screen below, and replay its ticks
correctAnswerText: The screen below stays mounted in the stack, so its effect is never cleaned up
explanation: A stack keeps the screens underneath mounted (that is why their scroll position survives), so their effects run on out of sight. useFocusEffect, with its callback in useCallback, starts work on focus and cleans up on blur. Clean-up works normally; it simply never runs because nothing unmounted.

prompt: A dish screen reads { id } with useLocalSearchParams and never finds a dish, though the ids in local data are numbers. Why?
optionA: Route params come from a URL, so id is the string "101", not 101
optionB: Params arrive after the first render, so find runs on undefined
optionC: Numeric ids are stripped from the URL unless the route is typed
optionD: useLocalSearchParams returns only the params of the parent layout
correctAnswerText: Route params come from a URL, so id is the string "101", not 101
explanation: In Expo Router every screen is a URL, so params are strings even if a number was passed; 101 === "101" is false, and strict TypeScript reports the comparison (TS2367). Convert once with Number() and treat a non-integer as not found. The other options misdescribe the hook.

prompt: Why should an app decide its Android notification channels, and their importance, before the first release?
optionA: Once a channel exists on a phone, the app cannot raise its importance
optionB: FCM drops messages for channels created after the app was installed
optionC: Play Console freezes every channel id once the first review has passed
optionD: Channels are compiled into the APK and cannot be created at runtime
correctAnswerText: Once a channel exists on a phone, the app cannot raise its importance
explanation: From creation the user owns a channel's settings, so raising "orders" later does nothing for existing installs; the fix is a new channel id. Channels are created at runtime with setNotificationChannelAsync, and neither Play Console nor FCM freezes them.

prompt: Why is a React Native app registered with an identity provider as a public client that holds no client secret?
optionA: Hermes bytecode cannot store strings longer than a few dozen characters
optionB: Identity providers refuse client secrets from any app that is written in JavaScript
optionC: Anything compiled into the app can be read out of the package anyone downloads
optionD: Client secrets only work over Wi-Fi, and phones mostly use mobile data now
correctAnswerText: Anything compiled into the app can be read out of the package anyone downloads
explanation: A secret in the APK is a secret anyone can extract, so OAuth gives mobile apps none and relies on PKCE to make a stolen code useless. Secrets have nothing to do with the network type, Hermes stores strings as strings, and the rule applies to native apps as much as JavaScript ones.

prompt: Why does a fare sheet built with Reanimated and Gesture Handler keep following the finger while the JavaScript thread is busy?
optionA: The gesture, shared value and animated style all run on the UI thread
optionB: The JavaScript thread gets top priority whenever a finger is touching
optionC: Shared values are React state batched once per frame by the renderer
optionD: Reanimated pauses React rendering until the drag has fully finished
correctAnswerText: The gesture, shared value and animated style all run on the UI thread
explanation: Gesture Handler recognises touches on the UI thread, and worklets update the shared value and style there, so nothing waits for JavaScript. Reanimated does not pause React, shared values are not React state, and thread priority does not change on touch.

prompt: A checkout screen is wrapped in an error boundary, yet an error thrown in the Pay button's onPress is not caught by it. Why?
optionA: Boundaries are disabled in release builds and work only in development
optionB: Boundaries catch errors thrown while rendering; handlers run outside it
optionC: Pressable swallows every error its handlers throw before React sees it
optionD: Boundaries catch only errors from their own component, not from children
correctAnswerText: Boundaries catch errors thrown while rendering; handlers run outside it
explanation: An error boundary catches errors during rendering and lifecycle methods of its children; an event handler or async callback needs its own try/catch that sets an error state. Boundaries do cover children, Pressable does not swallow errors, and boundaries work in release builds, where an uncaught render error is otherwise fatal.

prompt: A product grid on a 412 dp wide window has 16 dp of padding on each side, 2 columns and an 8 dp gap between them. How wide is each card?
optionA: 206 dp
optionB: 198 dp
optionC: 190 dp
optionD: 186 dp
correctAnswerText: 186 dp
explanation: (412 − 2 × 16 − 8) / 2 = 186 dp. 190 forgets the gap, 198 subtracts one side's padding only, and 206 ignores padding and gap. Compute it from useWindowDimensions() rather than hard-coding it, so other widths work too.

prompt: A FlatList has a 700 dp viewport, 2,000 dp of content and onEndReachedThreshold={0.5}. Which is the smallest of these scroll offsets at which onEndReached qualifies to fire?
optionA: 600 dp
optionC: 900 dp
explanation: The threshold is in visible lengths, so it fires when less than 0.5 × 700 = 350 dp is left below. The distance left is 2,000 − 700 − offset: 700 at 600, 400 at 900, 300 at 1,000. 1,300 also qualifies (0 left) but is not the first.

prompt: A filter sheet must close on Android Back, and only after that may Back leave the screen. Which listener does that?
optionA: While open, a hardwareBackPress handler that closes and returns true, removed in clean-up
optionB: From mount, a hardwareBackPress handler that calls BackHandler.exitApp() after closing
optionC: From mount, a hardwareBackPress handler that closes and returns true, never removed after
optionD: While open, a hardwareBackPress handler that closes and returns false, removed in clean-up
correctAnswerText: While open, a hardwareBackPress handler that closes and returns true, removed in clean-up
explanation: Handlers run newest first, and returning true marks Back as handled, so the screen's own Back does not also run. Subscribing only while open and removing in clean-up lets the next Back reach the navigator. Returning false lets the screen close too, a listener never removed swallows Back for good, and exitApp leaves the app.

prompt: In a bus-booking app with tabs, the payment screen must hide the tab bar, and Back must not reach it after a successful booking. Where does it go?
optionA: In the Trips tab's stack, with the ticket pushed on top of it once it succeeds
optionB: In the root stack above the tabs, with the ticket replacing it on success
optionC: In a drawer beside the tabs, opened by the Pay button on the seat screen
optionD: As a hidden fourth tab, shown by switching to it when payment is needed
correctAnswerText: In the root stack above the tabs, with the ticket replacing it on success
explanation: Screens that should not show the tab bar belong in the root stack, and router.replace (or dismissTo) swaps payment for the ticket so Back cannot return to it. A tab's stack keeps the tab bar, pushing leaves payment underneath, and a drawer or hidden tab is the wrong navigator for a one-way task.

prompt: useCameraPermissions returns status "denied" with canAskAgain false. What should the parcel-scan screen offer?
optionA: An explanation, an Open settings button and a type-the-code fallback
optionB: A notice that scanning is unavailable, ending the delivery flow there
optionC: Nothing new; request the permission again in an effect until granted
optionD: An Allow camera button that calls requestPermission once more on tap
correctAnswerText: An explanation, an Open settings button and a type-the-code fallback
explanation: With canAskAgain false only Settings can change the answer, so Linking.openSettings() is the way forward, and the app must still work without the camera. A request now resolves "denied" with no dialog, which looks broken; an effect loop requests forever; and ending the flow abandons the rider.

prompt: A home screen needs only the city the user is in, to pick a store. Which expo-location approach fits best?
optionA: startLocationUpdatesAsync with a foreground service running
optionB: getLastKnownPositionAsync, falling back to a Low accuracy fix
optionC: watchPositionAsync at BestForNavigation for the whole session
optionD: getCurrentPositionAsync at Highest accuracy on each screen open
correctAnswerText: getLastKnownPositionAsync, falling back to a Low accuracy fix
explanation: Accuracy is a battery decision: a recent cached fix or a kilometre-level fix answers "which city" without keeping the GPS on. Continuous navigation-grade updates, background updates with a service, and the highest accuracy on every open all spend battery for precision the screen does not use.

prompt: Before upload, a 3000 × 4000 portrait photo is resized so its longer edge is at most 1280 px, keeping the aspect ratio. What size results?
explanation: The longer edge is the height, so it becomes 1280 and the width scales by the same factor: 3000 × 1280 / 4000 = 960. Setting the width to 1280 instead gives 1280 × 1707, taller than the limit; 1280 × 960 swaps the orientation; and 3000 × 1280 distorts the photo.

prompt: Where should a React Native app keep its short-lived access token and its long-lived refresh token?
optionA: Access token in memory; refresh token in expo-secure-store
optionB: Both in a persisted Zustand store, saved to AsyncStorage
optionC: Access token in expo-secure-store; refresh token in app.json
optionD: Both in AsyncStorage, under a key name that looks harmless
correctAnswerText: Access token in memory; refresh token in expo-secure-store
explanation: The refresh token must survive a restart and is valuable, so it goes to the Keystore or Keychain through expo-secure-store; the access token is used on every request and can live in memory. AsyncStorage (directly or through a persisted store) is a plain file, a key name hides nothing, and app.json is build configuration.

prompt: A card has shadowColor, shadowOpacity and shadowRadius, and shows a shadow on iPhone but none on Android. Which change gives both a shadow?
optionA: Platform.select: the shadow props on iOS, elevation on Android
optionB: A larger shadowRadius, which Android needs before it draws one
optionC: A .shadow.css file imported into the card component module
optionD: shadowOffset added, since Android draws only offset shadows
correctAnswerText: Platform.select: the shadow props on iOS, elevation on Android
explanation: The shadow* properties are iOS-only; Android uses elevation (with a background colour on the view). With the new architecture boxShadow also works on both. Radius and offset are still iOS properties, and React Native has no CSS files.

prompt: The link thaligo://pay?orderId=4521&amountPaise=100 opens the app. What should the pay screen do with amountPaise?
optionA: Use it if it matches the cart total saved on the phone, then pay at once
optionB: Show it beside the cart total and let the user choose which one to pay
optionC: Ignore it; fetch the order's amount from the server and ask to confirm
optionD: Use it, since links in SMS messages come from the company's own server
correctAnswerText: Ignore it; fetch the order's amount from the server and ask to confirm
explanation: Any app, page or message can open a custom-scheme link, so a link may name an order but never set an amount, payee or role; the server supplies the amount and the user taps to confirm. Matching phone-side data can be tampered with, SMS senders are not proof, and offering a choice still trusts the link.

prompt: A cart badge renders <View>{count && <Text>{count}</Text>}</View>. With an empty cart the phone shows "Text strings must be rendered within a <Text> component". Why?
optionA: A Text rendered conditionally needs a key prop, or React Native throws
optionB: count is undefined for an empty cart, and undefined can never be rendered
optionC: A View cannot hold a conditional child, so every && needs a ternary
optionD: With count 0 the expression is 0, a bare number placed directly in a View
correctAnswerText: With count 0 the expression is 0, a bare number placed directly in a View
explanation: 0 && x is 0, and React renders numbers, so a raw 0 lands inside a View, which only native Text may hold. count > 0 && ... makes the condition a real boolean. undefined renders nothing, conditional children are fine when the condition is boolean, and keys are for lists. A jest render did not throw here, so check the rendered tree.

prompt: A delivery-slot FlatList uses renderItem = useCallback(..., []). The tick never moves to a newly chosen slot, even with extraData={selected}. Why?
optionA: extraData accepts only arrays, so a single selected id is silently ignored by the list
optionB: FlatList re-renders rows only when data changes identity, never otherwise
optionC: renderItem keeps the first selected value; extraData cannot refresh a stale function
optionD: The tick needs getItemLayout, without which rows are never measured again
correctAnswerText: renderItem keeps the first selected value; extraData cannot refresh a stale function
explanation: An empty dependency list freezes the closure, so FlatList re-runs the same function that still sees the first selection. Honest dependencies ([selected]) plus extraData, or a memo row that receives selected as a prop, fix it. extraData takes any value, it is exactly the way to re-render on other changes, and getItemLayout is about measurement.

prompt: Order history sometimes shows page 2 twice after a fast fling. The list has onEndReached={() => fetchPage(page + 1)}. What is the cause?
optionA: keyExtractor returned the index, so React copied the second page twice
optionB: The threshold must be 0, or onEndReached fires twice on every Android
optionC: FlatList always requests each page twice to fill its windowSize buffer
optionD: onEndReached fired again before page 2 arrived, and nothing guarded it
correctAnswerText: onEndReached fired again before page 2 arrived, and nothing guarded it
explanation: onEndReached can fire more than once for the same end (a fling, a re-render), so guard with a loading flag and hasMore, advance the page only when a page arrives, and de-duplicate by id when appending. FlatList requests nothing itself, index keys cause other bugs, and threshold 0 does not make the event fire once.

prompt: Signed-in users who tap an order link land on Home. The root layout sets signedIn = status === "signedIn" and renders its guarded Stack straight away. What is happening?
optionA: The link opens before the splash screen, so Expo Router discards its path
optionB: While restoring, the guard sees "signed out", redirects, and the link is lost
optionC: Stack.Protected ignores deep links unless the user signs in again every time
optionD: Guards always send the user to the anchor first and only then to the link
correctAnswerText: While restoring, the guard sees "signed out", redirects, and the link is lost
explanation: Reading the saved session is async, and a boolean treats "not read yet" as signed out, so the guard redirects to sign-in and then, once restored, to Home. Keep three states and return null (with the splash up) while restoring. Guards do honour links, the splash is not the cause, and guards redirect only when false.

prompt: A notification opens /orders/4521, and Back goes to the Home tab instead of the orders list. The Orders stack holds only [orderId]. Which fix addresses the cause?
optionA: Move [orderId].tsx into the root stack, above the tab navigator
optionB: Set unstable_settings = { anchor: 'index' } in the orders layout
optionC: Push /orders and then /orders/4521 from the notification handler
optionD: Set backBehavior to 'history' on the bottom tab navigator itself
correctAnswerText: Set unstable_settings = { anchor: 'index' } in the orders layout
explanation: Opened cold, the nested stack has nothing under the detail, so Back leaves the tab; the anchor puts the list underneath. Two pushes break for links from outside the app, backBehavior governs moves between tabs, and the root stack would hide the tab bar.

prompt: useEffect(() => { if (!permission?.granted) requestPermission(); }, [permission]). Riders who blocked the camera say the scanner hangs. Why?
optionA: requestPermission throws for blocked users, and the effect has no catch
optionB: Each request yields a new denied object, which re-runs the effect forever
optionC: The dependency should be permission.status, which never changes at all
optionD: The effect runs only once, so a blocked rider is never asked a second time
correctAnswerText: Each request yields a new denied object, which re-runs the effect forever
explanation: Every request resolves a fresh response object; for a blocked user it is still denied, so the effect sees a new value and requests again (a test counted 50 requests from one visit before its stop). Request on a tap and branch on canAskAgain instead. The effect does re-run, request resolves rather than throws, and depending on status hides the loop rather than fixing the design.

prompt: After a user has opened the cart screen three times, returning to the app refreshes the cart three times. Its effect calls AppState.addEventListener and returns nothing. Why?
optionA: AppState fires change three times on Android for every single return
optionB: The cart refresh retries twice by default whenever the app comes back
optionC: React runs effects three times in release builds, to detect any side effects
optionD: Each visit added a listener that outlived the screen, as none was removed
correctAnswerText: Each visit added a listener that outlived the screen, as none was removed
explanation: addEventListener returns a subscription; without return () => sub.remove() each mount adds another listener that keeps firing after unmount (a test showed 3 listeners and 3 refreshes). The same rule covers watchPositionAsync and notification listeners. AppState sends one change per transition, and release builds do not repeat effects.

prompt: Sign-outs spike each morning. At launch five requests get 401 together and each calls /auth/refresh; the server rotates refresh tokens. What is the client bug?
optionA: Each request refreshes alone; a reused token makes the server end the session
optionB: Five requests at launch exceed the API's limit and trigger a forced logout
optionC: The access token lifetime is too short, so users must log in every morning
optionD: expo-secure-store loses its saved contents overnight on most budget Android phones
correctAnswerText: Each request refreshes alone; a reused token makes the server end the session
explanation: The first refresh wins; the next presents the now-spent token, reuse detection revokes the whole family, and the user is signed out. One shared refresh promise that every 401 awaits (cleared in finally), then one replay, fixes it. Short access tokens are expected, and neither rate limits nor secure storage explain it.

prompt: Corporate sign-in reaches the provider and returns, then the token exchange fails with invalid_grant. The challenge comes from digestStringAsync with no options. Likely cause?
optionA: invalid_grant means the user typed the wrong company password
optionB: The redirect URI must be an https link, never a custom app scheme
optionC: The verifier is too long; PKCE accepts at most 32 random characters
optionD: The digest is hex by default; a PKCE challenge must be base64url
correctAnswerText: The digest is hex by default; a PKCE challenge must be base64url
explanation: code_challenge is BASE64URL(SHA-256(verifier)); hex (and plain base64 with + / =) never matches, so the server rejects the exchange. Ask for base64 and convert, or let expo-auth-session build the pair. Verifiers are 43 to 128 characters, custom schemes are allowed redirect URIs, and a wrong password fails at the provider's page, before any code exists.

prompt: App Links open the app for debug builds installed over USB, but Play Store users get a browser chooser instead. assetlinks.json lists the upload key's SHA-256. Cause?
optionA: Play re-signs the app, so the file must list the app-signing key's fingerprint
optionB: assetlinks.json is read only after the user has opened the app at least once
optionC: Play Store builds ignore intent filters unless the scheme is a custom one
optionD: App Links work only when the app is installed by USB with developer options on
correctAnswerText: Play re-signs the app, so the file must list the app-signing key's fingerprint
explanation: Verification compares the file with the key that signed the installed app, and Play signs releases with its own app-signing key (shown in Play Console). adb shell pm get-app-links shows the verification state. Store installs support App Links, verification happens at install with autoVerify, and https intent filters are the point of App Links.

prompt: A new consumer app needs Android first, iOS later, and one payments SDK with its own native code. Which setup is the soundest default?
optionA: Expo with a development build, adding the SDK through its config plugin
optionB: Expo Go only, asking the SDK vendor to add its module to the Expo Go app
optionC: The bare CLI, because an Expo app cannot contain native libraries at all
optionD: Two native apps, because one native SDK rules out React Native entirely
correctAnswerText: Expo with a development build, adding the SDK through its config plugin
explanation: React Native's docs recommend a framework, and with development builds, config plugins and prebuild an Expo app can include any native library. Expo Go's module set is fixed, "Expo cannot use native code" is outdated, and one SDK is no reason to maintain two codebases.

prompt: A start-up's core feature is AR try-on with heavy live camera processing, and its web team writes React. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Native may fit better here; React Native suits apps less tied to the platform
optionB: React Native, since one shared codebase is always cheaper in the long run
optionC: A WebView shell, since the web team can then reuse all of its React code unchanged
optionD: Flutter, since drawing its own widgets speeds up the whole camera pipeline
correctAnswerText: Native may fit better here; React Native suits apps less tied to the platform
explanation: Apps that live on platform features (heavy camera and media work, AR) are where native's full access pays off; React Native shines when a React team needs both platforms with native UI. "Always cheaper" ignores the feature, Flutter's own rendering does not speed camera processing, and a WebView is not React Native at all.

prompt: A food-delivery app's team proposes certificate pinning for its API. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Usually skip it: a bad pin cuts off every install; spend the effort server-side
optionB: Pin in native config, since an over-the-air update can fix a wrong pin quickly
optionC: Pin the leaf certificate, since a renewed certificate always keeps its pin
optionD: Pin with no backup pin, since a second pin weakens the protection it gives
correctAnswerText: Usually skip it: a bad pin cuts off every install; spend the effort server-side
explanation: TLS already validates the chain; pinning adds protection at the risk that a rotated key stops every installed copy talking to the server, which banking and payment apps accept with a backup pin and an expiry. Pins are of the public key (SPKI), a backup pin is essential, and native pins cannot be changed by an OTA update.

prompt: A payment gateway secret and a maps API key are both set as EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables in an Expo app. What should change?
optionA: Move both into app.json extra, which is never shipped inside the app
optionB: Drop the EXPO_PUBLIC_ prefix so the bundle stores both values encrypted
optionC: Move the payment secret to the server; restrict the maps key to the app
optionD: Keep both, since Hermes bytecode hides string constants from inspection
correctAnswerText: Move the payment secret to the server; restrict the maps key to the app
explanation: EXPO_PUBLIC_ values are inlined into the bundle, and a simple scan of an unzipped APK finds them; Hermes keeps strings as strings. A payment secret must stay on the server, which calls the provider; a key that must ship is restricted by package name and signing certificate. Without the prefix the value is simply undefined in the app, and app.json extra ships too.

prompt: A grocery company has a customer app that shows the rider on a map, and a rider app that reports position during shifts. Which location permissions fit?
optionA: Neither: geofences need no location permission and cover both cases
optionB: Customer: foreground only; rider: background, with a foreground service
optionC: Customer: background, so the map is ready the moment the app is opened
optionD: Both apps: background, so that tracking survives when the screen is locked
correctAnswerText: Customer: foreground only; rider: background, with a foreground service
explanation: The customer only looks at a map while the app is open; the rider must report with the screen off, which needs background permission, a visible foreground-service notification and an End shift that stops it, and both stores ask for justification. Asking customers for background access costs trust for nothing, and geofences need background location themselves.

prompt: A 40-row results list stutters on a mid-range Android phone, and a teammate wants to switch to FlashList today. Which response is soundest?
optionA: Profile a release build on that phone first, then switch if the list is the cause
optionB: Profile in development mode first, since that is where slowness is easiest to see
optionC: Raise windowSize to 50 first, since keeping more rows mounted always scrolls better
optionD: Switch now, since FlashList is faster than FlatList for every kind of list there is
correctAnswerText: Profile a release build on that phone first, then switch if the list is the cause
explanation: The cause may be unstable props defeating memo, inline styles, or full-size images, none of which a new list fixes; measure with the Profiler and performance monitor on a release build on the slow phone. Development mode is much slower than what users run, and a larger window keeps more rows (and images) in memory.

prompt: A reminder must appear exactly 30 minutes before a customer's delivery slot, even if the app is closed. Which tool is right?
optionA: A local notification scheduled for that time
optionB: A setTimeout started on the slot's screen
optionC: A foreground service kept running till then
optionD: An expo-background-task registered for that time
correctAnswerText: A local notification scheduled for that time
explanation: The OS delivers a scheduled local notification at its time with no server and no running JavaScript. Background tasks are inexact (the OS chooses when, often hours apart), a setTimeout stops when the app is suspended or killed, and a foreground service is for continuous, user-visible work such as a rider on shift.

prompt: A consumer food app with four main sections must choose between a side drawer and bottom tabs. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: A drawer: it hides navigation, which gives each screen more room for content
optionB: Bottom tabs: visible and thumb-reachable; drawers suit staff apps with many areas
optionC: A drawer nested inside each tab, so both styles are available to every user
optionD: Bottom tabs on Android only, since iPhones cannot show a tab bar at the bottom edge
correctAnswerText: Bottom tabs: visible and thumb-reachable; drawers suit staff apps with many areas
explanation: A few top-level sections belong in tabs, where a thumb reaches on a large phone and users can see where they are; a drawer fits a partner app moved through by staff. Hidden navigation is the drawer's cost, nesting navigators this way confuses users, and iOS apps use bottom tabs all the time.

prompt: A bottom sheet must follow the finger and close on a quick flick, on mid-range phones. Which approach is soundest?
optionA: Reanimated with Gesture Handler, using velocity and distance to decide
optionB: A CSS transition on top, since Reanimated 4 animates gestures that way
optionC: setState on every move event, so React re-renders the sheet each frame
optionD: Animated with useNativeDriver, animating the sheet's height per frame
correctAnswerText: Reanimated with Gesture Handler, using velocity and distance to decide
explanation: Finger-driven motion belongs on the UI thread, and checking velocity as well as distance makes a flick dismiss as users expect; translate with transform, not height. useNativeDriver cannot animate layout properties such as height, per-move setState sends every frame through JavaScript, and CSS transitions are for state changes, not gestures.

prompt: A lending app's regulator expects root detection. A teammate proposes that transfers from phones passing the check skip some server-side checks. Your judgement?
optionA: Add detection to raise the cost, but the server still checks every transfer
optionB: Refuse detection entirely, since every client-side check can be bypassed
optionC: Agree, but only for transfers made over Wi-Fi rather than mobile data
optionD: Agree, since a phone that passes root detection can then be trusted completely
correctAnswerText: Add detection to raise the cost, but the server still checks every transfer
explanation: Root detection, obfuscation and tamper checks raise an attacker's cost and can all be bypassed, so the server remains the only security boundary; Play Integrity or App Attest give the server a signal it decides how to use. Trusting the client is the flaw, refusing a regulator's requirement is not an option, and the network type proves nothing.

prompt: In Kotlin, which keyword declares a reference that cannot be reassigned, the counterpart of const in TypeScript?
optionA: fun
optionB: val
optionC: var
optionD: let
correctAnswerText: val
explanation: val declares a read-only reference, like const: it cannot be pointed at another value after it is set. var is the reassignable form, like let; let in Kotlin is a scope function, not a declaration, and fun declares a function.

prompt: What does the Kotlin expression coupon ?: "NONE" evaluate to?
optionA: coupon, after throwing if it is not "NONE"
optionB: true if coupon equals "NONE", else false
optionC: coupon if it is not null, otherwise "NONE"
optionD: "NONE" if coupon is blank, otherwise coupon
correctAnswerText: coupon if it is not null, otherwise "NONE"
explanation: The elvis operator ?: returns its left side unless that is null, and the right side otherwise, like ?? in TypeScript. It checks only for null, not for a blank string, it never throws, and it is not a comparison.

prompt: Which functions does a Kotlin data class generate from the properties in its primary constructor?
optionA: equals, hashCode, toString, copy and componentN
optionB: compareTo, sort and a builder for each property
optionC: getters only, plus a no-argument constructor
optionD: serialize and parse, for writing it to JSON files
correctAnswerText: equals, hashCode, toString, copy and componentN
explanation: A data class gets field-based equals and hashCode, a readable toString, copy for changing one field, and componentN functions for destructuring. Ordering is not generated, there is no builder, and JSON needs a serialisation library.

prompt: What does minSdkVersion decide for an Android app?
optionA: The oldest Android version the app can be installed on
optionB: The Android API level the code is compiled against
optionC: The Android behaviour changes that the app has opted into
optionD: The lowest Gradle version that can build the project
correctAnswerText: The oldest Android version the app can be installed on
explanation: minSdkVersion is the oldest API level the app installs on; raising it drops older phones. compileSdkVersion is what the compiler builds against, targetSdkVersion is the behaviour the app opts into, and the Gradle version is set by the wrapper.

prompt: Which file declares an Android app's permissions, its activities and the intent filters for its deep links?
optionA: AndroidManifest.xml
optionB: app/build.gradle
optionC: settings.gradle
optionD: gradle.properties
correctAnswerText: AndroidManifest.xml
explanation: The manifest is what the system reads before running any code: permissions, the application class, each activity and its intent filters. app/build.gradle holds the app ID, versions and dependencies, gradle.properties holds build switches, and settings.gradle lists the projects in the build.

prompt: In what order does Android call an activity's callbacks as it is created and becomes visible and interactive?
optionA: onResume, onStart, onCreate
optionB: onCreate, onResume, onStart
optionC: onStart, onCreate, onResume
optionD: onCreate, onStart, onResume
correctAnswerText: onCreate, onStart, onResume
explanation: An activity is created (onCreate), becomes visible (onStart) and then interactive (onResume); React Native reports that last state as AppState "active". Leaving runs onPause then onStop, the mirror of the last two.

prompt: In Jetpack Compose, what is recomposition?
optionA: Running composables again when state they read has changed
optionB: Rebuilding the activity from scratch after a rotation event
optionC: Merging the manifests of every library into a single file
optionD: Recompiling the Kotlin source while the app is still running
correctAnswerText: Running composables again when state they read has changed
explanation: Recomposition is Compose re-running the composables that read a piece of state when it changes, the counterpart of a React re-render. Activity recreation is a lifecycle event, Compose does not recompile code, and manifest merging is a build step.

prompt: In an Expo Modules API definition, which component exposes a native function that returns a Promise to JavaScript?
optionA: Function
optionB: AsyncFunction
optionC: OnStartObserving
optionD: Constant
correctAnswerText: AsyncFunction
explanation: AsyncFunction returns a Promise and runs off the JavaScript thread, so it suits slow work. Function is synchronous on the JavaScript thread, Constant is a read-only property, and OnStartObserving is a hook that runs when the first listener is added.

prompt: Which coroutine dispatcher is meant for disk and network work in an Android app?
optionA: Dispatchers.Main
optionB: Dispatchers.Unconfined
optionC: Dispatchers.IO
optionD: Dispatchers.Default
correctAnswerText: Dispatchers.IO
explanation: Dispatchers.IO is the pool for blocking I/O such as files and network calls, usually entered with withContext. Main runs UI work, Default is for CPU-heavy computation, and Unconfined does not pin work to any particular thread.

prompt: What does the gradlew script in an Android project do?
optionA: Starts Metro and serves the JavaScript bundle to the emulator
optionB: Signs the release build with the upload key from the keystore
optionC: Installs the Android SDK and sets ANDROID_HOME for the whole machine
optionD: Runs the Gradle version the project pins, downloading it if needed
correctAnswerText: Runs the Gradle version the project pins, downloading it if needed
explanation: The wrapper runs the Gradle version named in gradle-wrapper.properties, much as a lockfile pins packages, so every machine builds with the same Gradle. It does not install the SDK, has nothing to do with Metro, and signing is configured in the app's build file.

prompt: Kotlin promises that a String cannot hold null. Why can a value read from a Bundle through a Java API still crash with a NullPointerException?
optionA: Kotlin drops its null checks in release builds to run faster
optionB: Java APIs return platform types whose nullness Kotlin cannot check
optionC: Values from a Bundle are read lazily on a thread that may not exist
optionD: A Bundle converts a missing value to undefined, which Kotlin rejects
correctAnswerText: Java APIs return platform types whose nullness Kotlin cannot check
explanation: A value from Java code has a platform type: Kotlin lets you treat it as non-null but cannot prove it, so a missing value fails at run time. Null checks stay in release builds, Kotlin has no undefined, and nothing here is read lazily. Treat such values as nullable at the boundary.

prompt: Why does declaring a screen state as a sealed interface make a when expression over it safer than one over a plain interface?
optionA: Sealed types are immutable, so the when cannot change the state
optionB: A sealed interface runs its when branches in a fixed, sorted order
optionC: The compiler knows every subtype, so a missing case fails to compile
optionD: Sealed types can only be used on the main thread, avoiding races
correctAnswerText: The compiler knows every subtype, so a missing case fails to compile
explanation: Because every subtype of a sealed type is known at compile time, a when used as an expression must cover them all, so adding a new state breaks every incomplete when, like an exhaustive switch with never in TypeScript. Sealed says nothing about mutability, branch order or threads.

prompt: Why should an app save what must survive when it goes to the background, rather than in onDestroy?
optionA: onDestroy is called on every rotation, so it would save too often
optionB: Writing to disk is not allowed inside onDestroy on recent Android
optionC: A process killed in the background may never get an onDestroy call
optionD: onDestroy runs before onStop, so the screen is already gone by then
correctAnswerText: A process killed in the background may never get an onDestroy call
explanation: When Android needs memory it can kill a background process outright, without calling onDestroy, so a save there may never happen; save as the user goes or by onStop. onDestroy comes after onStop, disk writes are not banned there, and the rotation point is not why it is unreliable.

prompt: Why does a counter declared as var count = 0 inside a composable reset, when the same value inside remember does not?
optionA: Plain var values are stored on disk and are cleared on each recomposition
optionB: The body runs again on recomposition; remember keeps a value across runs
optionC: remember turns the composable into a class whose fields are never reset
optionD: Compose copies plain locals into a new thread that starts from zero again
correctAnswerText: The body runs again on recomposition; remember keeps a value across runs
explanation: A composable is a function that runs again on every recomposition, so a plain local starts fresh each time, like a let inside a React component. remember stores the value in the composition so later runs get it back. Nothing is stored on disk, no thread is involved, and no class is generated.

prompt: Why does Compose recompose when a new set is assigned to a mutableStateOf holder, but not when add() is called on a plain list kept in remember?
optionA: add() is a suspend function, so its change is applied after the frame is drawn
optionB: remember makes the list read-only, so the add() call is silently thrown away
optionC: Compose compares lists by size, and add() leaves the remembered size unchanged
optionD: Compose observes writes to state holders, and add() on a plain list writes none
correctAnswerText: Compose observes writes to state holders, and add() on a plain list writes none
explanation: Compose tracks reads and writes of snapshot state such as mutableStateOf; assigning a new value is a write it sees. A plain list changes its data with no notification, the same symptom as mutating state in React. Size is not compared, add() is not a suspend function, and the list really does change.

prompt: What does structured concurrency give a request started in viewModelScope that GlobalScope.launch does not?
optionA: Automatic retries when the request fails because the phone is offline
optionB: An owner: clearing the ViewModel cancels the work and failures reach a parent
optionC: A faster thread pool, because viewModelScope always runs on Dispatchers.IO
optionD: Survival after the app process is killed, until the request has completed in full
correctAnswerText: An owner: clearing the ViewModel cancels the work and failures reach a parent
explanation: In structured concurrency every coroutine belongs to a scope; viewModelScope is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared, so work cannot outlive its screen, and failures propagate to the parent. GlobalScope has no owner. viewModelScope uses the main dispatcher by default, there are no automatic retries, and nothing survives process death.

prompt: A release build of an app declares a permission that nobody on the team wrote into any manifest. How is that possible?
optionA: The Play Store inserts permissions it detects the app needs at upload time
optionB: Kotlin code that calls a protected API declares the permission at compile time
optionC: Gradle merges each library's manifest into the app's, permissions included
optionD: Android adds every permission a phone supports to apps built in release mode
correctAnswerText: Gradle merges each library's manifest into the app's, permissions included
explanation: Every library ships its own manifest and the build merges them into one, which is how a camera library adds CAMERA for you and also how unexpected permissions appear. In Expo, android.blockedPermissions removes ones you do not want. The system, the store and the compiler do not add permissions.

prompt: In an Expo project that uses Continuous Native Generation, why are lasting native changes made in app config or a config plugin rather than in android/?
optionA: Edits in android/ apply to debug builds only, while app config covers release
optionB: android/ is generated by prebuild, so hand edits are overwritten on regeneration
optionC: Expo encrypts android/ during a build, so edits there cannot be read by Gradle
optionD: Gradle refuses to read any file in android/ that was edited after it was created
correctAnswerText: android/ is generated by prebuild, so hand edits are overwritten on regeneration
explanation: With CNG the native folders are output: npx expo prebuild and EAS Build generate them from app config and plugins, so only changes expressed there survive. Gradle reads edited files normally, nothing is encrypted, and android/ is the same project for debug and release.

prompt: Why can a custom Kotlin module never run inside Expo Go, however the JavaScript is reloaded?
optionA: Metro sends only TypeScript files to Expo Go and skips the Kotlin source files
optionB: Expo Go runs JavaScript without JSI, so it cannot call into any native module at all
optionC: Native code is compiled into the binary, and Expo Go's binary does not contain it
optionD: Expo Go blocks Kotlin modules for security but allows those written in Java
correctAnswerText: Native code is compiled into the binary, and Expo Go's binary does not contain it
explanation: Kotlin is compiled into the app binary, and Expo Go is a fixed binary with only Expo's own native modules, so a custom module needs a development build of your project. Expo Go does call native modules (its own), the language is irrelevant, and Metro never bundles native source.

prompt: Why does it matter whether an activity in the manifest has android:exported set to true?
optionA: Only exported activities are included in the release build that Gradle produces
optionB: An exported activity is uploaded to Play separately and can be updated on its own
optionC: Other apps can start an exported activity, so its intent extras are untrusted input
optionD: Exported activities keep running after the app's process has been killed by Android
correctAnswerText: Other apps can start an exported activity, so its intent extras are untrusted input
explanation: exported says whether components of other apps may start this one, which makes the manifest a security boundary: set false where outside access is not needed, and validate every extra an exported component receives. It does not affect what is built, uploaded, or kept alive.

prompt: A TypeScript line in a Pune laundry app reads const pin = user?.address?.pincode ?? "000000". Which Kotlin line behaves the same?
optionA: val pin = user!!.address!!.pincode ?: "000000"
optionB: val pin = if (user) user.address.pincode else "000000"
optionC: val pin = user?.address?.pincode ?: "000000"
optionD: val pin = user.address.pincode ?? "000000"
correctAnswerText: val pin = user?.address?.pincode ?: "000000"
explanation: Safe calls ?. stop at the first null and yield null, and the elvis ?: supplies the fallback, exactly like ?. and ?? in TypeScript. !! throws on a null user instead of falling back, ?? is not a Kotlin operator, and Kotlin does not accept a nullable object as an if condition.

prompt: UI state is data class OrdersState(val isLoading: Boolean, val orders: List<Order>). Which line makes a new state with isLoading false and the same orders, leaving state unchanged?
optionA: val next = state.copy(isLoading = false)
optionB: val next = state.clone().also { it.isLoading = false }
optionC: val next = OrdersState(state).apply { isLoading = false }
optionD: state.isLoading = false; val next = state
correctAnswerText: val next = state.copy(isLoading = false)
explanation: copy builds a new instance with the named fields changed and the rest carried over, the Kotlin form of { ...state, isLoading: false }. isLoading is a val, so assignment does not compile, there is no constructor taking an OrdersState, and data classes have no clone.

prompt: A native Compose screen in a Kochi ferry app must load the timetable for routeId, and load it again whenever routeId changes. What should it use?
optionA: A call to viewModel.load(routeId) at the top of the body
optionB: remember { viewModel.load(routeId) } above the layout code
optionC: LaunchedEffect(routeId) { viewModel.load(routeId) }
optionD: SideEffect { viewModel.load(routeId) } beside the layout
correctAnswerText: LaunchedEffect(routeId) { viewModel.load(routeId) }
explanation: LaunchedEffect starts a coroutine when it enters the composition and restarts it when its key changes, cancelling the old one: useEffect with [routeId]. A call in the body runs on every recomposition, remember without the key never reloads, and SideEffect runs after every successful recomposition.

prompt: A LazyColumn lists parcels, each row with an expanded flag in remember, and new parcels arrive at the top. Which items() call keeps each flag with its parcel?
optionA: items(parcels.size) { i -> ParcelRow(parcels[i]) } instead
optionB: items(parcels, key = { it.trackingId }) { ParcelRow(it) }
optionC: items(parcels.reversed()) { ParcelRow(it) } with no key set
optionD: items(parcels) { ParcelRow(it) } with the list sorted by id
correctAnswerText: items(parcels, key = { it.trackingId }) { ParcelRow(it) }
explanation: A stable key lets Compose match rows to items when the list changes, so state stays with the parcel rather than the position, as keyExtractor does for FlatList. Without a key, row state follows the index, which shifts when items are inserted at the top; sorting or reversing does not change that.

prompt: A native module must tell the JavaScript side every time wired headphones are unplugged. Which Expo Modules API pieces fit?
optionA: An AsyncFunction that resolves once and is called again in a JS loop
optionB: A Constant holding the plug state, read again by JavaScript each second
optionC: A synchronous Function that blocks until the next unplug event arrives
optionD: Events plus sendEvent, registering the receiver in OnStartObserving
correctAnswerText: Events plus sendEvent, registering the receiver in OnStartObserving
explanation: A push from native to JavaScript is an event: declare it with Events, send it with sendEvent, and register the Android receiver only while someone listens via OnStartObserving and OnStopObserving. A Constant never changes, a blocking Function freezes the JS thread, and polling an async call wastes battery.

prompt: A user presses Home in a ticketing app, reads a message, then taps the app in recents a minute later; the process was not killed. Which callbacks run on the way out and back?
optionA: onDestroy; then onCreate, onStart and onResume again
optionB: onStop only; then onResume, without onStart again
optionC: onPause, onStop; then onRestart, onStart, onResume
optionD: onPause, onStop, onDestroy; then onCreate, onResume
correctAnswerText: onPause, onStop; then onRestart, onStart, onResume
explanation: Leaving runs onPause and onStop; returning to a stopped activity runs onRestart, onStart and onResume. onDestroy and a fresh onCreate happen only if the activity is finished or the process died, onPause always precedes onStop, and onStart always precedes onResume.

prompt: A team using Expo with Continuous Native Generation has agreed to raise the minimum Android version for a new SDK. Where does the change go?
optionA: An android.minSdk field in the project's package.json
optionB: minSdkVersion in the generated android/build.gradle
optionC: The uses-sdk element added by hand to AndroidManifest.xml
optionD: The expo-build-properties plugin options in app config
correctAnswerText: The expo-build-properties plugin options in app config
explanation: In CNG, SDK levels are set through the expo-build-properties config plugin so every prebuild and EAS Build reproduces them. The generated build.gradle and manifest are overwritten on the next prebuild, and package.json has no such field.

prompt: val fares = listOf(450, 1200, 800, 1500). What does fares.filter { it < 1000 }.sumOf { it } return?
explanation: filter keeps 450 and 800, the fares under 1000, and sumOf adds them: 1250. 3950 is the sum of every fare, 2700 is the sum of those at or above 1000, and 800 is only the larger of the two kept values. it is the implicit name of the single lambda parameter.

prompt: A bill-payment app wants the user to choose which of their installed UPI apps completes a payment. Which kind of intent fits?
optionA: An implicit intent describing the action, matched by apps' filters
optionB: A PendingIntent with FLAG_MUTABLE that each UPI app can rewrite
optionC: A broadcast sent to every app that holds the INTERNET permission
optionD: An explicit intent naming one UPI app's activity class directly
correctAnswerText: An implicit intent describing the action, matched by apps' filters
explanation: An implicit intent describes what to do, and the system offers every app whose intent filter matches, which is how one payment request opens the user's choice of UPI app. An explicit intent picks one app, a mutable PendingIntent is a security risk with a different purpose, and a broadcast does not start a payment.

prompt: Testers suspect a KYC form resets because Android kills the app while users fetch an OTP. How can a developer reproduce that on demand?
optionA: Press r in Metro while the form is open, so the JavaScript bundle reloads
optionB: Background the app, run adb shell am kill with the package, reopen from recents
optionC: Rotate the phone several times while the KYC form is still open in the foreground
optionD: Clear the app's storage in Settings, then open it again from the launcher
correctAnswerText: Background the app, run adb shell am kill with the package, reopen from recents
explanation: am kill on a backgrounded app imitates the system reclaiming memory, and reopening from recents is how the user would return, so the restore path is exercised. Rotation tests configuration changes, a Metro reload is a developer action, and clearing storage tests a fresh install rather than a restore.

prompt: A clinic app's native screen does val slotId = intent.getStringExtra("slotId")!!. It works from the app's own button and crashes when opened from a reminder notification. What is the cause?
optionA: The !! operator only works in debug builds, and the reminder runs in release
optionB: The notification's intent lacks the extra, and !! throws on the null it returns
optionC: Notifications open activities on a background thread, where intents are empty
optionD: getStringExtra cannot read extras from a PendingIntent until onResume has run
correctAnswerText: The notification's intent lacks the extra, and !! throws on the null it returns
explanation: getStringExtra returns null for a missing key, and !! turns that into a NullPointerException; the reminder was built without the extra. The fix is to decide what a missing id means, with ?: and a fallback or finish(). Activities start on the main thread, extras are readable in onCreate, and !! behaves the same in every build.

prompt: In a native Compose form, OutlinedTextField(value = name, onValueChange = { name = it }) shows each typed letter briefly and then goes blank. name is declared as var name = "". What is wrong?
optionA: name is a plain local: Compose never sees the change and the body resets it
optionB: OutlinedTextField needs a key so Compose knows which field received input
optionC: onValueChange runs on a worker thread, so the assignment arrives too late
optionD: The field must be wrapped in a LaunchedEffect for its value to be stored
correctAnswerText: name is a plain local: Compose never sees the change and the body resets it
explanation: A controlled field shows whatever value it is given. Assigning a plain var is invisible to Compose, and any recomposition runs the body again and sets it back to "". var name by remember { mutableStateOf("") } fixes both. Keys are for lists, the callback runs on the main thread, and an effect is not a place to hold state.

prompt: In a plain native Compose activity, a half-typed address held in var address by remember { mutableStateOf("") } vanishes when the phone rotates. Recomposition alone keeps it. Why does rotation lose it?
optionA: remember keeps strings only up to a fixed length, and the address was too long
optionB: The keyboard closes on rotation, and that cancels any pending state writes
optionC: Rotation recreates the activity, and remember lives in the discarded composition
optionD: Rotation clears every mutableStateOf in the app to free memory for the new layout
correctAnswerText: Rotation recreates the activity, and remember lives in the discarded composition
explanation: A configuration change destroys and recreates an activity that does not declare configChanges, and remember is rebuilt with the new composition. rememberSaveable writes the value into saved state, and a ViewModel also survives the change. There is no global clearing, no length limit, and closing the keyboard cancels nothing.

prompt: A payments SDK works in debug, but the release build crashes at launch and adb logcat shows ClassNotFoundException for one of the SDK's classes. What is the most likely cause?
optionA: Play App Signing strips classes that are not signed by the upload key
optionB: Hermes is off in release builds, so Java classes cannot be looked up
optionC: R8 removed or renamed a class the SDK loads by name; it needs a keep rule
optionD: The release build cannot reach Metro, so the SDK's classes never arrive
correctAnswerText: R8 removed or renamed a class the SDK loads by name; it needs a keep rule
explanation: Release builds shrink and obfuscate native code with R8, and a class that a library loads by reflection can be removed or renamed; a keep rule in proguard-rules.pro (or the library's own rules) fixes it. Release builds embed their bundle, signing does not strip classes, and Hermes runs JavaScript, not Java class loading.

prompt: Right after adding a maps library, the build fails: "Manifest merger failed : uses-sdk:minSdkVersion 24 cannot be smaller than version 26 declared in library". What does it tell the team?
optionA: The SDK installed on the laptop is older than the version the library needs
optionB: The library needs a newer Android than the oldest one the app installs on
optionC: The library was built with a newer Gradle than the one the wrapper downloads
optionD: Two manifests declare the same activity name, and the merger cannot pick one
correctAnswerText: The library needs a newer Android than the oldest one the app installs on
explanation: The merger compares minSdk values: the app installs down to 24 and the library requires 26, so the build refuses rather than ship a crash on older phones. The fix is a decision to raise minSdk or choose another library, not tools:overrideLibrary. Laptop SDKs, duplicate activities and Gradle versions give different errors.

prompt: A module's TypeScript declares the event "onNetworkTypeChanged" and tsc passes, but listeners never fire on a new development build. A log in OnStartObserving never prints. What should be checked first?
optionA: That the event payload is a Map, since other types are dropped silently
optionB: That the Kotlin Events(...) name matches the TypeScript name exactly
optionC: That Metro was restarted with --clear after the Kotlin file changed
optionD: That tsc runs in strict mode, so it can check the Kotlin event names
correctAnswerText: That the Kotlin Events(...) name matches the TypeScript name exactly
explanation: OnStartObserving runs when the first listener for a declared event is added; if it never runs, the listener was added for a name Kotlin does not declare. tsc cannot see Kotlin in any mode, so the declaration is only as true as the team keeps it. Metro does not bundle Kotlin, and the payload matters only after an event is sent.

prompt: After visiting a map screen five times, five handlers run on every battery-saver change and the native receiver is never unregistered. The effect calls addListener and returns nothing. What explains both symptoms?
optionA: No subscription is removed, so the module never sees its last listener go
optionB: addListener is called during render, so it runs once per recomposition
optionC: The receiver is registered with RECEIVER_EXPORTED, so it cannot be removed
optionD: The effect has an empty dependency array, so React runs it on every render
correctAnswerText: No subscription is removed, so the module never sees its last listener go
explanation: Each mount adds a listener and nothing calls sub.remove(), so they accumulate, and OnStopObserving, which unregisters the receiver, runs only when the last listener is removed. Returning () => sub.remove() from the effect fixes both. The call is in an effect, not render; the flag does not block removal; and [] runs the effect once per mount.

prompt: ANR reports for a photo app show the main thread inside a native module Function that reads image metadata from disk. JavaScript profiling looks clean. What is the diagnosis?
optionA: Slow disk I/O runs synchronously on a thread that must answer input
optionB: The module throws an exception that the system shows as an ANR dialog
optionC: The JavaScript thread is overloaded, which Android reports as an ANR
optionD: The app lacks the storage permission, so the read waits for a prompt
correctAnswerText: Slow disk I/O runs synchronously on a thread that must answer input
explanation: An ANR means the main thread did not respond to input in time; a synchronous Function doing disk reads blocks it. Moving the work into an AsyncFunction (or another background thread) fixes it. A busy JS thread freezes taps without an ANR, an exception is a crash, and a permission problem fails rather than blocking.

prompt: Analytics shows a native Compose screen logging "screen_viewed" dozens of times per visit. The log call sits at the top of the composable body. Why?
optionA: Analytics SDKs retry each event until the composable leaves the screen
optionB: Compose renders each composable twice per frame to check that the function is pure
optionC: The body runs on every recomposition, so the call runs each time state changes
optionD: The call runs once per child composable that the screen contains
correctAnswerText: The body runs on every recomposition, so the call runs each time state changes
explanation: Work in a composable body runs whenever that body recomposes, which can be many times per visit, just as a fetch in a React component body runs on every render. A side effect belongs in LaunchedEffect with a key. Compose does not double-render for purity checks, and the other two describe nothing Compose does.

prompt: data class Seat(var row: Int, var no: Int). A Seat is added to a HashSet, then its no is changed, and set.contains(thatSameSeat) returns false. What explains it?
optionA: contains uses compareTo, which data classes do not generate for var fields
optionB: Data classes compare by identity once a field has been reassigned in place
optionC: Its hashCode changed after insertion, so the set looks in the wrong bucket
optionD: HashSet stores a copy, so the original object is no longer the one inside
correctAnswerText: Its hashCode changed after insertion, so the set looks in the wrong bucket
explanation: A data class hashCode is computed from its fields, so changing a field after insertion means the set searches a bucket where the object is not. That is why value types used as keys should have val fields. Equality stays field-based, the set holds the same reference, and hash sets use equals and hashCode, not compareTo.

prompt: Ankur Pharmacy's React Native app needs barcode scanning. A developer wants to write a Kotlin module for it this sprint. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Avoid native code and decode barcodes in JavaScript from raw camera frames on every phone
optionB: Write the module, but load it in Expo Go so that no development build is required
optionC: Write the module, since native code is always faster than any library could ever be
