optionD: Check Expo's modules and maintained libraries first; write native code only if none fits
correctAnswerText: Check Expo's modules and maintained libraries first; write native code only if none fits
explanation: Your own native module means Kotlin and Swift to maintain, upgrades you own and a development build, so an Expo or well-maintained library comes first and custom code is for an API no library covers. Libraries are native too, Expo Go cannot load custom native code, and decoding frames in JavaScript is the slow path.

prompt: A new native module powers an optional "lite mode", and some testers still run older development builds. Which loading choice is best?
optionA: A try/catch around each call site, with requireNativeModule left unchanged
optionB: Ship the module only in production builds, and stub it in development builds
optionC: requireOptionalNativeModule with a fallback, so callers must handle null
optionD: requireNativeModule, so any build without the module fails loudly at launch
correctAnswerText: requireOptionalNativeModule with a fallback, so callers must handle null
explanation: For an optional feature, the optional loader returns null when the binary lacks the module, and its type makes every caller handle that, so old builds degrade instead of crashing. requireNativeModule throws at import, so a red screen on old builds; scattered try/catch misses the import-time throw; and differing builds hide bugs until release.

prompt: A live-tracking library needs a higher minSdk than a rural bus app supports. One engineer suggests tools:overrideLibrary to keep the old minimum. Which judgement is best?
optionA: Check what share of users the change drops, then raise minSdk or pick another library
optionB: Fork the library and lower its declared minSdk so both values match each other
optionC: Raise minSdk silently in the generated build.gradle so the business is not bothered
optionD: Use tools:overrideLibrary, since the merger check is only a cautious warning
correctAnswerText: Check what share of users the change drops, then raise minSdk or pick another library
explanation: The library calls APIs older phones lack, so overriding moves the failure to crashes on those phones. Dropping old phones is a business decision best made with data on who uses them, then made through app config. Editing generated files is overwritten, and lowering the library's number does not add the missing APIs.

prompt: A native loan screen holds a selected tab, a list of 300 offers from the server, and a six-step application draft. Which placement is best?
optionA: All three in a ViewModel, since it survives configuration changes and process death
optionB: All three in remember, and reload everything from the server after any restart
optionC: Tab in rememberSaveable, offers in a ViewModel, the draft persisted to storage
optionD: All three in rememberSaveable, since it survives both rotation and process death
correctAnswerText: Tab in rememberSaveable, offers in a ViewModel, the draft persisted to storage
explanation: Small UI choices fit saved state; a large list belongs in a ViewModel and can be reloaded from the repository; a draft the user would hate to lose must be persisted, since only storage survives everything reliably. rememberSaveable does survive process death, but saved state is for small values and is gone once the user closes the task; a ViewModel does not survive process death, and remember survives neither.

prompt: An Expo team keeps needing small manifest and Gradle tweaks. One lead wants to commit android/ and edit it by hand. Which assessment is soundest?
optionA: Avoid both and ask users to apply the tweaks in the phone's developer settings
optionB: Prefer idempotent config plugins; committing android/ means owning every upgrade
optionC: Commit android/ and keep running prebuild --clean, so both approaches combine
optionD: Commit android/, since config plugins run only on EAS and never on local builds
correctAnswerText: Prefer idempotent config plugins; committing android/ means owning every upgrade
explanation: Config plugins re-apply each change on every prebuild and keep upgrades a matter of regenerating, so they suit a stream of small tweaks. Leaving CNG is allowed, but then the team hand-maintains those files through every React Native upgrade. Plugins run locally too, prebuild --clean would wipe the hand edits, and users cannot patch a manifest.

prompt: A reviewer finds forty uses of !! in a native module. Which team rule is the best replacement?
optionA: Keep !! but wrap each module function in try/catch that returns null silently
optionB: Replace each !! with lateinit var, which removes the possibility of a crash
optionC: Declare every value as non-null String, so the compiler stops asking about it
optionD: Handle real absence with ?: or ?.; use requireNotNull with a message for bugs
correctAnswerText: Handle real absence with ?: or ?.; use requireNotNull with a message for bugs
explanation: Where a value can legitimately be missing, the code should say what happens, with ?: or ?.; where null can only mean a bug, requireNotNull fails with a message that explains it. Swallowing exceptions hides failures, lateinit only delays the check to run time, and a non-null declaration cannot stop a Java API returning null.

prompt: A Kotlin module ports order totals that include paise. Which type for the amount is the best choice?
optionA: String, holding the formatted amount
optionB: Int, holding the rupees with paise cut
optionC: Long, holding the amount in paise
optionD: Double, holding the amount in rupees
correctAnswerText: Long, holding the amount in paise
explanation: Whole paise in a Long are exact and leave plenty of range, the same reason money is never a float in TypeScript. A Double cannot represent many decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift; truncating to rupees loses money; and a formatted string must be parsed again for every calculation.

prompt: A delivery app builds a PendingIntent for a notification that opens one order. Which flag choice is best, and why?
optionA: FLAG_MUTABLE, since immutable intents cannot carry extras such as the order id
optionB: FLAG_IMMUTABLE, since nothing needs to fill in the intent and holders cannot alter it
optionC: No flag at all, since the system picks the safest option for notifications automatically
optionD: FLAG_MUTABLE, since the notification system may need to change the order id later
correctAnswerText: FLAG_IMMUTABLE, since nothing needs to fill in the intent and holders cannot alter it
explanation: A PendingIntent lets another app run an intent with your app's identity, so it should be immutable unless the receiver genuinely must fill something in, because a mutable one can be altered by whoever holds it. Recent Android requires choosing explicitly, and immutable intents still carry the extras you set.

prompt: A native seat-selection screen loads seats from the network and must show loading and error states. Which structure is best?
optionA: A network call inside the composable body, with the result kept in remember
optionB: A rememberSaveable holding the full seat list, refreshed on every rotation
optionC: A top-level var in the file, assigned by a GlobalScope coroutine on launch
optionD: A ViewModel exposing StateFlow, collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle
correctAnswerText: A ViewModel exposing StateFlow, collected with collectAsStateWithLifecycle
explanation: The ViewModel owns loading and errors, survives rotation and cancels its coroutines when cleared, and lifecycle-aware collection stops in the background, the same split as screens versus a data layer in React Native. A body call repeats on recomposition, a GlobalScope global has no owner, and saved state is for small values.

prompt: A team must decide how to test a Kotlin module that pushes events to a hook. Which plan covers the risks best?
optionA: Snapshot tests of the screen, which cover both the hook and the native events
optionB: Jest with a mocked module for the hook, plus a recorded check on a real device
optionC: Jest with a mocked module alone, since tsc already checks the Kotlin signatures
optionD: Device checks alone, since mocking the module tests nothing that is real
correctAnswerText: Jest with a mocked module for the hook, plus a recorded check on a real device
explanation: A Jest mock proves the JavaScript behaviour quickly and repeatably, but nothing checks the TypeScript declaration against the Kotlin, so a device check that the event really arrives covers the other side. tsc cannot see Kotlin, skipping unit tests loses fast feedback, and a snapshot never exercises the native side.

prompt: Under Play App Signing, which key signs the APKs that users actually install from Google Play?
optionA: The app signing key, which Google keeps
optionB: The debug key, which Android tools create
optionC: The EAS access token, which CI stores
optionD: The upload key, which the developer keeps
correctAnswerText: The app signing key, which Google keeps
explanation: With Play App Signing, Google keeps the app signing key and signs what users install with it; the developer signs each upload with the upload key, which Play checks and then replaces. The debug key signs only debug builds, and an access token is not a signing key.

prompt: Which Android version field is an integer that must be higher on every upload to Google Play?
optionA: runtimeVersion
optionB: versionCode
optionC: versionName
optionD: minSdkVersion
correctAnswerText: versionCode
explanation: Play compares versionCode, so each upload needs a higher integer than any before. versionName is the text users see, minSdkVersion is the oldest Android the app supports, and runtimeVersion decides which over-the-air updates a build accepts.

prompt: Which list gives the Play Console's release tracks from the narrowest audience to everybody?
optionA: Open testing, closed testing, internal testing, production
optionB: Internal testing, open testing, production, closed testing
optionC: Internal testing, closed testing, open testing, production
optionD: Closed testing, internal testing, production, open testing
correctAnswerText: Internal testing, closed testing, open testing, production
explanation: Internal testing is a short email list, closed testing uses larger lists or groups, open testing lets anyone join from the listing, and production is everyone. A release moves up by being promoted, so the tested bytes are the bytes users get.

prompt: What does Google Play do with the Android App Bundle (.aab) a developer uploads?
optionA: Generates and signs per-device APKs from it
optionB: Installs the bundle on each phone as it is
optionC: Converts it to an iOS build for the App Store
optionD: Stores it only as a backup of the source code
correctAnswerText: Generates and signs per-device APKs from it
explanation: The bundle holds code and resources for every device; Play builds APKs with just the CPU architecture, density and languages each phone needs, and signs them. A bundle cannot be installed directly, it has nothing to do with iOS, and it contains compiled code rather than source.

prompt: With EAS Update, which installed builds can receive an update published for runtime version "4.1.0"?
optionA: Every build on the channel, whatever its runtime
optionB: Builds whose runtime version is "4.1.0" or higher
optionC: Builds whose runtime version is lower than "4.1.0"
optionD: Builds whose runtime version is exactly "4.1.0"
correctAnswerText: Builds whose runtime version is exactly "4.1.0"
explanation: An update is served only to builds whose runtimeVersion is the same string, which stands for "this JavaScript fits this native layer". There is no ordering or range, and the channel narrows which builds are eligible rather than overriding the runtime check.

prompt: In the usual eas.json set-up, which build profile produces a debug build with expo-dev-client that loads JavaScript from Metro?
optionA: preview
optionB: development
optionC: production
optionD: submit
correctAnswerText: development
explanation: The development profile is a debug build with the dev client, installed on team phones and fed by Metro. preview is a release build installed directly for QA, production is a release build in store format, and submit is a separate section for uploading, not a build profile.

prompt: What does a source map record for a minified release bundle?
optionA: The signing certificate fingerprint that the bundle was signed with
optionB: A hash of the native layer, used to choose a runtime version
optionC: For positions in the bundle, the original file, line, column and name
optionD: The list of screens in the app and the order users visit them in
correctAnswerText: For positions in the bundle, the original file, line, column and name
explanation: A source map maps positions in generated code back to the original file, line, column and name, which is how a crash tool turns bundle:1:84512 into a line of TypeScript. It is not navigation data, a fingerprint of native code, or signing information.

prompt: What does the crash-free users rate measure for a release over a period?
optionA: The share of users who opened the app and did not uninstall
optionB: The share of crash reports that were fixed in the period
optionC: The share of users who had no crash at all in that period
optionD: The share of sessions that did not end in a crash that day
correctAnswerText: The share of users who had no crash at all in that period
explanation: Crash-free users counts a user as crashed if any one of their sessions crashed, and reports the share with none. The share of sessions without a crash is the crash-free sessions rate; uninstalls and fixed issues are different measures.

prompt: Which eas-cli command republishes the update before the latest one on a branch, undoing a bad over-the-air update?
optionA: eas update:rollback
optionB: eas credentials
optionC: eas submit --latest
optionD: eas build:cancel
correctAnswerText: eas update:rollback
explanation: eas update:rollback republishes the previous update group, or rolls back to the bundle embedded in the build if there is none. build:cancel stops a queued build, submit uploads a binary to a store, and credentials manages keys and certificates.

prompt: On TestFlight, which testers can install a build only after it passes Beta App Review?
optionA: Every tester, before any build can be installed
optionB: Internal testers, the App Store Connect team
optionC: Ad hoc testers, whose devices EAS registered
optionD: External testers, invited by email or public link
correctAnswerText: External testers, invited by email or public link
explanation: External testers need the build to pass Beta App Review; internal testers, who belong to the App Store Connect team, get builds after processing. Registered-device installs are ad hoc internal distribution, outside TestFlight.

prompt: Android installs an update only if it carries the same signing certificate as the installed app. Why does that make the split into an app signing key and an upload key valuable?
optionA: The split lets Play accept uploads that have not been signed at all
optionB: A lost upload key can be reset while installs stay signed by the same key
optionC: The upload key lets phones install updates signed by any team member
optionD: Two keys double the encryption, so the APK cannot be unpacked by anyone
correctAnswerText: A lost upload key can be reset while installs stay signed by the same key
explanation: Because phones only see the app signing key, which Google keeps, a lost or leaked upload key can be replaced through an upload key reset without breaking updates. Signing is not encryption, phones accept only the one certificate, and every upload must still be signed.

prompt: Why can a team not roll users back from version 5.2.0 to 5.1.3 through Google Play after a bad release?
optionA: A rollback would need the upload key, which only Google is holding
optionB: Play will not install a lower versionCode over a higher installed one
optionC: Play deletes earlier versions from its servers once a new one is live
optionD: Older versions fail review again because their target level is stale
correctAnswerText: Play will not install a lower versionCode over a higher installed one
explanation: Play orders builds by versionCode and does not downgrade, so the way back is forward: a fix with a higher versionCode, or an over-the-air update for a JavaScript bug. Old releases are not the issue, the developer holds the upload key, and re-review is not the reason.

prompt: Why is any variable whose name starts with EXPO_PUBLIC_ treated as public, even when it is stored as an EAS secret?
optionA: Metro sends the value to the dev server, which is open on the network
optionB: Its value is inlined into the JavaScript bundle, which anyone can unpack
optionC: The prefix uploads the value to the Play listing as public metadata
optionD: EAS prints every EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable in its build logs in plain text
correctAnswerText: Its value is inlined into the JavaScript bundle, which anyone can unpack
explanation: EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables are written into the bundle at build time, and an APK can be unzipped and read, so the value ships to every phone whatever its EAS visibility. That is fine for an API URL and wrong for a payment secret. Logs, listings and Metro are not the reason.

prompt: With expo-updates defaults (check on load, fallbackToCacheTimeout 0), why does a published fix usually run only on the second launch after it is published?
optionA: The store must approve the update during the first launch on each phone
optionB: The app starts on its cached bundle and runs the downloaded one next time
optionC: Updates wait for the phone to be on Wi-Fi, which is checked at launch
optionD: The first launch only registers the phone; the update is sent on the next
correctAnswerText: The app starts on its cached bundle and runs the downloaded one next time
explanation: The app checks for an update at cold start but does not wait for it: it runs the bundle it has while the new one downloads, and the new one runs on the next cold start. There is no registration launch, stores do not review OTA updates, and Wi-Fi-only checking is not the default.

prompt: Why does the fingerprint runtime version policy protect old binaries better than the appVersion policy?
optionA: It is checked by Google Play, which blocks updates that do not match
optionB: It changes by itself when native code changes, and JavaScript leaves it alone
optionC: It encrypts the bundle so that only the matching binary can decrypt it
optionD: It changes on every JavaScript commit, so no update ever reaches an older binary
correctAnswerText: It changes by itself when native code changes, and JavaScript leaves it alone
explanation: The fingerprint hashes everything that affects the native layer, so adding a native library makes a new runtime version without anyone bumping a number, while JavaScript-only changes keep it. appVersion is safe only if every native change comes with a version bump. Nothing is encrypted, and stores do not check runtime versions.

prompt: Users of a news app average four sessions a day. Why is its daily crash-free users rate normally lower than its crash-free sessions rate?
optionA: Crash-free users is sampled at 10%, so it is always the lower of the two estimates
optionB: Crash-free users leaves out users on old versions, who crash the least
optionC: A user counts as crashed if any of their sessions crashed, over fewer users
optionD: Sessions that crash are retried, so each one is counted as two sessions
correctAnswerText: A user counts as crashed if any of their sessions crashed, over fewer users
explanation: Each crashed session marks one user as crashed, and the user count is about a quarter of the session count, so the same crashes are a larger share of users. Neither rate drops old versions, crashed sessions are not double counted, and neither is a fixed sample.

prompt: The Sentry config plugin uploads source maps during each EAS build. Why must the pipeline also upload maps after every eas update?
optionA: Each update is a new bundle, and its maps exist only from that publish
optionB: Updates are not minified, so they need a different kind of source map
optionC: The build-time maps cover only native code, never the JavaScript bundle
optionD: Sentry deletes the build's maps as soon as a phone downloads an update
correctAnswerText: Each update is a new bundle, and its maps exist only from that publish
explanation: A source map matches one exact bundle, and an update is a new bundle produced by eas update, so its maps must be uploaded from that output, or its crashes show minified frames. Sentry keeps the build's maps, updates are minified too, and the build-time upload does cover the embedded JavaScript bundle.

prompt: Why does every eas command in a GitHub Actions job get the --non-interactive flag?
optionA: Interactive mode builds locally on the runner instead of on EAS servers
optionB: Without the flag, eas skips validating eas.json before it starts a build
optionC: The flag is what makes eas read its EXPO_TOKEN from the environment
optionD: With no one to answer a prompt, eas should fail with a message instead
correctAnswerText: With no one to answer a prompt, eas should fail with a message instead
explanation: In CI a prompt waits for input that never comes, so the job hangs until the timeout; --non-interactive makes eas stop with an error that says what is missing. It does not move the build, EXPO_TOKEN is read either way, and validation happens in both modes.

prompt: A minimum-version check compares app versions as plain strings. Why does it wrongly treat "3.12.0" as older than "3.9.1"?
optionA: Strings ignore everything after the first dot when they are compared
optionB: Version strings must be zero-padded, or JavaScript cannot read them
optionC: Text compares character by character, and "1" sorts before "9"
optionD: Comparing strings uses their length, and both have the same length
correctAnswerText: Text compares character by character, and "1" sorts before "9"
explanation: String comparison is lexical: after "3." it compares "1" with "9" and stops, so "3.12.0" < "3.9.1" is true. Versions must be split and compared part by part as numbers. Nothing is ignored after a dot, padding is a workaround rather than a rule, and length is not used.

prompt: Why do teams give the preview and production variants of one app different application IDs, set through app.config.ts?
optionA: Android treats one ID as one app, so separate IDs can sit side by side
optionB: Play rejects any upload whose ID was ever used by an internal build
optionC: The application ID decides which EAS Update channel a build listens to
optionD: Different IDs let both variants share one versionCode without a clash
correctAnswerText: Android treats one ID as one app, so separate IDs can sit side by side
explanation: Two builds with one ID are the same app to Android, so one replaces the other, and a different signature makes the install fail; separate IDs let QA keep both and tell them apart. Internal builds do not block an ID, versionCode rules are per app on Play, and the channel comes from the build profile.

prompt: A grocery app is at 3.7.2. The next release adds a "repeat last order" button and changes nothing else. What should its version be?
explanation: A new feature that breaks nothing is a minor bump, and the patch number goes back to zero: 3.8.0. 3.7.3 signals only a fix, 4.0.0 signals a breaking change, and 3.8.2 keeps a patch number that belongs to the old minor.

prompt: A team derives versionCode = ((major × 1000 + minor) × 100 + patch) × 100 + build. What is the code for version 3.12.4, build 2?
explanation: 3 × 1000 + 12 = 3012; × 100 + 4 = 301204; × 100 + 2 = 30120402. The scheme keeps codes rising with the version, so 3.10.0 (30100000) sorts above 3.9.99 build 99 (30099999). The other values drop a factor or place digits in the wrong slots.

prompt: A pharmacy app plans four changes: a typo fix on a screen, a festival banner imported from JavaScript, adding a native maps library, and a new app icon. Which can ship with eas update?
optionA: The banner image and the new app icon
optionB: The typo fix, banner and maps library
optionC: The typo fix and the banner image
optionD: All four, if they go out on one channel
correctAnswerText: The typo fix and the banner image
explanation: An update replaces the JavaScript bundle and the assets it imports, so the typo and the imported banner can go over the air. A library with native code and the app icon live in the native layer and need a store build. A channel chooses who gets an update, not what it may contain.

prompt: Installed builds: production 6.0.0, production 5.9.1 and preview 6.0.0. With the appVersion policy, a fix is published with eas update --channel production from a commit at version 6.0.0. Which builds get it?
optionA: Only the production 6.0.0 build
optionB: Production 6.0.0 and preview 6.0.0
optionC: All three builds that are installed
optionD: Both production builds, 6.0.0 and 5.9.1
correctAnswerText: Only the production 6.0.0 build
explanation: Delivery needs both the channel and the runtime version to match. Under appVersion the update's runtime is "6.0.0", which 5.9.1 does not have, and the preview build listens on a different channel. 5.9.1 users need the fix published again from the 5.9.1 release commit.

prompt: Yesterday a ride app had 3,20,000 sessions, 1,120 of which crashed, from 80,000 users, 540 of whom crashed. What are its crash-free sessions and crash-free users rates?
optionA: 99.33% sessions and 99.65% users
optionB: 96.50% sessions and 93.25% users
optionC: 99.65% sessions and 98.60% users
optionD: 99.65% sessions and 99.33% users
correctAnswerText: 99.65% sessions and 99.33% users
explanation: Sessions: 1 − 1,120 / 3,20,000 = 99.65%. Users: 1 − 540 / 80,000 = 99.325%, about 99.33%. The users rate is lower because a user with any crashed session counts as crashed and there are a quarter as many users. 98.60% divides crashed sessions by users, and the last option slips a decimal place.

prompt: An app has 2,40,000 daily users averaging 2.5 sessions a day. Its rollout gate needs 45,000 sessions on the new version before widening. Roughly how long does a 5% staged rollout take to get there?
optionA: About three hours
optionB: About fifteen days
optionC: About a day and a half
optionD: About seven and a half days
correctAnswerText: About a day and a half
explanation: 5% of 2,40,000 users is 12,000, and at 2.5 sessions each that is 30,000 sessions a day, so 45,000 needs about 1.5 days. A 1% slice would give 6,000 a day and need 7.5 days, which is why the slice size is chosen with the gate in mind.

prompt: A team is restricting its Maps API key to its Android app before the first Play release. Which certificate fingerprint must the key allow for users who install from Play?
optionA: The debug keystore's, from the developer laptop that built it
optionB: The app signing key's, from App integrity in the Play Console
optionC: The upload key's, from keytool -list on the EAS keystore backup
optionD: A SHA-256 of the AAB file, computed just before it is uploaded
correctAnswerText: The app signing key's, from App integrity in the Play Console
explanation: Play re-signs what users install with the app signing key, so Google services see that certificate; its fingerprints are shown under App integrity. The upload key signs only uploads (and preview builds signed with it), the debug key only debug builds, and a file hash is not a certificate fingerprint.

prompt: A team must place two values: the Sentry DSN the app reports to, and the Sentry auth token that uploads source maps during builds. Where does each go?
optionA: DSN in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable; token as an EAS secret variable
optionB: Token in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable; DSN kept only on the backend
optionC: Both committed in app.json, with the repository kept private
optionD: Both as EXPO_PUBLIC_ variables, since Sentry needs both at run time
correctAnswerText: DSN in an EXPO_PUBLIC_ variable; token as an EAS secret variable
explanation: The DSN only says where to send events and is designed to be public, so it may sit in the bundle. The auth token can upload and change project data, so it stays a build-time secret on EAS (and in GitHub secrets for CI). The app never needs the token, and a private repository is not a secret store.

prompt: A clinic-booking app logs in only by phone OTP. What should the team set up so Play's reviewers and pre-launch report can get past the login?
optionA: A test number with a fixed OTP on the server, declared under App access
optionB: Nothing, since Play's crawler skips any screen that asks for a login
optionC: A separate build for the testing tracks with the login screen removed
optionD: The developer's own phone number, given to Google with each release
correctAnswerText: A test number with a fixed OTP on the server, declared under App access
explanation: Reviewers and the pre-launch crawler use the credentials declared under App access, so a number whose fixed OTP works only for that number lets them in safely. A build without login tests a different app, a personal number is unsafe and unworkable, and the crawler otherwise sees only the login screen.

prompt: A tutoring app wants more store ratings using StoreReview.requestReview(). Where in the app should it be called?
optionA: On the error screen, to collect feedback when something failed
optionB: Behind a "Rate us" button on the settings screen, every time
optionC: On every cold start, so the prompt appears as often as it can
optionD: After a good moment, such as a student finishing a fifth lesson
correctAnswerText: After a good moment, such as a student finishing a fifth lesson
explanation: The operating system decides whether the in-app review prompt appears and limits how often, so it should be asked at a moment of satisfaction and never relied on. A button may do nothing when the prompt is suppressed, asking after an error invites a bad review, and asking at every launch wastes the limited prompts.

prompt: Uploads keep failing because the versionCode "has already been used", though the production profile in eas.json says "autoincrement": true. What is wrong?
optionA: The versionName must change too, or Play rejects a new versionCode
optionB: autoIncrement works only for iOS builds, so Android codes never change
optionC: The key is misspelt; it is autoIncrement, so the setting was never applied
optionD: Play caches the last versionCode for a day, so uploads must be spaced out
correctAnswerText: The key is misspelt; it is autoIncrement, so the setting was never applied
explanation: eas.json keys are case-sensitive: "autoincrement" is not a known key (the eas-json parser reports it as not allowed), so every build kept the versionCode from app config. Fix the spelling, use appVersionSource remote, and validate eas.json in CI. Auto-increment covers both platforms, and Play has no cache or versionName rule.

prompt: QA installs a preview APK on a phone that has the Play version, and adb prints INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE. Both builds use the ID in.example.tiffin. What is happening?
optionA: APKs built by EAS cannot install on phones that have used the Play Store
optionB: The preview APK targets a newer Android than the phone is running on
optionC: The preview APK has a lower versionCode, so Android refuses the downgrade outright
optionD: Same ID, different certificates: Play's copy is signed by the app signing key
correctAnswerText: Same ID, different certificates: Play's copy is signed by the app signing key
explanation: Android treats the APK as an update of the installed app, and an update must carry the same certificate; the Play copy is signed by Google's app signing key and the APK by the upload key. A downgrade or an SDK problem gives different errors. The lasting fix is a separate ID per variant, not "uninstall first".

prompt: An urgent fix was published with eas update to production, yet hours later the dashboard shows almost no downloads. Phones run 2.4.0, the policy is appVersion, and main already says 2.5.0. What happened?
optionA: The update reached phones but will not run until they reinstall
optionB: Phones only download updates overnight while they are charging
optionC: The update was made for runtime 2.5.0, which no installed build has
optionD: The update is waiting for Google Play to review it before release
correctAnswerText: The update was made for runtime 2.5.0, which no installed build has
explanation: Under appVersion the runtime version is the version string, and it must match exactly, so an update built from a 2.5.0 commit reaches no 2.4.0 phone. Publish from the 2.4.0 release commit, or adopt the fingerprint policy. Stores do not review OTA updates, and there is no overnight or reinstall rule.

prompt: Minutes after an update, crash reports spike with "Cannot find native module 'ExpoLocation'" whenever the new delivery screen opens. What went wrong?
optionA: The update was rolled out to 100% at once instead of a small percentage first
optionB: The update used a native library that the installed binaries do not contain
optionC: Sentry has no source maps for the update, so it reports the wrong module
optionD: The phones denied location permission, which removes the native module
correctAnswerText: The update used a native library that the installed binaries do not contain
explanation: JavaScript cannot add native code, so an update that imports a newly added native library crashes on binaries built without it. Roll back with eas update:rollback now, and ship the feature in a store build. Missing maps make traces unreadable, not wrong; the percentage only limits the damage; and a denied permission does not remove a module.

prompt: Crashes tagged updateId "embedded" show TypeScript lines in Sentry; crashes tagged with last Tuesday's update show index.android.bundle:1:52190. What does the pipeline lack?
optionA: Sentry.wrap on the root component, so errors inside updates are caught
optionB: A step uploading source maps from the eas update output after publishing
optionC: A higher tracesSampleRate, so that update sessions record full stacks
optionD: The Sentry config plugin, which wires the native SDKs into the build
correctAnswerText: A step uploading source maps from the eas update output after publishing
explanation: Embedded-bundle crashes are readable, so the build-time upload works; only the update lacks maps, because nobody uploaded them for that new bundle. The plugin is clearly in place, trace sampling affects performance data rather than stack frames, and errors are being captured already.

prompt: A release shows 99.76% crash-free sessions (960 crashes in 4,00,000) but 99.952% crash-free users (48 of 1,00,000). What pattern does that point to?
optionA: A few users crashing about twenty times each, likely a crash on launch
optionB: A counting bug, since crash-free users can never exceed crash-free sessions
optionC: Crashes only in sessions of users who have no account on the server
optionD: Many users each crashing once, spread evenly across all their sessions
correctAnswerText: A few users crashing about twenty times each, likely a crash on launch
explanation: 960 crashed sessions from 48 users is 20 crashes per affected user, which is what a crash that loops on launch looks like. Many single crashes would pull the users rate down more than the sessions rate. The users rate can be the higher one when crashes concentrate, and nothing here points to accounts.

prompt: Baseline crash rate is 0.20%. The gate needs 20,000 sessions to widen and halts when the 95% lower bound exceeds 0.30%. At 9,000 sessions there are 45 crashes: 0.50%, interval 0.37%–0.67%. What should happen?
optionA: Halt now: even the lower bound is clearly above the halt line
optionB: Hold where it is: the rate may settle as more sessions come
optionC: Wait: the gate needs 20,000 sessions before any decision at all
optionD: Widen: forty-five crashes is a small number for a whole release
correctAnswerText: Halt now: even the lower bound is clearly above the halt line
explanation: The minimum session count guards widening, not halting: a lower bound of 0.37% is above 0.30% (1.5 × baseline), so even the optimistic reading is too high. Waiting would let more users get a bad build, a raw count means nothing without its denominator, and holding keeps serving a build the evidence already condemns.

prompt: A new job runs eas update on merges to main and hangs until the timeout. The expo-github-action step has no token input, and the eas step has no extra flags. What is the cause?
optionA: eas update cannot run on a merge, only on a version tag that names a release
optionB: GitHub limits jobs on main to one step, so the update step never starts
optionC: eas is not logged in and waits at a prompt; add EXPO_TOKEN and --non-interactive
optionD: The runner has no Android SDK, so eas update waits for Gradle to download it first
correctAnswerText: eas is not logged in and waits at a prompt; add EXPO_TOKEN and --non-interactive
explanation: Without a token the CLI is not logged in, and without --non-interactive it waits for an answer nobody can give. Pass token: ${{ secrets.EXPO_TOKEN }} to the action and add the flag so failures are immediate. eas update needs no Android SDK, it can run on any trigger, and GitHub has no one-step rule.

prompt: A new version passes every fresh-install test, but upgraded users find an empty cart. The persisted store's data shape changed and its version was bumped. What is missing?
optionA: A larger storage quota, since the new cart shape takes up more space on the phone
optionB: A migrate function, so the old saved shape is converted rather than dropped
optionC: A new application ID, so the upgrade installs as a separate app
optionD: A cleared cache on first launch, so the new code starts from nothing
correctAnswerText: A migrate function, so the old saved shape is converted rather than dropped
explanation: An upgrade starts with the old version's saved data; with the version bumped and no migrate function, the persisted store discards the old state and starts empty. A migrate step per version, tested from a saved old blob, keeps the cart. Storage size is not the issue, clearing data is the bug itself, and a new ID abandons every user.

prompt: A reviewer flags this step: run: eas update --message "${{ github.event.head_commit.message }}". What is the risk, and the fix?
optionA: eas update rejects multi-word messages; use the commit hash instead
optionB: The message is pasted into the shell script; pass it through env instead
optionC: GitHub never expands expressions in run, so the message is always blank
optionD: Commit messages are secrets, so they would appear unmasked in the logs
correctAnswerText: The message is pasted into the shell script; pass it through env instead
explanation: GitHub substitutes the expression into the script before the shell runs it, so a message with quotes or $(...) becomes shell code. Setting env: MSG: ${{ ... }} and using "$MSG" keeps it as data. GitHub does expand it there, which is the problem; commit messages are not secrets; and multi-word messages are fine.

prompt: Sitara Learning has twice sent an update to binaries it did not fit, both times after a native library was added without a version bump. Which runtime version policy is the best choice?
optionA: appVersion, with a reminder in the pull request template to bump it
optionB: A fixed string, edited by the release manager before each update
optionC: nativeVersion, so every build gets only updates published after it
optionD: fingerprint, so a native change makes a new runtime version by itself
correctAnswerText: fingerprint, so a native change makes a new runtime version by itself
explanation: Both incidents came from a human forgetting a bump, so the best policy removes the human step: the fingerprint follows the native layer automatically. A reminder or a hand-edited string keeps the same failure mode. nativeVersion is safe but forces a fix to be published once per build in use, a cost the team does not need here.

prompt: A team proposes widening a staged rollout whenever the new version's raw crash rate is below the old one's. Which change to the rule is most valuable?
optionA: Widen on a fixed daily schedule, so no one has to read the crash numbers at all
optionB: Use crash-free users only, since sessions are too noisy to be useful
optionC: Compare against last month's average crash rate instead of the old version
optionD: Require a minimum session count and act on interval bounds, not the point value
correctAnswerText: Require a minimum session count and act on interval bounds, not the point value
explanation: A crash rate from a few thousand sessions is noisy, so a rule on the raw value widens and halts on luck; a minimum sample and interval bounds act only on clear evidence. A fixed schedule ignores the data, last month is the wrong comparison (compare with the previous release at the same stage), and both rates are worth reading.

prompt: Version 7.3.0 is at 20% of production and a TypeScript bug double-counts a delivery fee. The fix is one line. Which plan is best?
optionA: Ask Play to roll the 20% back to 7.2.0 while the fix goes through review
optionB: Halt the rollout, publish the fix to that runtime with a small rollout, then resume
optionC: Leave the rollout running and include the fix in 7.4.0 next month as the team planned
optionD: Publish the fix to every runtime version at once, so all users get it today
correctAnswerText: Halt the rollout, publish the fix to that runtime with a small rollout, then resume
explanation: Halting stops the spread, and a JavaScript bug can be fixed over the air for the matching runtime, itself rolled out by percentage and widened when it holds. Waiting a month leaves users overcharged, Play cannot downgrade, and an update made from 7.3.0 code may not fit other runtimes' native layers.

prompt: A backend team wants to delete an endpoint that the app's 3.x versions still call; many users rarely update. Which plan is soundest?
optionA: Delete it now, since Play updates every installed app within a few days
optionB: Keep it, use the in-app minimum-version check, remove once usage is low
optionC: Rename the endpoint so old versions fail fast with a clear 404 message
optionD: Publish an OTA update telling every installed version to use the new one
correctAnswerText: Keep it, use the in-app minimum-version check, remove once usage is low
explanation: Store releases are not deployments; old binaries stay for months. Keep the API compatible, raise the minimum version through the config endpoint so 3.x users see an update screen, and remove the endpoint when analytics by version show 3.x is rare. Play does not force updates, OTA reaches only matching runtimes, and a 404 locks users out.

prompt: A start-up is deciding where its Android upload keystore should live. Which arrangement is best?
optionA: Only on the lead developer's laptop, so exactly one person can sign uploads
optionB: Committed to the private repository, so every build machine can reach it
optionC: Shared in the team chat with its password, so anyone can rebuild in a hurry
optionD: EAS-managed credentials, plus a backup in the company vault, never in Git
correctAnswerText: EAS-managed credentials, plus a backup in the company vault, never in Git
explanation: Builds need the key without exposing it, and losing it causes an upload-key reset at best, so EAS holds it for builds and a vault holds a backup outside any one laptop. Git history spreads it to every clone, one laptop is a single point of loss, and chat is a leak with a search box.

prompt: A team ships a store build every fortnight and OTA updates in between. When crashes spike, it cannot tell which change caused it. Which practice helps most?
optionA: Name every Sentry release after the date the build was made on EAS
optionB: Raise tracesSampleRate to 1.0, so that every session has a full trace
optionC: Stop OTA updates altogether, so that every change arrives in a build
optionD: Tag every event with the app version and the update ID it is running
correctAnswerText: Tag every event with the app version and the update ID it is running
explanation: With the version and update ID on each event, a spike lines up with the exact build or update that started it, and the same tags on analytics tie funnel changes to releases. Giving up OTA loses fast fixes, full tracing adds cost without naming the change, and a build date says nothing about which update a phone runs.

prompt: A product manager wants a whole new paid loyalty section shipped by OTA update to skip store review, since it is all JavaScript. Which judgement is soundest?
optionA: Ship it through a store release; use OTA for fixes and small adjustments
optionB: Ship it by OTA at a 1% rollout, which keeps it outside the store rules
optionC: Ship it by OTA, but hide it from reviewers with a remote feature flag
optionD: Ship it by OTA, since stores allow any change written in JavaScript
correctAnswerText: Ship it through a store release; use OTA for fixes and small adjustments
explanation: Both stores allow updating interpreted code within limits: an update must not change the app's purpose or add features that would need review. Fixes and small changes go over the air; new features go through review. The rollout percentage does not change the rules, and hiding features from reviewers is deception.

prompt: Two developers built production apps on the same day and both uploads carried the same versionCode. Which way of managing versionCode is best for this team?
optionA: Each developer edits versionCode in app config just before starting each build
optionB: Keep one versionCode per versionName and reuse it for every rebuild
optionC: appVersionSource remote with autoIncrement, so EAS issues each code once
optionD: Derive versionCode from the build's date in DDMMYYYY form each time
correctAnswerText: appVersionSource remote with autoIncrement, so EAS issues each code once
explanation: With remote versions, EAS keeps the current code on its servers and bumps it per build, so parallel builds cannot collide. Hand edits recreate the race, a DDMMYYYY code is not ordered (1 March sorts below 31 January) and repeats on one day, and Play never accepts a reused code.

prompt: A release passed its crash-rate gate and reached 100%, and next week orders fell because checkout silently stopped working on one bank's UPI app. What should the release process add?
optionA: A longer wait at 1%, so the crash rate has more sessions behind it
optionB: An extra round of fresh-install tests on the newest flagship phone
optionC: A funnel check by version and payment app alongside the crash gate
optionD: A stricter crash gate, halting at any rise in the crash rate at all
correctAnswerText: A funnel check by version and payment app alongside the crash gate
explanation: The gate compares crash rates only, and a broken step that does not crash passes it; a funnel from checkout_started to payment_succeeded, split by app version and payment app, shows the drop. A stricter or longer crash gate still sees no crash, and a flagship fresh install does not exercise that bank's hand-off.

prompt: With half a day before submitting a release candidate, which check plan finds the most bugs that development never shows?
optionA: The exact store build on a budget phone: upgrade over the live version, process death
optionB: The debug build on the emulator, repeating every flow until nothing goes red
optionC: The preview build on the newest flagship phone, with a fresh install every time
optionD: The full Jest suite run three more times on the release branch to rule out any flaky tests
correctAnswerText: The exact store build on a budget phone: upgrade over the live version, process death
explanation: A release build is a different program: minified Hermes bytecode, no Metro, __DEV__ false, R8 on native code, and real data from the previous version. Testing that exact build on a budget phone, including an upgrade and process death, covers what debug runs miss. Debug builds, re-run unit tests and fresh flagship installs repeat what already passed.
